# The Options Trading Master Document

### Complete Notes from Adam Khoo's *Options Trading Course — Level 1 & Level 2*

---

## About This Document

A complete, exhaustive written record of the **core strategy curriculum** across both
Options Level 1 and Level 2 — **130 videos, 56h 20m of instruction**,
transcribed in full and rewritten as connected explanatory prose (not bullet-point notes).

Every strategy is covered leg-by-leg with its full entry rulebook, payoff arithmetic,
trade management, and every live/worked case study narrated end-to-end with real numbers.
Only the bullish and neutral strategy families are covered in depth per instruction; the
Level-2 duplicate credit-spread lessons (identical GLD/COST/CRWV trades already covered in
Part IV) were skipped to avoid repetition.

**Provenance note:** everything below comes from the course videos. Where the instructor
points at an on-screen value without saying it aloud, the text says so explicitly rather
than inventing a number.

---

# Part I — Selling Covered Calls & Selling Cash Secured Puts

## Selling Covered Calls and Selling Cash Secured Puts

### Introduction: Two Strategies, One Idea

The two strategies that occupy this chapter — selling covered calls and selling cash secured puts — are usually taught as separate techniques, and in the course they are indeed presented as separate lessons with separate entry rules, separate case studies and separate risk warnings. But they are best understood as two halves of a single idea, and if you grasp that idea first, every individual rule that follows will feel like a consequence rather than an arbitrary instruction.

The idea is this. A long-term investor who owns great companies makes money in two conventional ways. The first is capital gain: the share price rises over the years and the investor's stake becomes worth more. The second is the dividend: some companies distribute a portion of their profits in cash, and the investor collects that cash without doing anything at all. Both of these are passive, both are well understood, and both are entirely dependent on things the investor does not control — the trajectory of the share price and the dividend policy of the board.

There is, however, a third stream of income that most investors never touch, and it is available precisely during the long stretches of time when the other two streams are producing nothing interesting. That third stream is option premium. By selling call options against shares already owned, or by selling put options against cash already earmarked to buy shares, the investor collects money from other market participants in exchange for accepting a specific, defined obligation. When you have three streams of income running simultaneously — capital gain, dividends and option premium — the overall return on the portfolio is higher than it would be with two, and the improvement is not marginal.

The reason this matters so much is a fact about how share prices actually behave, as opposed to how beginners imagine they behave. A fundamentally strong business will always rise in the long run. That is the premise of the entire value momentum investing approach and it is not in dispute here. But the share price does not go up every day, every week, every month, or even every year. Prices move in seasons and cycles. A stock will run very strongly for a period, and then it must pull back, go back down, consolidate, and rest. After resting a while, it continues rising. On average, any stock you buy will be going sideways or going nowhere something like 60% to 70% of the time, and will be rallying strongly only 30% to 40% of the time.

For the ordinary investor, those dead periods are simply dead. He waits. If the stock pays a dividend he collects a little something while he waits, but many technology stocks pay no dividend at all, and during those flat months and years the investor is, in the course's own blunt phrase, just sucking his thumb. The strategies in this chapter convert that dead time into income. During the flat seasons — the periods when the stock is going nowhere — a disciplined seller of covered calls can make roughly 2% to 3% a month. Two to three percent a month annualises to 24% to 36% a year, which as a supplement to capital gain and dividends is not a small thing.

Cash secured puts attack the same problem from the other end. Instead of asking what to do with shares you already own during a flat period, they ask what to do with cash you are holding while you wait for a stock you want to buy to come down to a price you are willing to pay. The conventional answer is to wait, place a limit order, and hope. The answer taught here is to get paid for waiting. You sell a put option at the price at which you would happily buy the stock, you collect the premium immediately, and one of two acceptable outcomes follows: either the stock falls to your price and you buy it at a discount that the premium makes even deeper, or the stock does not fall, the option expires worthless, and you keep the money and repeat.

Both strategies rest on the same non-negotiable foundation, and it is worth stating it at the outset because everything else collapses without it: **you only do this on fundamentally strong companies that you genuinely want to own for the long run.** Not on penny stocks, not on unprofitable companies, not on businesses whose share price may never recover. The whole risk profile of both strategies depends on the assumption that if you end up holding the shares, holding the shares is a good outcome. If the underlying business is rotten, no amount of clever option mechanics will save you.

---

## PART ONE: SELLING COVERED CALLS

### The Position, Leg by Leg

A covered call is a two-part position, though in the most common case only one of the two parts is actually traded at the moment of entry because the other is already sitting in the account.

The first leg is the stock: at least 100 shares of a fundamentally strong company or a high-quality ETF, owned outright. This is the "covered" part of the name. The shares are what make the obligation you are about to accept harmless.

The second leg is a short call option — one contract sold for every 100 shares held. Selling a call means accepting an obligation. Specifically, the seller of a call is obligated to deliver, that is to sell, 100 shares of the underlying stock at the strike price if the option is exercised. In exchange for accepting that obligation, the seller receives a premium in cash, credited to the account immediately at the moment the trade is filled.

That is the entire structure. Own 100 shares, sell one call. Own 800 shares, and you may sell up to eight calls. The share count is the constraint, and it is a hard one: without the shares behind it, the short call is a naked call, an entirely different and vastly more dangerous animal that is not taught here at all.

The practical consequence of the 100-share minimum deserves attention because it determines which stocks are accessible to which account sizes. If one share of a company costs around $20 — Bank of America is given as the example — then 100 shares costs roughly $2,000 and the strategy is affordable to almost anybody. If one share costs $3,000, as Amazon once did before its split, then 100 shares costs $300,000 and very few retail investors are in a position to run the strategy on that name at all. Beginners with smaller accounts are therefore steered toward lower-priced shares, without ever compromising on the requirement that the underlying business be excellent.

### The Market Outlook That Justifies the Trade

A covered call is not a bullish trade and it is not a bearish trade. Asked directly whether the covered call setup is a bullish setup or a bearish setup, the honest answer given in the course is: it depends — and specifically it depends on whether you already own the shares.

Consider the two situations separately, because they are genuinely different trades that happen to share a name.

In the first situation, you already own the shares. You bought them long ago, you hold them as a long-term investment, and you are not selling. The question is merely whether now is a good moment to rent out the upside for a month. Here the outlook that justifies selling the call is mildly bearish or neutral *in the short term only*: you believe the stock has run up too far too fast, that it is over-extended, that it is bumping into resistance, and that over the next thirty to forty-five days it is more likely to consolidate sideways or retrace than to keep climbing. Your long-term view remains bullish — that is why you still own the shares — but your one-month view is that nothing much good is about to happen, and you would rather be paid 2% to 3% for that month than collect nothing.

In the second situation, you do not yet own the shares, and you intend to buy them and sell the call simultaneously as a single package. Now the setup is unambiguously bullish, because you are about to spend real money buying stock. Here you want the opposite technical picture: you want to buy the shares when they are cheap, on a wave down, at a support level, at a point where you believe the price cannot easily go lower and is likely to bounce. The analogy offered is property: you want to buy a property when the price is cheap, not when it is expensive. The SCHW case study narrated later in this chapter is exactly this second kind of trade.

For the first and more common situation — selling a call against shares you already hold — the technical trigger is described in terms of wave patterns. Share prices move in waves: wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down. The rule is emphatic and repeated: **never sell a covered call after a wave down. Always sell the covered call after a wave up.** The reasoning is probabilistic rather than certain. After a wave up, especially one that has gone up in a near-vertical, ninety-degree fashion and has stretched a long way from its moving averages, the probability favours consolidation or retracement. It is likened to breathing: once the market has breathed out, it must breathe in. A stock that has just breathed out is a stock whose short-term upside is, on the balance of probabilities, limited — which is exactly the condition under which selling that upside is a good bargain.

A second, related trigger is resistance. If the stock has risen and stalled beneath an identifiable resistance level, and you judge that it is unlikely to break above that resistance in the short term, you can sell a call with a strike at or above that resistance. This is described as a good-to-have rather than a must-have; the wave-up condition is the primary trigger and the resistance is a bonus confirmation.

### A First Worked Example: Yum China

The clearest first illustration in the course is a real position in Yum China, a company held in the instructor's own portfolio and owned because it is a good business — it operates KFC in China, and Chinese consumers love fried chicken. Over the long run the stock had risen very nicely. But recently the price had waved up, waved down, waved up, waved down and waved up again, and the most recent wave up had left it over-extended, printing what is described as a bearish pin bar at the top. The expectation was that the price would come back down toward its moving average.

At that moment the stock was trading at $53.34. The trade taken was to sell the Yum China August $55 call options — a strike $1.66 above the market, chosen because the price was not expected to reach it within the life of the option — with roughly 30 days to expiration. The premium collected was $1.30 per share.

The arithmetic that justified the trade is the arithmetic that justifies every covered call in this system. The premium of $1.30 divided by the share price of $53.34 gives 2.4%. That is 2.4% earned in thirty days on capital already committed to the stock, and 2.4% a month is roughly 29% a year on top of whatever the shares themselves do. The threshold is at least 2%; this cleared it, so the trade was taken.

The position was not one contract but eight, because 800 shares of Yum China were held, and one contract covers 100 shares. Eight contracts at $1.30 per share on 100 shares per contract produces $1,040 of premium collected up front — the transcript momentarily says "one thousand three hundred dollars" before correcting itself to $1,040, which is the arithmetically correct figure.

What happened next is instructive about how these positions behave day to day. After the sale, time decay went to work and the calls fell in value from $1.30 to $0.64 — they had already lost roughly half their value. On the interactive brokers screen this appeared as an unrealised profit of $503, with another $580-odd still to be collected if the calls went all the way to zero. At the moment of the recording Yum China was trading at $54.51, still below the $55 strike, and the hope was simply that it would stay there for the few remaining days.

One point of platform mechanics is worth extracting here because it confuses almost every beginner. When you first sell a covered call, the position shows a **negative** market value in the account. Negative does not mean you have lost money. The negative sign simply denotes that this is premium you have collected — the option is a liability you owe, not an asset you hold. It is not yet truly yours. It only becomes yours when you close the position by buying the call back, or when the option expires and the liability goes to zero, at which point the profit equals the full premium collected.

### The Three Outcomes at Expiration

Every covered call resolves into one of three scenarios, and the entire management discipline of the strategy consists of knowing which one you are in and what to do about it.

#### Scenario One: the shares stay at or below the strike

This is the best case and, statistically, the common case. In the Yum China example, the share price may drift up a little, drift down, wander sideways, but by the expiration date it is at $55 or below. The call expires worthless. There is nothing to buy back — the liability simply evaporates — and the full premium of $1.30 per share, $130 per contract, is retained as profit.

Once that happens, the process repeats. You sell a new call option under the same rules: a strike at roughly 35 to 45 delta, out of the money, with another 30 to 45 days to expiration, collecting another round of premium.

#### Scenario Two: the shares finish above the strike and you do nothing

If Yum China trades above $55 at expiration — above the strike by even one cent, at $55.01 or more — and you take no action, the calls you sold are automatically exercised and you are assigned. Assignment means you are obligated to sell your 100 shares per contract at the strike price. The next morning your shares are gone, and cash appears in their place.

Crucially, the cash you receive is not merely the strike price. You keep the premium as well. So the effective sale price is $55 plus $1.30, or $56.30 per share, and for one contract $5,630 in cash is credited to the account.

The question the course insists you ask *before* selling the call is whether you would be content with that outcome. If the shares were bought at $40 or $45, then selling at an effective $56.30 is a good result and there is nothing to complain about. If losing the shares at that price would upset you, you should not have sold the call at that strike in the first place. And if you do find yourself upset after the fact, the remedy is straightforward: you now hold $5,630 in cash, and you may use it to buy the shares back at the prevailing market price, or wait for a pullback and buy them back cheaper.

#### Scenario Three: you act before expiration to avoid assignment

If you do not want the shares called away, you are not obliged to sit and watch it happen. You can buy the calls back before they are exercised. Depending on where the stock has gone, buying them back may cost you a small loss, may be break-even, or may even leave a profit. Having bought back the old call, you simultaneously sell a new call at a higher strike that is less likely to be reached, or at a higher strike with a longer expiration, buying yourself more time and collecting a fresh round of premium in the process. This is rolling, and it is treated in detail below.

Seen across all three scenarios, the strategy is described as a win-win. If the share price does not go up, you win, because you keep your shares and the premium was free money. If the share price does go up and the shares are called away, you also win, because you sell at a price you were happy to sell at *plus* the premium on top.

### The Catch: Capped Upside and the High-Growth Trap

There is always a catch, and the catch here is precisely defined. When you sell a covered call, you are locking in a return of 2% to 3% for the month. You are, in effect, converting the stock's uncertain short-term return into a fixed salary. The consequence is that if the stock happens to run very hard during that month, you have capped your upside and you miss the extra gains. If the stock rises 20% in thirty days, you do not participate in that 20%; you participate in the 2% to 3% you agreed to.

This is described using two images that are worth keeping. The first is the fixed salary: you have taken a wage instead of a bonus, and if there is a bonus that month, you do not get it. The second is the Ferrari: you have bought a Ferrari and fitted it with a limiter so that it cannot exceed eighty kilometres per hour. The car is capable of far more; you have contractually prevented yourself from using that capability.

From this follows the single most emphasised prohibition in the covered call lessons: **do not sell covered calls on high-growth stocks.** This is presented not as theory but as a personal regret — a mistake made in the early years and regretted a lot. High-growth stocks move very fast; the price goes up quickly, retraces briefly, then moves up quickly again. Selling calls against them means being repeatedly run over. The instructor notes seeing many people kick themselves for having sold covered calls on stocks like Nvidia and Amazon, taking a small premium and forfeiting an enormous capital gain.

The working definition of high growth given is a company growing at more than 20% a year. Named examples of stocks to avoid for this purpose include Nvidia, Palantir, AMD and Palo Alto. The stocks that are appropriate are low-growth to moderate-growth companies, often the defensive names: McDonald's, Pepsi, Costco, Walmart, Thermo Fisher, Waste Management, 3M, and — now — Apple. Apple is used deliberately as an illustration of a stock that has migrated between categories: it used to grow at around 20% and was therefore off-limits, but it has since become a moderate-growth company and is now an acceptable covered call candidate.

The practical method for checking which category a company falls into is to look up the projected growth rate — the course refers to stock screening data and the Stock Oracle tool. The examples given are concrete: Apple's projected growth is about 11% over the next five years, which is moderate; Waste Management grows at about 9.9%, which is low to moderate and defensive; Nvidia grows at 23% a year, which is high growth; and Palantir grows at 65% a year, which is emphatically high growth. Anything above 20% is high growth and is excluded.

### Entry Rules for Selling Covered Calls

The entry rules are stated formally and are worth setting out in an ordered list, since this is one of the places where the source material is genuinely an enumerated procedure. Each rule, however, carries a reason, and the reasons matter more than the numbers.

1. **Stock selection.** Write covered calls only on fundamentally strong stocks or ETFs that you already own. Writing and selling are the same thing; the terms are interchangeable. The company should pass the seven-step value momentum investment criteria taught in the whale investor course; if you cannot assess that yourself, the Dow 30 is offered as a reasonable starting universe, and the ideal hunting ground is the S&P 500 — names like McDonald's, Thermo Fisher, Visa, MasterCard, Pepsi, Costco, Walmart and Apple.

2. **ETFs are eligible.** High-quality index ETFs work well: the SPY ETF and the VOO ETF, which track the S&P 500, and ETFs tracking the NASDAQ or the Dow Jones. For ETFs the required return threshold is relaxed — 1.5% a month is acceptable rather than the 2% to 3% demanded of individual stocks, because the volatility and therefore the premium is lower.

3. **Stocks to avoid.** High-growth stocks are excluded for the capped-upside reason already given. Biotech and pharmaceutical companies are also avoided — not merely for covered calls but as investments generally — because they tend to be extremely volatile with inconsistent profits, with only a few exceptions.

4. **Own at least 100 shares per contract.** One contract of covered calls requires 100 shares of cover. Four hundred shares permit up to four contracts, and so on.

5. **The current share price must be above your average cost.** Before selling a call, check that the market price exceeds what you paid. If Apple was bought at $150 or $200 and now trades at $298, you are safely above cost, and even if the shares are called away you will be selling above your purchase price. Selling a covered call at a strike below your cost basis would risk locking in a loss on the shares, which defeats the purpose.

6. **Sell only when the stock is over-extended, and ideally beneath resistance.** Sell after a wave up, never after a wave down. Resistance beneath the strike is a good-to-have.

7. **A further valuation condition, stated in the Apple walkthrough:** sell the covered call when the share price is above the intrinsic value of the business. In the Apple example the intrinsic value was $241 and the market price $298, so the stock was trading above fair value — precisely the condition under which having it called away is not a tragedy.

8. **Strike selection by delta: 35 to 45 delta.** The rule of thumb is to choose the strike whose option carries a delta between 35 and 45. In the live Apple demonstration the range quoted while scrolling the chain was narrowed to 40 to 45 delta, and the strike actually chosen sat at 42 delta. This range places the strike comfortably out of the money while still generating a meaningful premium.

9. **Expiration: 30 to 45 days.** Any expiry in that window is acceptable — 29 days, 35 days and 43 days are all described as fine in the Apple example. This is the sweet spot where time decay is meaningful but there is still enough premium to be worth collecting.

10. **Premium target: at least 2% to 3% return for 30 to 45 days.** This is the binding constraint. If the delta-appropriate strike does not produce a premium clearing 2%, the trade is not taken.

11. **Implied volatility, as a bonus.** Ideally sell when implied volatility is high, meaning roughly 35 to 40 or above. This is explicitly not a requirement, only a bonus, because high IV means richer premium for the same strike.

#### Calculating the Return: Two Schools of Thought

There is a small ambiguity in how the return on a covered call should be computed, and the course resolves it by declaring that both conventions are acceptable. You may divide the premium by the **strike price**, or you may divide the premium by the **current share price**. These are two different schools of thought and the answers they produce are quite similar in practice, since the strike sits only a little above the market. As long as the result is roughly 2% or better, the trade qualifies. The Yum China example divided $1.30 by the $53 share price to get 2.4%; the Apple example divided $6.675 by the $305 strike to get 2.1%; the SCHW example divided $2.26 by the $89.01 share price to get 2.5%. All three methods appear, and all three are treated as legitimate.

A refinement appears in the SCHW discussion: because the expiry chosen was 35 days rather than exactly 30, the yield can be time-adjusted by multiplying by 30/35 to express it as a true monthly rate. Doing so on the 91-strike figure still left the result above 2%, and on the 92-strike figure it left it at roughly 2%, so both passed.

### A Live Covered Call: Apple, Step by Step

The Apple demonstration is the course's canonical walkthrough of entering a covered call on shares already held, and it is worth following in full because it includes the order-entry haggling that most textbooks omit.

The position going in was 485 Apple shares at an average cost of $162.99 — call it $163 — with the stock trading at $298. Three conditions were checked before anything was done. The current share price of $298 was above the intrinsic value of $241, so the stock was overvalued. The current share price was above the average cost of $163, so a called-away outcome would be profitable. And the chart showed the familiar wave pattern with the most recent move being a wave up, so the timing condition was met. All three conditions being satisfied, the trade was authorised.

With 485 shares, four contracts could have been sold. Only one was, which is itself a lesson in position sizing: there is no obligation to write calls against your entire holding, and writing against a fraction leaves the remainder free to participate fully in any rally.

The expiry chosen was 35 days out, sitting in the middle of the 30-to-45-day window, expiring on 18 June. Scrolling the option chain for a delta between 40 and 45 landed on the $305 strike at 42 delta. The mark price — the midpoint between the bid and the ask — was $6.675, and $6.675 divided by the $305 strike gives 2.1%, which clears the 2% minimum. The trade was therefore approved.

The order entry itself was done on Interactive Brokers, using either the Options Trader window or the option chain; both are described as equally acceptable. Selling means clicking the bid side of the chain, which populates a sell order. A **limit price must always be used**, never a market price. A limit price on a sale means "this price or higher."

What follows is a small masterclass in not leaving money on the table. The mid was around $6.70. Rather than simply accepting the mid, the order was first entered at $6.75 — a deliberate attempt to do slightly better than the midpoint, on the reasoning that you never know until you try. It did not fill. The price was then walked down step by step: $6.73, no fill; $6.72, no fill; $6.71, no fill; $6.70 — filled. One contract sold at $6.70, which is $670 in cash credited immediately.

The advice embedded in this sequence is that an unfilled limit order can simply be left to sit — it may or may not eventually fill — or the limit can be lowered incrementally until it does. The only constraint is that you must not walk it down so far that the premium falls below the 2% threshold that justified the trade in the first place.

With the trade on, the picture was as follows. A red line at $305 marks the strike on the chart. Over the next 35 days the share price may go sideways, may go down, may even poke above $305 temporarily — none of that matters. What matters is only where the price sits on the expiration date. If it closes at $305 or below, the call becomes worthless.

The stated intention, however, was not to hold to expiration. The normal practice is to buy the call back once it has lost most of its value. If, after a couple of weeks, the call has decayed from $6.70 to around $1.70, buying it back nets $5.00 per share of profit and closes the risk entirely.

The alternative outcome was also spelled out. If the price rises above $305 and stays there, and the call is left alone through expiration, it is exercised automatically, 100 shares are sold at $305, and the account is credited $30,500. Adding the $6.70 premium gives an effective sale price of $311.70 against a cost basis of $162.99 — a very substantial profit. Once again the conclusion is the same: either you keep the shares and collect free premium, or you sell the shares at an excellent price and collect the premium too.

### Trade Management and Taking Profits

Having entered, the covered call seller manages the position according to which of three developing scenarios is unfolding. These map onto the three expiration outcomes but are framed in terms of action rather than outcome.

#### Managing Scenario One: the stock behaves, and you take profit early

If the stock goes down, sideways, or up only modestly, the short call bleeds value every single day through time decay. From $6.70 it drifts to $6.50, $6.40, $6.30, $6.00, and so on. If the share price actually drops, the decay accelerates sharply.

You may simply let it run to zero. On the day of expiration the call becomes worthless, there is nothing to buy back, and the full $670 per contract is kept. That is the maximum profit and it is the theoretical ideal.

But the practice taught is different, and the reasoning is explicitly about risk rather than about return. Waiting for the last few percent of the premium means keeping the position open, and while it is open the share price could suddenly run higher and turn a comfortable win into a rolling problem. So the rule adopted is: **once you have captured roughly 70% to 80% of the maximum profit, close the trade early, take the money and run.**

The arithmetic is illustrated with the Apple position. The call was sold at $6.70. If it decays to $1.34 and is bought back there, the net profit is $6.70 minus $1.34, which is $5.36 per share. Expressed as a fraction of the maximum, $5.36 divided by $6.70 is about 80%. Capturing 80% of the maximum with certainty, well before expiration, is preferred to gambling on the remaining 20%.

The same calculation is run at a different exit price: sold at $6.70, bought back at $1.50, net profit $5.20 per share, which on one contract of 100 shares is $520.

The counter-example is equally instructive. On the day after the Apple call was sold at $6.70 — net $6.69 after commission — the option had fallen only to $6.11. Buying it back at that point would have realised $58, which is 8.6% of the maximum profit after one day. That is explicitly *not* enough. The 70%-to-80% threshold is a threshold, not a suggestion, and a one-day gain of 8.6% does not come close to meeting it.

The mechanics of closing are simple. You highlight the option position in the platform and right-click — on a Mac, two fingers on the trackpad. The menu offers both "buy" and "close," and they are the same thing for a short position: closing a short call is a purchase. Either choice opens an order ticket to buy back one contract. You enter the price at which you are willing to buy it back — much lower than what you sold it for — and you may attach a good-till-cancelled instruction so that the order rests in the market until it fills. In the demonstration a good-till-cancelled buy order was placed at $1.50 against a call sold at $6.70, so that whenever the option decayed to that level the profit would be taken automatically.

#### Managing Scenario Two: the stock runs, and the short call shows a growing loss

If the stock climbs above the strike and keeps going, the short call will display a larger and larger loss in the account. The instruction is not to panic, and the reason is arithmetic rather than reassurance: as the stock rises, the call loses money but the 100 shares gain more. The capital gain on the shares exceeds the loss on the call. On a net basis you are still making money; you are simply making less than you would have made unhedged.

At that point there is a genuine decision. If you do not mind selling the shares, do nothing. Let the call expire in the money, let the shares be called away at the strike, and keep the premium as well. If you *do* mind losing the shares, then you must roll the call, and you must roll it before assignment becomes likely.

#### When to Roll: the two triggers

The timing of a roll is governed by two specific triggers, and both derive from an understanding of when the person on the other side of your trade will choose to exercise.

The person who bought your call may exercise at any time — these are American-style options and there is no requirement to wait for expiration. In practice, though, a call buyer will rarely exercise early, because exercising throws away whatever extrinsic value remains in the option. The buyer only finds early exercise attractive when there is essentially no extrinsic value left to throw away, which happens when the option is deep in the money.

The first trigger is therefore **delta**. As the stock rises, the delta of the call you sold climbs from 40 to 50 to 60 to 80. Once it reaches **90 delta or above**, there is a high chance the call will be exercised early. In the assignment lesson this is stated more precisely still: early exercise becomes likely when the delta exceeds 90 **and** the extrinsic value of the call has fallen below 20 cents. You can check the delta at any time simply by looking at the option chain.

The second trigger is **time**. Roughly two to three days before expiration, if the call is in the money, assignment at expiration is effectively certain unless you act. So the rule is: roll when delta reaches 90 or above, or roll in the last two to three days before expiry, whichever comes first.

#### The Mechanics of Rolling a Covered Call

Rolling is a two-legged transaction executed as close to simultaneously as the platform allows.

The first leg is to **buy back the call you sold, at a loss**. This loss is unavoidable and must be accepted without flinching. In the Apple illustration, a call sold at $6.70 might have risen to $16.70 as the stock climbed, so buying it back costs $16.70 and crystallises a $10.00 per share loss on that leg.

The second leg is to **sell a new call at the same strike or a higher strike, with a later expiration, choosing a strike where the new premium exceeds the loss on the old call.** The new option should carry at least 30 to 45 days to expiration, though it may be longer — 60 days, 80 days, whatever is required to generate enough premium. The governing constraint is not delta and not any fixed strike distance; it is simply that the credit received must be larger than the debit paid. This is called **rolling the call for a credit**.

The purpose of the roll is threefold and it is worth being explicit about each. You raise the strike, which means that if the shares are eventually called away it will be at a better price. You buy more time, which gives the stock room to fall back below the strike. And you collect net additional premium, which means you are being paid to do all this rather than paying for the privilege.

Rolling is not a one-time event. You may roll once, twice, three times or more, until eventually the call expires worthless and you keep both your shares and the accumulated premium.

### Rolling in Practice: the SPY Covered Call

The course includes a full live demonstration of a roll, recorded on 12 August, on a covered call sold on SPY one month earlier. It is worth following closely because it exposes the judgment involved as well as the mechanics.

The starting position was 100 shares of SPY bought at $286, with the ETF now trading at $336 — a large unrealised gain on the shares themselves. One month earlier a call had been sold at the $322 strike, expiring 21 August, for a premium of $10.85. The share price at $336 was well above the $322 strike, so the call was in the money, and there were eight days left to expiration.

The first thing done was to price out the do-nothing alternative honestly. If no action were taken, the call would be exercised and the shares sold at $322. Adding the $10.85 premium retained gives an effective sale price of $332.85 per share. Against a purchase price of $286 that is a very good profit, and the transcript is explicit that this outcome would not be objectionable in itself. The problem is not the money — it is that the shares would be gone, and the decision made was to keep the shares.

The cost of keeping them was then quantified. The call sold at $10.85 could be bought back at $4.68, meaning a loss on that leg of $3.81 per share, or $381. The figure drifted during the recording as the market moved — $384, $390, $388, eventually settling near $394 and rounded to $4.00 per share for planning purposes. The candid response to the obvious question of why the call was sold at all is simply that the share price was not known in advance; and the loss is tolerable because the gain on the shares over the same period was larger. Net-net, the position was still making money.

The next step was to choose the replacement call. The option chain was opened and the expiry set to 30 days out, 11 September. Longer expiries — 50, 60 or 90 days — were noted as available and would generate more premium, but were not required.

Then came strike selection under the governing constraint. With approximately $4.00 per share to recover, any strike whose premium exceeded $4.00 was eligible. Reading down the chain: the $340 call was paying $5.60, comfortably more than $4.00, so it qualified. The $341 call also qualified. The $342 call did **not** qualify — its premium was insufficient to cover the $4.00 loss — and was therefore ruled out. So the eligible range was $341 and lower.

Here the judgment call arose. Selling the $341 call, with the ETF at $336, would be selling out of the money at 39 delta, leaving $5 of room for further appreciation before the shares were at risk again. Selling at the money, at $336, would collect around $7.00, a much larger premium, but would leave no room at all. The correct choice depends entirely on whether SPY was about to keep rising or was about to stall — and the honest observation was that SPY was approaching its all-time high of $339, and nobody can predict whether a market breaks through an all-time high or reverses off it. The transcript dwells on the genuine indecision here, which is more useful pedagogically than a false confidence would be.

The decision made was to sell slightly closer to the money, at the $337 strike, which sat at approximately 50 delta with SPY at $336, collecting around $6.40 to $6.45. The reasoning: $6.40 pays for the $4.00 loss and leaves roughly $2.00 of net new credit.

The execution order matters. The new call was sold **first**, and then the old call was bought back immediately afterwards. The final numbers as recorded were a realised loss of $4.37 on buying back the old $322 call, and a premium of $6.39 to $6.40 collected on selling the new $337 call. Since $6.40 exceeds $4.37, the roll was net positive.

The summary of what the roll accomplished is a good summary of what every roll should accomplish: more time was bought — the new call expires 11 September, thirty days out; the strike was raised from $322 to $337; and additional money was collected on net. The shares were retained throughout.

The demonstration also notes in passing that the same chain can be read on Think or Swim as well as Interactive Brokers, and on Think or Swim the September 11 chain showed the $341 call paying $4.29 — a slightly different quote from a different data feed, which is normal.

### Assignment: What Actually Happens

The final scenario is that you allow the call to be exercised. This happens under two conditions, stated precisely.

The first is early exercise: the share price rises far above the strike, the call is deep in the money, its delta exceeds 90, and its extrinsic value has fallen below 20 cents. Under those conditions there is a high chance the call buyer exercises well before expiration.

The second is expiry in the money: on the expiration date the share price closes above the strike by one cent or more. The call is then automatically exercised.

The consequences are mechanical and worth stating in sequence. First, you keep the option premium — that was collected at the outset and is never at risk. Second, you do not buy the call back; once exercised, the call ceases to exist and cannot be repurchased. Third, you are assigned: 100 shares per contract are deducted from your account, which is why you must genuinely hold them. Fourth, cash is credited: the strike price multiplied by 100 shares. In the Apple case, a $305 strike means $30,500 credited per contract.

What you do with that cash is your choice. You may buy the shares back — the $30,500 is more than enough to repurchase 100 shares at $305 — and then repeat the whole process by selling a new call at 35 to 45 delta with 30 to 45 days to expiration.

### Advantages and Risks of Covered Calls

The advantages are summarised in four parts.

First, the strategy generates premium as additional monthly income on top of the dividends and capital gains already earned from the portfolio, producing something on the order of an extra 30% to 40% annualised return on a stock even when it moves sideways or down in the short term.

Second, it transforms the economics of holding dull stocks. The example given is 3M: a stock bought without any expectation of dramatic appreciation, expected to go sideways for years. That would ordinarily be an unattractive holding. But with a roughly 4% dividend plus 2% to 3% a month from covered calls, the sideways behaviour stops mattering. Who cares if the stock goes nowhere, when going nowhere pays that well?

Third, it reduces the cost basis of owning the stock, as the accumulated premium gradually pays back the original purchase price.

Fourth — and this is an under-appreciated use — a covered call can serve as an **exit strategy**. Suppose you bought a stock at $100, it has run to your target price of $300, it is now overvalued, and you have decided to sell. Instead of simply selling at $300, sell a call at the $300 strike. If the shares are called away, that is exactly what you wanted; but you have collected extra premium on top of the sale price. If they are not called away, you keep the premium and remain free to try again.

On the question of risk, the answer given is deliberately provocative: there is **no** risk to this strategy, as long as you already own the shares of fundamentally good companies. That claim is then immediately qualified in two ways, and the qualifications are the substance.

The first qualification is the capped upside already discussed at length: in the short term you have taken the fixed salary and forfeited the bonus.

The second qualification is that you retain the same downside risk you already had as a shareholder. If the stock falls, you lose money on the stock — but you would have lost that money anyway, whether or not you sold a call. The covered call neither creates nor removes that exposure; it merely offsets a small part of it with the premium collected. And if you own a lousy company, it can fall regardless of what you do with options. This is why the entire edifice rests on owning great businesses.

The point about the absence of downside protection is made even more directly in the SCHW case study, where a covered call is entered as a fresh position rather than written against existing stock. There, the observation is that a covered call has no protection on the downside, because it is fundamentally an investment concept rather than a hedged trade, and one does not buy protection for a long-term investment. A small decline is absorbed by the premium collected. A decline of $5, $6 or $10 will put the position into loss, and the response to that is not a stop-loss but continued premium collection — keep selling calls to offset the downside impact while the business recovers.

---

### Case Study: The Covered Call on Charles Schwab (SCHW)

The Schwab trade is the most complete covered call in the course, because it was entered live, monitored for five weeks, carried through to expiration, assigned, and then summarised with full accounting. It also differs from the Apple and Yum China examples in an important structural way: the shares were not already owned. The stock and the call were bought and sold together as a single two-legged order.

#### The Company and the Fundamental Case

Charles Schwab is described as one of the largest fund managers in the world, managing trillions of dollars of assets, and as the owner of the Think or Swim platform following its acquisition of TD Ameritrade. From a fundamental standpoint it is a good stock to own — which is the precondition for any covered call, because the strategy is an investment concept and one does not invest in lousy businesses.

On valuation, the position was clear. The Stock Oracle screen displayed a value of about $260 per share against a market price of about $89, which would make the stock worth roughly three times its price. That figure is treated with appropriate scepticism — described as possibly a little too optimistic — but the independent assessment offered was that intrinsic value was somewhere above $100, comfortably above the $89 market price. The stock was therefore significantly undervalued.

#### The Technical Case and the Direction of the Setup

Because the shares were not yet owned, this was explicitly a **bullish** setup, and therefore the technical requirement was the opposite of the classic covered-call trigger. Instead of selling after a wave up, the shares needed to be bought after a wave down, at support, where the price was unlikely to fall further.

The chart supplied exactly that. The price was at $89, and $89 was a support level that the stock had tested several times in the past, bouncing off it each time. The long-term trend was up, and the price was now bouncing off support. This made it a good entry point for buying the shares.

The three income streams were laid out before entry: capital gain if the share price rises; premium from the call sold at, say, $95 (the figure floated before the chain was examined); and dividends collected while the shares are held. Three streams justified proceeding to the option chain to check the numbers.

#### Selecting the Expiry and the Strike

The expiry candidates on screen were 28 days and, further out, 12 June at about 35 days. The 35-day expiry was chosen because it sits inside the 30-to-45-day window. Earnings had already passed, so there was no earnings event inside the option's life — noted as convenient, though not treated as a disqualifying concern either way.

The strike was then selected on the 40-to-45 delta rule, and two candidates were evaluated arithmetically rather than by eye.

| Candidate strike | Delta | Mark premium | Premium ÷ share price ($89.01) | Time-adjusted (×30/35) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $91 | ~42 | $2.26 | 2.5% | still above 2% | Qualifies; more premium |
| $92 | (higher strike, lower delta) | $1.92 | 2.1% | roughly 2% | Qualifies; more room for capital gain |

The trade-off between the two is the central trade-off of strike selection. The $91 strike collects more premium but caps the capital gain sooner. The $92 strike collects less premium but leaves more room for the stock to appreciate before the gain is capped. Both cleared the 2% hurdle, so either was acceptable. The $91 strike at 42 delta was chosen.

#### Executing the Two-Legged Order

On Think or Swim, the order was constructed by right-clicking the chosen option and selecting "buy covered stock," which builds a two-legged order automatically: leg one buys 100 shares, leg two sells one $91 call expiring 12 June at about 42 delta. The platform quoted a net debit of $86.69.

That net debit number is worth dwelling on, because it makes the economics of the position visible in a single figure. The stock was trading at $88.92. The net debit of $86.66 is $2.26 lower — exactly the premium collected on the $91 call. In other words, executing both legs together means **buying the shares at a price $2.26 below the market**. The premium collected up front partially offsets the cost of the shares.

That in turn defines the break-even. Because $2.26 is collected up front, the cost of owning the shares falls by $2.26, so the break-even point sits below the current stock price. The entry price and the break-even point are the same thing in this structure.

#### The Payoff Profile Before Entry

The profit and loss analysis was examined before the order was sent, which is the correct sequence. The findings were as follows.

If the share price simply stayed around its current level, the position would make roughly $200 at expiration five weeks out. If the share price rose, more would be made, up to a cap. The maximum gain shown on the expiration curve was **$433** — the figure that would be realised if the price finished at or above the $91 strike.

The maximum profit is computed as the strike price minus the net cost of the position, multiplied by 100 shares per contract: $91.00 minus $86.65 is $4.35 per share, which on 100 shares is $435. (The on-screen analyser showed $433 and the later summary used $435; the small difference reflects the fill price drifting between the simulation and the execution.)

Crucially, the return on investment is computed against the **net cost of $86.67, not against the $89 share price**, because the premium received up front genuinely reduces the capital committed. On that basis the maximum return is about **5% in a month** — described as very good, and explicitly accepted as satisfactory in the knowledge that the gain cannot exceed it no matter how far the stock runs. And if the stock never reaches $91, the premium alone still delivers more than 2% a month, which is also satisfactory. Both branches were acceptable before the trade was placed, which is the correct condition for entering any trade of this kind.

Implied volatility was checked as a bonus condition and was found to be excellent: Schwab's implied volatility percentile was 63, which is high, and that is why the premium was so generous. The Interactive Brokers equivalent metric is the IV rank or 52-week rank, which measures the same thing. Selling into high IV always produces a better premium — but, once again, it is a bonus rather than a requirement, and 2% a month remains the actual gate.

Before executing, the growth-stock warning was repeated. Schwab is a stable, steady stock that has gone sideways over the past year — exactly the kind of business that suits covered calls. Nvidia is the counter-example: if you own 100 shares of a stock that is shooting up and looks overbought at resistance, selling a call above resistance to collect premium while you wait feels reasonable, but it is a mistake, because Nvidia is a growth stock that could double and become a multi-bagger. Selling covered calls on such a stock caps precisely the upside you bought it for.

#### Placing the Order on Interactive Brokers

The execution was then repeated on Interactive Brokers, which requires a different sequence for a multi-leg order. The 34-day expiry was selected, and the **Strategy Builder** must be turned on to build an order with two or more legs. The 42-delta call at the $91 strike was selected first and marked as a sell, collecting a little over $2.00 — clearing the 2% yield test.

To add the stock leg, one clicks the **Advanced Plus** button and adds a stock leg, which appends "buy 100 shares of Charles Schwab" to the order. An error was made and corrected on camera: the expiry was initially set to June 5 rather than the intended June 12, and was corrected, after which the premium was still above $2.00 at approximately 42 delta, within the 40-to-45 range.

The order was priced at the mid of the combined bid and ask, around $86.61, entered as a **debit** because cash must be paid out to buy the shares. Because this is a debit order, the negotiation runs in the opposite direction from the Apple call sale: you start with a lower price — offering less — and raise it gradually until you get filled. The sequence recorded was to start around $86.60, observe the mid drift to $86.65, raise the limit to $86.65, and fill there.

#### Capital and Margin

The capital consequences were spelled out carefully. One contract requires paying roughly $8,665 in cash. The account held about $10,600 in US dollars, which covers one contract with room to spare. Two contracts would have exceeded the available US dollar cash, pushing the US dollar balance negative and incurring interest, unless Singapore dollars were first converted. Rather than borrow, one contract was traded. After the fill, the cash balance fell from about $10,600 to about $2,000.

Separately from cash, the broker blocks margin: roughly $6,000 at entry, falling to about $3,000 as maintenance margin. The observation is added that a larger account would typically have less margin blocked, since this was a small account and the broker was conservative.

#### The First Day and the Nature of the Risk

Immediately after the fill the position showed two legs: 100 shares of Schwab, showing a small loss, and one short $91 call, also showing a small loss. Combined, the trade was down about $2 — nothing at all.

The explanation of why this is unconcerning is a good summary of how covered calls make money. Time passing benefits the trade, because the call sold will decay. If the price stays below $91, the call will bleed to zero and the entire $2-plus of premium becomes profit, so the P&L drifts from negative to positive simply as days pass.

The genuine risk was then stated plainly. Because the shares were bought with no protection, a falling share price hurts the trade — that is the typical profile of a covered call, which has no downside protection because it is an investment position. A small decline is covered by the premium collected. A decline of $5, $6 or $10 puts the trade at a loss. The response to that scenario is not to cut, but to keep selling calls to collect more premium and offset the downside impact — on the strength of the fundamental conviction that the business is sound and undervalued.

#### Entry Summary

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Date of entry | 8 May |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Shares bought | 100 at $88.92 (summary states $88.992) |
| Call sold | $91 strike, expiring 12 June, ~42 delta |
| Premium collected | $2.26 (summary states $2.27) |
| Net debit | $86.65 per share |
| Cash paid | $8,665 |
| Days to expiration | 35 |
| Maximum profit | ($91.00 − $86.65) × 100 = $435 |
| Maximum ROI | 5.02% over 35 days |

#### Five Weeks Later: 12 June, Expiration Day

The update was recorded on 12 June, five weeks after entry and on the expiration date itself. Schwab had been consolidating for several months. After entry the price initially dipped, then rebounded strongly; there was a period in which it fell significantly and again recovered strongly; and on the final day it rose by another $2 to trade at $91 — very slightly above the $91 strike.

Both legs were profitable at the same time, which is the ideal configuration. The call sold for $2.26 had decayed to a mark price of about $0.36, and later in the session $0.35, so the short call showed a gain. The stock, bought at $88.99-ish and now at $91-plus, showed a gain of roughly $200. Together the two legs produced a combined profit of about $400-plus, with the two legs contributing almost equally.

The remaining extrinsic value was tracked minute by minute, because on expiration day that is what determines whether waiting is worth anything. With the stock at $91 and the strike at $91, the call was in the money by about eleven cents, and the remaining extrinsic value was quoted as 25, 24 and 23 cents as the session ran — all of which would go to zero by the close. Waiting a few more hours would therefore capture roughly $22 more.

The analyser expressed the same fact graphically. The pink curve showed the current profit and the blue curve the profit at expiration. At the current share price the pink curve read **$413** and the blue curve read **$435.25** — a difference of about $24 to $25, which is precisely the remaining extrinsic value. At expiration the pink curve converges into the blue curve, and that convergence is the last of the profit.

#### The Choice: Roll, or Let It Expire

At that point the position sat exactly at its maximum profit point — the optimal outcome, beyond which no further gain is possible. Two courses of action were laid out.

The first was to roll. The chart looked over-extended and overbought and was starting to reverse down. If a pullback were expected, one could buy back the $91 call and sell a new $91 call. If further upside were expected, one could sell the new call at a higher strike. Concretely: buy back the $91 call for about $0.25, then go out another five weeks — another 35 days — and sell the $92.50 call, $1.50 higher, creating more headroom for capital gain, collecting about **$2.67**. Since $2.67 comfortably exceeds the $0.25 cost of closing, this would be a roll for a net credit of about $2.40.

This is described in the most useful possible terms: rolling the $91 up to $92.50 and out by five weeks, for additional credit, is an upgrade to the trade for which you are being paid. It is a repeatable monthly routine — open the account every five weeks, roll up and out, keep collecting premium. The caveat is honest: you will not always get a premium as good as this one, because prices move in different ways.

The second course of action was to do nothing and let expiration resolve the trade. Three sub-scenarios were laid out for that choice:

1. **Close below $91.** The option expires worthless, an additional $22 to $23 of decay is captured between now and the close, the shares are retained, and a new call can be sold on Monday.
2. **Close exactly at $91.** It becomes a coin flip. The counterparty may exercise or may decline to exercise; it is a 50-50 chance. If exercised, the shares are sold at $91 — perfectly acceptable, since they were bought at $88.99 and the premium is retained on top.
3. **Close above $91 — at $91.01 or higher.** Exercise is likely, assignment follows, and the 100 shares are sold away.

The decision made was to let it expire, precisely so that the assignment mechanics could be demonstrated. The reasoning was that being assigned at $91 produces a very good profit, and the resulting cash can be used to buy the shares back on Monday and re-enter the trade. Losing the shares was explicitly described as no problem at all. But the alternative advice for a reader who does *not* want the shares sold was given just as clearly: roll it up now — buy back the $91 call for $0.25 and sell a new one at a higher strike a month out, and keep collecting premium.

#### Saturday: The Outcome

The final update was recorded the following Saturday. Schwab closed on Friday at **$91.10**, ten cents above the strike. Because it expired in the money by more than one cent, the short call was liable to assignment — though the ultimate decision rests with the buyer, and the point is made that even in-the-money options are sometimes not exercised.

In this case the notification confirmed assignment. The counterparty exercised, forfeiting all the premium they had paid for the call, and in exchange acquired the shares at $91 per share — a slight discount to the $91.10 closing price. The Schwab position disappeared from the account.

The consequence was $91 × 100 shares × 1 contract = **$9,100 in cash** credited to the account, and that cash could immediately be used to buy the shares back and re-establish the trade on Monday.

#### Full Trade Accounting

The final summary is the clearest single accounting of a covered call in the entire course.

| Line item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry date | 8 May |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Shares bought | 100 @ $88.992 |
| Call sold | $91 strike, 12 June expiry |
| Premium collected | $2.27 per share |
| Net debit at entry | $86.65 per share |
| Cash out at entry | $8,665 |
| Maximum profit (defined at entry) | ($91 − $86.65) × 100 = $435 |
| Days held | 35 |
| Closing price at expiration | $91.10 |
| Outcome | Assigned; cost to close the call = $0 |
| Cash in at exit | $91 × 100 = $9,100 |
| **Net profit** | $9,100 − $8,665 = **$435** |
| **Return on capital** | **5.02% in 35 days** |

The trade achieved its maximum profit exactly. Two features of the accounting deserve emphasis.

First, the cost of closing the call was **zero**. Because the option was assigned rather than bought back, the buyer forfeited the option's value and nothing was paid to extinguish it. The trade-off is that the shares had to be sold at $91 rather than the market's $91.10 — the profit is capped at the strike, and that ten cents is the price of the cap.

Second, the 5.02% return decomposes cleanly into its two sources:

| Source | Amount | Return |
|---|---|---|
| Option premium | $227 | 2.62% |
| Capital gain on shares ($91.00 − $88.99) | ~$208 | 2.4% |
| **Total** | **$435** | **~5.02%** |

The premium yield of 2.62% in a single month is exactly what the strategy targets — the 2% to 3% per month rule, met precisely. The capital gain of 2.4% is the bonus that arises when the underlying cooperates. Together they produced more than 5% in five weeks.

---

## PART TWO: SELLING CASH SECURED PUTS

### Purpose and Premise

Selling cash secured puts is described as the instructor's favourite strategy, executed almost every other day to generate income for the investment portfolio. Its purpose is stated in a single sentence: it is used when you want to buy 100 shares of a particular stock at a discount, and eventually perhaps even for free.

The logic runs as follows. You identify a company you genuinely want to own — one that consistently produces higher revenue and higher profits year after year, generates positive free cash flow, and possesses a wide economic moat. Microsoft, Google, Apple, McDonald's, Visa and MasterCard are named as the kind of businesses that qualify.

Having identified the company, you apply two additional filters before doing anything. The first is valuation: you only buy shares of a stock if it is undervalued, trading below intrinsic value. The second is technical: the price must have dropped, must have waved down, and must be at a level of support.

At that point you face a choice. You could simply buy the shares at the market. Or you could play hard to get, insisting on an even lower price and a bigger discount. If you take the second path, the conventional approach is to place a limit order below the market and wait. The problem with waiting is that the stock may never come down — it may simply keep rising, and you never own it at all.

The solution taught is to make money while waiting. Instead of waiting like an idiot, you sell a put option at the strike price at which you would happily buy. Selling a put means accepting the obligation to buy 100 shares at the strike price if the option is exercised, and in exchange you collect premium immediately. You are being paid to wait for the shares to drop to your level.

### The Position, Leg by Leg

The cash secured put is a single-leg position with a cash requirement attached.

The traded leg is one short put option per 100 shares you are prepared to buy, sold out of the money — that is, at a strike below the current market price. The premium is credited to the account at the moment of the fill and represents the maximum profit the trade can ever produce.

The untraded but mandatory component is the cash: enough money in the account, or immediately transferable to it, to purchase 100 shares per contract at the strike price. This is what makes the put "cash secured." Selling a put without that cash is selling a **naked put**, and the course's position on naked puts is unambiguous: do not do it.

### The First Example: Buying at a Discount

The first worked example concerns a company the transcript renders as "MetPace," with the ticker letters spoken as "M-D-E-P" — the automatic transcription is clearly garbled here and the exact name should be treated with caution, though the numbers themselves are stated consistently and are usable.

The chart showed the familiar sequence: wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down. The rule for puts is the mirror image of the covered call rule: **only buy shares, or sell puts, after a wave down. Never after a wave up.** On the daily candles there is a further specification: you want the price to have dropped to at least the 50-day moving average, drawn as a blue line on the chart. In this case the price had dropped to the moving average and appeared to be turning up.

Intrinsic value was $336. The price had fallen to a little over $290 — $289 in the detailed version — so the stock was undervalued. Buying at $289 was therefore entirely reasonable. But the desire was to buy at a bigger discount, at $270.

The trade taken was to sell the $270 strike put expiring in February, about 30 days away, collecting **$9.10** per share. One contract of 100 shares means **$910 in cash received up front**.

The obligation accepted is to buy 100 shares if the price drops and stays below $270 at expiration — which was regarded as a desirable outcome, not a feared one, since the whole purpose was to acquire the shares at a discount.

#### How the Strike Was Chosen

The natural question — why $270 and not $260 or $250 — is answered with a two-part rule.

The first part is the expiry: sell puts with **30 to 45 days** to expiration. That is the sweet spot.

The second part is the return: choose a strike where **the premium divided by the strike price gives at least 2% for the month**. Here, $9.10 divided by $270 gives **3.3%** for 30 days. Repeated monthly, 3.3% × 12 is a 39% annual return, which is excellent. You may always sell at a lower strike, but the lower you go the less premium you receive, so the 2% floor sets the practical limit on how conservative you can be.

A third observation ties the strike back to probability. A strike selected this way typically carries a delta of about **0.30 negative — 30 delta**, possibly 30 to 35. The interpretation of that delta is the useful part: it means there is roughly a **30% probability that you will end up buying the shares**, and therefore roughly a **70% probability that the put expires worthless and you simply keep the premium**.

#### The Two Outcomes

**Outcome one: the share price drops below the strike and stays there.** At expiration the put is exercised, either by the put buyer or automatically by the exchange, and you are obligated to buy 100 shares at $270. This is a welcome outcome, because it is a good company being acquired at a discount to the price at which you were already willing to buy. And the effective purchase price is better still, because the premium was collected up front: $270 minus $9.10 gives a net purchase price of **$260.90**.

This is where the cash requirement bites. To take delivery you need 100 × $260.90, approximately **$26,000 in cash**, ready and waiting. Without it, you were selling a naked put. For those who cannot commit $26,000 to a single position, the advice is to run the strategy on lower-priced stocks in the $50 to $80 range — but always, without exception, on very good companies that make money consistently, never on unprofitable companies or penny stocks.

**Outcome two: the share price does not stay below the strike.** The price may go up, may go sideways, or may dip below $270 and bounce back before expiry. In any of those cases the put expires worthless, the obligation to buy disappears, and the premium is kept in full. You then repeat the process — sell another put, collect more premium — until eventually you either get the shares you wanted or you have collected so much premium along the way that you no longer mind.

This trade was executed for real on 18 January and notified to subscribers of the Ultimate Investors Playbook: one contract of $270-strike puts, expiring 16 February, collecting $9.10 per share.

### A Second Worked Example: Motorola Solutions (MSI)

The Motorola Solutions example is used to demonstrate strike selection on a stock already owned, where the motive is to acquire more shares rather than to establish a first position.

The fundamental screen came first. Using Stock Oracle, the Oracle IQ ranks the business across predictability, profitability, growth, moat, financial strength and valuation. The shortcut rule is that **as long as every rank is at least medium or high, the company counts as high quality**. For MSI the readings were: predictability high, profitability high, growth medium, moat very high, financial strength high, valuation medium — all medium or better, therefore high quality. A further filter is applied on the moat specifically: buy only companies with a wide moat or a narrow moat, and avoid companies with **no** moat, because they tend to be risky in the long run.

The Oracle value — the intrinsic value — was $413 against a share price of $391, so the stock was undervalued. Both conditions of the fundamental screen were met.

The technical screen came next, and it introduced a useful piece of craft. On the **daily** time frame Motorola looked choppy — up, down, up, down, with no clear trend. When the daily chart is that noisy, the instruction is to step up to the **weekly** time frame, where the trend is smoother and the wave structure legible. On the weekly candles the wave up, wave down structure was clear, and the most recent move was a wave down to a support level. That is the moment to sell a put, provided you want to own the shares.

The option chain was then worked through methodically. The available expiries were 3 days, 37 days and 66 days. The 3-day expiry is far too short and the 66-day expiry too long; the 37-day expiry sits inside the 30-to-45-day window and was selected. The stated preference is nearer to 40 to 45 days, though 30 days is fine as well.

On the chosen expiry, attention goes to two columns: the **delta** and the **mark price**. The mark is the midpoint between the bid and the ask, and it is the realistic indication of what the option is worth right now. Scanning the delta column for a value near −0.30, the closest available was **−0.33**, which corresponded to the **$380 strike**.

The return test: the mark price was **$7.45**, and $7.45 divided by $380 gives about **1.9%** for 37 days. That is not quite 2%, and the judgment applied is that it is close enough — "that's fine." This is a useful calibration point: the 2% rule is a target, not a tripwire, and 1.9% is acceptable.

The order entry rules mirror those for calls. Clicking the **bid** enters a sell; clicking the **ask** enters a buy. The platform will default to the bid price, but the bid is not what you want — you want at least the mark. **Always use a limit price; never use a market order.** A limit on a sale means this price or higher. You may set the limit above the mark — $8.00 was floated as an option — accepting that you may not get filled. If you want to be sure of a fill, enter the limit at roughly the mark, in this case $7.45.

The position, translated back onto the chart, looks like this. The put strike sits at $380, the market is at $391, and there are 37 days to run. If, at expiration, the price is at or above $380, the put decays to worthlessness and the full **$745** per contract is retained. Anything can happen in between — the price can rise, fall, go sideways, even trade below $380 temporarily — and none of it matters, because only the expiration price determines the outcome.

If instead the price is below $380 at expiration and the option is allowed to expire, it is exercised and 100 shares of MSI must be bought at $380. Against the $7.45 already collected, the effective purchase price is **$372.55** — an attractive entry against an intrinsic value of $413.

### Capital, Collateral and the Meaning of "Cash Secured"

The capital mechanics of a cash secured put are frequently misunderstood, and the MSI example is used to separate two different numbers that are easy to confuse.

The first number is the **notional value**: the total amount of stock you have committed to buy, which is the strike price multiplied by 100 shares. For the MSI trade that is $380 × 100 = **$38,000**. This is the money you must genuinely have available, because if assigned you must actually pay it.

The second number is the **buying power reduction** or margin collateral: the amount the broker actually blocks in your account as security. This is very much smaller. On the MSI trade the buying power effect displayed was about **$6,689** — roughly 17.6%, described as "about 20%, in fact less than 20%." The general rule given is that a broker requires collateral of about **20% of the notional value** in an ordinary margin account.

The critical warning attached to this gap is that the small collateral requirement is precisely what seduces people into selling more puts than they can afford. The broker will let you sell the put with $6,689 blocked; the broker will not stop you from doing so without the $38,000 behind it. That restraint has to come from you. If you do not have the money ready to buy the shares, you are selling a naked put, and you should not.

Two refinements are added. First, the collateral requirement is **not static**: if the stock price drops and the put moves further into the money, the buying power requirement rises from 20% to 30% to 40% to 50%. This dynamic is the mechanism by which unprepared sellers receive margin calls in a crash. Second, account type matters: with a **portfolio margin account** at Interactive Brokers — available with at least US$100,000 — the buying power blocked can be considerably less than 20%. On the SHLD example the blocked buying power was $663 on a $6,200 notional, only about 10%, because of portfolio margin. The instructor's own comment on this is the correct attitude: it does not matter what the broker blocks, because the cash to buy the shares is there anyway.

### The Payoff Profile

The profit and loss diagram of a short put is worth reading carefully, because two of its features are routinely misread.

On the vertical axis is profit and loss, with anything above zero a profit and anything below a loss. On the horizontal axis is the share price, rising to the right and falling to the left. Two curves are drawn: the **green or blue line** is the profit at expiration, and the **purple line** is the profit today.

The first commonly misread feature is that **the P&L today, at the moment of entry, is zero**, despite the cash having been credited. This confuses people who expect to see an immediate profit. The explanation is that the P&L curve shows what would happen if you bought the put back right now — and buying it back immediately means paying the same $7.45 you just received, so nothing has been made. The cash is in the account, but it is offset by the liability of the open option. It becomes profit only as the option decays.

The second feature is the movement of the purple line over time. Stepping the analysis date forward — 14 May, 15 May, 17 May, 18 May — the purple line drifts steadily upward. It does so because every day that passes strips time value out of the short put, so the option can be bought back cheaper, so more profit is locked in. Time is working in your favour and the purple line rising toward the blue line is the visual expression of that. At expiration the two curves coincide.

The **maximum profit** is the premium, collected in full at the moment of the sale: $7.45 × 100 = $745 for the MSI trade. There is no way to make more than that, no matter how far the stock rises.

The **break-even** is the strike minus the premium: $380 − $7.45 = **$372.55** for MSI. Below that point the diagram shows losses, and this is where the third misreading occurs. Looking at the diagram, it appears that as the share price falls you could lose a great deal of money. The response is twofold. First, the break-even is not really a loss threshold in the ordinary sense — it is simply the **average purchase price of the 100 shares** you will end up owning. The line merely reflects that you have effectively bought stock at $372.55. Second, if the price falls below that, you are making paper losses, exactly as any shareholder does when a stock falls below their cost — but on a high-quality business bought below intrinsic value, that is a temporary condition, and in the long run a good company's share price goes up and the investment makes money.

The caveat is stated with equal clarity: this reasoning holds **only** for high-quality businesses. If you do this on an unprofitable stock, or on a stock whose price can never come back, then yes, you can lose a lot of money.

The **theoretical maximum loss** is the strike minus the premium, multiplied by 100 — the loss you would take if the company went to zero and stayed there. On the CELH trade discussed later this is computed explicitly as $2,642 per contract. It is described as a theoretical scenario that will not happen in 31 days, but it is the honest arithmetic definition of the risk.

### Practice Case Study: SHLD

The SHLD case is presented as a self-test, with the reader invited to pause and calculate. It is worth reproducing because the deliberate simplicity makes the arithmetic transparent.

The instrument is the Global X Defense ETF, ticker SHLD. Being an ETF there is no intrinsic value to compute; the qualifying test is simply that it is a high-quality ETF made up of great businesses that will rise over the long run. The technical picture showed wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down, with a recent wave down to a support level. The share price was **$64.64** — a much lower share price than MSI or META, and therefore far more accessible to a small account.

The trade: sell one contract of the SHLD **$62 strike put**, expiring in June, **36 days** to expiration.

**Question one: what premium is collected per contract?** The mark price on the $62 strike was $1.20, so the total is $1.20 × 100 = **$120 per contract**. Either answer — $120 per contract or $1.20 per share — is correct.

**Question two: what is the return on investment for 36 days?** Premium divided by strike: $1.20 ÷ $62 = **1.9%**. Close enough to 2%, and reasonable.

**Question three: if assigned, what is the net purchase cost of the 100 shares?** Strike minus premium: $62.00 − $1.20 = **$60.80 per share**.

**Cash required:** 100 × $62 = **$6,200**, which must be set aside. Collateral blocked at the standard 20% would be roughly **$1,240**, though on the portfolio margin account actually used it was $663.

The strike was chosen at 30 delta, and the point is made that other deltas are permissible — 36 delta or 25 delta would both be defensible — provided the premium still clears roughly 2%.

The SHLD trade also carries a small but valuable platform lesson. On Interactive Brokers, the column called **mid** performs the same function as Think or Swim's **mark**: the midpoint between the bid and the ask.
