On this chain the bid was $1.40 and the resulting mid was $1.20 (the transcript's spoken figures are partially garbled here, but the operative number, the $1.20 mid used for the trade, is stated consistently). If your option chain lacks the delta column, the mid column, or the full range of strikes, all of these can be configured by right-clicking the chain and adding or removing columns, and by choosing "all" to display every available strike. Once the order is entered — one contract, limit price $1.20 — the platform displays the buying power that will be blocked before you transmit. After transmitting, right-clicking the position and opening a **What If** analysis produces the same profit and loss analyser seen on Think or Swim.

### Entry Rules for Selling Cash Secured Puts

Drawing the rules together into their formal statement:

1. **Stock selection.** Sell puts only on fundamentally strong, undervalued stocks that you would not mind owning. Stock Oracle provides a shortcut for assessing quality: all Oracle IQ ranks at medium or high, and a wide or narrow moat rather than no moat. High-quality ETFs also qualify, with the intrinsic-value test replaced by a judgment of the underlying basket's quality.

2. **Have the cash.** Cash sufficient to buy 100 shares per contract at the strike price must be in the account, or in an account from which it can be transferred immediately. Without it the trade is a naked put.

3. **Wait for the wave down.** Sell only after the price has retraced to a support level, is undervalued, and is within **5% to 10% of your intended purchase price**. On daily candles look for a drop to at least the 50-day moving average; if the daily chart is too choppy, use the weekly.

4. **Sell out of the money.** The strike must be below the current market price.

5. **Delta around 30.** The typical strike sits near −0.30 delta, implying roughly a 70% probability of expiring worthless. Lower deltas are acceptable — the CELH trade was executed at 14 delta — provided the premium test is still satisfied.

6. **Expiration 30 to 45 days.** The sweet spot, with a stated preference for the 40-to-45 end.

7. **Premium at least 2% to 3% of the strike for the month.** Premium divided by strike price. More is better; the higher the yield the better the deal, subject to the strike still being one you are content to buy at.

8. **High implied volatility is a bonus.** Above 40 is high. It produces richer premiums but is explicitly not required. The requirement is 2% a month; implied volatility merely makes reaching it easier.

### Exit Scenario One: The Put Expires Worthless, or You Close Early

If the stock stays at or above the strike at expiration — whether it rose, went sideways, or dipped below and recovered — the put expires worthless. There is nothing to buy back, and 100% of the premium is realised as profit. You then sell a new put with another 30 to 45 days to expiration, at the same or a different strike, and repeat indefinitely. This is the income engine.

But, as with covered calls, the practice differs from the theory. Most of the time the put is bought back before expiration. The rule is: **buy to close once you have realised at least 70% of the maximum profit.**

The rationale is a comparison of what remains against what it costs to obtain it. If a put with 30 days to expiration has lost most of its value after only seven days, and closing now captures 70% to 80% of the profit, then holding for the remaining 20-plus days to collect the last 20% to 30% is a poor use of both capital and risk. Close it, take the profit, and redeploy.

#### The Visa Trade: Closing After Seven Days

A live example makes this concrete. On 22 April an alert was issued to Ultimate Investors Playbook subscribers: a cash secured put sold on **Visa at the $300 strike, expiring 29 May** — about 37 days to expiration — for a credit of **$6.15**. Two contracts were sold.

Within seven days Visa's share price jumped substantially, and the put collapsed in value to **$0.86**. The unrealised profit was 86% of maximum, roughly $1,000 across the two contracts, with only about $164 of value left in the position and a full month still to run. Holding another thirty days to capture $164 does not make sense.

The close was executed by highlighting the position, right-clicking, and selecting close — which, for a short put, means buying it back. The negotiation is again visible and again instructive, but in the opposite direction from a sale: because you are buying, you start low and walk up. The mark was $0.82. An offer at $0.80 was tried and did not fill — described self-deprecatingly as being a bit greedy. Then $0.81, no fill; $0.82, no fill; then $0.83, $0.85, and finally a fill at **$0.86**.

The accounting: sold at $6.15, bought back at $0.86, net **$5.29 per share**. On two contracts — 200 shares — that is **$1,058** profit (the platform displayed $1,055 before the final fill). Expressed as a fraction of maximum: $5.29 ÷ $6.15 = **86% of the maximum profit**, captured in seven days rather than thirty-seven.

#### The Pattern in the Trade Log

This is not an isolated case but the standard operating procedure, and the Discord notification history is presented as evidence. Several closes are read out:

| Underlying | Strike | Expiry | Sold at | Closed at | % of max profit realised |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Google | $255 | 15 May | $7.21 | $1.10 | 84% |
| Nvidia | $155 | — | — | — | 69% |
| Meta | — | — | — | $1.63 (stated as "163") | 85% |
| Amazon | — | — | — | — | 78% |
| Visa | $300 | 29 May | $6.15 | $0.86 | 86% |

The Google close, notified on 8 April, is spelled out: sold at $7.21, closed at $1.10, capturing roughly $6.11 per share, which is 84% of the maximum profit, achieved in just a few days. This, the transcript says plainly, is how the game is actually played in real life — closing puts early once 70% to 80% of the profit is in hand.

### Exit Scenario Two: Assignment

If the stock drops below the strike and stays there until expiration, you are assigned. The mechanics deserve careful statement because the timing is not entirely within your control.

The person who bought your put — whoever they may be, and you will never know — may exercise at any time, because equity options are **American style**. The moment they exercise, you are obligated and you are assigned 100 shares.

In practice, most of the time the put buyer will not exercise early, because early exercise forfeits the option's remaining extrinsic value. The dominant path to assignment is therefore automatic: if the put expires in the money by one cent or more, the exchange exercises it automatically.

What happens next is straightforward. The following morning, 100 shares appear in your account, and the broker deducts the purchase cost — the strike price times 100 shares, or $6,200 in the SHLD example. Your effective cost, however, is lower than the strike because of the premium you collected: $62.00 minus $1.20 gives a net cost of **$60.80** per share.

From there you have choices. Many people simply keep the shares as a long-term investment, which is fine and is usually the whole point. Others begin selling covered calls against the newly acquired shares — and that combination, cash secured puts to acquire, covered calls to generate income on what you acquired, is the **wheel** or cash flow wheel strategy, treated in its own lesson.

#### Early Assignment

Early exercise does happen, and the conditions are the mirror image of those for calls. It becomes likely when the stock drops far below the strike — from $64 down to $55, say — so that the put is deep in the money. As the price falls, the put's delta rises from 30 to 40 to 50 and onward. **Once the delta reaches 90 or higher there is a high chance of early exercise**, and likewise **if the extrinsic value falls below 10 cents** there is very little left for the buyer to forfeit and exercise becomes attractive to them. (Note that the threshold quoted for early exercise of a short *call* was an extrinsic value below 20 cents; for the short put it is stated as below 10 cents. Both express the same idea — negligible remaining time value — and both should be treated as approximate.)

You can monitor this directly on the option chain by watching the delta column. The SHLD chain is used to demonstrate: with the ETF at $64, the $62-strike put carried a delta of only about −0.30, so early exercise was remote. But further up the chain, the **$73-strike put** — a strike far above the market — showed a delta of **91, and elsewhere on screen 94**. Anyone who had sold that $73 put a couple of weeks earlier, before the ETF fell to $64, was now sitting at 91 delta with 36 days still to run, and faced a high probability of early assignment.

If you are assigned early and you do not want the shares, the remedy is simple and immediate: sell the shares. Click sell, dispose of the 100 shares at the market, and the proceeds return to your account. There is nothing catastrophic about early assignment; it merely accelerates a decision you had already accepted in principle.

### Exit Scenario Three: Rolling the Put

The third scenario applies when the stock has fallen below your strike, assignment is approaching, and you have changed your mind — you no longer want the shares.

#### When to Roll

Two triggers, exactly parallel to those for covered calls. Roll when it is close to expiration — typically **two to three days before expiry** — and it appears likely the price will remain below the strike. Or roll when the put is already **deep in the money with a delta of about 0.90 or more**, regardless of how much time remains.

#### How to Roll

The process has two steps.

**Step one: buy to close the existing put, at a loss.** This is unavoidable. A put sold for $1.20 may, after the share price falls, be worth $5.20, and buying it back therefore costs $5.20 and crystallises a loss of $4.00 per share.

**Step two: sell to open a new put, at the same strike or lower, with a further expiration date, collecting enough premium to cover the loss.** The new expiry is typically another 30 to 45 days, though a longer expiry may be chosen if more premium is required. The binding requirement is that the new credit exceeds the old debit. This is **rolling for a credit**, and because the new strike is normally lower, it is more specifically **rolling the put down** — down in strike, out in time.

The purpose is precisely stated: the premium collected from the new put covers the loss on the initial short put, while lowering your break-even and buying more time for the share price to recover.

#### The Pepsi Roll

A compact real example is given. A Pepsi put was sold at the **$165 strike** for **$2.99**, across three contracts. Pepsi then declined below the strike, and with expiration approaching, assignment was certain unless something was done. The shares were no longer wanted.

The put was bought back at **$5.60**, producing a loss of **$2.61** per share. Immediately a new put was sold at the **$160 strike** — a lower strike — with a further expiration, collecting **$3.60** in premium.

The net effect: $3.60 collected minus $2.61 lost equals a **net credit of $0.99 per share**. Across three contracts — 300 shares — that is **$297**.

What happened subsequently was the desired outcome: Pepsi rebounded above $160, the new put expired worthless, and the trade closed with the $297 profit intact.

The honest qualification follows immediately. It does not always work out on the first roll. Sometimes the share price keeps falling and the new put must itself be rolled, and then again, and again. Rolls of three or four times are described as routine; the longest roll on record for the instructor was **six times**. But the underlying principle holds: as long as you keep rolling, you never have to take the shares, and if the company is genuinely good, the price eventually rebounds and the put eventually expires worthless. Provided you have the buying power to hold and keep rolling, this can be done indefinitely.

### The Lockheed Martin Roll: A Full Back-Tested Walkthrough

The most detailed demonstration of rolling in the course is a back-test conducted on Think or Swim's **On Demand** feature, which allows the platform to be rewound to any historical date and traded as though live. The chosen episode is deliberately extreme: a cash secured put sold on Lockheed Martin immediately before the COVID-19 crash. The purpose is to show what rolling can accomplish in genuinely adverse conditions.

The simulated account begins with $100,000.

#### The Original Trade: 26 February 2020

The platform was rewound to **26 February 2020** — with the clock set carefully to the New York market session, 11 a.m. New York time corresponding to 11 p.m. Singapore time. At that date the chart showed the familiar wave structure, with the most recent move a wave down, and the level appeared to be support. The reasonable expectation was a bounce. Nobody watching that chart on that date had any idea what was about to happen.

The trade taken was the standard one: expiry chosen at **35 to 45 days**, landing on the **3 April** expiry at about 37 days; strike chosen at approximately **30 delta**, landing on the **$390 put**; premium collected **$7.45 per share**, or **$745** for one contract. The simulated cash balance rose from $100,000 to $100,745.

#### 3 April 2020: The Crash

Fast-forwarding to 3 April, the expiration date, the price had plunged. The short put was deep in the money, showing a loss of **−$2,815**, and the account's net liquidation value had fallen from $100,000 to **$97,185**.

At this point the honest alternative was available: simply let the put be exercised, buy 100 shares of Lockheed Martin at $390, and keep the $745 premium. That is the ordinary, intended outcome of a cash secured put, and it would have been a defensible choice on a business of Lockheed's quality.

But the demonstration proceeds on the assumption that, for whatever reason, the shares are no longer wanted.

#### Roll One: 3 April

Buying the put back was quoted at **$35.60**, against $7.45 collected — a loss of **$28.15** per share. The actual fill in the simulation was at **$38.50**, executed at market for demonstration purposes; the summary spreadsheet subsequently used **$35.60** for the accounting, and the round-number loss carried forward was **$28.15**. The account dropped from $100,000 to about $97,000, and the loss was realised.

Now the offsetting sale. The requirement was a new put collecting **more than $28**, at a strike **lower** than the original $390, with a further expiration. Returning to the chain at the default 35-to-45-day window, the **42-day** expiry (15 May) was selected — noted as no more right or wrong than 35 days.

The strike chosen was **$370**, twenty dollars below the original, collecting **$32.85**. Against the $28.15 loss, this left a **net credit of $4.70**.

Here the treatment of delta at the roll stage is given explicitly, and it is important because it contradicts the entry rule. The $370 strike carried a delta of about **57** — far from the 30 delta demanded at entry. The instruction is blunt: **do not worry about the delta when rolling.** Delta governs only the first sale. Thereafter, what matters is getting enough premium to cover the loss and lowering the strike. Those two things are what count.

The account cash returned to approximately $100,000, though net liquidation remained at a loss because the new short put was itself under water. The running credit was recorded as **$4.70**.

#### Roll Two: 15 May

Advancing to 15 May, the price was still below the new $370 strike. Doing nothing meant assignment at $370 — which, it is noted, is not a bad outcome at all, since it is $20 per share better than the original $390 and the second premium is retained on top. But the demonstration continues on the premise of not wanting the shares.

The $370 put, sold for $32.85, was now quoted at about **$12.00** — falling in real time as the simulation ran, which is a nice reminder that these are live quotes. It was bought back at **$12.00**, producing a **profit of $20.85** on that leg.

The running accounting was then laid out on a spreadsheet, with positive figures denoting money received and negative denoting money paid:

| Transaction | Cash flow |
|---|---|
| Sell $390 put | +$7.45 |
| Buy back $390 put | −$35.60 |
| *Subtotal (loss on first put)* | *−$28.15* |
| Sell $370 put | +$32.85 |
| Buy back $370 put | −$12.00 |
| *Subtotal (profit on second put)* | *+$20.85* |
| **Running net** | **−$7.30** |

The headline observation is the one that matters: the net position had improved from a **−$28.15** loss to a **−$7.30** loss. The loss was shrinking with each roll. Keep rolling, and the loss reduces until it becomes a profit.

#### Roll Three: 18 May

The simulation being on a Friday, the third sale was placed the following Monday, 18 May, with Lockheed trading at $375. The requirement was now to recover $7.30.

The **39-day** expiry was chosen as closest to 40 days. Scanning the chain for a premium of at least $7.00, several candidates presented themselves — the $350 strike at $8.50, and the $355 and $360 strikes. The $350 strike at 28 delta was considered, and then the **$360 strike** at about **34 delta** was chosen instead, collecting **$9.30**, expiring **26 June**.

#### 26 June: The Final Close

Advancing to 26 June, the price had fallen again. The $360 put now sat almost exactly at the money — the strike at $360 and the stock at $360. If left alone it could still be assigned.

The close was executed against a moving quote: initially $1.67, then $2.50, and finally filled at **$1.68**. The profit on this third put was therefore $9.30 − $1.68 = **$7.62**.

The full accounting, as summarised:

| Round | Sold | Bought back | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1: $390 put | +$7.45 | −$35.60 | −$28.15 |
| 2: $370 put | +$32.85 | −$12.00 | +$20.85 |
| 3: $360 put | +$9.30 | −$1.68 | +$7.62 |
| **Net** | | | **+$0.32 per share** |

The final cash balance in the simulated account was **$100,032**, with net liquidation matching. A net profit of about **$32**.

#### What the Lockheed Exercise Demonstrates

The point of the exercise is not the $32. The point is stated directly: if you sell a cash secured put, you normally *want* to be assigned the shares and you do not want to buy the put back. But if for some reason you no longer want the shares, there is an alternative — you can roll the put, and keep rolling it, until you no longer lose money on the put and no longer have to own the shares. Each roll buys time for the share price to recover. The trade began in the teeth of the worst crash in a decade, saw a $28 per share loss, and was ground back to break-even and slightly beyond over four months of rolling.

And the exercise ends where every lesson in this chapter ends: none of it works unless the underlying company is genuinely good. You must only sell cash secured puts on fundamentally strong companies that you know will rise in the long run — companies with a wide economic moat and consistent profits — and the stock should already be undervalued when you sell the put. The COVID crash demonstrates that something undervalued can become far more undervalued; the roll is the tool that lets you wait that out.

### Advantages and Risks of Cash Secured Puts

#### The Advantages

The advantage is that you can buy great companies at a discount, or eventually for free. You are paid premium while waiting for the stock to fall to your ideal purchase price, and you keep collecting that premium as profit until it does. By the time the price finally drops to your level, you may have collected so much accumulated premium that the shares are effectively free.

#### The First Risk: You Never Get the Shares

The catch, and it is a real one, is that you may never actually own the stock if the share price simply keeps rising.

This is illustrated with a personal failure. A couple of years ago Microsoft was trading at around $150. A few shares were bought outright, but greed intervened, and rather than buying more, puts were sold at around $130 in the hope of a better entry. Microsoft then simply kept climbing — $160, $170, $180. Every put expired worthless and every premium was collected as free money, but the shares were never acquired, and the position in one of the great compounders of the era remained very small. The premium collected was trivial compared with the capital gain forgone.

The conclusion drawn shapes how the strategy should be used: **sell puts only when you already own a reasonable number of shares** and are playing hard to get for additional shares at a genuine discount. Cash secured puts are a supplement to a position, not usually the way to build one from nothing on a stock that is running.

#### The Second Risk: The Shares Themselves

Once assigned, you carry exactly the same risk as buying the stock outright. Buy a company that is losing money, carrying too much debt, or trading above fair value, and you should not be surprised when the shares fall 20% and you lose money on them. There is nothing about the option structure that protects you from a bad investment decision. This is why the ability to identify great companies and buy them at a discount is the actual prerequisite.

#### The Third Risk: Naked Puts and the Seduction of Free Money

The most emphatic warning in the entire chapter concerns selling naked puts — selling puts with no intention or capacity to own the shares.

The psychology is described with unusual precision because it is so common among students and friends. During a bull market, with stocks rising, a trader sells puts far below the market — Microsoft at $210, puts sold at $180 — reasoning that the stock is very unlikely to fall that far. The stock rises, the put expires worthless, and the premium is free money. It happens again, and again. It becomes lucrative and, crucially, it becomes *easy*. The trader concludes that this is simply free money every month and that assignment will never come, and begins to size up — selling puts on far more shares than they could ever afford to buy.

The mechanism of ruin is then laid out step by step, and it hinges on the dynamic margin requirement described earlier. Markets crash on a schedule that is statistically reliable even if individually unpredictable: roughly **once a year the market drops 5%; once every two years it drops 10%; once every five years it drops 20%**. It is the nature of the game. When that happens to a trader who is short more puts than they can cover, the broker increases the buying power required to hold those puts. If the account lacks the buying power, the broker issues a **margin call**, demanding cash immediately. If the cash cannot be produced, the broker force-closes the positions — at the worst possible prices, at the bottom of a crash — and the loss can be very large indeed.

The two rules that prevent this are stated as absolutes. **Only sell puts when you have the intention to own 100 shares at the strike price.** And **always ensure you have the cash ready to purchase 100 shares in the event of assignment** — in the account, or in a bank account from which it can be transferred immediately.

#### A Student's Cautionary Tale

The warning is reinforced by a message from a student named Alice, posted in the course chat groups as a caution to others, describing her own experience with cash secured puts before and during the COVID-19 crash.

She began as a newbie, sold 3M puts, and found it astonishingly easy — about $500 per contract in free money. She did it again with VEEV puts and Yum puts, collecting around a thousand dollars. She concluded she had found a fantastic deal producing free money.

Then COVID-19 hit and the market crashed. Her buying power requirement shot up, and because she did not have enough cash in the account to meet the increased requirement, she received a margin call: the broker demanded she top up cash the next day. She had to keep topping up over many days. She was fortunate — she had spare cash set aside for rainy days — and without it, in her own phrase, she would have been *jialat mati*, finished.

Her conclusion, and the reason the message is reproduced in the course, is that from that day on she never sold puts or calls naked. Her preferred solution was to always enter a trade with two legs, both puts and calls, so that the position carries its own insurance.

#### The Bridge to Credit Spreads

That last remark points directly at the next strategy in the curriculum, and the chapter closes by making the connection explicit.

If you believe a stock is going up — Microsoft at $210 — and you want to sell a put at $180, you have two legitimate ways to do it safely. The first is the one taught throughout this chapter: have the cash ready to buy the shares. The second is to hedge the position by **buying another put at a lower strike**, say $175, against the $180 put you sold.

The image offered for this is precise: you are selling insurance to collect premium, and simultaneously buying reinsurance to cap your own exposure. The long put at $175 defines and limits the loss on the short put at $180, so that no crash, however severe, can produce an unbounded outcome or a forced liquidation.

That two-legged structure has a name. It is the **bull put spread**, also known as a credit spread, and it is the subject of the lessons that follow.

---

### Summary of Rules

For convenience, the operative thresholds from both strategies are collected here. Every one of these figures is stated explicitly in the lessons, and each carries the reasoning developed above.

#### Selling Covered Calls

| Rule | Specification |
|---|---|
| Underlying | Fundamentally strong stock or high-quality ETF, already owned |
| Growth filter | Low to moderate growth only; avoid anything growing above 20% a year |
| Sector filter | Avoid biotech and pharmaceutical |
| Share requirement | 100 shares per contract |
| Cost basis condition | Current share price must exceed your average cost |
| Valuation condition | Share price above intrinsic value |
| Technical trigger | After a wave up; ideally below resistance; never after a wave down |
| Strike selection | 35 to 45 delta (40 to 45 in the live examples) |
| Days to expiration | 30 to 45 |
| Premium target | 2% to 3% of share price or strike per month; 1.5% acceptable for ETFs |
| Implied volatility | 35 to 40 or above — a bonus, not a requirement |
| Profit taking | Buy to close at 70% to 80% of maximum profit |
| Roll trigger | Short call delta reaches 90+, or 2 to 3 days before expiry while in the money |
| Roll method | Buy back at a loss; sell same or higher strike, 30 to 45+ days out, for a net credit |
| Early exercise risk | Delta above 90 and extrinsic value below $0.20 |
| Maximum profit | (Strike − net cost of shares) × 100 + premium |
| Maximum risk | The same downside as owning the stock, less the premium collected |

#### Selling Cash Secured Puts

| Rule | Specification |
|---|---|
| Underlying | Fundamentally strong, undervalued stock you want to own; or high-quality ETF |
| Quality screen | All Oracle IQ ranks medium or high; wide or narrow moat, never no moat |
| Cash requirement | Strike × 100 per contract, available in cash |
| Broker collateral | Roughly 20% of notional in a margin account; less with portfolio margin; rises as the put goes in the money |
| Technical trigger | After a wave down, at support, within 5% to 10% of your intended purchase price; at least the 50-day moving average on daily candles, or use weekly candles if daily is choppy |
| Strike selection | Out of the money, around 30 delta; lower delta acceptable if premium still qualifies |
| Days to expiration | 30 to 45, preferring 40 to 45 |
| Premium target | At least 2% to 3% of the strike price per month |
| Implied volatility | Above 40 is high — a bonus, not a requirement |
| Maximum profit | The premium collected, in full |
| Break-even | Strike − premium |
| Maximum theoretical loss | (Strike − premium) × 100, if the stock goes to zero |
| Profit taking | Buy to close at 70%+ of maximum profit; examples realised 69% to 86% |
| Assignment trigger | In the money by $0.01 or more at expiration |
| Early exercise risk | Delta at 0.90 or above, or extrinsic value below $0.10 |
| Roll trigger | 2 to 3 days before expiry with the price below the strike, or delta at 0.90+ |
| Roll method | Buy to close at a loss; sell same or lower strike, further out in time, for a net credit; ignore delta on the roll |
| Prohibited | Naked puts — selling without the cash or intention to buy the shares |

---

# Part II — The Cashflow Wheel & The Bull Call Spread

## The Cashflow Wheel and The Bull Call Spread

### Introduction: Two Machines, Two Purposes

The two strategies covered in this chapter sit at opposite ends of the options temperament spectrum, and understanding why they differ is more instructive than learning either one in isolation.

The Cashflow Wheel is a patient, capital-heavy, income-producing machine. It is built out of two strategies you have already met — the cash secured put and the covered call — bolted together into a continuous cycle that runs indefinitely on a single high-quality stock. It does not try to predict direction. It does not try to catch a move. It asks only one thing of the underlying: that the company be good enough that its share price will eventually recover from whatever happens to it in the short term. The Wheel makes money from the relentless collection of option premium, month after month, and it explicitly renounces any claim on the capital gains of the stock itself. Adam is completely direct about this: "my intention is not to make any money from the stock. My intention is to just generate monthly cash flow from selling puts and selling calls on the stock." The Wheel is a cash-flow business dressed up as a stock position.

The Bull Call Spread is the opposite animal. It is a small-capital, short-horizon, directional bet. It is a debit spread, meaning you pay money out to put it on, and that payment is the entirety of what you can lose. It is deployed for roughly thirty days at a time on a stock you believe is about to rise, and it is designed to be closed and recycled quickly. It has a low probability of maximum success — the ANET case study opens with a stated 38% chance of winning at expiration — and it compensates for that low hit rate with a risk-to-reward ratio of at least one-to-two. The Bull Call Spread does not care whether the underlying is a wonderful business. It cares whether the chart is bouncing off support in an uptrend.

One strategy is designed to be right most of the time and to earn little each time it is right. The other is designed to be wrong most of the time and to earn a great deal on the minority of occasions when it is right. Both are profitable if executed with discipline; both are catastrophic if the discipline is dropped. What follows is a complete treatment of each, including every rule, every threshold, and every case study exactly as taught.

---

## PART ONE — THE CASHFLOW WHEEL

### Chapter Section 1: The Building Blocks Reviewed

Before the Wheel can be assembled, the two components must be understood precisely, because the entire strategy is a consequence of the obligations those two components create.

#### Selling a Put

When you sell any option — put or call — you receive a premium. That premium is cash. It is not a promise of cash, not a paper credit, not something that settles later. As Adam puts it, "This is cash, you receive immediately that goes into your cash account, into your balance." That money is yours from the moment the trade fills, and no subsequent development in the trade can take it away from you.

What you have sold in exchange is an obligation. Selling a put obligates you to buy 100 shares of the underlying stock at the chosen strike price, and you must be prepared to buy those 100 shares at any moment that the put buyer chooses to exercise. The put buyer holds that right from the moment of purchase until the expiration date.

In practice, early exercise is rare. The put buyer will typically not exercise unless the put is very deep in the money and very close to expiration, because exercising early destroys whatever extrinsic value remains in the contract. The buyer would generally be better off selling the option than exercising it. But on the final day there is no such thing as extrinsic value, and the rule becomes mechanical and unforgiving: if on the expiration day the stock price closes below the strike price by even one cent, the put is automatically exercised. You will be assigned 100 shares of stock, and the cash required to buy them will be deducted from your account without ceremony.

From this follows the single most important safety rule attached to selling puts. You should only sell a put if you have the money ready to buy the 100 shares if they are assigned to you. That is what makes it a *cash secured* put. The instruction is stated twice, in successive sentences, for emphasis: "Never, never sell a put if you don't have the money to buy the 100 shares. If you do that, you are selling a naked put. Never do that."

#### Selling a Call

The call side is the mirror image. When you sell a call you again receive cash immediately, and in exchange you take on the obligation to sell 100 shares of the underlying stock at the strike price to the call buyer. Again, the buyer may exercise at any time before or on expiration; again, early exercise is rare and generally happens only when the call is very deep in the money or very close to expiry; and again, on the expiration day the process becomes automatic. If the stock closes above the strike price, the call you sold is exercised, 100 shares are deducted from your account, and the cash proceeds from selling those shares are credited to you.

And so the corresponding safety rule: before you sell that call, you must already own the 100 shares. That is what makes it a *covered* call — you are selling a call against shares you already hold, so the obligation to deliver can always be met from inventory. "Never ever sell a call option if you don't own the 100 shares to begin with. If you do that, you're selling a naked call. Never sell a naked call."

The Wheel is nothing more than these two obligations arranged in a loop. You sell puts until one of them assigns you shares. Then you sell calls against those shares until one of them takes the shares away. Then you sell puts again. Each rotation of the loop deposits premium into your account.

### Chapter Section 2: Stock Selection — The Part That Actually Determines Your Outcome

Adam does not begin the Wheel discussion with option mechanics. He begins it with stock selection, and he is blunt about the hierarchy: "the most important thing for this strategy is choosing the right stock. That's the most important thing. It begins with stock selection."

The reason for this priority becomes obvious once you trace what the Wheel actually commits you to. If you are assigned shares, you own them. If the shares fall, you own them at a loss. And the Wheel's entire risk-management posture consists of refusing to sell at a loss — of holding the shares and continuing to write calls until the price recovers. That posture is only rational if recovery is close to certain. A recovery assumption applied to the wrong business is not a strategy; it is a slow-motion disaster.

So the qualifying criteria are demanding.

**The business must be fundamentally excellent.** The Wheel should only be performed on fundamentally great stocks that will increase in value over time. Concretely, these are high-quality businesses with consistent growth in sales revenue, in earnings, and in cash flow from operations. Adam's confidence standard is deliberately absolute: "You've got to be 100% confident that this company, the stock price will always go up in the long run."

**The company should have an economic moat, ideally a wide one.** A wide moat is the safest; a narrow moat can be considered. A company with no economic moat at all is disqualified, as is anything speculative.

**The stock must be undervalued at entry.** The share price should be trading below the intrinsic value of the company. This is not a preference but an entry condition, and it recurs at every stage of the cycle — each time you return to the top of the Wheel to sell a fresh put, you must re-check that the stock is still undervalued. If the price has risen so far that the stock is now overvalued, you do not sell another put on it. You either wait for it to become undervalued again or you find a different undervalued company.

**The ten-year chart should show a clear uptrend.** This is a useful sanity check that sits alongside the fundamental analysis. Look at a decade of price history and confirm the stock has been rising over that period. "If the stock is like going down for 10 years, then obviously it's not a very good business."

For students of the Value Momentum Investing course, the analytical machinery for all of this already exists — the business analysis, the intrinsic value calculation. For those who want a shortcut, the Stock Oracle tool renders the verdict immediately across the relevant metrics, and the rule of thumb given is that the company should rank at least medium to high on each of them.

#### The Budget Constraint

There is a purely practical filter layered on top of the quality filter, and it is one that many students underestimate. To run the Wheel you must be able to buy 100 shares of the stock. That means the capital requirement is one hundred times the share price. A $150 stock demands $15,000 of buying capacity. A $400 stock demands $40,000.

This is where a real tension emerges, and Adam names it directly. If you have a relatively small account, you are forced to focus on stocks selling below $100. But — and this is the trap — "many stocks below 100 could be lousy company. So please don't do this on a low-price stock that's a lousy company." The budget constraint must never be allowed to override the quality constraint. There are good companies with share prices below $100; there are simply not very many of them.

He supplies worked examples in three price brackets so that students can start their search in the right place:

| Price bracket | Example companies given |
|---|---|
| Below $100 | Coca-Cola (KO), Bank of America (BAC), Monster Beverage (MNST), Arch Capital (ACGL) |
| $100 to $200 | McDonald's (MCD), Yum! Brands, Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), Cintas (CTAS), PepsiCo (PEP) |
| Above $200 | JPMorgan, Chubb, Linde (industrial gases), MSCI, Visa, Waste Management |

McDonald's is flagged as a boundary case that drifts between the middle and top brackets depending on where it is trading; at the time of recording it sat above $200. These lists are illustrative rather than exhaustive — the point is to demonstrate that quality exists at every price point, and that the search should be conducted within your bracket rather than by abandoning your standards.

To operate comfortably in the above-$200 bracket, at least $20,000 in the account is stated as the requirement. More generally, the strategy's account-size guidance is a $10,000 minimum, with $50,000 to $100,000 described as the level at which the strategy becomes genuinely comfortable to run.

#### The Holding-Power Requirement

The final selection criterion is not about the stock at all — it is about you. You must have the holding power to keep 100 shares for an extended period. The reason is that a bear market or a large correction can drive the share price down a long way, and the Wheel's answer to that is to wait. If you do not have the temperament or the financial capacity to sit on a losing stock position for a year or more, the instruction is unambiguous: "do not use this strategy, use other option strategies that we teach where you can cut loss a lot earlier."

### Chapter Section 3: Timing the Entry — The Wave and the Support Level

Having established *what* to trade, the next question is *when*. The Wheel's timing rule rests on an observation about how good stocks actually move.

Share prices of good companies always go up, but they do not go up in a straight line. They move in wave patterns — wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down. Adam's metaphor is respiratory: "breathe out, breathe in." The stock exhales upward and inhales downward, and the inhalation is your opportunity.

So the entry condition is: wait for the price to wave down to a support level.

Two quantitative markers are given for what constitutes an adequate wave down. The first is a percentage: ideally the price should have dropped by at least 10% to 15% from the recent high. The second is technical: ideally the price should be at a strong support level such as the 50-period moving average. The formal statement of the rule is that the price "should wave down to at least the 50 moving average on daily candles or lower."

There is a practical note about chart timeframes that is worth preserving because it addresses a real difficulty. Daily candles on many stocks look choppy, and choppiness makes the wave structure hard to read. In those instances you can switch to weekly candles, which smooth the trend and make the alternation of wave up and wave down legible. The ICE demonstration does exactly this — the daily chart is described as "a bit choppy," and the weekly chart is used instead to identify the sequence of waves.

There is also an important concession about how strictly to apply the support rule, and it is one that separates the demonstration from actual practice. When walking through ICE, Adam points out a deeper, stronger support level further down the chart and volunteers that in reality he would probably wait for the price to fall all the way there before executing. He is only entering at the shallower level because he has to record the video. The student is explicitly told they may hold out for the stronger support: "Of course you can. Of course you can." The lesson embedded here is that support levels come in grades, and waiting for a better one is always permitted.

To illustrate with the abstract McDonald's example used at the start: imagine a stock you are 100% confident in. It has run up, and now it falls. It drops roughly 10%, down to about $90, and arrives at a strong support level such as the 50-period moving average. At that point you would reasonably expect a bounce. That is the moment to sell a cash secured put.

### Chapter Section 4: Step One — Selling the Cash Secured Put

#### Choosing the Strike by Delta

The put is sold below the current price — in the abstract example, by something like 5% to 10%. But the percentage is not the governing rule. The governing rule is delta.

The instruction is to sell the cash secured put at a delta of between 20 and 30. In the McDonald's illustration, a 30-delta put happens to carry an $80 strike price.

Understanding *why* delta is used requires understanding what delta approximates in this context. A 30-delta put means there is roughly a 30% chance that the price will stay below the strike price at expiration. That is the probability of assignment. Adam frames it as a frequency: "out of 100 times I do this, 70 out of 100 times, the stock price would not stay below the $80 strike price." Seventy percent of the time the put expires worthless and you simply keep the premium. Thirty percent of the time you are assigned.

Selecting a 20-delta put instead of a 30-delta put is described as "a lot more conservative," because a 20-delta strike sits further below the market and is therefore harder to breach. The trade-off is premium: the further out of the money you go, the less you collect, and at some point the premium becomes too small to be worth the capital commitment. This is why the range has both a floor and a ceiling. You want the strike as low as possible — "so it's harder for the stock price to drop below that strike price" — subject to still receiving an adequate premium.

#### The Premium Floor: 2% of the Strike Price

The premium adequacy test is quantitative. Before selling the put, check that you are receiving at least 2% of the strike price in premium.

The worked example uses Intel. If the strike price is $61.50, then 2% of $61.50 is $1.23, so you should receive at least $1.23 in premium. The timeframe qualifier matters: that 2% is stated as the target "ideally within 30 days," and if you are selling 45 days out you should expect somewhat more than 2%.

#### Expiry Selection

Days to expiration for the cash secured put leg is 30 to 45 days.

#### The ICE Illustration of Strike Selection

The Intercontinental Exchange example demonstrates the strike-selection process end to end and shows the 2% rule actually rejecting a candidate.

ICE is introduced as an S&P 500 company that owns the New York Stock Exchange along with other exchanges — a very profitable business. Run through Stock Oracle, it scores medium on predictability, high on profitability, medium on growth, wide on economic moat, and high on financial strength. The intrinsic value is $165 against a current share price of $154, so the stock is undervalued. The quality and valuation gates are passed.

The chart, read on weekly candles, shows the price has waved down to a support level. The gates are now all open.

Turning to the option chain, the two candidate expiries are 18 June and 26 June. Either is acceptable, with the note that the longer expiry collects "more juicy premium." The demonstration proceeds with the 41-day expiry.

Two strikes fall in the 20-to-30 delta band: the $145 strike and the $150 strike. Working from the preference for the lowest viable strike, the $145 is tested first. It pays $1.90 in premium. Dividing $1.90 by the $145 strike gives approximately 1.3%. That fails the 2% test, and Adam's reaction is immediate: "not attractive."

The $150 strike pays $3.12. Dividing $3.12 by $150 gives 2.08%, which clears the bar. The trade is therefore the $150 strike put, sold for $3.12, with 41 days to expiration.

The return-on-capital framing is stated explicitly: $3.12 divided by $150 is about 2% return for 41 days.

The platform's own probability figure is then read off: there is about a 34% chance the price will drop from $154 and stay below $150 through expiration, which means a 66% chance the put expires worthless. Note that this is consistent with the 20-to-30 delta guidance — the delta and the probability of finishing in the money are approximately the same number.

Finally, the strike is drawn onto the chart in red so the trade can be visualised. The mental model for the next 41 days is then laid out: the share price may bounce up, go sideways, go down, or even dip below $150 temporarily — none of that matters. What matters is only where it sits at expiration. If it is at or above $150 at expiration, the put expires worthless. If it is below $150 at expiration, the put is exercised and 100 shares are assigned. And whichever of those happens, the $3.12 premium was credited on day one and is kept.

#### Buying Power and the Margin Account

There is an operational recommendation attached to selling cash secured puts that materially affects how much capital the strategy ties up. The suggestion is to hold a margin account with your broker, because a margin account causes the broker to reserve much less buying power against a short put position than the full notional obligation.

The typical reservation is approximately 20% to 30% of the stock value. The Intel worked example makes this concrete. Selling one put contract at the $61.50 strike creates an obligation to buy $6,150 worth of shares, since one contract covers 100 shares. Taking the upper end of the range, 30% of $6,150 is $1,845. So if you hold $10,000 cash in the account, $1,845 is blocked when you open that put rather than the entire $6,150.

This is a convenience, not a licence to over-leverage, and the caveat is delivered immediately. Buying power reserved against the position can *increase*. If the stock price continues falling towards the strike price, the reservation can climb from 20–30% to 40% or even 50%. This is precisely why the underlying requirement never changes: you must still have enough buying power ready to actually buy the shares. The margin account reduces the reservation; it does not reduce the obligation.

### Chapter Section 5: The Two Outcomes of the Put, and Step 2A

Forty-one days later, exactly two things can have happened.

#### Outcome One: The Put Expires Worthless

If at expiration the stock is at or above the $150 strike, the put expires worthless. You are no longer obligated to buy the stock, and — importantly — you do not have to buy the put back to close it. It simply evaporates. You keep the full premium, which at $3.12 per share across 100 shares is $312 of realised profit on the option. You received no stock, so there is no profit or loss on the stock side.

The response to this outcome is Step 2A: repeat Step One. Wait for the stock price to wave down again to a support level and sell another cash secured put. You continue doing this — selling puts, collecting premium, selling puts again — for as long as the stock remains undervalued.

The exit condition on that loop is valuation. If the price has risen enough that the stock is now overvalued, you stop. You either wait for it to become undervalued once more, or you go and find a different great company that is undervalued and sitting near support.

#### Outcome Two: Assignment

If instead ICE drops from $154 to, say, $148 and stays there through expiration, the put is in the money at expiration. It is exercised — either by the put buyer or automatically by the exchange — and you are assigned 100 shares.

Your option P&L is unchanged: still $312, because the premium was collected up front and is unaffected by assignment. But now you also own 100 shares of stock. You bought them at the strike price of $150 — that is your cost basis, and it is the number that will govern everything that follows. With the stock trading at $148, you are sitting on an unrealised loss of $2 per share, or $200 across the position.

Adam's response to that $200 unrealised loss is the psychological centrepiece of the entire strategy: "Am I worried about this $200 unrealized loss? No, I'm not." The justification chains back to stock selection. This is a high-quality company. It is a company he does not mind owning. He knows the share price will go up over time even if it drops in the short term. Therefore he will not sell the stock at a loss; he will hold it until it becomes profitable. "So to me this unrealized loss is irrelevant."

That sentence only survives contact with reality if the stock-selection work was done properly. This is the single point at which the Wheel's front-end discipline is cashed in.

Assignment sends you to Step 2B.

### Chapter Section 6: Step 2B — Transitioning to the Covered Call

You now own 100 shares and you still want monthly cash flow. So you immediately sell a covered call against those shares.

#### The Cost-Basis Rule for Strike Selection

The strike-selection rule for the covered call leg is the most important single rule in the Wheel, and it is different in kind from the delta-based rule used for the put. The strike you choose must be at or above the purchase cost of your 100 shares.

The logic is arithmetic rather than probabilistic. You were assigned the shares at $150. If you sell a call at $150 and the shares are called away, you sell them at $150 and your P&L on the stock is exactly zero. If you sold a call at a strike below $150 and it were exercised, you would be forced to sell your shares below your cost and lock in a real, realised loss on the stock — which would defeat the entire premise of the strategy. So the rule: "if my shares get taken away, I don't lose money on the shares."

In the ICE example the covered call is therefore sold at the $150 strike, matching the assignment price exactly.

#### Expiry and Premium Requirements for the Call

Days to expiration is again 30 to 45 days, mirroring the put leg. The ICE demonstration uses another 41 days for symmetry.

The premium adequacy test for the call is stated as at least 1% to 2% of the strike price, with higher being better. Note that this floor is lower than the 2% required on the put. The reason is structural: the covered call strike is pinned to your cost basis, so you have no freedom to move it to chase premium the way you can with a put.

#### The ICE Covered Call Walkthrough

With ICE at $148 and 100 shares held at a $150 cost basis, a covered call is sold at the $150 strike, 41 days out. The premium is estimated at $3.00 per share, and Adam is careful to flag this as an estimate — "it's impossible to know exactly how much, but we just use an estimate." That $3.00 becomes $300 of premium for the contract.

Forty-one days later, two outcomes again.

**If ICE rebounds above $150 and stays above $150 at expiration**, the covered call is exercised and the 100 shares are called away at $150. You bought at $150 and sold at $150, so your stock P&L is zero — exactly as designed. You keep the $300 call premium. Added to the $312 from the original put, total option premium collected across the cycle is $612.

**If ICE instead falls further, to $147**, it is below the $150 covered call strike, so the call expires worthless. You keep the $300 premium regardless, bringing the running total to $612. But you still hold the shares, and at $147 against a $150 cost basis you now carry a $300 unrealised loss. Again, that unrealised loss is treated as irrelevant, because you will not sell at a loss and you expect eventual recovery. In the meantime, you are collecting cash flow from the options.

This second outcome sends you to Step 3A.

### Chapter Section 7: Step 3A — Re-selling the Call, and the Diminishing-Premium Problem

If the call expires worthless, you repeat Step 2B: sell another covered call. And you keep repeating it until the share price finally exceeds the strike and your shares are called away.

The ICE walkthrough continues to show what this looks like in practice, and in doing so it surfaces the strategy's central mechanical friction.

With ICE now at $147, another covered call is sold — again at the $150 strike, because $150 remains the cost basis and that rule does not move. Again 41 days to expiration. But the premium is now lower. When the call was sold with the stock at $148, the $150 strike collected $3.00. With the stock at $147, that same $150 strike is further out of the money, so it collects less. The illustrative figure used is $2.50, with the acknowledgement that it could be even less — "could be even $2, for example, you know? We never know."

This is the fundamental problem the Wheel faces when a stock keeps falling. Your call strike is frozen at your cost basis. The stock is moving away from that strike. Every step down widens the gap, reduces the delta of the call you must sell, and shrinks the premium you can collect.

Continuing the example: if ICE now rebounds above $150 by expiration, the call is exercised, the 100 shares are called away at $150, and you break even on the stock. Total option profit is now $312 plus $300 plus $250, which is $862 collected across three option sales.

The full ICE cycle, laid out as a table:

| Stage | Trade | Stock price context | Premium per share | Premium for contract | Running option P&L | Stock position |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sell $150 put, 41 DTE | ICE at $154.36 | $3.12 | $312 | $312 | none |
| 2 | Assigned at $150 | ICE at $148 | — | — | $312 | 100 shares, cost $150, unrealised −$200 |
| 3 | Sell $150 covered call, 41 DTE | ICE at $148 | ~$3.00 (est.) | $300 | $612 | 100 shares held |
| 4 | Call expires worthless | ICE at $147 | — | — | $612 | 100 shares, unrealised −$300 |
| 5 | Sell $150 covered call again, 41 DTE | ICE at $147 | ~$2.50 (est.) | $250 | $862 | 100 shares held |
| 6 | Called away at $150 | ICE rebounds above $150 | — | — | $862 | flat, zero stock P&L |

#### The Income Expectation

The ICE cycle is then converted into a return figure, and this is the number that defines what the Wheel is actually worth.

Total option profit across the cycle is $862. The capital deployed was the 100 shares purchased at $150, which is $15,000. So the return on investment is $862 divided by $15,000, which is approximately 8% over four months. Annualising by multiplying by three gives roughly a 17% annualised return, which Adam characterises as "not too bad."

Elsewhere, when listing the advantages of the strategy, he states that "getting 24% annualised return a year is very, very possible." The two figures are not in conflict — the 17% comes from one specific illustrated cycle that included a drawdown and two rounds of call-writing at diminishing premium, while the 24% represents what the strategy can produce when conditions are more favourable. Both numbers should be understood as premium-driven; neither includes any contribution from stock appreciation, because by construction there is none.

#### The Trap: When the Stock Falls Too Far

Now the risk that the ICE example only gestures at is confronted head-on, and it is the risk that determines whether a student should run this strategy at all.

The problem is what happens when the share price has fallen so far below your cost basis that the call you are obligated to sell at that cost basis no longer generates a worthwhile premium.

The Intel example makes the mechanics visible. You were assigned Intel at a $61.50 strike, so $61.50 is your cost basis and your call strike. Intel falls to $59. At $59, selling a $61.50 call still yields a reasonably decent premium of about 2% — the machine still works. But suppose Intel keeps falling, to $55. Now your $61.50 call is very far above the current price, and the delta on that strike may be less than 20. The premium available from selling it becomes very small, and "it may not be worth selling the call at all."

The rule for this situation is explicit and it is a rule of inaction: **if the stock price has fallen too low and a decent premium — meaning at least 1% to 2% of the strike price — cannot be received from the covered call, then do not sell the covered call.** Wait. Wait for the stock price to rise and recover high enough that selling the call at your cost-basis strike once again produces at least 1% to 2%. In the Intel case, that would mean waiting for the price to rebound to around $58 or $59 before writing again.

The consequence of that rule is the Wheel's trap. During the entire waiting period you are holding 100 shares at an unrealised loss and generating no cash flow whatsoever. The income machine is switched off precisely when you would most like it running. As stated: "you're stuck with holding the 100 shares until it recovers and you can't get any cash flow in the time being because it's dropped too much. So there is a risk that you have to be willing to accept. It can happen."

The duration of that trap is quantified. In a sustained bear market, you may have to wait up to one to two years for the stock price to recover. Such bear markets do not happen often — the estimate given is once every five, six, or seven years — but they will happen. And the conclusion drawn is a gating condition on the whole strategy: "If you're not prepared to hold 100 shares of the stock for at least a year or so, you should not be using the wheel strategy."

### Chapter Section 8: Step 3B — Closing the Loop

The other branch of Step 3 is the happy one. The stock rebounds, the covered call is exercised, the 100 shares are sold at the strike price, and you are left holding no shares.

At that point you return to the top of the Wheel: sell another cash secured put, provided all the entry criteria are met again. Those criteria are unchanged and must be freshly verified. Is the stock still undervalued? Has it waved down to a support level? If the stock has now risen too much and become overvalued, you wait for it to become undervalued again, or you look for a different undervalued stock on which to sell the next cash secured put.

That completes the cycle. The Wheel, stated as a sequence:

1. Sell a cash secured put on a great, undervalued company that has waved down to support, at 20 to 30 delta, 30 to 45 days to expiration, for a premium of at least 2% of the strike price, with the cash ready to buy 100 shares.
2. If the put expires worthless, keep the premium and repeat step one, provided the stock is still undervalued.
3. If the put is assigned, take delivery of 100 shares at the strike price and note that strike as your cost basis.
4. Sell a covered call against those shares at a strike at or above your cost basis, 30 to 45 days to expiration, for a premium of at least 1% to 2% of the strike price.
5. If the call expires worthless, keep the premium and repeat step four — unless the stock has fallen so far that no adequate premium is available, in which case wait for a rebound before writing again.
6. If the call is exercised, deliver the 100 shares at your cost basis, book zero P&L on the stock, and return to step one.

### Chapter Section 9: The Risks of the Wheel

Three distinct risks are identified, and they are worth separating carefully because they have different causes and different remedies.

**The first risk is that the stock price drops too far below the purchase cost.** This is the trap described above. After assignment at $61.50, the share price falls all the way to $55, $54, $51. The covered call at your cost basis no longer yields meaningful premium, so you cannot write it. You are stuck holding 100 shares with no cash flow until the price recovers enough to resume writing. In a sustained bear market that wait can extend to one or two years. The remedy is holding power — capital and temperament sufficient to sit through it.

**The second risk is choosing a stock that is severely overvalued.** The example used is Tesla, described at the time as trading around $700 against an estimated intrinsic value of around $200. The danger with a stock trading far above intrinsic value is that when the bubble bursts, the price can drop 30%, 40%, or 50% — "and it may never come back. Or it may take a long time to come back." This is why knowing the intrinsic value before selling the cash secured put is not optional. The Wheel's tolerance for drawdown assumes a floor set by fundamental value; if the price was never anchored to fundamental value in the first place, there is no floor.

**The third risk is choosing a fundamentally weak company.** If the business cannot withstand recessions or shocks — the examples given are the airlines and hotels during the pandemic, both of which "got killed" — the stock may never recover. And if it never recovers, you may eventually be forced to sell the shares for a significant loss, which is the one thing the entire strategy is constructed to avoid. This loops back to the opening insistence: "the most important thing in this strategy is stock selection, is to pick a very fundamentally good company."

### Chapter Section 10: Pros, Cons, and the Apparent Contradiction

#### The Advantages

The headline advantage, stated as a personal opinion rather than a guarantee, is that if you choose the right stocks — fundamentally strong, undervalued — there is almost no chance of losing money. The reasoning is that the share price will eventually come back, so any unrealised loss on the stock will eventually be recovered, and in the meantime you are generating cash flow by selling options. A 24% annualised return is described as very possible.

#### The Disadvantages

**It requires a sizable account.** A $10,000 minimum is stated, with $50,000 to $100,000 described as the comfortable operating range.

**You should not expect to make any money from owning the shares.** This is stated as something the student must accept up front rather than discover later. You do not participate in the upside potential of the stock, because your gains on the stock will always be capped by the covered call you sold. The illustration is stark: you sold a covered call on Intel at the $61.50 strike when Intel was at $59, and then Intel jumps to $100. Because you sold a call at $61.50, the most you can get on the stock is break-even. "You cannot be upset if the stock goes to $100 and you say, I've got to make all that money, but I'm not making all that because I sold my shares at 61.50. You have to accept that for the wheel strategy."

**You must be prepared to hold the 100 shares for one to two years if a sustained bear market arrives.** "That will happen one day. I don't know when, but it will happen."

#### Resolving the Contradiction

The section closes by answering a question that alert students inevitably raise, and the answer clarifies the Wheel's place in a portfolio better than any other passage.

Adam has taught elsewhere that he only sells covered calls on shares he owns when those shares are way overvalued, when he is very profitable on them, and when the price is way overextended — selling the call then to harvest a large profit. That appears to contradict the Wheel, which sells covered calls at break-even.

The resolution is that the two behaviours belong to two different parts of the portfolio, serving different objectives. In his investment portfolio, he buys shares because he wants to make money *from the shares*. Since that is the objective, he will not cap that upside with a covered call unless the price is very high, the stock is way overvalued, and the call sale locks in a huge profit.

The Wheel is not that. The Wheel is performed on stocks he does not intend to make money from as stocks. The only intent is to generate cash flow by trading options on them. "So in other words, in my portfolio, this particular strategy doesn't really fit into my investment... this strategy fits into a part of my portfolio that's purely for trading."

That distinction is worth internalising. The Wheel is a trading operation that happens to use stock as collateral. It is not an investment in the stock. Judging it by the standard of an investment — asking whether you captured the stock's appreciation — is a category error, and one that will make a perfectly successful Wheel feel like a failure.

---

## PART TWO — THE BULL CALL SPREAD

### Chapter Section 11: The Position, Leg by Leg

A bull call spread is a two-legged position with one purpose: to express a bullish view on a stock more efficiently than simply buying a call.

The construction is as follows. You buy a call option at one strike price, and you simultaneously sell a call option at a higher strike price. Both legs must share the same expiry date. Because the call you buy is nearer the money than the call you sell, the call you buy costs more than the call you sell brings in, so the net effect is that money leaves your account. This is why the bull call spread is also called a **debit spread**.

The first worked construction uses Citigroup. Citigroup is trading around $63, and you believe the price is going to rise.

The long leg is placed near the current market price — at the money or slightly in the money. Here, that is the $62.50 strike call, which costs $2.41 per share. That is a debit; money goes out.

The short leg is placed at where you think the price will reach within the period of the trade. If your view is that Citigroup will reach around $67 or $68, you sell a call at a strike near that target — here, the $67.50 strike, which brings in $0.53 per share. That is a credit; money comes in.

The netting is the whole point. You pay $2.41 and collect $0.53, so your net debit is $1.88 per share. Multiplied by the 100 shares in a contract: you pay $241 for the long call, you receive $53 for the short call, and your net cash outlay is $188 for one contract.

The rights and obligations stack up cleanly. Buying the $62.50 call gives you the right to buy 100 shares at $62.50. Selling the $67.50 call obligates you to sell 100 shares at $67.50. You buy at $62.50 and sell at $67.50, and you make the difference.

An important reassurance is attached here for students who have just been told never to sell a naked call. In a bull call spread you are not selling the call naked. You hold the long call, which gives you the right to acquire the shares you would need to deliver if your short call is assigned. The long call covers the short call. "This is what we call a hedge trade. You're not selling the call naked in case some of you are wondering."

### Chapter Section 12: Why Not Just Buy a Call?

The bull call spread only makes sense against the alternative it replaces, so the case is built by first enumerating what is wrong with simply buying a call.

**Buying a call is expensive.** You pay a high premium, and — crucially — the stock price must move above the strike price by the amount of the premium for you to break even at expiration. If the stock rises but not enough to cover the premium, you lose money on the trade even though your directional view was correct. This is the most common way a novice loses on a long call: being right and still losing.

**Time decay works against you.** A long call has negative theta. Every day it loses time value, and the closer it gets to expiration the faster it loses value, until eventually no extrinsic value remains at all.

**A fall in implied volatility works against you.** If implied volatility drops after you buy the call, the value of the call falls. This produces one of the most confusing outcomes for new traders: the stock price goes up and the call option goes *down*. The stock rose, but the collapse in implied volatility hit the extrinsic value harder than the price move helped it.

The bull call spread reduces or eliminates all three problems.

**On cost:** the credit from the short call finances part of the long call. In the Citigroup example you pay $188 rather than $241 — a lower outlay and therefore a lower maximum risk. This in turn lowers the break-even price, so the stock has to move less for the trade to work at expiration.

**On theta:** selling the call reverses the sign of your time decay exposure on that leg. "Now theta works in your favour because every day that passes, the call you sold is making you more money." The result is the defining behavioural property of a bull call spread — as long as the share price has gone above your break-even price, the more time passes, the more profitable the trade becomes.

**On implied volatility:** a decline in implied volatility makes your short call more valuable to you, offsetting the damage the same decline does to your long call. Holding both a long call and a short call means the volatility effects "kind of like even off," so you are not negatively affected by a volatility crush the way an outright call buyer is.

**On probability:** the combined effect of the lower cost and lower break-even is a higher probability of a profitable trade than a straight long call on the same stock.

#### The Cost of These Benefits

There is no free lunch here, and the trade-off is stated plainly twice.

The first disadvantage is that your maximum profit is limited to the strike of your short call. If the share price goes way above that strike, you make nothing more. The defence offered is empirical rather than theoretical: "most of the time when you buy a stock or you buy a call the price doesn't go to infinity. The price has to go up a certain amount and then come down again. So most of the time it is worth it to buy a bull call spread at a lower cost than just buying a call option that is a lot more expensive."

The second disadvantage is subtler and catches many traders by surprise: you only get the maximum profit at expiration. If the share price shoots up very quickly right after you enter, you will not immediately have the maximum profit. You have to wait for time to pass — for the "purple line" of current P&L to rise up to the "green line" of expiration P&L — before that profit is fully realised.

### Chapter Section 13: When to Enter — The Chart Setups

The bull call spread is deployed when you are bullish. Three specific chart configurations justify that stance.

**The first is a retracement to support within an established uptrend.** An uptrend is identified by the price making higher highs and higher lows, and by moving averages sloping upward. Within such a trend, the best time to buy a bull call spread is after the price has retraced to a support level and is bouncing back up. The pattern repeats: it waves up, drops to support, bounces — you enter to catch the upside. It waves up, drops to support again, bounces — you enter again.

**The second is a bounce off the bottom of a consolidation range.** If the price is moving sideways in a range, and there is a strong support level at the bottom of that range, you can enter a bull call spread at that lower boundary in order to capture the move back up through the range.

**The third is a breakout from consolidation.** If the price has been consolidating beneath a resistance level and then breaks out above that resistance, there is usually substantial upward momentum, and a bull call spread can be entered at that point.

The generalisation is simple: any time you think the stock price is going to go up, you can enter a bull call spread.

The counter-cases are stated with equal clarity in the ANET lesson, and they are worth committing to memory because they define when *not* to trade this structure. If you are not sure, do not enter the trade. If you think the price will consolidate before it goes higher, do not enter the trade. If you are bearish, definitely do not enter. "Only enter the trade using bull call spread if you are bullish that the stock price will go up very shortly."

That phrase — "very shortly" — is the operative constraint. A bull call spread with 30 days on it is a bet on both direction *and* timing. Being right about direction on a two-month horizon is a losing trade on a one-month structure.

### Chapter Section 14: The Goldman Sachs Construction

The first full worked example uses Goldman Sachs, and it establishes every formula the strategy needs.

Goldman Sachs is on an uptrend. The technical confirmation is layered: the 20 EMA (the red dotted line) is above the 40 EMA, which signals a short-term uptrend, and the 50 moving average is above the 150 moving average, which signals a medium-term uptrend. On an uptrend, the price has a higher probability of moving higher in the short term.

At the point of entry, Goldman Sachs is trading at $384.44. The target price is $405.

**Leg one:** buy the Goldman Sachs $385 call. The $385 strike is chosen because the long call should be placed near the market value — at the money — and with the stock at $384.44, the $385 strike is just at the money. The cost is $8.45 per share.

**Leg two:** sell the Goldman Sachs $405 call, placed at the target price. This brings in a credit of $2.26 per share.

**Net premium:** $8.45 paid minus $2.26 received gives a net debit of $6.19 per share. Multiplied by 100 shares, the total premium paid is $619 for one contract.

From these numbers, every characteristic of the trade follows.

**Maximum risk** is the net premium paid: $619. That is the worst that can happen — even if Goldman Sachs collapses all the way to zero, your loss is capped at $619.

**Break-even at expiration** is the long call strike plus the net premium paid: $385 + $6.19 = $391.19. So Goldman Sachs must rise from $384.44 to $391.19 for the trade to break even at expiration. An important qualification is added: before expiration, the break-even is lower than this, because the trade still contains extrinsic value.

**Maximum profit at expiration** is the strike of the short call minus the strike of the long call, minus the net premium. The strike difference is $405 − $385 = $20. Subtracting the $6.19 premium gives $13.81 per share, which across 100 shares is $1,381.

**Risk-to-reward ratio** is maximum reward divided by maximum risk: $1,381 ÷ $619 = 2.2. You are risking $1 to make $2.20. The verdict: "Is that a good trade? Yes."

Summarised:

| Metric | Formula | Goldman Sachs values |
|---|---|---|
| Net debit | Long call cost − short call credit | $8.45 − $2.26 = $6.19 |
| Max risk | Net debit × 100 | $619 |
| Break-even at expiry | Long strike + net debit | $385 + $6.19 = $391.19 |
| Max profit | (Short strike − long strike − net debit) × 100 | ($405 − $385 − $6.19) × 100 = $1,381 |
| Risk-to-reward | Max profit ÷ max risk | $1,381 ÷ $619 = 2.2 |

#### Executing It on the Platform

The mechanics of entering a two-legged order on thinkorswim are demonstrated. Goldman Sachs is at $384.44. On the Trade tab, the option chain offers expiries at 26 days and 33 days; either is acceptable, and the 26-day expiry — options expiring 15 March — is chosen. The general guidance stated here is that a bull call spread is usually given about 30 days, plus or minus.

Calls appear on the left of the chain with strikes down the centre. The $385 call is bought at $8.45; the $405 call is sold at $2.26.

The click convention matters and is stated explicitly: **when you are buying, you click the ask; when you are selling, you click the bid.** So you click the ask price on the $385 strike to create the buy leg. To add the second leg to the same order rather than starting a new one, you hold down the Control key and click the bid on the $405 strike. The result is a single order buying one contract of the $385 call and selling one contract of the $405 call, with a net debit of $6.19.

Clicking Confirm and Send displays the platform's own calculation of maximum loss ($619) and maximum profit ($1,381), matching the hand calculations. Clicking through to Analyze generates the profit-and-loss graph, on which the green line is P&L at expiration, the current stock price sits at $384.88, the maximum profit of $1,381 is reached above $405, the maximum loss of $619 is the floor if the stock collapses to zero, and the break-even sits at $391.19.

#### Reading the Payoff Diagram

The shape of the payoff diagram is worth dwelling on. A plain long call produces the familiar hockey-stick — the "Nike sign" — with unlimited upside. Adding the short call truncates that upside at the short strike, converting unlimited reward into limited reward. What you get in exchange is limited risk at a *lower* level than the naked long call would have carried, and a lower break-even.

### Chapter Section 15: How Time Works For and Against the Position
