The behaviour of the bull call spread through time is the single most important thing to understand about managing it, and it is best explained through the two lines on the platform's analysis graph. The green line is P&L at expiration. The purple line is P&L right now.

At the moment you enter the trade, the purple line sits at the break-even point relative to your entry. As days pass, the purple line migrates toward the green line. Whether that migration helps or hurts depends entirely on where the share price sits.

**If the share price is above the break-even point**, the green line is above the purple line at that price. As time passes, the purple line rises toward the green line, and the trade becomes more and more profitable. Maximum profit is realised only at expiration. But — and this is the operationally important point — "we don't have to wait for the actual date of expiration to close the trade. We could actually close it earlier and take like 80–90% profit." Once the share price has gone up, time is no longer working against you. Time is working in your favour.

**If the share price does not move up, or moves down**, the relationship inverts. The green line is below the purple line at that price, so as time passes the purple line falls toward the green line. The value of the trade drops, and drops, and drops. If you hold to expiration you lose the maximum amount.

This asymmetry generates the core management principle: when the trade is working, patience is rewarded; when the trade is not working, patience is punished. "If the price doesn't go up, the price stays there or goes down, then you don't want to hang around the trade for too long. You want to get out as early as possible so that you salvage some of the premium that's left in the trade. If you wait to expiration, you get nothing left."

The ANET lesson restates this from the other side: if the price doesn't move at all, time decay hurts the trade, because you paid a debit and that money decays over time. At the current price, if nothing happens, you will end up losing the max loss anyway.

### Chapter Section 16: The Seagate Exercise

A second construction is worked through as a student exercise on Seagate Technology (ticker STX), and it introduces the standard-deviation method for setting the short strike.

Seagate is on an uptrend by the same criteria used for Goldman Sachs: the 20 EMA is above the 40 EMA, the 50 moving average is above the 150 moving average, and the price overall is rising. The price has waved up, waved down, waved up a bit, waved down a bit, and is now sitting at a support level. Current price is $87.52.

**The long call.** The rule is to choose a strike near the current price — in the money or slightly out of the money is fine, as long as it is near the market price. With the stock at $87.52, the closest available strike is $87.50, which is slightly in the money. The long call is the $87.50 strike expiring 15 March, 28 days out. The premium paid is $3.20 per share, or $320 for the contract.

**The short call, and the one-standard-deviation method.** Here a systematic method for setting the target price is introduced. On the thinkorswim platform, the option chain displays a figure on the right — in this case ±$6.68. That is the **one standard deviation move**: over the 28 days to expiration, there is a 68% probability that the price will move up or down by no more than $6.68. This is used as a rough gauge of where the price can realistically travel within the timeframe.

Applying it: target price equals current price plus one standard deviation, so $87.52 + $6.68 = $94.20. The nearest available strike to $94.20 is $95, so the short call is the $95 strike. It brings in a credit of $0.715 per share.

**Working the numbers.** Net debit is −$3.20 + $0.715 = −$2.485, rounded to $2.49. Maximum risk is $2.49 × 100 = $249.

Break-even at expiration is the long strike plus the premium: $87.50 + $2.49 = $89.99.

Maximum profit is the strike difference minus the premium: $95 − $87.50 − $2.49 = $5.01 per share, which is $501 for the contract.

Risk-to-reward is $501 ÷ $249, which is approximately 2. You are risking a maximum $1 to make a maximum $2 — "that's a good trade."

#### The Direct Comparison

The Seagate example is then used to demonstrate the advantages numerically against simply buying the call, and this side-by-side is the clearest statement of the case for the spread:

| | Buy the $87.50 call outright | $87.50 / $95 bull call spread |
|---|---|---|
| Cost / maximum loss | $320 | $249 |
| Break-even at expiration | $90.70 (stated as $90) | $89.99 |
| Upside | Unlimited | Capped at $501 |
| Theta exposure | Negative throughout | Offset by short call |
| Volatility crush exposure | Full | Largely neutralised |

You take less risk on the same stock, and your break-even is lower. The summary of advantages is: lower cost of trade and hence lower risk; a lower break-even price; less affected by time value decay and by volatility crush; and a higher probability of a profitable trade. The summary of disadvantages is: maximum profit is capped at the short call strike, and maximum profit is only obtained at expiration.

### Chapter Section 17: The Complete Entry Rules

The entry procedure is now stated as a formal sequence.

**Step one: identify a bullish stock.** Identify a stock you believe is going to go up. Two practical filters apply: the stock price should be more than $20, and options must be available on it. If there are no options, you cannot do a bull call spread.

**Step two: choose the expiry.** Look at the option chain and choose the date to expiration. Usually about 30 days. It need not be exactly 30 days — it can be more or less. If you believe the share price is going to go up very fast, 15 days is acceptable, and there is nothing wrong with that. If you want more time, 50 days is acceptable too. But there is a specific reason 30 days is described as optimal: because maximum profit only arrives at expiration, giving yourself too much time means that even if the share price does go up, you must wait a long time to collect the maximum profit. Longer expiry buys you room to be right, at the cost of slowing down how fast being right pays.

**Step three: choose the long call strike.** Choose a strike at the money or one strike in the money. In delta terms, this is usually roughly 0.5 to 0.6 delta.

**Step four: choose the short call strike.** The simplest method is to place the short call at one standard deviation above the current price, read off the platform. Alternatively, you can place the target at a very strong level of resistance if you believe such a level exists at a particular point. Either is acceptable. But there is a hard minimum on the width: "generally, we want to sell the call at a strike at least $5 above the call that you're buying — at least a $5 difference in the strike price." A spread narrower than $5 does not leave enough room between the strikes for the position to be worth the transaction.

**Step five: choose the number of contracts, using the 2% position-sizing rule.** The total premium you are risking should be less than 2% of the net liquidation value of your account. The arithmetic is demonstrated: if your account is worth $10,000, 2% of that is $200, so the total premium on any one bull call spread must not exceed $200. If it exceeds $200, skip the trade. If you find a spread whose total premium is $100, you can enter two contracts, because two contracts at $100 risks exactly $200, which is exactly 2%.

The rationale is survival: "the whole idea about trading is to always keep your risk small. So even if you have a losing trade, even if you've got a few losing trades, you won't damage your capital that much, and you stay in the game so that when the winning trades come, they will more than offset your losing trades. It's all about risk management."

**Step six: analyse the risk-to-reward profile.** Plot the profit and loss on your platform, identify the maximum loss, the maximum profit, and the break-even point, and confirm the ratio. The requirement is that you are risking a maximum $1 to make a maximum profit of at least $2.

The justification for that 1:2 requirement is a statement about realistic expectations that deserves emphasis. "Realistically, when you are betting on the stock going up or going down, in the long run, you will only be right half the time. You will only be right 50% of the time. And that's fine. You can make a lot of money even if you are right 50% of the time." The reason is the asymmetry: when you are wrong you lose $1, because that is your capped maximum loss, and when you are right you make close to $2. Across many trades, the winners more than make up for the losers.

**Step seven: enter using a limit order.** Once you are happy with the trade, place a limit order on the bull call spread.

### Chapter Section 18: The Complete Exit Rules

Three exit rules govern the position, and each has a specific numeric threshold.

#### Profit-Taking: 80% of Maximum Profit

The general rule is to close the bull call spread to take profit once **80% of the maximum profit has been reached**.

Applied to the Goldman Sachs trade, where maximum profit is $1,381, 80% of that is approximately $1,104. Once the position shows about $1,104 of profit, you close it and move to the next trade.

The reasoning behind not holding for the last 20% is straightforward risk management: "sometimes the risk is that if you wait too long, the share price may drop back down and then you lose everything. So because of that, we're saying you get 80%, take and run. Okay, that's a pretty good return already."

There is an important calibration for newer traders offered in the GOOGL case study. For those new to bull call spreads, targeting about 70% of max profit is suggested instead, on the basis that 70% or 80% is "a nice number you should aim for" while you build confidence, and that reaching for 90% exposes you to losing all your profit if the stock drops. The ANET presenter offers a third, more aggressive variant of the same principle from personal preference: if he can capture more than 50% of the max profit in less than half the elapsed time — say $280 or more of profit within a week on a 30-day trade — he will close and recycle the capital, on the reasoning that staying in the trade longer to squeeze out more profit always carries the risk of the price reversing.

The common thread across all three variants is that they are all early exits, and they are all motivated by the same thing: unrealised profit in a directional debit spread is fragile.

#### Cutting Losses: 50% of Maximum Loss

Not all trades will be winners. Some trades you enter and the share price simply does not go up — it sits there or it drops. Below the break-even point, time is actively working against you, because the purple line falls toward the green line and each passing day costs you money.

So the rule is: once you enter the trade, give it some time to move up. But if it does not move up and you start losing money, close the bull call spread and cut losses **once 50% of the maximum loss has been realised**.

Applied to Goldman Sachs: the maximum loss is $619. You never want to lose $619. Once you are down half of that — around $310 — you cut the loss, close the trade, and look for the next one.

The effect of pairing an 80%-of-max-profit exit with a 50%-of-max-loss exit is a substantial improvement in the realised risk-reward of the strategy over its theoretical risk-reward. "By doing that, we keep our losses small, we keep our profits big, and we will have a very profitable strategy."

#### The Gap-Down Exception: Beyond 80% of Maximum Loss

There is one carefully bounded exception to the cut-loss rule, and it applies to violent adverse moves.

Sometimes the share price drops violently or gaps down on news. If such a move takes you past your 50% stop before you can act, and you find you have suddenly lost more than 80% of your maximum loss, then closing is no longer worthwhile. The reasoning: you have already lost nearly everything, so the remaining downside is small, while the potential upside from a bounce is not.

The condition attached is time. "If you still have time left, you still have two weeks left before it expires, I would just hold on to it because I've really lost 80%. But if there's two weeks left, there could be a chance where for some reason it may bounce back up again."

Restated in its final form: if you have lost 50%, close the trade. If you have lost 80% — almost everything — and you have at least two weeks left, leave it and hope it goes up. If it does not go up, you accept the 100% loss. Such cases exist but are not many. "Most of the time, we want to cut loss at 50% of the max loss."

#### The Rules in Summary

| Rule | Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Stock price minimum | Above $20, options available | Qualifies for the strategy |
| Expiry | ~30 days (15–50 acceptable) | Choose from chain |
| Long call strike | At the money or one strike ITM; ~0.5–0.6 delta | Buy |
| Short call strike | 1 standard deviation above price, or a strong resistance level; minimum $5 above long strike | Sell |
| Position size | Total premium < 2% of account net liquidation value | Sets contract count |
| Risk-to-reward | At least 1:2 | Otherwise skip the trade |
| Profit target | 80% of max profit (70% for beginners) | Close |
| Stop loss | 50% of max loss | Close |
| Gap-down exception | >80% of max loss with ≥2 weeks remaining | Hold and hope |
| Expiration handling | Always close before expiration | Avoid assignment risk |

---

## PART THREE — THE CASE STUDIES

### Chapter Section 19: Case Study One — GOOGL

#### The Chart Read: Four Points of Confluence

The GOOGL trade is presented as a live trade, entered on the 1st of March, and it opens with a demonstration of what a properly qualified entry looks like.

The macro picture: Google was on an uptrend before 2021, came down during COVID, and has since recovered from that downtrend and resumed the uptrend. Technically, there is a diagonal channel sloping upward, and the price has bounced off the lower boundary of that channel several times. Zooming in, the bounces are counted individually — once, twice, a third time, a fourth time — and the current bounce is the fifth. A support level that has held five times is a strong support level.

That is point one. Three more are then accumulated, and the deliberate stacking of independent confirmations is the methodological lesson of this case study.

Point two: Google is oversold on the stochastic oscillator, which is reading below 30.

Point three: Google is bouncing off the 150 moving average, drawn as the green line on the chart. Zooming in on that level, the bounces are counted again — once, twice, almost a third time, and this is the fourth.

Point four: the price is testing the previous swing lows, which are previous horizontal support levels.

So there are four independent reasons to expect a bounce: diagonal channel support, stochastic oversold, the 150 moving average, and horizontal swing-low support.

On top of that confluence sits a timing trigger. Google made a **confirmation candle** the previous day, which establishes a confirmed reversal. The honest caveat is attached immediately: "now whether this reversal is going to continue, we don't know." A confirmed reversal is a valid entry signal, not a guarantee. But by the entry rules, four points of reversal plus a confirmation candle constitute a valid entry.

#### Structuring the Trade

The intended structure is stated before any strikes are chosen: buy at the money, sell at one standard deviation.

There is a useful aside about alternatives to the one-standard-deviation exit. You do not have to go all the way out to one standard deviation. You could exit at the previous swing high at $149, or at $153. "It's up to you where you want to exit." The presenter's own default is one standard deviation, and its distance depends on the days to expiration chosen.

Before choosing strikes, a compact revision of the payoff structure is drawn out by hand, and it consolidates the three formulas:

- **Break-even price** = long call strike + premium paid
- **Max loss** = the premium paid
- **Max profit** = short call strike − long call strike − premium paid

#### Platform Setup on Interactive Brokers

Three practical Interactive Brokers configuration points are covered, and they matter because without them the required strikes and the one-standard-deviation marker are simply invisible.

First, if you do not see all the expiry dates, click on "More" and ensure that **weeklies and quarterlies** are activated. That checkbox must be ticked before weekly and quarterly expirations appear.

Second, the option chain defaults to displaying 8 strikes. Switching that setting from "8 strikes" to "1 SD" reveals the one-standard-deviation range. In the default colour scheme, the chain shows two shades of blue — a darker blue and a lighter blue — and the boundary between them is the one standard deviation level. Hovering the cursor over a strike pops up the standard deviation reading, and the same boundary appears on the downside.

Third, for better legibility, the colour scheme can be changed. Clicking the gear icon at the top of the option chain, going to Settings, and changing the colour scheme to option 4 produces a dark green and brownish green pairing that is easier to differentiate than the two blues.

Fourth, because this is a two-legged order, the **Strategy Builder** must be switched on. Without it you cannot construct a combo order.

#### Strike and Expiry Selection

Google is trading at $137.76 to $137.77.

For the expiry, two candidates are considered: 27 days and 35 days.

**The 27-day candidate.** The long call is placed at the strike closest to the current price. With Google at $137.76, both $137 and $138 are viable, and the closest is $138. The 28 March $138 call costs between $3.65 and $3.75. The one standard deviation level for this expiry is $146, so the short call is the 28 March $146 call, which brings in $0.96 to $1.02. The net premium is $2.58 to $2.79. Checking the Profile tab, the max loss shows as $274 and the risk-reward ratio is **1.91**.

**The 35-day candidate.** With more time, the one standard deviation move is wider, so the short strike moves out to $147. The long call remains $138. The net premium is $2.92 to $3.14, and the risk-reward ratio comes out at **1.85**.

The comparison is the method being taught: "that's how I usually choose, I'll choose between two DTEs at the money and one standard deviation and see which gives me a better risk reward." The 27-day version at 1.91 is better than the 35-day version at 1.85, so the 27-day trade is selected.

#### The Resistance Check

Before committing, one further check is performed, and it is a check many traders omit. Being at one standard deviation does not automatically make a strike a good place to sell. What matters is whether there is resistance *below* your short strike — because price hitting resistance below your short call and turning back down is exactly the failure mode that kills the trade.

So the chart is revisited and a line drawn at $146. The verdict: at $146 there is "probably a small little one, okay, but not a concern." The resistance that would worry him is one that has been tested many times, and the level around $145 has not been tested many times. "All I need is for the stock price to go beyond 146. All right. So it's good to go."

#### Working the Limit Order

The order-entry sequence that follows is a small masterclass in not overpaying, and it is worth reproducing in detail because spread fills are where a good trade quietly becomes a mediocre one.

The order shows a cost between $2.59 and $2.74. Because this is a debit and money is going out, the strategy is to start at the lowest price and negotiate upward: "I will start from the lowest price, okay, at 259. Then I'll bargain my way up."

A note is made about the mid price — even placing at mid does not necessarily get filled, so the mid is not treated as a target.

Two contracts are entered. The Profile tab then shows $548 rather than $518, because the platform estimates using the higher price of $2.74 rather than the $2.59 being offered. The risk-reward remains 1.91.

The order is placed as a day order, with the plan that if it does not fill, it will be re-entered tomorrow. It is submitted and appears as a working order — and to monitor it, a separate window is opened via Order Management, under Orders, showing live orders. The trade shows at $2.59, two contracts, zero out of two filled.

Then the negotiation:

| Limit price offered | Result |
|---|---|
| $2.59 | No fill |
| $2.60 | No fill |
| $2.66 | No fill — still far from the last price |
| $2.68 | No fill |
| $2.70 | **Filled** |

The reasoning at each step is instructive. At $2.60 there is no fill and the price is "still very far." Since the ask is at $2.82 and the bid is at $2.71, and Google is relatively liquid, going closer to $2.71 is acceptable — so $2.66. Still nothing, and the observation is that $2.66 is "not even close to the last price." Then $2.68, with the note that offering higher is optional: "If you do not want to offer high, you can just leave it alone and see if it gets filled overnight." Finally $2.70 fills.

The post-mortem is honest and useful: the average price shows $2.707 and the last price shows $2.69. "So if just now I didn't go a bit aggressive, I just go at 269, it could be filled at 269. And I save myself $2." The lesson is that pushing the limit up too quickly costs money, and that in a liquid name a slightly more patient walk-up would have got the same fill for less.

#### The Trade's Numbers

With the fill at $2.69 to $2.70 (Interactive Brokers reports $2.70, likely including commission), the trade metrics for one contract are:

| Metric | Calculation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Long call | 28 March $138 call | — |
| Short call | 28 March $146 call | — |
| Days to expiration | 1 March to 28 March | 27 days |
| Net debit | — | $2.69 per share |
| Max loss | $2.69 × 100 | $269 |
| Max profit | ($146 − $138 − $2.69) × 100 | $531 |
| Break-even | $138 + $2.69 | $140.69 |
| Contracts | — | 2 |

The break-even of $140.69 is drawn onto the chart so the level is visible: above $140.69 at expiration, the trade is profitable.

#### Managing the Trade: The Near-Stop-Out

The first update comes on 20 March, with 8 days to expiration.

The exit target is set explicitly. Maximum profit is $531 per contract across two contracts, so 80% of the total maximum profit is $849.60. "So remember this magic number 849.6 is the point where I will intend to exit."

Then comes the most instructive passage in the entire case study. After entry, the trade went *against* the position. The stop-out level was 50% of maximum loss. And the trade came within a hair of triggering it: "I was lucky enough not to stop out. So my target stop-out level was 50% of my maximum loss. I was lucky. It was like 49% of my maximum loss. So I was lucky. It was around 50% when I was sleeping. But the trade managed to recover."

That is a 49% drawdown against a 50% stop. One more percentage point and the trade — which ultimately captured 98.6% of maximum profit — would have been closed for a loss.

The rule extracted from this is stated cleanly and is worth taking seriously precisely because the outcome was lucky rather than skilful: **"very importantly, if it didn't hit your 50% loss, keep the trade."** The stop is a line, not a zone. You do not exit early because you are uncomfortable, and you do not exit late because you are hopeful. You exit at the line.

After surviving the drawdown, the price hit the support level — the strong horizontal support previously drawn on the chart — and rallied. There was a gap up, attributed to rumours of a partnership between Microsoft and Google, with the explicit caveat that the news is irrelevant to the trading decision: "which we don't really care when we trade — there is just a coincidence that it gapped up." The technical setup produced the entry; the news was noise that happened to break in the right direction.

#### The 80% Decision

On the gap up, the position came very close to the 80% profit target, and then over the following two days the price came back down somewhat. Google is now at $147 — still above the $146 short strike.

Reading the P&L profile: the trade is showing $819 to $821 profit, against a platform-calculated maximum profit of $1,059 for the two contracts (slightly different from the hand-calculated $1,062 because the platform includes commission). The 80% target of $849.60 has not quite been reached.

Three choices are laid out.

**Choice one: take the profit now at roughly 70% and run.**

**Choice two: hold and let theta work.** The purple dotted line is the P&L as of today, and if the price stays where it is, every day collects money. This is the favourable side of the time-decay asymmetry: "when I'm making profit in the bull call spread... however, if you look at the loss side, if I'm making losses or I'm close to making losses, the theta decay works against me and it goes down towards my max loss every single day." The risk of choosing this is explicit: if Google drops over the next few days, the profits evaporate.

**Choice three: close one contract and hold the other.** Since the position is two contracts, half can be closed to bank profit while the other half continues to run. The framing offered: "you get some profit, put it in your pocket, and take the rest of the banker's money to continue trading."

The decision taken is to hold, on the reasoning that the 80% target has not been hit and the price remains well beyond the short call, where the position still earns money. But a condition is attached: "if I do see Google dropping significantly over the next few days, I will immediately close it."

The theta figure is then read off the risk profile: approximately **$15 per day**. With roughly eight days remaining, that is the pace at which the remaining profit will accrue if the price simply stays where it is. "So what I'm hoping now is it stays where it is."

#### The Exit

The next update is dated the 26th of March, with two days to expiration — and this contract is unusual in that it must be closed on the Thursday rather than the Friday, because the Friday is Good Friday. So expiration is effectively tomorrow.

Google has gone well above the $146 short strike. The question raised is whether to close or simply let it expire, since letting it expire in the money on both legs would in theory collect the full spread without paying closing commission.

The answer is a general best-practice rule that applies to every spread, not just this one: **always close your contracts before expiration.** The reason is assignment risk. "There might be cases where the price moves violently in a certain direction that caused your contracts to be assigned accidentally. The price could drop and one leg gets assigned whereas the other leg does not get assigned, and that will be a big headache." A partially assigned spread leaves you with an unhedged stock or option position you never intended — which is precisely the naked exposure the spread structure was designed to prevent.

The spread is closed at **$7.93**.

#### The Full P&L

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Opening premium paid (per share) | $2.70 |
| Closing premium received (per share) | $7.93 |
| Profit per share | $5.23 |
| Profit per contract | $523 |
| Contracts | 2 |
| Total profit per share across both | $10.46 |
| Total profit | $1,046 |

Three separate return calculations are then performed, and the fact that three exist at all is a useful lesson in how ROI can be framed.

**Against the expected cut-loss level (aggressive).** The stop loss is 50% of the $2.70 premium, which is $1.35. So $5.23 divided by $1.35 gives **387.4%**. "So for every $1 I risk, I earn back $3.87." This is the most flattering framing, and it is legitimate only because the 50% stop is genuinely enforced — the actual capital at risk under the rules is $1.35, not $2.70.

**Against the maximum possible loss (conservative).** $5.23 divided by the full $2.70 premium paid gives **193%**. "Not bad. In fact it's very good."

**As a percentage of maximum profit.** Maximum profit is $146 − $138 − $2.70 = $5.30. So $5.23 divided by $5.30 is **98.6% of maximum profit** captured.

That 98.6% is far beyond the 80% rule, and the deviation is explained rather than glossed over: "under normal situation, I would have exited at 80%. It's just that because it's very near the expiration, I decided to wait a bit longer for the theta to work in my favour." The justification is that with expiration imminent and the price well above the short strike, the remaining risk window was short. This is a discretionary override of a standing rule, made under specific conditions, and it is not offered as a general licence.

#### The Lessons Drawn

Three closing lessons are attached to the GOOGL trade, and they are the most important content in the case study.

**Beginners should target 70–80%, not 90%.** "If you consider yourself a new trader in bull call spreads, target maybe about 70% of your max profit... because if you aim for even higher, 90%, remember when the stock price dropped, you could lose all your profit. So for a start, you want to build your confidence. 70%, 80% will be a nice number you should aim for."

**Be patient and only take great trades.** Mediocre trades are defined precisely: a trade that is not at a support level that has been tested multiple times, or a trade that does not give you a good risk-reward, should not be taken.

**Expect a low win rate.** This is the passage that should recalibrate expectations most sharply. "While bull call spread is very profitable when you get winning trades, the winning trades don't come often. In fact, for most traders, winning trades come about 30%. 30% win rate, that's quite normal. If you are really good, you're very patient, you find your trades and you wait for them to really hit the support level, tested many times, maybe you can push it up to 40%, 45%."

And then the arithmetic that makes a 30–45% win rate acceptable: "a 40% to 45% win rate at 2R, at 80% profit, you are going to be very profitable." The strategy does not need to be right often. It needs to be right occasionally while adhering to the 1:2 minimum and the 80% profit-taking rule.

The final instruction follows from all of this: "Be patient, wait for the trades to come to you. If there's no trade that is ideal — because bull call spread needs to be directional — if there's no trade that is ideal, it's okay. Don't take any trade. Go ahead and trade other strategies. Bull call spread strategies need to be very, very strict in order to get winning trades."

### Chapter Section 20: Case Study Two — ANET (Arista Networks)

#### Why This Stock, on This Day

The ANET trade is entered on 12 May 2026, and the entry logic is different in character from the GOOGL trade — less about multiple confluent support levels and more about relative strength against a hostile market.

The trend context is established first: ANET is on an uptrend, with the 200, 150, and 50 moving averages all sloping up.

The recent development is that the share price dropped significantly after earnings, about a week prior. And today it looks like it is stabilising.

Then comes the observation that makes this setup interesting. The whole market is down significantly on this day — the S&P 500 and the NASDAQ are both down by 1% or more. "But this stock is going against the trend of the market. So it looks like there's some momentum going on, and I like that setup. So a stock that is going strongly in a very bad tape in today's market."

Relative strength on a bad day is treated as a real signal. A stock that refuses to fall when everything else is falling is being bought by someone with conviction.

Two further technical confirmations complete the picture. The stock is holding above the 200 moving average, with the caveat that the day has not closed yet but it looks very promising. And the stochastic — the presenter's preferred indicator for gauging oversold and overbought conditions — shows the stock deeply oversold and beginning to reverse back up. "That means there's some momentum coming into the stock in the very near future. And I expect the stock price to go higher from here in a pretty quick manner."

That expectation of speed is what makes the bull call spread the right structure: "the bull call spread is a suitable strategy to use, as long as I think the price will go up very fast in the near future."

#### Constructing the Trade

The analysis is done in thinkorswim and the execution in Interactive Brokers.

**Expiry.** The stated acceptable range is anywhere between 30 days and about 45 days, with 30 days as the ideal. Exactly 30 days is not available, but 31 days is, expiring 12 June. Close enough.

**Long call.** The stock is at close to $139, so the long call is bought near the money at the **$139 strike**.

**Short call via one standard deviation.** ThinkorSwim indicates that the price could move up or down within $17 over the next 31 days. So one standard deviation out of the money is $139 + $17 = $156. The strike $156 does not exist; the neighbouring strikes are $155 and $157.50. The $155 strike is selected as the one-standard-deviation strike.

The order is constructed the same way as before: click the ask on the $139 call to buy, then hold Control and click the bid on the $155 strike to sell. The result is a vertical spread — long the $139 call, short the $155 call — costing **$5.67 per share**, or $567 for one contract.

#### The Trade's Numbers at Entry

| Metric | Calculation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Long call | 12 June $139 call | — |
| Short call | 12 June $155 call | — |
| Days to expiration | — | 31 |
| Net debit (thinkorswim analysis) | — | $5.67 per share, $567 |
| Break-even | $139 + $5.67 | $144.62 (stated variously as $144.62 and $144.67) |
| Max loss | Net debit × 100 | $567 |
| Max gain | ($155 − $139 − $5.67) × 100 | $1,033 |
| Probability of winning at expiration | Platform figure | ~38% |

The break-even is explained again from first principles — the long call strike plus the premium paid — and its implication is stated bluntly: the price definitely needs to go above that level by expiration for the trade to be profitable. There is a nuance worth preserving: if the price rises immediately after entry, the trade shows a profit right away even though it is below the expiration break-even, because extrinsic value remains. But if it does not go higher and simply sits there until expiration, it turns into a loss.

The probability figure is the honest headline of this case study. There is only about a **38% chance of winning at expiration**. This is described, correctly, as a low-probability trade. What redeems it is the risk-reward: risking $567 to make $1,033 is close to a 1:2 ratio, "which is a very favourable risk-reward profile."

And then the structural insight that ties the whole course together: "So it's a typical profile of a bull call spread where you have a lower probability of winning, but better risk-reward ratio. So this is the opposite of the credit spread, like bull put spread or bear call spread." Debit spreads buy a large payoff at low probability; credit spreads sell a small payoff at high probability. Neither is superior — they are opposite ends of the same trade-off, and a complete trader uses both.

#### The Alternative Short Strike

Before executing, an alternative to the one-standard-deviation method is demonstrated, and it echoes the option offered in the entry rules: you may set the short strike at a technical resistance level instead.

Examining the ANET chart, resistance is identified at about $152 — a previous swing high, and also the level from which the price fell after earnings, which makes it a plausible resistance. So the short call could be sold at $152 instead of $155. The nearest available strike is $152.50.

Clicking $152.50 to sell shows the effect: the trade costs less, because a lower short strike brings in more premium. Consequently the max loss is lower. But the risk-reward changes.

The decision is to stay with $155, and the reasoning is about upside room: "maybe I just choose the 155 to give me a little bit better risk reward, just in case the price breaks a little bit above that, then it will not cap the upside so much." A short strike at $152.50 would cap the trade right at the resistance level; a short strike at $155 gives the position room to profit if the price pushes through.

#### Execution and the Fill

Switching to Interactive Brokers, ANET is entered in the option chain, the 31-day expiry (12 June) is selected, and the Strategy Builder is turned on because this is a two-legged trade. Leg one buys the $139 call by clicking the ask; leg two sells the $155 call by clicking the bid.

The mid price on Interactive Brokers is $5.66, very close to the $5.67 seen in thinkorswim.

The negotiation principle is the same as in the GOOGL trade: because this is a debit, start with a lower number and raise from there. The opening offer is **$5.60** for one contract.

The order is transmitted and fills immediately — and at a *better* price than offered: **$5.57**. The reflection is candid: "so maybe I have overpaid a little bit, but that's okay. A few cents here and there. Ideally, you start lower and then raise it gradually until it is filled. But it's okay, it got filled at a better price than what I put here."

An immediate observation about the newly opened position: it shows a small loss. The explanation is important for anyone who has been alarmed by this. It is not time decay and it is not implied volatility — neither has had time to act. It is that the bid-ask spread is wide, and the broker assumes that if you exited right now you would exit at an unfavourable price in order to get filled immediately. "So that's why it shows as a loss, but I'm not concerned because this is a trade for one month."

#### Managing the Trade

The management plan is stated at entry, before anything happens, which is the correct order of operations.

**On cutting losses:** "I will never let my trade lose at the max loss." The fill was $5.57, so the max loss is $557. The stop is half of that: $557 ÷ 2 = approximately $280, or $2.80 per share. "So if my trade loses, let's call it $280, I will cut loss on it."

That stop level is then mapped onto the price chart, which is a valuable exercise because it converts an abstract P&L threshold into a concrete price you can watch. If the price drops significantly tomorrow — to $130, $128 — that is roughly where the $280 stop would be hit. Knowing this in advance produces calm: "So I still have some margin for error until that stop loss point. So right now I'm not worried."

**On the flat scenario:** if the price doesn't move, that also hurts the trade, because time decay works against a debit position. At the current price, held to expiration, the trade loses the max loss.

**On taking profit:** the standard rule is restated — if the trade hits about 80% to 90% of max profit with a week or two still to run, there is no point waiting; take the profit. Adam and YY are noted as preferring 80–90%. The personal preference offered is more aggressive on time: "if I can get more than 50% of the max profit in less than half of the time, I would close the trade and run. So if I get $280 profit or more in, let's say, a week or one-third of the time — why not? So I will close the trade, take the profit, and recycle my capital on other trades."

The condition attached is a sensible piece of judgement: if the price has already shot up to a very high level and there is very little chance of it reversing back below the break-even, you can keep it as long as you want, closer to expiry, to get the most out of it. But if the price has only moved moderately and the trade is already up $280 or $300, closing is preferable, because there is still real risk of the price coming back down.

#### Three Weeks Later

The update comes on 2 June 2026, three weeks after entry.

The chart tells the story. Since entry the price has gone up significantly, and today alone it is up $5. Reviewing the entry: on 12 May the trade was entered as the price was rebounding from a dip in an uptrend, bouncing off the moving averages — a key support level — with the stochastic in the oversold region. The reliability of that indicator is emphasised: "whenever it is deep in the oversold region here, it has a good chance to rebound. And in fact, it did."

But the path was not straight. After entry the price rebounded initially, then retraced and tested the support level again, and only then rebounded strongly. This is worth noting alongside the GOOGL trade: both winners went against the position first. A bull call spread that immediately works is the exception, not the rule.

**At half time — one week before this update, roughly two weeks into a 31-day trade — the position was showing about $500 profit.** Against a max profit of $1,043, that was slightly less than half. Under the stated personal rule (more than 50% of max profit in less than half the time), it did not quite qualify: "I was hesitant to close it because it's not exactly at half of my max profit yet. So I decided to hold."

That decision was rewarded. The price continued to rally, and at the time of this update the position shows **$933 profit** on one contract.

#### The Exit Decision

The arithmetic driving the exit is laid out precisely. Max profit is recomputed from first principles: the short call at $155 minus the long call at $139 gives $16, times 100 shares gives a $1,600 spread, minus the $557 entry debit gives **$1,043** max profit.

Current profit of $932 divided by max profit of $1,043 is approximately **90% of maximum profit**, with 10 days still remaining until the 12 June expiration.

"So it makes sense to close the trade to realise 90% of the max profit in two-thirds of the time. There's no point to wait another one-third of the time to get the remaining 10% of the max profit."

The counter-argument is given fair treatment. Time is currently working in the trade's favour, because the price well exceeds the $155 short strike and sits in the profit zone. Holding for the remaining 10 or 11 days, if the price stays where it is, would collect the remaining ~$100. The pink curve (current P&L) rises toward the blue curve (expiration P&L) as time passes. So it is genuinely acceptable to hold "if you strongly believe that the price would not decline so much and definitely not decline below the $155 short call."

But experience overrules the theoretical case: "there's only 10% profit left. And with 10 days to go, anything can happen. The market can collapse and the trade can turn into a loss as well. Yes, it's safe because it still has a significant margin for error, but you never know. The price can move very fast. It moved fast when it went up. It can move fast when it declines as well."

Two additional benefits of closing are named: you release the capital for other trades, and you eliminate the risk entirely. "Because if you stay in the trade, that means the risk is still there."

It is also worth recording that the stop loss was never tested. "As you can see there, since I entered the trade, the price never declined to that level. So I did not have to cut loss because the price was steady and went up from there."

#### Closing the Position

Two mechanical routes to closing a spread on Interactive Brokers are demonstrated.

The first is through the option chain with Strategy Builder open: click **buy** to close the short call, and click **sell** (on the bid column) to close the long call. So the closing order buys to close the $155 short call and sells to close the $139 long call.

The second is simpler: right-click on the trade in the combo view and choose Close, which takes you to the order entry where the price can be negotiated.

The critical check when closing a debit spread is the direction of cash flow. "The plus or minus sign can be very confusing, but just when you set it out, make sure it is a credit — C, right? In a green box, it needs to be a C credit trade when you close it." At entry you only paid money out; at exit you must receive money back, so the closing order must show as a credit. The higher the credit, the better.

The negotiation runs in the opposite direction from the entry. Because you want to *receive* money, you start high and work down. The credit available is around $14.9, with the mid price showing $14.5. The opening offer is $15, then down through $14.95, then $14.92. Watching the mark price in the position (14.92) guides the descent. The fill comes at **$14.88 credit**.

#### The Full P&L

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry date | 12 May 2026 |
| Exit date | 2 June 2026 |
| Days in trade | 21 |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Entry debit | $5.57 per share = $557 |
| Max risk / capital deployed | $557 |
| Max profit | ($155 − $139) × 100 − $557 = $1,043 |
| Exit credit | $14.88 per share = $1,488 |
| Profit | $1,488 − $557 = $931 |
| Return on investment | $931 ÷ $557 = **167%** |
| Percentage of max profit captured | ~90% |

The summary judgement: "basically, I got almost 90% of the max profit. So if I hold the trade for the next 10 days, there could be a good chance that I get the remaining, let's say, $110. But again, there's no point to wait for another 10 days to get only $100 profit. Just close the trade — the trade already realised a very good return on investment. Closing the trade early means I can release the capital now for other trades."

Note the contrast with GOOGL. The GOOGL trade rode to 98.6% of max profit because expiration was two days away and the risk window was almost closed. The ANET trade closed at 90% with 10 days left because the risk window was still wide open. The percentage of max profit is not the decision variable on its own — it must be weighed against how much time remains for the position to be taken away from you.

### Chapter Section 21: Case Study Three — The Bull Call Spread on the VIX

The final case study is presented as a bonus lesson, and it is qualitatively different from the two that precede it. It is not a directional bet on a company. It is a portfolio hedge.

#### What the VIX Is and Why It Matters

The VIX is the CBOE market volatility index, ticker VIX, and it is also known as the fear index. Its defining property is that it tends to move opposite to the market.

The inverse correlation is demonstrated by overlaying the VIX against SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, over a year of data. When the S&P rises, people feel complacent and confident, and the VIX falls. When the market drops, people are scared, and the VIX rises. The COVID crash provides the extreme illustration: "look at the VIX — wow, the VIX went to the moon."

#### The Hedging Logic

The purpose of buying call spreads on the VIX is stated directly: to hedge the investment portfolio. You buy VIX call spreads when you anticipate the market could be dropping — when you think the market is complacent and due to "breathe in."

The payoff of that hedge is not merely defensive. "When the market drops, our call options on the VIX will make a lot of money, and we can take those profits to buy more of the great shares at a discount." The hedge is a mechanism for converting a market decline into buying power at exactly the moment when buying power is most valuable. This connects the strategy back to the value investing framework that underpins the whole course.

#### Timing the Entry: Two Conditions

Entry requires two things to be true at once — a condition on the S&P and a condition on the VIX itself.

**Condition one: the S&P 500 is overextended.** You start buying calls on the VIX when the market is near the top of a wave up and is stretched far from its moving averages. The rubber-band metaphor is used: "when the price waves up and it gets really far from the moving averages, I think it's overextended, I anticipate it's going to drop soon."

The honesty about precision here is refreshing and should be preserved: "we can't always catch the top, you never know where the top is, but you kind of have a feeling that once it gets a bit far from the moving averages, like a rubber band, it gets really far, it will snap back... You can't always guess the exact snapping back. Sometimes I'm a bit early, sometimes I'm a bit late, so it's not perfect."

Two indicators can sharpen the read: the **Bollinger Bands** and the **full Stochastic**. The signal is when the S&P is outside the upper Bollinger Band *and* the stochastic is above 80. That combination means the market is overbought and due to snap back.

**Condition two: the VIX itself is near support.** For the VIX chart, only horizontal support and resistance levels are drawn — no moving averages, no indicators. At the time of the lesson, the support zone is identified at roughly 20 to 21, extending to 22, and resistance is identified at roughly 29 to 30, with further, higher resistance levels above that.

So the operating range is stated as a rule: **when the VIX is between 20 and 22, it is near support and you start buying calls on the VIX. When it reaches 29 to 30, you start taking profits.**

The upper bound is deliberately conservative. The VIX could always jump to 40, but this is rare — "normally the VIX would only shoot up all the way in 10 years, and I wouldn't bet on it going all the way back up." So the approach is explicitly range-trading: buy at support, sell at resistance, repeat.

At the moment of the lesson, the VIX is at 24, which is "neither here nor there." So the honest answer to whether he would buy right now is no — he would wait for 20 to 22.

#### The Scaling Technique

A refinement is offered for those trading multiple contracts. When the VIX goes to 21 or 22, you might buy a number of contracts — 10 or 20. When it gets halfway to your target, at around 26, you sell half to take profits. The other half you sell when it reaches 29 to 30. "So there are many ways to skin the cat."

#### The VIX Spread's Special Rules

Three rules apply to VIX spreads that differ from the standard bull call spread rules, and each has a specific reason.

**Rule one: at least 60 days to expiration.** Where a standard bull call spread uses about 30 days, VIX spreads are entered with at least 60 days.

**Rule two: exit 30 days before expiration.** This is stated as applying to the VIX specifically. "For the VIX, especially for the VIX only, for the spreads, I like to exit 30 days before expiration."

These two rules are connected, and rule one exists to serve rule two: "So I've got to enter way more than 30 days. So I'm going to go 60 days. Why 60 days? Means that I've got 30 days for the VIX to go up. And if it doesn't go up in 30 days, I get out with 30 days left." The 60-day expiry buys you a 30-day window in which to be right, plus a 30-day cushion of remaining extrinsic value that lets you exit without having suffered full time decay.

The purpose is explicitly loss limitation: "If VIX falls, I want to get out early so that I don't hit the max loss. I get out when there's still above extrinsic value left."

**Rule three: strikes are chosen by delta, not by proximity to price.** This is the most counterintuitive VIX rule and it needs careful explanation.

For the long call, choose a delta of about 50 — "roughly about 50 delta." For the short call, choose a delta of about 35 to 40.

The reason this is unusual becomes clear in the demonstration. With the VIX around 24, the 50-delta call is the **$30 strike** — six points above the index level. A student would reasonably object that "at the money" should mean the strike equals the market price. The answer is that the VIX is a special instrument: "Yes, normally for other stocks, but the VIX is a special animal. Don't ask me why, it's just special. So for the VIX, we look more at the delta. We're going to buy where the delta is close to 50 or slightly more than 50."

(The underlying reason surfaces later in the lesson, in the discussion of VIX futures — see below.)

#### Structuring the Trade

The date is 18 January; the market is closed for a holiday. Expiries are examined, and the closest to 60 days is **57 days**, expiring 17 March.

**Long call.** Looking at the deltas, two candidates present themselves: a 54-delta strike and a 48-delta strike. Either would be acceptable, but the one further in the money is chosen — the **54 delta**, which is the $30 strike. Buying alone would cost $3.70, which is described as expensive: "if you just buy a call alone, it's going to be expensive. So I'm going to sell another call to finance that first call."

**Short call.** The target delta band is 35 to 40. Available candidates include the $40 strike, the $37.50 strike, and the $35 strike — "either one would be fine, and you can experiment with the different strikes to see which one gives you a better risk-to-reward ratio." The choice made is the **42-delta strike**, which is the $35 strike, because 42 is close to 40.

**The order.** Buy the $30 call, sell the $35 call. Cost: **$0.90 per share**, or $90 for one contract.

Clicking Confirm and Send shows a maximum loss of $90 and a maximum profit of **$410**.

But this is where the VIX case study departs decisively from the previous two, and the departure is the most important teaching point in the lesson.

#### Why the Maximum Profit Is Irrelevant

A $90 risk for a $410 maximum profit looks like a spectacular 1:4.5 risk-reward. It is not, and treating it as such would be a serious error.

The reason: maximum profit requires the VIX to reach $35, and "it's going to be really difficult for VIX to jump to $35 unless it's another major crash." The stated profit-taking target is 29 to 30, not 35. "So I'm not even dreaming about that maximum profit."

This is a general principle disguised as a VIX-specific note. **The theoretical maximum profit of a spread is only meaningful if your exit plan actually involves reaching it.** If your plan is to exit at a level below your short strike, then the relevant risk-reward is not max-profit-over-max-loss — it is the P&L at your actual target over the P&L at your actual stop.

#### Simulating the Real Risk-Reward

The method for computing the *real* risk-reward is then demonstrated on the analysis graph, and it is a technique worth learning thoroughly.

Today is 18 January; expiration is 17 March, roughly 60 days away. Since the plan is to exit 30 days before expiration, the P&L must be evaluated as of 30 days from today — 18 February. So the analysis date is set forward to 18 February, and the purple line now shows what the P&L will look like on the day of the planned exit.

Then the price scenarios are set. Current VIX (as shown by the platform) is 23.75. The upside target is 29. The downside scenario is 20, the low end of the support zone. The graph's price range is stretched to span 20 to 29.

Reading the results off the purple line as of 18 February:

| VIX scenario | P&L at 30 days |
|---|---|
| Drops to 20 | −$66 |
| Rises to 29 | +$76 (quoted first as ~$58, then settled at $76) |

So the real trade is risking $66 to make about $76 — roughly 1:1, or 1.15:1.

The transcript wobbles slightly on the upside figure, quoting approximately $58 at first and then settling on $76 when the comparison is drawn. The conclusion, stated repeatedly, is that the ratio is roughly one to one.

#### Why 1:1 Is Acceptable on the VIX

An objection is anticipated and answered directly, and the answer is the core justification for treating the VIX differently from stocks.

"Some of you will be thinking, hey, I'm supposed to risk one to make 1.5. Yeah, under normal assets like stocks. But VIX is different. For VIX, if you can get one-to-one, that's good enough."

The reason is win rate. "Because VIX tends to move up a lot more than it moves down if you buy it at the lows. So your win rate for VIX should be really, really high."

This is a direct application of the trade-off that governs the whole subject. The 1:2 minimum for stock bull call spreads exists because the win rate on stock bull call spreads is only 30–45%. If the win rate is much higher — as it is when you buy VIX calls at a well-defined support level in an instrument that spikes upward far more violently than it drifts downward — then a lower payoff ratio is still highly profitable. Risk-reward and win rate are two sides of one equation, and neither number means anything without the other.

#### Optimising the Short Strike Through Trial and Error

The demonstration then tests whether a different short strike would improve the risk-reward. This is trial and error, done systematically.

| Short strike (long = $30) | Loss if VIX → 20 | Gain if VIX → 29 | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| $35 | −$66 | +$76 | ~1.15 |
| $37.50 | −$89 | +$103 | 103 ÷ 89 ≈ 1.15 |
| $40 | −$108 | +$124 | 124 ÷ 108 ≈ 1.15 |

The conclusion after three tests: "You can see it's all about the same. No difference whichever strike I choose."

And from that, a clean decision rule: "So I might as well choose a strike where I pay the lowest debit, which is 35." Since the risk-reward ratio is invariant across the strike choices, the tiebreaker is cost — pick the cheapest structure, which is the $30/$35 spread. A closing note observes that the debit had moved from $0.90 down to $0.85 as the market shifted, "so it will change along the way as the market moves."

This principle generalises usefully: when several structures give you the same risk-reward, take the one that ties up the least capital.

#### The VIX Futures Explanation

A common student question is then answered, and the answer resolves the earlier "special animal" mystery.

The question: the VIX chart shows the VIX at 24.34, but the analysis window shows 23.90. Why the discrepancy?

The answer: "When you buy options on the VIX, you're not really buying options on the VIX. Nope, you're not. You're buying options on the VIX futures. And the VIX futures could sometimes be a bit different from the VIX. So what you're seeing here, 23.90, are the VIX futures."

To verify this, you can chart the futures directly by typing `/VX` and choosing the nearest month — in this case the January futures. Doing so shows the futures trading at 23.85, which matches the figure in the option analysis window rather than the spot VIX figure on the chart.

"So in other words, when we place the trade we are placing the trade using VIX, but it's actually based on the VIX futures. It's a bit confusing, but it's just something peculiar about the VIX."

This explains why strike selection on the VIX must be done by delta rather than by proximity to the quoted index level. The options are not priced off the spot index you are looking at. They are priced off a futures contract that can sit meaningfully away from spot, and delta — which is derived from the actual pricing input — tells you the truth about where a strike sits, while the spot quote does not.

#### Placing the Order

On thinkorswim, the order is finalised through Confirm and Send, with the max loss of $90 and max profit shown, and transmitted. Since the market is closed, the order sits as a working order and will only execute when the market opens.

A note on fills: sometimes the order will not fill and you must wait. If you are eager to get in, you can increase the price you are willing to pay — from $0.90 to $0.91 and upward — until it fills. But the constraint is explicit: "don't increase too much that the risk-reward ratio is no longer relevant." The whole point of computing the risk-reward before entry is that it constrains how far you may chase the fill.

The order is then cancelled, with a general best-practice note: "usually for options, I only like to place the trade when the market's open. Then the prices we see are more accurate. When the markets close, the prices we see sometimes are not that accurate."

#### The Same Trade on Interactive Brokers

Finally, the identical VIX trade is placed on the Interactive Brokers Trader Workstation, and the setup steps mirror those from the GOOGL case study.

Enter VIX in the option chain to display all strikes. Click "More" and check weeklies and quarterlies so those expirations appear. Set the strike display to "all strikes" so the full ladder is visible.

To create a multi-leg combo — a spread — the **Strategy Builder** must be switched on.

With calls displayed on the left, click the ask on the $30 strike to buy the $30 call, then click the bid on the $35 strike to sell the $35 call. Two legs, quantity one contract.

For pricing, the bid-ask is $0.80 to $1.00, so the midpoint of roughly $0.90 is used as the limit. It is a debit, and the order is submitted. Since the market is closed, it may or may not fill at that price when trading opens, and the price can be updated — to $0.91, for instance — and the order updated. The order can also simply be cancelled, which is what is done here.

#### Summary of the VIX Trade

| Element | Value |
|---|---|
| Date | 18 January (market closed, holiday) |
| Instrument | VIX (options actually priced off VIX futures) |
| Spot VIX on chart | 24.34 |
| VIX futures / analysis price | 23.85–23.90 |
| Expiry | 17 March, 57 days (target ≥60 days) |
| Planned exit | 30 days before expiration (~18 February) |
| Long call | $30 strike, 54 delta (target ~50 delta) |
| Short call | $35 strike, 42 delta (target 35–40 delta) |
| Net debit | $0.90 per share, $90 per contract (later $0.85) |
| Theoretical max loss | $90 |
| Theoretical max profit | $410 (not a realistic target) |
| Entry zone | VIX at 20–22 |
| Profit-taking zone | VIX at 29–30 |
| Realistic loss at exit date if VIX → 20 | −$66 |
| Realistic gain at exit date if VIX → 29 | +$76 |
| Realistic risk-reward | ~1.15 : 1 (1:1 acceptable for VIX) |

---

### Chapter Section 22: Drawing the Threads Together

Placing the three case studies side by side reveals how much of options trading is judgement operating within rules, rather than rules operating on their own.

| | GOOGL | ANET | VIX |
|---|---|---|---|
| Setup | 4-point confluence + confirmation candle | Relative strength on a down day, post-earnings stabilisation, oversold stochastic | S&P overextended, VIX at range support |
| Long strike method | Closest to price ($138) | Near the money ($139) | ~50 delta ($30) |
| Short strike method | 1 SD ($146), resistance-checked | 1 SD ($155), resistance considered at $152.50 | 35–40 delta ($35) |
| DTE at entry | 27 | 31 | 57 |
| Debit | $2.69–$2.70 | $5.57 | $0.90 |
| Max profit | $531/contract | $1,043 | $410 (not targeted) |
| Planned exit | 80% of max profit | 80–90%, or >50% in <half the time | VIX at 29–30, or 30 days before expiry |
| Actual exit | 98.6% of max profit, 2 days to expiry | ~90% of max profit, 10 days to expiry | Not executed (market closed) |
| Result | $523/contract, 2 contracts, 193% ROI on premium | $931, 167% ROI | — |
| Path | Nearly stopped out at 49% of max loss | Retested support before rallying | — |

Several patterns are worth naming.

**Both winning trades went against the position first.** GOOGL came within one percentage point of its stop. ANET rebounded, retraced back to test support, and only then rallied. A bull call spread that works immediately is not the norm, and traders who exit on discomfort rather than on their stop level will convert winners into losers with alarming regularity.

**Both exits deviated from the 80% rule, in opposite directions, for the same underlying reason.** GOOGL held past 80% to 98.6% because expiration was two days away and the remaining risk window was almost closed. ANET closed at 90% rather than holding for 100% because ten days remained and the risk window was still open. The variable being managed in both cases was not the profit percentage but the exposure to reversal over the remaining time. The 80% rule is a good default precisely because it produces sensible behaviour without requiring this judgement; but understanding the reasoning behind it lets you adjust when circumstances are clear.

**Position sizing was conservative in every case.** GOOGL used two contracts at roughly $270 each. ANET used one contract at $557. VIX used one contract at $90. Under the 2% rule, these correspond to accounts of roughly $27,000, $28,000, and $4,500 respectively — though the VIX trade is a hedge rather than a directional bet and may be sized differently.

**The strategy expects to lose most of the time.** A 30% win rate is called normal; 40–45% is called good and achievable through patience. This is not a defect. Combined with a 1:2 minimum risk-reward, a 2% position size, and an 80% profit-taking discipline, a 40% win rate produces a strongly profitable expectancy. What it demands is that you keep taking the trades after a run of losses, and that you never let a loss run past 50% of the maximum in the hope of a recovery — because that single behaviour is what converts a positive-expectancy system into a negative one.

**And the final, repeated instruction is to do nothing when nothing qualifies.** "If there's no trade that is ideal, it's okay. Don't take any trade. Go ahead and trade other strategies." The bull call spread is a directional instrument with a 30-day clock, and forcing it onto a chart that has not given a signal is the most reliable way to lose money with it.

The Cashflow Wheel and the Bull Call Spread ask for opposite things from the trader. The Wheel asks for capital, for patience measured in years, and for the willingness to sit through an unrealised loss without flinching, in exchange for a steady 17% to 24% annualised premium yield. The Bull Call Spread asks for very little capital, for a short attention span, and for the discipline to cut a loss at exactly half of maximum and to take a profit at exactly 80% — in exchange for returns of 167% and 193% on the occasions when it works, and a great many small losses on the occasions when it does not.

Neither is better. They occupy different parts of a portfolio and serve different objectives, and the trader who understands both — and, crucially, understands which one a given market condition and a given account size call for — is in a far stronger position than the trader who has mastered only one.

---

# Part III — The Bear Put Spread & Hedging a Portfolio in Bear Markets

## The Bear Put Spread and the Art of Hedging a Portfolio in Bear Markets

### Introduction: The Mirror Image of the Bull Call Spread

Every strategy taught so far in this course has been built on the same underlying insight: that a naked long option — a bought call or a bought put standing on its own — is an honest instrument but an expensive one, and that most of its expense can be recovered by selling a second option against it at the price level where you actually expect the underlying to arrive. The bull call spread applied that insight to a rising market. The bear put spread, which is the subject of this chapter, applies exactly the same insight to a falling one.

The instructor introduces it in precisely those terms. "In this lesson, you're going to learn the bear put spread, which is a lot more cost effective than just buying a put option if you're bearish on a stock. So essentially a bear put spread is kind of like the opposite of the bull call spread." That single sentence is worth pausing over, because it tells you two things at once. It tells you what the structure is — a mirror image, with puts replacing calls and the direction of the strike ladder inverted — and it tells you what the motivation is. The motivation is not cleverness for its own sake. The motivation is cost. Everything else in this chapter follows from the observation that buying protection or buying downside exposure through a naked put is a financially punishing way to express a bearish view, and that a two-legged debit structure recovers a meaningful fraction of that punishment without materially damaging the trade's usefulness.

The chapter then broadens. Having built the bear put spread on individual equities — the instructor works through Amber and then Cisco in full arithmetic detail — the material moves to the strategic question that most students actually care about, which is what to do with a long-only investment portfolio when the market rolls over into a genuine bear market. The answer he gives is that you do not sell your long-term investments; you buy bear put spreads on the S&P 500 in a size calibrated to your portfolio and your account, and you keep rolling them every twenty to thirty days for as long as the downtrend persists. And finally the material extends into futures, where the same bear put spread structure is placed not on SPY or SPX but on the E-mini and Micro E-mini S&P 500 futures contracts, for the specific and quite narrow reason that futures trade for roughly twenty-three and a quarter hours a day while the cash index and its ETF do not.

This chapter covers all of that in the order he teaches it: the construction of the position leg by leg, the chart setups that justify entering it, the case against the naked put, the exact selection of strikes and expiries, the full arithmetic of maximum profit, maximum loss and breakeven, the behaviour of theta and implied volatility inside the structure, the complete entry and exit rulebook with every numeric threshold he states, the argument for hedging a long portfolio during a bear market, and the mechanics and multipliers of futures hedging.

---

### Part One: Constructing the Bear Put Spread

#### The Position, Leg by Leg

A bear put spread is a two-legged debit position on a single underlying, in a single expiration cycle, made up of one long put and one short put at a lower strike. The instructor states the construction with no ambiguity: "A bear put spread involves buying a put option at one strike price, which is usually the price where the stock is trading at, which is at the money or slightly in the money, and simultaneously we sell another put at a lower strike price, and they both have the same expiration date."

Three conditions are baked into that sentence and each of them matters. The first is that the long put is placed at or very near the current market price. This is the leg that does the work — it is the leg that gains value as the stock falls, and placing it at the money means it begins gaining value the moment the stock moves down a single cent, rather than requiring a long journey before it enters the money. The second is that the short put is placed at a lower strike, and specifically at the strike corresponding to where you actually believe the stock will be trading by expiration. That is not an arbitrary choice and the instructor devotes considerable time to how the target is derived. The third is that both legs share the same expiration date. This is what makes the structure a vertical spread rather than a calendar or diagonal, and it is what makes the maximum profit and maximum loss finite and computable in advance.

Because the at-the-money long put is worth more than the further out-of-the-money short put, the premium you pay for the long leg always exceeds the premium you collect on the short leg. The position is therefore a net debit, and the instructor is explicit about the terminology: "we call this a debit spread, because to enter the trade, we have to pay a debit." Money leaves your account on entry. That money — and only that money — is what you can lose.

#### The Bearish Outlook That Justifies It

The strategy is directional. It makes money if the underlying falls and loses money if it rises or stagnates. It follows that the entire edge of the trade lives in the quality of the bearish thesis, and the instructor grounds that thesis entirely in trend structure rather than in opinion, news, or valuation. "When we deploy this strategy, we deploy it when we are bearish on a target price. When is the best time to be bearish on the stock? Well, when a stock is on a downtrend, the probability is that the price will keep going lower."

The downtrend definition he uses is a two-tier moving-average alignment, and he states it identically every time it appears in these lessons. The short-term trend is judged by the 20-period exponential moving average, drawn as a red dotted line, sitting below the 40-period exponential moving average. The medium-term trend is judged by the 50-period simple moving average, drawn in blue, sitting below the 150-period moving average, drawn in green. When both conditions hold — 20 EMA below 40 EMA, and 50 MA below 150 MA — the stock is in a confirmed downtrend across both horizons, and the probabilistic case for a further decline is at its strongest. He is careful to frame this as probability and not certainty: the trend tells you which direction is more likely, not which direction is guaranteed.

Beyond the raw trend condition, he identifies two specific chart events that mark the moment to actually put the trade on, because a downtrend by itself is a state and not a trigger.

The first trigger is a rejection at resistance during a counter-trend rally. His description of downtrend price behaviour is worth quoting because it explains why waiting matters: "on a downtrend, it goes again into these wave patterns. So you can wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down. So it doesn't go down in a straight line. It waves up and goes up and whenever it goes up temporarily to a level of resistance and it's going to start waving back down, that's the time to deploy a bear put spread." The chart he points to on the right of the slide shows price bouncing off a level of resistance within an established downtrend and turning back over. The logic is that entering after a bounce gets you a higher entry price for your long put and therefore more room for the subsequent decline to run, whereas entering after the market has already fallen for several sessions means buying puts into elevated premium with the easy part of the move already gone.

The second trigger is a breakdown through support. On the left-hand chart he describes price in a downtrend approaching a horizontal level that has repeatedly held it up, and then failing: "you can see if the price broke the support. And once that support is broken, then there's a lot more downward momentum and that would be a great time to enter a bear put spread as well." A broken support level is significant because it removes the nearest structural obstacle beneath price and because it typically triggers stop-loss selling from holders who had been leaning on that level, which supplies the momentum that a bear put spread needs in order to reach its short strike before expiration.

Both triggers are therefore about the same thing: entering at a point where the next move is more likely to be immediate rather than delayed. Time is the enemy of a debit spread, and both of these setups are attempts to minimise how much time the trade needs in order to work.

#### Why Not Simply Buy a Put?

The instructor poses the obvious challenge himself. "If we are bearish on a stock, why don't we just buy a put option like what we learned in the previous lessons?" He answers with three disadvantages, and they are the exact mirror of the three he raised against the naked long call in the bull call spread lesson.

The first disadvantage is cost, and cost expressed specifically as its consequence for breakeven. "It's relatively expensive because when you buy a put option, you have to pay the premium up front and the stock price has to drop enough to cover the cost of the premium for you to make money. So on the expiration date the stock price has to move below the strike price minus the premium for you to start breaking even." The breakeven of a naked long put sits a full premium below the strike. Every dollar of premium you pay is a dollar of decline the stock must deliver before you have made anything at all, and on an at-the-money put with thirty days of life that premium can easily represent several per cent of the stock's price. You are, in effect, betting not merely that the stock will fall but that it will fall by more than the option market has already priced in.

The second disadvantage is time decay. "If you just buy a straight put option, there's the risk of time decay. Because every day that passes, the put option is losing extrinsic value. It's losing time value every single day. And the more time that passes, the less profit you make. So time is working against you." A naked long put has unambiguously negative theta. Holding it is a daily expense. If the stock does nothing at all, the position bleeds toward zero on a schedule that accelerates as expiration approaches.

The third disadvantage is exposure to falling implied volatility. "Once again, whether you buy a call option or put option, the moment the volatility of the stock falls, the implied volatility falls, the value of the put or the value of the call will fall because there's a drop in extrinsic value." This is the risk traders sometimes call volatility crush. It is particularly insidious for bearish trades, because implied volatility tends to be elevated precisely when markets are falling and fear is high — which is exactly when a novice is most tempted to buy puts. If the market then merely stabilises rather than continuing lower, the collapse in implied volatility can destroy the value of a long put even when the underlying has not moved against you at all.

The bear put spread does not eliminate any of these three problems, but it reduces all three simultaneously, and it does so by the same mechanism. Selling the lower-strike put brings in premium, which directly reduces cost and directly improves breakeven. Selling that put also creates a position with positive theta and positive vega — a short option gains as time passes and gains as implied volatility falls. Netted against the long put's negative theta and negative vega, the result is a structure whose sensitivity to both variables is dramatically muted. The instructor puts it plainly: "when you sell a put, theta works in your favour. As time passes, and implied volatility, works in your favour. So selling of the put offsets the buying of the put in terms of the theta and vega risk."

The word to hold onto is *offsets*, not *eliminates*. A bear put spread still decays if the stock does not move — that is exactly what the profit-and-loss diagrams in this lesson show, and it is the reason the exit rules exist. What it does not do is decay at the brutal rate of a naked long put.

#### The Generic Numerical Example: XYZ at $49.50
