Before touching real charts, the instructor builds a fully invented example that isolates the arithmetic from the market noise. The stock is called XYZ and it is trading at $49.50. You are bearish.

The long leg goes at the strike nearest the market. "You buy a put option at or near the current strike price. So of course you have to choose the closest strike price. So in this case, for example, we buy a put option at a strike price of $50." He restates what that ownership means in the most literal terms available, because he wants the mechanical meaning of the contract to stay in view underneath the arithmetic: "by buying the put, we have the right to sell the shares at $50."

The short leg goes at the target. "At the same time, we will sell a put option at a lower strike price where we think the price is going to drop to within that time frame. So if we think that the stock price is going to drop to, let's say, $45 in 30 days — from 49, it's going to drop to $45 in 30 days — then we sell a put option at a strike price of $45."

Now the money. The $50 put is quoted at $1.50. Because one option contract controls one hundred shares, that quoted price of $1.50 per share becomes a cash outlay of $150 per contract. The $45 put is quoted at $0.50, which becomes a cash inflow of $50 per contract. His framing of the relationship between the two is the essential intuition of the whole strategy: "this $50 that we collect in premium from the put we sold helps to offset the cost of buying this put, which we bought at $150."

The net debit is therefore $150 paid less $50 collected, which is $100 per contract. And the benefit is stated in exactly the terms a trader cares about: "if we just buy the put option, it costs us $150. But by doing a bear put spread, it now only costs us $100. So it's more cost effective. And because of that, it helps to increase our break-even price on the trade. So now the stock price doesn't have to drop so much for us to break even."

That phrase — *increase our break-even price* — is one that trips up students the first time they meet it, so it is worth being explicit about the direction of the benefit. For a bearish position, a higher breakeven price is better, because the stock has less distance to fall before the position becomes profitable. The naked $50 put breaks even at $50 minus $1.50, or $48.50. The spread breaks even at $50 minus $1.00, or $49.00. Since the stock sits at $49.50, the spread requires a fall of only fifty cents to reach breakeven while the naked put requires a full dollar. The spread starts making money sooner and requires less from the market.

The cost of that advantage is stated immediately and without evasion. "Of course there's a catch, and the catch is that it limits our potential profit as the price drops. So if the stock drops way below $45, then any extra profit, we don't get it. We get the profit up to $45." His justification for accepting that cap is a statement about how stocks actually behave rather than about mathematics: "which is fine, because most of the time the stock wouldn't just keep dropping all the way down. It would drop and bounce up again. So most of the time, it is more effective to use a bear put spread." You are selling away a tail outcome that rarely occurs, and being paid for it up front in the form of a lower entry cost that applies to every trade you ever place.

#### Worked Example One: Amber at $53.35

The first live example uses a stock the instructor calls Amber, and here every number is drawn off an actual option chain rather than invented.

The stock is trading at $53.35 and the chart satisfies both tiers of his downtrend test. "The 20 EMA, the red dotted line is below the 40 EMA, so the short term trend is down. The 50 moving average is below the 150 moving average, so the medium term trend is down." His conclusion is once again probabilistic rather than absolute: "we think that it is going to more likely go down than go up."

**Selecting the long put strike.** The rule is proximity to the market price, applied literally against the available strike ladder. "We buy or we long one contract of the Amber put options at the $53 strike price. Why $53? Because that's closest to the current market price. If you take a look at the option chain, the closest to $53.35 would be the 53 strike." He then does something important, which is to relax the rule before a student can turn it into dogma: "Could you choose the 54 strike? Yeah, you could do that as well. So whichever is close, you can choose that one." The 53 put is slightly out of the money with the stock at $53.35; the 54 put would be slightly in the money. Either is acceptable. What is not acceptable is a strike far from the money, because the whole point of the long leg is to begin participating in the decline immediately.

The premium on the 53 put is $4.15 per share, so a single contract costs $415 before considering the short leg.

**Selecting the short put strike.** This is where the analytical work sits, and the instructor offers two independent methods and then treats their agreement as confirmation.

The first method is structural. "One way is to look at the previous swing low of the stock. You can see over here, 43.59, that was a previous swing low. So if you think that the stock is going to drop all the way to that, you can use that as your target price." A prior swing low is a level at which buyers previously appeared in sufficient size to reverse the decline, and it therefore represents a reasonable estimate of where the current decline may also be arrested. Placing the short strike at or near that level means you are capping your profit exactly where you expect the market to stop cooperating anyway.

The second method is statistical, and it recycles a tool taught earlier in the course. "Another way to do it is to look at the one standard deviation, or one SD, which I taught you in the previous lesson. So for this particular expiry date, what's the one standard deviation? It's plus minus $9.42. What does that mean? That means that in 30 days for this expiry date, this stock is likely to drop or go up by $9.42. But since we are bearish, then we're saying that it's likely to drop by $9.42."

The expected-move figure is displayed on the platform for each expiration and is derived from the implied volatility of that cycle. It represents the range within which the underlying is expected to remain, with roughly sixty-eight per cent probability, by that expiration. Using it as a downside target is a way of saying: I will take profit at the edge of what the option market itself considers a normal move, rather than at a level that would require an abnormal one.

The arithmetic is straightforward. $53.35 minus $9.42 gives $43.93, which he rounds to "roughly about $44.00 is the target price." And then comes the confirmation: "which is interestingly also close to the previous swing low. That's also near $44. So they both are aligned, fantastic."

That alignment is the ideal case. When a purely statistical estimate of the likely move and a purely structural estimate drawn from price history land on the same number, the confidence in the target is much higher than either method alone would justify. The short strike is therefore set at 44.

The 44-strike put trades at $1.10 per share, delivering a credit of $110 per contract.

**The full arithmetic of the Amber trade.**

| Component | Per share | Per contract (×100) |
|---|---|---|
| Buy 1× Amber 53 put | $4.15 debit | $415 paid |
| Sell 1× Amber 44 put | $1.10 credit | $110 received |
| Net debit | $3.05 | $305 paid |

The net debit of $3.05 per share, or $305 per contract, is simultaneously the cost of the position and the definition of its risk. The instructor makes the identity explicit: "that is also my maximum risk in the trade. So the worst that can happen is that if the price does not drop, the price goes up and my entire spread is a loss. The most I can lose is $305. Remember that the maximum risk is the premium that you paid, the net premium."

**Breakeven.** The formula is the long put strike less the net premium paid. "The break-even price would be the strike price of my long put minus the net premium paid. So what's the strike price of the long put? It's 53. $53 minus 3.05, so my break-even price is $49.95."

The reason the formula works is worth spelling out. At expiration, if the stock closes at $49.95, the 53 put is worth its intrinsic value of $53 minus $49.95, which is $3.05, and the 44 put expires worthless because the stock is well above 44. The spread is therefore worth exactly the $3.05 you paid for it, and you are flat. Below $49.95 the long put's intrinsic value exceeds what you paid and you are in profit; above it, you are in loss. Note that this breakeven requires a decline of only $3.40 from the entry price of $53.35 — a fall of about 6.4 per cent — whereas a naked 53 put purchased at $4.15 would not break even until $48.85, a decline of $4.50 or roughly 8.4 per cent.

**Maximum profit.** "The maximum profit at expiration would be the difference in the strike price of the two puts, which is the long put strike price minus the short put strike price, and then minus the net premium paid. So in this case, what's the difference in the strike price? The difference will be 53 and 44. So 53 minus 44, the difference is $9. Then minus 3.05, and then you multiply by 100 shares. So per contract, our maximum profit is $595."

The intuition behind that formula is that the widest the spread can ever become is the distance between its strikes. If the stock closes at or below 44 at expiration, the long 53 put is worth $9 of intrinsic value and the short 44 put is worth zero — the spread is worth its full $9 width, which is $900 per contract. Since you paid $305 to acquire it, your profit is $595. Nothing the stock does below $44 can improve on that, because every additional dollar of gain on the long 53 put is exactly offset by an equal dollar of loss on the short 44 put. That offsetting is what the profit cap physically consists of.

**The risk-to-reward assessment.** "So do we have a good risk to reward ratio? We're risking $305 to make $595. So roughly, it is roughly close to risking 1 to 2. Well, it's actually slightly less than 2, but it's close enough."

The precise figure is 1.95 to 1. His willingness to call that "close enough" while explicitly naming the shortfall is characteristic — the one-to-two threshold is a guideline for filtering trades, not an arithmetic gate to be enforced to the second decimal place.

**The complete Amber payoff at expiration.**

| Stock price at expiration | 53 put value | 44 put value | Spread value | Profit / loss on $305 debit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $56.00 (rally) | $0 | $0 | $0 | −$305 (maximum loss) |
| $53.35 (unchanged) | $0 | $0 | $0 | −$305 (maximum loss) |
| $51.00 | $2.00 | $0 | $200 | −$105 |
| $49.95 (breakeven) | $3.05 | $0 | $305 | $0 |
| $48.00 | $5.00 | $0 | $500 | +$195 |
| $46.00 | $7.00 | $0 | $700 | +$395 |
| $44.00 (short strike) | $9.00 | $0 | $900 | +$595 (maximum profit) |
| $40.00 (below short strike) | $13.00 | $4.00 | $900 | +$595 (capped) |

The final two rows are the important ones. Once the stock is at or below $44, further declines change nothing, because the short put begins losing value at exactly the rate the long put gains it. That is the cap, made concrete.

**Placing the trade on the platform.** The instructor walks through the mechanics on Thinkorswim so that the abstraction becomes a sequence of clicks. He selects the 22nd of March expiry, "about 32 days to expiration, so usually I would choose about 30 days." He navigates to the put side of the chain. To buy the 53 put he clicks the ask price, which populates the order with "plus one, means one contract of 53 puts I'm buying." To add the second leg he holds the control key and clicks the bid on the 44 strike, which sells it. "So plus one, buy 53, minus one, sell 44. My net premium I'm paying would be $3.05 debit."

He then opens the analysis tab, and the resulting graph is described as matching the hand-drawn diagram exactly. The two lines on that graph are the central visual tool of this entire chapter, and their meaning must be held clearly. "The green line is the profit and loss at expiration. And the purple line is the profit and loss now. And this purple line changes every day as we move towards expiration."

The green line is the hockey-stick payoff of the position on the final day: flat at −$305 above the breakeven region, sloping down-left through breakeven, and flat again at +$595 below the short strike. The purple line is the position's mark-to-market value today, smoothed and rounded by the remaining extrinsic value in both options. Over the life of the trade the purple line migrates continuously toward the green line, and at expiration the two coincide.

#### How Time Actually Moves the Position

This migration of purple toward green is the mechanism by which theta expresses itself in a spread, and the instructor makes the crucial observation that its effect is not uniformly bad — it depends entirely on which side of the breakeven you are standing.

If the stock refuses to fall: "if I enter the trade right here and if the stock price doesn't drop, the stock price stays there — not very good for me. Because what happens to the purple line as time passes, and I'm losing time value? Notice as time passes, the purple line moves to the green line until it becomes the green line at the date of expiration." Above breakeven, the green line lies below the purple line, so time pulls your mark-to-market downward. "If the stock price doesn't drop below this break even point, you can see that the longer I hold the trade, the more I'm losing."

If the stock falls as expected: "the moment I enter the trade and the stock price starts to drop, and it can drop way below this break even point — it drops to let's say $46 or $44 — then you can see that I'm in the profit zone, and at this point notice that the more time that passes, the more the purple line will go up to the green line, and the more profit I make, and I maximize my profit on the expiration date when the purple line hits the green line."

This is the single most operationally important consequence of using a spread rather than a naked put, and it has a direct behavioural implication that the exit rules formalise. When you are wrong, time is destroying you and you should leave quickly. When you are right, time is *paying* you and you should stay — but staying carries the risk that the stock reverses before expiration, which is why the profit-taking rule exists at all.

---

### Part Two: Reinforcement Through the Cisco Example

The instructor then runs a second complete example on Cisco, and structures it as a guided exercise in which the student is repeatedly asked to pause the video and compute the answer before it is revealed. Because the pedagogical intent is repetition, the numbers are worth reproducing in full.

#### The Setup

Cisco is trading at $48.44, and the chart passes both tiers of the trend test: "it's on a downtrend. We've got the 20 EMA, red dotted line, below the 40 EMA, and the 50 moving average is below the 150 moving average. So the moving averages are pointing downwards."

The trigger in this case is the breakdown variant rather than the resistance-rejection variant. "There was a previous support level over here where the price broke below the support and there's a chance it will continue going down to the previous swing low, which is the target at $46. So right now, from $48.44, we think that Cisco may drop all the way down to $46."

The expiration selected is once again the 22nd of March, "32 days to expiration."

#### The Legs

The long put goes at the 48 strike. "We are choosing to buy or go long the Cisco put at the 48 strike price. Why $48? Because that is near the market price." And again the rule is loosened rather than made rigid, but this time with an important qualifier attached: "we could choose 48, we could also choose 49. So you basically choose either one, but you have to make sure at the end of the day, you have a good risk-to-reward ratio of risking a dollar to make close to $2."

That qualifier converts strike selection from an aesthetic judgement into a constrained optimisation. You are free to slide the long strike up or down the ladder by one increment, but the choice you make must survive the risk-reward test at the end. If a particular combination of strikes produces a ratio meaningfully worse than one-to-two, the answer is to change the strikes or to abandon the trade — not to accept the ratio.

The 48 put is priced at $0.83, a debit of $83 per contract.

For the short leg he weighs the same two target-setting methods. "How do we select the strike price of the put to sell? Again, we can look at where is the next swing low, or we can look at the one standard deviation, which is in this case plus minus $2.27. So in this case, I've decided to put the target price at the previous swing low, which is roughly about $2 below this strike price. So 46 would be the short put strike."

It is worth noticing that here the two methods do not coincide as neatly as they did on Amber. The one-standard-deviation move of $2.27 from $48.44 implies a downside target of $46.17, while the previous swing low sits at $46. He chooses the structural level, which is fractionally more ambitious, and it happens to land on an available round strike. When the two methods disagree modestly, choosing the one that corresponds to a real level on the chart is defensible, because the market has demonstrated that price actually stops there.

The 46 put is priced at $0.26, a credit of $26 per contract.

#### The Arithmetic, Worked in Full

| Component | Per share | Per contract |
|---|---|---|
| Buy 1× Cisco 48 put | $0.83 debit | $83 paid |
| Sell 1× Cisco 46 put | $0.26 credit | $26 received |
| Net debit | $0.57 | $57 paid |
| Spread width | $2.00 | $200 |

**Maximum risk.** "Your maximum risk would be the premium that you paid for the contract. So the net debit is 57 cents times 100 shares. So that gives you a maximum risk of $57."

**Breakeven.** "It's the strike price of your long put, which is 48, minus your net premium, which is 57 cents. So the break even price would be 48 minus 0.57, $47.43."

Cisco must therefore fall $1.01 from $48.44, a decline of about 2.1 per cent, for the position to reach breakeven at expiration. That is a far more modest demand than the Amber trade made, which is a direct consequence of the spread being narrow and cheap relative to the stock's price.

**Maximum profit.** "It will be the strike price of the long put, which is 48, minus the strike price of the short put, which is 46, minus the net premium, which is 57 cents, and you have to then multiply that by 100. So 2 minus 0.57 times 100, maximum profit $143."

**Risk-to-reward.** "So we are risking $57 to make $143. So the risk to return ratio would be 143 divided by 57, which is risking 1 to make more than 2.5. So this looks like a pretty attractive trade."

At 2.51 to 1 this comfortably clears the one-to-two guideline and is materially better than the Amber trade's 1.95 to 1. The structural reason is that the Cisco spread is narrow — only $2 wide — and the short put, being only $2.44 out of the money, still carried enough premium at $0.26 to fund a meaningful fraction of a cheap long put. Narrow spreads placed on stocks with modest expected moves frequently produce better nominal ratios than wide spreads, though they also produce smaller absolute profits and require a correspondingly precise directional call.

**The Cisco payoff table.**

| Cisco price at expiration | 48 put value | 46 put value | Spread value | Profit / loss on $57 debit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $50.00 | $0 | $0 | $0 | −$57 (maximum loss) |
| $48.44 (entry, unchanged) | $0 | $0 | $0 | −$57 (maximum loss) |
| $47.43 (breakeven) | $0.57 | $0 | $57 | $0 |
| $47.00 | $1.00 | $0 | $100 | +$43 |
| $46.50 | $1.50 | $0 | $150 | +$93 |
| $46.00 (short strike) | $2.00 | $0 | $200 | +$143 (maximum profit) |
| $44.00 | $4.00 | $2.00 | $200 | +$143 (capped) |

#### Reading the Graph, and a First Statement of the Exit Discipline

Describing the Cisco profit-and-loss graph, the instructor introduces a subtlety about breakeven that many students miss. "You can see that the break even point on the expiration date is $47.43, as we calculated. But of course that's at expiration. Before it expires our break even point is higher, but as time goes on the expiration price will keep dropping until it reaches $47.43."

The point being made is that the purple line and the green line cross the zero axis at different places. Because the long put retains extrinsic value before expiration, the position becomes profitable on a mark-to-market basis at a stock price *above* $47.43. The formal breakeven of $47.43 is a statement about the final day only. In the interim, a smaller decline than the formula suggests can already put you in the black — which is a good thing, and which is part of why early profit-taking is viable.

He then previews the loss discipline that will be formalised in the next lesson: "our maximum loss is $57 if the share price goes up and we leave it to expire. Are we going to do that? No. Because if the share price goes up, then as the purple line is dropping, before it drops to the green line, we want to cut our losses and at the most lose 50 per cent of that $57."

And he previews the corresponding profit condition, with its inherent tension: "to make the maximum profit, we have to wait for the expiration date, because as it moves to expiration, the purple line will move up to the green line and we make more and more money."

#### The Complete Advantage and Disadvantage Ledger

Having worked two examples, the instructor consolidates. He begins by noting that the logic transfers wholesale from the bullish structure: "the advantages of the bear put spread are the same as bull call spreads versus buying straight calls."

The advantages, as he enumerates them, are four.

The first is lower cost and therefore lower risk. Because the credit from the short put reduces the debit, less capital is committed to the position and the maximum possible loss falls proportionally. On Amber the reduction was from $415 to $305, a saving of just over a quarter of the outlay.

The second is the improved breakeven, and here he returns to the Amber figures for a direct comparison. "If you just buy a put option, in this case, you can see that the share price has to drop to $48.85 before you get profitable at expiration. Whereas if you use a bear put spread, you can see that the break-even price is higher at $49.95. So the stock price has to drop less before you start breaking even." The naked 53 put costing $4.15 breaks even at $48.85. The spread costing $3.05 breaks even at $49.95. That is a $1.10 improvement in the stock price required, which is the entire credit collected from the short put — a demonstration that the credit converts one-for-one into reduced distance required.

The third is muted sensitivity to time and volatility: the spread is "less affected by time value decay and by volatility crush, which means volatility dropping doesn't affect the value of the bear put spread very much."

The fourth is the summarising consequence of the first three: "overall, you have a higher probability of a profitable trade versus just buying a straight put." This follows directly from the improved breakeven. A position that requires a smaller move in order to profit will, other things equal, profit more often.

The disadvantages are two, and he does not soften either.

The first is the profit cap. "Your maximum profit is capped to the strike price of the short put. So if you just buy a put option and the stock price goes to zero, you get the maximum profit. But again, that's very rare. It's like striking the lottery." The comparison to a lottery is the honest framing. The naked put's unlimited-ish upside — bounded only by the stock reaching zero — is real but is realised so infrequently that paying for it on every trade is a poor bargain.

The second is that the full profit arrives only at the end. "You only get the maximum profit at expiration. So if the share price drops, but drops too fast, you may not get the full profit until the expiration date. You have to wait for the purple line to go up to the green line." A trader whose stock collapses to the short strike in the first week does not immediately hold $595 or $143 of profit. The short put still carries extrinsic value that must decay away before the spread can be worth its full width, and until it does, closing the position early realises less than the theoretical maximum. This is precisely why the eighty-per-cent profit-taking rule exists rather than a hundred-per-cent rule.

---

### Part Three: The Entry and Exit Rulebook

The instructor devotes a full lesson to converting everything above into a checklist that can be executed without deliberation. Because the rules carry specific numeric thresholds, they are the most operationally valuable material in the chapter.

#### Entry Rules

**Step one: identify a bearish setup, and check the instrument qualifies.** "Step number one is to identify a bearish trade on a stock, index or ETF. So you think that the stock price is going to go down because it's on a downtrend, then you can execute a bear put spread. Ideally, we want the stock price to be above $20, and of course, options must be available."

Two filters are embedded here. The instrument must have a listed and reasonably liquid options market, which excludes a large fraction of the equity universe. And the underlying should be trading above $20. The reason for the price floor, though he does not elaborate on it here, is structural: below $20 the strike ladder is typically spaced too coarsely relative to the stock's price for a meaningful spread to be constructed, the premiums involved become so small that bid-ask spreads consume a disproportionate share of the edge, and the ratio of transaction cost to potential profit deteriorates badly.

**Step two: select the expiration.** "Step two is to check the option chain. And when you look at the option chain, choose your date to expiration. 30 days, choose the ideal time."

He then discusses the trade-off in both directions rather than treating thirty days as sacred. "Could you choose less than 30 days? Sure. If you think that the price will drop in five days, you could choose five days. If you think it's going to drop in 10 days, you could choose 10 days. But of course, if you give 30 days, you have got more time to be right. But if you give too much time and the share price drops, then you have to wait quite a while to get the maximum profit. Because recall that you only get the maximum profit at expiration."

The tension is genuine and symmetric. A longer expiration buys you more time for the thesis to play out, which raises the probability of being directionally correct at some point during the trade's life. But it also means that if the move happens early, you sit holding a position whose short leg still contains substantial extrinsic value, unable to harvest the full spread width without waiting weeks. Thirty days is the compromise he settles on as a default, and the actual trades in these lessons use thirty-two days on the equities and twenty-five to thirty days on the index and futures hedges.

**Step three: select the long put strike.** "You have to choose the strike price of your long put that you're buying and the short put that you're selling. For the long put that you're buying, I choose a strike price that is near the current market price, usually between 50 to 60 deltas. Of course, for puts the deltas are negative. So usually it's at the money or one strike in the money. Now could it be slightly out of the money? That's fine as well."

The delta band of fifty to sixty is the precise version of "near the money." A delta of fifty corresponds almost exactly to at-the-money; deltas above fifty correspond to in-the-money puts, meaning strikes above the current stock price. His parenthetical about negative delta is a reminder of convention: put deltas are conventionally quoted as negative numbers because puts gain as the underlying falls, so a "50 to 60 delta" put is displayed on most platforms as −0.50 to −0.60. On the Amber trade the 53 put with the stock at $53.35 was slightly out of the money and would have carried a delta slightly below fifty in magnitude; on Cisco the 48 put with the stock at $48.44 was likewise marginally out of the money. Both sit at the permissive edge of the band, which is consistent with his explicit statement that slightly out of the money is acceptable.

**Step four: select the short put strike.** "For the strike price of the put I'm selling, I would choose the strike at a target price below the market price. So how do I decide the target price? A few ways. One is to just look at the one standard deviation move, the one SD move. If it's like plus minus $3, then the target price would be $3 below the market price. And or you can look at the previous support level or previous swing low to identify where's your target price."

The word "and or" is doing real work. The two methods can be used independently, but when they agree — as they did on Amber, where the statistical target of $43.93 and the swing low of $43.59 both pointed to a 44 strike — the resulting confidence is substantially higher.

**Step five: size the position.** This is the step the instructor treats as the most consequential, and it is where the single most important numeric rule in the chapter appears.

"So once you do that, then you have to choose how many contracts you want to trade. Remember, one contract is always equal to 100 shares. So how many contracts you trade depends on how big your account is. The rule is that the total premium that you pay for the trade should be less than 2 per cent of the net liquidation value of your account."

He then works the arithmetic explicitly. "Let's imagine your account is a $10,000 account. What is 2 per cent of $10,000? 2 per cent of $10,000 would be $200. So that means that if you find a trade where one contract, the premium is more than $200, then you can't take the trade because it's beyond your budget. You only take trades where the net premium that you have to pay is below $200. Now, if it's $100, for example, then you can trade two contracts. If it's $200, you can trade one contract. If it's more than $200, you can't take the trade."

The rule is unusually clean in application because the maximum loss of a bear put spread equals the net debit exactly. There is no need to model scenarios or estimate a stop-loss level in order to size the position, because the worst case is already known at the moment of entry. The position sizing question therefore reduces to simple division.

| Account net liquidation value | 2% risk budget | Max contracts at $57 debit (Cisco) | Max contracts at $305 debit (Amber) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $5,000 | $100 | 1 | 0 — trade not permissible |
| $10,000 | $200 | 3 | 0 — trade not permissible |
| $25,000 | $500 | 8 | 1 |
| $50,000 | $1,000 | 17 | 3 |
| $100,000 | $2,000 | 35 | 6 |

The table makes visible something the instructor states in the Cisco and Amber examples only implicitly: the Amber trade at $305 per contract is simply unavailable to a trader with a $10,000 account. Not undesirable — unavailable. The rule is a hard gate, and the correct response to a trade that fails it is to find a different trade, not to shave the rule.

His justification for the rule is a statement about survival rather than about optimisation. "Always limit your risk so that every one trade, you only risk 2 per cent or less of your capital. Because remember, in trading, we will have periods of losing trades and winning trades. You want to make sure that when you get a series of losing trades, your account is able to survive the losing trades so that when the winning trades come, you can make up for the losing trades and make a net profit."

And he names the specific failure mode with unusual bluntness: "The mistake a lot of traders make is that they risk too much. They think that this is a sure win trade and they risk too much and they get one big loss or three big losses and their account is wiped out so much so that they're out of the game. And once you're out of the game, you can't play the game anymore. When the winning trades come, you're not there to capture the winning trade. So it's all about risk management, very important."

The structure of that argument is important. It is not that large positions have negative expectancy — a good strategy has positive expectancy at any size. It is that a strategy with positive expectancy still produces losing streaks, and a position size that cannot survive a normal losing streak converts a profitable strategy into a terminal one. The two per cent rule is a solvency constraint, not a return-optimisation constraint.

**Step six: verify the risk-reward on the platform before committing.** "Next is to analyse the profit — you can use the trading platform and look at your maximum profit, your maximum loss and your break-even price. And again, before you enter the trade, always ensure that your risk-reward ratio is one is to two or better."

This is the final filter and it applies after all the structural choices have been made. If the completed spread does not offer roughly two dollars of potential profit for every dollar risked, the trade is rejected regardless of how attractive the chart looked.

**Step seven: place the order correctly.** "Once you're happy with the trade, you can just place a limit order at the market price. And of course, you can always change the limit order as long as you're getting a 1 to 2 return ratio. You can change the limit order until you get the order filled."

Two disciplines are contained here. The first is that the order must be a limit order rather than a market order. A two-legged spread executed at market can slip badly, because you are crossing two separate bid-ask spreads simultaneously and the combined slippage can consume a meaningful share of a small net debit. The second is that the limit price may be adjusted upward to achieve a fill, but only within the constraint that the resulting risk-reward ratio still satisfies the one-to-two threshold. Paying up to get filled is acceptable; paying up until the trade is no longer worth taking is not.

Finally, a rule about timing within the session: "usually we place the order when the market opens. We don't place the order before the market opens, because when the market opens then, the prices you see are more accurate." Option quotes outside regular trading hours are stale or wide, the underlying is not actively trading, and the displayed mid-price may bear little relation to what is actually achievable. This particular rule turns out to be the seed of the entire futures discussion later in the chapter, because futures options do trade nearly around the clock and therefore relax this constraint.

#### Exit Rules

The exit rules split into a profit branch and a loss branch, with an important exception attached to the loss branch.

**Taking profit: close at eighty per cent of maximum profit.**

The instructor first establishes why one would not simply hold to expiration. "Once we enter the trade and if the share price drops, then our trade becomes profitable. Initially, your profit will be at the purple line. But as time passes, remember the purple line will start to go up to the green line, and you will get the maximum profit only at expiration. But once the price drops, we don't have to wait until expiration to get the maximum profit. Why? Because sometimes if you wait too long, the share price may go back up. If it goes back up, the profits may disappear."

That is the trade-off in its entirety. The last twenty per cent of a spread's profit is the slowest and most grudgingly delivered portion — it consists almost entirely of residual extrinsic value in the short put that decays only in the final days — while the exposure required to capture it is a full additional stretch of directional risk in a market that has already moved a long way in your favour and is therefore statistically more prone to bouncing.

The rule follows: "usually what we do is we will close the bear put spread, we close the trade and take profit once 80 per cent of the maximum profit is realized. So in the case of Cisco, what's the maximum profit that we can achieve? The maximum profit is $143. So once we get 80 per cent of that, which is about $114, then we can close the trade and move on to the next trade. We don't have to be greedy and squeeze out every single last dollar of the trade."

Applying the same eighty-per-cent rule across the examples in this chapter:

| Trade | Maximum profit | 80% profit-taking level | Effective risk-reward if exited at 80% |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cisco 48/46 put spread | $143 | approximately $114 | $114 on $57 risk = 2.0 to 1 |
| Amber 53/44 put spread | $595 | $476 | $476 on $305 risk = 1.56 to 1 |

The phrase he attaches to the rule — "we don't have to be greedy and squeeze out every single last dollar" — reframes the eighty per cent target as a discipline about capital velocity rather than about maximisation. Closing at eighty per cent frees the capital and the risk budget to be deployed into the next setup, and over many trades the compounding effect of faster turnover typically outweighs the twenty per cent surrendered on each individual position.

He restates the underlying tension honestly rather than pretending it away: "once the share price drops, the longer you stay in the trade, the more profits that you get, but of course there's always a risk that the share price will bounce back up."

**Cutting losses: close at fifty per cent of maximum loss.**

The loss branch covers three distinct ways a bear put spread can fail, and the instructor enumerates all of them because a novice tends to think only of the first.

The first failure mode is the stock moving against you. "If you enter the trade and the share price doesn't go down, the share price goes up, then of course you are in the loss zone. Now initially, you are not losing the full $57 at the green line. Initially, your loss would be at the purple line, which could be half of that maximum loss or maybe 20 per cent of the maximum loss. So once you're in the losing zone, you do not want to wait for yourself to lose everything at expiration. You want to close the trade and get out while you still have got value in the bear put spread."

The second failure mode is stagnation. "If the share price doesn't go up but stays there, you will also lose value as time passes. The purple line will drop, drop, drop to the green line." A bear put spread on a stock that goes nowhere loses its entire debit. Doing nothing is not a neutral outcome for this structure — it is the maximum-loss outcome.

The third failure mode is insufficient movement in the right direction. "Or if the share price goes down, but it goes down not enough — it goes down a bit, but not enough to cross the breakeven line — again, eventually at expiration, you will end up losing money on the green line." This is the subtlest of the three and the one most likely to lull a trader into complacency, because the chart appears to be cooperating. But a decline that stalls above the breakeven price delivers a full loss at expiration exactly as a rally would.

Against all three, the rule is identical: "the general rule is that once we are losing 50 per cent of the maximum loss, we close the trade. We don't want to lose everything."

| Trade | Maximum loss | 50% stop-loss level | Residual value recovered on exit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cisco 48/46 put spread | $57 | close at roughly $28–29 of loss | roughly $28–29 |
| Amber 53/44 put spread | $305 | close at roughly $152 of loss | roughly $153 |

**The gap-risk exception: do not cut at eighty or ninety per cent loss if two weeks remain.**

The final rule is the most counter-intuitive in the lesson, and the instructor introduces it by first describing the situation that produces it. "Similar to the bull call spread, for the bear put spread there is sometimes a chance where the price can suddenly jump up a lot. It gaps up. So from $48.44, the share price, boom, jumps up to say $53. And we lose more than 50 per cent very, very fast. So we may end up losing 80 or even 90 per cent."

Overnight gaps are the mechanism by which a stop-loss rule fails. A fifty-per-cent stop assumes the ability to exit at fifty per cent, and a stock that opens five dollars higher than it closed gives no such opportunity. The trader wakes up already past the threshold, and the question becomes what to do about a position that is nearly worthless.

"So if you find that you're losing 80 per cent or more on the trade, and there's still time left — you still have two weeks to expiration — then I wouldn't close it. Because if I close it, then I already almost lose everything. So I might as well hold on to it because there's two weeks left, and who knows, in two weeks the share price could collapse and it could be a profitable trade. So the general rule is that yes, if you're losing 50 per cent, cut loss, but if you suddenly lose 80 or 90 per cent, you've got very little left to lose. I would just leave it there if there's still at least two weeks to expiration."

The logic is an asymmetry argument rather than a hope argument. Closing a position worth ten or twenty per cent of what you paid recovers a trivial sum, while the option value that remains — however small — retains genuine convexity. If the stock reverses sharply within the remaining two weeks, that residual stake can multiply many times over. The expected value of holding a nearly worthless spread with meaningful time remaining exceeds the expected value of liquidating it, because the downside of holding is capped at the small residual amount you would have recovered anyway.

The two-week condition is essential and is stated twice. The convexity argument depends entirely on there being enough calendar time for a reversal to occur and to be reflected in the option's value. With three days left, a deeply out-of-the-money spread has effectively no chance of recovering, and the argument collapses.

**The consolidated exit rulebook.**

| Situation | Threshold | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Trade profitable, thesis working | 80% of maximum profit realised | Close the spread, bank the profit, redeploy capital |
| Trade losing — adverse move, stagnation, or insufficient decline | 50% of maximum loss reached | Close the spread, preserve remaining value |
| Sudden gap against the position | 80–90% of maximum loss, and at least 2 weeks to expiration | Do not close; hold the residual value for possible reversal |
| Sudden gap against the position | 80–90% of maximum loss, and less than 2 weeks to expiration | The two-week condition fails; the exception does not apply |

---

### Part Four: Hedging a Long Portfolio During a Bear Market

Having established the bear put spread as a directional trading instrument on individual equities, the instructor now repositions it as something quite different — a portfolio management tool. "In this video I'll be talking about how I use bear put spreads, or how I trade bear put spreads on the SPY, on the S&P 500 ETF, to hedge my investment portfolio during a downtrend or during a bear market."

The framing is important and he returns to it repeatedly. The purpose of the trade is not to make money in isolation. It is "to create profits to hedge the short-term, unrealized losses on my long-term investments." The investor is assumed to hold a long-term equity portfolio that he does not wish to sell — for reasons of tax, of conviction, of transaction cost, or simply because selling a long-term portfolio on a technical signal defeats the purpose of holding it long-term. What he wants is a temporary overlay that generates gains while the portfolio generates paper losses, so that the aggregate account drawdown is reduced and so that the investor is emotionally and financially able to hold on.

#### When Hedging Is Worth Its Cost

The instructor treats the timing question as the whole ballgame, because a hedge put on at the wrong time is a pure expense.

The signal to begin hedging is the short-term moving average cross. "I'll only do this when the market is on a downtrend. How would I know what's a downtrend? I would want to see the 20 EMA, the red dotted line, crossing below the 40 EMA. So when the 20 is below the 40, that is a short-term downtrend signal. The 20 crossed below the 40, that was a signal of the downtrend. So you can start buying put spreads when that happens."

The confirmation of a genuine bear market is the medium-term cross. "When the 50 moving average, the blue line, crosses below the 150 moving average, that is a confirmation of a bear market."

He then supplies the duration expectation that justifies the whole exercise. "Usually bear markets last six months to a year and a half or two years. And so you could actually make quite a lot of money as the market goes down."

This is the economic case for hedging. If a genuine bear market runs for six months to two years, then a hedge that must be renewed every twenty-five to thirty days will be renewed somewhere between six and twenty-four times, and each renewal is an opportunity for the position to profit as the decline continues. The cumulative gain across a long sequence of successful bear put spreads can meaningfully offset the unrealised drawdown in the underlying portfolio.

But he is scrupulous about the case where it does not work, and he uses a real and recent example. "In February of last year, you could see that the moment the bear market started, it ended. It was the fastest bear market in history. So if you had started buying puts only here, you would probably have lost money on those puts."

His attitude to that outcome is the essential insight about hedging generally, and it is delivered as an analogy: "That is fine. It's like buying insurance and the house started burning and then it recovered."

The analogy repays attention. Insurance that is never claimed is not a failed purchase; it is the normal outcome of owning insurance. A hedge that expires worthless because the market recovered is not evidence that hedging was a mistake — it is evidence that the outcome you were insuring against did not materialise, which is the outcome you should have preferred anyway. The cost of the hedge is the premium of the insurance, and the two-per-cent position sizing rule ensures that premium stays affordable.

Implicit in his framework is also a clear statement of when hedging is *not* worth its cost, and it is simply the negation of the entry signal. When the 20 EMA is above the 40 EMA and the market is in a clear uptrend, you do not hedge. He demonstrates this by refusing to place the very trade he is about to teach: "would we buy a put or put spread on the SPY right now? Right here right now, no. Because you can see the market is still on a very clear uptrend. We won't. But let's imagine that now is a downtrend and we're going to do it right now. So this is a simulation." He repeats the disclaimer several times throughout the demonstration, which is itself a lesson: the discipline of not trading against your own signal is stronger than the desire to demonstrate a strategy.

#### Choosing the Instrument: SPX versus SPY

The first practical decision is which index vehicle to hedge with, and the answer is determined by account size.

"First of all, you can buy bear put spreads on the SPX itself, but it's going to be really expensive. And only if you've got a very big account, like a $50,000, $100,000, million dollar account, then it would make sense. But for most of you with smaller accounts it would be more cost effective to buy bear put spreads on the SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, because the SPY is basically 10 per cent of the value of the SPX. So I'm going to use the SPY as an example because I think it's more affordable for most of you."

The ten-to-one relationship is the key fact. SPY is an exchange-traded fund designed to track the S&P 500 at approximately one-tenth of the index level, so a one-point move in the index corresponds to roughly a ten-cent move in SPY. Since both SPX options and SPY options use a one-hundred multiplier, one SPX option contract carries roughly ten times the notional exposure of one SPY option contract. He restates this later in the lesson to make sure it is not missed: "you can do this on the SPY, or you can also do this on the SPX. But bear in mind that for the SPX, the contract value would be 10 times the contract value of the SPY."

The practical implication for hedge sizing is direct. A trader who needs a hedge of a given notional size can achieve it either with ten SPY spreads or with one SPX spread, and the choice between them is a matter of granularity and capital. A small account cannot afford the indivisible chunk that one SPX spread represents; a large account may prefer the reduced commission and administrative burden of a single SPX position.

#### Choosing the Expiration: The Rolling Insurance Model

The expiry decision is framed as an admission of ignorance rather than a forecast.

"We have to select the date to expiration — how long we think this downtrend is going to last. We've got to guess. Now I can't predict how long the downtrend is, no one can predict it. So usually what I do is I will choose an expiry of roughly about 20 to 30 days. And if the market continues going down more than that, what do I do? I buy another put spread, and another, until the downtrend ends."

The insurance analogy returns and is extended into a full operating model: "It's kind of like I'm buying fire insurance and I'm buying 30 days fire insurance, and if there's a fire and it keeps burning, I'll keep renewing my insurance for the next 30 days. So normally that's what I do, I buy in 30 day intervals. That's my style."

This is a materially different mental model from buying a single long-dated hedge. A twenty-five to thirty day spread that is systematically renewed has three advantages over a six-month put. It costs far less per period. It allows the strikes to be repeatedly reset lower as the market falls, so that the hedge continues to be positioned at the money rather than becoming deeply in the money and losing its leverage. And it permits the hedge to be abandoned cheaply the moment the trend signal reverses, rather than leaving the investor holding an expensive long-dated instrument that has become inappropriate.

He is careful, as always, to present this as a personal preference rather than a law: "my style, like I said, is I would select roughly 25 to 30 days. You can select longer than that, there's nothing wrong. I'm just sharing my style."

#### The SPY Hedge, Worked in Full

The demonstration trade uses SPY trading at $375, with the market closed and in an uptrend — both facts he flags explicitly as departures from live conditions. "Right now the market's closed. Usually when we do this, the market's open, so we see the actual live price. But since this is a demo, I'm doing it while the market's closed. And also, the market is not on a downtrend. So I don't actually want to do it. But I'm just demonstrating."

The expiration chosen is twenty-five days out, expiring on the 12th of February. The current date is stated as the 18th of January.

**The long leg.** "We choose the strike which is near or at the money, 375." He briefly considers 376 before settling on 375 with the comment that "375, that's a bit cheaper." The premium is $8.23 per share, and because SPY options carry the standard one-hundred multiplier, that is $823 for a single naked put. His reaction is the whole argument for the spread compressed into one line: "just buying the put is going to be $823, pretty expensive. So to lower the cost, we're going to sell a put where we think it's going to reach."

**The short leg, derived from expected move.** "So where do we think the market's going to go in 25 days? To help us guess, look at this number on the right. Can you see plus minus 20.374? What does this mean? This means that based on current volatility, the SPY will go up by 20 points or go down by 20 points in 25 days based on current volatility. So if you think the market is going to go down, it means that in 25 days, the market would go down by 20. So we use this as a rough gauge. So what's 375 minus 20? It would be 355."

He then selects 356 rather than 355, on the grounds that it is the nearest available strike to the computed target: "So I'm going to sell a put at 356 because that will be close to this."

The premium collected on the 356 put is $3.68 per share, or $368 per contract. His comment on the effect is the same offset logic as the equity examples: "the $3.68 will help to offset the cost of $8.23. So that lowers my cost to about five bucks."

**The completed SPY hedge.** He constructs it on the platform by clicking the ask on the 375 put to buy and control-clicking the bid on the 356 put to sell.

| Component | Per share | Per contract (×100) |
|---|---|---|
| Buy 1× SPY 375 put | $8.23 debit | $823 paid |
| Sell 1× SPY 356 put | $3.68 credit | $368 received |
| Net debit (platform confirmation: $4.56) | $4.56 | $456 paid |
| Spread width | $19.00 | $1,900 |

There is a small internal inconsistency worth noting honestly: $8.23 less $3.68 equals $4.55, while the platform displayed and he quoted $4.56. The one-cent discrepancy arises because he was reading the mid-price of each leg separately while the platform computed the spread price from the actual bid and ask. The figure he uses throughout is the platform's $4.56, which becomes $456 per contract.

**Maximum loss and maximum profit.** He confirms both on the order ticket rather than computing them: "click on confirm and send to check what's my maximum loss. My maximum loss will be $456. My maximum profit would be $1,444."

The maximum profit figure is consistent with the structure. The spread is nineteen points wide, worth $1,900 at full value, less the $456 debit, giving $1,444.

**Risk-to-reward.** "So is that a good risk to return ratio? Well, we take 1,444 divided by 456, that is risking a dollar to make $3. Now, is that a good trade? It's not bad, right? So if I'm wrong, if the market doesn't go down, the market keeps going up instead, I lose a dollar. But if the market goes down to the target price in 25 days, I make $3. That's a good trade. I'm going to take the trade."

At 3.17 to 1 this substantially exceeds the one-to-two minimum. Index spreads placed with the short strike a full standard deviation out tend to produce better nominal ratios than tight equity spreads, because the width of the spread is large relative to the net debit.

#### The Exit Plan for the Hedge

The instructor is emphatic that the exit plan must exist before entry. "Before you take any trade, always look at the profit and loss chart. Ensure that it's today's date, 18 of January." He then works through both branches on the analysis graph.

**The profit branch.** "My game plan would be if the market goes down to 355, I'm going to wait as it nears expiration. It expires on the 12th of February. So as it moves towards expiration, I will hit the maximum profit of about $1,444."

For the hedge application specifically, he is willing to hold closer to expiration than the eighty-per-cent rule would suggest for a standalone directional trade, because the hedge is serving a portfolio function throughout its life and not merely a profit function.

**The loss branch, with a chart-based trigger.** Here he introduces a stop-loss criterion that is different in kind from the percentage rules of the previous lesson — a price-based technical trigger rather than a percentage-of-premium trigger.

"If the market doesn't go down, the market reverses back up, I'm going to cut my loss. So when am I going to cut my loss? I've got a plan. Usually what happens is that if the market, instead of going down, goes back up and it goes above the previous swing high, I'll cut my loss at, say, 382, for example."

The reasoning is that a move above the previous swing high invalidates the downtrend structure that justified the hedge in the first place. Once the reason for holding the position has disappeared, the position should disappear too, regardless of what percentage of the premium happens to have been lost at that moment.

He then does something valuable, which is to use the analysis tool to price that stop in advance. "And I will get out before expiration. So instead of letting it expire on the 12th of February, I may get out say 10 days before. I may get out on the 2nd of February. So if I get out on the 2nd of February, how much would I lose? I put my cursor there and check the number here. I would lose $261, which is roughly half of the premium."

This is the two rules — the technical trigger and the fifty-per-cent maximum-loss guideline — converging on the same answer. A loss of $261 on a $456 debit is 57 per cent, close enough to the fifty-per-cent guideline that both frameworks endorse the same exit. The instructor treats this convergence as validation: "when I take a trade, if I'm wrong in direction, I don't lose 100 per cent. If I'm losing half of the premium, I get out."

**The realised risk-reward.** He then recomputes the trade's economics using the actual planned exit rather than the theoretical maximum loss, which is a more honest measure of the opportunity. "So if I'm wrong, I lose $261. And if the market indeed keeps going down and I let it go closer to expiration, I could get out near the green line, I'm making $1,000. Now that would make it a really good deal. Cut loss at $261 and make $1,400 — $1,400 divided by $261, that's not bad. That's risking a dollar to make $5."

There is a slight looseness in his figures here: he says "$1,000" and then computes with $1,444, arriving at a ratio he calls five to one. The arithmetic of $1,444 divided by $261 is 5.53, so the "risking a dollar to make $5" characterisation is accurate for the maximum-profit case. The underlying point stands regardless of which profit figure is used: because the planned stop-loss is roughly half the theoretical maximum loss while the profit target is close to the theoretical maximum, the *practical* risk-reward of a disciplined trade is considerably better than the ratio computed from maximum loss to maximum profit.

#### Rolling the Hedge Down as the Bear Market Continues

The final and most distinctive element of the hedging framework is the rolling process, which is what converts a single twenty-five-day trade into an ongoing portfolio overlay.

"This trade ends in 25 days. What if after 25 days, the market keeps going down and the bear market lasts for six months? Well, I'll buy another bear put spread. I keep buying new ones every 20 days, and I keep rolling it and keep making money as it goes down."

He then walks through a concrete second cycle using the chart. "So example, right now let's imagine it's 375, and my target price is 356 somewhere. So I enter the trade right here. Market drops. Once it reaches my target price, this trade, I'm already making my profits. Now, if I think it's going to keep going down — if the trend remains down, the moving averages remain down, the 20 EMA remains below the 40 EMA — what do I do? That's right. I buy another put spread. So this time I'll buy another put at 357, for example, and I sell another put at 337."

The pattern is now visible and is entirely systematic. The second spread's long strike of 357 sits at the market, which is where the first spread's short strike of 356 was. The second spread's short strike of 337 sits twenty points below, matching the width of the first spread. The hedge is being marched down the price ladder in twenty-point increments, each increment corresponding to one expected-move interval, each new spread re-established at the money so that it retains maximum sensitivity to the next leg of the decline.

The condition for continuing to roll is the trend signal itself, restated: the twenty EMA must remain below the forty EMA. And the condition for stopping is its reversal.

"I keep repeating the process until the market bottoms, and once the market reverses back into an uptrend — when the 20 EMA goes back above the 40 EMA — then I'll close all my bear put spreads and I go long on the market again."

That final sentence is the unwind rule in its entirety, and it is notable for its decisiveness. There is no partial unwind, no scaling out, no waiting for confirmation from the slower moving averages. The same short-term signal that initiated the hedging programme terminates it, and the terminal action is both to close every remaining spread and to resume adding long exposure. The hedge is treated as a temporary state of the portfolio that persists exactly as long as the technical condition that created it, and no longer.

The complete rolling hedge cycle, as he describes it:

| Phase | Trigger | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Initiate | 20 EMA crosses below 40 EMA | Buy first SPY (or SPX) bear put spread, 25–30 days out, long strike at the money, short strike one expected move lower |
| Confirm | 50 MA crosses below 150 MA | Bear market confirmed; continue the programme with increased conviction |
| Roll | Spread approaches expiration or reaches target while 20 EMA remains below 40 EMA | Buy a new spread with the long strike at the new market price and the short strike one expected move below |
| Cut a failed leg | Market rallies above the previous swing high, or loss reaches roughly 50% of premium | Close that spread before expiration, salvaging remaining time value |
| Unwind | 20 EMA crosses back above 40 EMA | Close all bear put spreads and go long the market again |

#### The Bridge to Futures

The lesson closes by identifying the one limitation of the SPY and SPX approach that futures solve, and it is a limitation of trading hours rather than of strategy.

"Sometimes I may use bear put spreads on the S&P 500 futures instead of doing it on the SPX or SPY. Why? Because remember that the SPX and the SPY, they are only open during the market hours, which is 9:30 a.m. Eastern time, New York time, to 4 p.m. So I have to wait for the market to open before I place my bear put spreads. When the market is closed, I can't do it. So sometimes if I feel that I want to get in earlier than everyone else — I want to start shorting the market, I want to start hedging my portfolio before the market opens — what can I do? That's right. Instead of buying put options on the SPX or SPY, I buy put options or bear put spreads on the S&P futures, which is slash ES or slash MES. And the futures contract is 23 hours a day. I can get in before everyone else."

This connects back to the entry rule about placing orders only after the open. That rule exists because pre-market equity option quotes are unreliable. Futures options do not have that problem, because the futures market itself is genuinely trading throughout the night, which means the quotes are live and the fills are real.

---

### Part Five: Hedging Using Futures

#### What a Futures Contract Is, and How It Differs

The instructor opens with a definition that is deliberately narrow and functional. "What are futures? Futures are a derivative of the index. And the main difference is when you trade options on the index, like the SPX, or on the index ETF, like the SPY, you can only trade during market opening hours, which is 9:30 a.m. Eastern time to 4 p.m. Eastern time. Now, sometimes I like to enter the market before the market actually opens. So if I want to get in early, I will trade the S&P 500 futures. Because the futures runs for almost 24 hours. It's about 23 and a half hours."

He then details the schedule precisely, and the precision matters because the near-continuous nature of the market is the entire justification for using it. "During the weekday, futures basically run from Monday to Friday. Weekend is closed. But Monday to Friday, it is open almost throughout, except the futures market closes at 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time. So the stock market closes at 4 p.m. 15 minutes later, the futures market will close for only 15 minutes, which means from 4:15 to 4:30, it takes a short break. And then the futures market starts again. And it closes as well at 5:30 p.m. Eastern time for half an hour. So basically it only closes for 15 minutes, plus half an hour. It only closes for 45 minutes. And the rest of the time, it is running."

Forty-five minutes of closure across the trading day leaves roughly twenty-three and a quarter hours of continuous access. For a hedger, this means that news arriving at two in the morning — an overseas selloff, a geopolitical shock, a central bank announcement in another time zone — can be responded to immediately, rather than watched helplessly until 9:30 Eastern by which time the market has already gapped.

There is a second and quite different way in which futures differ from options, which the instructor addresses through his risk warnings rather than through a formal definition. A futures contract is a *symmetric* obligation. A long futures position gains and loses linearly with the index, with no cap in either direction and no premium paid; a short futures position does the same in reverse. That symmetry is what makes outright futures dangerous as a hedging instrument — a short futures position placed as a hedge will lose without limit if the market rallies, and unlike a put spread there is no bounded maximum loss defined at entry.

His response to that danger is not to warn against it abstractly but to sidestep it structurally. He never places an outright futures position in these lessons. What he does is place *bear put spreads on futures options*, which reintroduces the bounded-risk profile of a debit spread while retaining the twenty-three-hour access of the futures market. "I only use the futures to hedge as a hedge to my investment portfolio. So for example, if I find that the market is on a downtrend, it's going into a bear market, and I don't want to wait for the market to open, I want to quickly hedge my position, I would usually buy bear put spreads on the E-mini futures or the micro futures."

The maximum loss of the futures option spreads he demonstrates is the net debit paid, exactly as on equities. The unlimited-loss characteristic of futures belongs to the outright contract, not to the defined-risk option structure he builds on top of it.

#### The Two Contracts and Their Multipliers

The most important technical content in this lesson is the contract specification, because the multipliers differ from the familiar one-hundred multiplier of equity options and getting them wrong is the fastest way to place a position ten times larger than intended.

**The E-mini S&P 500 futures, symbol /ES.** "If you're trading the S&P 500 futures, there are two products that you can trade. The first product is known as the S&P E-mini futures. The ticker symbol would be slash ES."

He derives the multiplier from the tick size rather than simply stating it, which makes it memorable. "You can see that it moves in 25 cent increments. So the smallest move would be 25 cents. Now each 25 cent move represents $12.50 — whether you make $12.50 or you lose $12.50. So a $1 move would be times four. So you multiply this by four. What do you get? You get $50. So a $1 move in the E-mini futures represents a $50 profit or loss for you as a trader. $1 move equals $50. So the options contract, one contract, would be multiplied by 50."

**The Micro E-mini S&P 500 futures, symbol /MES.** "Recently, they have a new product, which is called the S&P E-mini micro futures, and the ticker symbol would be slash MES. Usually for people with bigger accounts, like a hundred thousand dollar account, a million dollar account, you would trade the slash ES. But for those of you who have got smaller accounts, like a two thousand dollar account, three thousand dollar account, then it's more affordable to trade the MES."

The multiplier derivation follows the same pattern, though the transcription of the tick value is garbled in the recording. He says "a $1 move times four would be $1.25 times $4 is $5. So for the micro E-mini futures, one option contract, multiply by 5." The tick size on the Micro E-mini is likewise 0.25 index points, and the value of that tick is $1.25, which multiplied by four gives the $5 per one-point move that he states as the contract multiplier.

He then insists on the distinction being written down, because it is the single most error-prone fact in the lesson. "Let me just write it down, and I want you to also note it down. For the E-mini futures, one contract would be times 50. Remember that if you trade stocks and ETFs, it's always one contract is 100 shares. It's always times 100 shares. But for the E-mini futures, it's times 50. Not times 100. And for the E-mini micro futures, one contract would be times 5."

| Instrument | Symbol | Tick size | Tick value | Multiplier per 1.00 point | Relative size |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Equity or ETF option (e.g. SPY) | — | $0.01 | — | ×100 | baseline |
| E-mini S&P 500 futures option | /ES | 0.25 | $12.50 | ×50 | large |
| Micro E-mini S&P 500 futures option | /MES | 0.25 | $1.25 | ×5 | one-tenth of /ES |

The relationship between the two futures products is exactly ten to one, which is the same ratio that exists between SPX and SPY. This gives the hedger a four-rung ladder of position granularity — MES at the smallest, SPY next, then ES, then SPX at the largest — and the correct rung is determined entirely by account size.

#### Broker Permissions and the Risk Warning

Before any trade is placed, the instructor inserts a gate that does not exist for equity options. "First of all, if you want to trade futures or trade options on futures, you're going to get special permission from your broker. So you've got to go to the account management section and apply for futures trading and options on futures trading, and you've got to fill in a lot of forms of declarations — I understand the risk — because it is very risky if you don't know what you're doing. So you've got to know what you're doing, then the broker will give you permission. Of course, they'll ask you how many years of experience you have. If you say none, they say I'm sorry, you can't trade this."

Two things are being communicated. The first is procedural: futures and futures-options permissions are a separate application from equity options permissions, and they are not granted automatically. The second is substantive: the reason brokers gate this product is that the leverage embedded in a fifty-times multiplier makes it genuinely dangerous for an inexperienced trader, and the gate is a feature rather than an obstacle.

#### The Futures Expiration Structure

Futures introduce a complication that equity options do not have, which is that the *underlying itself* expires.

"Futures are contracts that also have expiry dates. So let's take a look at the E-mini futures, ticker symbol slash ES. You can see that these are the futures — you've got the March contract, the June contract, the September contract, and the December contract. There are basically four contracts."

The S&P futures follow a quarterly cycle: March, June, September, December. At any moment one of these is the front month and carries essentially all the volume and open interest.

He then reassures the student that this need not be managed manually. "You don't have to worry too much about this. You know why? Because the options that you see here, they are already based on the most recent month contract, which is the active contract. So we only care about the active contract. And the active contract — can you see the word 'active' over there? — is basically the March. So this is the futures contract that will expire in March."

But there is a hard constraint that follows, and he states it twice for emphasis. "So all the options that we trade must expire before March. I repeat, the options contract must expire before the futures contract."

The logic is that an option on a futures contract cannot outlive the contract it is written on. In the demonstration the March futures contract has sixty days remaining, which establishes the outer bound: "the March contract, 60 days. So all the option contracts we trade must be within 60 days."

Since his preferred hedging horizon is twenty-five to thirty days, this constraint is comfortably satisfied in practice. It becomes binding only if a trader attempts to place a long-dated futures option hedge, or attempts to place a thirty-day hedge when the front-month futures contract has only two weeks left — in which case the correct response is to move to the next quarterly contract.

#### Selecting the Expiration, and a Convention Worth Knowing

The expiration selection follows the same rule as SPY. "How many days should I choose? Similar to the SPX, I'll choose about 25 to 30 days. Usually that's my style."

In doing so he flags a platform convention that catches out newcomers. "Notice that this one expires on Monday. This expires on Wednesday. Now, they don't give you the day here. When they don't give you the day, it's a Friday. So always remember, if there's no day, it's a Friday."

S&P futures options list expirations on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. Thinkorswim labels the non-standard ones explicitly and leaves the standard Friday expirations unlabelled, so an unlabelled entry in the expiration list is a Friday. He then verifies the choice by counting days on a calendar, arriving at 25 days from the 18th of January to the 12th of February, which he confirms falls on Chinese New Year that year.

He also contrasts this unfavourably with the alternative platform he demonstrates later: "what I like about Interactive Brokers is that they put down the actual date for you, 12 of February. Whereas for this platform, they just put Friday or Monday or Wednesday and you've got to go figure out the actual day."

#### The /ES Hedge, Worked in Full

With the futures trading at 3761, he begins with the naked put in order to establish the scale of the problem.

**The naked put, and why it is unaffordable.** "So right now the market is at 3761. That's the current price of the futures. So let's look for 3761. Close enough, 3760. So we're going to buy this put. So if we just buy the put itself, it's going to cost $76.50. Remember times 50. So 76 times 50 is $3,825. Don't believe me? Click confirm and send. There you are — the premium is the maximum loss, $3,825. That is the cost of buying the put. Really expensive. So it's like $3,800 to just buy a put. I told you it's expensive."

That figure is the whole argument for the spread in the futures context, and it is far more dramatic than in the equity context. A single at-the-money put on the E-mini requires nearly four thousand dollars of premium, which under the two-per-cent rule would demand an account of over $190,000.

**Deriving the short strike from expected move.** "To make it cheaper, we sell a put at our target price. Where do we think the market is going to go down to in 25 days? Look at this figure over here. So based on current volatility, we expect the market to go up by 191 points or go down by 191 in 25 days. So we expect in 25 days, the market will drop by 191. So 3760 minus 191 — our target price in 25 days would be 3569. Let's round it off to 3570."

The method is identical to the SPY and equity cases: take the platform's displayed one-standard-deviation expected move for the chosen expiration, subtract it from the current price, and round to the nearest available strike.

**Assembling the spread.** He notes that the strike ladder must be extended to reach 3570 — "let's increase the strikes, more strikes, more strikes" — because the default display shows only strikes near the money. He then buys the 3760 put by clicking the ask and sells the 3570 put by holding control and clicking the bid.

| Component | Quoted price | ×50 multiplier |
|---|---|---|
| Buy 1× /ES 3760 put | $76.25 | $3,812.50 paid |
| Sell 1× /ES 3570 put | $32.75 | $1,637.50 received |
| Net debit (spread quoted at $43.50) | $43.50 | approximately $2,000 paid |
| Spread width | 190 points | $9,500 |

**The multiplier applied.** The instructor's arithmetic here is stated somewhat loosely in the recording — he says "the spread is going to cost us $43.50 times 50, that's going to cost us $2,000 per contract" and separately references $43.25 — but the platform confirmation resolves it: "click this, there we go. You see, the cost of the trade, which is the maximum loss, is $2,000."

The precise figure of $43.50 multiplied by 50 is $2,175, and $40.00 multiplied by 50 is $2,000, so the round $2,000 he quotes is the platform's confirmed figure for the fill he actually assembled rather than a computation from the quoted mid-prices. What matters pedagogically is the *method*: take the spread's quoted price and multiply by 50. He returns to this repeatedly and it is the point he wants retained.

His editorial comment on the result is honest about what has and has not been achieved: "It's cheaper, right? But still pretty expensive, yeah." The spread has cut the cost roughly in half compared with the $3,825 naked put, but two thousand dollars per contract remains a large commitment.

**Maximum profit and risk-reward.** "Maximum profit, if it goes down and hits our profit target, we make $7,000. So we're risking $2,000 to make $7,000. That's not a bad deal, right? Risking $1 to make $3."

A ratio of 3.5 to 1 comfortably exceeds the one-to-two minimum, and it is consistent with the geometry: a 190-point-wide spread worth $9,500 at full value, less a $2,000 debit, leaves roughly $7,500, which he rounds to $7,000.

**The exit plan.** He builds the same two-branch plan as on SPY.

For the profit branch: "our target is for the market to fall to 3570. So let's pull this to 3570. The market drops down to our target, and we hold it. As it moves to expiration, look at the purple line, the purple line is moving to the green line. So when it's near 25 days, we're going to take profit and we're going to make about $7,000 if the market goes down."

For the loss branch, he restates the general principle first: "If the market doesn't go down, the market goes up instead, we've got to cut our loss. Because if the market goes up, it means, hey, no longer downtrend, market's going back up, we've got to cut our loss. Remember, as a trader, you've got to have a profit target, you've got to have a stop loss. So the moment it goes up, at a certain point, I've got to cut my losses.
