It means that the market's not going down. Don't hold it to expiration and lose everything. Get out early, salvage some of the premium left."

Then the specific trigger, identical in kind to the SPY hedge: "usually what I do is, if the market instead of going down goes up, and it goes above the previous swing high, I would cut loss. So if the market goes above the previous swing high to say 3830, I'll cut my loss."

And then the crucial step of pricing that stop in advance on the analysis graph: "I will not get out near expiration. I'll get out before expiration, so I get some time value left in the option. So this expires on the 12th of February. So maybe by the 5th of February, if I find that the market's not going down, I get out early. I won't lose the entire green. I'll lose the purple, which would be roughly $1,423."

The realised economics are then computed against that planned stop rather than the theoretical maximum loss: "if I'm right and it goes down and I take profit near expiration, I could make six grand or seven grand. So I'm risking $1,400 to make $6,000 to $7,000. That's risking a dollar to make $5. Pretty good trade."

A planned loss of $1,423 against a planned gain of $7,000 is 4.9 to 1, so the "dollar to make $5" characterisation holds. And once again the planned stop of $1,423 on a $2,000 maximum loss represents roughly seventy per cent of maximum — somewhat looser than the fifty-per-cent guideline from the equity lesson, and the difference arises because the stop is being set by the technical trigger at 3830 rather than by a percentage of premium. When the two frameworks diverge, the disciplined trader takes whichever fires first.

#### The /MES Hedge: The Same Trade at One-Tenth Scale

The instructor anticipates that two thousand dollars per contract will be prohibitive for most students and immediately offers the alternative. "If losing $1,400 or losing about $2,000 is too big for your account because your account is a small account, no worries — trade the Micro E-mini futures, which is a lot smaller."

He calls /MES "the budget one, the budget futures," and stresses that nothing changes except the multiplier. "The way you trade it is exactly the same, except instead of multiplying by 50, you multiply by 5. So again, just look at the active contract, which will be expiring in March. So everything is the same."

He assembles the identical structure: the same 25-day expiration, the same 3760 long put, the same 3570 short put. "So we buy a put at the money, 3760, and sell the put at 3570."

**The /MES arithmetic.** "So now one contract will be $44.50 times five. And that will only be $222. So pretty affordable. If you lose everything, you only lose $222. But if it goes down, like you expect, you could make $700. So you're risking $200 to make $700. Again, risking $1 to make $3."

| Component | /ES version | /MES version |
|---|---|---|
| Spread quoted price | approximately $43.50 | $44.50 |
| Multiplier | ×50 | ×5 |
| Net debit / maximum loss | approximately $2,000 | approximately $222 |
| Maximum profit | approximately $7,000 | approximately $700 |
| Risk-reward | roughly 3.5 to 1 | roughly 3.2 to 1 |

The small difference in quoted spread price between the two products — $43.50 versus $44.50 — reflects the separate order books and slightly different liquidity of the two markets rather than any structural distinction. The economics are otherwise proportional at exactly ten to one.

He then applies the same realistic-exit reasoning: "in reality, we won't lose the entire $222. If it doesn't go our way, we cut loss, we lose maybe $100 or $150. So it's really affordable."

The significance of /MES for the student cannot be overstated. Under the two-per-cent position sizing rule, a $222 debit is permissible for an account of $11,100 or more, whereas the $2,000 /ES version requires an account of $100,000. The Micro E-mini is what makes a genuinely round-the-clock futures hedge accessible to an ordinary retail account, and it is why the instructor describes it as being for "a two thousand dollar account, three thousand dollar account" holder — though strictly, applying his own two-per-cent rule to a $222 debit would require closer to eleven thousand dollars, so the smaller account figures he mentions describe who the product was designed for rather than who can afford this specific spread under his own sizing rule.

#### Placing the Trade on the Interactive Brokers Mobile Application

The lesson closes with a walkthrough of the same trade on a second platform, which serves both to demystify the interface and to reinforce that the strategy is platform-independent.

The sequence he demonstrates is as follows. He opens the order ticket and searches for the symbol /ES, which returns the E-mini S&P 500 futures. From the results he selects "futures options chain and combo builder," explaining the choice: "this is the one I'll choose because I want to build a combo, which is a spread."

He selects the 12th of February expiration from the loaded chain, noting approvingly that Interactive Brokers displays the calendar date directly rather than requiring the Friday-inference used on the other platform.

He then enables the combo functionality: "you have to click this on, Strategy Builder. Turn this on. So this strategy builder will allow you to add multiple combos or multiple legs."

He addresses a display limitation that will otherwise obstruct the trade, since the 3570 strike sits far from the money: "if you don't see enough strikes, you want to create more strikes, click on this button here and you can choose all strikes or four strikes. Normally I choose all strikes. Time period, you can just leave it as maximum. And class, all classes — in other words, weekly and monthly options."

The two legs are then entered. "We're going to buy the 3760 put. So click ask to buy, click on this, and you can see the first leg appears. So now we sell the 3570. Let's scroll down to look for 3570. There we are. So we click bid to sell. Buy 3760, sell 3570."

He reviews the assembled order: "once we've got the two legs, click order, and it builds the order. So again, double check, we're buying the spread, which is buying the 3760, selling the 3570, and this will cost us one contract, right now the market price is 43.50."

And then he restates the multiplier rule one final time, because this is the moment at which a mistake would be irreversible: "again, this is the slash ES, so we have to take this and multiply by 50 to get the value of the contract. If you're trading the MES, then we multiply this by five, remember?"

On order type and price, he repeats the limit-order discipline established in the entry rules, together with the practice of negotiating: "you can put your limit order at the market price, or you can bargain by putting it lower. You can try $43 or $43.25 until it gets filled."

And on scaling: "this is one contract. If you buy two contracts, then just add two contracts, three contracts and so on and so forth." This is where the two-per-cent sizing rule enters the futures workflow — the number of contracts entered here is the number the risk budget permits, computed by dividing two per cent of net liquidation value by the per-contract debit.

The order is submitted with a slide gesture, and the lesson concludes with a summary of everything covered: "this concludes our lesson on bear put spreads. We've covered how to create bear put spreads on individual stocks, how to do it on the SPX index, SPY ETF, and finally how to trade options on the futures contract."

---

### Part Six: Synthesis — The Bear Put Spread as a Single Coherent System

Stepping back from the four lessons, what emerges is not four separate techniques but a single structure applied across four instrument classes with the parameters scaled to fit each.

The structure is invariant. In every case the trader buys an at-the-money or near-the-money put and simultaneously sells a further out-of-the-money put in the same expiration cycle, paying a net debit. In every case the maximum loss equals that debit, the maximum profit equals the spread width less the debit, and the breakeven sits at the long strike less the debit. In every case the expiration is chosen at twenty-five to thirty-two days, the long strike is placed near the market at fifty to sixty delta, and the short strike is placed at a target derived from either the platform's one-standard-deviation expected move or a prior swing low, with the two methods used to corroborate each other where possible. In every case the position is sized so that the net debit does not exceed two per cent of the account's net liquidation value, and rejected outright if that constraint cannot be met with a single contract. In every case the trade is only accepted if the resulting risk-reward is one to two or better. In every case the entry is a limit order placed after the open, or in the futures case at whatever hour the trader chooses. In every case profits are taken at eighty per cent of maximum, losses are cut at fifty per cent of maximum or at a technical invalidation such as a break above the previous swing high, and a gap-driven loss of eighty to ninety per cent is held rather than realised provided at least two weeks remain to expiration.

What varies across the four instruments is only scale and access.

| Instrument | Multiplier | Typical debit in the examples | Suits an account of roughly | Trading hours |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Individual equity (Cisco 48/46) | ×100 | $57 | $2,850 and up | 9:30–16:00 ET |
| Individual equity (Amber 53/44) | ×100 | $305 | $15,250 and up | 9:30–16:00 ET |
| SPY (375/356) | ×100 | $456 | $22,800 and up | 9:30–16:00 ET |
| SPX | ×100, ten times SPY notional | roughly ten times the SPY figure | $50,000–$100,000 and up per his guidance | 9:30–16:00 ET |
| /MES Micro E-mini (3760/3570) | ×5 | $222 | $11,100 and up | roughly 23¼ hours |
| /ES E-mini (3760/3570) | ×50 | approximately $2,000 | $100,000 and up | roughly 23¼ hours |

The account figures in that table are derived by applying the instructor's own two-per-cent rule to the debits he quotes, and they illustrate why the product ladder exists. The strategy does not change as an account grows; only the rung of the ladder does.

The final and most important reframing in the material is the shift from thinking about the bear put spread as a speculation to thinking about it as insurance. When it is placed on an individual stock in a confirmed downtrend after a rejection at resistance or a break of support, it is a directional trade and is judged as one — by its risk-reward ratio and its win rate. But when it is placed on SPY, SPX, /ES or /MES against a long-term investment portfolio during a bear market, it is something else. It is a recurring premium paid to convert an unbearable drawdown into a bearable one, renewed every twenty-five to thirty days for as long as the twenty EMA remains below the forty, rolled down the strike ladder as the market falls, and abandoned in full the moment the twenty crosses back above the forty.

The instructor's own summary of that function is the sentence around which the entire hedging half of this chapter is organised: he uses these spreads "to go short on the market, to make money as the market goes down, in order to create profits to hedge the short-term, unrealized losses on my long-term investments."

And his defence of the cost when the insurance is not needed is the sentence that makes the practice sustainable: "It's like buying insurance and the house started burning and then it recovered." The premiums you pay on hedges that expire worthless are not losses in the ordinary sense. They are the price of being able to hold your portfolio through the bear market that eventually does arrive — and, just as importantly, the price of being able to hold it through the many that do not.

# Part IV — Credit Spreads: Bull Put, Bear Call & Risk Management (+ Live Q&A)

## Credit Spreads — The Bull Put Spread, The Bear Call Spread, and Risk Management

### Part One: The Conceptual Shift From Debit to Credit

Everything taught up to this point in the course has been built on a single financial posture: the student was a net buyer of options. The bull call spread, used to express a bullish view, was constructed by buying a call near the money and selling a further call at the target price, using the premium collected from the sold call to defray the cost of the call that was bought. The bear put spread mirrored that construction on the downside. In both cases, once the two legs were netted against one another, money still left the account at the moment the position was opened. That outflow is what gives these structures their name. They are debit spreads, and the trader who uses them is, in the language of the market, a net buyer of options.

Credit spreads invert that posture completely. When a credit spread is opened, money comes *in*. The trader is a net seller of options, the broker deposits the net premium into the account on the day the trade is filled, and the entire subsequent life of the position is spent hoping that what was sold decays into worthlessness. This is not a cosmetic difference in cash flow. It changes the fundamental economics of the trade in three ways, and understanding those three ways is the whole point of the introduction to this section.

The first change concerns *how many outcomes pay you*. When a bull call spread is opened, there is exactly one scenario in which the trade makes money: the price must rise, and it must rise before the expiry date. If the stock goes sideways, the trade loses. If the stock rises only slightly, the trade loses. If the stock falls, the trade loses. Adam's own summary of the debit spread is blunt on this point — you make money in one scenario and you lose money in all the others. A credit spread is the opposite. With a bull put spread, if the price goes sideways you win, if the price rises a little you win, if the price rises a lot you win, and even if the price falls — provided it does not fall through the strike of the option you sold — you still win. There is, in his phrase, a wide zone of profits. That wide zone is the entire structural reason credit spreads carry a much higher win rate than debit spreads.

The second change concerns *the direction in which time flows*. A net buyer of options is fighting the clock. Every day that passes drains a little time value out of the long option, and the position must therefore be right not merely in direction but in direction *and speed*. A net seller of options has the clock as an ally. Every day that passes drains a little value out of the option that was sold, and that drainage is precisely the seller's profit. As Adam puts it, there is no concern about being right fast; in fact the longer it takes, the better it is for you. Nothing happening is not a neutral outcome for a credit spread. Nothing happening is the *best* outcome.

The third change concerns *what the edge actually is*. In a debit spread, the edge is directional forecasting: you are being paid to be correct about where price is going. In a credit spread, the edge is probabilistic: you are being paid to be correct about where price will *not* go. Those are very different bets. It is a great deal easier to say with confidence that a stock trading at $82.55 will not fall below $70 within forty-two days than it is to say that the same stock will rise to a particular level within the same window. The credit spread converts the trader's job from prediction into probability estimation, and the option chain — through the delta column — hands the trader a live estimate of that probability on every strike.

There is a fourth point which is less about economics than about survival, and it deserves to be stated early because it explains why the strategy has two legs rather than one. A trader who merely sold a put and stopped there would be short an unhedged obligation. If the stock collapsed, the loss would be limited only by the distance from the strike to zero. Adam's insistence throughout the course — and repeated forcefully in the live webinar — is that options must never be sold naked. Never sell calls naked, never sell puts naked; that, he says, is how people go bankrupt and lose their houses. The second leg of a credit spread exists to convert an open-ended obligation into a defined-risk position. The best metaphor he offers is the insurance business. When you sell the put, you are the insurance company writing a policy for someone who owns the stock and is afraid it will fall; you collect the premium from that customer. Then you take a portion of the premium you just collected and you buy *reinsurance* — a further out-of-the-money put — so that if the catastrophe actually arrives, your own liability is capped and someone further down the chain absorbs the tail. You still make money up front, but you have bounded the disaster. That is the whole architecture of a defined-risk credit spread in one sentence.

There are exactly two credit spreads in this section of the course. The first, labelled strategy 1A, is the **bull put spread**, deployed when the trader is bullish. The second, labelled 1B, is the **bear call spread**, deployed when the trader is bearish. Adam is unusually candid about the split between them: 99.9% of the time he trades only 1A. He hardly ever trades bear call spreads, and the reason is structural rather than aesthetic. The market spends most of its life going up. Using a bear call spread means wanting the market to fall while the market's natural drift is upward, which is trading against the tide. He reserves bear call spreads for genuine bear markets — the sort of environment that arrives, in his estimate, once every five or six years — and teaches the strategy anyway in case a student's temperament suits the bearish side better than his own.

#### The bull put spread in outline

The bull put spread is executed on a stock that is in a clear uptrend. Adam defines the uptrend with moving averages, and the definition is worth committing to memory because it recurs at every stage of the strategy. The short-term trend is up when the 20-period exponential moving average (drawn as the red dotted line on his charts) is above the 40-period exponential moving average (the blue dotted line). The medium-term trend is up when the 50-period moving average (the solid blue line) is above the 150-period moving average (the green line). When both conditions hold simultaneously, the trend is strong in both timeframes and the stock is a legitimate candidate.

But an uptrend alone is not an entry. Prices move in waves — up, down, up, down — and the timing rule is that the bull put spread is executed when the price has waved *down* into a level of support, not when it is sitting at a high. Adam's reasoning is entirely about the geometry of what happens next: after an impulsive wave up, the probable next move is a pullback, and entering a bullish credit spread just before a pullback is asking to have your short strike tested. Entering after the pullback, ideally where price is touching a moving average that has repeatedly acted as support, means the stock has already done the falling and is unlikely to fall much further. He would not do this at a new high; he waits for price to come back down nearer the moving average first.

With that setup in place, the mechanics are simple. Sell an out-of-the-money put below the current price, which collects premium. Then, because you have no desire to actually own the shares, buy a second put further out of the money — further down — with the same expiration date, which caps the risk of the first. Because the put you buy is further from the money than the put you sold, it costs less than what you collected. Net, money comes in. That net inflow is the credit, and the position is a put spread because both legs are puts with the same expiry.

The profit mechanism follows directly. Because you are a net seller and you have already been paid, you maximise the profit by having both options decay toward worthlessness. As long as the stock price rises, moves sideways, or even falls somewhat — provided it does not go below the strike of the put you sold — the sold option will expire worthless, the bought option will expire worthless, and you keep the entire credit collected on day one.

#### The bear call spread in outline

The bear call spread is the mirror image and is executed on a stock in a clear downtrend, defined by the same moving averages in reverse sequence: the 20 EMA below the 40 EMA for the short term, and the 50 below the 150 for the medium term. The waves run the other way too — the entry is taken when price has waved *up* into a resistance level and looks ready to resume the decline.

The construction is to sell a call above the current price, which is superficially like a covered call except that no shares are owned, and then — precisely because no shares are owned and the position cannot be left naked — to buy a second call further above that to cap the risk. The call bought further out of the money costs less than the call sold nearer the money, so once again money comes in net. As long as the stock falls, goes sideways, or even rises somewhat without exceeding the strike of the call that was sold, both options decay toward worthlessness and the full credit is retained.

---

### Part Two: The Bull Put Spread in Full — Construction, Entry Rules, and the Arithmetic

#### The market filter before the stock filter

Before any individual stock is considered, Adam applies a top-down filter. He wants the overall market to be bullish in the first place, and he quantifies that with the same medium-term test he uses on stocks: the S&P 500 should have its 50-period moving average above its 150-period moving average. When that condition holds, the index is on a medium-term uptrend, and a bullish credit spread is being placed with the prevailing current rather than against it.

Only then does the individual name matter. The stock itself must show the full moving-average sequence — 20 EMA above the 40 EMA on the short term, 50 above the 150 on the medium term — and it must be *retracing into support* rather than extended at a high. His own phrasing on the timing is emphatic and repeated: never do this during the wave up, because what usually follows a wave up is a drop. Wait for the drop first, and then execute, so that the probability of further downside is small and the probability of a rebound is large. Ideally the retracement lands on something structural, and his preferred structure is the 50-period moving average, which on the charts he shows has a visible history of acting as a springboard.

#### The volatility filter

Because the trader is a net seller, expensive options are good news. High implied volatility means richer premiums, and richer premiums mean more credit collected for the same structural risk. The metric used is the **IV percentile** (equivalently, IV rank on Interactive Brokers), which compares current implied volatility to its own range over the trailing period rather than to some absolute standard. The threshold Adam gives is **35% or higher**, stated as an ideal rather than an absolute requirement. In the live GLD trade, Bang restates this as explicitly nice-to-have rather than mandatory: a reading above 35% or even 40% is considered good, but the trade is still valid on the credit-to-width test alone. The higher the implied volatility, the higher the premiums, and the better the trade.

#### Selecting the short put: delta as a probability dial

This is the heart of the strategy and the single most important numeric rule in the section. The short put — the option you sell — is chosen not by price, not by "feel", and not by picking a round number, but by **delta between 20 and 25**.

The reason is that delta, for this purpose, is a probability estimate. A 20-delta put carries roughly a 20% chance that the price will expire below that strike, which means an 80% chance that it will not. A 25-delta put carries roughly a 25% chance of finishing below, meaning a 75% chance of not. The strike is therefore chosen by dialling in the desired win rate. Choose 20 delta and the theoretical win rate is 80%; choose 25 delta and it is 75%. Everything else about the trade — the credit, the width, the risk-reward — is downstream of this one decision, because the delta chosen *is* the probability that the trade works.

Within that 20-to-25 band, the lower delta is the safer one. Bang states the preference directly in the GLD lesson: "the lower is safer," because a lower delta corresponds to a strike further from the money, and a strike further from the money is harder for the stock to reach. Adam expresses the same preference in a different way when choosing an expiry: among several acceptable candidates he likes to choose the one where the short strike sits as low as possible, because the lower it is, the less likely the price is to get there.

#### Selecting the long put: the hedge leg

Once the short put has been chosen by delta, the long put is chosen by *distance*, not by delta. Adam is explicit that you do not need to look at the delta of the put you buy at all — you only look at the delta of the put you sell. The long put goes **one or two strikes lower** than the short put, with the same expiration date.

Whether to go one strike or two is decided by trial and error on the platform. Both are legitimate; the trader tests each and takes whichever produces the better combination of credit and risk. Bang, working on GLD where the strikes are spaced $1 apart because the underlying is enormously liquid, frames the same rule in dollar terms rather than strike-count terms: he buys the protective put roughly **$5 or $10 below** the short put, and in that instance chose $5 for simplicity. In practice, on stocks whose strikes are spaced $5 apart, "one strike lower" and "$5 wide" are the same instruction.

#### The credit test: the 1-to-4 rule and the 20%-of-width rule

Having chosen both legs, the trader must now check whether the trade is worth doing at all, and this is where Adam introduces the rule he tells students to write down: **for every $1 of credit received, the maximum risk must not exceed $4.** Less than $4 is excellent. More than $4 disqualifies the trade.

The reason is that the maximum loss on a defined-risk vertical is also the buying power the broker will block, which makes it the capital committed. If $4 of capital is committed to earn $1 of credit, the return on capital is 25%, and that 25% is earned within the 30-to-45-day holding window. Anything worse than 1-to-4 fails to clear his minimum return on capital hurdle. Anything better than 1-to-4 — a risk of $3 or $3.50 per dollar of credit — improves the return.

Bang states the identical test from the other end, in a form that is often easier to apply at the option chain: **collect at least 20% of the width of the spread**. On a $5-wide spread, 20% of the width is $1.00, so the minimum acceptable credit is $1.00. On a $10-wide spread the minimum would be $2.00. The two formulations are the same rule seen from opposite sides, because a $1.00 credit on a $5 spread leaves $4.00 of risk, which is exactly the 1-to-4 boundary. Bang's version generalises cleanly to any width the trader chooses: "you can choose a $5 spread, you can choose a $10 spread, or you can choose whatever spread you want, as long as you can collect at least 20% of the strike difference."

This test is not a formality. It is the reason trades get abandoned mid-execution. In the live NET trade, when the fill price slipped to $0.84 of credit against $4.16 of risk, the ratio became roughly 5-to-1 and Adam refused to take the trade at all, stating that a dollar of credit was the lowest he was willing to accept: "either one dollar or nothing."

#### Expiration window

The date to expiration is **30 to 45 days**. In the summary lesson Adam narrows the ideal to 30 to 40 days, and in practice across the case studies the entries land between 29 and 42 days. The band is genuinely a band and not a single number: in the live NET trade he lists three acceptable candidates on the chain — 19 February at 20 days, 26 February at 35 days, and 5 March at 42 days — and notes that all three would be fine, that he experiments among them by trial and error to see which offers the best risk-to-reward, and that he prefers the one whose short strike sits lowest for a given delta.

Two considerations push in opposite directions inside this window. A longer expiry collects more premium, which is why in the CRWV trade he chose the 39-day expiry over the 31-day one — "usually I like to choose the one that's further date to expiration, so I collect more premium." But a longer expiry also holds capital hostage for longer and raises the chance of crossing an earnings announcement.

#### The earnings prohibition

This is an absolute rule and it applies to every vertical spread, not just the bull put spread. **Do not enter a trade whose expiry falls after the stock's next earnings announcement.** The reason is gap risk. When a company reports, the price can jump or collapse overnight. If it collapses through the short put strike while the market is closed, there is no opportunity to cut the loss at the intended level, and the trade can lose far more than the planned amount — potentially the full maximum loss.

Bang adds an important refinement. It is technically acceptable to enter a trade that spans an earnings date *if* you commit to exiting before the announcement. But even then there is a hidden cost: options retain most of their value until the event, so if you close before earnings you will not have captured much decay, and the trade will not have made a good profit even if the direction was right. The clean rule is therefore to avoid the situation entirely. GLD, being a gold ETF with no earnings date at all, is used as the example of a candidate that is structurally immune to this problem.

Adam adds the management-side corollary: if earnings are coming up and you are still in a trade, close it before the announcement whether you are up, down, or flat. "Whether it's a small loss or a break even or making some profit, just close the trade. Just be safe."

#### The sector prohibition

Alongside earnings, Adam gives a categorical sector exclusion which he tells students to write down: **never trade this strategy on biotech or pharmaceutical companies.** The reason is the same gap risk in a more chronic form. These companies live and die on binary drug-trial outcomes, and they have a tendency to gap violently as trials pass or fail. In the live scan he runs, he strikes out BIIB and BNTX on sight purely on sector grounds, without even looking at their charts. "Never trade stocks in this sector."

#### The universe filter

The stocks that qualify are large, liquid, and heavily optioned. The specific criteria Adam encodes into his scanner are:

| Filter | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Share price | at least $50 | Below this the premium collected per contract is too small, forcing more contracts and more commissions to reach the same credit |
| Market capitalisation | at least $20 billion | Large companies only; no speculative small caps |
| Average volume | at least 1 million shares per day | Ensures liquidity in the underlying |
| IV percentile | 35% or higher | Ensures options are expensive enough to be worth selling |
| Options available | optionable stocks only, ideally with weekly series as well as monthly | Weekly series are a proxy for high option liquidity and give a wider choice of expiries |

The preference for names that offer weekly expirations, not just monthly ones, recurs in the Q&A: Bang uses the presence of a weekly option series as a direct liquidity signal, noting that among the thirty Dow components a name like Travelers lacks weeklies and correspondingly shows a wide bid-ask spread.

---

### Part Three: The NET Trade — Every Number Explained

The teaching example that carries the theory is a real trade on Cloudflare, ticker NET, executed on 22 January. It is worth walking through slowly, because every rule above appears in it.

**Why the setup qualified.** NET was in a clear uptrend on both timeframes: the 20 EMA above the 40 EMA for the short term, the 50 above the 150 for the medium term. Price had waved up, waved down, and retraced to a support level. Adam is honest that the entry was not perfect — ideally he would have entered at the very bottom of the retracement, but by the time he saw it price had already lifted off the low. He took it anyway to have a live example to teach with, noting that it was still acceptable because price remained relatively near the support, and that he would categorically not have taken it at a new high.

**The chain.** He chose the 5 March expiry, which was 42 days out from the 22 January trade date. The IV percentile on the day was in the mid-to-high fifties — quoted as 56% in one place and 58% in another as the reading moved intraday — comfortably above the 35% threshold and therefore excellent conditions for selling.

**The legs.** He sold the 70-strike put, which carried a delta of 21, sitting squarely in the 20-to-25 band. The bid-ask on that put was $2.15 by $2.97, and his order filled at **$2.68**, in between the two. He then bought the 65-strike put, one strike lower, which carried a delta of 15 — noted only in passing, since the long leg is not selected by delta — and paid **$1.57**, again a fill between the bid and ask.

**The arithmetic.** The following table sets out every derived quantity in the trade and how it is computed.

| Quantity | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Premium received (short 70 put) | — | $2.68 per share, $268 per contract |
| Premium paid (long 65 put) | — | $1.57 per share, $157 per contract |
| Net credit = maximum profit | premium received − premium paid | $1.11 per share, **$111 per contract** |
| Spread width | 70 − 65 | $5.00 |
| Maximum loss = buying power used | width − net credit, times 100 | $5.00 − $1.11 = $3.89, **$389 per contract** |
| Risk-to-credit ratio | 3.89 ÷ 1.11 | **3.50 to 1** (passes the 1-to-4 test) |
| Return on capital if held to max profit | 111 ÷ 389 | **28.5% in 42 days** |
| Break-even at expiration | short strike − net credit | 70 − 1.11 = **$68.89** |
| Probability of finishing below the short strike | delta of short put | 21% |
| Theoretical win rate | 100% − 21% | **79%** |

The current price at the time of the analysis was $82.55, so the short strike at 70 sat roughly 15% below the market. The distance is the point. As long as NET rose, went sideways, or fell — but did not reach or breach $70 by expiration — the position collected its maximum profit of $111.

**The objection, and the answer.** Adam anticipates the obvious complaint, because it is the standard reason people dislike this strategy: why would anyone risk $389 to make $111? Why make $1 to lose $4? He calls it a legitimate question and gives a two-part answer.

The first part is that the $4 loss is not the loss you actually take. The maximum loss is only realised if the trade is left completely unmanaged — if you let the price collapse through the short strike and hold to expiration without acting. That will not be allowed to happen. Under the risk-management rules, a losing trade is closed long before that point, and the realised loss is dramatically smaller.

The second part is the win rate. A strategy that wins 75-80% of the time and loses roughly what it wins on the occasions it fails is a very profitable strategy, even though it looks unattractive when only the maximum figures are compared.

#### What the loss actually looks like — the point of no return

The exit trigger is stated with no ambiguity: **cut the loss the moment the price reaches the strike price of the short put.** Adam calls the short strike "the point of no return." For the NET trade, that level is $70.

The interesting part is how much is lost at that level, because the answer changes as time passes. This is where the profit-and-loss simulation in the analysis tab earns its keep. The green line on the chart is the profit and loss at expiration, which the trader will never actually reach because the position gets closed first. The purple (or black) line is the profit and loss *today*, or on whatever date the trader sets in the simulator. As the calendar advances, the purple line migrates upward toward the green line, and because it migrates upward, the loss taken at the point of no return shrinks.

Running the NET simulation on the trade as analysed in the theory lesson produced the following:

| Date the short strike is touched | Days elapsed of the 42 | Loss if closed at $70 | Loss as a multiple of the $111 credit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22 January (entry day) | 0 | $121 | ~1.1x |
| 22 February | ~30 | $82.90 | ~0.75x |
| 4 March (day before expiry) | 41 | $12.89 | ~0.12x |

The pattern is the entire argument for the strategy's risk profile. On day one, hitting the stop costs about as much as the credit — a roughly one-to-one loser against a roughly one-to-one winner, but with a 79% win rate attached. Thirty days in, hitting the stop costs *less* than the credit, so the loser is smaller than the winner *and* the win rate is 79%. On the eve of expiry, hitting the stop costs almost nothing.

A parallel simulation run three days later in the rules lesson, on the same position, gave slightly different figures because the market had moved: $126.20 if the strike was touched on 25 January, $113 if touched on 10 February, and only $22 if touched on 4 March. And the live execution session, running the numbers on the actual fill, produced a third set: $71 if the price dropped to $70 immediately, and $65 if it dropped there on 22 February. These figures differ because the underlying's price, implied volatility, and the exact fill all shifted between the recordings; the shape of the relationship — smaller and smaller losses as expiry approaches — is identical in all three, and that shape is what matters.

**The one warning attached to the simulation.** The purple line is not only a function of time. It is also a function of implied volatility. Adam demonstrates this by shocking volatility upward in the analysis tool: with a 20% increase in volatility, the purple line drops, meaning the loss at the point of no return becomes larger. With a 50% increase it drops much further. This is one of the strongest arguments for the IV percentile filter. If you enter when implied volatility is already high, it is unlikely to go much higher, and the volatility component of your short-term risk is largely spent. If you enter when the IV percentile is 20, a volatility spike can enlarge your loss materially before time decay has had a chance to help you.

---

### Part Four: The Live Execution — Order Entry, Fills, and Broker Mechanics

The live trade recorded on 22 January is valuable less for the setup, which repeats the NET analysis, than for what it shows about the gap between the price on the screen and the price you actually get.

#### Working the order down

Adam opened the 5 March chain on Think or Swim, confirmed the IV percentile at 58%, and located the only strike in the 20-to-25 delta band, which was the 70 put. He notes there is no 25-delta strike available, so the choice is effectively made for him. He then tested the two candidate hedges — buy the 65, or buy the 60 — as trial and error, and the 70/65 combination showed a **$1.21** credit on screen.

He ran that through the confirm-and-send dialog to check the ratio before transmitting. The dialog reported a maximum profit of $121 and a maximum loss of $379, giving a risk of $3.13 per dollar of credit. That comfortably passes the 1-to-4 test, and he judged it a very good trade — with the caveat that "it remains to be seen if we can get the order filled."

What followed is the practical education. The order at $1.21 did not fill; the market was at $1.19. He lowered to $1.19, checked the ratio again ($3.81 of risk against $1.19 of credit, or 3.2 to 1) and confirmed it still passed. Still no fill; the market had moved to $1.15. He tried $1.16, rechecking the ratio each time. Then the displayed market fell to $0.84, at which point he stopped and did the arithmetic in front of the student: $0.84 of credit against $4.16 of risk is a ratio of roughly five to one. "Not worth it." He declared a hard floor — at least $1.00 of credit, "either one dollar or nothing" — placed the order there, and was filled.

The realised fill was **$1.11**, better than the $1.00 he was prepared to accept. That is the number that carries forward as the trade's actual credit: sold the 70 put, bought the 65 put, collected $111 per contract.

The lesson embedded in that sequence is that the displayed mid-price is an aspiration, not a quote you are entitled to. The correct procedure is to start high, lower the limit incrementally, and re-verify the credit-to-risk ratio at every step, abandoning the trade entirely if the ratio breaks the 1-to-4 boundary rather than chasing a fill.

Alongside the new position, the screen showed his existing book: one open credit spread up $684, total open profit of $3,004, and an account up roughly $3,400 in the first twenty days of January — offered as evidence that this is a routine, repeated activity rather than a one-off demonstration.

#### Closing a credit spread — the direction of the money

Adam repeats a point that trips up new traders: **you open a credit spread for a credit, and you close it for a debit.** Money comes in at entry and money goes out at exit. The profit is the difference between the two, and since you sold the spread expensively and buy it back cheaply, anything you pay back below the original credit is profit.

He demonstrates on an existing open position in a name transcribed as CHDR. He had opened it a couple of weeks earlier for a **$0.95** credit. Time had passed, the options had decayed, and the spread was now worth **$0.02** — an unrealised profit of **$832** across his position size, very near the maximum. To close it on Think or Swim he highlights the position, right-clicks (or, on a Mac, taps with two fingers on the trackpad), selects "create closing order," and chooses to buy it back. He tries a $0.03 debit; it does not fill; and he shrugs — he is not desperate, and if he were, he would raise the debit to four cents, five cents, six cents until it filled.

He also states his general preference on expiry, which is elaborated further in the risk-management lesson: he does not like to let positions expire worthless even when they are deep out of the money. He prefers to buy them back for a small debit, because it is safer.

#### Interactive Brokers: the sign convention

Interactive Brokers uses a different and initially confusing convention, and Adam relates that he learned it the hard way by getting it wrong when he started.

On IBKR, when *opening* a credit spread, **the price must be entered as a negative number, because negative means credit**. He replicates the same NET trade on the IBKR option chain: same symbol, same 5 March expiry (shown as 41 days), open the strategy builder because more than one leg is involved, sell the 70 by clicking the bid, buy the 65 by clicking the ask, set quantity to one contract, always use a limit price, and enter the price as negative to match the $1.11 credit obtained on the other platform. His warning is emphatic: if you do not put the negative sign, you will pay money instead of receiving it, and you will lose money the instant the trade opens. If the platform offers you a positive market price, do not accept it, because positive means you are paying.

To *close* on IBKR, the position is highlighted, right-clicked, and closed — and here the convention inverts in meaning if not in sign: **when closing, negative means debit**. He demonstrates on an open Amazon spread that had been opened for a **$1.75** credit and had since decayed to **$0.61**, showing about **$1,100** of unrealised profit. Entering minus 75 cents to close would mean paying $0.75 to exit, still leaving a dollar of profit — but he does not want that; he wants to wait until the spread is trading around $0.20, at which point he would close for a minus-0.20 debit and keep nearly the full credit.

Bang, working in the same platform on GLD, offers the cleanest way through the confusion: **ignore the plus and minus signs entirely and read the letter.** When the order preview shows a green **C**, you are receiving a credit, which is correct for opening. When it shows a red **D**, you are paying a debit, which is correct for closing. "Just focus on C or D and ignore the plus or minus sign."

Adam's broader counsel on the whole issue is to pick one broker and stay with it, precisely so that the terminology stops being a source of error. The point is reinforced later when the same closing action is described as "buying back the bull put spread" on Think or Swim and "selling the bull put spread" on Interactive Brokers — the same economic act with opposite verbs.

---

### Part Five: The Complete Rulebook and the Scan

#### Finding candidates

Candidates can be found by eye, but Adam demonstrates a scanner on Think or Swim, reached through Scan and then Stock Hacker. He notes an Option Hacker exists and can screen specifically for spreads with far more granularity, but says he keeps it simple. Four filters are added through the "Add filter" control, which distinguishes stock filters, option filters, fundamental filters, and study filters:

1. **Stock closing price**, minimum $50, added as a stock filter.
2. **Market capitalisation**, minimum 20,000 — the field is denominated in millions, so this is $20 billion — added as a fundamental filter.
3. **IV percentile**, set from 35 to 200, added as a study filter under volatility.
4. **Average volume**, minimum one million shares, added as a study filter.

The scan is then restricted to optionable stocks rather than all stocks, and run. He notes that more filters could be added — one could encode the moving-average sequence directly, requiring the 20 above the 40 and the 50 above the 150 — but he prefers to do that part visually.

The results are saved to a dated watchlist and reviewed as daily candles over a six-month window, with the chart panel synchronised to the watchlist so that clicking a symbol brings up its chart. The review he narrates on 25 January is the most instructive part of the lesson, because it shows how many scan hits get rejected and why:

- **Amazon** — a genuine uptrend, but currently consolidating in an up-down-up-down chop rather than sitting on support. He rejects a fresh entry because from a mid-range position it could still fall. He notes he is already up about $500 on an Amazon position entered earlier, when it *was* at support.
- **Alibaba** — rejected, because the 20 is below the 40 and the uptrend is therefore not confirmed. "A bit risky to take that one."
- **Baidu** — the chart shows the ideal pattern historically (wave up, wave down, bounce at support), but price has already flown up from support, so entering now would be entering high. Rejected on timing.
- **BIIB** and **BNTX** — rejected instantly on the biotech prohibition, without further analysis.
- **DDOG** — already in the book, entered at the support bounce and now showing about $700 of profit. He would not enter it fresh at the current extended level.
- **GSX** — rejected, not a clear uptrend.
- **LBRDK** — accepted as an interesting candidate. Clear wave structure, bouncing, roughly halfway back up rather than fully extended, and an IV percentile of 38%, above the 35% threshold.
- **NET** — the position he had just entered a couple of days earlier, found through exactly this process.
- **PINS (Pinterest)** — acceptable, on the condition that the short strike is placed below the visible support level.
- **PLUG** — rejected as too extended; he wants it to fall back to the strong support visible lower on the chart.
- **PYPL** — rejected as a bit too high, despite being in an uptrend.
- **SNAP** — the ideal entry had already passed; still acceptable but a worse entry than it would have been at the low.
- **SPOT** — an acceptable uptrend with the right wave structure, already moving up off the low.

The general principle he draws out of the exercise is the discipline of refusal: "Don't force a trade. Only take trades when they're great. If they're not great, skip it. You're not forced to take a trade."

#### The full entry procedure, in order

Assembling everything, the procedure to enter a bull put spread runs as follows.

1. **Identify a bullish setup** on a stock or ETF: the broad market on a medium-term uptrend (S&P 50 above 150), the underlying itself with the 20 EMA above the 40 EMA and the 50 above the 150, and price retracing into a support level rather than extended at a high. The name must be a large company of at least $20 billion market capitalisation, trading at least a million shares a day, priced at $50 or more, offering both monthly and weekly option series, and ideally showing an IV percentile of 35% or better. It must not be a biotech or pharmaceutical company.
2. **Choose a date to expiration** between 30 and 45 days, verifying first that no earnings announcement falls before that expiry.
3. **Select the short put** at a delta of −20 to −25, which sets the theoretical win probability at 75-80%.
4. **Select the long put** one or two strikes lower (equivalently, about $5 or $10 below on a widely spaced chain), with the same expiration, testing both distances to see which produces the better package.
5. **Verify the credit test** before transmitting: the maximum loss must not exceed four times the net credit, equivalently the credit must be at least 20% of the spread width, equivalently the return on the committed capital must be at least 25% over the 30-to-45-day window. Remember that the maximum loss is also the buying power the broker will block.
6. **Size the position** so that the *realistic* loss — 1.5 times the net credit, not the maximum loss — is no more than 3% of the account's net liquidation value.
7. **Check the risk-and-return profile** in the analysis tab before committing, simulating what the loss would be if the stock fell to the short strike today, in ten days, in fifteen days, and just before expiration, and additionally shocking implied volatility upward to see how much worse a volatility spike would make an early loss.
8. **Place a limit order, never a market order.** Start at the midpoint or even at the ask — as high as possible — and lower the limit incrementally until filled, re-verifying at every step that the credit still satisfies the 1-to-4 rule. If the ratio breaks, abandon the trade. On Interactive Brokers, confirm the order shows a credit.

---

### Part Six: Trade Management — Taking Profit and Cutting Loss

#### Monitoring cadence

The position must be looked at **at least once a day**. Adam is insistent that this is not a set-and-forget strategy: "please don't forget about it." Any time after the market opens is acceptable, including a couple of hours after the open. Over the long run he expects to close roughly 20-25% of positions for a loss and 75-80% for a profit, which is simply the delta-selected win rate expressing itself.

#### The three reasons to close

**Reason one: the stock reaches the short put strike.** This is the point of no return, and the instruction is unconditional — the moment it reaches there, close the trade, no questions asked. He extends the trigger slightly forward in time as well: if it looks like the strike will be reached very soon, by the next day, just close it. Executed at that level, the expected loss is roughly **1.5 times the credit received**. Collect $100, expect to lose about $150.

**Reason two: earnings are approaching.** If the stock is going to report and there is any risk that the price could gap below the short strike, close the trade — at a small loss, at break-even, or at a partial profit, whichever it happens to be.

**Reason three, and the best one: the profit is substantially banked.** This is the profit-taking rule, and it is expressed in terms of *percentage of the credit decayed*, not dollars. Once the spread has lost about **90%** of its opening value — meaning about 90% of the maximum profit has been realised — Adam closes. He does not try to squeeze out the last of it.

He also closes considerably earlier than 90% in a specific circumstance: when a large fraction of the profit has arrived in a small fraction of the time. If 80% of the profit is already realised with twenty days still to run, he will close to free the capital and redeploy it into a fresh position where a full new credit can be collected.

Bang formalises exactly the same idea into a time-versus-profit ratio: **if more than half of the maximum profit has been earned in less than half of the time, exit.** His reasoning is that the return on investment is enhanced by recycling capital — there is no sense waiting two more weeks to earn the final third when two-thirds is already in hand — and, crucially, that while you remain in the trade the risk is still live. "The moment you are still in the trade, that means the risk is still there. Just better close the trade to lock in the profit and run." He allows that a more patient trader might hold for 60% or 75% of the maximum, and calls that a matter of personal tolerance.

#### Worked profit-taking decisions

The risk-management lesson walks through a live book on 25 January and makes the decision explicitly for each position. (Adam notes in passing that the positions shown are actually "bull put spread extreme" trades, a modification of the base strategy taught in a later lesson, but that the management is essentially the same.)

| Position | Expiry | Opening credit | Current value | Percentage of profit captured | Unrealised P&L | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon | 5 February (~10 days out) | $1.68 | $0.62 | ~64% | +$400 | Hold. Wait for the spread to reach roughly $0.17, which is a 90% decay from $1.68 |
| Second position | — | $0.95 | $0.47 | ~50% | +$400 | Hold; roughly another $400 still to be made |
| DDOG | 19 February (25 days out) | $1.10 | $0.19 | ~80% | +$700 | **Close.** No point waiting another 25 days for the final 20%; free the capital and open a new position |

The DDOG decision is the cleanest illustration of the principle. Twenty-five days of remaining risk exposure is a poor price to pay for the last fifth of the profit when four-fifths is already sitting there.

#### The prohibition on holding to expiration

Adam refuses to let credit spreads expire, even ones that are far out of the money and apparently certain to expire worthless. The risk he is protecting against is a last-moment gap: if the price collapses after the market closes near expiry, a position that looked safe can produce a large loss with no chance to react. His rule is to always close before expiration — options expire on a Friday at 4 p.m. Eastern, so at the latest close that day, and preferably the day before.

He states the danger in its sharpest form as a standing warning: **you can lose more than four times your net credit if you allow the trade to expire below your short strike.** The bounded maximum loss assumes an orderly close; assignment mechanics and gap risk around expiry can exceed it. Do not take that risk.

#### Adjustment and rolling

On the question of adjusting a losing position, the course is deliberately restrictive at this level. Bang answers the general question in the webinar by pointing out that every strategy taught specifies its entry point, exit point, and adjustment criteria before the trade is placed, and that the trader's job in the trade is to follow the plan rather than let ego or emotion produce improvisation — "that would be a perfect setup for disaster."

Adam then states the level-one position plainly: **the strategies taught in this course do not require adjustments.** Adjustments belong to the advanced strategies — iron condors, iron butterflies, and the rest of the advanced course. In the basic course, the management is binary: hold to the profit target, or close at the short strike. He acknowledges that some traders are content to sit through to the maximum loss, and says that if that is genuinely acceptable to them, they may; but if it is not, the rule is to stick to the game plan and cut early.

The nearest thing to a roll taught in this section belongs to the covered-call strategy rather than the credit spread, and Adam explains it in the webinar for completeness. If a short covered call is out of the money at expiry, let it expire worthless and do nothing. If it is at the money or in the money and you do not want your shares called away, then before expiration you buy back the short call and simultaneously sell another call further out of the money at a further expiration date. You lose money on the call you buy back, but you make more on the appreciated long shares, so the net is still positive.

#### Assignment risk

Assignment is the risk that most preoccupies new sellers, and the course's answer is that it is technically real but practically remote.

The mechanism, explained through a question about a SPY put spread with a 288 long put and a 281 short put, is this. Early assignment on a short option is irrational for the option's holder as long as that option still carries extrinsic value, because exercising early forfeits that extrinsic value. The holder would be giving up money. So while time remains and the option retains extrinsic value, early assignment is very unlikely.

And if it happens anyway, it is not a catastrophe — it is, in that particular case, the maximum profit arriving early. If the short 281 put is assigned, you are put 100 shares of SPY at $281. But you still hold the long 288 put, which you can exercise to sell 100 shares at $288. The long shares and the short shares neutralise each other, and you are left having bought at 281 and sold at 288 — the full width of the spread. As Bang puts it: low probability of happening, and even in that case you get the maximum profit.

Mechanically, exercising the long leg is done by the trader, not the broker: in the platform, right-click the specific option (or two-finger tap on a Mac trackpad), choose exercise from the drop-down menu, and it converts. The reminder attached to it is that exercising always forfeits the remaining extrinsic value, which is why neither instructor does it voluntarily.

How often does this actually occur? Bang, with twelve years of options trading behind him at the time of the webinar, reports that he has *never* had a short option assigned. Adam's comment: "If you ever get assigned, go buy the lottery."

One asymmetry is worth flagging, and it appears in the dividend discussion. Once an ex-dividend date is confirmed, option pricing has already incorporated the expected price adjustment. But a holder of a call option that is in the money may rationally exercise early *specifically to capture the dividend* by converting the call into long shares before the ex-date. This means early assignment risk is materially higher on short *calls* around dividends than it is on short *puts*. Bang's summary: watch out when you trade the call side around dividends; on the put side you do not have to worry about that.

---

### Part Seven: Risk Management — Position Sizing and Portfolio Construction

This is, by Adam's own framing, the part of the lesson where accounts are saved or destroyed. His warning is direct: the strategy is genuinely powerful and can make a great deal of money, and there are exactly two ways to lose money with it. The first is failing to follow the rules — specifically, failing to cut the loss when the rules say to cut. The second is overtrading: taking too many contracts, so that when a losing trade arrives it does disproportionate damage.

The statistical foundation of the warning is worth stating carefully. A 75% win rate means that 25% of trades lose. In a hundred trades, twenty-five will be losers. **Those losses do not arrive politely spaced out.** They can arrive consecutively. If the size is too large and the losers cluster, the account can be wiped out by a strategy whose long-run expectancy is positive. Everything in this section exists to make a losing streak survivable.

#### The unit of risk is the realistic loss, not the maximum loss

The critical modelling decision is that position size is computed from the **1.5x credit realistic loss**, not from the 4x credit maximum loss. If the net credit is $100, the maximum loss is $400 but the *actual risk*, given that the trade will be cut at the short strike, is $150.

#### The 3% rule

**Risk a maximum of 3% of the account's net liquidation value on any single trade.** Net liquidation value is the total capital of the account as the broker reports it, and it is visible on the account summary on any platform.

The arithmetic is then mechanical. For a $10,000 account, 3% is $300. If each contract carries a $100 credit and therefore a $150 realistic loss, then $300 divided by $150 gives **two contracts**. That is the position size. Worked in the other direction, if the position size is fixed at two contracts, the credit per contract must be $200 for a $10,000 account to be risking its full 3% allowance — which is the assumption used later in the expectancy calculation.

Adam shows the same computation against his own live accounts. His Think or Swim account showed a net liquidation value of **$112,000**, giving a maximum risk per trade of 3% × $112,000 = roughly **$3,000**. He then turns to his Interactive Brokers account, which he describes as around $2 million in net liquidation value; the corresponding per-trade risk figure spoken in the transcript is garbled by the transcription and cannot be reliably reconstructed, so it is not reproduced here — but the method is unchanged, and 3% of a $2 million account would be $60,000 per trade. He closes with the reminder that 3% is a ceiling, not a target: "you can risk 1% or 2%, but not more than 3%."

#### Concurrent positions and correlated ruin

Having sized each trade, the second question is how many trades to run simultaneously. Adam's answer is refreshingly honest about what the constraint actually is: "It depends on how strong your heart is." Since each position risks 3%, the worst-case aggregate drawdown scales linearly with the number of open positions — and the scenario in which they all lose together is precisely a broad market decline, which is exactly the environment in which a portfolio of bullish credit spreads on correlated large-cap stocks *will* fail together. That is the correlation risk built into the strategy, and the sizing table is the mitigation.

| Concurrent positions | Aggregate risk if all lose | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | 15% drawdown | Suitable for a conservative trader |
| 7 | 21% drawdown | Intermediate |
| 10 | 30% drawdown | The stated hard ceiling |
| more than 10 | — | **Do not.** "I don't suggest taking more than 10 positions." |

The choice among five, seven, and ten is the trader's own tolerance decision. If a 30% drawdown would end your participation in the market, take no more than five. If you can genuinely absorb 30% and remain functional — "I'm okay, my capital can drop 30%, I'm still there, baby" — ten is permitted. Above ten is not.

#### The buying-power ceiling

There is a second, independent ceiling based on capital utilisation rather than loss. Adam works a table for a $10,000 account running ten concurrent trades, each with a $200 credit, each with a maximum loss (and therefore buying power blocked) of $800, and each with a realistic loss of $300:

| Metric | Per trade | Across 10 trades |
|---|---|---|
| Credit received | $200 | $2,000 |
| Maximum loss / buying power used | $800 | $8,000 |
| Realistic loss if cut at the short strike | $300 | $3,000 |

Ten such trades consume $8,000 of buying power out of $10,000 of capital, which is **80% utilisation**. That is stated as the maximum: "I do not suggest you exceed that."

The three outcomes of that portfolio are then laid out. If every one of the ten positions loses simultaneously — very unlikely, but possible in a crash — the account loses $3,000, a 30% drawdown. If all ten win, the account collects $2,000, a 20% return. And in the expected case, at a 75-80% win rate, roughly eight win and two lose: eight winners at $200 is $1,600 of profit, two losers at $300 is $600 of loss, and the account nets **$1,000**. (The spoken arithmetic in the lesson misstates the winners' total, but the net figure of $1,000 he arrives at is correct: $1,600 − $600 = $1,000.)

Adam adds an important portfolio-construction caveat to this table. It assumes the entire account is running this one strategy. In practice, a student finishing the course knows more than a dozen strategies, and a realistic portfolio would allocate across several of them — some bull put spreads, some bull call spreads, some covered calls, and so on — diversifying by strategy as well as by underlying.

#### Expected profit: the expectancy formula

Adam then derives the strategy's expectancy from first principles, using the general formula that applies to any trading strategy whatsoever:

> **Expected profit per trade = (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss)**

For the bull put spread, the inputs are as follows. The theoretical win rate from the 20-25 delta selection is 75-80%, but for the purposes of estimating profit he deliberately uses a more conservative **70%**, leaving a 30% loss rate as a buffer against reality. The average win is the credit received, denoted C. The average loss is 1.5 times the credit, or 1.5C — with the honest acknowledgement that in practice many losses come in below 1.5C, while occasionally a gap below the strike produces a loss larger than 1.5C.

Substituting:

> Expected profit = (0.70 × C) − (0.30 × 1.5C) = 0.70C − 0.45C = **0.25C per trade**

Every trade, on average, across wins and losses combined, returns a quarter of the credit collected.

Scaling that to a year: at ten trades a month, or 120 trades a year, the annual expectation is 120 × 0.25C = **30C**. The final step is to determine C for a given account, and C is determined by the position-sizing rule. For a $10,000 account, 3% is $300 of risk per trade, which at a 1.5x loss multiple corresponds to a credit of $200 per trade. Therefore:

> 30 × $200 = **$6,000 per year on a $10,000 account, a 60% return on capital.**

Adam attaches every appropriate caveat to that figure. There are no guarantees; a hundred trades will not reliably deliver exactly a 70% win rate; some periods will run hotter at 75%, and some will run colder than 70%. Sixty percent a year is an average expectation across a large sample, not a promise for any particular year — "some years it could be higher, some years it could be lower."

#### The advantages and the risks, summarised

The three advantages of the bull put spread over its debit-spread counterpart:

First, a much higher probability of winning. A bull call spread wins roughly 50% of the time or slightly better, because the share price must actually rise for it to pay. A bull put spread wins 70% or more, because the share price can rise, stay flat, or even fall modestly and the trade still pays. The profit zone is far wider.

Second, time decay works for you rather than against you. You are paid up front, and every day that passes bleeds value out of the options you sold, converting more and more of the maximum profit into realised profit.

Third, you do not have to be right on direction. This is the same point as the first stated from the trader's perspective rather than the statistician's: the maximum profit is achievable in a scenario where your directional view turns out to be wrong in a mild way.

Against those, two disadvantages:

First, profit is capped at the premium collected. There is no upside participation beyond the credit, however far the stock rises.

Second, and far more seriously, **gap risk**. If the share price gaps down below the short put strike, the loss will exceed 1.5 times the credit, because the intended exit level was never available. And if the position is left to expire below the short strike, the loss can reach the full four times the credit or more. The mitigations are the ones already given: avoid stocks with earnings inside the trade window and close before earnings if one appears; avoid stocks with a history of gapping; and confine the strategy to very large, profitable companies whose price behaviour is comparatively orderly. Adam is explicit that the risk cannot be eliminated — "we can't prevent it 100%; it may happen from time to time" — only mitigated.

---

### Part Eight: Case Study One — GLD, A Losing Trade Managed Correctly

The GLD trade is the most valuable case study in the section precisely because it loses money. It demonstrates the full lifecycle including the part that the theory lessons can only simulate: what it actually feels like to have a stop level violated overnight, what happens when the level is repeatedly tested and repeatedly holds, and what the discipline of cutting a loss at less than half the maximum actually saves. (The transcript dates the trade to "2006"; from the surrounding material this is plainly a transcription error for a recent year, and only the month and day — 6 May entry, 27 May exit — are reliable.)

#### The setup

Bang opens on GLD, the gold ETF, and reads the chart as textbook. The trend is solid: all the key moving averages are sloping up. The recent decline is characterised as a dip on an uptrend rather than a trend change, and the reading is supported by history — roughly two months earlier price had dipped, bounced off the 150-period moving average, and rebounded; the more recent dip had done the same thing; and on the day of entry price was bouncing off it again. The inference is that gold will go higher from here.

He restates the strategy's tolerance for being wrong: with a bull put spread you do not need to be right on direction. If price rises, good. If it goes sideways, the trade is fine. And even if it falls somewhat, as long as it does not hit the short put strike, the trade is fine.

GLD carries a structural advantage that Bang draws attention to explicitly: as an ETF it has no earnings date, so the gap risk that forces the earnings prohibition on individual stocks simply does not exist. This removes the single largest source of uncontrolled loss from the trade.

#### Construction

Working the Interactive Brokers option chain with the 30-to-45-day rule, he considers the 5 June expiry at about 29 days and the 12 June expiry at about 36 days, and elects to try the shorter one first.

Scanning the delta column for the 20-to-25 band, the 25-delta strike is the **413 put**, which becomes the short leg. For the protective leg he applies his dollar-distance version of the rule — $5 or $10 below — and notes something interesting about GLD's chain: because the ETF is so liquid, strikes are spaced $1 apart, which gives an unusually fine granular scale and means he could pick any width he likes. He chooses **$5** for simplicity, buying the **408 put**.

Because more than one leg is involved, the strategy builder must be turned on. The two legs are sell the 413 put and buy the 408 put, both expiring 5 June.

#### The credit test

At the mid-price the two-leg package showed a credit of about **$1.03**. Bang immediately runs both forms of the test. First the ratio form: the width is $5, so the maximum risk is $5.00 minus $1.03 = $3.97, essentially $4 — "you risk four to get one." Second, and more directly, the width form: a $1.03 credit on a $5 width is 20.6% of the width, which clears the 20% minimum. Since 20% of $5 is exactly $1.00, the minimum acceptable credit here is $1.00, and $1.03 passes with a small margin.

For a single contract, therefore:

| Quantity | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Net credit / maximum profit | $1.03 x 100 | **$103** |
| Spread width | 413 minus 408 | $5.00 |
| Maximum loss | ($5.00 x 100) minus $103 | **$397** |
| Ratio | 397 divided by 103 | ~3.9 to 1 (inside the 1-to-4 limit) |

He notes the IV percentile — the IBKR equivalent being IV rank — at about **37%**, above the 35-40% threshold that counts as good, which means the premium is decent. But he repeats that this is nice-to-have and not required: "as long as you can get at least $1 for a $5 spread, meaning 20% of the spread, that is good enough."

#### Pre-trade simulation

Before transmitting, he analyses the profit-and-loss profile on Think or Swim, setting the analysis date to the day after expiry so the curve shows the terminal payoff. With GLD trading around **430** at entry, the picture is a very wide profit zone: rising is profitable, flat is maximally profitable, and modestly falling is still profitable. The transcript's spoken break-even figures are garbled by the transcription (one reading suggests 409, another 412); the arithmetic break-even is unambiguous and is the short strike minus the credit, 413.00 minus 1.08 = **$411.92**. The platform reported a probability of profit of about **71%**, consistent with a 25-delta short strike.

He then simulates the loss at the point of no return under two timings. If price fell immediately to the 413 short strike and he cut, the loss on one contract would be somewhat under **$100** — "you gain 100 and you lose less than 100, right, if you cut loss on time." If instead two weeks passed before price fell there, the loss would be smaller, about **$60**, because time decay has already moved the near-term curve toward the expiry curve. And if price simply sat still while time passed, that same unrealised loss would eventually turn into a profit.

#### Sizing up and the fill

Satisfied with the structure, he increases the position from one contract to **two**, which doubles everything: maximum gain about **$200**, maximum loss about **$800**, and buying power blocked around **$797**. He confirms that the broker blocks approximately the maximum loss amount, which is the practical meaning of the "max loss equals buying power" identity.

As the market moved, the mid drifted up to **$1.07-$1.08**. He works the order the same way Adam does — start above the mid and come down — beginning at $1.10 with two contracts, reducing gradually, and getting filled at **$1.08**, first partially and then completely.

The recorded entry is therefore: 6 May, two contracts, short the 5 June 413 put, long the 5 June 408 put, credit $1.08 per share, **$216 received up front**. The cash balance in the account visibly increases at the moment of the fill, which is the tangible expression of what "credit spread" means. Maximum loss, and thus capital committed, is $1,000 minus $216 = **$784**.

#### Bang's pre-stated exit plan

Before anything happens, he states both exits.

On the profit side: with $216 collected, if he can realise half of that in less than half the elapsed time, he will exit. His general formulation is that capturing the majority of the profit in a fraction of the time justifies closing and recycling the capital into a new trade, because return on investment is a function of time as well as size. He allows that a greedier trader might hold for 60% or 75% of the maximum, and calls that a matter of personal tolerance.

On the loss side: if price falls and hits the 413 short strike, he exits. He restates the simulated cost — roughly $65 to $70 per contract at that moment, so about **$140** for two contracts — and contrasts it with the consequence of not cutting: "if you don't cut loss at that point in time and the price keeps going down, you could potentially lose three times, four times of the premium you receive, and that will be massive."

#### What actually happened

Twenty-one days later, on 27 May, the trade was closed for a loss, and the sequence of events is instructive.

Initially the trade went the right way: after entry GLD rose, which moved the position favourably. Then it consolidated. Then it fell significantly.

On **15 May** the price came almost exactly to the short strike without quite reaching it, and rebounded the following day. Then it went lower still — and here the real-world complication arrives. Price went *below* the short put strike while Bang was asleep. By the rule he should have closed on that day; in practice, the move happened outside his waking hours and he could not act. The next morning he was ready to cut the loss, but at the open GLD rebounded strongly and closed back above the stop level. The day after that it traded around the level again but again closed above it. And this pattern repeated for several days: each session opened below 413 and then recovered to close above it. By the rule as he applies it — and this is a meaningful nuance in how the stop is interpreted in practice — he did not cut, because 413 was behaving as a very strong support.

On **27 May**, that changed decisively. GLD dropped **$4.50** on the day, breaking convincingly below the 413 short strike, and in fact trading down to around the 408 long strike as well. At that point the entire spread was in the money and the position, if left alone to expiry with price unchanged, would settle at the full maximum loss.

Bang's reasoning for acting immediately is the clearest statement of why a stop matters even after it has already been breached: there was still time left in the trade, so the maximum loss had not yet been realised. The position still had value to preserve. "If I don't do anything and the price stays right here until the expiration, my trade would hit the max loss, and that's something I don't want."

#### The exit and the accounting

He closed with a two-leg closing order — buy to close the short 413 put, sell to close the long 408 put, quantity two — and worked the debit upward from the mark. Starting at **$2.70**, then **$2.73** (no fill), **$2.74** (no fill), and finally **$2.75**, where one contract filled and then the second.

| Line item | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Entry date | — | 6 May |
| Position | short 413 put / long 408 put, 5 June expiry | 2 contracts |
| Credit received | $1.08 x 100 x 2 | **+$216** |
| Maximum profit potential | equals the credit | $216 |
| Maximum loss potential / capital committed | ($5.00 x 100 x 2) minus $216 | **$784** |
| Exit date | — | 27 May (21 days in trade) |
| Debit paid to close | $2.75 x 100 x 2 | **minus $550** |
| Realised loss | $216 minus $550 | **minus $335** (he cites $335, allowing for the roughly $1.07 net credit after commission) |
| Return on capital | minus 335 divided by 784 | **minus 47.7%** |
| Loss avoided by cutting | $784 minus $335 | **$449** |

The comparison in that final row is the point of the entire case study.
