The realised loss was less than half of the maximum loss that would have been incurred had the position been abandoned to expiry at the prevailing price. Bang's framing is unsentimental: "It's not good, but it's not too bad, because I cut loss at less than half of the max loss, and that saved my capital as well. Otherwise I could have lost 100%."

His closing reflection is the philosophical companion to the expectancy arithmetic. High probability does not mean certainty. This was a high-probability trade, and it lost, because a 71% probability of profit is also a 29% probability of loss and that 29% has to show up sometimes. "It's okay to take the loss, bite the bullet, and then move on. In the long run, as long as you continue to play with high probability trades, you will be winning over the long time."

The GLD trade also illustrates something the theory does not: the practical friction between a rule stated as "close the moment it reaches the short strike" and a market that touches, breaches, and recovers a level repeatedly over several sessions in a timezone the trader is not awake for. Bang did not close on the first intraday breach and, given the subsequent recoveries, was not immediately punished for it — but he was ultimately forced to take a loss at a considerably worse level than the first violation would have offered, which is precisely the cost of allowing discretion into a mechanical stop.

---

### Part Nine: Case Study Two — COST, Scaling Into a Winner

The Costco trade demonstrates the opposite outcome and adds two dimensions the earlier examples did not: the experience of chasing a fill that keeps deteriorating, and the practice of scaling a position up after the initial contract.

#### The setup

Adam looks at Costco after an earnings announcement has produced a decline into what he identifies as a strong support level around **960**, which is where price was trading. His reading: after a retracement into support, there is a high probability of either a bounce or a sideways consolidation. He acknowledges plainly that it could also go a lot lower — "of course it's possible as well" — but the trade is about probabilities, not certainty.

The trend qualification holds: the 50-period moving average remains above the 150, so the medium-term uptrend is intact, and this is a dip within it. The support has a second confirmation in that it coincides roughly with the 200-day moving average, a long-term level.

He raises a legitimate refinement here and then declines it. A more cautious trader would wait for a green candle — a bullish candle confirming the bounce — before entering, and he says there is no problem with that approach. His own entry is deliberately more aggressive, taken before the confirming candle, justified by the strength of the support and its coincidence with the 200-day average.

Note also that this is a case where earnings have already been announced and are therefore behind rather than ahead of the trade, which satisfies the earnings prohibition from the other direction: the event risk that would have contaminated the position has already passed.

#### Strike selection and the fill grind

On the Think or Swim chain he considers two expiries in the 30-to-45-day range — 2 July and 10 July — and takes the longer one, 10 July.

Scanning the delta column, the 20-to-25 delta band on this chain is wide: the **895, 900, 905, and 910** strikes all fall within it. He notes the general preference that the lower the strike, the harder it is for price to reach, which argues for 895.

He first tries the more conservative structure: sell the 900 put, buy the 895 put. This produces only **$0.97** of credit on a $5-wide spread — below the $1.00 minimum, and therefore a failing trade. His response is exactly what the rule prescribes: if you cannot get at least a dollar, move up to a higher strike price until you can.

Moving up one notch to sell the **905** and buy the **900**, the screen showed **$2.25** — an implausibly good number on a $5 spread. Adam's reaction is one of the most practically useful moments in the section. He does not take it at face value. His stated expectation for a $5 spread is something in the region of **$1.50 to $1.70**, so $2.25 is unrealistic, and he attributes it to a glitch or a temporarily wonky quote. "Sometimes when you see it's too good to be true, it is too good to be true."

What followed was a long descent, and the sequence is worth recording in full because it is the most detailed record of order-working in the section:

| Limit attempted | Result |
|---|---|
| $1.60 | No fill; market shown dropping to $1.40 |
| $1.50 | No fill |
| $1.40 | No fill |
| $1.35 | No fill; market shown at $1.27 |
| $1.30 | No fill |
| $1.28 | No fill |
| $1.25 | No fill |
| $1.20 | No fill |
| $1.18 | No fill |
| $1.15 | No fill |
| $1.12 | **Filled** |

His comment on landing at $1.12 is that it is "actually not bad, because it's more than a dollar, so I can't really complain." The discipline held throughout: at no point did the ladder go below the $1.00 floor, and every rung was a limit-order fill attempt rather than a market order.

#### The position

| Quantity | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Short put | 905 strike, 10 July expiry | delta in the 20-25 band |
| Long put | 900 strike, 10 July expiry | one strike lower |
| Width | 905 minus 900 | $5.00 |
| Net credit / maximum profit | $1.12 x 100 | **$112 per contract** |
| Maximum loss | ($5.00 x 100) minus $112 | $388 per contract |
| Cut-loss level | short strike | **$905** |
| Simulated loss if cut at 905 | from the analysis tab | **~$102** |

At an underlying price of 960 against a short strike of 905, the buffer is roughly 5.7%. The analysis tab shows the familiar shape: a profit zone spanning everything above the break-even, with the purple line converging on the green line as expiry approaches. Adam observes that the risk-to-reward is good — making $112 against a realistic $102 loss, with the delta-implied win rate attached.

He states the management plan at entry: he will not normally hold to expiration but will close once 70-80% of the maximum profit has been captured, and if price drops to 905 he closes for a loss.

#### Replicating on Interactive Brokers, and failing to get filled

He then rebuilds the identical trade on IBKR — same 10 July expiry, sell 905 by clicking the bid, buy 900 by clicking the ask, via the strategy builder, quantity one, limit order, price entered as a negative because negative means credit.

Here the trade would not fill at all. He tried **$1.15**, then **$1.13**, then **$1.12** — the very price he had been filled at minutes earlier on the other platform — and then **$1.11**, and got nothing. His explanation is simply that the market moves every second, and the deeper reason becomes apparent when he returns to the chart: price had already begun moving up, which reduces the value of a put spread and therefore reduces the credit available to a seller.

His conclusion is the appropriate one and worth quoting for its restraint: "I'm not going to chase it. I'm just going to leave it. And we'll see whether it gets filled. If it doesn't get filled, then, too bad, so sad, never mind, move on, because I already entered the trade on Think or Swim at $1.12."

#### Scaling up, and the outcome

The follow-up is recorded on **4 June**, only six days after entry. Two things had happened.

First, Adam had scaled the position. After the initial single contract at $1.12, he added **nine more contracts at $1.15**, bringing the total to **ten contracts** at an average credit of a little over **$1.14**.

Second, Costco had gapped up. When the underlying jumps in the favourable direction, a bull put spread loses value very quickly, and the spread that had been sold for $1.12-$1.15 was now trading at **$0.25**.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Days elapsed | 6 of roughly 40 |
| Opening credit (average) | ~$1.14 per share |
| Current spread value | $0.25 |
| Percentage of maximum profit captured | **78%** |
| Profit if closed | roughly **$800** across ten contracts |
| Days remaining to 10 July expiry | ~36 |

The decision follows directly from Bang's time-versus-profit principle and Adam's own early-exit practice: 78% of the maximum profit had been captured in about 15% of the time. "Of course I could wait to expiration on the 10th of July, but if I'm already making 78%, why wait? I might as well close it early."

#### An aside on closing mechanics

While demonstrating the close, Adam uses a then-open CRWV bull put spread as a worked example of *not* closing yet. He had sold that spread for **$1.32**; it was then trading at **$1.04** on Think or Swim, representing about 20% of the maximum profit captured — explicitly "not good enough." He shows placing a good-till-cancelled buy-to-close order at **$0.10**, so that the position closes automatically if and when the spread decays that far.

The same position on Interactive Brokers had been opened at **$1.30** and was showing **$0.34**, or about a 27% profit if closed there and then — again refused on the same grounds, with a resting order at $0.10.

The vocabulary asymmetry is highlighted once more: on Think or Swim, closing this position is described as *buying back* the bull put spread; on Interactive Brokers, the same action is described as *selling* it. Adam's advice remains to pick one broker and internalise its language rather than translating on the fly.

---

### Part Ten: Case Study Three — CRWV, A Complete Round Trip

The CoreWeave trade, ticker CRWV, is the only case study followed from entry through to a realised profit, and it is therefore the cleanest illustration of the full cycle.

#### The setup

On **19 May**, CRWV was in an uptrend with a clear wave structure — up, down, up, down — and had just completed a **double bottom** pattern, finding support at the **101** level with the stock trading around **$100**. Adam describes his stance as moderately bullish: after a wave down into support, he expects either sideways consolidation or a bounce, and both of those outcomes pay a bull put spread.

#### Construction

Two expiries fell within the window: **18 June at 31 days** and **26 June at 39 days**. Either would be acceptable, and he took the longer one on the grounds that more time collects more premium.

In the delta column, the **85-strike put** carried a delta of **23**, sitting near the middle of the 20-to-25 band, and he calls it "the perfect candidate." The hedge went one strike lower to the **80-strike put**, giving a $5 width.

| Quantity | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Short put | 85 strike, 26 June expiry, delta 23 | — |
| Long put | 80 strike, 26 June expiry | one strike lower |
| Width | 85 minus 80 | $5.00 |
| Credit shown at analysis | — | $1.36, fluctuating between $1.31 and $1.36 |
| Maximum profit at $1.36 | $1.36 x 100 | **$136** |
| Maximum loss at $1.36 | ($5.00 x 100) minus $136 | **$364** |
| Credit as a share of width | 1.36 divided by 5.00 | **27%** — comfortably above the 20% minimum |
| Cut-loss level | short strike | **$85** |
| Simulated loss if cut at 85 | from the analysis tab | **~$99.60**, effectively $100 |
| Probability of finishing below 85 | platform figure | ~33% |
| Approximate win rate | — | **~70%** |

Adam is careful to note the fluctuation in the quoted credit — it moved between $1.31 and $1.36 while he was looking at it, "it keeps changing as the market changes" — which is the same instability that produced the fill grind on Costco.

His summary of the trade's attractiveness is the risk-reward comparison in realistic rather than maximum terms: a maximum profit of about $134 to $136 against a realistic loss of about $100 at the stop, with a roughly 70% win rate. "I think it's a pretty attractive trade."

#### The fills

On Think or Swim he entered a limit at **$1.34**; the market drifted to $1.31; he adjusted to **$1.32** and was filled. He observes that he had plenty of buffer above the $1.00 floor, so lowering the limit cost him nothing in terms of trade validity.

He then replicated on Interactive Brokers — 26 June expiry, sell the 85 by clicking the bid, buy the 80 by clicking the ask, through the strategy builder, one contract, price entered as a negative because negative means credit — and worked down through **$1.35** (no fill), **$1.34** (no fill), **$1.33** (no fill), and **$1.32**, where it filled. A figure of **$1.30** for the IBKR entry surfaces later in the same lesson, reflecting the account's actual recorded fill.

For teaching purposes he entered only one contract, noting that a real position would be sized by the 3% rule to two, three, five, or ten contracts depending on the account.

#### The chart, marked up

Adam draws the short strike at 85 as a red dotted line and the long strike at 80 as a second line, and restates the payoff geography in plain terms: over the next 39 days the share price may rise, go sideways, or fall, and in all of those scenarios the trade is profitable, provided it does not touch 85. If it touches 85, he closes for a loss of roughly $100 per contract. If it does not, he keeps up to $132.

#### The first checkpoint: 22 May

Three days after entry, price had jumped up. The effect on the spread was immediate and disproportionate:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Days elapsed | 3 of 39 |
| Opening credit (Think or Swim) | $1.32 |
| Current spread value | $0.80 |
| Percentage of maximum profit captured | **39%**, moving to **45%** intraday |
| Opening credit (Interactive Brokers) | $1.30 |
| Current spread value on IBKR | $0.92 |
| Percentage captured on IBKR | **29%** |

Adam declines to close, restating the target: he wants roughly 70-80% of the maximum profit before exiting, and 37-45% is not enough. But he uses the moment to make a point about the mechanics of the strategy that is easy to miss: "when the share price jumps up very quickly, the value of the options drop a lot. It drops pretty fast when that happens." A credit spread does not only decay with time; a favourable directional move accelerates the decay dramatically, because it simultaneously reduces the delta of both legs and typically compresses implied volatility.

#### The exit: 2 June

On 2 June, fourteen days after entry and twenty-five days before expiry, CRWV gapped up sharply again. The spread had fallen from $1.30-$1.32 to **$0.32**.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Days elapsed | 14 of 39 |
| Days remaining | 25 |
| Opening credit | $1.30 on IBKR, $1.32 on Think or Swim |
| Spread value at decision | $0.32 |
| Percentage of maximum profit captured | **74%** |
| Debit actually paid to close | **$0.33** |
| Realised profit | **$95 per contract** |
| Maximum profit had it been held to expiry | about $130 |

The exit itself was worked in the same disciplined way as the entries, only in reverse: because a close is a debit, the aim is to pay as *little* as possible, so he started below the market at **$0.30**, got no fill, moved to **$0.32**, got no fill, and filled at **$0.33**.

The closing logic is stated cleanly: "I sold it 25 days before expiration. If I had to hold it for the next 25 days, I'll get the full profit, which is like $100-plus dollars. What's the point? So I just close it, take the money and run, and open another trade."

Put in the terms of the profit-taking rule, holding for a further 25 days — nearly two thirds of the trade's entire duration — in order to earn the remaining $35 would be a poor use of both capital and risk exposure, when that same capital could be redeployed immediately into a fresh spread earning a fresh full credit.

#### Side-by-side comparison of the three case studies

| | GLD | COST | CRWV |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entry date | 6 May | ~29 May | 19 May |
| Expiry | 5 June (~29 DTE) | 10 July (~40 DTE) | 26 June (39 DTE) |
| Underlying at entry | ~430 | ~960 | ~100 |
| Short put strike | 413 | 905 | 85 |
| Long put strike | 408 | 900 | 80 |
| Width | $5 | $5 | $5 |
| Short-put delta | ~25 | 20-25 band | 23 |
| Credit per share | $1.08 | $1.12 first contract, $1.15 for the next nine | $1.32 TOS, $1.30 IBKR |
| Credit as a percentage of width | 21.6% | 22.4% | 26.4% |
| Contracts | 2 | 10 | 1 (demonstration size) |
| Max loss per contract | $392 | $388 | $368 |
| Capital committed | $784 | roughly $3,860 | $368 |
| Outcome | Cut at a loss on day 21 | Closed at 78% of max on day 6 | Closed at 74% of max on day 14 |
| Result | **minus $335, or minus 47.7% on capital** | **roughly plus $800** | **plus $95 per contract** |

Two structural observations fall out of this table. First, every one of the three trades used a $5 width and a credit slightly above the 20%-of-width minimum, confirming that the rule is not theoretical but is the actual operative constraint on strike selection. Second, the two winners were both closed early — on day 6 of 40 and day 14 of 39 — because the profit arrived far faster than the calendar, which is exactly the circumstance the early-exit rule is designed to exploit. The single loser, by contrast, ran 21 of its 29 days before being cut. That asymmetry — winners closed fast, losers closed at a defined level — is the mechanical shape of the strategy's expectancy.

---

### Part Eleven: The Bear Call Spread — The Mirror Image

Adam introduces the bear call spread by reassuring the student that it will not take another two hours to learn, because once the bull put spread is understood, the bear call spread is simply its inverse. He restates his own position on it up front: he very rarely trades it, because it is a bearish strategy and the market goes up roughly 90% of the time. He would probably only use it in a genuine bear market of the sort that arrives every five or six years. But he teaches it because some students are temperamentally more bearish, and because there are periods when it is the right tool.

#### When to deploy it

The ideal environment is a market-wide bear market — the 50-period moving average below the 150 on the index, with the whole market declining. This is not a requirement but it maximises the probability. It is possible to use a bear call spread in a bullish market, but then the individual stock chosen must be genuinely, distinctly bearish.

For the stock itself, the downtrend definition is the exact reverse of the uptrend definition: the **20 EMA below the 40 EMA** for the short-term downtrend, and the **50 below the 150** for the medium-term downtrend. When the moving averages line up in that sequence, the stock is in a confirmed downtrend.

The timing rule inverts as well. On a downtrend, price makes waves up and waves down while trending lower. The entry is taken when price is **retracing upwards into a resistance level** and looks ready to resume falling — the mirror of waiting for a retracement into support on the bullish side. Critically, Adam adds a placement rule: **the strike price of the option you sell should be above that resistance level**, so that the resistance sits between the current price and your short strike as an additional barrier.

The implied volatility filter is unchanged: IV rank or IV percentile of **35% or above**, for the same reason as before — you are a net seller and you want expensive options.

#### Construction

Sell an out-of-the-money call above the current price at a delta of **20 to 25**, and buy a further out-of-the-money call **one to two strikes higher** to cap the risk, both with the same expiration date. The delta interpretation is symmetrical: a 20-to-25 delta short call means a 20-25% chance the price finishes above that strike, and therefore a **75-80% win rate**. Price can fall, go sideways, or even rise — it simply must not exceed the short call strike.

The rationale for the second leg is the same as on the put side, and Adam is careful about it: selling the call alone superficially resembles a covered call, "except you don't own the shares." Without shares to deliver, the position would be naked and must be hedged, which is what the long call accomplishes.

#### The SPLK worked example

The teaching trade is on SPLK on **25 January** with the stock at **170.90**.

The setup qualifies on every count. The 20 is below the 40, and the 50 has just crossed below the 150, so both timeframes confirm the downtrend. Price is making lower highs and lower lows. And there is a well-defined level of former support that has turned into resistance, which price has recently rallied into and is expected to be rejected from.

The expiry chosen is **5 March**, which is **40 days** out from the trade date.

Scanning the call side of the chain for the 20-to-25 delta band, several strikes qualify — **192, 195, and 197.5** are all within the band. Adam takes the highest of them, and states the reason explicitly: the higher the strike price, the more difficult it is for the stock to reach it, so 197.5 is materially safer than 192, which sits much closer to the current price. The short call carries a delta of **21**.

For the hedge he considers buying the **200** or the **205**, either being acceptable at one or two strikes higher, and chooses the **200**.

| Quantity | Computation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Premium received (short 197.5 call) | — | $3.06 per share, **$306 per contract** |
| Premium paid (long 200 call) | — | $2.56 per share, **$256 per contract** |
| Net credit equals maximum profit | $3.06 minus $2.56 | $0.50 per share, **$50 per contract** |
| Spread width | 200.0 minus 197.5 | **$2.50** |
| Maximum loss equals buying power used | ($2.50 minus $0.50) x 100 | **$200 per contract** |
| Risk-to-credit ratio | 200 divided by 50 | **4 to 1** — exactly at the limit, and therefore acceptable |
| Return on capital | 50 divided by 200 | **25% in 40 days** |
| Break-even at expiration | short strike plus net credit | 197.5 plus 0.50 = **$198.00** |
| Probability of finishing above the short strike | delta of the short call | 21% |
| Theoretical win rate | 100% minus 21% | **79%** |

This trade is worth studying precisely because it sits *exactly* on the 1-to-4 boundary rather than comfortably inside it. Adam checks the ratio explicitly — "$200 divided by $50, that is 1 to 4. So is that within our criteria? $1 credit, maximum loss $4. Yes, within that criteria, but not more than $4. Anything 4 or less." A worse ratio would have required moving strikes or abandoning the trade.

Note also that the width here is $2.50 rather than $5, because SPLK's chain is spaced at $2.50 intervals in this region. The rules adapt without modification: "one to two strikes" is the operative instruction, and 20% of a $2.50 width is exactly $0.50, which is exactly the credit collected. Both formulations of the credit test agree, as they must.

#### The payoff geography and management

Plotted, the position shows the same shape as a bull put spread reflected left to right. The current price sits to the left of the profit plateau; the profit zone extends downward and sideways without limit and upward as far as the break-even at $198.00. Maximum profit is $50, achieved anywhere at or below 197.5 at expiration; maximum loss is $200, reached at or above 200.

The **point of no return is the short call strike at 197.5**, and the management rule is identical to the bull put spread in mirror image: if the stock price rises to the short call strike, cut the loss.

The simulated cost of doing so decays with time in exactly the same way:

| Date the short strike is touched | Days elapsed of the 40 | Loss if closed at 197.5 | Loss as a multiple of the $50 credit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25 January (entry day) | 0 | **$75** | **1.5x** |
| 25 February | 30 | **$70** | **1.4x** |
| 4 March (day before expiry) | 39 | **$59** | **1.18x** |

This is the cleanest demonstration in the entire section of where the "expect to lose 1.5 times the credit" heuristic comes from. On entry day, the loss at the point of no return is exactly 1.5 times the credit received. As time passes it decays toward 1.18 times, and would continue to fall toward parity at expiry. The 1.5x figure used throughout the position-sizing arithmetic is therefore a conservative worst case within the trade's life, not a long-run average.

Adam's closing instruction on the strategy is procedural rather than theoretical: before taking any bear call spread, look at the profit-and-loss chart and establish, under several different time scenarios, exactly how much you would lose if price ran up to the point of no return and you cut. And the answer, at most, should be about 1.5 times your credit.

#### Bull put versus bear call, side by side

| | Bull put spread (1A) | Bear call spread (1B) |
|---|---|---|
| Market view | Bullish to neutral | Bearish to neutral |
| Index condition preferred | S&P 50 MA above 150 MA | S&P 50 MA below 150 MA (bear market) |
| Stock trend required | 20 EMA above 40 EMA; 50 above 150 | 20 EMA below 40 EMA; 50 below 150 |
| Entry timing | Retracement down into support | Retracement up into resistance |
| Structural placement | Short strike below support | Short strike above resistance |
| Sell | Out-of-the-money put, delta 20-25 | Out-of-the-money call, delta 20-25 |
| Buy | Put one to two strikes lower | Call one to two strikes higher |
| Maximum profit | Net credit | Net credit |
| Maximum loss | Width minus credit | Width minus credit |
| Break-even | Short strike minus credit | Short strike plus credit |
| Point of no return | Short put strike | Short call strike |
| Loss at the stop | about 1.5x credit | about 1.5x credit |
| Win rate | 75-80% | 75-80% |
| IV percentile filter | 35% or higher | 35% or higher |
| Days to expiration | 30-45 | 30-45 |
| Credit test | max risk 4x credit, or credit at least 20% of width | max risk 4x credit, or credit at least 20% of width |
| Frequency of use by Adam | 99.9% of credit spread trades | Very rare; bear markets only |

### Part Twelve: The Live Q&A Webinar

The section closes with a live question-and-answer webinar conducted by Adam Khoo together with Bang Van, broadcast from Singapore to students working through the course. Questions had been submitted in advance and grouped into themes, with additional live questions taken as the session ran. Adam opens by apologising for having lost his voice — "usually my voice is not that sexy, but bear with me" — and the session runs a little over two hours, punctuated by several platform crashes which he works around.

What follows organises the substance of the session by theme rather than by chronology, because questions on the same subject were scattered across the two hours.

#### Theme one: finding the entry on the chart

The opening question asked how to find the right entry point on a chart for buying a call or a put. Adam's answer reframes the question before answering it: options are a tool, nothing more. If you want to go long you may buy the stock or buy the option, so the real question is not "when do I buy a call" but "when is the best time to go long," and that question is answered by technical analysis, identically whether the instrument is a stock, an option, a currency, or a futures contract.

His definition of a clear uptrend uses four moving averages: the **20 EMA**, and the **50, 150 and 200 simple moving averages**. The trend is up when they are in sequence — the 20 above the 50, the 50 above the 150, the 150 above the 200. On a downtrend the sequence reverses: the 200 above the 150, above the 50, above the 20.

Within a confirmed trend, there are exactly two optimal entry types, and both are about avoiding buying at extremes.

The first is the **retracement entry**. A stock in an uptrend does not go up in a straight line; it moves in impulsive waves up and corrective waves down, making higher highs and higher lows. You never want to enter at the top of an impulsive wave. You wait for price to pull back toward a moving average — Adam's personal favourite is the 50 — and you enter as it bounces off that average. On a downtrend, the mirror: wait for a retracement up toward the 50 and enter short there.

The second is the **breakout entry**, which comes in two forms. Sometimes an uptrend develops a counter-trend line of lower highs; the entry is the break of that counter-trend line. Sometimes an uptrend runs into a horizontal resistance and tests it repeatedly; three or more tests indicates a strong resistance, and the entry is the breakout above it. A refinement on the same idea: after a resistance is broken, it becomes support, and the retest of that new support from above is also a valid entry. On a downtrend, all of the same structures apply inverted — the break of a counter-trend line of higher lows, the break below a repeatedly-tested horizontal support, and the retest of broken support from below as new resistance.

Bang interjects with the volatility overlay: whenever you buy a call or a put, check the IV percentile first, because it tells you whether the option is cheap or expensive. To buy, you want the IV percentile **below 40, or better still below 30**. Buying when IV is 60 or 70 — which is typical immediately before earnings or a key event — means paying a great deal for the option. "Don't buy options when the options are expensive."

#### Theme two: day trading with options

A student asked about day trading with options — entering and exiting on the same day. Bang defines the term first: a day trade is a position opened and closed within the same session; buying today and closing tomorrow is not a day trade.

His guidance is that it can be done, but it demands nimbleness, and nimbleness demands liquidity. Choose highly liquid underlyings — the Dow components, the S&P 500 — trade **at the money**, where liquidity is greatest, and prefer short-dated options, which carry more liquidity than long-dated ones.

Adam adds his own preference, which is not day trading at all: he focuses on calls and puts on ETFs, and argues that a trader can be extremely consistent by concentrating on a handful of good companies or ETFs. His recurring claim throughout the webinar is that if you did nothing but trade calls and puts on the S&P 500 ETF, SPY, consistently, that alone would generate good profits.

He demonstrates on the SPY chart. The ideal periods to have bought calls were those when the moving averages were in full sequence — the 20 above the 50, the 50 above the 150, the 150 above the 200 — and price was retracing to the 50. Buy a call or a call spread at each of those retracements and repeat the process. He is equally clear that these conditions do not always exist: sometimes SPY is choppy and there is no clear trend, and in trading there are three available actions — go long, go short, or do nothing. "Sometimes it's best to do nothing when you don't have a clear trend. It's better to go fishing."

Turning to the SPY at the time of the webinar, he read it as still technically in an uptrend — 20 above 50, 50 above 150 — despite a sell-off over the preceding days, with price having found support at **280**, a level that had previously been strong resistance. Could you buy a call there? Not a bad trade, but not a perfect one, because price was trading *below* the 50 moving average and he prefers to buy above it. A more conservative trader would wait for price to recover above the 50 at around **286 to 287** before buying. And if IV percentile were high, he would prefer a call spread — buying an at-the-money call and selling another at a target price around 295 or 296 — because a spread is much less sensitive to elevated implied volatility than an outright call.

#### Theme three: macro news and world events

Asked how the US-China trade war would affect the strategies taught in the course, Bang answered that it does not affect them at all, and in fact provides opportunity: if you think the market will crash, buy a put or a put spread; if you think a deal will be signed and the market will bounce, buy a call or a call spread. In the advanced course there are further strategies that allow a trader to profit in any of the three market directions, including no direction at all.

Adam's answer to the same question is one of the strongest statements of principle in the session, and he generalises it well beyond trade wars. **Ignore the macro news.** There will always be a conflict, always a trade war, always something. Focusing on presidential tweets or the news cycle will drive you crazy and will not help. Traders look at price action and technical analysis; investors look at fundamentals. Is it an uptrend? A downtrend? A breakout? A dip? Those are the questions that generate trades. *Why* it is in an uptrend does not matter — "we don't care. It's not important." The same discipline applies whether the instrument is options, forex, or stocks. "It's only noise that serves to distract you."

The follow-up question was more concrete: if you have an open call spread and bad news hits, do you close immediately or wait for the news to subside?

Bang answers first, from the plan-based perspective. When you entered, you already knew your maximum loss and your cut-loss threshold. If the news-driven move has not hit that threshold, close if you wish and redeploy your attention, but the plan governs. He then makes an observation that is peculiar to options and easy to overlook: when you are wrong on direction as an option buyer, you do not lose 100% of your maximum loss immediately, because time value remains until expiration. That remaining time can be enough for the market to recover. He tells a story against himself here — he once speculated that a company would not go bankrupt; the day after, the company announced it was filing Chapter 11, which was his maximum-loss scenario; a week later the decision was reversed, the share price recovered, and the position made all the money back. "When you play options, you won't hit the max loss until the last day."

Adam's answer is different in emphasis and reflects his own style. He enters a call spread when there is a clear uptrend, and he exits the moment there is no longer a clear uptrend — for example, when price breaks below the moving average, or makes a lower low. He closes well before expiration so that he never loses his maximum loss; typically he loses only about 50% of it. And crucially, the trigger is never the news itself: "I close the trade, not because of bad news, because I don't read the news. It's a complete waste of time. I close the trade when I see the trend is no longer going up... Always make decisions on price action, because ultimately it is all built into the price."

#### Theme four: which stocks to trade options on

Asked whether options should be traded only on blue-chip stocks, Bang gave a two-part answer. Blue chips have high liquidity and lower volatility, which makes them ideal for steady income strategies like covered calls, where you want a stock that grinds upward while you sell premium against it. But that is not the whole picture: options can also be used to speculate on sharp moves, and for that purpose other securities are legitimate. The instrument should follow the strategy.

Adam's personal practice is narrower. He trades options mainly on SPY and on blue chips, and his reason is entirely mechanical rather than philosophical: large companies have the most strike prices and the widest range of expiration dates, so it is easy to select exactly the strike he wants. Smaller companies may not offer the strike he needs, or the expiry he needs, which constrains the trade before it starts.

This point recurs later in a form worth emphasising, when he demonstrates the FinViz screener. He finds a stock with a beautiful channel-up structure, bouncing off both trendline support and a moving average — an excellent *trading* setup. But it is an $8 stock and not a well-known company, so the options may be illiquid, the bid-ask spread may be too wide, and there may be no suitable strike or expiry. His conclusion is a principle in its own right: **a good trading setup is not necessarily a good option-trading setup.** There are two independent questions — is this a good setup, and are options a suitable instrument for expressing it? If the setup is good but the options are not, simply trade the stock.

#### Theme five: option buyer versus option seller

A student challenged the whole framing of the course, asking why the lessons teach buying options when the probability of winning as a buyer is low.

Adam rejects the premise. It is not true that being an option buyer is inadvisable; you can make a great deal of money on either side, and it is a matter of style. He and Bang differ: Adam prefers to be a buyer — buying calls, call spreads, put spreads — while Bang prefers to be a seller, and most option-selling strategies are covered in the advanced course. Both are profitable.

He then lays out the trade-off with numbers, and this is one of the most useful passages in the webinar because it explains exactly why the credit spread's unattractive-looking risk-reward is not a defect.

As an **option buyer** taking directional trades, your win rate is roughly **50% to 60%**. That is acceptable only because you insist on a favourable payoff: Adam's rule is to always risk $1 to make at least **$1.50 to $2**. If you consistently risk one to make two, then being right half the time produces a positive expectancy.

As an **option seller**, your win rate is much higher — Adam quotes **80% to 90%** for the selling strategies — but there is no free lunch, and the price of that win rate is the payoff. You typically risk $3 or $4 to make $1. The teaching then is that management converts that theoretical 4-to-1 loss into something much smaller: "we'll teach you how to repair your trade, to manage your trade so that you will never lose $4... we will quickly adjust it or close it so that we'll only lose 20% of the maximum loss."

That last figure — losing only about 20% of the maximum loss — is the webinar's own restatement of the credit spread cut-loss rule. In the bull put spread, the maximum loss is four times the credit and the realistic loss is 1.5 times the credit; 1.5 divided by 4 is 37.5%, so the webinar's "20% of max loss" is a rougher and more optimistic version of the same idea, but the principle is identical: never take the full defined loss.

Bang adds the portfolio dimension. Even though he prefers selling, a well-diversified portfolio needs both. Selling strategies give you positive theta — time working for you — while buying strategies carry negative theta. The goal is a mix such that the portfolio, taken as a whole, gains a little every day that passes.

#### Theme six: choosing strikes and expirations

Several questions circled the same practical problem: which strike, and which expiration?

Adam's honest answer is that he does not have a formula; he has a process. He experiments. He tries different strikes and different expiries, analyses the profit-and-loss chart for each, and selects the combination with the best risk-to-return profile. Sometimes buying a straight call has a poor risk-to-return, in which case he buys a call spread instead. Even within spreads he iterates — buy the 280 call and sell the 290, and if the risk-to-return is unsatisfactory, try buying the 285 and selling the 295 — until the chart shows an acceptable profile.

On the specific question of **in-the-money versus out-of-the-money** for buyers, both instructors gave the same structural answer from different angles.

A deep in-the-money option has a high delta — 70, 80, even 90 — which means a $1 move in the stock produces close to a $1 move in the option. The advantage is that you make money on small moves. The disadvantage is cost, and correspondingly larger losses when you are wrong. Bang describes deep-in-the-money buying as a **stock replacement strategy**: rather than committing the capital to buy 100 shares of Amazon or Google outright, you buy a deep in-the-money call for a fraction of the cost and get almost dollar-for-dollar participation. The risk is symmetrical — if the direction is wrong, you lose a lot, exactly as a shareholder would.

An at-the-money option has a delta around **50**, so a $1 stock move produces a $0.50 option move, and the stock therefore has to move meaningfully for the trade to pay. This is Adam's own preferred style, and he correspondingly selects strikes with **delta of about 50 to 60**.

An out-of-the-money option is cheapest, requires the largest move to become profitable, but pays the most when a large move actually occurs. Bang's summary of the choice: there is no black-and-white answer; it depends entirely on how strong your conviction in the direction is, and on how fast you expect the move. Adam's version: if you believe the move will be large, buy slightly out of the money; if you believe it will be small, buy at the money or in the money.

Adam ties the delta choice back to strategy explicitly when asked about the role of delta in strike selection. It depends on the strategy: at the money means about 50 delta, deep in the money means 80 or 90 delta, out of the money means around 40 delta or lower. "That's basically it."

He adds a hard rule for buyers that has no equivalent on the selling side. **When buying a straight call or put, buy at least 60 days to expiration, and exit at least 30 days before expiration.** The reason is that the final 30 to 40 days carry the heaviest time decay, and an option buyer should not be holding through that. This has a corollary for how he analyses trades: he sets the analysis date in the simulator to the intended exit date — 30 days before expiry — and reads his profit and loss from that line rather than from the expiration line, which he will never reach. Spreads are different: because a spread's profit is maximised at expiration, he can and does buy much shorter-dated spreads and hold them close to expiry.

#### Theme seven: liquidity, open interest, and bid-ask spreads

A student noticed that open interest is not used as a selection criterion in the course and asked why.

Bang's answer is that for the stocks actually being traded — Apple, Facebook, Google, the Dow components, the S&P 500 — liquidity is so high that open interest is never a binding constraint, which is why it is not mentioned. Open interest matters when trading less liquid stocks or unusual strikes, where it tells you how many contracts are available for someone to transact with you at a given strike and expiry. On common large-cap names, it is simply not an issue.

On bid-ask spreads specifically, his practical benchmark is that on a stock priced under $100 the bid-ask on a liquid option should be a **few cents**. That is what you see on names like Apple, Facebook and Twitter. Wide spreads cost you on entry and again on exit, so tight spreads directly reduce slippage.

He offers a shortcut for assessing option liquidity without examining the chain in detail: **if the stock has a weekly option series, its options are liquid; if it only has monthlies, they are not.** He gives Travelers, a Dow component, as the counterexample — low option liquidity, no weekly series, and a correspondingly wide bid-ask.

Asked directly what makes a good option to buy — whether to focus on delta, theta, gamma, or implied volatility — Bang's answer is that you plan the whole trade profile before entering: the Greeks, the maximum risk, the maximum profit, and the profit-and-loss chart both at expiration and before it. Adam's answer is that everything is already built into the profit-and-loss chart, so he goes to the analysis tab, reads the maximum loss and maximum profit, and applies his rule: when net buying options, the maximum profit must exceed the maximum loss, and he wants to be risking a dollar to make at least $1.50 to $2. "If it's less than that, it's not a good option trade."

The session also touched on gamma. Several attendees asked about gamma and about "long gamma" setups; Adam declined both, on the grounds that gamma trading is a very short-term activity that is not part of the course's strategies.

#### Theme eight: stop losses on options

Two students asked whether it is possible to place a stop loss on an option based on the underlying's price, and both instructors advised against it.

The technical objection comes first. There is a correlation between the stock price and the option price, but there is no exact way to convert a stock-price stop into an option-price stop, because delta is only one of the inputs. Vega, theta and even interest rates all move the option's value, and theta moves it every single day. So there is no reliable mapping from "the stock fell to X" to "the option is now worth Y."

The practical objection is stronger and concerns execution quality. Option bid-ask spreads are not always tight, and a stop order dumps your option at whatever the market will pay, which can be a very poor price. "Don't let it happen, because then you will give your decision into the machine to do it for you, and often that is not a good thing."

Bang's preferred alternative is active monitoring and manual management. His justification is the same time-value argument he made earlier: because an option retains value until expiration, you do not lose everything in a single day, so you always have time to exit deliberately at a smaller loss rather than automatically at a bad price. He confirms later that the same reasoning applies on the selling side taught in the advanced course.

#### Theme nine: adjustments and repair

Asked how to fix or adjust a trade that goes against you, Bang's answer is procedural. Every strategy in the course specifies, before entry, the entry point, the exit point, and the adjustment criteria. Understand the risk profile, the risk-reward ratio, the chart, and every parameter before you enter. Then, once in the trade, stick to the plan and do not let emotion or ego pull you away from it — "that would be a perfect setup for disaster."

Adam sharpens this into a level-specific statement: **the strategies in this level-one course do not require adjustments.** Adjustments belong to advanced structures like the iron condor and the iron butterfly. In the basic course, the discipline is to respect the defined loss limit and cut. If a trader is genuinely content to take the maximum loss, that is a choice they may make; but if they are not, the game plan governs and they cut early.

#### Theme ten: assignment, exercise and dividends

The webinar received several versions of the same anxiety, most fully articulated by a student who had bought a SPY put spread — long the 288 put, short the 281 put — speculating on a market decline, and had watched the price fall below 281, putting the entire spread in the money. He feared his short put would be assigned.

Bang's answer proceeds in two steps.

First, on likelihood: it is very unlikely. The 281 put retains extrinsic value until expiration, and as long as it does, exercising early would force the option's holder to forfeit that extrinsic value — that is, to lose money voluntarily. "Why would you want to lose money? He will not exercise early." The possibility exists, but it is remote.

Second, on consequence: even if it happens, the outcome is *good*, because in a fully in-the-money debit put spread, assignment simply delivers the maximum profit early. If assigned on the short 281 put, you are put 100 shares. But you hold the long 288 put, which you exercise to sell 100 shares at 288. The long and short share positions neutralise, and you are left having bought at 281 and sold at 288 — the full spread width, which is the maximum profit. "So you should not be concerned about this one. One, low probability of happening. Two, even in that case, you get the max profit."

A follow-up asked whether the broker handles the neutralising exercise automatically. It does not; the trader initiates it. In the platform you right-click on the specific long option — or, on a Mac, place two fingers on the trackpad — select "exercise" from the drop-down menu, and the option converts. The standing caution is that exercising always forfeits the remaining extrinsic value, which is why neither instructor exercises voluntarily.

The rarity of the whole scenario is underscored by the instructors' own experience. Bang, with twelve years of options trading, states that he has never had a short option assigned. Adam's comment: "If you ever get assigned, go buy the lottery."

The dividend question produced the one genuine asymmetry. Once an ex-dividend date is confirmed, option pricing has already factored in the expected price adjustment — on the ex-date, the share price is marked down by the dividend amount, and the options reflect that in advance. The complication is behavioural rather than mathematical: a holder of an in-the-money **call** may rationally exercise early precisely in order to convert the call into long shares before the ex-date and collect the dividend. This means that as a **seller of calls**, you may find yourself assigned early around dividends. Bang's conclusion: watch out on the call side around dividends; on the put side, this particular risk does not apply.

A related question asked whether an Interactive Brokers margin account can be used to pay for assigned stock. The answer is yes, within the account's margin capacity: once you are assigned, you own shares (or short shares), and the broker will let margin absorb the position provided it fits your borrowing limit. If it does not fit, the broker does not wait — it will liquidate the position before assignment or before expiration, dumping your shares or options at whatever the market price happens to be. The lesson is that a position which cannot be absorbed by your account will be closed for you, on the broker's timing rather than yours.

#### Theme eleven: covered calls

Covered calls attracted a cluster of questions, and Adam's answers assemble into a complete set of selection rules that complement the credit spread material.

**The premium rule.** He wants the premium received to be at least **2% of the stock price**. On a $100 stock, that means at least $2 of premium for a call expiring in about 30 days. The reasoning is annualisation: 2% a month, repeated across a year, is at least 20%, which makes the activity worth doing.

**The profitability rule.** Only sell covered calls on a position that is already showing a profit. If you bought at $100 and the stock is at $110, sell calls against it. If you bought at $100 and the stock is at $80, do not — he does not want to be writing calls against a losing stock position.

**The technical rule.** He prefers to sell covered calls when the stock is facing a resistance level, or when it has run far from its moving averages and looks overstretched. In either case, he does not expect the stock to reach his strike within the next 30 days, and expects it to come back down toward him.

**On implied volatility.** Asked whether IV must be above 50% to sell covered calls, Bang's answer is that ideally yes, above 50% is best because it produces good premium — but if the premium is good enough at a lower reading to serve as regular income, go ahead.

**On selling calls against a larger holding.** A student holding 200 shares asked whether to sell two contracts at the same strike and expiry or to split them across different strikes and expiries. Either works. Bang notes you can ladder them — one short-dated and one long-dated, or one at a lower strike and one higher. Adam's own practice is to keep it simple and use the same strike and the same expiration.

**On rolling.** If the short call is out of the money at expiry, do nothing and let it expire worthless. If it is at or in the money and you do not want the shares called away, then before expiration you buy back the short call and sell another call further out of the money at a later expiration. You take a loss on the call you buy back, but the long shares have appreciated by more, so the net is positive.

**On consistency when the stock is not consistent.** A student asked how covered calls can be sold monthly if the stock itself does not move consistently. Adam's answer distinguishes the regimes. When the stock is trending up strongly, price will tend to exceed your strike; you lose on the short call but make more on the long shares, so net you still make money — the call simply caps your upside. If you do not want the shares called away, you buy back and roll, which costs money on the option leg but is more than offset on the share leg. His conclusion is that selling covered calls into a strong up-move may not be very profitable, but stocks do not go up every day; after a strong advance they will go sideways, and it is during those sideways periods that the calls expire worthless and the premium is kept in full. Across the cycle of advances and consolidations, the accumulated premium reliably adds to annual returns.

**A structural correction.** One student asked whether he could begin selling covered calls now, against shares he expected to be assigned at the end of the month from a short 47-strike Intel put with the stock at 45. Bang's answer is a firm no: **you cannot sell a covered call when you do not own the shares.** You must wait for expiration and actual assignment. Doing otherwise means being simultaneously short a put and short a call with no stock — a short strangle, which is a far more advanced and far riskier position than the student intended.

A related question asked about selling a covered call and a cash-secured put on the same underlying at the same expiration — for example, on Alibaba. Bang works through the exposure. On the upside there is no problem: the stock rises, you lose on the short call but gain more on the shares. On the downside there is a **double whammy**: the stock falls, you lose on the shares *and* you lose on the short put. He therefore advises against it unless you genuinely want to buy another 100 shares at that strike. "You have to be extremely bullish on the share price to do it."

There is also a small but useful piece of market-structure reassurance in this theme. A student, having learned that a covered call may be closed and re-opened before expiration, asked what happens to the person who paid the premium for the original call. Bang's answer: you never know who your counterparty is, because the exchange performs the matching. When you buy, the exchange finds a seller; when you close, your counterparty is likely a different person entirely; and when that other person decides to close their position, the exchange will find a counterparty for them. "You don't have to care about it. The exchange does the matching."

#### Theme twelve: cash-secured puts

Asked what the best strike is when selling puts, Bang's answer is that there is no best strike — there is only the strike you are genuinely comfortable owning the shares at. Because assignment means buying the stock, the strategy should be used only on companies with good fundamentals and a good technical setup, so that ending up as a shareholder is an acceptable outcome rather than a disaster.

The trade-off between strikes is a pure probability trade-off. A strike far below the current market gives you a high probability of keeping the premium and a low probability of assignment — but the premium is small. A strike closer to the market gives you a larger premium but a higher probability of being assigned. Neither is right; it depends on the individual's preference.

Adam attaches the categorical rule that dominates the whole strategy: **never sell options naked.** Never naked calls, never naked puts. When you sell a put it must be a cash-secured put, meaning the cash to buy the stock is actually there. And you sell it only if you were prepared to buy the stock anyway — because it is a good company you already wanted to own — using the put as a way to collect extra money before buying. "If you have no intention of buying the stock, please do not sell the put. It is suicidal."

His own premium threshold on cash-secured puts is stated in absolute rather than percentage terms: on a $100-to-$200 stock like Apple, he wants at least **$400 to $500 per contract**. If a contract only offers $100 or $200, he is not interested.

On whether an elevated IV percentile of around 50% is required, Bang's answer parallels his covered-call answer: high IV gives better premium, but if you want to own a particular stock at a particular price, go ahead regardless, because the worst case is owning a stock you wanted at a price you liked. "It's a good thing."

#### Theme thirteen: implied volatility

Several questions probed implied volatility from different angles, and the answers assemble into a coherent framework.

**What the metrics mean.** The platform will display several volatility figures — implied volatility, IV percentile, IV last, historical IV. The one to focus on is the **IV percentile**. Bang offers the clearest analogy in the whole webinar: historical volatility is the road behind you, telling you how bumpy the past year has been; implied volatility is the road ahead of you, telling you how bumpy the market expects the next stretch to be. IV percentile compares the two — it tells you how bumpy the road ahead looks *relative to the road you have just travelled over the past 52 weeks*.

**What drives it.** IV does not rise or fall as a function of time passing. It is driven by events. It rises ahead of a key event and collapses afterwards. Adam's list of drivers is characteristically direct: implied volatility is driven by presidential tweets and by approaching earnings; when the tweeting stops, IV falls. His conclusion is that it is impossible to predict when IV will rise or fall, so the practical response is positional rather than predictive: **when IV is high, don't buy options — if anything, sell them; when IV is low, that's a great time to buy.**

A student asked whether IV automatically becomes high after 30 days have passed on a 60-day option. The answer is no — IV is event-driven, not calendar-driven. The 60-day/30-day rule for option buyers exists to avoid the acceleration of time decay in the final month, not because of anything IV does.

**Whether IV matters for spreads.** Asked whether IV percentile should be considered when buying a vertical call or put spread, both instructors said it matters much less than for outright options. Because a spread involves both a purchase and a sale, the volatility exposures partially offset, and the net impact is smaller. Adam's practice reflects this exactly: "personally, when I use spreads, I don't really bother much about the IV percentile — only if I buy a straight call or straight put."

**Whether to use a spread because IV is high.** This follows directly. When IV is very low, just buy the straight call, because options are cheap. When IV is high, a spread is better. But Adam's actual method is comparative rather than rule-based: he looks at the risk profile of the straight call — how much he loses if wrong, how much he makes if right — and compares it against the same analysis for a call spread, and takes whichever offers the better risk-to-return. Sometimes that is the call, sometimes the spread.

A short factual question confirmed that the IV figure displayed on Interactive Brokers is the same as the one on Think or Swim.

#### Theme fourteen: scanning and watchlists

Asked how he identifies candidates, Adam gives two complementary methods.

The first is the daily watchlist. He recommends maintaining a watchlist of common stocks and ETFs on the trading platform and reviewing it every day for developing setups. His own list of usual suspects includes SPY, the US oil ETF, VGK (the European ETF), and a handful of common stocks. Each day he runs down the list asking the same three questions: is it in an uptrend, is it making a dip, is there a breakout? He notes that Bang covered watchlist construction in lesson two of the course.

The second is a screener. He demonstrates **FinViz**, which offers pattern-based scans directly from the main page. Selecting **Channel Up** returns stocks in clear ascending channels; he browses through them looking for one that has retraced to support and is bouncing off either a trendline or a moving average. He also points to **Channel** for range-bound stocks moving sideways between support and resistance, where a bounce off support is a long entry, and **Channel Down** for the bearish equivalent.

It is in the course of this demonstration that he delivers the caution described earlier: a beautiful channel-up setup on an $8 stock is a fine *stock* trade but may be untradeable with options because of illiquidity, wide spreads, or an inadequate range of strikes and expiries. There are always two questions — is the setup good, and are options the right instrument for it?

Asked when to run the FinViz scan, he answers: any time before the market opens at 9:30 a.m. Eastern. Do the research, find the setup, check whether options exist on the name, check whether they are liquid, check whether IV is low, and if all of that holds, go for it.

He notes that scripts for scanning these setups on TC2000 are provided in his separate stock trading course, along with the full treatment of retracement, breakout and reversal setups.

Bang, asked separately how to scan for the best spread by risk-to-reward, gives a corrective answer that is important enough to restate. Finding the spread with the greatest risk-to-reward is *not* the most important criterion. A very speculative, far out-of-the-money spread will show a spectacular risk-to-reward ratio precisely because the probability of collecting is low. "What's the point?" The decision must weigh probability alongside payoff, not payoff alone.

#### Theme fifteen: platforms, brokers and costs

A number of housekeeping questions were answered.

On **charting and setup for Interactive Brokers**, Bang had already recorded a dedicated video; it is lesson two, part three of the course.

On **Bang's proprietary covered-call and cash-secured-put scanner**, which is a self-built Excel file synchronised to Think or Swim through Visual Basic: it requires a Think or Swim account to feed prices, but not a *funded* live account — a simulated account will feed the data adequately. It does not work with Interactive Brokers, because IBKR does not use the same Visual Basic bridge, and it runs only on Microsoft Windows. To change the expiration date in the scanner, the target date is typed manually into the light blue cell, following the format year, month, day, then P.

On **countries where Think or Swim does not accept clients**, Adam is deliberately oblique. He says that with creativity there is always a way to open an unfunded Think or Swim account for the purpose of using the tools, that he has students in restricted countries who have found ways to use a demo or unfunded live account, and that he cannot say more than that.

On **commissions**, students in Singapore get a group rate with lower commissions on stocks and options through an arrangement with Think or Swim Singapore, obtained by emailing the company. Adam is careful to correct a misunderstanding raised late in the session: there is no special *fee* for signing up, there is a special *commission rate*. For students outside Singapore who cannot access that arrangement, Interactive Brokers offers a better commission on options — around **$0.75 to $0.80 per contract** — which he calls a very low commission and a perfectly good deal.

Bang qualifies the comparison. IBKR has a lower headline per-contract commission, but he has found additional charges appear later, particularly on advanced strategies — selling iron condors on oil or natural gas, or selling strangles, can attract items like an oil exposure fee or a weekend position exposure fee. His objection is transparency rather than magnitude: he prefers Think or Swim's slightly higher but completely clear fee schedule, with no hidden items.

On **maintenance fees**, Adam's understanding is that Think or Swim requires a minimum funding balance of around $3,500 but charges no ongoing maintenance fee once funded.

On **which broker to use for options**, Adam confirms both work, and notes that he personally tends to execute his own option trades through Interactive Brokers.

On **buying power showing as negative** in the position statement: when you buy an option the broker blocks a certain amount of capital, and when you sell an option you collect cash but incur an obligation, so the broker blocks capital as collateral against that obligation. The negative figure in the buying power column is that blocked amount — capital reserved, not money lost.

On **trading hours**: options on commodities and futures trade roughly 23 hours a day, five days a week. Options on ETFs and indices trade only within regular market hours. Bang's preference is to trade within the regular session, between 9:30 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. Eastern, because that is when option liquidity is highest.

#### Theme sixteen: realistic returns and trading frequency

Asked how many trades he does in a month and what return he expects, Bang gave a set of numbers that function as a reality check on the entire course.

On **frequency**: he holds roughly **ten positions at any one time** in a single account, with a typical holding period of **one to two months**. That works out to entering and exiting perhaps one or two positions per week at most. He is explicit that this is not a high-turnover, in-and-out-daily style, and that a student who is not a heavy day-trading type can work at an even slower pace — once a week, or once every two weeks — without that being an obstacle to making money. "Slowly, boring, it's okay."

On **returns**: his stated expectation is **20% to 25% a year**, which he calls a decent expectation, with the acknowledgement that some periods do much better.

Adam supplements this with observed extremes from watching Bang trade. In a good year he has seen Bang do **150%**, and has seen him double his money in a year. He has also seen him at **minus 10% in a month**. The point of quoting both is that neither is the expectation: "it's impossible to predict when it's a good year... you may not be positive every single month. But overall, if you can do an average of 20, 30% a year, that's pretty good."

Bang's own summary of his psychological framing is worth preserving because it connects directly to the credit spread material: "I'm seeing myself as selling insurance. Sometimes you get hit because there's some big accident and typhoon and stuff like that. But over the long run, I make money."

#### Theme seventeen: small accounts, leverage and instrument choice

Asked whether a small account is better served by stocks or options, Adam first corrects the framing of the question. The questioner used the word "invest," and Adam separates the concepts: **options are not for investing, options are for trading.** Investing means buying a stock and holding it for a long time.

With that distinction made, options genuinely help a small account, because buying 100 shares of an expensive stock costs a great deal of money while an option on the same stock does not. Options are a form of leverage, and there are several ways to obtain leverage — margin, CFDs, and options. He notes that CFDs are not permitted in the United States, which makes options the best available leverage tool for American traders. In Singapore, where CFDs are available, he chooses between them situationally: when IV is very low he prefers options, and when IV is high and he wants to take a directional trade he uses CFDs instead.

#### Theme eighteen: what the instructors actually trade

Asked to name their favourite go-to strategies, both answered candidly.

**Adam's favourites** are spreads — specifically call spreads — concentrated mostly on SPY. His whole routine on that instrument is: wait for SPY to be in a clear uptrend, wait for it to retrace toward the moving average, buy a call spread. "That's all I do, and doing really well on that." His second favourite is the **earnings probability spread**, a three-legged structure invented by Bang and taught in the advanced course, used two to three days before a company reports on names judged likely to beat: the risk is $1 and the reward is $5 to $10. Third, he is a heavy user of **covered calls**, because he owns a great deal of stock in his long-term investment portfolio and writes calls against it regularly. Fourth, he uses **put spreads during short-term corrections** — he mentions having bought a lot of put spreads during the trade-war-driven correction of the preceding days — as a hedge that profits while his long-term portfolio takes an unrealised drawdown he has no intention of selling into.

**Bang's favourite** is the **iron condor**, which he trades on oil, natural gas, gold and the euro. His reasons are precise: a better risk-to-reward and a high probability of winning, but above all **defined risk** — "it's not like unlimited risk. When you are selling, you're afraid that things can go wrong and you can lose a lot. But in this case, I have my max loss." He also values that the trade runs for about two months, so he is not forced to manage it constantly, which suits him because he holds a full-time job. His second is a bottom-fishing strategy that students named after him, a three-leg structure used when a stock has fallen enough to be due a bounce: enter long, but buy protection in case the timing is wrong. Both are taught in the advanced course.

Adam notes that trade calls and alerts are not currently offered for options, but will be offered when the advanced course launches, because the majority of the trades Bang takes come from the advanced material.

#### Theme nineteen: assorted questions

Several questions fell outside the main themes.

**On the VIX.** A student observed that on the VIX, short-dated and long-dated options carried almost the same premium, and asked why the longer-dated option was not more expensive despite having more time. Bang answers with appropriate humility, saying that after thirteen years he does not consider himself a master of VIX products, and that VIX is a different animal that does not behave like a normal stock. His interpretation of the specific observation is that market participants were fearful about the near term and relatively unworried about the longer term — buying short-dated insurance while negotiations were unresolved, but believing things would sort themselves out eventually — which compresses the term structure.

**On intrinsic value.** Asked whether there is an easy way to determine a company's intrinsic value by entering a ticker, the answer is no; it must be calculated, and a calculator is provided in the separate value momentum investing course. Adam adds the important framing: intrinsic value is useful for *investing*, not for short-term trading. Short-term trading has nothing to do with intrinsic value; it has to do with technical analysis and chart setups.

**On the probability figures on the risk graph.** A student asked what the percentage figures shown at both sides of the risk analysis graph mean. They are simply the probability of the price moving within that range. Bang notes it is not covered in the technical session and is not especially important — it is a probability estimate for the price staying within a band, and there is not much more to read into it.

**On the dual-chart layout.** A student noted that Bang had shown how to set up two side-by-side charts on Think or Swim but had not explained the use of the left-hand one. Bang's answer is that he prefers to hold both a short-term and a long-term view simultaneously: a two-day chart alongside a one-year chart, so that he can see both how the stock has behaved over the past year and how it has behaved over the past two days. Any timeframe can be substituted on the left — five days, one week, one month — according to preference.

**On protective puts and beta weighting.** A student reported a portfolio with a beta-weighted delta of 66, calculated that two SPY put contracts would be required for a full hedge, but found that using put *spreads* instead of outright puts only brought the portfolio delta down to 40, and asked whether buying straight puts would solve the problem. Bang confirms that it would. The reason is arithmetic: when you buy a put spread you buy a put and sell a lower put, so the net delta of the package is smaller in magnitude than the delta of the long put alone — less than 50 — and a structure with less delta hedges less. The correct construction for a portfolio hedge, as shown in the video, is to buy a straight **at-the-money** put.

**On directionless markets.** Asked what short-term strategies work when SPY cannot break resistance but remains in an uptrend, Adam's answer is the one he gave earlier in a different context: if there is no clear direction, do not trade. Directional strategies need direction. "You don't always have to trade."

**On whether stock ownership is required for a call spread.** No. Aside from covered calls — the one strategy in which shares are owned first and calls are written against them — none of the strategies involve owning the stock. "We just trade options without wanting to ever buy the stock."

**On applying the course's stock-trading setups to options.** Asked whether a call spread can be traded off the bounce strategy from the professional stock trading course, the answer is yes, absolutely — with the same caveat about option liquidity. A good trading setup on a stock whose options are illiquid, thinly struck, or badly spaced should simply be traded as a stock.

#### The closing demonstration: straight call versus call spread on SPY

Adam ended the webinar with a live worked comparison, which is the single most useful passage in the session because it shows the decision procedure rather than describing it. (The demonstration was interrupted twice by the platform crashing, which he handled with good humour and a promise to record it separately if he could not get it running.)

**The setup.** SPY was trading at **283**. The moving averages remained in uptrend sequence — 20 above 50, 50 above 200 — and price had retraced and bounced off support at **280**, a level that had previously been significant resistance. His short-term target was the previous high at **295**. He noted the trade was imperfect, because price was below the 50 moving average and he prefers to go long above it, and said that his lack of full confidence would express itself in size: perhaps one contract here, where a high-confidence setup above the 50 would justify many more.

**Option one: the straight call.** Applying his rule for outright option buying, he selected an expiry with at least 60 days: **19 July, at 65 days to expiration**. Applying his at-the-money preference, he selected the **283 strike**, with a delta of **54**. The cost was **$797** for one contract.

He then set the analysis date not to expiration but to **19 June** — 30 days before expiry, which is where he intends to exit — and read the purple line at his two scenario prices:

| Scenario | SPY price | Profit or loss on 19 June |
|---|---|---|
| Target reached | 295 | **+$529.50** |
| Support decisively broken | 278 | **−$511** |

His verdict: "it's kind of like risking one for one. So it may not be that profitable if it just goes to 295." He allows that if SPY went far beyond target — to 300 or 310 — the upside is unlimited, but observes that it is rare for a move to run that far, and a strategy should not be justified by its tail.

**Option two: the call spread.** Because a spread's maximum profit is realised at expiration rather than before it, he does not need a long-dated option, and can choose an expiry matched to his expected timeframe. If he expects SPY to reach 295 within 14 days, he can buy the **14-day** expiry. He constructed the spread by buying the **283 call** and selling the **295 call** — the short strike placed exactly at his target price, which is the standard construction for a debit call spread.

| Metric | Straight call | Call spread |
|---|---|---|
| Expiry | 19 July, 65 DTE | 14 DTE |
| Structure | Long 283 call | Long 283 call / short 295 call |
| Cost | **$797** | **$426** |
| Profit at target | +$529.50 (measured 30 days before expiry) | **+$774** (maximum, at expiration) |
| Loss if wrong | −$511 at 278 | **−$426** maximum |
| Reward-to-risk | roughly 1 to 1 | **774 divided by 426 = about 1.8 to 1** |

The conclusion is decisive and follows directly from his stated rule that a net-buying trade must risk $1 to make at least $1.50 to $2: the spread costs nearly half as much to enter, has a defined and smaller maximum loss, and offers a materially better payoff for the same directional view and the same target price. "So you can see in this particular case, it is more profitable to use the call spread."

The methodological point is more important than the specific answer. Adam does not decide between an outright option and a spread by rule of thumb. He builds both, analyses both on the profit-and-loss chart at the date he actually intends to exit, reads off the profit at his target and the loss at his invalidation level, computes the ratio, and takes whichever structure wins. That is the same process the credit spread rules encode — the 1-to-4 ratio test, the 20%-of-width test, the simulated loss at the point of no return — applied to the debit side of the book.

---

### Part Thirteen: The Section in Summary

Everything in this chapter reduces to a small number of load-bearing propositions.

A credit spread pays you at the start and asks only that nothing much happen. That single structural fact changes the win rate from roughly 50% to roughly 75-80%, turns time from an adversary into an ally, and replaces directional forecasting with probability estimation as the source of edge.

The probability is not guessed; it is selected. The delta of the option you sell *is* the probability that the trade fails. Choosing a 20-to-25 delta short strike is choosing a 75-80% win rate, and everything else in the trade follows from that decision.

The second leg is not optional and is not there to improve the payoff — it makes the payoff worse. It is there to convert an unbounded obligation into a bounded one, so that no single trade can end your participation. Never sell options naked.

The trade must clear an economic hurdle before it is placed: maximum risk no greater than four times the credit, equivalently a credit of at least 20% of the width, equivalently a return of at least 25% on committed capital over a 30-to-45-day window. Trades that fail this test are not entered, and orders whose fill price causes them to fail the test are abandoned rather than chased.
