The maximum loss is a number the trader must know and must never experience. The short strike is the point of no return, the position is closed there, and the realistic loss is about 1.5 times the credit — a figure that only shrinks as expiration approaches.

Position size is computed from the realistic loss, not the maximum loss, and is capped at 3% of net liquidation value per trade, at ten concurrent positions, and at 80% of buying power. These three ceilings exist because a 75% win rate guarantees that 25% of trades lose and does not guarantee that the losers arrive politely spaced apart.

Profits are taken early and deliberately. At 80-90% of maximum profit captured, or whenever the majority of the profit has arrived in a minority of the time, the position is closed, the capital is recycled, and — just as importantly — the remaining risk is retired.

Nothing is held through earnings, and nothing is held to expiration.

And finally, the arithmetic that makes it all worth doing: at a conservative 70% win rate, winning the credit and losing 1.5 times the credit, the expectancy is a quarter of the credit per trade, which across 120 trades a year is thirty times the credit — about 60% on capital for an account sized according to the rules, on average, over the long run, with no guarantees in any particular year.

---

# Part V — The Jade Lizard

## The Jade Lizard

### Introduction: A Strategy Introduced Fresh From Testing

Of all the positions taught in Level 2, the Jade Lizard is the one Adam Khoo introduces with the most visible enthusiasm, and the reason is worth stating up front: he is not teaching it from a textbook. He opens the lesson by telling the class that this is "a brand new strategy called Jade Lizard, which I've been testing over the past four months, and the result has been so good that I'm so eager to share with you right now." That framing matters, because everything that follows in the chapter — the delta targets, the credit rule, the days-to-expiration window, the profit-taking percentage — is not generic internet advice. It is the residue of a live experiment conducted across more than two hundred real trades in a real account over roughly five months, and the specific numbers he settles on are the ones that survived that experiment.

He is explicit about the distinction. "If you search the Jade Lizard option strategy on YouTube or on Google," he says, "you could find a very generic rule of the Jade Lizard, which is sell bear call and sell a put. But I've been testing it over hundreds of trades, and now I have narrowed down the entry rules such that it would help optimize the trade for you. So the Jade Lizard strategy that I'm teaching here will be a very specific version, which works very well for me." The generic Jade Lizard is a shape. The version taught in this course is a shape plus a rulebook, and the rulebook is where the edge lives.

The name itself has a history. The structure was named and popularized by Tanya (Tammy) Andrews and Liz Dierking of tastytrade — in the transcript the names come through the automatic transcription as "Cheney Andrews" and "Liz Dekkin on Tseid trade," which are clearly Andrews and Dierking at tastytrade — and Khoo credits them openly as the origin of the name. He abbreviates it throughout as "JL."

The one-sentence characterization he gives is this: the Jade Lizard is a strategy that allows a trader to benefit from a neutral to slightly bullish price movement, and its unique feature is that it has a very high probability of winning. Both halves of that sentence carry weight. The directional bias is deliberately mild — not bullish, not bearish, but tilted very slightly to the upside of flat. And the probability of winning is high because, as we will see, the structure collects premium from both sides of the market simultaneously and places its two short strikes far enough apart that the underlying has to do something fairly dramatic before the position is in trouble.

But high probability is not the same as low risk, and Khoo is careful to say so more than once. "It's high probability of winning," he warns, "but it doesn't mean that it has no loss. In some cases, where the share price collapses, you could incur some significant loss as well." The Jade Lizard has an asymmetry built into it: the upside is capped and safe, while the downside is uncapped and unprotected. That asymmetry is the whole personality of the trade, and understanding it properly is the difference between a strategy that compounds and a strategy that gives back a year of gains in a single week.

---

### The Anatomy of the Position: Three Legs, One Expiration

The Jade Lizard is a three-legged spread. All three legs must share the same expiration date — Khoo repeats this constraint twice in the opening minutes, because it is the thing that makes the payoff diagram behave the way it does. If the legs sit in different expiries, the position becomes a diagonal construction with entirely different Greeks and an entirely different risk profile, and none of the arithmetic in this chapter applies.

The three legs decompose naturally into two familiar sub-positions that most students have already met in Level 1.

The first sub-position is a **bear call spread**, sometimes called a short call vertical, which occupies legs one and two. You sell a call, and you buy a higher-strike call above it to cap the upside risk. "You sell a call, you buy a higher call to protect the upside risks," Khoo says. "So that's a bear call." On its own, this is a bearish-to-neutral structure: it profits if the stock stays below the short call, and its maximum loss is the width between the two call strikes minus the credit received.

The second sub-position is a **short out-of-the-money put**, leg three, which Khoo describes as being functionally identical to a cash-secured put: "the third leg is to sell an out-of-the-money put, which is like a cash-secured put." On its own, this is a bullish structure: it profits if the stock stays above the put strike, and its risk extends all the way to zero.

Put them together and you have a position that collects two separate credits at entry. "So you can imagine now you sell a bear call and you sell a put option at the same time. So in combination, you get two sets of credits or premiums at the entry."

The complete leg structure, in the order Khoo builds it, is set out below.

| Leg | Action | Instrument | Target | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sell | Out-of-the-money put | ~25 delta or lower | Collects the largest single credit; expresses the mild bullish tilt; carries all the downside risk |
| 2 | Sell | Out-of-the-money call | ~45 delta (±2–3) | Collects the second credit; sits close to the money where premium is richest |
| 3 | Buy | Higher-strike call | Chosen so total credit ≥ call-spread width | Caps the upside; converts unlimited call risk into a bounded, and ideally zero, upside exposure |

Notice the ordering of the delta targets, because it is not symmetric and the asymmetry is intentional. The short call is placed at roughly 45 delta — very close to the money, which is where option premium is richest per unit of strike distance. The short put is placed at roughly 25 delta or lower — much further out of the money, deliberately conservative. Khoo is putting the aggressive leg on the side where his risk is capped, and the defensive leg on the side where his risk is open-ended. That single design decision explains most of the trade's behavior.

---

### The Defining Property: No Upside Risk

Here is what makes a Jade Lizard a Jade Lizard rather than merely an iron-condor-shaped pile of options. Khoo states the condition plainly: "this strategy is created in a way that it has no risk on the upside. How could you get that kind of risk reward profile? Well, you need to collect a total credit that is equal or greater than the width of the bear call spread, the difference between the short call and the long call. So the total credit has to be equal or greater than that."

The arithmetic is worth writing out explicitly, because once you see it the structure becomes obvious rather than clever.

Consider what happens at expiration if the stock closes above the long call strike — that is, above every strike in the position, in the worst possible case for the call spread. The short put expires worthless, so it keeps its full credit. The call spread, however, is fully in the money and is worth exactly the width between the two call strikes. You are obliged to pay that width to close it.

So the profit at any price above the long call strike is:

> **Profit (upside) = Total credit received − Call spread width**

If the total credit exceeds the width, that expression is positive. There is no price on the upside, however extreme, at which the position loses money. If the total credit exactly equals the width, the expression is zero: the upside flattens out precisely at breakeven, no matter how far the stock runs. And if the credit falls slightly short of the width, there is a small, strictly bounded loss zone on the upside equal to the shortfall — which, as we will see, Khoo is often willing to accept in exchange for a better put strike.

Applied to the numbers from his Tesla demonstration: the call spread was 260/270, a width of $10.00, and the total credit collected was $10.47. The upside profit is therefore $10.47 − $10.00 = $0.47 per share, or $47 per contract, and that $47 is guaranteed regardless of whether Tesla finishes at $271 or at $500. In the Risk Navigator simulation he runs later, he points at exactly this region of the chart and says "that is area of $42 profit," reading a slightly different number off a slightly different fill — but the principle is identical. "Really because the trade has no risk on the upside in this case, you will be guaranteed a profit if the price goes higher."

This is the property that makes the payoff diagram look the way it does. Plot the position at expiration and you get a shape with three distinct regions. Far on the left, below the put strike and continuing down toward zero, is a steep, unbounded loss line. In the middle, between the short put and the short call, is a flat plateau at maximum profit. And on the right, above the long call, is a second flat line sitting just barely above the zero axis — a small, permanent, guaranteed profit. Khoo describes this right-hand shelf as "a break even zone. So this one for me is a break even zone," and he treats it as such: "It always has some small profit or break even. Or sometimes a small loss is okay. I consider it as a break even zone."

The result is that the Jade Lizard is not a two-sided risk trade at all. It is a one-sided risk trade wearing the costume of a two-sided one. "The risk is on the downside," he summarizes at the end of the first lesson. "So because of that, Jade Lizard has no downside protection, and it's important for us to manage the risk properly and cut loss on time."

---

### Why Each Leg Is There

It is worth pausing on the logic of each individual leg, because students who understand only the shape will misconstruct the trade the first time a strike ladder does not cooperate.

**The short put exists to generate the bulk of the credit and to express the directional view.** This is the leg that does the heavy lifting. Because the position needs total credit to exceed the call spread width, and because the call spread by itself can never produce a credit larger than its own width, the excess must come from somewhere else — and that somewhere else is the put. Without the short put there is no Jade Lizard; there is only a bear call spread that loses money above its short strike. The put is also the leg that makes the trade neutral-to-slightly-bullish rather than neutral-to-bearish: it is the reason the position wants the stock to stay up, and it is the leg that will hurt if the stock falls.

**The short call exists to add credit cheaply at a point on the curve where premium is dense.** At 45 delta the call is close to at-the-money, which is where extrinsic value per contract peaks. Selling here maximizes the credit contribution per unit of risk taken. It is also the leg that defines the top of the maximum-profit plateau: as long as the stock finishes below this strike, the call side contributes its full credit.

**The long call exists purely as insurance, and its strike is a free parameter.** This is the single most important construction insight in the lesson, and Khoo returns to it repeatedly. The long call is not chosen for a delta. It is chosen for arithmetic. "The long call will be at the strike price such that when you combine the premium you collect, that would be equal or greater than the spread within the long call and the short call." You pick it last, after the two short legs are set, and you pick it by testing candidate strikes until the credit-versus-width inequality is satisfied on terms you like.

That "on terms you like" clause hides a genuine tradeoff, and Khoo works through it explicitly with live numbers, which we will follow in detail shortly. Buying a *closer* long call costs more premium, shrinks the net credit, and lifts the guaranteed upside profit higher above zero — but at the cost of a higher downside breakeven and a lower maximum profit. Buying a *further* long call costs less premium, increases the net credit, pushes the downside breakeven lower and the maximum profit higher — but flattens the upside shelf down toward zero, or even slightly below it. Khoo has a clear preference here, and he states it: "Typically, I would prefer to have this zone to be near to break-even, near to zero. That would be okay. Because in that case, I would have a wider profit zone between here and here."

In other words, he deliberately gives away almost all of the guaranteed upside profit in order to buy a wider maximum-profit plateau and a lower downside breakeven. He is trading a certainty he does not much value — a few tens of dollars if the stock rockets — for protection on the side where the real money can be lost.

---

### Market Outlook and Stock Selection

#### The Directional View

The Jade Lizard wants the stock to go approximately nowhere, with a mild preference for drifting up rather than down. Khoo's phrasing is precise and he draws a boundary on both ends of the spectrum. "Neutral to slightly bullish kind of setup would be best. You don't need to be like super bullish. In fact, super bullish in this strategy is not even good. Slightly bullish would be best, or neutral would be okay. But definitely not a super bearish one. Slightly bearish is okay. Super bearish, no."

The reason super-bullish is "not even good" is structural rather than stylistic. If you genuinely expect a large rally, the Jade Lizard caps you at a few cents of guaranteed profit above the long call — you would be far better served by a bull call spread or a long call. The Jade Lizard converts a strong directional view into a weak payoff. And the reason super-bearish is disqualifying is even simpler: the short put is naked to the downside, and a collapsing stock is precisely the scenario the position cannot survive.

The technical setup he favors is a stock that has already sold off and is showing signs of stabilizing. "Ideally, when the price shows that it has been stabilizing after a sell down and could be due for a rebound." This is a deliberate choice: entering after a decline means implied volatility is already elevated (which fattens the premium), the stock has already given back some of its downside potential, and the odds of a further collapse are somewhat reduced compared to entering at the top of an extended run.

#### Fundamental Quality

Khoo's first stated preference is that the Jade Lizard "should be used on fundamentally good stocks that are trading undervalue, I mean, below the intrinsic value. So we will typically trade it on VMI stock or UIP stock that are undervalued, and it has been beaten down and it's now stabilizing or is due for a rebound." VMI here is the Value Momentum Investing framework and UIP the Ultimate Investing Programme universe — in both cases, the point is that the candidate should be a business whose intrinsic value provides a floor under the share price.

He immediately softens this into a preference rather than a rule: "In those cases, it's going to be best, but it is not a must. It's not a must. You can trade it on other stocks as well."

What is not optional is the prohibition. "Please avoid trading Jade Lizard on highly speculative stocks." His reasoning is a direct consequence of the payoff shape: "Often you see highly speculative stocks have very good premium, right? And it's very tempting to enter those kinds of trade. But those are the stocks that could also be very risky. The stock could have a good chance of plunging or collapsing. So avoid those kinds of stocks. Speculative stocks, like meme stock kind of thing, avoid those. Yes, the premium could be very good, but the probability of the stock price collapsing is also high."

This is the single most important selection filter in the strategy, and the logic is worth spelling out. The Jade Lizard is short a naked put. A naked put on a speculative name is a bet that the tail risk priced into the option is overpriced — and on meme stocks and story stocks it usually is not. The rich premium that makes those names superficially attractive is rich precisely because the market correctly assesses that they can lose forty percent in a session. You are being paid fairly for a risk you cannot afford to take with a high-frequency, high-turnover strategy. The whole edge of the Jade Lizard depends on the losing 13% of trades being survivable; on a speculative name, a single loser can erase a quarter of winners.

When he goes hunting for actual candidates in the live sessions, the names he picks are instructive: Tesla, TSM, JPMorgan, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft. Every one is a mega-cap. He says so directly when introducing the Meta trade: "I like mega cap stocks because many of them are still undervalue and if they're on uptrend, they're making a lot of money and they're also producing a ton of cash. So I like them." And when justifying the Tesla trade despite its volatility: "That's obviously one of the high volatility stocks, but it's not like a small stock. It's not like a meme stock. It's not like the stock can crash like 10, 15% easily. It's a mega cap stock. It's a trillion dollar stock. So obviously, there's some push and there's fundamentals to support it."

#### Liquidity

The second hard requirement is option liquidity, and Khoo is unusually specific about what he means by it. "I only use this strategy on high liquidity stocks. The stock with a good option liquidity, for example, it has weekly options, it has very tight bid and ask spread, and it has very granular strike price ladder. Like every strike price, it's near each other, or half of the dollars, that would be best. If it's like $5 or $10, it would not be so ideal."

Three separate criteria are packed into that sentence, and each one matters for a different reason.

*Weekly options* matter because the strategy targets a four-to-six-week window and needs the ability to pick a specific expiry rather than being forced into the nearest monthly. In the live examples he selects 44 DTE, 37 DTE, and roughly 30 DTE expiries — none of which would exist on a monthly-only chain.

*Tight bid-ask spreads* matter because the position has three legs, each of which must be crossed on entry and again on exit. Six crossings of a wide spread will consume the entire edge of a trade whose average return is 2.4% of margin. In the execution walkthroughs, Khoo spends a great deal of time negotiating pennies around the mid-price precisely because those pennies are a meaningful fraction of the trade's expectancy.

*A granular strike ladder* matters because the construction method requires fine-tuning. The long call is chosen by testing strikes until the credit-versus-width arithmetic works; the short put is often nudged one or two strikes lower to buy extra margin of safety. Both of those adjustments are impossible on a $5 or $10 ladder. This is not a theoretical concern — it actually blocks a trade during the live session. When he attempts a Microsoft Jade Lizard in the 30-day expiry, he runs into exactly this problem: "the problem with this series, there's no more granular strike prices. So there's like $5 increment, which is not so ideal." The candidate construction produces only $8.76 of credit against a $10 spread, which he rejects — "this is less ideal because I have less than $10 spread" — and he solves it by moving out to the December 1 expiry where a $9-plus credit against the same $10 width is achievable.

#### Implied Volatility

Because the Jade Lizard is a net-premium-selling structure, it wants to be entered when premium is expensive. Khoo's threshold is stated as follows: "Ideally, when you have the high IV, like IV implied volatility percentile, if it's greater than 40 in thinkorswim, you can check it out and you see the premium is good, then you could enter the trade. Or if you use Interactive Brokers, you can use 52-week IV ranking, which is equivalent to IV percentile in TOS. So either way, if you see the number is more than 40 percent, that could be a good time to enter the trade."

He then explicitly demotes this from a rule to a hint: "But this is not the must. It's one indicator to tell you that this stock could be a good candidate for the trade."

The reason IV rank is a soft criterion rather than a hard one becomes clear once you look at how he actually sources elevated volatility in practice. Rather than waiting for a stock's IV percentile to climb above 40 on its own, he deliberately places these trades into earnings events, which manufacture the volatility premium on demand.

---

### Trading Through Earnings: A Deliberate Reversal

Almost every other income strategy in the course carries a standing instruction to avoid earnings. The Jade Lizard reverses it. "The Jade Lizard strategy can be used during the earnings period. So unlike many strategies that we taught so far, we say avoid earnings period. This one, you can trade through earnings. In fact, if you trade through the earnings event, you could have a better premium, or you can sell the short put at the lowest strike price."

The mechanism he describes is precise and repays attention. When implied volatility is elevated ahead of an earnings release, the entire option chain reprices. Delta is a function of implied volatility as well as of moneyness, so a given delta corresponds to a strike that is further from the money than it would be in a calm market. Khoo spells this out when constructing the Alphabet trade: "With the earnings coming, the premiums get expensive, so then the 25 delta can be pushed further out. That's how it works. When the IV elevated, the one standard deviation or the delta will be further out from the current stock price. So I can afford to sell further out at 25 delta. So 25 delta here is 128. And right now the stock price is close to 137. So almost 10 points, 9 points below the current stock price."

This is the earnings trade's genuine attraction. You are not merely being paid more premium for the same risk; you are being allowed to place your short put further away from the money while still collecting enough credit to satisfy the no-upside-risk condition. The margin of safety widens at the same time the payment increases.

He does not pretend this is free. "Yes, there would be a risk that the price would gap down a lot, but there will be a criteria for you to cut loss and move on in those scenarios." The earnings gap is the specific mechanism by which the Jade Lizard's stop-loss rule can be jumped over. In the six live trades that follow, exactly this happens once — on Tesla — and it produces the only loss of the sequence.

---

### The Complete Entry Rulebook

Before working through the live examples it is worth assembling every entry criterion Khoo states, with its numeric threshold, in one place.

| Criterion | Rule | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying quality | Fundamentally sound, ideally trading below intrinsic value (VMI / UIP names) | Preferred, not required |
| Prohibited underlyings | No highly speculative or meme stocks, regardless of premium | Hard rule |
| Option liquidity | Weeklies available, tight bid-ask, granular ($0.50–$1) strike ladder | Hard rule |
| Technical setup | Neutral to slightly bullish; ideally stabilizing after a sell-off | Required (super-bearish disqualifies) |
| Implied volatility | IV percentile (TOS) or 52-week IV rank (IBKR) above 40 | Indicator, not required |
| Days to expiration | 4 to 6 weeks; roughly 28–45 days | Optimal window from testing |
| Short call strike | ~45 delta, tolerance of a few points either way (42–47 observed) | Core rule |
| Short put strike | ~25 delta **or lower**; lower is safer and better | Core rule, one-directional |
| Long call strike | Chosen so total credit ≥ call spread width | Defining rule |
| Credit vs. width | Credit ≥ width preferred; slightly below acceptable "approximately" | Core rule with tolerance |
| Maximum ROI | Max profit ÷ buying power blocked must exceed 10%; 14–20% preferred | Hard minimum |
| Earnings | Permitted and often desirable | Deliberate exception |

On the DTE window he is explicit that this came out of testing rather than theory: "In terms of the time frame, again, I tested out over a different time frame one week to a few months, and so far, the best optimal time frame would be anywhere between four to six weeks. Four to six weeks, that's an optimal time for you to enter this trade." In practice he stretches this slightly — the Tesla and JPMorgan trades are entered at 44 DTE, "a little bit more than six weeks, but that's okay."

On the delta tolerances, he is relaxed about the call and strict about the put, and the asymmetry is once again deliberate. For the call: "you sell the lower call strike at about 45 delta. When I say 45, it doesn't need to be exact 45. Sometimes, you know, like 46, 47 is fine, or 43, 42, 44, that's okay." For the put: "the short put should be at the 25 delta, or lower. The lower is the better. So when you sell a put, remember, the trade has potentially significant risk on the downside. So if you sell a lower delta put, that would be safer. So delta at 25 would be minimum or lower, it would be better."

Read carefully, the put rule is not "target 25 delta." It is "25 delta is the maximum you may sell; go lower whenever the arithmetic allows." Every live trade in the sequence ends up with a put delta *below* 25 — 23 on Tesla, 23 on Alphabet, roughly 20–21 on Meta, 24 on Microsoft — because Khoo systematically spends surplus credit on pushing the put strike down.

#### The Return-on-Investment Test

The one criterion that has nothing to do with the option chain and everything to do with capital efficiency is the ROI floor, and it functions as a genuine veto. After constructing a candidate, you submit it to the broker to discover how much buying power or margin will be blocked, and then compute:

> **Maximum ROI = Maximum profit (net credit) ÷ Buying power blocked**

"If the maximum return on investment, which is equal to the maximum profit, which is the credit you receive, divided by the buying power or by the margin, it needs to be greater than 10%. Don't settle for anything less than 10%. Minimum, you need to achieve at least 10%. Often, I want to achieve like 14, 15%. Sometimes I could get even 20%. So get the best out of your capital. Don't settle for less than 10%, max return on investment."

This is the criterion that makes the strategy scalable. The Jade Lizard's headline per-trade returns are modest — his measured average across 237 trades is 2.4% of margin — and the only way that compounds into something meaningful is by cycling capital fast and never tying it up in a trade that cannot pay at least 10% at its theoretical best.

The ROI test is also where the choice of broker begins to matter materially, and Khoo demonstrates this side by side. The identical Tesla structure blocked approximately $8,443 of buying power on thinkorswim but only about $4,621 of maintenance margin on Interactive Brokers, roughly half. "ID blocks less buying power if you have a margin account. So in my case, it blocked even less because I have a portfolio margin in this particular account. So that's why it blocks almost half of thinkorswim." His conclusion is direct: "So it's a better use of buying power or capital if you use IB for these kinds of trade. Again, the risk is still the same. The downside risk is still the same. It's just that you use less capital for the trade."

He adds a second, unrelated advantage of the broker choice that bears on a credit strategy specifically: "on this trade, you collect premium up front, you collect the cash at the entry. Remember, thinkorswim pays almost zero for the cash sitting in your account. Interactive Brokers pay you very decent interest income."

He also flags an important caveat about margin figures on IBKR, discovered while entering the Meta trade. Because portfolio margin nets exposures across a whole account, the margin quoted for a new Jade Lizard on a symbol where you already hold positions will be distorted: "The reason why it blocks me less because I have other meta position. Perhaps that would impact the margin. But the typical trade here would block me about maybe $3,000, $4,000. So fine, this one they blocked me less. To be fair, I would simulate a similar trade in a different account where I don't have meta position to get exact margin for the trade. This one gets mixed up with other trade." For anyone computing ROI honestly, this is a real trap: a margin number that is artificially low because of unrelated hedging positions will flatter the ROI calculation of the new trade.

---

### The Payoff Profile in Full

With the construction rules established, the payoff arithmetic can be stated completely.

**Maximum profit** equals the total net credit received at entry, and it is achieved when the stock finishes at expiration anywhere between the short put strike and the short call strike. "The max profit will be equal to the total credit you collect from selling a bear call and selling the put at the same time." And on where it is realized: "that is a max profit area. So this max profit would be achieved if the stock price stays within the two short strikes at the expiration."

**Upside profit** above the long call equals the total credit minus the call spread width — a fixed, guaranteed amount when the credit exceeds the width, and a small fixed loss when it does not.

**Downside breakeven** is the short put strike minus the total credit per share. "The break-even point on the downside would be, well, the short put strike minus the credit that you receive." On the Tesla example: short put 230, credit approximately $8.97 in the first construction, giving a breakeven near $221.20 — the transcript renders this as "$2212," which is the platform's display of 221.2. When he improves the credit to $10.67 by moving the long call from 270 to 275, the breakeven drops to approximately $219. "So I can lower my break-even point by almost $2 because I collect $2 more from the premium."

**Downside loss** below the breakeven is unbounded and grows dollar for dollar with the decline. "There's a loss zone as well. That is when the share price collapses."

A summary of the full payoff surface at expiration:

| Stock price at expiration | Outcome |
|---|---|
| Above the long call strike | Fixed profit = total credit − call spread width (guaranteed positive if credit ≥ width) |
| Between short call and long call | Profit declining from maximum toward the upside shelf as the short call goes further in the money |
| Between short put and short call | **Maximum profit** = full net credit |
| Between breakeven and short put | Profit declining from maximum toward zero |
| At the breakeven (short put − credit) | Zero |
| Below the breakeven | Loss, growing one-for-one with the decline, unbounded to zero |

#### Where the Breakeven Sits Relative to Expected Movement

One of the more useful observations Khoo makes concerns the relationship between the Jade Lizard's downside breakeven and the market's own estimate of how far the stock can move. "Often you see that break-even point would be close to one standard deviation point or even lower. And the trade would have very high probability of winning, something like 70% or even 80% of probability of winning sometimes."

He then demonstrates this concretely on the Tesla trade. With the stock near $250 and a breakeven around $215, the required decline is roughly 35 points. He compares that against the option market's implied move: "based on the current implied volatility, which is saying that the share price could potentially move up or down by 15 points after the earnings today. So after the earnings, the market expects the stock price to move either $15 up or $15 down with one standard deviation probability. But it could move more, but that would be beyond the expectation of the market. So when I have like 35 points margin of error on the downside, when the market expects the share price to move already 15 points tomorrow, I feel comfortable with the trade."

And over the full life of the trade: "even if you keep the trade until the expiration, which is 44 days, the market also expects the share price to move within 37 points up or down, right at my break-even point. So remember, in this Jade Lizard, with the margin for error there, the break-even point tends to be close to the one-standard-deviation point. So in this case, one-standard-deviation point at the expiration is $37 below the current stock price, which is close to $225, which is fine."

The Tesla platform display showed a probability of profit close to 75% at entry, with a 25% probability of loss. That is the theoretical expectation of a properly constructed Jade Lizard.

---

### The Statistical Record: 237 Trades

What elevates this lesson above a strategy explanation is that Khoo brings his own trading record to the class. Between late May and mid-October — "almost five months now" — he executed 237 Jade Lizard trades in a live account, of which all but fewer than ten had closed by the time of the recording.

| Metric | Result |
|---|---|
| Total trades | 237 |
| Winning trades | 206 |
| Win rate | 87% |
| Losing trades | 13% |
| Total profit | Over $32,000 |
| Average ROI per trade (on margin) | 2.4% |
| Average holding period | 11 days |
| Cumulative capital deployed (arithmetic sum) | ~$1.3 million |
| Actual capital in use at any one time | Roughly $40,000–$50,000 |

Several features of this table deserve comment.

The 87% win rate is materially higher than the ~75% probability of profit the platform assigns to an individual trade at entry, and Khoo notices the gap himself: "in the trade that I showed you earlier, there would be something like 75% of probability of winning. And that would be the case for most of the trades. But in reality, based on the 200 plus trades that I've done so far, the actual win rate for me is 87%." The most likely explanation, though he does not state it as such, is active management: he closes at 50% of maximum profit rather than holding to expiration, which converts a large number of trades that *would* have finished near the breakeven into early winners.

The 2.4% average ROI figure is deliberately unglamorous, and he explains why it should not be judged in isolation. "2.4 looks a little bit low, but keep in mind that this is a fast-moving trade. So every trade, on average, I've been in a trade for only 11 days, less than two weeks, 11 days per trade. So within 11 days, if I could make 2.4% with the high probability of winning. And by the way, 2.4 is an average between losing and winning. So 2.4, very consistent profit. And for 11 days, if you do the math, 2.4 divided by 11 days and times 365 days, you annualize it. You would come up with something like 80% return on investment on the annual basis."

That annualization — 2.4% ÷ 11 × 365 ≈ 79.6% — is a simple non-compounded extrapolation and should be read as such, but it makes the point: the strategy's return comes from velocity, not from magnitude.

The $1.3 million capital figure is the one most likely to alarm a student, and Khoo addresses it directly: "don't be scared or overwhelmed by a $1.3 million here. This is just a mathematical cumulative capital that I use for all 237. In reality, at any point in time, with less than 10 open trades, I use a lot less capital, roughly about maybe $40,000 or $50,000 max. So I just recycled that $50,000 every 11 days on average."

He also shows the raw trade log on screen, colour-coded — closed trades greyed out, open trades in white — and describes what the equity curve looks like in practice: "most of the trades are profitable. From here, you see a series of profitable trades, and then I have a big hit here on the Coinbase price collapse. And then I have some losing trades here once in a while. But most of the time, I have winning trades."

That single reference — a "big hit" on a Coinbase collapse — is the most honest data point in the lesson. It is a concrete illustration of exactly the risk the speculative-stock prohibition is meant to avoid, and it is worth noting that even the author of the strategy took a large loss from one.

Finally, a note of transparency on the numbers themselves: at one point he says he has done "almost 300 trades now" and at another "over 200 trades." The tabulated figure he presents on screen is 237, and that is the number this chapter treats as authoritative.

---

### Worked Construction I: Tesla on thinkorswim

The first construction is done live on thinkorswim, before the market opens, on a day when Tesla is due to report earnings after the close. Khoo is recording pre-market and will enter the trade after the open, which puts the position deliberately through the earnings event.

The setup analysis is brief and technical: "From the technical standpoint, it looks like the price has retraced and maybe near kind of the oversold region right now. So it looks like it's a good setup for our earnings. Because the price has sold off before the earnings, if the earning is not too bad, I think there's a good chance that the price won't drop further, or even increase."

**Step one — choose the expiry.** "First of all, what DTE? 4 to 6 weeks. Anytime between 28 days and 42 days, or 44, 45 days, it's okay. So maybe I look at 44 days, a little bit more than six weeks, it's okay." He selects the December 1 expiry at 44 DTE with the stock at approximately $254.

**Step two — locate the short call at 45 delta.** "I look at the delta column on the call side, and I also look at the delta column on the put side together. So on the call side, I will look for a call that has the delta of 45. There's no exact strike price with the 45 delta, so I can choose something like 44 delta to sell. So this is the one that I will sell the call at. So I will sell the call at 265 strike price."

**Step three — locate the short put at 25 delta.** "On the put side, I would need to sell something like 25 delta. Remember this one, 25 delta or lower. So let's say I choose 25. So it means I will sell 230 on the trade."

**Step four — solve for the long call.** This is where the real work happens, and Khoo tests two candidates against each other.

*Candidate A: buy the 270 call.* "Let's say if I buy 270 call, then net of the credit, I have something close to $9, which is definitely greater than $5.5 between a long call and a short call." The call spread is 265/270, a width of $5.00, and the credit is roughly $8.97 — comfortably above the width, so there is no upside risk. "You see that obviously there's no loss zone on the upside. So if the share price goes higher, I would make money as well. The break-even point will be somewhere $221, which is about the short put strike here, minus the credit that I received. So minus almost $9."

He then applies the ROI test. "Check out the max return on investment. So the max profit is $897. How much is the buying power? The buying power would be $8,126. So then you do the math here, $897, divided by $8,127. So you have something like 11%, max return on investment, which is okay. Also meets the criteria." Eleven percent clears the 10% floor — but only just. "So this one, 11%. It's okay. But it's not the optimal trade."

*Candidate B: buy the 275 call.* "The one I like better would be, why don't I buy 275? So I buy a higher call, I pay less money, and therefore the net credit would be increased. So if I choose 275 strike to buy instead of 270, look at the credit I will receive. Well, in this case, I will receive $10.67, which is a higher max profit for the trade."

The call spread is now 265/275, a width of $10.00, against a credit of $10.67. The guaranteed upside profit shrinks from $3.97 per share to $0.67 per share — the shelf drops nearly to the zero line. Khoo watches this happen on the chart and accepts it: "the profit zone up here would be lower. But it's still positive. It's still above zero line. So still the trade doesn't have the loss zone on the upside, no risk on the upside. So it's still okay."

What he gains is threefold, and he enumerates it: "in this case, I buy a higher call. I have the benefit of a wider profit zone, the lower break-even point, and the higher max-profit potential." The breakeven moves from approximately $221 to approximately $219. "So I can lower my break-even point by almost $2 because I collect $2 more from the premium."

The cost is equally clear: "the trade-off would be if the share price rallies sharply, then I would make less profit on that side."

The ROI test on Candidate B: "If I confirm and send, it says it would block me 8,443. So if I do the math here, then 10.67, that's the credit I received, which is also the max profit, divided by 8,443. So I would have close to 13% max return on investment as compared to only 11% earlier."

Khoo's verdict is unambiguous, and it encodes his general preference: "the version I like better would be the one that would have almost break-even on the upside, which is the 275 here." He then adds a fair-minded note that the other choice is legitimate for a trader with a different view: "if you like the other trade, that's okay, too. You just choose $270. You collect less premium, and they will block you slightly less buying power, but then the return on investment would be less. But in this case, if you choose this trade and the share price rallies very sharply, then you will benefit more from the trade."

**The resulting position**, as he summarizes it back to the class:

| Element | Value |
|---|---|
| Underlying / price | Tesla, ~$254 |
| DTE | 44 (December 1 expiry) |
| Leg 1 | Sell 230 put (~25 delta) |
| Leg 2 | Sell 265 call (~44–45 delta) |
| Leg 3 | Buy 275 call |
| Call spread width | $10.00 |
| Net credit | $10.67 ($1,067 per contract) |
| Credit ≥ width? | Yes — no upside risk |
| Guaranteed upside profit | $0.67 per share ($67) |
| Max profit | $1,067, achieved between 230 and 265 |
| Downside breakeven | ~$219 |
| Buying power blocked (TOS) | $8,443 |
| Max ROI | ~13% |
| Probability of profit (platform) | ~75% |

"In this case, the distance is $10, so I need to collect at least $10, which is the case, because I'm collecting $10.67, or $1,067 for one contract. And the buying power it blocks me is about $8,000. And if I do the math, the max return on investment is more than 10%. Anything more than 10%, that is good."

#### The Same Trade, Adjusted at the Open

When the market actually opens the next session, conditions have moved and Khoo demonstrates something important: the plan is re-derived from current deltas, not copied from the pre-market notes. The broad market is down roughly half a percent on both SPX and Nasdaq, and Tesla is down more than $4. He also notes his standing habit of waiting out the opening auction: "you know that I usually don't take any action during the first half an hour or 45 minutes, and now it's time for me to take action."

The delta shift is exactly what a lower stock price implies. "Right now, I'm looking at 25 delta. Earlier, 25 delta was at this one, 230. But because the price is dropping right now, the 25 delta has increased to 27 delta. So I can afford to sell maybe a slightly lower strike. Instead of 230, I can sell 225, which has a lower delta, which means the trade would be safer."

The same logic applies on the call side: "on the call side earlier I was planning to sell 265 which is 45 delta, this becomes 42 now. So now I need to sell something like 260." The entire structure shifts five points lower. "So instead of 230, now I sell 225 for the put. Instead of selling 265 call, I'm now selling 260 call, and then I will buy $10 higher strike for the long call, which is $270 now."

The revised construction still satisfies the defining condition: "with that, I will still collect more than the spread of the call, which is 10 points. So if I enter the trade right now, I can get $10.47, which is, again, no risk on the upside. And then I have $5 lower on the put side, which protects me better."

He explicitly abandons the pre-market plan: "earlier the trade was like 230 to 65 to 75. Now I no longer want to enter that trade."

He then briefly explores a shorter-dated alternative at 37 DTE — sell the 222 put at 22 delta, sell the 260 call at 46 delta, buy the 270 call — which produces a credit roughly 50 to 55 cents short of the $10 width. This is his clearest demonstration of the tolerance around the credit rule. "So if I do this one, I have less than $10. Not too much lower. Maybe 50 cents, 55 cents lower, which is still acceptable. You have a small loss zone on the upside. But again, as long as you don't hold the trade until expiration and the price goes higher, you can always get some profit, small profit on the upside. So this one is also okay."

The tradeoff between the two expiries is stated as a genuine choice rather than a right answer: "the benefit of this trade will be you can let the trade decay faster and the profit will come faster. But again, the other trade, you have better premium, you have to wait a little longer." He returns to the 44-day version.

---

### Worked Construction II: Tesla on Interactive Brokers

Khoo then rebuilds the identical trade on Interactive Brokers, both to serve students on that platform and because — as established above — IBKR blocks materially less capital for the same risk.

#### The Mechanics of Entry

The workflow he demonstrates is worth recording because a three-legged credit spread cannot be entered leg-by-leg without incurring uncontrolled slippage.

He begins in the Option Trader window: "My preferred way to trade options on Interactive Brokers is to open the option trader. It will open up the option trader. So the new window will pop up like this. So here you just type in Tesla and then choose Stock and Smart. It will pull up the data on options chain from call side and put side."

The critical instruction is the strategy builder: "in the option trader, you need to use strategy builder for the multi-legged strategy. So multi-leg strategy, please use the strategy builder. If you only use the one-legged strategy like buy a call or sell a cash-secured put, you don't need the strategy builder, just here and then click into buy or sell. That's good enough. But if you want to use a multi-leg kind of trade order, then you need to use the strategy builder."

Forgetting to switch it on is a mistake he makes on camera during the Microsoft entry — "I need to turn on the strategy builder. This is a mistake. Turn it on, do it again" — which is a useful reminder that the platform will happily let you build the wrong thing.

He also demonstrates two ways to obtain the margin figure before committing: "Sometimes I just press the transmit and they tell me how much margin they will block me. Or you can right click on that box, right click, and check margin and performance profile."

An important distinction surfaces here between two margin numbers the platform reports. "So maintenance margin, that's what I'm looking at. Initial margin, fine. I use either of them, but I normally use 4,621 because this is the one I need to tie up my cash or buying power to maintain the trade." When entering the JPMorgan trade later he makes the same distinction: "they will block me 4,662 ... But the margin that they keep to maintain my trade is actually less. 4,154. That will be an ongoing margin, not the 4,663."

For ROI computation, the maintenance margin is the figure that matters, because it is the capital that remains locked for the life of the trade.

#### Analyzing the Trade in Risk Navigator

The IBKR analysis tool is Risk Navigator, and the setup sequence Khoo teaches is precise enough to be reproduced step by step.

1. From the classic Trader Workstation, click the Risk Navigator button.
2. Open a new "what-if" window. "By default, it pulls up your positions in your portfolio. But I want to open the new one, blank, without any position in it. So new window, and then it will ask whether the new what-if window here. And then it will ask whether the new one I want to include the positions in my portfolio in it or no. Normally I just use No."
3. Confirm you are in simulation mode. "Once you see this Risk Navigator with the border in red here, that means it's a simulation. It's in the simulation mode."
4. Add the underlying and select the option chain and expiry, then click each of the three legs to add them to the scenario.
5. Assign quantities, which do not populate automatically. "It has zero quantity here. So you need to assign the number of contracts into the simulation... negative means sell, positive means buy."
6. Switch from the default P&L view to the equity tab to see the payoff chart.
7. Expand the position with the plus sign to reveal all three legs.
8. Right-click the chart and choose the last trading day scenario to plot the expiration payoff, and separately select today's date to plot the current-date curve.
9. Right-click again to activate a vertical crosshair for reading values off the chart.
10. Change the x-axis from percentage change to dollar increments by selecting the underlying: "On the x-axis, it's percentage of the price change. If you want to show a dollar increment up or down, you need to choose an underlying... So click onto the underlying here and choose the stock you want to analyze. And here now the x-axis will show the price increment, $5 each."

There is one further setting that Khoo initially gets wrong on camera and later corrects, and it is genuinely important for anyone monitoring a live position rather than simulating a new one. When reviewing an existing trade, the default equity-portfolio plot shows the payoff of a hypothetically newly-opened position, not the actual profit or loss on your fill. "If you look at the chart right now, it simulates the new trade. It's not showing you the real P&L of the current trade. Because the current P&L of the trade is showing that the trade is making $423. And if you look at the curve here, it's a break even. So that means this is meant to be the new trade, not the existing one. Now for you to view the right P&L of the existing trade, you need to change this one, the block here, to the unrealized P&L. Then you have it. Now the dotted purple curve will reflect the real P&L of the trade."

He also notes a cosmetic quirk — a stray dot on the chart that is not the current stock price — and the fix: "This dot is not the current stock price. The vertical line here is where the current stock price is. Now, to make this dot disappear, you just untick on this one and tick it again, then it disappears. This is something to do with the VaR here, which I don't know how to use."

Reading the completed Tesla simulation, he confirms all the key regions. "You see that the max profit is $1,041. How about if the price moved to this area? That is an area of $42 profit." And the loss region: "if the price drops below the break-even point here, it would be a loss zone, and the loss would be significant, a few thousand dollars, or even higher if the price dropped significantly."

He re-derives the maximum-profit zone from the chart: "if the price stays between the two short strikes, 225, which is a short put, and the 260, which is a short call, that is a max profit... But the break-even point is not within this. The break-even point is about $10 lower. Remember, the break-even point is equal to the short put minus the received premium, which is about $10 plus. So your break-even point is near 225, or slightly lower than $225."

And then, unprompted, he restates the central risk: "from the trade standpoint, you can see the risk is not on the upside, the risk is on the downside because it has no protection. And therefore, in this kind of trade, first of all, please don't over trade it. Trade with small quantity, see how it goes. More importantly, manage the risk timely, meaning cut loss."

#### Execution and Fill

Before pulling the trigger, Khoo weighs one final adjustment — spending some of the surplus credit on a safer put. "I can choose to keep the same trade, or I can choose to collect less than this, but have a better protection on the downside. So if I go $5 lower than this, I will need to reduce the premium by $1.50. So that would be net $9. So that's a little bit too low." Nine dollars against a ten-dollar width would open a full dollar of upside loss — beyond his tolerance — so he declines.

He works the order around the mid-price rather than crossing the spread: "You go to the mid price, it's 10.93, similar to thinkorswim. And again, it blocks me about $4,600." He starts at 10.92 and is filled immediately, which prompts a small trader's regret: "so it looks like I could have got a better price than this one, but it's okay."

The final Tesla position: short the December 1 225 put, short the 260 call, long the 270 call, one contract, filled at approximately $10.92 credit, with maintenance margin of $4,621 on IBKR against roughly $8,000 on thinkorswim.

He closes the entry with a restatement of the three exit branches: "if the price goes nowhere, that would be best. So after the earnings, you will see if the price doesn't move, the trade will immediately bring out a lot of profit. If the price drops significantly, I need to be ready when it hits the short put, 225, and I need to cut loss there. But if the price goes significantly higher beyond the long call 270 — well, guess what? I would still make money, though the money would be less. So in that case, I would probably take the profit early and don't hold the trade until expiration to avoid the small profit being disappeared."

---

### Worked Construction III: TSM and the "Reinvest the Upside" Technique

The second construction of the session is on Taiwan Semiconductor, and it introduces the single most characteristic adjustment technique in the entire lesson.

The thesis is fundamental first: "TSM is a fundamentally good stock. Based on my valuation, the fair value of the stock is about $110. Right now, it is trading below 90, which is well below the intrinsic value of the stock. So obviously, it's a good stock. It has the fundamentals to support."

The technical read is neutral, and he says so honestly: "Technically, the stock price is retracing right now, and the earnings is coming tomorrow before the market open. For me, it's below intrinsic value. It's not like overstretched or overbought. It's not even oversold. So it's something like in the middle. In this case, the technical is neutral, in my opinion. And the price will be purely driven by the outcome of the earnings tomorrow." His conclusion for the downside: "I like the stock, and I think the stock has some good fundamental to support on the downside, so I don't think it's going to collapse."

He chooses a shorter expiry than Tesla deliberately, to vary the illustration: the November 24 expiry at approximately 37 DTE.

**The initial construction.** Sell the 84 put at approximately 25 delta; sell the 92 call at 43 delta ("I don't have 45 exact delta here. So I choose 43, which is a 92 call to sell"); buy the 94 call, $2 above. The credit is $2.26 per share against a $2.00 width — comfortably clear of the no-upside-risk condition. Reading the chart: "the chart looks okay because there's no risk on the upside here because the lowest point on the upside is still above zero line. So it's zero risk on the upside kind of trade. If the price moves between the short put and the short call, the trade would make $226 for one contract. And the break-even point is about 81 something, which is 84 minus the collected premium, which is $226."

**The adjustment.** And here is the technique, stated as a choice: "either I can go with this, or I can reinvest the small profit here on the upside to push the short put a little bit lower, so that my trade would be safer. So instead of selling 84 put, I will sell 83 put instead."

The word *reinvest* is exactly right. The surplus credit above the call spread width is, in effect, an asset sitting on the upside shelf doing very little. Because that shelf will almost never be reached and, even when it is, pays only a token amount, the surplus is far more valuable if it is converted into downside distance. Moving the put strike down one dollar costs credit but buys a dollar of additional room before the position starts losing money.

He runs the substitution in Risk Navigator by zeroing the 84 put and adding a short 83 put: "So now the trade is short 83 put, short 92 call, and long 94 call. So in that case, I still have zero risk on the upside. I collect less premium, about $200 instead of $224. But I have a lower break-even point because I push the put strike $1 lower. So then I will reduce the risk on the downside. So I like this trade better than the other one."

The trade gives up roughly $24 of maximum profit per contract to move the breakeven a full dollar lower — a straightforwardly good exchange for a strategy whose only real risk is a downside gap. This same reinvestment move recurs on Alphabet (128 put moved down to 127) and on Meta (285 put moved down to 280), and in each case Khoo makes the substitution for the same reason.

**Position sizing.** TSM introduces the sizing convention Khoo uses throughout. "Normally I go with about $1,000 premium. So this one $200, then I need to enter like five contracts. The Tesla, I collected $1,000. So I just entered one contract. This one, only $200 premium or the max profit. I want to have the same size of the trade. Then I need to increase the number of contracts."

The unit of position size, in other words, is not a number of contracts — it is roughly $1,000 of collected credit. This normalizes risk across underlyings with wildly different share prices and premium levels, and it is why the six live trades range from one contract (Tesla, Meta, Microsoft) to three (JPMorgan, Alphabet) to five (TSM).

**The ROI check.** With five contracts: "check margin. It will block me about $4,100, and collecting $1,000 plus premium. So max return on investment, in this case, it's about 25%. You do the math, a thousand plus divided by 4,000 plus. So 20 plus percent return on investment, which is a very good ratio."

That is comfortably above the 10% floor and at the very top of his stated 14–20% aspiration.

**The fill.** The negotiation is instructive about how a multi-leg credit order actually behaves. "So the midpoint is 203. Then we start with 204 and send. So 204, it's still on the blue. I mean, it has not been received by the other side. So wait a little bit for the blue to turn green. Then it would be fine." He explains the colour convention: "Once it's green, I mean there will be a counterparty, we think, but we have not agreed on the price yet. So we need to negotiate the price with the counterparty here."

He then watches the mid-price deteriorate against him while he holds out — "the midpoint now drops to $203, no, 202, no. The midpoint now drops to $199" — and fills at 201. Five contracts at $2.01 credit, blocking approximately $4,125 of margin.

He closes the session with a practical tip for anyone who has forgotten what margin a live position consumed: rebuild the same structure in the strategy builder at the same contract count and right-click for the margin report without transmitting. "You want to simulate a similar trade, but don't execute it. Just check the margin only... And here you go, then you have 4125, same."

---

### Worked Construction IV: JPMorgan — A Non-Earnings Trade

Five days later Khoo enters four more positions, the first of which is deliberately chosen as a control: JPMorgan has already reported. "Let me start with the one that is not earnings driven, the one that has released earnings, which is JP Morgan Bank."

The construction sequence follows the standard template but produces an instructive failure on the first attempt.

The expiry is December 1, "slightly more than six weeks." He sells the 25-delta put, which sits at the 137 strike. He sells the 146 call at 44 delta. And then he tries the long call four dollars up, at 150: "maybe I buy about $4 higher strike. See if I can get $4 for the spread."

It does not work. "So with this, I collect only $340, $3.40, which is less than the spread of the call, which is $4. So it's not good."

This is the moment that demonstrates the rule has teeth. A $3.40 credit against a $4.00 width would leave sixty cents of upside loss — outside the "approximately fine" tolerance he applied to the fifty-cent shortfall on the shorter-dated Tesla candidate, and in any case unnecessary because a fix is available. "So I need to change the simulation here. I need to buy something like $149."

Narrowing the call spread from four dollars wide to three dollars wide costs credit (the 149 call is more expensive than the 150) but reduces the width by more than the credit falls. "I collect about $300 or $3 per share, that is equal to the spread between $146 and $149. So the credit that I receive should be equal or larger than the spread of the call, which is the case here. So this is fine."

The resulting payoff is textbook: "This is a P&L chart of the trade. When you see that there's no loss zone on the upside, the trade is good... Right now, the stock price is here, as long as it stays within the profit zone, 134, and then 149, that would be very nice. If it goes higher, there's no risk on that upside. Nothing to worry. I could still make some money here, small money, if it goes higher. And I could take profit and run if it goes beyond the 149. Otherwise, if it drops below the 134, I will cut loss and move on."

Sized to the standard unit: "probably I will increase the number of contracts to about three contracts so that I can collect $1,000 premium." At three contracts the maximum profit is approximately $924 and the breakeven sits at $134.

The technical confirmation is added after the fact rather than before, which is worth noting as a departure from strict process: "check the chart also on JPM. Yeah, it looks like the chart is having a support right beneath the current price. So looks like it's a good entry point. Today it's bouncing off a little bit. And there's a good chance that it could be a support line for the price. And then if it goes higher, it's good for the trade. As long as it's not collapsing, it's okay."

The order is worked from a starting credit of $3.10 down through $3.05, $3.04, $3.03 as the mid-price drifts, filling three contracts at $3.02 for a total credit of $906. Initial margin quoted at $4,662; maintenance margin at $4,154.

Before transmitting he pauses on a point that trips up many students, and it is worth quoting: "Check the midpoint now, 305. So let me just start with 310 credit. Remember, this is credit. This is what I'm receiving when I enter the trade. So this is all important, that credit or debit. In the Jade Lizard, at the entry, you need to collect premium up front. So it's a credit. So credit, you want to receive more. So start with a higher number."

The Jade Lizard is always a credit at entry and always a debit at exit, and the direction of price negotiation reverses accordingly — start high on entry and walk down; start low on exit and walk up.

---

### Worked Construction V: Alphabet — Earnings and Maximum Margin of Safety

Alphabet is the third construction, and it is an earnings trade. The chart read comes first: "Google looks good. The chart looks solidly up, and the 50 moving average seems to be a very good support. And recently it retraced, and today it seems just bounced off it. So I like it that it continues its uptrend."

The elevated pre-earnings IV does exactly what Khoo predicted it would. With the stock near $137, the 25-delta put sits all the way down at the 128 strike — nine points, roughly 6.5%, below spot.

The initial construction is short 128 put, short 140 call (45 delta), long 144 call. "So this one, I can collect $4.70, more than the $4 spread of the call, which is good."

And then comes the reinvestment move again, this time stated as a general policy for earnings trades rather than as a one-off: "Normally, when I play earnings, I want to play safe. So if I can collect more than the spread here, I will choose a slightly lower put option so that it gives more margin for error in case the share price falls after earnings. So instead of 128, I will check if I can get a good premium on the 127 put."

Substituting the 127 put for the 128: "With that, I collect almost $4, which is equal to the spread of the call. So I like this trade better because it gives me extra margin of safety on the downside. It's close enough to the $4. So call it $4."

He then measures the resulting protection in percentage terms, which is the clearest statement of the risk framing anywhere in the lesson: "my break-even point is 123. So 123 versus right now the stock price at 136, 137. So I have like $13 downside protection. The margin of safety is $13, which is 10% of the stock right now, which is quite safe, in my opinion, because Google is a fundamentally good stock, and it's on uptrend and it's still undervalue, and now it has 10% margin of safety on the downside."

Note how the fundamental and the structural arguments are stacked rather than substituted: the stock is undervalued *and* the structure gives a 10% buffer. Neither alone is the reason for the trade.

Sized at three contracts, the ROI screen is exceptional: "the max profit here is 1,200 divided by 2,113 margin. So the max profit is like 50%, which is good." He immediately adds an honest caveat about why the number is so flattering: "I mean, maybe because I have a portfolio margin, so it blocks me less. But for those who have a Reg-T margin, I think they will block you about 4,000. Still, you have 20 plus percent max return on investment, which is still very good."

The fill negotiation ends slightly below the $4.00 target, at $3.90 for three contracts, and he explicitly accepts the resulting sliver of upside risk: "Don't drop too much. I think $390 is still okay because the chart shows that there's a little loss on there, but when the price goes up, I will still make money."

He then quantifies the sliver from the simulation, and in doing so gives the clearest statement of why a small upside loss zone is tolerable: "if I keep the trade until expiration, the trade would lose like $22. But if I take the profit early, I would make like $100 plus. So normally, if it goes beyond the break-even point on the upside, I make small profit, I would just close the trade and run."

This is the resolution of the credit-versus-width tolerance. A ten- or twenty-cent shortfall creates a theoretical loss that only materializes if you hold to expiration in the one scenario — a strong rally — where you would have closed early anyway. The rule is a rule about expiration risk, and the management rule dissolves it.

Total credit: $1,170 for three contracts. Margin: $2,113. Position: short December 1 127 put, short 140 call, long 144 call.

---

### Worked Construction VI: Meta — Testing the Put Ladder

Meta is the fourth construction, also an earnings play. The chart: "Meta chart looks also good, uptrend, long term and short term. Looks like there's a support at 50 moving average as well. Earnings coming. If we have a good margin of safety, I think I still like the trade."

The call-side selection illustrates the discretion inside the 45-delta band: "on the call side, I would sell 46 or 42. 42 means I have more profit upside. 46 is I have less profit on upside. Maybe 46 is okay." Selling the higher-delta (lower-strike) call collects more premium but caps the maximum-profit plateau at a lower price; selling the lower-delta call widens the plateau but collects less. He takes the 325 call at approximately 46 delta and buys the 335 call, a $10 width.

The initial construction with the 285 put clears the width comfortably at more than $11. And so, once again, the surplus goes into the put strike — but this time Khoo does something he does not do elsewhere: he ladders down through candidates to find the boundary.

First candidate down: "instead of collecting $10 plus, or $11 plus here, I will reduce the put here, let's say, to $280 to be safer in case the share price falls after the earnings." At the 280 strike, which is 21 delta, "I collect like still more than 10. This is good."

Second candidate: "Why don't I test another one? Let's sell even lower put to see how low I can go. Let's say if I sell 275." The result fails the test: "Then I collect less than 10. All right, so that's a little bit too low."

He settles at 280. "Maybe I go back to the 280, sell 280, and then zero out this one. So I collect $10.54. This is good."

This ladder is the cleanest demonstration in the lesson of the actual optimization problem the Jade Lizard poses. You are minimizing the short put strike subject to the constraint that total credit remains at or above the call spread width. Meta's answer is 280; going to 275 violates the constraint.

The payoff analysis confirms the shape: "there's no loss zone on the upside here. I would make some money even if it goes beyond a break-even point on the upside. On the downside, where's my break-even point? That's 270. 270 at expiration."

He then does something he does on every trade — he prices the stop-loss scenario in advance: "Now, if I cut loss, when the price drops below the short put, which is 280, how much is a loss? The loss would be about $900. It's less than the premium I receive here. So that's the typical risk-reward profile. If it drops so much below my short put of the trade, then the trade will be losing approximately near the premium that I receive."

And a crucial qualifier that governs how the stop actually behaves: "But that is on that date only. If the price stays there until the expiration, this loss will turn into a max profit, actually. So depends on how much time I've been in the trade before the price drops, it could have a different P&L implication."

That sentence contains the whole subtlety of managing this trade, and we will return to it.

Finally, the fundamental case, offered as the reason he is comfortable with the residual risk: "I strongly believe Meta has turned around. They're making good money. They restructured their cost structure, and they reduced their investment. So cash flow has improved a lot. A lot of fundamental stuff has been improved over the past few quarters. That's why you see the share price has performed very well this year."

Sized at one contract because the premium is already at the $1,000 unit, the order fills after walking down from $10.60 through $10.55 and $10.50 to $10.40. Total credit $1,040; margin $2,413.

---

### Worked Construction VII: Microsoft — When the Strike Ladder Fights Back

Microsoft is the fourth entry of the day and the one where construction genuinely fails on the first pass, which makes it the most instructive.

The chart read is lukewarm but acceptable: "Chart looks okay. So on uptrend, on the long term, on the short term, it's kind of neutral, sideways. It's fine. It's not like a terrible chart looking like sloping down. So it's not. It looks okay. A decent chart here."

He deliberately varies the expiry to demonstrate the process: "maybe I choose different DTE now. Let's see if I can have a good trade. So now, this time I choose November 24, which is about a month."

The construction: short put at approximately 24 delta, short call at approximately 45 delta, long call ten points higher at 345. And the strike ladder immediately becomes the problem. "You know, the problem with this series, there's no more granular strike prices. So there's like $5 increment, which is not so ideal."

The result: "So I collect only 876, not like 10. I need to have like $10 or $1,000 for one contract. So this is less ideal because I have less than $10 spread."

An $8.76 credit against a $10.00 width leaves $1.24 of upside loss — more than double the largest shortfall he has accepted anywhere else, and clearly outside tolerance. Rather than compromise, he changes expiry: "therefore I may simulate a different trade. Maybe I choose the longer DTE. Maybe I go all the way to December 1 again, same DTE as I use for others."

In the December 1 chain: "sell 310, which is 25 delta. And then on the call, I would sell 46 delta. And then I will buy this 345, which is $10 spread. Same strike price structure. Now I will check if I can get a good premium or not... This one I got like $9 plus, which is close to 10. I think this one is better."

Roughly $9.25 against a $10.00 width leaves about $0.75 of theoretical upside loss — acceptable under the "approximately fine" tolerance, and he justifies it exactly as he did on Alphabet, by reference to the management rule: "even if the share price exceeds the long call, which is the profit zone on the upside, the trade would still make some money. So if I don't hold the trade until the expiration, I don't have the loss here. So I'm not worried about this dotted blue line below here, because I'm not going to keep the trade until expiration. I will close the trade if it goes beyond $345. So then I will make money if it goes higher."

The downside: "on the downside, where's my break-even point? That is here, 300 on the chart. How does it look? Let me see. 300 is somewhere here. Quite a good margin for error. The share price needs to collapse kind of thing to hit the 300."

And the pre-computed stop: "I would need to cut loss if it hits the 310, which is the short put strike, at which I will lose this money, which is about $500, which is not bad, because that is half of the premium that I'm collecting here."

The order walks down from $9.60 through $9.50, $9.45, $9.40, $9.30 and fills at $9.27. One contract, credit $927 (reported later as $927 inclusive of commission).

---

### Trade Management: The Three Scenarios

Khoo organizes management around exactly three price scenarios, and he gives each a defined action. This is the operating manual for the strategy and it is worth setting out completely before following the live trades.

#### Scenario One: The Stock Goes Nowhere (or Drifts Mildly)

This is the design case and the profitable one. "If everything goes okay, the price stays stagnant or going a little bit higher or even drops a little. In those scenarios, the trade would be doing very well. And as long as the price continues to stay within this neutral, slightly bullish kind of zone, the time decay would bring more profit."

The action is to take profit at approximately half of the maximum profit: "I would take profit at about half of the max profit. So max profit is $1,067. If I got like $500 or $600, especially in less than half of the time, I would take it. Release the capital for a new trade."

Later, when actually managing the live trades, he widens this into a band: "you recall my exit criteria is I would take profit if the trade hits about 50 to about two-thirds of the max profit."

Note two important features of this rule. First, the denominator is the maximum profit — the credit received — not the margin. Second, the *rate* of profit accumulation matters as much as the level: "especially in less than half of the time." Fifty percent of the maximum profit earned in a quarter of the time is a far better annualized outcome than the remaining fifty percent earned over the other three quarters.

He makes this explicit when closing Meta: "I would take the profit on this trade today, because it's good enough. There is still four weeks to expiration. So I only make like 60% of the max profit in two weeks. No point to wait for another four weeks to make the rest of like 40%. Just close it, release the buying power for new trades. Holding onto the trade to earn the remaining 40% is fine. But just keep in mind that the time that you need to wait will be longer, four weeks from now, double of the time that has passed. And then you just get a smaller portion of the profit if the price remains in the profit zone. Now, holding on to the trade for the next four weeks, anything can happen. The price could move a lot higher. The price could drop a lot as well. Just don't know. So in this case, just stick to the rule, take the profit and run."

#### Scenario Two: The Stock Collapses

This is the loss case and the one that requires discipline. The stop trigger is stated unambiguously: **exit when the stock price falls below the short put strike.** "The stop loss would be when the share price drops falling below the short put strike. The short put strike is 230, right?"

The expected size of that loss is approximately half the maximum profit, and Khoo emphasizes the symmetry: "I would cut loss where it hits my short put, and I would incur something like $500 loss, which is half of the max profit. So you see the consistency here. I take profit at half of the max profit. Or take loss at half of the max profit as well."

He is then careful to head off a misreading: "not the return on investment. Return on investment would be less because if I incur only $500 loss and the broker blocks me like $8,000 plus, then the loss would be around 7 or 8%. So the 50% here is not the 50% return on investment, but rather the 50% of the max profit. To be consistent, either take profit or take loss at 50% of the max profit."

Crucially, the *actual* loss at the stop depends heavily on how much time remains. Khoo qualifies the rule in several places, and this is the piece most students get wrong.

If the stock touches the short put strike late in the trade's life, the position may still be profitable, because time decay has already lifted the current-date curve close to the expiration payoff.
