"If the trade is expiring on the same day, then the trade would still make money because at that point in time, it's still above the break-even point. So in that scenario, depends on how long you've been in the trade. If the trade is almost expiring and the price starts to plunge, then the trade would probably still be okay. And in that case, take a profit and run."

If, on the other hand, the stock collapses immediately after entry, the loss is at its worst. "Now, the worst-case scenario would be right after I enter the trade, and the price already started to plunge. So in that case, I would cut loss if the price drops below the put strike."

And there is a third gradation, which is what actually happens on Tesla. If the stock does not merely touch the short put but gaps decisively *through* it, the loss escalates from roughly half the credit to roughly the full credit: "That's a typical profile of the trade when the price drops well below the short put. In this case, exceeding the short put, you would typically lose that kind of money. If it just barely hits the short put, the loss would be about 50% of the received premium. But in this case, it drops all the way lower than that and even lower than the break-even point. So the trade is losing 100% of the premium that I received."

The three gradations can be summarized:

| Situation when short put is breached | Approximate outcome |
|---|---|
| Stock drifts down to the short put late in the trade's life | Position may still be profitable; take the profit and exit |
| Stock reaches the short put with meaningful time remaining | Loss of roughly 50% of the credit received |
| Stock gaps well below the short put, near or through the breakeven | Loss of roughly 100% of the credit received |

#### Scenario Three: The Stock Rallies Sharply

This is the "okay but not ideal" case. "What if the share price suddenly rallies very strongly? So in that scenario, you see the price suddenly rallies. That is an okay scenario. It's not ideal. But it's okay because the trade would still be making some money, especially when the time is not near the expiration."

The action is to take the small profit and exit, and the reasoning is entirely about the decay of the current-date curve toward the expiration curve — in this region, that decay works *against* you. "I would take profit at that point in time because the trade would make some small profit, and I would just close it and move on. And the reason for it is, if you let the trade run through the expiration, this profit will turn into a break even. The pink curve will go down and become the blue curve. In that case, the small profit would turn into a break even. I don't want that to happen. If the share price goes very sharply, I just take a small profit and move on."

This is the one region of the Jade Lizard where theta is your enemy rather than your friend. Between the two short strikes, the current-date curve rises toward the expiration plateau as time passes. Above the long call, the current-date curve *falls* toward the flat upside shelf. Holding a runaway winner is therefore strictly value-destructive.

He restates this repeatedly. On the trade sitting above the long call at Microsoft: "if I don't close it now and the price either continues to go higher and I would make less profit, or even if it stays right here until the expiration, this $110 will turn into a small loss here, which I don't want. So better take the profit and run in this case."

And he explicitly refuses to speculate on a retracement, which is a discipline point worth underlining: "Because I don't know if the price will ever retrace back here or not. If you have a conviction that the price has run up so much so fast and it could go down into the profit zone — if you have that foresight, yeah, go ahead and keep the trade, and you have the chance to make good profit here. But you never know. The price could continue to stay here or even go higher and then you will turn the profit into a loss. I don't want that situation. I don't have to guess. I just take the chance of the probability of the trade here. So now it's outside the profit zone. I would still make some profit. Why not? So I just close it for small profit. It's okay."

#### The Complete Exit Rulebook

| Condition | Action |
|---|---|
| Unrealized profit reaches 50%–66% of max profit | Close for profit; release capital |
| Profit target hit unusually early relative to DTE | Close — the annualized return is what matters |
| Stock falls below the short put strike, early in trade | Cut loss (expect ~50% of credit lost) |
| Stock gaps well below the short put toward breakeven | Cut loss immediately (expect ~100% of credit lost) |
| Stock at/below short put but near expiration and still profitable | Take the profit and exit |
| Stock rises above the long call strike | Close early for the small profit before theta erodes it |
| Stock rises above the short call but below the long call | Monitor; profit is shrinking; consider closing |
| Any position approaching expiration | Do not hold to expiry — close it |

#### Monitoring: Theta as the Confirming Indicator

Throughout the review sessions Khoo uses theta as the quantitative check on whether time is working for him. On the TSM position: "The theta should be positive, $17 a day. So as long as it stays within this range, theta continues to be positive and the trade will bring some money." On a later review of the same position: "Theta is $15 a day. So I would just keep the trade, wait for the theta to work its magic."

He also offers a graphical shortcut for anyone who does not want to read the Greeks: "even if you don't look at the theta, look at the chart, you would know theta is positive. Why? Because the price is right here. And right here, you see the profit is just less than half of the max profit. So the longer it stays around here, the more profit will come, and you hit the max profit at the expiration."

The general principle is that the vertical gap between the current-date curve and the expiration curve *at the current stock price* is the profit that time decay will deliver if nothing moves. Where that gap is positive, theta is your friend and holding is rational. Where it is negative — above the long call — holding is irrational.

---

### The Six Live Trades, Followed to Completion

What makes this lesson unusually valuable as a record is that all six positions are followed from entry to exit with real fills and real P&L. The narrative that follows tracks each one.

#### Tesla: The Loss

Entered October 18 with the stock at approximately $248–250, short the December 1 225 put, short the 260 call, long the 270 call, one contract, credit $10.92.

The trade went wrong immediately, and it went wrong twice. "Two days ago, when I entered the trade, the price was at about 250. And then on that particular day, after I entered the trade, the price closed significantly lower than the entry point. So it dropped all the way down to 235. Yesterday, after the earnings was released and it was bad, the stock plunged another 8% or 9% and today it's dropping another 4% or 5%."

Khoo separates the causes honestly: "part of the reason is the whole market is now selling off and because of the 10-year treasury yields have been spiking up. And partly because the earnings have been bad and the guidance going forward is also not a good story."

By October 20 the stock was around $212–213, well below the 225 short put and near the trade's breakeven. The position was showing an unrealized loss of $1,063 against a credit of $1,090 — "which is almost 100% of the collected premium at the entry... so 99% of the premium."

Khoo makes the decision to cut without hesitation, and the reasoning is a small clinic in probabilistic discipline: "I would say this is a little bit unlucky because the trade itself has a high probability of winning. I've been trading this for almost 300 trades now, and the probability of winning is like 87%. So 13% of the time, the trade lost money, and this is one of those situations. So just treat it that way. It's just part of the rare cases where I lose money. I just need to play with the odds here. I will win some, I will lose some... In this case, I cannot bet that the price will reverse because I don't know. By right, I just stick to the plan. I will cut loss right here, and let the future trades hopefully make more money to offset."

He closes by rebuilding the reverse order in the strategy builder — buy to close the two shorts, sell to close the long — starting the debit below the mid and walking up in five-cent increments until filled at $21.80. He decomposes the fill: "the exit price is 21.8, in which 21.1 is from the short put that I bought back, and the other two is from the call spread." That is, the short put alone accounted for over 96% of the closing cost. The call spread — the leg with capped risk — was almost irrelevant to the outcome.

The final tabulated result differs slightly from the figures quoted during the live exit, and this chapter reports the summary numbers as authoritative: entry credit $1,092, exit debit $2,080, loss $988, held five days, margin $6,138 (this margin figure is higher than the $4,621 maintenance margin observed at entry and Khoo does not reconcile the difference on camera), loss equal to 16.1% of margin and roughly 90% of the credit collected. Tesla was at $248 at entry and $211.99 at exit.

His epitaph for the trade is brief: "Well, you win some, you lose some. So in this case, I lose on the trade."

#### TSM: The Full Cycle

Entered October 18, five contracts, short the November 24 83 put, short the 92 call, long the 94 call, credit $2.01 per share, $1,005 total, margin approximately $4,125.

TSM did the opposite of Tesla. "TSM actually is the other way around. I entered it here when the price was dropping. And yesterday, the earnings were released, and the company beat the expectations from both top line and bottom line and provided a very bullish guidance. And the stock jumped yesterday. Today it's retracing a little bit, but it's still higher than my entry point."

At the first review (October 20) the position showed $119 unrealized. Khoo held, applying the rule mechanically: "Normally, I would take profit at 50% of the max profit. So in this case, my entry price is $2 and five contracts. I collected $1,000. That is my max profit. Right now, I'm making about $120, so less than $500. So I will continue to hold the trade here, to wait for the time decay to bring more profit."

At the second review (October 23) it was $116 with theta at $17 a day, and the projected profit if the stock stayed put was $535. "Right now, time is our friend. I just leave it there, nothing to worry about."

At the third review (November 3) it had reached $418 — "41% of the max profit" — with theta at $15 a day and the stock at $91.70, comfortably inside the 81-to-94 profit zone. Khoo held once more: "I would wait. I would wait for a few more days, and then the trade would make more money, and then I would take the profit at 50% or better at that point in time."

By November 8 the stock had risen to about $92.50, which put it *above* the 92 short call. This changes the calculus, and Khoo says so: "this trade has a break-even point between 81 and 94. Today, the price is approaching the high end of the break-even point... The stock price currently at about 92.5. So it's still within the profit zone." The unrealized profit was $439, or about 44% of maximum — slightly short of the 50% target.

He closed anyway, and gave two reasons. The first was schedule: "By right, I can hold the trade because it has not hit the 50% of the max profit yet, 44%, and I would still wait for a few more days because theta is still working in my favor. $13 a day... But the video on the lesson has been a little long, so I just want to close it here. In reality, you can hold the trade for a few more days."

The second reason, added during the summary, is the substantive one and it is a genuine management insight: "I forgot to mention one of the reasons why I want to close this trade today is because the price has gone beyond the short call. The short call of the trade is 92, and the stock price was 92.46 at the time I exited the trade. So it's slightly above the short call, and I don't want to risk losing the profit."

That is a real management principle worth extracting even though it is not in his formal rulebook: once the stock trades above the short call, the position has left the maximum-profit plateau and is sliding down the right shoulder toward the upside shelf. Further holding no longer maximizes profit.

He exits by rebuilding the reverse order — buy to close both shorts, sell to close the long, quantity five — and walking the debit up from $1.08 through $1.12, $1.13, $1.15 to a fill at $1.16.

Result: entry credit $1,005, exit debit $580, profit $425, held 21 days, ROI approximately 10% on margin, and 42–43% of maximum profit.

He also notes in passing something the platform does that reinforces the strategy's capital-recycling logic: "when I submit, the broker will release the margin, release margin for new trades. That should happen. When I enter the trade, it increased the margin, so it blocked more margin for my account. But when I close the trade, the broker will release or reduce the buying power or the margin for new trades."

#### Meta: The Ideal Outcome

Entered October 23, one contract, short December 1 280 put, short 325 call, long 335 call, credit $1,040, margin $2,413. Stock at entry: $315.

Meta reported and the stock fell — but not far enough to matter. Khoo describes the sequence: "for META, the earnings was solid, but the price dropped about $10, and it was still within the profit zone of the trade. So therefore, I held on to the trade, and the price recovered after that day, and it has stayed within the profit zone since then. So the trade has been very profitable from the get-go until today when I closed it."

This is precisely the scenario the strategy is designed for: an earnings move that is real but contained inside the very wide gap between the short put and the short call. The IV crush after the announcement collapsed the option prices on both sides simultaneously, delivering profit immediately.

By November 3 the position was at "almost 60%" of maximum profit with four weeks still to run, which triggered the profit-taking rule and the annualization argument quoted earlier.

The exit demonstrates both closing methods on IBKR. The first is via the portfolio: right-click the combined position and select Close, then negotiate the debit — but Khoo notes the sign confusion this can create. "It knows credit, debit, plus side or minus side. Confusing. So the other way, it just turned on the strategy builder here where you have a negative one, then you click the ask to buy. Leg number one. Leg number two, you also have a short position here. You click the ask to buy. And then the 335 strike, I have a long call here. So I click bid to sell. So I just do a reverse order of the existing position."

He starts at $4.06 against a $4.19 mid, raises to $4.15, then $4.16, and finally fills at $4.23 as the mid drifted to $4.24. He is candid that his impatience cost him: "of course, because I start with a lower number, most of the time it won't be filled. I really want to close it. Then I need to raise the price. So just gradually raise the price until it is filled. Now, if I'm not so keen, then I just leave it there for a while and then I come back and I will negotiate again. But in this case, I just make sure that I show you how I exit the trade."

Result: entry credit $1,040, exit debit $423, profit $617, held 11 days, ROI 25.6% on margin, 59.3% of maximum profit.

Khoo singles out the price behavior as the ideal: "look at the price at entry, that is 315, and at the exit time, that was 314.6. It's almost the same. That's the best thing about this trade. The price doesn't move and the profit is like 60% of the max profit, which is what it's all about. After 11 days, price doesn't move. That's a very good scenario. In this trade, you don't want the price to move so much higher or so much lower. As long as it stays in the range within the profit zone, that would be the best."

Forty cents of stock movement over eleven days produced a 25.6% return on capital. That single sentence is the clearest statement of what the Jade Lizard is actually monetizing.

#### Microsoft: The Upside Escape

Entered October 23, one contract, short December 1 310 put, short 335 call, long 345 call, credit $927 inclusive of commission, margin approximately $1,914 (derived from the reported 5.8% ROI on $111 profit; the exact figure is shown on his screen but not read aloud). Stock at entry: approximately $330.

Microsoft reported spectacularly. "Microsoft released an outstanding set of numbers, and the stock price jumped significantly. It retraced a little bit, and after that, it just kept going higher. Because of that, the stock price is right here, and it went outside the profit zone."

By November 3 the stock had run to roughly $350, above the 345 long call — beyond the entire structure. The unrealized profit was approximately $108–110.

This is Scenario Three, and Khoo frames it explicitly against the Tesla outcome: "this is the opposite scenario of the Tesla trade when the price fell significantly after the earnings. This one, the price went way higher after the earnings, and it went outside the profit zone into the upside of the trade. But this is a better scenario because in such a scenario, the trade would still make some money. Unlike when it drops outside the profit zone on the downside, it would lose money. So it's not the bad scenario here when the stock price went outside to the upside. Because remember, the trade doesn't have risk on the upside, if you construct it correctly."

He identifies the residual issue precisely: "In this case, I have a small loss zone on the upside only if I keep the trade until expiration and the price stays outside the profit zone here. But I want to close it early so that I would still realize some profit here, which is about $110."

This is the payoff of the Alphabet/Microsoft tolerance decision, tested live. The construction had accepted a roughly seventy-five-cent shortfall against the width, which implies a small theoretical loss at expiration above the long call. Because he closes early, the current-date curve is still above zero and he realizes a profit rather than the theoretical loss.

He exits by right-clicking the position, starting the debit at $8.10 against a mark of $8.14, then walking up through $8.12, $8.14, $8.15 to a fill at $8.16.

Result: entry credit $927, exit debit $816, profit $111, held 11 days, ROI 5.8% on margin, 12% of maximum profit. Microsoft went from $330 at entry to approximately $350 at exit — a move Khoo describes as "up like $23. So that is too much on the upside, but yet the trade is still profitable, which is very good."

Twelve percent of the maximum profit is a poor outcome relative to the Meta trade, but it is a positive outcome from a twenty-dollar adverse move in the underlying. That is the no-upside-risk property paying for itself.

#### Alphabet: The Discretionary Override

Entered October 23, three contracts, short December 1 127 put, short 140 call, long 144 call, credit $1,170, margin $2,113. Stock at entry: $136.60.

This trade contains the most interesting and most carefully caveated episode in the whole lesson, because Khoo breaks his own rule and says so.

Alphabet reported and the stock fell hard. "Alphabet released very good earnings with a slight miss on the cloud growth. But the rest of the numbers are fantastic, very solid. Stock price drops something like 10% after the earnings. After the earnings, the price drops below the profit zone here, and I was ready to cut loss on the trade. I was ready to do it."

A 10% decline on a stock at $136.60 puts it near $123 — at or through the 127 short put and close to the trade's breakeven. By the rulebook, that is an unambiguous exit.

He did not exit. "But before that, I did a study, and I found that everything looked so good with a very tiny thing in their numbers in the result. And I truly believed that the market got it wrong. And the decline in the stock price was just purely an overreaction. So at that point, I made an adjustment call that the stock price would recover. And in fact, it did. So the stock has recovered very strongly. So it went into the profit zone here again. So that's why the trade has turned around from a losing trade to a profitable trade."

Khoo then does something that deserves credit: rather than presenting this as skill, he flags it as a rule violation. "So you can argue that I was a little bit cheating here. That's fine. But I told you, perhaps in many venues, that I have very strong conviction on the Alphabet fundamentals. And that's why I believe it was just pure overreaction on the earnings."

And then, more directly still: "So if I play by the rule, I should have cut loss. To be very transparent, I should have cut loss on this one. But in this case, it's one of the very rare cases where I have very strong conviction that the stock price falling after the earnings was wrong. Somehow I felt that was wrong. And I took the risk to hold onto the trade because it's a good stock anyway. So I held onto the trade and then the whole thing turned around."

The comparison he draws to Tesla is the important teaching point, because it shows the two branches side by side: "Like the Tesla trade at the beginning, I cut loss, I moved on, no regrets. I think the stock price also recovered, but it's okay. Once you cut loss, you close the trade, it's not relevant anymore. But in this particular case, I made an adjustment call. I took the risk, and it paid off handsomely."

His framing for how students should treat this is careful and non-prescriptive: "So it's a little bit on the art, not the science part of the trade. So just take it in the right context." And elsewhere: "If you want to apply this strategy, sometimes you have to make a hard call, whether you want to cut loss and move on."

The honest reading of this episode is that the discretionary override worked and Khoo does not recommend it. He also notes that Tesla — the trade where he followed the rule — subsequently recovered too, which means the rule cost him money on that occasion and the override made him money on this one. Neither outcome tells you anything about whether the rule is correct; only the 237-trade sample does.

By November 8 the position was at $781 unrealized, "which is equivalent to 67% of the max profit" — the top of his 50–66% band. He closed. "So I would like to take profit today because it's well within that range. In fact, it is at the high end of the range. So two-thirds of the max profit now is being realized. So the profit is good, and I just take it and release the buying power or the margin for new trades. There's no point to hold the trade until December 1, which is still like three weeks from now, and to get only one-third of the profit left in the trade."

His reason for not pressing further is a general one: "There could be a lot of uncertainties while you're holding the trade, especially now the stock has rallied quite strongly, and a retracement can reduce the profit or even wipe out the profit. You never know. So the profit is good. Just take it and run."

He exits by strategy builder, walking the debit from $1.28 up through $1.29, $1.30, $1.32, $1.33 and finally $1.34, where it fills.

Result: entry credit $1,170, exit debit $402, profit $768, held 16 days, ROI 36.3% on margin, 65.6% of maximum profit.

The most striking feature of this trade, which Khoo highlights, is the direction of the stock over the holding period: "look at the price. The price at the entry was 136.6. And today, when I exited it, it actually dropped by 5 points. And it's still making good profit. That is the nature of this kind of trade. It has a significant margin of safety on the downside. So after the earnings, remember, Google's share price fell and then recovered, versus the entry price, it's still $5 down. But the trade made very good profit."

A stock that finished five dollars lower than where it started produced a 36.3% return on capital in sixteen days. This is the clearest possible illustration of what "neutral to slightly bullish" actually means in practice: the position does not need the stock to go up, only to not go down very much.

#### JPMorgan: The Control Case

Entered October 23, three contracts, short December 1 137 put, short 146 call, long 149 call, credit $906, margin approximately $4,050–4,154.

JPMorgan is the only one of the six with no earnings event in the holding period, and its behavior is correspondingly undramatic.

At the November 3 review the position was showing $340, "which is about 38% of the max profit." Khoo assessed the risk on both sides: "it is quite safe to hold the trade here because it's not very far from the break-even point on the upside, and it's very far from the break-even point on the downside... Again, time is my friend here, and every day it will bring me $15 from the time decay standpoint for three contracts here. It's good."

By November 8 it had reached "about 400 plus or 46% of the max profit" with the stock in the upper part of the 134-to-149 profit zone. As with TSM, he closed slightly short of the 50% target and said openly that he was doing so for the convenience of the lesson: "if I hold it for a few more days, I'm sure this will bring more profit, and I could exit at 50% or more, like the Google when I exited at 66, 67% of the max profit. I could do the same for JPM here. But again, holding the trade always comes with some risk. And just for the illustration purpose, I just take the profit here. In reality, I could just hold it for a few more days."

The exit walks the debit from $1.62 up to a fill around $1.68.

Result: entry credit $906, exit debit $504, profit $402, held 16 days, ROI approximately 10% on margin, 44% of maximum profit.

---

### The Combined Scorecard

| Trade | Entry | Days | Contracts | Credit | Margin | Exit debit | P&L | ROI | % of max profit | Stock at entry → exit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tesla | Oct 18 | 5 | 1 | $1,092 | $6,138 | $2,080 | **−$988** | −16.1% | −90% | $248 → $211.99 |
| TSM | Oct 18 | 21 | 5 | $1,005 | ~$4,125 | $580 | **+$425** | ~10% | 42% | ~$89 → $92.46 |
| Meta | Oct 23 | 11 | 1 | $1,040 | $2,413 | $423 | **+$617** | 25.6% | 59.3% | $315 → $314.60 |
| Microsoft | Oct 23 | 11 | 1 | $927 | ~$1,914 | $816 | **+$111** | 5.8% | 12% | $330 → ~$350 |
| Alphabet | Oct 23 | 16 | 3 | $1,170 | $2,113 | $402 | **+$768** | 36.3% | 65.6% | $136.60 → ~$131.60 |
| JPMorgan | Oct 23 | 16 | 3 | $906 | ~$4,050 | $504 | **+$402** | ~10% | 44% | — |
| **Total** | | **avg 13** | | | **$28,000+** | | **+$1,335** | **6.4%** | | |

Khoo's own summary: "I got only one losing trade, and the next five are winning trades. Total combined six trades, I made a profit of 1,335. Total combined buying power or margin I use on the six trades, $28,000 plus, that translates into an average 6.4% return on investment."

And on velocity, which is the point of the whole exercise: "the good thing about this one is I do not tie up my capital on the trade for long. So in the case of Tesla, I quickly cut loss. TSM, 21 days, Meta 11 days, Microsoft 11 days, Google 16 days, JPMorgan 16 days, so on average, I've been in the trades for 13 days per trade. Within 13 days, I could generate 6.4%. That is pretty good. So imagine if I keep doing this, every 13 days, I got 6%. So in a month, I could get like 17, 18%."

The win rate over the six: "I got 5 out of 6 trades as winning trades. So 5 over 6, that translates into 83% win rate, which is very similar to my overall Jade Lizard trades so far. So I've done like over 200 trades, and my win rate on average is also over 80%. So this one is not unusual. It's very consistent with what I have achieved over the past five, six months now."

There is one honest observation to add that Khoo does not make: five of these six trades were entered on the same two days into a market that subsequently rallied. The 83% win rate over six correlated trades is not independent evidence of anything; the 87% over 237 trades across five months is. The six-trade sequence is best read as a detailed demonstration of process, not as a statistical result.

---

### Adjustments and Rolling

It is important to be precise about what Khoo does and does not teach here, because the Jade Lizard's adjustment repertoire in this course is narrower than students might expect from other credit strategies.

**Adjustments made before entry are extensive and systematic.** These are the ones taught in full:

The *long call selection* is itself an adjustment lever, and Khoo demonstrates iterating over candidate strikes on Tesla (270 versus 275) and on JPMorgan (150, which failed, versus 149, which worked). Moving the long call further out increases credit, raises maximum profit, lowers the downside breakeven, and flattens the upside shelf; moving it closer does the reverse.

The *short put reinvestment* is the signature technique — spend surplus credit above the call spread width on moving the put strike down. Demonstrated on TSM (84 → 83), Alphabet (128 → 127), and Meta (285 → 280, with 275 tested and rejected as too far). The general rule: "if I can collect more than the spread here, I will choose a slightly lower put option so that it gives more margin for error."

The *short call delta selection* within the 42–47 band trades premium against plateau width: "42 means I have more profit upside. 46 is I have less profit on upside."

The *expiry substitution* is used when the strike ladder in one series is too coarse to satisfy the credit rule, as on Microsoft where a 30-day series with $5 increments was abandoned for the 44-day series.

The *pre-market to open re-derivation* on Tesla, where the entire structure shifted five points lower because the stock had moved and both deltas had shifted, is an adjustment discipline in its own right: the plan is a method, not a set of strikes.

**Adjustments after entry are, in this lesson, essentially absent — and that is deliberate.** Khoo does not teach rolling the short put down and out. He does not teach rolling the call spread up. He does not teach converting the position into a different structure when tested. The management rulebook contains exactly two post-entry actions: close for profit at 50–66% of maximum, or close for loss when the stock breaches the short put. There is no third branch.

The only post-entry deviation demonstrated anywhere in the six trades is the Alphabet override, and Khoo explicitly labels it as a rule violation driven by fundamental conviction rather than a technique — "so if I play by the rule, I should have cut loss. To be very transparent, I should have cut loss on this one" — and files it under "the art, not the science part of the trade." It should not be read as an adjustment method.

This absence is coherent with the rest of the design. The Jade Lizard is a high-turnover strategy with an eleven-to-thirteen-day average holding period and a 2.4% average return. Adjustment techniques consume time, add commission, and — most importantly — extend the duration of a position whose entire edge comes from cycling capital quickly. When a Jade Lizard is wrong, the correct response is to release the capital and put it into the next one, where the 87% base rate applies again from a clean start. The Tesla trade is the model: five days from entry to stop, capital freed, move on.

---

### Assignment Considerations

Assignment risk in a Jade Lizard is concentrated entirely in the short put, and it follows directly from the structure. The short put is the only leg that is naked, and it is the only leg that will be deep in the money in the scenario the trade fears.

Khoo's framing of the put leg from the outset is that it is functionally a cash-secured put — "the third leg is to sell an out-of-the-money put, which is like a cash-secured put" — which carries with it the entire assignment framework taught in Level 1. If the stock falls below the put strike and the option is exercised, the trader is obliged to buy the shares at the strike.

There are three practical observations that follow from the material.

First, the stop-loss rule is itself the primary assignment defense. The trigger to exit — the stock falling below the short put strike — is precisely the condition under which the put moves into the money and assignment becomes a live possibility. A trader who follows the rule closes the position at or near the moment assignment risk begins to accrue, rather than after it. On Tesla, Khoo bought the short put back for $21.10 rather than holding it in the money.

Second, the short call side carries essentially no assignment concern in normal operation, because it is protected by the long call. Even if the short call is assigned, the long call caps the resulting exposure at the spread width, and the position's economics are already accounted for by the no-upside-risk arithmetic. This is a structural benefit of the bear call spread over a naked short call.

Third, the injunction against holding to expiration removes most residual assignment exposure. Khoo never holds a Jade Lizard to expiry in any of the six trades, and the management rules push toward closing well before the final week: profit-taking at 50–66% typically triggers around the halfway point of the trade's life, and the upside rule explicitly requires closing early rather than letting the current-date curve decay into the expiration curve.

The related capital consideration is the one Khoo does emphasize repeatedly: the broker's margin hold. On thinkorswim the Tesla structure blocked roughly $8,443 of buying power; on Interactive Brokers with portfolio margin the same structure held about $4,621 of maintenance margin. Because the ROI floor is computed against this number, and because it is the constraint on how many concurrent positions can be carried, the margin treatment is functionally more important to the strategy's economics than assignment mechanics.

---

### The Risks, Stated Completely

Khoo returns to the risk discussion more often than to any other topic in the lesson, which is appropriate for a structure whose headline feature is a very high win rate. The complete list follows.

**The downside is unprotected and open-ended.** This is the fundamental risk and it is stated more than half a dozen times. "Any trade like that would have no downside protection. So you need to be careful here as well." The short put has no long put beneath it. Below the breakeven, losses grow dollar for dollar with the decline all the way to zero. The structural asymmetry — capped and safe above, uncapped and exposed below — is not a flaw to be engineered around; it is what the position is.

**A single loss can exceed the credit collected.** The Tesla trade lost $988 against a credit of $1,092 in five days, or roughly 90% of the premium. Because the profit target is 50% of the credit, a single full-size loss undoes roughly two winning trades. The strategy's arithmetic requires the 87% base rate to hold; if selection discipline slips and the loss rate rises, the edge disappears quickly.

**Losses can exceed the stop-loss estimate through gapping.** The stop rule anticipates a loss of about 50% of the credit when the stock reaches the short put. But a stock that gaps down through the strike overnight — as Tesla did after earnings — delivers a loss closer to 100% of the credit, because the stop level was never available for trading. Khoo describes this gradation precisely: "If it just barely hits the short put, the loss would be about 50% of the received premium. But in this case, it drops all the way lower than that and even lower than the break-even point. So the trade is losing 100% of the premium."

**Earnings gaps are the specific mechanism that defeats the stop.** The strategy deliberately seeks out earnings events for the volatility premium, and in doing so it accepts overnight gap risk on the one side where it has no protection. This is a conscious trade, not an oversight — "yes, there would be a risk that the price would gap down a lot, but there will be a criteria for you to cut loss and move on" — but the Tesla loss is exactly this risk materializing.

**Speculative underlyings can produce outsized losses.** The Coinbase reference in the trade log — "then I have a big hit here on the Coinbase price collapse" — is a live example of what happens when the stock-selection filter is not applied. It is the largest single loss visible in his 237-trade record.

**Over-sizing converts a high-probability strategy into a fragile one.** Khoo's instruction is direct and given twice. "Please don't over trade it, okay? Trade with small quantity, see how it goes." And earlier: "Don't overtrade it. It's high probability of winning, but it doesn't mean that it has no loss." The $1,000-of-credit sizing unit exists precisely to prevent any single position from dominating the portfolio, and the practice of running fewer than ten concurrent positions against roughly $40,000–$50,000 of deployed capital keeps individual position size to a small fraction of the whole.

**Holding to expiration destroys upside profit.** In the region above the long call, theta works against the position. A profitable rally that is held into expiry converts into breakeven or a small loss as the current-date curve decays onto the expiration curve. "If you let the trade run through the expiration, this profit will turn into a break even... I don't want that to happen."

**Holding past the profit target risks the entire gain.** Khoo raises this on Alphabet and on JPMorgan: "There could be a lot of uncertainties while you're holding the trade, especially now the stock has rallied quite strongly, and a retracement can reduce the profit or even wipe out the profit." The remaining third of a maximum profit is not worth the risk of the first two-thirds.

**Broker margin figures can be misleading under portfolio margin.** The Meta entry showed an artificially low margin because unrelated Meta positions netted against it, which would have inflated the computed ROI. Anyone using portfolio margin should verify the standalone margin of a structure before applying the 10% ROI test to it.

**Execution slippage is material relative to the edge.** Six spread crossings per round trip against an average per-trade return of 2.4% of margin means that careless order entry can consume a meaningful share of the expected profit. This is why the liquidity filter is a hard rule and why Khoo negotiates so patiently around the mid-price on every entry and exit.

**Discretionary overrides are not a strategy.** The Alphabet trade worked. Khoo says plainly that he should have cut. A student who generalizes from that outcome — who begins holding tested positions on conviction — has replaced a rule with a base rate of 87% by a judgment with an unknown base rate.

---

### Summary: The Jade Lizard in One Page

The Jade Lizard sells a bear call spread and an out-of-the-money put in the same expiration, sized so that the total credit received equals or exceeds the width of the call spread. That single arithmetic condition eliminates risk on the upside entirely, converting what would be an unbounded short-call exposure into a small guaranteed profit no matter how far the stock rallies. What remains is a one-sided risk position: unbounded on the downside, safe above, with a wide flat maximum-profit plateau between the two short strikes.

The entry recipe is to find a liquid, fundamentally sound, non-speculative underlying that is neutral to mildly bullish and preferably stabilizing after a decline; select an expiration four to six weeks out; sell the call at approximately 45 delta and the put at 25 delta or lower; then solve for the long call strike such that the credit clears the width. Verify that maximum profit divided by blocked buying power exceeds 10%, and prefer setups that deliver 14–20%. Elevated implied volatility, including that produced by an upcoming earnings release, is welcome rather than disqualifying, because it lets the put be placed further from the money for the same credit.

The management recipe is to close for profit when unrealized gains reach 50% to two-thirds of the credit collected — sooner if that level arrives early relative to the days elapsed; to close for a loss when the stock breaches the short put strike, expecting a loss of roughly half the credit if the move is orderly and closer to all of it if the move is a gap; and to close early for a small profit whenever the stock has run above the long call, because in that region time decay works against you. Never hold to expiration.

The evidence Khoo brings is 237 live trades over roughly five months producing an 87% win rate, more than $32,000 of profit, a 2.4% average return per trade on margin, and an eleven-day average holding period. The six trades demonstrated in full — Tesla, TSM, Meta, Microsoft, Alphabet, JPMorgan — produced five winners and one loser, $1,335 of net profit on $28,000-plus of cumulative margin, a 6.4% blended return over an average thirteen-day hold, and an 83% win rate consistent with the larger sample.

The final word belongs to the risk. The Jade Lizard wins often, and the frequency of winning is seductive. But its returns are small, its losses are not, and its entire economics rest on the assumption that the losing 13% remain survivable. That assumption holds only if the underlying is high quality, the position is small, and the stop is honored. Remove any one of those, and a strategy that wins nine times out of ten becomes a strategy that gives it all back on the tenth.

---

# Part VI — The Crouching Bull Strategy

## The Crouching Bull Strategy

### Introduction: A Bullish Strategy Built for a Bear Market

There is a particular kind of frustration that afflicts the fundamentally-minded investor during a bear market. He looks at his watchlist and sees companies he genuinely admires — businesses with durable moats, strong balance sheets and management teams he trusts — trading at prices twenty, thirty, forty per cent below where they were a year earlier. Every instinct built up over years of value investing tells him this is exactly the moment to buy. And yet every instinct built up over years of *surviving* markets tells him that a stock which has fallen thirty per cent can fall another thirty per cent, that catching a falling knife is a well-worn cliché precisely because so many investors have been cut doing it, and that the difference between "cheap" and "cheaper" has ruined more portfolios than outright fraud.

The Crouching Bull Spread — abbreviated throughout this chapter as CBS — is Adam Khoo's answer to that frustration. He introduced it to students in December 2022, and he introduced it with an unusually long explanation of its provenance, because the provenance is the point. He had invented the strategy, in his own words, roughly a year earlier, and had then spent eleven months trading it with his own money before teaching it to anybody. The reason for that delay was deliberate. "The reason why it took me quite some time to finish the testing and then now introducing it to you," he explained, "is because I really want to know whether this strategy could work well in a very tough market condition like the one we had just experienced since the beginning of this year 2022."

He began testing at the end of January 2022. He recorded the introductory lesson on 23 December 2022 — his words, "just one week from crossing to the new year." Over that testing window the S&P 500 index had fallen roughly twenty per cent from its high, and had fallen fifteen to sixteen per cent from the point at which he began testing. The Nasdaq had fallen more — "thirty plus per cent." This was not a strategy backtested in a spreadsheet against a decade of rising prices. It was a strategy forward-tested, with real capital, through one of the ugliest twelve-month stretches equities had seen since 2008.

And it worked. That is the claim, and the six lessons that constitute this chapter are Adam's evidence for it: three live trades entered on camera during a public webinar on 21 November 2022, then followed forward through four subsequent recording sessions across four and a half months, with every roll, every strike selection, every profit-and-loss calculation shown on screen and narrated aloud, right through to the final closing trades in April 2023. Two of those three trades made substantial money. One lost a little. All three lost less — or made more — than simply owning the underlying shares would have done over the same period.

The single most important framing sentence in the entire lesson comes early, and it is worth pausing on: "And just to be clear, this is not even a bearish strategy. It's a bull strategy, bullish strategy, but it works during the bearish market condition."

That sentence contains the entire thesis. The Crouching Bull is unambiguously, structurally bullish. Every leg of it profits if the stock goes up. It has no bearish component whatsoever — no long puts, no short calls placed to profit from decline, no delta-negative hedge. And yet its architecture is arranged so that the trader is compensated for waiting, protected across a wide band of adverse movement, and given the ability to keep pushing his risk further down the price ladder for as long as the bear market lasts. It is bullish in its ultimate payoff and defensive in its posture. Hence the name.

### The Name, and Why It Matters

Adam is candid that the name came before any real precision. "For lack of better word, I call it Crouching Bull," he says. But the image he then paints is a genuinely useful mental model for how the trade behaves, and it is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing as branding.

The bull, in his description, "is not at the attacking mode yet." The animal has lowered its head, its feet are gathered beneath it, its weight is set — it is crouched. It is not fleeing. It is not attacking. It is *waiting*, storing energy, watching for the moment when the balance of the fight shifts and a charge becomes profitable rather than suicidal. "It needs to be defending first before attacking. Defending, it's nothing wrong with that and wait for the right time to attack."

This maps onto the structure with unusual precision. The long-dated bull call spread is the horn — the attacking apparatus, the part that will do enormous damage when the charge finally comes, but which does nothing at all while the animal is stationary. The short-dated cash secured put is the crouch — the defensive posture, the part that feeds the animal while it waits, that lowers its centre of gravity, that can be re-set month after month after month without ever committing to the charge.

Adam returns to this image repeatedly across the six lessons, and it functions as a decision rule as much as a metaphor. When he looks at a Meta chart that has run up hard and then paused, he describes it as the bull "resting, it's resting and the bull is resting and then waiting and getting some energy back and then charging it again." When he explains why he adds the third leg to what would otherwise be a plain bull call spread, the reason is that a naked bull call spread is a bull that is charging *now*, with no ability to wait — and in a bear market, charging now is how bulls get killed.

### The Structure: Three Legs, Two Expiries

The Crouching Bull is a three-legged position. Adam calls it "a three-legged strategy" and constructs it, in the platform, as a single combined order most of the time. Its distinguishing structural feature — the thing that separates it from every strategy taught earlier in the course — is that the three legs do not share a common expiry. Two legs are long-dated; one leg is short-dated. That asymmetry is not incidental. It is the entire engine of the strategy.

Let us take the legs one at a time, because the reasoning behind each is different.

#### Leg One: The Long At-the-Money Call, Roughly Six Months Out

The first leg is a long call, bought at or very near the money, with a days-to-expiration of approximately six months. Adam's phrasing: "You buy a call at the money strike price with the DTE of around six months."

Two decisions are embedded here. The first is the strike: at the money, or near it. This is the strike that gives the position genuine directional participation. An at-the-money call has a delta in the region of 0.5, which means that if the stock rallies, the call captures roughly half of that rally immediately and progressively more as the move extends. A deep out-of-the-money call would be cheaper, but it would also be nearly inert against a modest recovery — and the whole premise of the Crouching Bull is that the recovery, when it comes, may be gradual rather than explosive. Adam's actual entries confirm the discipline: Google at $97.50 spot, he bought the 97 call; XBI at $80 spot, he bought the 80 call; Meta at $110 spot, he bought the 110 call. In each case he took the listed strike sitting closest to the live price and did not agonise over it.

The second decision is the expiry, and this is where the strategy diverges sharply from the standard bull call spread taught in Level 1. A conventional bull call spread might be placed at thirty to ninety days. Adam places the call legs at *six months or more*. The November 2022 entries all used the June 2023 expiry, which he acknowledged was slightly more than six months — "Go to June, which is about more than six months, right? Seven months, six and a half months, which is fine." He was explicitly relaxed about the precision.

The reason for the long dating is stated plainly: "Because in this bear market, it could take a long time for the bull to return. So that's why I use this strategy to wait for the right time when the bull returns, it will bring on the benefit to the trade." Bottoms are processes, not events. A stock that has been sold off for eleven months does not typically turn on a dime and rally in the following fortnight; it grinds sideways, retests, forms a base, fails, forms a better base, and eventually breaks out. Buying a thirty-day call on that thesis is buying a lottery ticket on the timing of a process that has no reason to respect your calendar. Buying a six-month call gives the process room to complete.

The cost of that room is premium. A six-month at-the-money call is expensive — Adam paid roughly $12 for the Google 97 call and something over $10 for the XBI 80 call. Which brings us directly to the second leg.

#### Leg Two: The Short Out-of-the-Money Call, Same Expiry

The second leg is a short call at a higher strike, in the same expiry as the long call. Together, legs one and two form an ordinary long-dated bull call spread — a vertical debit spread.

Its function is financing. "You sell a higher call and use part of the premium you collect from selling that call to finance the long call that you buy," Adam explains. "So it's a bull call spread. You know when you buy a call at the lower strike price and you sell a higher strike price call, you collect some premium that reduce the cost of the trade."

The magnitude of that reduction, in his live examples, ran between roughly thirty and forty per cent of the long call's cost. On Google he paid about $12 for the 97 call and the spread came out at a net $8.43 debit — the short 120 call had contributed something on the order of $3.50 in credit. On XBI he described the effect exactly: "So instead of paying $10 plus, now I cut the cost by 30%. Same, right? You cut the cost by 30%. So I get the cost now to 7.3." The short 100 call had brought in $3.35.

Where should the short call sit? Adam offers two methods, and he is explicit about the hierarchy between them.

The default, in the absence of a technical view, is **one standard deviation above the current stock price**. He uses the platform's own standard deviation indicator, which displays the expected one-standard-deviation move for the selected expiry, and simply adds it to spot. On Google, with the stock at $97 and the indicator reading $23, he took $97 + $23 = $120 and sold the 120 call. On XBI, with spot at $80 and the indicator reading approximately $20, he took the 100 strike. On Meta, with spot at $110 and the indicator reading roughly $40, he arrived at 150.

The alternative, which he prefers when he has a genuine chart-based opinion, is to **sell the short call at your target price** — typically a resistance level you do not believe the stock will exceed within the life of the spread. "If you look at the chart of the stock, if at a certain resistance level, you don't think the stock can break above that, you can also sell the short call at that level." He walks through this reasoning on both XBI and Meta. On XBI he considered a resistance around 95 and weighed selling the 95 call against the safer 100 — "so technically I can sell at 95 or sell 100 even safer, right? Because I sell, I don't want it to go beyond that." He chose 100. On Meta he identified a level around 155 which had been support many times and had, after being broken, converted to resistance — a textbook polarity flip — and noted that the 150 strike sat just under it and near the 150-day moving average. "So it makes sense to sell 150 something, right?" He sold the 150 and observed he could have sold 155 for slightly more upside.

The relationship between these two methods is worth stating clearly, because it is a general principle in Adam's teaching. One standard deviation is the *default for the trader with no view*. "Without knowing the technical part, I just blindly sell at one standard deviation for the short call." A chart-derived target is *superior when you actually have one*, because it encodes information the standard deviation calculation does not contain. The two frequently agree, which is reassuring; when they disagree, the chart wins, subject to the constraint that you never place the short call so close that you strangle the upside.

#### Leg Three: The Short-Dated Cash Secured Put

The third leg is what makes this a Crouching Bull rather than a bull call spread. It is a short put, struck below the current stock price, with a days-to-expiration of approximately one month.

"The third leg that I would like to add to the trade is to sell a put option below the current stock price, and the DTE is shorter. How short? Typically, one month expiry. So the third leg is actually a cash secured put."

Note the words *cash secured*. This is not a credit spread. There is no long put beneath it. The trader is naked short a put and must be prepared, in the worst case, to take delivery of one hundred shares per contract at the strike price. This is the single most important risk characteristic of the entire strategy and Adam flags it more times than any other point in the six lessons.

Strike selection for the put follows the mirror image of the short call: **one standard deviation below the current stock price**, subject to the additional and rather important qualification that the strike should sit at or near a technical support level. "You just sell a put option below the current stock price. Ideally, at one standard deviation below the current stock price." And in the checklist: "the put strike, the cash secured put that you are selling with the strike price is below the current stock price. And ideally, it should be at or near a support level so that it won't fall below it."

Again the live examples show the arithmetic. Google at $97 with a one-standard-deviation move of $8 gave $89, and he sold the 89 put. XBI at $80 with a move of $8 gave $72, and he sold the 72 put. Meta at $110 with a move of roughly $13 gave $97, and he sold the 97 put — and on Meta he then explicitly checked the chart, noting that 97 was "around near the bottom here, right? Quite close to the bottom," and concluding, "with a lot of good news, I still can own the stock price at the last swing low, which is good."

#### Why the Expiries Differ

This is the structural insight that the whole strategy hangs on, and it deserves its own treatment.

If all three legs shared the same six-month expiry, the trade would be a much less interesting thing. A six-month short put decays slowly, collects its premium once, and gives the trader nothing to do for half a year. By making the put a one-month instrument while the calls run for six, Adam creates a machine that can be re-loaded again and again against a fixed long-dated position.

He does the count himself: "because the short-dated cash secured put has about one month DTE and the long bull call has six months DTE. So technically you can roll the cash secured put four, five or six times, until the long bull expires."

Each roll is a fresh premium collection. Each roll is also a fresh opportunity to move the strike — usually downward, in a declining market — which progressively lowers the price at which the trader might eventually be assigned shares. "You could roll the cash secured put down and out, collecting more premium, buying more time for the price to go higher."

There is a second, more technical reason for the short dating, which relates to theta. A one-month at-the-money-ish option decays far faster in absolute terms per day than a six-month one, because theta accelerates as expiry approaches. By repeatedly harvesting the steep part of the decay curve on the put while holding the flat part of the curve on the calls, the trader arranges for time decay to work for him rather than against him — a point Adam demonstrates numerically in the next section.

#### The Structure in Summary

| Leg | Action | Instrument | Strike rule | Expiry | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy | Call | At the money or nearest to spot | ~6 months | Directional participation when the bull returns |
| 2 | Sell | Call | One standard deviation above spot, **or** chart target / resistance | Same as leg 1 (~6 months) | Finances leg 1, cutting its cost by roughly 30–40% |
| 3 | Sell | Put | One standard deviation below spot, ideally at or near support | ~1 month | Generates positive theta, provides margin of safety, is rolled repeatedly |

Adam summarises it himself in a single sentence: "So basically, it's just a combination of the long-dated bull call spread and a short-dated cash secured put as simple as that."

### The Problem the Third Leg Solves

To understand why the Crouching Bull exists at all, one has to look carefully at what is wrong with a plain bull call spread when the market refuses to cooperate — and Adam demonstrates this on screen, in real time, before adding the third leg.

Working on Google during the webinar, he first constructs only legs one and two: long the June 97 call, short the June 120 call, for a net debit of $8.43. He then analyses that two-legged position and immediately identifies the flaw:

"What I don't like about this is that right now at the current price, if the price just stays here, I will lose a max loss, which is about $843."

Read that carefully, because it is the crux. A bull call spread does not merely lose when the stock falls. It loses its *entire* maximum loss when the stock does *nothing*. Sideways is fatal. If Google sits at $97 for the next six months and expires there, both calls expire worthless and the $843 debit is gone in full. The position requires the stock to rise, and to rise before a specific date, merely to break even.

The second flaw follows directly: "the theta would be negative, like a dollar a day, dollar a day and then that will increase over time." Every day that passes with no upward movement costs money, and the daily cost accelerates as expiry nears. The trader is on a clock, and the clock is a meter running against him.

He acknowledges the compensation honestly. "The max profit is quite attractive, which is like $1,500. So I lose 800 to make 1,500 — one to two risk reward ratio. Like that's a typical bull call spread risk reward ratio." A one-to-two risk-reward on a debit spread is entirely respectable. In a bull market, that is a perfectly good trade.

But: "again, I don't like the negative theta so I need to sell cash secured put way out the money and turns the trade theta into a positive. So time works in my favor. So not only two legs here, I would add the third leg."

The third leg does three distinct things, and it is worth separating them because traders often conflate them.

First, it **reduces the entry cost**. On Google, the 89 put brought in about $1.00 in credit, taking the net debit from $8.43 down to roughly $7.43. That is a direct reduction in capital at risk and a direct improvement in return on investment for any given profit outcome.

Second, it **flips the sign of theta**. This is the effect Adam emphasises most. After adding the put, he checks the platform's Greeks display: "So if I move to the current stock price, if the stock stays at the current level, it's positive. And if it just stays here until expiration, this trade will still be profitable. So the bull call, if the stock stays the same until expiration, you lose. But this trade, if it stays the same, you look at the corner of the lower box here, you see the blue number. It will generate some profit."

That is a categorical change in the character of the position, not a marginal improvement. A trade that loses on sideways movement has been converted into a trade that makes money on sideways movement. On the XBI construction he quantifies it: "this trade would have a very good theta, $4 a day, $4 a day. Remember, this one will accelerate as the time is closer to the expiration of the short put." And then, in a line that captures the psychological benefit better than any Greek: "Not too bad, especially there's a lot of holidays coming, right? You will go out travel and then the trade is still generating some money for you. That's the best concept."

Third, it **creates a margin of safety on the downside**. Because the put credit reduces the net debit, the breakeven price of the combined position sits *below* the current stock price. On Google the breakeven came out around $95 against a $97 spot — "which is about $2 plus below the current stock price. So I get about 2-3% discount if the stock drops." On Meta the breakeven was $106 against a $110 spot — "which is about $4 below the current stock price. So worst case, worst case, I still own the stock at a discount versus the current market price." On XBI it was around $87 against $80 spot for the whole structure including the put obligation, which Adam explained as roughly the 72 put strike plus the $6 entry cost, giving approximately $78 as the point below which the position begins to lose on the assigned shares.

Adam generalises the breakeven result into a rule of thumb worth memorising: "typically when you analyze the trade, the break-even point for the trade would typically around three to five per cent below the current stock price, which is quite good because it's a good stock being trading at below intrinsic value, and now you can buy it at 3 to 5 per cent below the current stock."

That is the elegance of the structure. You are buying a fundamentally sound business below its intrinsic value, and the option structure then hands you a further three to five per cent of cushion on top, *and* pays you to wait.

### The Four Price Scenarios

Adam frames the payoff not as a single P&L curve but as four discrete outcomes, and he claims — accurately, on his own accounting — that the trader wins in three of them.

**Scenario one: the stock rallies.** This is the bull's charge. "If the stock price rallies, the trade should have a significant upside." The bull call spread converges toward its maximum value, the cash secured put expires worthless, and the trader collects both. The contrast Adam draws is with the plain cash secured put strategy taught in Level 1: "if you remember the cash secured put, you get the premium, but that premium is your max profit. You cannot earn more than that. Your trade profit is capped at the premium you collect. So this one is different." On Google the numbers made the point starkly — a cash secured put alone would have capped the trader at roughly $115 of premium; the Crouching Bull's bull call spread offered up to $1,500. On Meta the potential was "near $3,000 upside."

**Scenario two: the stock goes sideways.** "In that case, your cash secured put will continue to generate income for you. You continue to earn the premium, and the concept here is you are paid to wait. The trade should have a good positive theta, meaning the time decay works in the trade favour." This is where the Crouching Bull most decisively beats the plain bull call spread, which loses its entire debit in this scenario. Adam is emphatic that he is entirely comfortable here: "So I don't mind doing this trade and the price keep going sideways for a long time." And he confirms it happened repeatedly in practice: "many stocks that I've been doing over the past several months have been going sideways, but the trades are very profitable because the cash secured puts keep bringing me new money, new premium, and I don't mind because time is my friend."

**Scenario three: the stock drops modestly.** If the decline is contained — meaning it does not carry far below the put strike — the trade should still be at or near breakeven, because the put credit and the three-to-five per cent cushion absorb it. "If the price drops slightly, not significantly, the trade should still be profitable or at least break even. And then you can roll the short put down and out to collect more premium." The response is mechanical: roll the put lower and further out, harvest another credit, extend the runway.

**Scenario four: the stock collapses.** This is the losing case, and Adam does not soften it. "Now the fourth scenario where you lose money, that is when the share price kind of collapses and drops so much below your cash secured put strike price. In that case, you may end up with owning the shares."

But even here the consolations are structural rather than rhetorical, and they trace directly back to the entry filters. "But hey, this is a fundamentally good stock to start with, right? So you don't mind owning that shares. Number two, now you can own it at a discount versus the entry point. So good stock, trading at below intrinsic value. And third, you can buy it even at a lower price."

The full scenario map, then:

| Scenario | Bull call spread leg | Cash secured put leg | Net outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stock rallies above short call strike | Approaches maximum profit | Expires worthless, full credit kept | Best case — take profit and close |
| Stock goes sideways | Bleeds slowly (long-dated, so slowly) | Expires worthless each month, roll and repeat | Profitable — theta positive, paid to wait |
| Stock drops modestly | Loses value | Loses some value but far less than shares | Roughly breakeven; roll put down and out |
| Stock collapses well below put strike | Loses significantly | In the money, assignment risk | Loss — but smaller than owning shares, and you acquire a good stock cheaply |

### Entry Criteria: The Checklist

Adam is unusually strict about the pre-trade filters for this strategy, and the reason is the naked short put. Because the worst case is share ownership, the entry criteria are essentially the entry criteria of a long-term investor rather than those of a short-term options trader.

#### Filter One: Fundamentally Good Stock

"I only use it on fundamentally good stocks to start with. Please don't use this strategy on lousy stocks. Because in the worst case scenario, when you use this strategy, you would have to own the shares. And you don't want to own shares of lousy stocks, right? You want to own shares of fundamentally good stocks because eventually when the bull returns or the market boom comes back, the stock will recover. So fundamentally good stocks always come back."

The checklist question he poses is deliberately personal: "fundamentally, is that a good stock that I don't mind owning? If the answer is yes, then go to the next step. If it's just a lousy stock, forget about it. Don't do it."

#### Filter Two: Trading Below Intrinsic Value

Being a good company is necessary but not sufficient. The price must also be attractive. "Technically, it has been beaten down or declining well below intrinsic value. So the stock has to be trading at below intrinsic value of the stock."

He restates this as an independent veto: "From the fundamental also, good stock is one, but the stock price has to be below the intrinsic value. If it has already exceeded the intrinsic value, no point to trade because you may end up with buying the share at the overvalue."

This filter has real teeth in his own practice. When he closes the Google trade in April 2023 and considers re-entering, the reason he permits himself to do so is precisely that the valuation test still passes: "even at this price, 105, it is still below the intrinsic value of the stock. Yeah, the intrinsic value of the stock is like 159. So technically, I could still enter the same trade." That $159 figure for Alphabet is his own valuation number, stated aloud. When he tried to check Meta's intrinsic value during the November webinar, he did not have it in front of him and said so honestly rather than inventing a figure: "I don't have here. But I believe it's like near 200 level. So clearly, I think I don't have it here, but I believe it is really below the intrinsic value."

Note also that the intrinsic value test is waived for ETFs, for the obvious reason that the concept does not straightforwardly apply. On XBI he said: "I look at, I mean, there's no intrinsic value for ETF. It's all technical, right? So, but this is a good ETF that I like to own in my portfolio. By the way, this strategy you can use on ETF as well."

#### Filter Three: The Technical Setup — Bottoming, Not Falling

This is the filter that most distinguishes a good Crouching Bull entry from a bad one, and it is the one that requires judgement rather than a number.

"Technically, as I mentioned, the price has already found the bottom or is now bottoming and is due for a rebound." He elaborates: "look for the stock, as I mentioned, fundamentally good stock, trading below intrinsic value, but the technical has to be, it is near the bottom or is now bottoming. How do we know? Look at the chart. You think the bottom has been found or is now being formed and is ready or poised for a rebound. That is a right set up for the Crouching Bull."

The XBI entry is his cleanest illustration of what a bottoming chart looks like. Describing it live: "I like the setup of XBI a lot. You see it's forming the bottom. It's forming the bottom. It has a lot of supports here. It's like support, support. I think it could go a little bit lower, but I think it's very near the bottom already. It's like building the base again. The wider the base, the higher the space." That last line — a slight mis-transcription of the well-known trader's maxim "the wider the base, the higher in space" — captures the logic: extended sideways consolidation after a decline builds the platform from which sustained advances launch. "So once the base has been built and then consolidated long enough, it will start to go higher."

The Meta entry illustrates a different and more difficult version of the same judgement: bottoming by exhaustion of bad news. Adam walks through the fundamental narrative explicitly. Meta had reported terrible earnings, given terrible guidance, halved its earnings, and was, in his phrase, "burning money like crazy on Metaverse," with a CEO who "doesn't seem to have a sense of urgency." That was the bad news that made the low. Then came the change: "recently he fired 11,000 of people... So he cut the workforce by 13%. It's significant. And market believes that it's just a beginning." His read on the significance is about signalling rather than the direct cost saving: "at least it shows the investor community that the management now is serious in terms of cutting costs, scale down investments and get the company back on track."

And then, crucially, he applies the crouching-bull image to the price action itself: "when the bull run too much, it's exhausted and feel like tired. It's now like resting, it's resting and the bull is resting and then waiting and getting some energy back and then charging again. So I like this one."

He follows this with one of the most important caveats in the entire course, and it is a caveat about the limits of teaching by example: "Now, if you don't believe that the stock has bottomed. And the bad news has been priced in the stock. Don't trade this one. Okay, this is what I'm doing. If you don't like it, don't do it. Okay. But it's my account. My money, I do what I think is right. So then if you like it, you can play it by yourself, but if you don't like it, skip it."

The bottoming judgement cannot be outsourced. It is the one part of the setup where the trader must form and own his own view.

#### Filter Four: The Put Strike Sits at or Near Support

The fourth filter is a constraint on strike placement rather than on stock selection, but it belongs in the checklist because it is checked before the order goes out. The put strike must be below the current price and, ideally, at or just below a level where the chart suggests buyers will appear.

Adam checks this on every single roll across all four management sessions, without exception, and the checks are instructive:

On the December roll of Google to the 81 put: "I need to check whether 81 is safe or not... The last swing low is 83. So 81 will be below that. I would say it's very safe because if it drops further from here, there's a good chance that it will bounce off this swing low support level... I'm selling the 81, which is below this level, so it gives me even better cushion on the downside."

On the December roll of XBI to the 74 put: "74 from the chart, you want to check it out. 74 is still like below the support level here, right? So the stock price need to break below this support level to hit my short put strike, which is unlikely."

On the March roll of XBI to the 77 put: "77 is right at the support level. 76, 77, right there, which is pretty good. So I don't mind to own XBI at $77 per share. And by the way, it's very near the support level. If it retraces to that level, the chances are it will bounce."

On the March roll of Google to the 86 put: "86 is very close to the last swing low, I mean the lowest in many years, right? So it's kind of a support level for me, and it's dirt cheap, and I don't mind buying Google share at 86."

#### The Delta Cross-Check

Alongside the standard deviation calculation and the chart check, Adam uses the option's delta as a probability read on the put strike. He does this consistently, and the numbers he cites are always around the same level.

On the December Google roll: "that, by the way, has about 19 delta. That means there's almost like 81% chance that the stock won't drop below that. So very safe, I would say."

On the January Google roll to the 90 put: "how do I know it's safe? I look at the delta, which shows about 19. That means I have more than 80% chance that the price won't drop below 90 by the expiration. I have 81% chance of winning in the trade."

On the December XBI roll to the 74 put: "there's 81% chance that the stock won't drop below $74 by the expiration on January 27. So very high probability of getting this money for free one more round."

On the December Meta roll to the 102 put: "If I sell this one, I have more than 80% chance of winning, because there's only 17% chance that the stock price could drop below 102. 83% chance that the stock price will stay above that."

The pattern is consistent and gives us a usable numeric target: **the short put's delta should land around 0.17 to 0.19, implying roughly an 81 to 83 per cent probability of expiring worthless.** This is not a coincidence — a one-standard-deviation move corresponds, under a normal distribution, to roughly the sixteenth percentile in each tail, so a strike placed one standard deviation below spot will naturally carry a delta in the high teens. The delta check and the standard deviation calculation are two views of the same underlying fact, and Adam uses them to confirm each other.

#### The Complete Entry Checklist

| # | Test | Pass condition | Fail action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fundamentals | A company you would genuinely be content to own outright | Abandon — do not trade CBS on weak businesses |
| 2 | Valuation | Stock price below your intrinsic value estimate | Abandon — no point buying above fair value (waived for ETFs) |
| 3 | Technical | Bottom formed or actively forming; base-building; poised to rebound | Wait — do not trade a stock still in free-fall |
| 4 | Put strike | Below spot, ~1 SD down, at or near a support level or swing low | Move the strike lower, or skip |
| 5 | Delta cross-check | Short put delta approximately 0.17–0.19 (~81–83% win probability) | Adjust strike |
| 6 | Breakeven | Roughly 3–5% below current stock price | Re-examine construction |
| 7 | Theta | Position theta positive after all three legs | Add or adjust the put leg until it is |
| 8 | Position size | You could afford to take delivery of the shares in cash | Reduce size |

#### Execution: All at Once, or Legged In

Adam's default is a single combined three-leg order, but he explicitly permits legging in, and describes both sequences.

"You can do in one shot three legs all together, same way you execute with a bull call — three legs, right? Buy a call, sell a call, sell put, three legs at the same time. But you can also leg in one at the time. You can leg in the cash secured put first to buy time, to collect premium, waiting for the stock price to stabilize and start to rebound, and then you leg in the second part, which is a bull call spread. Or vice versa — you can leg in with a bull call spread first and then sell the cash secured put later. Normally, I just execute all three legs together at one shot."

There is practical wisdom in the note about legging the put in first. If you like the fundamentals and valuation but are not yet convinced the bottom has formed, selling the cash secured put alone commits you to nothing directional, pays you to wait, and lets you add the bull call spread once the technical picture confirms.

One practical execution note from the live session: three-legged orders are harder to fill than two-legged ones.
