On XBI, Adam had to work the order patiently, adjusting a cent at a time — "just give there three legs, sometimes it takes some time, that's it takes some time to fill because three legs, right, it's harder to be filled." He observed the mark price oscillating between $6.08 and $6.12, put his order at $6.10 as the midpoint, then raised to $6.11 to get filled. He treats a cent or two as immaterial: "I'm okay with a few cents here and there, it's okay."

### The Three Live Trades: Entry, 21 November 2022

Everything above is theory. What follows is the record of three positions entered live during a public webinar on 21 November 2022 and tracked to their conclusions. These are the spine of the chapter, and they are worth following in complete detail because they collectively cover every scenario the strategy can produce.

#### Trade One — Alphabet (GOOGL)

Alphabet was trading at approximately $97.50. Adam went to the June 2023 expiry — "about more than six months, seven months, six and a half months, which is fine."

He bought the 97 call, at the money, paying about $12. He then read the one-standard-deviation indicator for that expiry as $23, added it to spot — "97 is a current stock price, plus $23, that is $120" — and sold the 120 call, holding the control key to add the leg to the same order ticket. "So the platform is telling me that I'm buying a bull call spread, the vertical debit spread here, buying one call option at 97 and then sell one call option, same expiration at the higher strike price. And I pay the debit of 8.43."

He then analysed that two-legged spread and rejected it for the reasons already discussed: max loss $843 if the stock merely sat still, max profit $1,500, negative theta of about a dollar a day and accelerating.

For the third leg he moved to the nearest monthly expiry — he wanted thirty days and the chain offered thirty-two, which he accepted without complaint. With spot at $97 and the one-standard-deviation figure at $8, he took $97 − $8 = $89 and sold the 89 put, collecting approximately $1.00 in credit. "Earlier, I have to pay like $8.50. Now I collect $1 on the cash secured put. I reduce the cost to $7.5."

He then worked the order, attempting $7.40 and eventually filling at $7.43. The broker blocked buying power of $2,041 — not the notional cost of the shares, and not the theoretical maximum loss.

| Alphabet — entry, 21 Nov 2022 | |
|---|---|
| Stock price at entry | ~$97.50 |
| Leg 1 | Buy 1 × Jun 2023 97 call (~$12) |
| Leg 2 | Sell 1 × Jun 2023 120 call |
| Bull call spread net debit | $8.43 |
| Leg 3 | Sell 1 × Dec 23 2022 89 put (~$1.00 credit, 32 DTE) |
| **Net debit paid** | **$7.43 ($743)** |
| Buying power blocked | $2,041 |
| Breakeven | ~$95 (about 2–3% below spot) |
| Bull call spread max profit | ~$1,500 |
| Theta after leg 3 | Positive |

#### Trade Two — XBI (SPDR S&P Biotech ETF)

XBI, a biotech ETF, was trading at $80. Adam's rationale was purely technical, since intrinsic value does not apply, combined with a portfolio-level desire to own the sector: "this is a good ETF that I like to own in my portfolio."

He liked the chart specifically because of the extended base — layered supports, an established trading range, the classic wide-base setup. He also noted a practical attraction: "The premium on XBI is good," which matters because the strategy's income engine is the put.

Same June expiry. He bought the 80 call at the money, paying something over $10. For the short call he read the one-standard-deviation move as approximately $20, giving 100. He considered instead selling the 95 strike, which he identified as a plausible resistance level on a recovery, but chose the safer 100 to preserve upside: "Because I sell, I don't want it to go beyond that. So I can sell 95 or can sell 100." He collected $3.35 on the 100 call, cutting the spread cost by thirty per cent to $7.30 net.

The put leg went out to the same thirty-two-day expiry. One standard deviation down was $8, giving $80 − $8 = $72, and he sold the 72 put. This brought the total cost down again — "so I cut the cost down further from 10 to 7 now to 6."

He worked the order at $6.05, then $6.10, then $6.11, watching the mark oscillate. It eventually filled at $6.12. Buying power blocked was $1,508.

He then analysed the completed position: theta of $4 a day, and a breakeven he computed live. When the platform showed the breakeven at $87, he explained the arithmetic aloud: "Why is the break even point 87? Well, because I need to buy the stock price at 72, no? Plus, I need to pay $6 for the entry. So it was $78 around that." (The $87 figure is the platform's own displayed breakeven for the composite position; Adam's $78 arithmetic describes the effective acquisition cost of assigned shares. He did not reconcile the two on camera, and both numbers should be understood as describing different things — one the composite curve's crossing point, the other the net cost of stock if assigned.)

Then the critical qualification, which applies to every Crouching Bull breakeven: "Again, this is a break even point for the one month, for the first month. But the bull call is six months out, right? So I could continue to roll the short put many rounds lower to get the lower potential entry price for me."

| XBI — entry, 21 Nov 2022 | |
|---|---|
| Stock price at entry | $80.00 |
| Leg 1 | Buy 1 × Jun 2023 80 call (~$10+) |
| Leg 2 | Sell 1 × Jun 2023 100 call ($3.35 credit) |
| Bull call spread net debit | $7.30 |
| Leg 3 | Sell 1 × Dec 23 2022 72 put ($1.11 credit, 32 DTE) |
| **Net debit paid** | **$6.12 ($612)** |
| Buying power blocked | $1,508 |
| Theta at entry | ~$4/day, positive |

#### Trade Three — Meta Platforms (META)

Meta was at $110 — "very easy to remember the share price at the entry point. 110." The fundamental case has been described above: catastrophic earnings, a wildly unpopular Metaverse spend, and then the 11,000-person layoff that signalled a change in management posture. The technical case was a bottom formed on maximum pessimism followed by a strong recovery move that had paused to consolidate.

Same June expiry. He bought the 110 call at the money. For the short call, one standard deviation was $40, giving $150 — and separately, the chart identified a resistance around 155, formed by a level that had served as support repeatedly before breaking. He sold the 150 call, noting it sat near the 150-day moving average and just under the 155 resistance, and observing he could have sold 155 for slightly more upside.

He then showed the two-legged spread's failure mode once more, and the numbers were larger because the underlying was more expensive: "if the stock doesn't go up, it just stays right as it is right now, I will lose the max loss, which is about $1,300 for the trade. And it has a negative theta, so it hurts me every day, and it accelerates."

For the put leg he went to the same thirty-two-day expiry, read the one-standard-deviation move as about $13, and sold the 97 put for about $1.70. He then reasoned about assignment explicitly: "Worst case, I own the stock at 97, minus $1.70. So 96 something. Let's say 97 is fine. 97 is around near the bottom here, right? Quite close to the bottom."

The breakeven came out at $106, "which is about $4 below the current stock price." The upside potential was "near $3,000."

He filled at $11.20. Buying power blocked was $2,250. He was careful to distinguish that from the real worst case: "Again, that is not max loss. Max loss is like 9,000 something when the stock goes to zero."

| Meta — entry, 21 Nov 2022 | |
|---|---|
| Stock price at entry | $110.00 |
| Leg 1 | Buy 1 × Jun 2023 110 call |
| Leg 2 | Sell 1 × Jun 2023 150 call |
| Leg 3 | Sell 1 × Dec 23 2022 97 put (~$1.70 credit, 32 DTE) |
| **Net debit paid** | **$11.20 ($1,120)** |
| Buying power blocked | $2,250 |
| Breakeven | ~$106 (~$4 below spot) |
| Upside potential | ~$3,000 |
| Theoretical max loss | ~$9,000+ (stock to zero) |

That last line deserves emphasis, because it is where the strategy's real risk lives. The broker blocks $2,250. The stock going to zero costs you something over $9,000. Those two numbers are not the same number, and confusing them is how traders blow up.

### Trade Management: The First Roll, 23 December 2022

Thirty-two days after entry, on the expiration date of all three put legs, Adam sat down to manage the positions. The market had been unkind in aggregate, and the three trades had diverged into exactly the three scenarios the strategy is designed to handle.

#### Alphabet: The Losing Case, and Why It Was Losing Less

Alphabet had fallen from $97.50 to just under $89 — a decline of about $8, or roughly 8.5 per cent. "Since I entered the trade, the stock price went up initially, but then has been declining over the past three weeks or so, which is really bad from the stock performance standpoint."

The direct comparison he draws is the one that justifies the strategy's existence: "$8 declining in the stock price. If I had bought 100 shares, I would have lost $800 because of the stock price declining, correct? How is this CBS trade doing?" The platform showed the open P&L at approximately negative $298. "Compared to $8 declining in the stock price, and then I would have lost $800 if I bought 100 shares. This trade is doing better, though it's still losing money."

He then broke the loss down leg by leg, which is worth reproducing because it shows exactly how the structure absorbs a decline:

| Alphabet leg P&L, 23 Dec 2022 (stock ~$89) | |
|---|---|
| Long Jun 97 call | −$577 |
| Short Jun 120 call | +$222 |
| **Bull call spread net** | **−$355** |
| Short Dec 89 put (sold at ~$1.70, now ~$0.52) | Profitable |
| **Total position** | **≈ −$298** |

Note the put leg's behaviour. Adam had sold it for about $1.70 and it was now marked around $0.52 — despite the stock having fallen right onto the strike. "Imagine the stock has dropped $8. Yet my cash secured put leg is making money. That's what I mean in terms of the good margin for error or good margin of safety. Even if I'm wrong here, I'm making money on the cash secured put, and that has helped reduce the loss of the trade overall."

The mechanism is theta overwhelming delta. Over thirty-two days, an out-of-the-money put with a delta around 0.19 lost enough extrinsic value to time decay that even an $8 move against it left the seller with a profit on that leg. This is the practical meaning of "positive theta" in a real position.

His decision process then ran through the checklist in reverse. First, the fundamental question: "is Alphabet still fundamentally good stock or not? And the answer is definitely yes. This is still one of my most favourite stocks." He was explicit about the bear case and equally explicit about why he discounted it: "Yes, it has been declining because of the recession fear because a lot of concern that the ad demand will slow down and it will affect Google in a big way. Yes, that is true. And I believe that has priced in the stock right now."

Conclusion: "So I just need more time. I'm still having a full conviction on the stock fundamental and eventual stock price recovery. So I would like to hold on to the trade. What I need is time."

The roll had two purposes, and he separated them cleanly: "I would need to roll the put option here. Ideally, down and out. Down because I want to have another layer of safety net. So I like to have more cushion on the downside, even when the stock drops further I could potentially own the stock at the much better price. So I just want to delay taking the stock."

The mechanics: buy to close the 89 put for about $0.40, and sell to open a new put further out in time and lower in strike. He chose the expiry deliberately — not the nearest monthly, but 35 DTE expiring 27 January 2023 — and the reason was earnings. "Where will Google release earning? That is on 31st of January. So the best would be I sell 35 DTE expiring on Jan 27 just before the earning. Because if I roll another one, after this one, crossing the earning, I would expect to collect a lot more premium. Every time I roll across the earning, the premium would be very good. So right now I roll it right before the earning, and then on that day, I roll one more round, and next round, the premium would be very good."

This is a genuinely sophisticated piece of expiry management. Implied volatility inflates ahead of earnings, so an option sold in a cycle that *contains* an earnings date carries fatter premium than one that expires just before it. By timing the roll to land the *following* cycle across the announcement, he positions himself to sell into inflated volatility one roll later.

For the strike, one standard deviation for the new expiry was $8. From $89 that gave $81. He checked the last swing low at $83 and confirmed 81 sat safely beneath it. The delta read about 19. He bought back the 89 put at $0.40 and sold the 81 put for about $1.16, working the order and filling at a net credit of $0.76.

"So with that, I would collect about 75 cents credit. So I'm paid to roll it down, meaning I can potentially buy the share at 81, not 89. And then I'm paid to do it."

That single sentence captures the whole point of rolling down for a credit. The trader simultaneously improves his worst-case acquisition price by $8 per share *and* gets paid $76 for the privilege.

#### XBI: The Sideways Case

XBI had gone nowhere. "The stock has been trading in the range, or sideways, for quite some time now... since I enter the trade, the price has gone up, has gone down, up and down, up, down. Today is down. So today, the stock price is at 81.5, just slightly better than my entry points at 80."

And this, Adam points out, is exactly the case where the Crouching Bull earns its keep against the plain bull call spread: "which is good, because in the CBS trade, you do not need the price to go higher to make money. If it just goes sideways like this, the trade should be making money because the cash secured put will be expiring worthless."

The position was showing +$134. The 72 put, sold for $1.11, was "almost worthless, almost like max out of the profit of the cash secured put. I make $110 here. I buy back, I pay a little one cent, two cents to close." The bull call spread had also contributed modestly — the long 80 call was up $73 and the short 100 call was down $48, netting a small gain.

He rolled anyway, on discipline rather than necessity: "So I can choose to let it expire worthless today, but by discipline, I just close it and I opened the new one. And buy more time for the stock price to eventually recover."

Because the stock had drifted *up* rather than down, the new one-standard-deviation strike was *higher* than the old one — an important demonstration that rolling down is a response to price decline, not an unconditional rule. Spot was $81.81 and one standard deviation was $7.81, giving approximately $74. "So in this case, I am selling at a higher strike price than the original one, which is still fine because the stock has gone up by dollars or so. And I still have very good margin for error, because the stock needs to drop $7 to hit my short put."

He checked the chart — 74 sat below a support level — and the delta gave 81 per cent probability of expiring worthless. He also compared the premium against the original: "The original trade when I enter, I collected 1.11. This one, I collect 1.15. It's almost the same. Same level of premium, which is good."

Filled: bought back the 72 put at $0.03, sold the 74 put at $1.12, net credit $1.09.

#### Meta: The Winning Case

Meta had risen from $110 to $117 — "up by $7 since I entered the trade." The position showed +$410.

The leg breakdown demonstrated the reverse of Alphabet's:

| Meta leg P&L, 23 Dec 2022 (stock ~$117) | |
|---|---|
| Long Jun 110 call | +$360 |
| Short Jun 150 call | −$138 |
| **Bull call spread net** | **+$230** |
| Short Dec 97 put | ~+$170 |
| **Total position** | **≈ +$400** |

"In this case, the price is going higher, that generates profit for both bull call and the cash secured put at the same time."

He rolled the put to the same 27 January expiry, which for Meta sat just before its 1 February earnings date — the same volatility logic. One standard deviation from $117 was $15, giving $102. The 102 put offered close to $1.90 in premium and a delta implying 83 per cent probability of success. He checked the chart and confirmed the strike sat comfortably above prior lows, and he checked the ownership question: "102 is something I don't mind owning the shares. Right? Now 102 is still very cheap for META. Well below its intrinsic value."

He bought back the 97 put for $0.01 and sold the 102 put, filling at $1.85 as the stock ticked higher and premium compressed. "So I paid one cent to close the existing CSP, and then I sold the new cash secured put, collecting $186, which is very good."

#### The Accounting Trap

At this point Adam introduces a piece of practical bookkeeping that trips up almost every trader who rolls positions, and he flags it three separate times because it matters.

"Now one thing you need to notice that once I roll, the P&L shown in the platform is no longer accurate. Earlier it was making like 130 something. Now suddenly it's down to 24. Why is it? Because the profit from the old cash secured put has now been removed from the system. That's why you see the profit drop because of the removal of the cash secured put P&L."

The broker platform tracks P&L per open position. Close a leg, and its realised profit vanishes from the display. Roll four times and the display will show only the P&L of the currently open legs plus the newest put — while four rounds of realised put credits sit invisibly in the account history.

His solution is manual and unglamorous: "For you to really track the real P&L, you need to keep in your notebook or in my Excel file I noted down how much is the realized profit from the rolling, and I need to add on top of the P&L, which is shown here, to really get the right P&L of the trade."

He maintains a spreadsheet for exactly this purpose and cross-checks it against his own arithmetic at every management session. The method he uses throughout is simple and worth adopting wholesale:

**Effective cost of the trade = original net debit − sum of all rolling credits received.**
**Current profit = current mark value of the open position − effective cost.**
**Return on investment = current profit ÷ buying power blocked at entry.**

Notice the denominator. He measures return against the *buying power the broker actually blocked*, not against maximum theoretical loss and not against the notional value of the shares. This makes his percentage returns comparable across trades and honest about capital efficiency, though a reader should keep in mind that it is a favourable denominator — the buying power blocked can be increased by the broker if the stock falls, a point Adam himself raises.

### Trade Management: The Second Roll, 27 January 2023

Thirty-five days later, on the expiration of the January puts, Adam returned to all three positions.

#### Alphabet: Flat Stock, Small Profit

Alphabet had recovered from the December low of $89 back to $99 — essentially flat against the $97.50 entry, "$1.50 or $0.50 up since I entered the trade," which he characterised as roughly flat, and notably weak relative to a market that "has now rallied quite a bit."

The full accounting:

| Alphabet P&L, 27 Jan 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $743 |
| Roll credit, 23 Dec (89 → 81 put) | −$76 |
| **Effective cost** | **$667** |
| Current mark: bull call spread | $8.30 ($830) |
| Current mark: 81 put | ≈ $0.00 |
| **Current value** | **$830** |
| **Profit** | **$163** |
| Buying power | $2,041 |
| **Return on investment** | **~8%** |
| Stock price | ~$99 |

"So the price flat up a little bit, and I'm making some money, which is pretty decent, right? It's performing in line with the stock price for this particular trade." He cross-checked against his spreadsheet, which showed $151 as the mark fluctuated, and accepted the discrepancy as ordinary intraday noise: "In that range, 160, 150, profit."

The management decision rested on time remaining. "The long call and the short call, which is the bull call spread, still has 140 days to expiration. It's still a long way to go. The trade is making some money, but not at the level that I would like to see. Pretty much flat. So probably I need more time for the price to eventually rally. And for that I would make money from the trade. So I just need to buy more time."

The 81 put had gone to zero — "the value has been depleted. It's expiring today, by the way." He bought it back for a cent.

For the new put he established what he now describes as a routine: "Again, I tend to make this like a regular monthly exercise. I will sell another maybe five weeks. So 35 days again from now." One standard deviation from $99 was $9, giving $90. He checked delta at 19 and the ownership question: "Alphabet is a good stock that I don't mind owning. Right now, the stock price at 99. I don't mind to own it at 10% discount at 90, right? Which is still a good deal."

He filled at $1.26 credit.

#### XBI: The Breakout

XBI had done exactly what the strategy is built to wait for. Adam's chart description is the clearest statement in the six lessons of what a successful Crouching Bull looks like as it plays out: "it looks like it has broken above the trading range, retraced, tested the resistance now turned support, and now on the way up. This is exactly the scenario I'd like to use for Crouching Bull Spread, meaning I know that one day the bull will return, I just need to buy more time for it. And that is exactly what happened to the XBI trade right here. It took me some time. The price is fluctuating, but it has now broken above the trading range and on the way to rally upside."

The stock was at $89.58, up nearly $10 from the $80 entry.

| XBI P&L, 27 Jan 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $612 |
| Roll credit, 23 Dec (72 → 74 put) | −$109 |
| **Effective cost** | **$503** |
| Current mark: bull call spread | $10.55 |
| Current mark: 74 put | $0.01 |
| **Current value** | **$10.54 ($1,054)** |
| **Profit** | **$551** |
| Buying power | $1,508 |
| **Return on investment** | **36.5%** |
| Stock price | $89.58 |

"So since I entered the trade, the price has gone up by almost $10, and I made about $550 profit for the trade, which is 36.6%, not so bad." His spreadsheet agreed: "Indeed, it's making like $550 here, exactly the same methodology that I show you."

He held. The reasoning was the same as Alphabet's — 140 days remained on the calls, and the technical picture had just improved dramatically. "It looks like the price has broken above the resistance, and it's on the way up. I'm still pretty bullish on the ETF price here, and I'd like to hold the trade further to get more upside."

The roll: buy back the 74 put for a cent, sell the 35-day put at one standard deviation. $89.58 minus $7.24 gave approximately $82. He checked the chart — "82 would be around in the middle of the range here. It's okay. It has plenty of support. So I don't mind. Even if it retraces to that level, I keep rolling the cash secured put again." Filled at $1.03 credit.

Note the position sizing of the risk here. Rolling *up* to 82 from 74 raised the assignment price, but the stock had risen $9.58 in the interim; the strike remained one standard deviation below spot and comfortably within the established range's support structure.

#### Meta: Taking the Profit

Meta had run to $150.30 — from $110 at entry. Adam's assessment of the chart was that the easy money had been made and the risks had inverted.

He listed four separate reasons for exiting, and it is instructive that no single one of them would have sufficed on its own.

First, **the stock had reached his target price**. "I buy 110 call, which is at the money. And I sold the 150, which is my target price. Right now, the price at 150, which is at my target already." The short call strike *is* the target price by construction; when spot reaches it, the bull call spread is at or near its maximum realisable value and further upside is structurally impossible.

Second, **technical resistance was immediately overhead**. "It's already at 150 level, which is near the resistance based on the technical chart here. You see, there's a strong support turned resistance now. So my concern is approaching 155. It will be a resistance for the stock price."

Third, **earnings were imminent and the run-up created sell-the-news risk**. "the earning is coming. When the stock has run up quite a bit before the earnings, there could be sell on news, right? Even the earning is good, the guidance is good, but because the stock has run up so much, too much, too fast, there's a good chance that the stock price could retrace after the earning because people just take profits." He added a momentum-oscillator confirmation: "The stochastic also shows the stock is overbought. It's very overbought here, and it could be due for a retracement."

Fourth, and decisively, **the profit had massively exceeded his target return**.

| Meta P&L, 27 Jan 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $1,120 |
| Roll credit, 23 Dec (97 → 102 put) | −$185 |
| **Effective cost** | **$935** |
| Current mark: bull call spread | $27.52 |
| Current mark: 102 put | ≈ worthless |
| **Current value if exited** | **$2,755** |
| **Profit** | **$1,820** |
| Buying power | $2,250 |
| **Return on investment** | **80.8%** |
| Stock price | $150.30 |

His articulation of the profit-taking discipline is one of the most quotable passages in the course: "Yes, good stock. I still believe the rally will continue. However, I would be cautious of the trading, right? When you have a good profit, you need to be disciplined as well. The discipline not just on the cutting loss, but also on taking profit."

And then the explicit target: "from the P&L standpoint, it already generated more than 80%, way ahead of my target. **My target normally is about 50% return on investment. That is good enough.** This is about two months' time. I didn't need a trade for two months. Now making like 80% plus, I think it's pretty good. I would not be greedier. I would take the profit and run, release the buying power for the new trade. There are so many other opportunities, so many other good stocks that are still at a reasonable price."

The **50 per cent return on buying power** figure is the single most important numeric management rule in the strategy, and Adam states it only once. It is the profit target. Meta hit 80 per cent, which was 60 per cent past the target, and he closed.

The exit mechanics were a single three-leg closing order: sell to close the 110 call, buy to close the 150 call, buy to close the near-worthless 102 put. He aimed for $27.52, tried for $27.54, and filled at $27.54.

Final Meta accounting: $2,754 received minus $935 effective cost equals **$1,819 profit, 80.8 per cent return on the $2,250 buying power, achieved in 67 days**.

### Trade Management: The Third Roll, 3 March 2023

Five weeks later, with Meta closed, two positions remained.

#### Alphabet: Down Again

Google had reversed once more, falling from $99 back to $92.64. Against the $97.50 entry, "the price has been declining, right, up and down, but overall is declining... I entered when the stock was like 97.5, and today is like 92.5. So, drop by $5. Had I bought the stock, I would have lost $500 for 100 shares."

| Alphabet P&L, 3 Mar 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $743 |
| Roll credit 1, 23 Dec | −$76 |
| Roll credit 2, 27 Jan | −$126 |
| **Effective cost** | **$541** |
| Current mark: bull call spread | $4.58 |
| Current mark: 90 put | $0.02 |
| **Current value** | **$4.56 ($456)** |
| **Loss** | **−$85** |
| Buying power | $2,041 |
| **Return on investment** | **−4.1%** |
| Stock price | $92.64 |

The comparison against share ownership is now stark and Adam makes it explicitly: "Since I entered the trade, the stock has dropped about, let's call it, 5. This trade is losing $85, which is not too bad. Had I bought the stock, I would have lost $500 for 100 shares. But because I use Crouching Bull Spread, my loss is limited. My loss is much smaller, only less than $100 for the trade."

The stock had fallen 5.0 per cent. The position was down 4.1 per cent of blocked capital, and in absolute dollars it was down $85 against the $500 that a hundred shares would have cost. Two rounds of rolling credits totalling $202 had absorbed most of the directional damage.

His decision: hold and roll again. "I still have plenty of time for my bull call spread when I can roll the cash secured put leg for many rounds. So it's okay. I just need to buy more time. Google share price has not been performing well as many other big stocks, but it's just a matter of time because it's a good stock, it will recover eventually."

The roll went to a 34-day expiry rather than 35, and he explained the calendar quirk rather than glossing it: "You could ask why 34 days, not 35 days. Well, April 6 is actually Thursday because April 7th is a Good Friday and that is a holiday. So it changed to Thursday."

He bought back the 90 put for $0.03. One standard deviation from $92.70 was $7.30, giving 85 or 86; he chose 86 for slightly better premium. The chart check: "86 is very close to the last swing low, I mean the lowest in many years, right? So it's kind of a support level for me, and it's dirt cheap, and I don't mind buying Google share at 86. So it's good. I mean, this is a very good entry level if I have to buy the share at that price." He bargained $1.12 down to $1.11 and filled.

#### XBI: Retraced

XBI had given back its gains, falling from $89.58 back to about $82.70 — still slightly above the $80 entry.

| XBI P&L, 3 Mar 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $612 |
| Roll credit 1, 23 Dec | −$109 |
| Roll credit 2, 27 Jan | −$103 |
| **Effective cost** | **$400** |
| Current mark: bull call spread | $6.79 |
| Current mark: 82 put | $0.21 |

| Buying power | $1,508 |

"So versus my entry time, the price has gone up a little bit, $2, $3, and my trade is making $258, which is pretty good. In this case, the stock price I consider it as flat, but the trade is making some nice money, not at the level that I would like to see, but it's okay, it's just a matter of time."

There is a small but instructive management detail here. The 82 put still carried $0.21 to $0.23 of value because the stock had drifted just below the strike. Adam's normal practice would be to wait for that residual to decay further before rolling. He explained the compromise he was making for the sake of the recording: "If I wait until the end of the day and the price doesn't drop, this $0.23 will go to zero. But it's okay. For illustration of this video, I would close it or I roll it right now without waiting. Typically, I would wait a little bit longer for the remaining value of the short put here to deplete further, and then I roll. But it's okay. 20 cents left that I just leave it on the table."

The roll: one standard deviation from $82.70 was $6.30, suggesting 76. He chose 77 "to get a little bit better premium," and checked it against the chart: "77 is right at the support level. 76, 77, right there, which is pretty good." He filled at approximately $0.92 to $0.93 credit.

### Trade Management: The Final Exits, 5 April 2023

The last management session was recorded on 5 April, a day before the 6 April put expiry, because Adam expected to be unavailable the following day. Both remaining positions were closed.

#### Alphabet: Closed for a 29.7 Per Cent Gain

Google had rallied to $105.12, its best level since the trade began. "Since I entered the trade, the stock has gone up by, do the math, 105.12 minus 97.5. Stock has gone up $7.62."

| Alphabet P&L, 5 Apr 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $743 |
| Roll credit 1, 23 Dec | −$76 |
| Roll credit 2, 27 Jan | −$126 |
| Roll credit 3, 3 Mar | −$111 |
| **Effective cost** | **$430** |
| Mark value of bull call spread | $10.76 |
| 86 put | ≈ worthless |
| **Unrealised profit at mark** | **$646 (31.7%)** |
| **Actual fill on exit** | **$10.37 ($1,037)** |
| **Realised profit** | **$607** |
| Buying power | $2,041 |
| **Final return on investment** | **29.7%** |
| Stock price at exit | ~$105 |

Adam's comparison against buy-and-hold is worth quoting in full, because it reframes what the strategy is competing against: "my trade is making $646, which is almost equal to buying the shares and holding since then, right? You would make a very similar profit with less capital. And therefore, return on investment is much higher than if you have bought the shares by your cash."

A hundred shares of Alphabet at $97.50 would have required $9,750 of capital and would have gained $762. The Crouching Bull required $2,041 of blocked buying power and gained $607 — eighty per cent of the dollar profit on twenty-one per cent of the capital.

But the *reason* he closed rather than rolling again is the most important management insight in the entire final lesson, and it concerns theta.

"So first of all, the trade theta is now negative. You click on the column here. The theta of the trade is negative right now. Why is it? It's because there's no more value left in the cash secured put. The time decay doesn't work in my favour anymore. Whereby the bull call spread is still there, and it is losing like $1.89 a day. The rate of decay will increase because the time is approaching the expiration. Very soon, right? So in the next 30 days or so, you will see this $1.89 a day will increase. And I don't want that to happen."

This is the endgame of every Crouching Bull. The bull call spread was entered at roughly 210 days to expiration; by April it had only 72 days left — "about two and a half months. So this is something that made me think about maybe I want to close the trade today." A six-month call spread decays gently. A seventy-day call spread does not. As the calls approach expiry, their theta accelerates, and the monthly put credit — which was ample cover against a slow bleed — becomes insufficient to offset the increasingly rapid decay of the long call.

"So instead of rolling one more round, which I can do, but again, I have this time decay increase that works against me. So I would rather close the trade. Take the profit. By the way, the profit is good, right? 31.7%. So good. Take the profit, release the buying power, and use that buying power to enter the new trade."

His stated preference for redeployment is instructive: rather than nursing an ageing position, he would rather open a *fresh* Crouching Bull with a full six-month runway. "If I could not find a new trade, a better deal, then I would perhaps continue to enter the new trade on Google, because even at this price, 105, it is still below the intrinsic value of the stock. The intrinsic value of the stock is like 159. So technically, I could still enter the same trade, but on a longer time frame — of course, the construct has to be at the money bull call and then one standard deviation on the cash secured put."

The exit was a single three-leg order: buy to close the put, sell to close the 97 call, buy to close the 120 call. He tried $10.40, saw the price falling and moved quickly — "The price is dropping, so I need to close earlier" — and filled at $10.37.

#### XBI: Closed for a 10.3 Per Cent Loss

XBI, which had been the strategy's best-behaved chart in January, had deteriorated badly. "XBI price has been performing very poorly. I entered on the same day. It went up steadily, and it continued to go higher, which is good. But then it retraced back down, and I rolled it here on the last March 3rd, and then since then it collapsed. And then it kind of finds the support at the 76 level, which is good. It's holding there. So overall, the price has gone down from $80, now down to $76, dropped more than $4."

Critically, the 77 put was now in the money — spot $76.10 against a $77 strike. "Because the stock price has gone down below the put strike... the cash secured put now goes in the money. And that's why you see it's not worthless. It's worth something."

| XBI P&L, 5 Apr 2023 | |
|---|---|
| Entry debit, 21 Nov | $612 |
| Roll credit 1, 23 Dec | −$109 |
| Roll credit 2, 27 Jan | −$103 |
| Roll credit 3, 3 Mar | −$93 |
| **Effective cost** | **$307** |
| Mark: bull call spread | $2.65 |
| Mark: 77 put (in the money) | −$1.47 |
| **Net mark value** | **$1.18 ($118)** |
| **Unrealised loss at mark** | **−$189 (−12.5%)** |
| **Actual fill on exit** | **$1.51 ($151)** |
| **Realised loss** | **−$156** |
| Buying power | $1,508 |
| **Final return on investment** | **−10.3%** |
| Stock price at exit | $76.10 |

The exit filled better than the mark suggested — "actually I got filled at 151, not so bad" — which reduced the loss from the estimated $189 to $156. Adam noted this without drama: "So the trade lost less than what I calculated before."

The comparison against ownership again: "the stock drops by $4. Had I bought 100 shares, I would have lost $400 right now. But because I use the Crouching Bull strategy, the loss of the trade is only 189. So half of the loss compared to holding shares. So it's a good strategy."

The reason for closing rather than rolling was the identical theta argument, with an additional wrinkle: "technically, I can still roll the cash secured put down and out to collect more premium, create more margin of safety on the downside, and then buying more time for the stock price to recover. But I'm also facing the same situation that the theta of the trade is positive because the cash secured put here will expire tomorrow and it still has positive right now. But after tomorrow, after this one expires, if the new cash secured put does not generate enough time decay benefit, my trade will be losing money every day. And this one will accelerate as well because the [long calls] will approach the expiration date in the next two months or so."

The decision rule emerges clearly: **when the remaining life on the bull call spread has shortened to the point where its accelerating theta can no longer be offset by a monthly put credit, close the position and, if you still like the thesis, re-enter fresh with full duration.** Adam applied it identically to a winner and a loser on the same day.

"So the same thing that I have here, I can roll it now and out, but I can also close the trade and use that buying power to open the new trade. Same on XBI, but on the longer DTE, so that the bull call spread does not decay fast as this one. With that I just close the trade. Take the loss, the small loss."

#### The Combined Result

| Trade | Entry | Exit | Days held | Stock move | P&L | ROI on buying power |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Meta | 21 Nov 2022 | 27 Jan 2023 | 67 | $110 → $150.30 (+36.6%) | +$1,819 | +80.8% |
| Alphabet | 21 Nov 2022 | 5 Apr 2023 | 135 | $97.50 → $105 (+7.8%) | +$607 | +29.7% |
| XBI | 21 Nov 2022 | 5 Apr 2023 | 135 | $80 → $76.10 (−4.9%) | −$156 | −10.3% |
| **Total** | | | | | **+$2,270** | |

Adam's own summary: "After I have closed the Meta trade for a very high profit... I closed the Meta trade for $1,800 plus, 81% return on investment. I closed the Google trade today for $600 plus, almost 30% return on investment, and I also closed the trade on XBI, which is not doing well from the stock performance standpoint, and the trade lost $156 or 10% return on investment. So overall, the three trades combined have been doing very well and generated a very good return on investment."

Three trades. Two winners, one small loser. A total of $2,270 of profit against roughly $5,800 of blocked buying power, achieved during a period in which two of the three underlyings were essentially flat and one fell.

### Exit Rules

Distilling the exit logic scattered across the six lessons produces a coherent set of rules. Adam presents four exit conditions and one exit mechanic.

#### Exit One: The Stock Exceeds the Short Call Strike

"If the share price rallies a lot and exceeds the short call target, which is the highest target price, so in that case, the trade would have the best possible profit. I would just take the profit. That is the best scenario."

The mechanics have a specific sequencing recommendation. "In the best case scenario, if the price exceeds the price target, you could just first step, let the cash secured put expire worthless, because that one has a shorter DTE. You let it expire worthless first, and then you just close the bull call spread to max out the profit."

And a specific warning against continuing to sell puts after a big rally: "There's no point to hold on to the trade because at that point in time, if you keep selling the cash secured put at the highest price, it would be dangerous because the price can pull back very drastically and that will hurt the cash secured put."

The valuation logic behind this is worth spelling out. "Normally, when the share price goes up a lot, it exceeds the target. That means it already approached or even exceeded the intrinsic value of the stock. In that case, I would just close the trade, take the profit." The trade was entered because the stock was cheap; once it is no longer cheap, the premise has expired.

#### Exit Two: The Fundamentals Deteriorate

"If the stock price falls well below the short put strike, the cash secured put, at the same time, the stock's fundamentals have changed significantly for the worse. It deteriorates a lot. Wow, so that is a very bad scenario, right? You thought this is a good stock, but now the stock fundamentals have changed a lot. You would have to cut loss and move on."

He is careful to characterise the frequency: "This does not happen very often. For the stocks to change the fundamentals significantly, I don't normally see it every day. It happens once in a while, but not very often. So it's a rare case, but it could happen as well."

Note the conjunction. The exit requires *both* a price collapse below the put strike *and* a genuine fundamental deterioration. Price weakness alone is not a cut-loss signal in this strategy — that is what the rolling machinery exists to handle. Only when the underlying investment thesis breaks does the trade become unsalvageable.

#### Exit Three: Fifty Per Cent Return on Investment

Stated once, in the Meta exit: "My target normally is about 50% return on investment. That is good enough." Measured against the buying power blocked at entry.

#### Exit Four: Theta Turns Negative as the Calls Age

The rule that closed both Alphabet and XBI. When the long-dated bull call spread has decayed to the point where its accelerating theta exceeds what a monthly put credit can offset, close and redeploy. In practice this triggered at around 70 days remaining on positions entered at around 210 days.

#### The Assignment-Accepting Exit

There is a fifth path, which Adam mentions but does not himself take: deliberately accepting assignment. "If the stock price drops below the put strike price, I mean, the cash secured put becomes in the money, what can you do? You could keep the cash secured put if you wish to own the stock at the strike price. In that case, the shares will be assigned to you after the expiration, and the remaining two legs, the bull call spread there, you then just close the remaining two legs. Then you own the shares only."

This is a legitimate outcome, and for an investor who genuinely wanted the stock at that price, it is arguably the intended one. But it is not what Adam does. "The next one would be the one I prefer to do, and I've been doing it every time. I want to delay owning the stocks. It's just a matter of time when the share price recovers. So I just want to delay owning the stock, buying more time for the share price to rebound."

### The Rolling Discipline

Rolling the cash secured put is the operational heart of the strategy, and Adam's rules for it are precise.

#### When to Roll: The Extrinsic Value Test

The timing rule is not calendar-based. It is based on how much extrinsic value remains in the short put.

"Now, when I roll the put option, when the cash secured put is going to expire in the next one or two days. So normally, I wait until the last day or the last two days before the cash secured put expires. If the extrinsic value of the cash secured put is almost zero, it's time to roll."

He gives a specific numeric threshold: "Now, look at the extrinsic value of the cash secured put when it is nearly depleted. **If it falls below 0.1, that's the time to roll.** If there's not much value left, no point to wait."

The logic in both directions is worth understanding. If the put is out of the money and nearly worthless, waiting achieves nothing — the remaining pennies are not worth the days. "Just roll early, you get the premium early. Probably you get more premium if you roll it early, and that's the way you keep the trade theta positive." If the put is *in* the money with no extrinsic value left, waiting is actively dangerous: "if it's in the money, it will likely be assigned early."

This is a correct and important point about American-style options. An in-the-money short put with zero extrinsic value gives the holder no reason to keep it alive; early exercise becomes rational, and assignment follows.

#### Where to Roll: Down and Out, for a Credit

"I just roll the cash secured put to a new cash secured put, and at the same time, I sell to open a new cash secured put at a lower price or even at the same price. It's okay, but for a credit. **That's important. The net of the two needs to be a credit or even or small debit. It's fine, but it cannot be a big debit.**"

The credit requirement is the constraint that keeps the machinery working. Every roll that produces a credit reduces the effective cost of the position — which is exactly how Alphabet's $743 entry became a $430 effective cost by April, and how XBI's $612 became $307. Those reductions, cumulatively $313 and $305 respectively, are the difference between the trades' actual outcomes and considerably worse ones.

The directional preference for lower strikes applies when the stock has declined: "ideally, if you could roll it to a lower strike price for a credit. Meaning you buy back the cash secured put and you sell the new cash secured put for a net credit, that would be the best. And the new cash secured put has the lower price. And you can collect a credit for it. That would be the best. Why? Because at the end of the day, if the price keeps going lower, you could eventually own the shares. You want to own the shares at the lower price, not at the higher price. That's why rolling it lower is a good thing, because you could lower the buying price of the shares eventually. And if you do it for multiple rounds, you could lower the price of buying the shares significantly compared to the first entry point."

When the stock has *risen*, the same one-standard-deviation rule naturally produces a *higher* strike, and that is correct — the XBI December roll from 72 to 74 and January roll from 74 to 82 both moved up, tracking a rising stock.

#### The Roll Sequence, Step by Step

| Step | Action | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Check extrinsic value of current short put | Roll when below $0.10, typically last 1–2 days before expiry |
| 2 | Buy to close the expiring put | Usually $0.01–$0.03 if out of the money |
| 3 | Choose the new expiry | ~35 DTE (adjust for holidays); prefer landing the *following* cycle across an earnings date to capture inflated premium |
| 4 | Read the one-standard-deviation move for that expiry | From the platform indicator |
| 5 | Compute the strike | Current spot minus one standard deviation |
| 6 | Check the chart | Strike should sit at or below a support level or swing low |
| 7 | Check delta | Should be approximately 0.17–0.19 |
| 8 | Check the ownership question | "Would I be happy to buy this stock at this price?" |
| 9 | Verify the roll produces a net credit | Credit required; break-even or tiny debit tolerable; large debit not |
| 10 | Sell to open, working the price a cent at a time | Adam routinely bargains 1–2 cents and accepts either outcome |
| 11 | Record the credit externally | The platform will delete the closed leg's P&L; log it in a notebook or spreadsheet |

#### Rolling Across Earnings

The earnings-timing technique deserves separate mention because it recurs and because it is subtle. Adam times rolls so that the *next* cycle straddles an earnings announcement, on the reasoning that implied volatility inflation before earnings makes the premium richer.

On the December Google roll he selected 27 January precisely because Google reported on 31 January: the January put would expire *before* earnings, and the roll executed on 27 January would then sell a put whose life *contained* the announcement. "if I roll another one, after this one, crossing the earning, I would expect to collect a lot more premium. Every time I roll across the earning, the premium would be very good."

He applied the same logic to Meta, noting that the 27 January expiry sat before Meta's 1 February report: "35 days to expiration, by the way, is the time before the earnings. So earnings for Meta will be on the 1st of February 2023. So this one is good before the earnings."

There is a risk embedded in this that Adam does not discuss explicitly but which the reader should note: a put sold across an earnings announcement carries inflated premium *because* it carries genuine event risk. The extra income is compensation for the possibility of a gap. Given the strategy's stance that assignment on a good stock is acceptable, the trade-off is coherent — but it is a trade-off.

### Assignment: What It Is and What It Is Not

Adam devotes a substantial passage to assignment, and his framing is deliberately corrective, because most traders react to assignment with alarm.

"in case you see the price drops so fast, and the extrinsic value is already depleted and you plan to roll it, but when you open your account, you see that the cash secured put has been assigned. So in that case, again, be calm. Nothing to worry. **Don't be afraid of assignment because the assignment in most cases is not a risk.** Assignment is not a bad thing. It's not a risk."

He gives two specific reasons why early assignment is, on balance, favourable.

The first is that early assignment accelerates your profit on the extrinsic value: "First of all, it means you earn the remaining extrinsic value ahead of time. You don't have to wait until the last day of the expiration to earn the last cents or last dollars of the extrinsic value. The moment the buyer of the put exercises his or her option, you earn the remaining extrinsic value. So you earn it ahead of time. It's a good thing."

The second is that assignment simply executes the transaction you had already agreed to: "your cash, which you already need to get ready on standby, will be used to buy the stock in this case. And by the way, this is a good stock, right? So you just use your cash to buy the stock. And then once you own the stocks or the shares, you could sell the shares and then you're back to cash again. Once you're back in cash, sell a cash secured put — that's very normal. Nothing to worry about when you get assignment early."

That last sentence sketches the natural continuation: assignment on a Crouching Bull's put leg drops the trader into the Cashflow Wheel, where he now owns shares of a good company at a discount and can begin selling covered calls against them.

The critical practical point is the cash. "You must be willing to own shares at the put strike price because that's a cash secured put. That means you would have to have the cash ready on standby, whether it is within your trading account or in your bank account and be ready to top up."

### Risks and Failure Modes

Adam's risk discussion is unusually candid, and it is worth setting out completely because the strategy's structural elegance can obscure how much downside it carries.

#### No Downside Protection Whatsoever

This is the headline risk and Adam states it in the bluntest terms available: "because you sell cash secured put, **there is no protection on the downside, exactly like you're holding shares**. So in that case, if the share price drops, if you own shares, right, owning stocks — if you own stock, even good stocks, it could go down 30, 40, 50%, and you have to suffer that kind of loss. That is a watch-out. **There's no invincible scenario here.** There could be a significant loss if the share price collapses and stays low for a long time."

The short put has no long put beneath it. Below the strike, the position's loss profile is that of long stock. A good company can fall fifty per cent; a good company that falls fifty per cent will assign you shares at a strike far above the market, and the Crouching Bull will have merely reduced, not eliminated, the damage.

#### The Buying Power Illusion

The second warning concerns a specific and dangerous asymmetry between what the broker blocks and what the trade can actually cost.

"when you enter the trade, the broker will block you a nominal buying power. **They don't block you with the total max loss.** When you enter, they block you about one fourth or one fifth worth of the share value. But then if the share price declines a lot, the broker can increase the buying power. Eventually, when you own the shares, you need to have cash as well if you don't want to borrow the money from the broker."

The Meta numbers make this concrete. The broker blocked $2,250. Adam's own stated maximum loss was "like 9,000 something when the stock goes to zero." A trader who sized his position against the $2,250 figure — treating it as the capital at risk — would be running four times the exposure he believed he was running.

Worse, the blocked amount is not fixed. As the stock falls and the short put moves toward and into the money, brokers increase the margin requirement. A trader who is fully deployed at entry can find himself receiving margin calls precisely when the market is falling and precisely when he has least appetite to sell anything.

#### Do Not Over-Trade

The conclusion Adam draws from the two risks above is a sizing rule stated with unusual force.

"Because of those watch-outs, please do not over-trade CBS. The same way, when you trade cash secured put, don't over-trade cash secured put. Similarly, don't over-trade CBS. **Only trade on the stocks at the size that you can afford owning the shares.**"

And he broadens it: "Again, do not over-trade CBS, only trade at the size that you can afford. And this is not just applicable to this strategy, it's applicable to all strategies. Don't over-trade any strategy, no matter how good it is. You always need to diversify — diversify across different strategies, across different sectors, across different securities."

The sizing test is therefore not "how much buying power do I have?" It is "if every one of my open Crouching Bulls were assigned simultaneously, could I pay for all the shares?" That is a far more restrictive constraint, and it is the correct one.

#### The Wrong Stock

The first entry filter exists because of this risk. Trading the Crouching Bull on a weak business converts a strategy whose worst case is "I own a great company cheaply" into one whose worst case is "I own a failing company that will keep failing." The rolling machinery — which is the strategy's principal defence — only works if the stock eventually recovers. Roll a put down on a company in terminal decline and you are merely chasing the price into the ground, collecting shrinking premiums for accelerating risk.

#### The Wrong Technical Timing

Entering before the bottom has formed exposes the position to exactly the scenario the strategy handles worst: a sustained, one-directional decline that carries through every put strike faster than the rolls can retreat. The Alphabet trade came close to demonstrating this in December — a $8 decline in thirty-two days — and survived because Alphabet's decline was contained and eventually reversed. A stock in genuine free-fall does not offer that courtesy.

#### Theta Decay in the Endgame

The failure mode that closed both surviving trades. The strategy's positive-theta property is not permanent. It is a function of the ratio between the short put's daily decay and the long call spread's daily decay, and that ratio deteriorates as the calls approach expiry. A trader who mechanically rolls the put without monitoring position theta will find, somewhere around two to three months before the calls expire, that he is paying more per day in call decay than he is collecting in put credits — and the position will bleed regardless of what the stock does.

#### The P&L Display Problem

Not a market risk, but a real operational one. Because rolling deletes realised P&L from the platform display, a trader who does not maintain external records will systematically *underestimate* his own performance and may make bad decisions — closing a winner he believes is flat, or misjudging whether he has hit his fifty per cent target. Adam raises it on every single management session. Keep a spreadsheet.

### Repairing a Losing Trade

Adam addresses the psychology of holding a Crouching Bull through a drawdown directly, and his framing is designed to keep the trader from panicking out of a position whose entire premise is patience.

"Of course, when you do the CBS trade in the bear market condition, you often see that even good stock, the stock price could drop a lot. And your CBS trade will be losing money. How to repair a losing trade in this case?"

The first move is a reframe: "in that scenario, the mindset has to be, holding a deep in the money cash secured put is similar to holding shares. That's nothing different there. And this is a fundamentally good stock, so holding its shares is not a bad thing."

An in-the-money short put has a delta approaching −1.00; economically, you are long the stock. If you would be comfortable holding the shares — and the first entry filter guaranteed that you would be — then you should be comfortable holding the put.

The second move is to re-run the fundamental test: "if you see the stock's fundamentals remain strong. Nothing to worry. Stay the course. Stay on. Keep holding the cash secured put. Or you could roll the put down to reduce the cost of buying shares, potentially, and that also buys you more time for the eventual price recovery. Because good stocks, the stock price always recover. Just buy more time by rolling the put down and out."

The third is explicitly psychological: "From the psychology standpoint, just ignore the short-term drawdown, okay? Because see it as a long-term investment in that case, wait for the right time for the bull to return, ignore the short-term temporary drawdown."

And he grounds this in his own eleven-month testing record rather than in exhortation: "in my experience over the past 11 months testing this strategy, many of my trades have gone through a similar situation. As you know, the whole market has been down 15 to 20% or 30% in case of Nasdaq. Many of my trades have been going through the same pattern. Good stock, but the price kept going lower. And I hold on to it. And then when it bottomed, it started to recover, the trade turns around."

The Alphabet trade in this chapter is that pattern in miniature: entered at $97.50, down to $89 within a month, rolled lower, recovered to $99, fell back to $92.64, rolled lower again, and finally closed at $105 for a 29.7 per cent return. A trader who panicked in December would have booked a $298 loss. A trader who followed the rolling discipline booked a $607 gain.

### How the Greeks Behave Over the Life of the Trade

Pulling together the scattered observations about the Greeks produces a coherent picture of the position's evolution.

**Delta** is positive throughout and comes from all three legs. The long at-the-money call contributes approximately +0.50 at entry. The short out-of-the-money call contributes a small negative, growing as the stock rallies toward the short strike. The short put contributes a positive delta of approximately +0.17 to +0.19 at each entry, rising toward +1.00 if the stock falls through the strike. The composite is meaningfully long the stock, which is why Adam's P&L tracked the stock's direction so faithfully in every one of the three trades.

**Theta** is the Greek the strategy is built around, and its behaviour is the most interesting. At entry, before the third leg, theta is negative — approximately −$1.00 per day on the Google spread. After adding the put, theta flips positive; XBI's was +$4.00 per day at entry. Over each thirty-five-day put cycle, the put's theta *accelerates* as expiry approaches, so the position becomes progressively more theta-positive within each cycle. But across cycles, as the long call spread's own remaining life shortens, its negative theta grows — and by April, with 72 days left on the Google calls, that leg alone was decaying at $1.89 per day and Adam observed the composite had turned negative once the put expired. The interplay between a repeatedly-refreshed short-dated positive theta and a monotonically-worsening long-dated negative theta is precisely what defines the strategy's useful life.

**Vega** is not discussed explicitly, but its structure follows from the construction. The long six-month call carries substantial positive vega; the short six-month call offsets part of it; the short one-month put carries modest negative vega. The net is positive vega, weighted long-dated — which means the position benefits from rising implied volatility, an unusual and welcome property for a bullish trade entered near a market bottom, since volatility tends to be elevated precisely when the entry conditions are met and tends to compress as recoveries take hold. The earnings-timed put rolls deliberately sell into local vega spikes.

**Gamma** on the short put is the risk that matters near expiry. As the put approaches expiration with the stock near the strike, its delta becomes highly sensitive to small price moves. This is one more reason Adam's extrinsic-value roll trigger — roll when below $0.10 rather than holding to the last tick — is prudent rather than merely convenient.

### What the Crouching Bull Is Not

It is worth closing with a set of contrasts, because the strategy's identity is clearest against the alternatives.

**It is not a cash secured put.** The cash secured put caps profit at the premium collected. Adam makes the comparison repeatedly and with real numbers: on Google, a cash secured put alone would have capped him at roughly $115; the Crouching Bull offered up to $1,500. "Here you could get $1,500 profit. So that's the higher profit there is a bull time, bull show."

**It is not a bull call spread.** The bull call spread loses its full debit on sideways movement and carries negative theta from day one. The Crouching Bull profits on sideways movement and carries positive theta. This is the specific problem the third leg was invented to solve, and Adam demonstrated the before-and-after on camera for all three underlyings.

**It is not a bear market strategy.** It has no bearish component. It profits from rallies. Its relevance to bear markets is that it can be *entered* during them, held through them, and financed by them — but it makes its money when the bull finally charges.

**It is not a hedged position.** There is no long put. Below the short put strike the loss profile is that of long stock. Every claim about "margin of safety" refers to a three-to-five per cent cushion at entry plus whatever the accumulated rolling credits provide — a meaningful buffer, but a buffer, not a floor.

**It is not a short-term trade.** The three trades in this chapter ran 67, 135 and 135 days. The design assumption is that the bottoming process takes months and that the trader will roll the put four, five or six times before the calls expire.

### Summary of Rules

| Category | Rule |
|---|---|
| **Underlying** | Fundamentally strong stock you would be content to own; ETFs acceptable |
| **Valuation** | Trading below your intrinsic value estimate (waived for ETFs) |
| **Technical** | Bottom formed or forming; base-building; poised to rebound. Do not trade a stock in free-fall |
| **Leg 1** | Buy at-the-money call, ~6 months DTE |
| **Leg 2** | Sell call at +1 standard deviation, or at chart target/resistance; same expiry as leg 1 |
| **Leg 3** | Sell put at −1 standard deviation, at or near support; ~30–35 DTE |
| **Short put delta** | ~0.17–0.19 (81–83% probability of expiring worthless) |
| **Cost reduction from leg 2** | Typically 30–40% of the long call's premium |
| **Breakeven target** | 3–5% below current stock price |
| **Theta check** | Must be positive after all three legs; if not, adjust |
| **Execution** | One three-leg order preferred; legging in permitted (put first to buy time, or spread first) |
| **Sizing** | Only what you could afford to take delivery of in cash; buying power blocked ≠ maximum loss |
| **Roll trigger** | Short put extrinsic value below $0.10, typically 1–2 days before expiry |
| **Roll target** | ~35 DTE; time it so the *next* cycle crosses earnings for richer premium |
| **Roll strike** | −1 standard deviation from current spot; lower if stock has fallen, higher if it has risen |
| **Roll economics** | Must produce a net credit; break-even or small debit tolerable; large debit not |
| **Profit target** | ~50% return on buying power blocked |
| **Exit — best case** | Stock exceeds short call strike: let the put expire worthless, then close the call spread |
| **Exit — theta** | Close when the ageing call spread's accelerating decay can no longer be offset by monthly put credits (~70 days remaining in Adam's practice) |
| **Exit — fundamentals** | Cut loss if price collapses below the put strike *and* fundamentals have genuinely deteriorated |
| **Record-keeping** | Log every rolling credit externally; the platform deletes closed-leg P&L |
| **P&L formula** | Effective cost = entry debit − all rolling credits; profit = current mark − effective cost; ROI = profit ÷ buying power |

### Closing

The Crouching Bull Spread is, in the end, an argument about time. Every other bullish options structure taught in this course asks the trader to be right about direction *and* right about timing. The bull call spread demands a rally before a date. The cash secured put pays you to wait but caps what waiting can earn. The covered call requires you to already own the shares.

The Crouching Bull separates the two questions. It asks the trader to be right about *direction and value* — is this a good company, is it cheap, has it stopped falling — and then it systematically buys time to be right about *timing*, financing that time with a monthly income stream that also lowers the price at which the trader might eventually be forced to buy. Six months of runway on the upside; four, five or six chances to reset the downside; and a payoff structure that wins in three of four price scenarios.

Its cost is genuine and should not be minimised. The trader is naked short a put and must be able to buy the shares. The broker's margin figure understates the true exposure by a factor of four or more. A company whose fundamentals genuinely break will hand the trader a loss that no amount of rolling will repair.

But within those constraints, the record Adam presents is a fair one. Three trades, entered live in front of an audience during the worst equity year since 2008, on underlyings that between them rose 37 per cent, rose 8 per cent, and fell 5 per cent. Two closed at 81 per cent and 30 per cent returns on capital blocked. The third lost 10 per cent — less than half what holding the shares would have cost. That is what a defensive bull looks like: not spectacular in any single position, but structurally difficult to hurt, and positioned to charge when the moment finally arrives.

# Part VII — Entry Criteria, Trade Management & Scanning for Trades

## Entry Criteria, Trade Management, and Scanning for Trades

### The Operational Backbone of Level 2

Every options course eventually arrives at the same uncomfortable truth: the strategy is the easy part. The mechanics of a bull put spread — sell one put, buy a further out-of-the-money put with the same expiration, collect the difference as a net credit — can be taught in ten minutes and understood in twenty. What separates the trader who compounds a ten percent monthly return from the trader who blows up an account inside a quarter is not knowledge of the structure. It is the discipline of the filter that decides which underlyings are even eligible, the precision of the strike selection, the position sizing that converts a probabilistic edge into a survivable equity curve, and above all the willingness to close a losing trade on a rule rather than on a hope.

This chapter is that operational backbone. It covers the four lessons that sit at the heart of Level 2 — the entry criteria, the trade management framework, the scanning workflow on thinkorswim, the consolidated summary of steps from blank screen to filled order, and the updated scanner build on Interactive Brokers. Taken together they describe a single repeatable process. The strategy they are wrapped around is what Adam Khoo calls the **bull put spread extreme**, abbreviated in his own journal and scanner names as **BPSX**. But the process itself — the liquidity screen, the trend definition, the implied volatility condition, the earnings avoidance, the buying-power ratio, the daily monitoring, the three-times cut-loss rule — generalises well beyond that one strategy. It is the process that decides *what* to trade and *when*, and it deserves to be learned as a system in its own right.

Before going further it is worth stating plainly what this strategy is and, more importantly, who it is not for. Adam is unusually direct on this point. He created the bull put spread extreme roughly three years before recording these lessons, and describes it as one of his favourite strategies — but he also says explicitly that it is **not recommended for inexperienced traders**. The reason is structural. Because the short put is sold extremely far out of the money, the credit collected is small relative to the width of the spread, which means the ratio of maximum loss to maximum profit is roughly ten to one. If a trader enters this strategy, does nothing, and allows a losing position to run to expiration, the loss will be ten times the premium collected. The entire strategy depends on the trader never allowing that to happen. As Adam puts it, if you are new to trading it is best to avoid this until you have got more experience — experience specifically in knowing how to cut loss fast and how to manage a trade well. Once that experience exists, he considers it a pretty lucrative strategy. The order of those two statements matters.

---

### Part One: Entry Criteria

#### What "Extreme" Actually Means

The bull put spread extreme is a modification and adaptation of the standard bull put spread taught in the credit spreads lesson of Level 1. Adam is explicit that the reader should fully understand and revise that original strategy before attempting this one, because the extreme version changes only two things — but changes them in a way that alters the entire risk profile.

The word "extreme" is earned for two reasons. The first is that the put option is sold very far away from the market price — extremely far. The whole point is to place the short strike at a distance where it is genuinely hard for the share price to drop that far and hit it. The second reason is the mirror image of the first: because the short strike is so far away and the credit so thin, the strategy can be considerably more risky than a standard credit spread if the trade is not managed well. If the trader does not cut loss early, and the share price does drop a lot, and the position is allowed to expire, the loss can be substantial.

So the structural bargain of this strategy is this. You accept a very high probability of winning — Adam quotes a win rate of **80 to 90 percent**, and says that averaged over a large sample of trades you can take about **85 percent** as the realistic figure — in exchange for a payoff structure where a single unmanaged loss can wipe out ten winners. The strategy is only viable because the trader's own discipline caps the loss well below the structural maximum. Everything in this chapter exists to enforce that cap.

#### The Directional Thesis: Moderately Bullish

Like the standard bull put spread, this strategy is a moderately bullish position. It profits if the underlying goes up, and it profits equally if the underlying goes sideways, and it even profits if the underlying goes down — provided it does not go down very much. That "not very much" is defined precisely by the strike selection, but the directional thesis is worth stating clearly because it drives the technical setup requirement.

Ideally the trader is looking for a stock that is on a clear uptrend. The logic is straightforwardly probabilistic: when a stock is on an uptrend, the probability is that the price will tend to go higher rather than lower. The strategy is not a bet on a specific move; it is a bet that the stock will not collapse. An uptrend is simply the market condition in which that bet has the best odds.

But an uptrend alone is not enough, and this is where a great many traders go wrong. Adam is emphatic that within an uptrend the trader must wait for the price to retrace to a strong level of support before entering. Uptrends move in wave patterns — wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down, and the pattern continues. The rule that follows from this is stated as a prohibition: **never enter a trade after a wave up.** The reasoning is intuitive. If you enter immediately following a strong upward wave, there is a high chance the next move is a wave down, which is precisely the move that hurts a bull put spread. So the trader always waits for the price to drop first — to wave down — but specifically to wave down *into* a strong level of support.

What qualifies as a strong level of support? Ideally a moving average that has been previously tested, or a horizontal support level the trader has identified on the chart. Adam's worked example is a stock in a clear uptrend that has waved up and is now finding support at the 50-period moving average. At that point the reasoning is that there is a high chance the price bounces back up from there, or at worst goes sideways, or drops just a little further near support. All three of those outcomes are profitable for a bull put spread. That is the best time to enter.

An important nuance on precision: the retracement does not have to touch support exactly. Adam asks the question directly — does it have to be exact? — and answers it himself: near the support is enough. This is a discretionary judgement about proximity, not a mechanical trigger.

#### Defining the Uptrend Mechanically

Because "uptrend" is the sort of word every trader thinks they understand and every trader defines differently, Adam replaces the intuition with a specific two-part moving-average test. Both parts must be satisfied.

The short-term trend is defined as up when the **20-period exponential moving average is above the 40-period exponential moving average**. The medium-term trend is defined as up when the **50-period simple moving average is above the 150-period simple moving average**. Ideally the trader wants both to be true simultaneously — short-term trend up and medium-term trend up — which together constitute a clear uptrend.

The chart setup that renders this is worth describing exactly, because it is the same setup reproduced later inside Interactive Brokers. The analysis is done on **daily candles**. On Adam's thinkorswim charts, the red dotted line is the 20 EMA and the blue dotted line is the 40 EMA; the short-term trend is up when the red dotted line sits above the blue dotted line. The thick blue line is the 50-period simple moving average and the thick green line is the 150-period simple moving average; the medium-term trend is up when the blue sits above the green. Reading the chart is then a matter of confirming both relationships hold, then locating the current position in the wave cycle, then waiting for a wave down into support.

| Trend component | Fast average | Slow average | Condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short-term trend | 20 EMA | 40 EMA | 20 EMA above 40 EMA |
| Medium-term trend | 50 SMA | 150 SMA | 50 SMA above 150 SMA |

Note that the fast pair are exponential moving averages while the slow pair are simple moving averages. This is not an accident of transcription; it is repeated consistently across the lessons and reproduced deliberately when Adam builds the chart study list inside Interactive Brokers, where he explicitly adds simple moving averages at 50 and 150 and exponential moving averages at 20 and 40.

#### Underlying Selection: Large, Famous, Liquid

The universe of eligible underlyings is deliberately narrow. Adam wants to use this strategy only on **large-cap companies** — big, famous companies, the sort of names everyone has heard of. His examples are Tesla, Apple and Microsoft. The formal screen he applies is membership in or equivalence to the **S&P 500**. The instruction is stated in the negative as well as the positive: do not do this on penny stocks that nobody has heard of.

The reasoning behind this restriction is developed further in the later scanner update lesson, and it is the single most important refinement Adam makes to the criteria over the course of these lessons. He explains that he now only wants to trade this strategy on really big companies because **big companies are less likely to gap down** compared to medium or smaller-sized companies. Large companies tend to be fundamentally a lot stronger and carry a lot less risk. Since the entire strategy is a bet against a catastrophic downward gap, restricting the universe to companies structurally unlikely to gap is a direct reduction in the tail risk that the strategy is most exposed to.

That reasoning produced a concrete tightening of the numbers, which is discussed in detail in the scanning section below: the minimum market capitalisation was raised from **$10 billion** in the original scanner build to **$30 billion** in the updated build.

#### Options Liquidity Requirements
