The second gate is options liquidity. Adam wants to trade this only on stocks whose options are very liquid and where there are a lot of options available — meaning a rich chain with many strikes and many expirations to choose from. Two concrete tests are given.

The first is the presence of a **weekly option series**. Adam's guidance is that the best quick way to check liquidity is to look at whether the underlying has weekly options. He is careful to hedge this: usually, though not always, if there is a weekly option series the options are more liquid to trade. It is a proxy rather than a proof, but it is a fast and usually reliable one.

The second is the **bid-ask spread**, which should not be that wide. The figure Adam gives is that the spread should ideally be less than about **40 cents, or 30 cents**. This matters more than it might appear for a strategy of this type. Because the whole trade collects a credit measured in tens of cents — the worked examples run at 45 cents, 50 cents, 91 cents and 96 cents per share — a bid-ask spread of comparable magnitude would consume a meaningful fraction of the expected profit on entry and again on exit. A spread of 40 cents against a credit of 50 cents is already marginal; the requirement exists to keep transaction friction from eating the edge.

Liquidity also shows up indirectly in the underlying's own trading volume, which is one of the four hard scanner filters. In the thinkorswim scanner build, average volume must exceed **one million shares** per day. In the consolidated summary lesson, Adam mentions a figure of **at least 200,000 shares traded per day on average** as the minimum threshold, and in the Interactive Brokers build he again uses one million. The one-million figure is the one he actually types into both scanners, and it should be read as the operating standard; the 200,000 figure appears once as a looser floor. Where the two differ, the scanner values are what he actually trades from.

#### The Implied Volatility Condition

The third gate is implied volatility, and this is the condition that most directly determines whether the trade is worth putting on at all.

The rule is that **IV percentile rank must be 35 percent or above**. Adam calls 35 the minimum. Higher is better — he says 50 or 60 is beautiful — but 35 is the floor below which the trade should not be taken.

The immediate reason is pricing. High implied volatility means richer option premiums, which means more money collected for the same structural risk. Since the credit is the numerator of the return calculation and the buying power is the denominator, and since the buying power is largely determined by the width of the spread rather than by volatility, a higher IV environment produces a materially better return on capital for an identical position structure.

The deeper reason is mean reversion in the volatility itself, and this is where Adam's explanation becomes genuinely important to understand rather than merely to memorise. He walks through the mechanics using the analyse tab, and the argument runs as follows. After you enter the trade, if volatility increases significantly, that is bad for the trade. On the profit-and-loss simulation, an increase in implied volatility causes the purple line — the current-date profit and loss curve — to drop lower on the downside. Because the trader's cut-loss point is defined as a fixed dollar loss (three times the credit received, as detailed below), pushing the purple line down means the price does not have to fall as far to reach that loss. In Adam's words, the break-even point, the cut-loss point, the point of no return, all move *higher* — closer to the current price — when IV surges. The trade becomes easier to lose.

Conversely, if implied volatility falls after entry, the purple line rises, the point of no return falls further away from the current price, and the trade becomes safer and more profitable.

This is why entering when IV is already high is not merely about collecting a bigger premium. It is a structural defence. Adam states it plainly: enter when IV is as high as possible, because if IV is really high then it is more likely to go down. Entering at a low IV percentile means the volatility has room to expand against you; entering at a high IV percentile means the statistically likelier path is volatility contraction, which works in your favour on both the premium and the shape of the risk curve.

He demonstrates this quantitatively on the analyse tab by using the volatility adjustment widget to simulate a **30 percent increase in volatility**. In the worked example fifteen days into a thirty-day trade, the point of no return sat at 432 under unchanged volatility. Simulating a 30 percent volatility increase pushed that point of no return back up — the exact adjusted level is read off the screen rather than stated aloud, so no number should be attached to it, but the direction and the mechanism are unambiguous.

#### Earnings Avoidance

The fourth gate is the avoidance of earnings announcements, and it is absolute enough to be treated as a hard rule.

The instruction is to **ensure that the stock is not releasing earnings any time before your spread expires**. The reason is the gap risk that the strategy has no defence against. If earnings are released and the stock price gaps down more than 15 percent, the position can take a very large loss instantaneously, without ever giving the trader an opportunity to cut. Every other risk control in the strategy assumes the trader can act; a gap through the short strike overnight removes that assumption.

In the consolidated summary lesson Adam states the screening window operationally: if earnings are coming within **30 to 45 days** — that is, within the horizon that overlaps the intended expiration — he skips the trade entirely. There is one carve-out, and it is narrow and conditional. If a genuinely great setup appears and he decides to take the trade even though earnings are coming, he always ensures that he **gets out before the earnings are announced**. He describes this as very, very important. The exception is therefore not permission to hold through earnings; it is permission to trade a shorter effective holding period that terminates before the announcement.

Earnings avoidance also appears in the trade management rules as a mandatory exit trigger, which is discussed in Part Two.

#### Volatility of the Underlying and Sector Exclusions

Beyond earnings, Adam applies a behavioural filter to the underlying itself. The stock should have **a history of not dropping more than 15 percent in 30 days**. Some stocks are simply very volatile — they drop 15 percent, they drop 20 percent — and the strategy does not want those names. Since the short strike is placed roughly 15 percent below the current price, an underlying with a demonstrated habit of 15 to 20 percent monthly drawdowns is by definition an underlying that routinely travels the entire distance the strategy is relying on it not travelling.

There is also an explicit sector exclusion. **Avoid biotech and pharmaceutical stocks.** The reason given is binary event risk: these companies can gap down catastrophically when they fail their drug trials. Adam demonstrates the rule in practice during the scanning workflow — scrolling through his scan results he reaches the ticker ALXN and dismisses it immediately, saying that the moment he sees the word pharmaceutical or biotech, forget it, don't trade these, they are very scary and they tend to gap up and gap down a lot. The exclusion is applied on the name, not on the chart. A biotech with a perfect uptrend and a perfect IV percentile is still excluded.

#### Days to Expiration

The choice of expiration is where the transcripts contain a genuine and instructive range rather than a single number, and it is worth laying out honestly.

In the opening framing of the strategy Adam says he would usually choose a date to expiration of between **30 to 45 days**. Shortly afterwards, when describing what he actually does, he narrows this considerably: he sells the bull put credit spread with **20 to 30 days to expiration**, and calls 20 to 30 days his **sweet spot**. In the consolidated summary lesson he returns to the wider framing and says the sweet spot is between **30 to 45 days**. During the live scanning demonstration on Alibaba he says ideally between 20 to 30 days and selects a 26-day expiration. In the live Interactive Brokers trade on TAL he says usually he would choose 30 days, but no 30-day expiration existed in that chain, so the closest he could choose was 46 days — and he took it.

The honest synthesis is this. The strategy operates in a window of roughly **20 to 45 days to expiration**, with a strong preference for the shorter end of that range. Adam gives the reason for the preference directly: usually the shorter days are better, because then the options can expire and you can take your profits and run faster. Faster capital turnover means the same buying power can be recycled into more trades per month, which is what drives the monthly return target. Against that, shorter expirations sometimes force compromises elsewhere in the criteria, which is why he will stretch to 46 days when the chain does not offer anything closer to his ideal.

| Aspect | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Stated general range | 30 to 45 days | Standard framing of the strategy |
| Stated operating sweet spot | 20 to 30 days | Faster capital turnover, faster profit realisation |
| Demonstrated range in live trades | 26 days (BABA demo), 46 days (TAL live) | Constrained by what the chain actually offers |
| Preference direction | Shorter is better | Take profits and recycle buying power sooner |

#### Strike Selection: The Short Put

The short put is where the word "extreme" becomes a number.

Whereas the standard bull put spread taught in Level 1 sells the put at approximately **25 delta** — and Adam elsewhere refers to that original teaching as being at **20 delta** when comparing the risk profiles — the extreme version sells at **10 delta**.

The ideal is a delta of **9 to 15**, with **10 as the favourite and the sweet spot**. Adam is comfortable anywhere near 10 — 9, 11, 12 are all fine — and states a hard ceiling: he will not go above **15 delta**. In the consolidated summary he repeats this precisely: the sweet spot is 10, it can be slightly below at 9, it can be above 10, but he will not go more than 15.

What does 10 delta mean in this context? Adam gives the interpretation that matters for the strategy: it means there is only about a **10 percent probability that the price will drop below this strike price and stay there at expiration**. That is a theoretical figure derived from the option's own pricing, not a guess. From it follows the **90 percent win probability** that the strategy is built on, and he is careful to stress that this is not something he is estimating — it is a statistical fact read directly off the delta. Ninety percent probability that the option expires worthless, and therefore ninety percent probability that the spread pays the full credit.

Averaged over real trades and accounting for the imperfection of delta as a probability estimate, the realistic expectation he quotes is the 80 to 90 percent band with an 85 percent midpoint.

Alongside the delta condition sits a distance condition. The short put strike should ideally be roughly **15 percent below the current stock price**. The purpose is intuitive — it makes it genuinely hard for the stock price to reach the strike. But Adam explicitly qualifies this as a rough rule of thumb rather than a hard requirement. He notes that some stocks are simply less volatile — his examples are Pepsi and McDonald's — and for those names the 15 percent buffer is unnecessarily conservative; a 10 percent buffer might be perfectly adequate. The 15 percent figure is a default calibrated to a typical large-cap, not a universal constant.

The two conditions interact. In the Netflix example, Netflix was trading at 516 when the trade was executed and the 10-delta put sat at the **420 strike** — a distance of about **19 percent**, comfortably beyond the 15 percent guideline, which Adam describes as pretty safe at 10 delta. In the Alibaba demonstration the arithmetic went the other way: the stock was at 272 and the 240 strike he was examining worked out to roughly **12 percent** away, which he judged not really ideal because the guideline calls for at least 15 percent. He said explicitly that he might not actually take that trade in reality because it was not 15 percent away, though he allowed that a trader confident in the strength of the trend could still take it. He proceeded with it only for demonstration purposes. This is the correct model for how the 15 percent rule should be used — as a strong prior that requires an articulable reason to override.

#### Strike Selection: The Long Put

The long put is bought **one to two strikes below the short put**, with the same expiration date. Adam's default in the worked examples is one strike, but he says two strikes is fine as well provided the resulting risk-to-reward ratio is acceptable.

The reason the choice is left open is that the width of the spread is the primary lever controlling the relationship between credit received and buying power blocked, and that relationship is itself a hard entry criterion. Widening the spread from one strike to two increases the credit — but it increases the maximum loss faster. Adam demonstrates this arithmetic explicitly during the Alibaba scan, and the demonstration is worth reproducing in full because it is the clearest illustration of why this criterion is binding.

Selling the 240 put and buying the 235 put — a five-point-wide spread, one strike apart — produced a credit of **50 cents**, or $50 per contract, against a maximum loss and buying power requirement of **$450**. The ratio is nine to one, slightly less than ten times, and therefore acceptable.

Selling the 240 and buying the 230 instead — a ten-point-wide spread — produced a larger credit of **$70**, but a maximum loss of **$930**. That is a ratio of over thirteen to one. Adam's verdict was immediate: not a good deal, this is not a good deal, we cannot do this.

Selling the 235 and buying the 230 produced a credit of **$20** against a maximum loss of **$480**, a ratio of twenty-four to one, which fails badly.

Of the combinations tested, only the 240/235 pairing satisfied the ratio requirement. The lesson generalises: the correct spread width is not a fixed preference but the output of a search over the available combinations, constrained by the buying power ratio.

#### The Buying Power Ratio: The Binding Constraint

This is the criterion that turns the loose collection of preferences above into an executable rule, and it is the one Adam checks last and most insistently before every single entry.

**The buying power used must not be more than 10 times the net credit received.**

The buying power blocked by the broker when a credit spread is opened is, for these structures, identical to the maximum loss on the position — Adam states repeatedly that buying power and maximum loss are the same thing here, differing only by commission. So the rule can be stated equivalently: the maximum loss must not exceed ten times the maximum profit.

The arithmetic is straightforward. If the trader collects a credit of $1.00 per share, one contract representing 100 shares yields a total credit of $100. The maximum permitted buying power is then $1,000. That configuration produces a return on capital of $100 on $1,000, or **10 percent**, over the 20 to 30 day holding period. That 10 percent per cycle is the engine of the entire strategy's return profile.

The rule is a ceiling, not a target — less than ten times is better, but never more than ten times. And it is checked at the moment of order entry, using the broker's own confirm-and-send screen, which displays the maximum profit and maximum loss for the proposed order before it is transmitted.

Adam is scrupulous about the flip side. The ten-times ratio is not only the buying power; it is also the **maximum loss if the trade is not managed well**. He repeats this warning multiple times: if you do not manage the trade, you could lose ten times the profit that you make. The rule permits a ten-to-one structure precisely because a separate, stricter management rule guarantees the loss is realised at three times rather than ten times.

#### Why 10 Delta Rather Than 20 or 35

Adam devotes real attention to justifying the choice of 10 delta over the alternatives, and the discussion is valuable because it makes the trade-off explicit rather than presenting 10 delta as obviously correct.

The relationship is monotonic. The nearer the short put is sold to the current stock price — the bigger the delta — the smaller the maximum loss relative to the credit. At **20 delta**, the configuration taught in the original bull put spread lesson, for every $100 of credit received the maximum loss or buying power used is about **four times**, or $400. Some of Adam's students sell at **35 delta**, and at that distance for every $100 of credit received the maximum loss is only about **$200** — a two-to-one structure.

| Short put delta | Credit per contract | Approximate max loss | Ratio | Probability short strike finishes ITM |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 35 delta | $100 | $200 | 1 : 2 | ~35% |
| 20 delta | $100 | $400 | 1 : 4 | ~20% |
| 10 delta (BPSX) | $100 | $1,000 | 1 : 10 | ~10% |

Read down that table and the trade-off is obvious. Selling closer produces a far less frightening maximum loss, but the strike sits nearer the current stock price and therefore gets hit a good deal more easily. Selling further away produces a terrifying maximum loss on paper, but the strike sits so far from the market that it is almost very difficult for the stock to ever reach it.

Adam refuses to declare one approach right and the others wrong. He says there is no right or wrong, it depends on your preference, and notes that he has students using each of these methods very happily and making a lot of money. His own preference for 10 delta is stated as a preference and defended on one ground: the strike price is so far away that it is almost very difficult for the stock to ever reach there.

And when he anticipates the obvious objection — that he is risking ten times his money — his answer is the pivot on which the whole strategy turns. Yes, he is. But he will never lose ten times his money, because he has got strict cut-loss measures to get out much earlier, so that even if he is wrong on the trade he will at most lose **three times his profit**.

The ten-to-one structure is therefore a theoretical maximum that the trader contracts never to experience. That contract is the subject of Part Two.

#### The Netflix Case Study

The Netflix example is the reference implementation of every criterion above, and running through it end to end shows how the pieces lock together.

Netflix satisfied the stock criteria on inspection: it is a large company, an S&P 500 constituent, on a clear uptrend, and it had retraced to a support level. The first quantitative check was the option statistics page, where the **current IV percentile read 40 percent** — above the 35 percent minimum, so the volatility criterion passed.

The expiration selected was **30 days** out. Scanning the put chain for the 10-delta strike located the **420 put**. Netflix was trading at **516** at execution, so the short strike sat about **19 percent** below the market — well beyond the 15 percent guideline.

The quoted premium on the 420 put was **$4.50**, but Adam is careful to make a point about fills that recurs throughout these lessons: just because the screen quotes 4.50 does not mean you actually get filled at 4.50. In this case the fill came at **$4.40**, which he judged close enough. The long put, one strike below at **415**, was bought for **$3.90**. Both legs executed together as a single spread order.

The resulting net credit was **$0.50 per share**, or **$50 per contract**, on one contract. The broker's confirm-and-send screen showed a maximum profit of $50 and a maximum loss — identical to the buying power blocked, differing only by commission — of **$450**. Nine to one. Slightly less than ten times. The criterion passed.

The return arithmetic: $50 of profit on $450 of capital committed for 30 days is a **return of approximately 11 percent**.

The final pre-entry step, which Adam treats as mandatory, was to run the position through the **analyse function** — he demonstrates on thinkorswim — to see the profit and loss profile before committing. That analysis is the bridge into trade management, because what it produces is not a single break-even but a schedule of cut-loss points that changes with the passage of time.

#### Reading the Analyse Tab: The Moving Point of No Return

The profit and loss chart in the analyse tab shows two curves. The **green line** represents profit and loss at expiration — the terminal payoff diagram. The **purple line** represents profit and loss as of a simulated current date, incorporating remaining time value and the current volatility assumption. The tool allows the trader to advance the simulated date and watch the purple line migrate toward the green line, which is exactly what happens in reality as time decay works through the position.

For the Netflix trade, entered on the **3rd of September** with a $50 credit and a self-imposed maximum loss of three times that, or **$150**, the schedule looked like this.

On the day of entry, the 3rd of September, the purple line sat well below the green line on the downside. To lose $150 the stock would have had to drop to approximately **439** — a level meaningfully *above* the 420 short strike. In other words, on day one, the trader would be forced to cut the trade before the stock ever reached the short put.

Advancing the simulation to the **18th of September**, fifteen days later and roughly halfway to expiration, the purple line had risen. The point of no return had fallen from 439 to approximately **432**. Still above the short strike, but closer to it.

Advancing to the **3rd of October**, essentially expiration day, the purple line had converged onto the green line entirely. The three-times loss point now sat at approximately **418**, which is *below* the 420 short strike.

The pattern this reveals is the single most useful piece of intuition in the entire trade management framework. **As time passes, the point of no return gets lower and lower, until at expiration it converges on the short strike price itself.** Adam attaches an explicit caveat: this holds assuming volatility does not change.

The practical implication, which he spells out during the Alibaba demonstration, is that the danger in this strategy is heavily front-loaded. The moment the trade is entered, if the price starts to fall, the position is in trouble quickly, because the purple line is at its lowest and the cut-loss threshold is at its highest and nearest. But if fifteen or twenty days pass uneventfully and *then* the price starts going down, it is far less dangerous, because by that point the purple line has risen substantially and the position will not lose much even on a meaningful adverse move.

The same simulation on the Alibaba demo trade, a 26-day expiration entered on the 20th of September with a $1,000 credit and therefore a $3,000 cut-loss threshold, produced this schedule: at entry, the price would have to drop to **242** to lose $3,000, which is slightly above the 240 short strike; around the 3rd to 5th of October, roughly halfway, the level had fallen to **241**; and very close to expiration on the 15th of October, with the purple line nearly coincident with the green, the level had fallen to approximately **239**, below the short strike.

The TAL trade demonstrates the same principle in dollar terms. Entered on the 31st of August expiring 16 October with three contracts at $45 credit each, total credit $135, the maximum loss at expiration was **$1,365** — the ten-times structure. If the stock crashed all the way to the 60 short strike and expired there, the position would still make the full $135, because at expiration the payoff is unimpaired until the short strike is breached. But twenty days into the trade, around the 21st of September, if the price crashed to 60 the position would show a loss of approximately **$400** — three times the premium. Hence the rule: the moment the price gets close to that 60 strike, close it and take the loss.

Adam's summary of what this schedule proves is worth quoting in substance: if you manage your trade, it is going to be almost impossible to lose ten times your money. You manage your trade, you lose three times your money, and the probability of losing is less than 10 percent. That is the whole architecture in two sentences.

#### Entry Criteria Consolidated

| # | Criterion | Threshold | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Company size | Large cap, S&P 500 calibre | Fundamentally stronger, far less likely to gap down |
| 2 | Market capitalisation | ≥ $10bn originally; raised to **≥ $30bn** | Bigger companies gap down less often |
| 3 | Share price | ≥ $50 (originally ≥ $20) | Below $50 the premium is too thin; forces excessive contract counts and commissions |
| 4 | Average daily volume | ≥ 1,000,000 shares | Underlying liquidity; supports options liquidity |
| 5 | Optionable | Must be optionable; weekly series preferred | Weekly series usually indicates a liquid chain |
| 6 | Bid-ask spread | Less than roughly 30–40 cents | Wide spreads consume a credit measured in tens of cents |
| 7 | Short-term trend | 20 EMA above 40 EMA | Defines short-term uptrend mechanically |
| 8 | Medium-term trend | 50 SMA above 150 SMA | Defines medium-term uptrend mechanically |
| 9 | Wave position | Enter after a wave *down*, near strong support | Never enter after a wave up; retracement into support offers the best odds |
| 10 | IV percentile / IV rank | **≥ 35%**, higher preferred (50–60 excellent) | Richer premiums; IV more likely to fall than rise from a high base |
| 11 | Earnings | None before expiration; skip if within 30–45 days | Gap risk that no stop can defend against |
| 12 | Historical volatility of the name | No history of dropping more than 15% in 30 days | The strategy relies on the stock not travelling 15% down |
| 13 | Sector | Exclude biotech and pharmaceutical | Binary drug-trial gap risk |
| 14 | Days to expiration | 20–30 sweet spot; 30–45 acceptable range | Shorter turns capital faster; longer sometimes forced by the chain |
| 15 | Short put delta | **9–15, ideally 10**, never above 15 | ~10% probability of finishing in the money → ~90% win rate |
| 16 | Short put distance | ≈ 15% below current price (rule of thumb) | Distance buffer; can relax toward 10% on low-volatility names |
| 17 | Long put | 1–2 strikes below the short put, same expiration | Defines the spread width and therefore the risk ratio |
| 18 | Buying power to credit | **≤ 10 : 1**, never more | Caps structural risk; produces the ~10% ROI per cycle |
| 19 | Order type | Limit order at the mark, locked | Do not chase; protect the credit and therefore the ratio |
| 20 | Pre-trade analysis | Mandatory run through the analyse tab | Establish the schedule of cut-loss points before committing capital |

---

### Part Two: Trade Management

If the entry criteria decide what to trade, trade management decides whether the trader survives the trades that go wrong. Adam presents this as a short list of exit rules, but the rules are not equal in character: some are mechanical, some are conditional on price action, and one is an explicitly acknowledged judgement call. Understanding which is which is essential to applying them.

#### Rule One: Take Profit at 90 Percent of Maximum

The first and most frequently exercised rule is the profit target. **Close the trade once 90 percent or more of the maximum profit has been realised.**

The mechanic is simple. The trade was opened for a net credit; it is closed by buying the spread back for a net debit. If the spread was sold for 50 cents and can be bought back for 5 cents, then 45 of the 50 cents has been captured — 90 percent of the maximum — and the position is closed for a 45-cent realised gain.

The reasoning is not about squeezing the last cent out of a trade; it is about capital efficiency. Adam's explanation is that closing at 90 percent frees up the buying power so that new trades can be taken. Because he operates under a hard cap on total open buying power (detailed in Part Three), every dollar of buying power tied up in a trade that has already delivered 90 percent of its potential is a dollar unavailable for a fresh trade with 100 percent of its potential ahead of it. Once all buying power is committed, no more trades can be taken at all. Recycling capital out of nearly-finished positions is what allows the monthly premium target to be hit.

How long does it take to reach 90 percent? Adam is clear that it varies enormously and depends on what happens after entry. If the stock price rises sharply, or if volatility drops, the spread can collapse in value very fast — 50 cents falling to 5 cents in as little as **15 days on a 30-day trade**, or **10 days on a 20-day trade**. In those cases the position is closed early and the remaining days are used to open a different trade. But if the price does not move up much, or moves down, or volatility rises, the spread may initially increase in value before eventually decaying, and the 90 percent level may not be reached until day 29 of a 30-day trade. Every trade is different, and it depends heavily on the post-entry path of both price and implied volatility.

In practice Adam applies this rule with some flexibility around the edges. Closing three expiring Interactive Brokers positions on the 18th of September, he assesses each against the 90 percent standard. On Okta, of a $457 credit only **$3** remained to be squeezed out — clearly past the threshold, so he closes. On Teledoc, only **$39** remained of a roughly $900 credit — he says he should take the $900 and run, since there are only about two cents left in the spread. On Amazon he had realised **$2,800** with about **$500** remaining, which he describes as almost there and roughly 80 percent; he decides to wait a few more hours to squeeze out another $200 to $300 and reach approximately 90 percent, while noting that if he wanted to be really cautious he could simply close it at 80 percent. The rule is a threshold, and being comfortably past it is what matters, not hitting exactly 90.

#### Rule Two: Always Close Before Expiration — Never Let It Expire

The second rule is stated as an absolute, and Adam is unusually insistent about it. **Close the trade at the latest just before the expiration day ends.**

Concretely: if the spread expires on, say, the 20th of September, the position is closed before the end of that trading day. The end of the day is **4pm Eastern time**, which in Adam's time zone is 4am Singapore time. Since he normally sleeps around 1am, the practical rule is that he always closes the trade before he goes to sleep on expiration day.

The obvious objection is that if both strikes are out of the money, the options will expire worthless and the trader keeps the full credit without paying a closing commission. Adam acknowledges this is possible but advises against it: even if it is out of the money, just close it, spend the extra money on the commissions, close it, and have a good night's sleep.

The justification is post-close risk. Things can happen after hours that cause huge losses in the account. An out-of-the-money short put that appears safe at 4pm can be assigned or can move sharply on after-hours news, and the position carries that exposure overnight into settlement if it is left open. The cost of avoiding this is one closing commission, and the trades demonstrated show that the closing debit can be genuinely trivial — one, two or three cents — so the economics of the insurance are excellent.

The rule as Adam states it is comprehensive: **close all spreads before they expire, before you go to sleep on expiration day.**

#### Rule Three: Close Before Earnings

The third rule enforces the earnings criterion from Part One as an ongoing management obligation rather than a one-time entry check. **Close the trade if earnings are going to be released before the expiration.**

The concern is identical to the entry-side concern: if earnings are released and for some reason the stock price gaps down more than 15 percent, the position can take a huge loss. Since the trader cannot know in advance which direction an earnings gap will take, and since the strategy's risk is entirely asymmetric to the downside, the correct action is to remove the exposure before the event. Adam's formulation is that you never know, so close it before earnings are released.

This rule matters because earnings dates move and are sometimes announced or revised after a position is opened. A trade that satisfied the no-earnings criterion at entry can find itself with an earnings date inside its remaining life, and when that happens the position must be closed regardless of its profit or loss.

#### Rule Four: The Point of No Return — Cut at Three Times the Credit

The fourth rule is the hard loss limit, and it is the rule that makes the entire ten-to-one risk structure survivable.

**If the loss on the position begins to exceed three times the net credit received, close the trade.**

Adam states the purpose explicitly: this ensures you never lose more than three times your premium. The rule converts a structural maximum loss of ten times the credit into a managed maximum loss of three times the credit — a reduction of about seventy percent in the worst case, achieved purely through discipline.

The arithmetic is done per trade. On the Netflix example with a $50 credit, the cut-loss level is $150. On the Alibaba demonstration with a $1,000 credit, it is $3,000. On the TAL trade with a $135 credit across three contracts, it is $405. On the Spotify trade with a $910 credit across ten contracts, it was **$2,730** — Adam states that figure directly as the worst case he had allowed himself.

The level at which this loss occurs in terms of the underlying's price is not fixed. As established in Part One, it moves lower as expiration approaches and moves higher if implied volatility rises. The trader therefore does not set a static price stop; the trader monitors the position's dollar profit and loss against the three-times threshold, and uses the analyse tab to understand roughly where that threshold sits in price terms at any given point in the trade's life.

#### Rule Five: Close on a Technical Breakdown

The fifth rule is discretionary and, in Adam's own account, the one he actually exercises most often when things go wrong. **Close the trade if the stock price is falling really sharply and it looks likely to hit the short strike before expiration.**

He acknowledges directly that this involves a degree of discretion. But he gives two concrete technical triggers that convert it into something close to a rule.

The first trigger is a **change in the trend from an uptrend to a downtrend**, defined by the same moving average relationship used at entry: the 20 EMA crossing below the 40 EMA signals that the short-term trend has turned down. Since the entry thesis required the short-term trend to be up, the destruction of that condition destroys the reason for holding.

The second trigger is a **break of a strong support level with the price falling fast**. Again this mirrors the entry logic: the trade was entered on a retracement *into* support, on the expectation that support would hold. If support fails, the premise of the trade has failed.

The critical practical observation is about the resulting loss. Adam notes that when you close on this rule, you usually will not lose that much — typically **one time or two times the net credit**, rather than the full three times permitted by Rule Four. This is because the technical breakdown is usually visible before the position has accumulated the full three-times loss. Rule Five, in other words, is what actually keeps average losses well below the theoretical cap. Rule Four is the backstop; Rule Five is the working mechanism.

#### The Spotify Case Study: Cutting a Loss Correctly

Adam devotes substantial attention to a single losing trade, and it is the most instructive material in the trade management lesson precisely because the trade would have been profitable had he not closed it.

The trade was a bull put spread on Spotify, entered on the **19th of August**, expiring the **8th of September** — approximately 29 days. Against a target of roughly $1,000 in premium per trade, the per-contract credit was **$0.91**, or $91 per contract, so he bought **10 contracts** for a total credit of **$910**. The short put strike was **220**.

The trade went well for most of its life and looked as though it would expire worthless. Then, two days before expiry, on the **16th of September**, the price began dropping rapidly on bad news — Adam attributes it to something Apple did that impacted Spotify. On that day the candle was red and shooting down, and it looked as though it would hit the 220 strike.

Three separate signals aligned. The price was falling fast. The **20 EMA had crossed below the 40 EMA**, confirming that the short-term trend had turned down. And a **strong level of support had been broken**. All signs pointed to the price hitting the strike, so he closed the position for a loss.

What happened next is the point of the story. After he closed, the red candle turned into a white candle. The price came down to within a few cents of the 220 strike, missed it, and reversed back up. Had the position been left alone it would have expired worthless and delivered the full $910 profit.

Adam asks himself directly whether he regrets closing it, and answers no — absolutely no regrets — and says the reader should feel the same in the same situation. His reasoning is worth reproducing carefully, because it is the psychological core of the whole framework. He followed his rules. There was no way to know that after he got out the price would go back up. Everything looks clear in hindsight, but we cannot predict the future. That is trading. Once a trade is closed, be happy with it; where the price goes afterwards, whether it reverses back up or collapses, is none of our business, because we cannot predict it. He describes it as a good trade even though he took a loss.

The loss itself was **$654** against a $910 credit — a ratio of about **0.71**, meaning the realised loss was less than one times the credit. This is exactly the pattern Rule Five predicts: acting on the technical breakdown produced a loss well inside the three-times cap, which would have been $2,730. Adam highlights the comparison explicitly and notes he is pretty happy to have taken the loss so much lower than his permitted maximum.

He also notes, at the time of recording, that this was the **only loss he had taken across all his trades in the strategy** to date — while immediately knocking on wood and observing that another one could come at any time. The strategy had been live for three months.

Elsewhere he quotes the Spotify loss slightly differently, at about $600 against a $1,000 target, or roughly **60 percent of the premium**. Either figure supports the same conclusion: a disciplined technical exit produced a loss materially smaller than the permitted maximum, and the strategy's win rate absorbed it comfortably.

#### When Not to Cut: Distinguishing Volatility Loss from Directional Loss

The most sophisticated element of the management framework is a refinement to Rule Four that Adam introduces while reviewing his Costco position, and it is genuinely important because a mechanical application of the three-times rule would have produced a wrong decision.

Reviewing his thinkorswim account, he finds Costco showing a paper loss of about three times the credit — entered at 57 cents, now trading around three times that. On its face this triggers Rule Four. But before acting he opens the analyse tab and examines *why* the loss exists.

Costco was trading at **336** and his short strike was **300**. Since entry the stock price had not gone down at all; in fact it had gone up. The stock had moved *away* from danger. Yet the position showed a loss, because the purple line had dropped — and the purple line drops for one dominant reason on a position like this: **implied volatility went up a lot.**

This produces the refinement, which Adam states as a rule of thumb. **If the stock continues to be on an uptrend, has not reversed downward, and is still above the support level, then even if the position is losing three times on paper, he may not cut loss** — because the reason for the loss is not that the stock is going down, but that IV has gone up temporarily. He labels this a judgement call, and says so twice.

The logic is sound. Time decay is a certainty; volatility expansion is not. As time passes the purple line rises toward the green line and a volatility-driven paper loss will resolve itself into a profit, provided the stock does not subsequently fall. He simulates exactly this on the analyse tab and shows the loss converting into a profit as the date advances. But he attaches a warning that must not be lost: do not always hope that is going to happen, because while you are waiting for the purple line to rise, the stock price could drop. The refinement buys patience, not immunity.

He identifies the same phenomenon on two other positions. On an Interactive Brokers position in a ticker rendered as SDG in the transcript, the price had actually gone *up* since entry — moving further away from the strike, which is good — and yet the premium had risen from 48 cents to 109 cents, producing a paper loss purely because implied volatility rose even more. His conclusion is stated as a general caution: sometimes even if the stock price goes up, you can be showing a temporary loss because IV has gone up.

On Amazon he shows the opposite case combined: since entry Amazon had kept going down *and* IV had gone up, so the spread had moved from a 96-cent credit to 136 cents, a paper loss of $0.86 per share equivalent. He notes the mechanic plainly — when the spread price goes up you lose money, when it goes down you make money, it is the opposite of a long position — and confirms the loss was still well inside three times the credit, so no action was required.

On Google, entered at 199 and now at 359, the position was down $797. Again his assessment was no worries: less than three times the net credit.

#### The After-Hours Pricing Caveat

Attached to the Costco discussion is a practical warning that deserves separate emphasis, because acting on bad data is one of the easiest ways to violate a good rule.

**When the market is closed, the option prices displayed are not accurate.** Adam says they can be very wonky and can go crazy. He was reviewing his positions after the close, and the Costco position was showing a near-three-times loss. He explains that he would in fact wait for the market to open, when prices normalise — and confirms that when the market was open, Costco was not showing a 3.5-times loss at all; it was in fact positive.

The operational rule that follows is that **cut-loss decisions should be made against live prices during market hours, not against stale closing marks.** A paper loss observed after hours is a prompt to look more closely when the market opens, not a trigger to act.

This connects directly to a point Adam makes at the start of the Interactive Brokers scanner lesson: it is best to run the scanner only when the market is open, because before the market opens you get pretty different results, since some prices — especially option prices — may not be updated. The same data-quality principle governs both scanning and management.

#### Daily Monitoring: The Actual Workload

The management framework requires daily attention, and Adam is honest about how much. He states that he monitors every one of his positions every day, and that between his accounts this takes **about an hour or so a day**.

The monitoring has two components, and he does both for every position.

The first is the **profit and loss graph** in the analyse tab. For each position he checks where the current stock price sits relative to the short strike, confirming that the price is still comfortably far away. Walking through his positions he does exactly this: Apple's current price is well above the short strike, still quite far away; Adobe's short strike is at 395 and the current price is far above it; Tesla's short strike is well below a price that has risen since entry; Netflix is still very safe.

The second is the **chart**, examined for two things: the distance from the current price to the short strike, and whether the uptrend is still intact. Adam demonstrates a small but useful technique here — he draws the short strike onto the chart as a horizontal line and colours it red, so the danger zone is visually unmistakable. On Apple, with a short strike at 95, he adds the line, colours it red, and says: so I know that is the danger zone, welcome to the danger zone. On Adobe the red line at 395 shows the price is still far away and the uptrend intact.

The judgements that come out of this daily review are graded rather than binary. Tesla is described as very safe: clear uptrend, far from the strike, price has risen since entry. Adobe is very far away and safe. Netflix is safe but flagged for attention — he notes that the trend looks like it is breaking down even though the price is still quite far from the strike, and says that if it suddenly falls he may have to close Netflix as well, so he has got to watch it carefully. Apple is likewise flagged as being watched carefully because it looks like it could be changing trend. Costco, which had appeared in danger on the profit and loss screen, looks quite safe on the chart, with a short strike at 305 against a price far above it and the trend still up.

That triage — safe, safe but watched, act — is the actual daily output of the process. It is also why Adam closes the trade management lesson by repeating the warning he opened the strategy with: this is not for newbies or new traders, it is for experienced traders who watch the markets and have the discipline to know where to cut loss, because if you do not, the losses could be quite big if you just let it run to expiration.

#### Trade Management Consolidated

| Rule | Trigger | Action | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Profit target | Unrealised profit reaches **≥ 90%** of maximum | Close and free the buying power | Timing varies from ~10 days to the final day; driven by price path and IV |
| Expiration | Expiration day, before the 4pm ET close | Close regardless of moneyness | Never let it expire; after-hours events can cause huge losses |
| Earnings | Earnings scheduled before expiration | Close before the announcement | Gap risk of more than 15% cannot be stopped out |
| Hard loss cap | Loss reaches **3× the net credit** | Close | Converts a 10× structural risk into a 3× managed risk |
| Technical breakdown | 20 EMA crosses below 40 EMA, or strong support breaks with price falling fast | Close | Usually realises only 1–2× the credit; the rule that does the real work |
| Volatility-driven paper loss | Loss near 3× **but** stock still in uptrend, above support, not falling | May hold | Explicit judgement call; loss is from IV expansion, not direction |
| Stale data | Loss observed while the market is closed | Do not act; re-check at the open | After-hours option marks are unreliable |

---

### Part Three: Position Sizing and Portfolio Architecture

Position sizing sits between entry criteria and scanning in the logical order of the process, because the scan produces candidates and the sizing rules determine how many contracts of each candidate are taken. Adam introduces it at the start of the scanning lesson, and it is best understood as the mechanism that converts a per-trade ten-percent return into a portfolio-level ten-percent monthly return with a bounded worst case.

#### Step One: Decide the Allocated Capital

The first question is how much of the overall account is dedicated to this strategy. Adam's framing is that a trader running multiple strategies — Snipex, Bull Bang, and others in his curriculum — should explicitly carve out a slice for the bull put spread extreme rather than treating the whole account as available.

His illustration: a trader with a $100,000 account who runs several strategies might allocate **$20,000** to this one. That $20,000 then becomes the **maximum open buying power** permitted for the strategy. A trader with a $10,000 account might allocate $2,000.

His own numbers are given transparently. His Interactive Brokers account totals about **$1.3 million**, across which he runs several strategies. Of that, he had allocated **$100,000** to the bull put spread extreme — and mentions that he had very recently decided to increase that allocation to **$150,000**.

#### Step Two: Derive the Premium Target from the Ten-to-One Ratio

Because every dollar of credit collected blocks at most ten dollars of buying power, the maximum open premium is simply the allocated capital divided by ten.

On a $20,000 allocation, the maximum open premium is **$2,000**. On a $100,000 allocation it is **$10,000**.

This is also, by construction, the monthly income target, since the ten-percent-per-cycle return on the ten-to-one structure means the total premium collected *is* ten percent of the deployed capital. Adam states the target for the $20,000 example as at least $2,000 per month, which is the 10 percent figure the strategy is designed around. For the $100,000 account he gives a slightly wider expectation: roughly **$10,000 to $15,000 a month in premium for every $100,000 of buying power**.

#### Step Three: Divide Across Ten Trades for Diversification

Adam does not put the entire premium target into one trade. His standard is to divide the total premium across **ten separate trades**, diversified across different sectors. The reason for sector diversification is stated directly: if you put everything into one sector and the whole sector crashes, you could be in trouble.

Dividing $2,000 of target premium by ten gives **$200 of premium per trade**. Dividing $10,000 by ten gives **$1,000 of premium per trade**. He operates accounts at both scales and mentions a third at **$500 per trade**, and describes the per-trade premium as fixed for a given account — always $1,000 for the large one, always around $200 to $300 for the smaller thinkorswim account.

**Maximum open positions is capped at ten**, which is what makes the arithmetic close: ten positions at $200 of premium equals $2,000 of open premium, which at ten times equals $20,000 of buying power, which is the full allocation.

#### Step Four: Derive the Contract Count

With a fixed premium target per trade and a known credit per contract, the contract count falls out of the division. This is the last calculation before the order is placed.

The examples are consistent. On Netflix, with a $50 credit per contract against a $200 target, the answer is four contracts. On an Amazon trade with a $100 credit per contract against the same $200 target, two contracts. On the Alibaba demonstration, with a $50 credit per contract against a $1,000 target, twenty contracts — and entering twenty contracts produced exactly $1,000 of premium and $9,000 of buying power, the latter being the maximum loss if the trade were not managed. On TAL, with a credit of 45 cents rounded to about $44 to $45 per contract against a $1,000 target, the answer is **23 contracts**, which is what he actually traded. On Spotify, with a 91-cent credit against a $1,000 target, ten contracts for $910.

The principle Adam states is that no matter which trade it is, he always sizes it so the credit hits the target. The credit is held constant; the contract count is the free variable.

#### Step Five: Understand the Doomsday Drawdown

The final piece is the honest calculation of the worst case, which Adam insists on performing before any of this is deployed.

If the maximum open premium is $2,000 and every position is cut at three times the credit, the maximum simultaneous loss is **$6,000**. Against a $20,000 allocation that is a **30 percent drawdown**.

He is careful about the probability. For any single trade to fail is roughly a 10 percent event. For all ten to fail simultaneously is statistically very, very low. But he insists that because everything is possible, the trader must still write down the doomsday scenario of a 30 percent drawdown and be mentally prepared for it. And he attaches the condition on which the number depends: **provided you cut loss at three times your premium.** Without that discipline the doomsday number is not 30 percent; it is the full allocation.

On his own larger account the same calculation runs: total open premium of $13,838 against a three-times cut produces a maximum risk of about **$41,000**, and he states that he must be mentally prepared to lose $41,000 in that scenario.

#### The Trade Journal Spreadsheet

To administer all of this, Adam maintains a simple spreadsheet, which he encourages the reader to recreate. Its structure is worth setting out because it is the control panel for every rule above.

At the top sit the plan parameters: **account allocation** (his was $100,000), the **monthly target** at 10 percent of that ($10,000), the **number of trades** to diversify across (10), the **targeted premium per trade** ($1,000), the **buying power required** ($100,000 at the ten-times ratio), and the resulting **ROI of 10 percent**.

Below that sits the trade log, with one row per trade and columns for the **date of entry**, the **stock**, the **strike price of the short put**, the **number of contracts**, the **expiry date**, the **premium collected**, and the **buying power used**. Closed trades are highlighted in green; open trades remain in black. On Interactive Brokers he uses a grey highlight to mark closed trades in the platform's own display for the same purpose.

Beneath the log sit the live control totals, and these are the numbers that actually gate new trades. **Total open premium** is the sum of the premium column across open rows, and it must not exceed the monthly target. **Maximum risk** is three times the total open premium, and it is the number the trader must be prepared to lose. **Total buying power used** is the sum of the buying power column across open rows, and it must not exceed the allocated capital. There is also a running **total premium collected** across both closed and open trades, and a **monthly premium** breakdown.

Adam uses this record to hold himself accountable in a way that is worth noting. At the time of the lesson his total open premium read **$13,838** against a $10,000 target, and his total buying power used exceeded the $100,000 allocation by about $30,000. He says openly that by rights the total open premium should not exceed $10,000, that he had exceeded it, and — in his own words — that he had been a naughty boy and the reader should not do that. The explanation is that he had recently decided to reallocate more capital to the strategy, raising the allocation to $150,000, which retroactively accommodates the excess. But the rule he states for the reader is unambiguous: the moment total open premium reaches the target, take no more trades. That is the maximum you can go.

The same gate is shown live on Interactive Brokers, where his maximum buying power for one account is **$100,000** and he had used **$75,000**; the moment it hits $100,000 he stops and does not allow himself to take more trades. On a second, smaller account the maximum buying power is **$50,000** against $38,000 used, targeting **$5,000 to $7,000 a month** in premium — and in the August shown, that account had collected **$7,600**.

The scale of the results he displays is worth recording as context rather than as a promise: across the year to that point he showed about **$40,000 collected in credit** from selling puts, and for August alone about **$13,000 to $13,600** in credit on the larger account.

---

### Part Four: Scanning for Trades on thinkorswim

The scan is where the process begins each day. Adam's description is that every day when the market opens he uses his scanner to produce a candidate list, then works through it manually. The critical framing point, delivered in the later Interactive Brokers lesson but applicable to both platforms, is that the scanner should only be run **when the market is open**, because before the open the results differ meaningfully — some prices, especially option prices, are not updated.

#### Navigating to the Scanner

On thinkorswim the path is **Scan → Stock Hacker**. The scan is then constructed by adding filters one at a time using the **Add Filter** control, which offers a choice between a **stock filter** and a **study filter**. Two of the four filters are stock filters and two are study filters.

#### The Four Filters

The scan uses exactly four filters, and Adam builds each one on screen.

**Filter one — closing price.** This is a stock filter. Add Filter → Stock → Price → Closing Price, with a minimum value. The original build used **$20 or above**, but Adam changes it live during the lesson to **$50**, and explains why. At $20 or $30 the premium per contract is very small, so reaching the premium target requires buying a large number of contracts, and more contracts means more commissions. He concludes that $50 is ideal, while being careful to say he is not claiming that trading below $50 is wrong. The Interactive Brokers build uses $50 as well, so $50 should be treated as the operating value.

**Filter two — market capitalisation.** Also a stock filter. The requirement is a minimum of **$10 billion** with no maximum, on the grounds that only big companies are wanted. This is the value that was later raised to **$30 billion** in the updated Interactive Brokers build, for the gap-risk reasons discussed in Part One. A reader building the scan today should use the $30 billion figure, since it reflects Adam's revised thinking.

**Filter three — IV percentile.** This is a study filter. Add Filter → Study → Volatility → **IV Percentile**, set to a range of **35 to 100**. This is the direct implementation of the implied volatility entry criterion.

**Filter four — average volume.** Also a study filter. Add Filter → Study → Volume → **Average Volume**, set to more than **one million shares**.

**Universe setting.** Alongside the four filters, the scan universe must be restricted to **optionable stocks only**. Adam sets the scan to run over all stocks but specifies optionable stocks so that only names with option chains are returned.

| # | Filter type | Path | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stock | Price → Closing Price | Minimum **$50** (originally $20) |
| 2 | Stock | Market Cap | Minimum **$10bn**, later revised to **$30bn**; no maximum |
| 3 | Study | Volatility → IV Percentile | **35 to 100** |
| 4 | Study | Volume → Average Volume | Minimum **1,000,000** shares |
| — | Universe | Scan in | **All optionable stocks** |

With the filters in place, click **Scan**.

#### Saving the Results as a Watchlist

The scan returns a list of potential candidates. Adam's next action is to save the result set as a watchlist, using the **Save as Watchlist** control and naming it by date — in the lesson he names it for the 21st of September. This matters because the manual review that follows is chart-by-chart, and a saved watchlist allows the trader to step through the candidates in sequence without re-running the scan.

He then opens the saved watchlist and reviews each name's chart in turn.

#### The Manual Chart Review

This is where the quantitative screen hands off to human judgement, and Adam's live walk-through of four candidates is the best available illustration of how the judgement is exercised.

**Apple.** Is it on an uptrend? Yes. The 20 is above the 40 and the 50 is above the 150, so both trend conditions hold. The IV rank reads **39**, which is above the 35 threshold. But there is a problem: the candle has broken below the 50 moving average, which he calls a bit iffy. His stated preference is for names that have *not* broken the moving average — he prefers the ones that are bouncing off the moving average, because once the moving average is broken the stock could start reversing into a downtrend. Apple is therefore a possible but not a preferred candidate. He also notes he already has a trade on Apple, so he would not take another one.

**ALXN.** Rejected instantly on sector. The moment he sees pharmaceutical or biotech, the name is out.

**Amazon.** On an uptrend with the 20 above the 40 and the 50 above the 150, so the mechanical trend test passes. But like Apple, the candles have broken the moving average, so he calls the uptrend a bit compromised. However, he argues that there is a visible level of support at the current price — and since the entry rule is to enter only when convinced the price is at a level, that argument makes Amazon a possibility. Moving averages are still in the correct sequence. Verdict: a possibility.

**Alibaba.** This is the one he selects. He calls it a pretty good setup: a nice uptrend, and critically it has **not broken below the 50 moving average**, which he says is even better. The wave pattern is clean — wave up, wave down, wave up, wave down — and the price is still pretty near the moving average, which is exactly the retracement-into-support condition the strategy wants. The IV rank reads **35**, right at the threshold.

He then validates the IV reading rather than trusting the scanner figure alone. The verification path on thinkorswim is **Trade → Option Statistics**, where the current IV percentile is displayed. It confirmed at 35, which he notes just passes the criterion.

This double-check is a small but important habit. The scanner is a coarse filter; the option statistics page is the authoritative reading for the specific name at the moment of trading.

#### Building the Order

With Alibaba selected, the workflow moves to the option chain.

The first decision is the expiration. The stated target is 20 to 30 days, and the chain offered a **26-day expiration on the 16th of October**, which he selects as pretty close to ideal.

Opening the puts side of that expiration, he searches for the 10 delta. The chain did not contain a clean 10 delta — the available strikes showed deltas of 12, 9 and 8. This is a routine situation and Adam's response is instructive: he does not force a strike, he tests combinations. He could sell the 12 delta and buy the 9, or sell the 9 and buy the 8, and there are many combinations available. The instruction is to test out the various combinations to see which one gives the best premium and buying power, always subject to the constraint that for $1 of premium you are not charged more than $10 of buying power. He is explicit that sometimes it is through trial and error that you find the perfect combination.

The mechanic for constructing the spread is: locate the intended short strike in the chain, **right-click → Sell Vertical**, which builds a vertical credit spread, then adjust the long strike as required.

The three combinations he tested and their outcomes were laid out in Part One. The 240/235 pairing produced a $50 credit against a $450 maximum loss and was the only one of the three that satisfied the ratio. He checked each by clicking **Confirm and Send**, which displays the maximum profit and the maximum loss — the latter being identical to the buying power blocked.

Then the distance check. Alibaba was at 272 and the short strike at 240, so the distance is 240 divided by 272, giving about 12 percent. Against the 15 percent guideline this is short, and Adam says so: not really ideal, usually you want it at least 15 percent away. He states he might not take this trade in reality, and proceeds only for demonstration.

Then the contract count. At $50 of credit per contract against a $1,000 per-trade target, the answer is **20 contracts**, producing $1,000 of premium and **$9,000** of buying power — which is also the maximum loss if the trade were left unmanaged.

Then the mandatory analyse step, which produced the schedule of points of no return described in Part One: 242 at entry, 241 around the 3rd to 5th of October, and approximately 239 near the 15th of October, together with the demonstration of what a 30 percent volatility increase does to that schedule.

#### Placing and Filling the Order

The order entry sequence is: **Confirm and Send**, ensuring the price is a **limit** and that the limit is **locked**, then send.

Adam demonstrates the order sitting in the queue waiting to be filled, since the market was closed at the time. His guidance on fills is practical and consistent across both platforms. The order does not always fill at the desired price. If it does not fill, the trader lowers the credit — from 50 cents to 49, to 48 — continuing to lower until it fills.

But this comes with a hard constraint that closes the loop back to the entry criteria. **Be careful not to lower the credit so much that the buying power becomes more than ten times the premium.** Because the buying power is fixed by the spread width while the credit shrinks with every concession, chasing a fill mechanically degrades the risk ratio. Adam's instruction is to keep checking — is my buying power not more than ten times the premium? — before every re-submission. A trade that satisfied the ratio at 50 cents may fail it at 43 cents, and at that point the correct action is to abandon the trade rather than accept the worse structure.

---

### Part Five: Scanning Using Interactive Brokers

The Interactive Brokers lesson serves two purposes. It updates the criteria, and it provides a complete alternative implementation for traders without thinkorswim access.

#### The Update to the Criteria

Adam opens by describing what changed over the weeks between the original scanner lesson and this one. He is clear that there were not many changes; there was one substantive one.

The **minimum market capitalisation was raised from $10 billion to $30 billion.** The reason, as covered above, is that he now wants to trade this strategy only on really big companies, because big companies are less likely to gap down than medium or smaller-sized companies, and are fundamentally a lot stronger with a lot less risk.

Everything else remained the same: minimum share price of **$50**, IV percentile of **at least 35 percent**, and average trading volume of **at least one million shares a day**.

He also delivers the timing rule already noted: run the scanner only when the market is open, because pre-market results differ, particularly for option-derived values.

#### The IV Percentile Versus IV Rank Terminology Problem

Before building the scan, Adam addresses a naming discrepancy that would otherwise confuse anyone moving between platforms, and it is one of the more genuinely useful pieces of platform knowledge in the course.

**Different brokers use different labels for the same measure.** On thinkorswim, the field is called **IV Percentile**. On Interactive Brokers, the equivalent field is called **IV Rank** — specifically **52-week IV Rank**. Adam says these use different names for the same definition, that the formula is roughly the same, and that he does not know why the industry has settled on inconsistent naming. His practical advice is to check it yourself, or simply follow what he does.

For the purpose of building the scan, the operational instruction is that the thinkorswim IV Percentile filter and the Interactive Brokers 52-week IV Rank filter are used interchangeably at the same threshold of 35.

#### Building the Scanner in Trader Workstation

The build sequence in Interactive Brokers Trader Workstation is as follows.

First, **create a dedicated tab.** At the bottom of the workspace, click the **plus** control to create a new tab and name it "scanner". This gives the scan and its associated chart a permanent home rather than floating over the trading layout.

Second, **open the scanner window.** Go to **New Window** at the top left, then navigate to **Scanners → Mosaic Market Scanner**.

Third, **create the scan.** Select **Create New Custom Scan** and name it. Adam names his **BPSX Scanner**, after the strategy.

Fourth, **define the universe.** Click **All Stocks**. Leave the region at the default of **US**. Under exchanges, leave all exchanges selected **except** that Adam unchecks **pink sheets** and **OTC**, on the grounds that these are usually small-cap companies and therefore outside the eligible universe by definition.

Fifth, **configure the fields and filters.** Open the **Fields and Filters** panel. Adam keeps the **Last Stock Price** field that is present by default and removes the change field, which he is not interested in. He then adds three further fields using **Add Field** and searching by name: **Market Cap**, **IV Rank** (selecting the **52-week IV Rank** variant), and **Average Volume**. The result is four filters: last stock price, market cap, 52-week implied volatility rank, and average volume.

Sixth, **enter the values.** Each filter is configured by clicking **Filter** on that row and entering the bounds.

For the **last stock price**, the minimum is **$50**. There is no meaningful maximum, but the field requires one, so Adam enters **$5,000** as a practical ceiling that covers essentially everything.

For **market cap**, the important detail is the unit. The Interactive Brokers market cap filter is denominated **in millions**. To screen for a minimum of $30 billion, the value entered is therefore **30,000** — thirty thousand million. Adam counts the zeros out loud on screen to make the point, because entering 30 or 30,000,000 would both be wrong.

For **IV Rank**, the range is **35 to 100**.

For **average volume**, the minimum is **1,000,000** — again counted out on screen as one, two, three, four, five, six zeros.

Seventh, **save.** Click **Done**, and the scan is saved under the name given.

| Step | Action in TWS | Setting |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Create tab (**+** at bottom) | Name it "scanner" |
| 2 | **New Window → Scanners → Mosaic Market Scanner** | — |
| 3 | **Create New Custom Scan** | Name: BPSX Scanner |
| 4 | Universe: **All Stocks** | Region **US**; all exchanges **except** pink sheets and OTC |
| 5 | **Fields and Filters → Add Field** | Add Market Cap, IV Rank (52-week), Average Volume; keep Last Stock Price |
| 6a | Last Stock Price → Filter | Min **50**, Max **5000** |
| 6b | Market Cap → Filter | Min **30000** (field is in millions = $30bn) |
| 6c | 52-week IV Rank → Filter | **35** to **100** |
| 6d | Average Volume → Filter | Min **1000000** |
| 7 | **Done** | Scan saved |

When Adam ran this configuration live, it returned **nine stocks** — all trading above $50, all with an IV rank of 35 or above, and all averaging at least a million shares a day. That number is worth internalising as an expectation: the screen is deliberately restrictive, and on a typical day it produces a handful of names, not a hundred. The manual chart review that follows is therefore a short task, not an all-day one.

#### Adding the Chart Panel

Because the mechanical screen does not test the trend or the retracement, the scan is only useful alongside a chart. Adam builds the chart directly into the scanner tab so that clicking a scan result immediately displays its chart.

The sequence is to open **New Window → Charts → Chart**, then resize the layout — squeezing the scanner panel narrower, since it does not need much width, and giving the chart the remaining space. He is candid that the Interactive Brokers charts are not as attractive as thinkorswim's and that he prefers thinkorswim for charting, but observes that they are better than nothing.

The chart is then configured to match the entry criteria exactly.

**Timeframe.** Set the time period to **one year** with **daily candles**. Daily candles are the required timeframe for the trend definition.

**Volume.** Remove the volume bar, since Adam does not use volume on the chart itself — underlying volume is already handled as a scanner filter.

**Moving averages.** Four are added, via **right-click → Add Study → Moving Averages**.

The first is a **simple moving average**, which defaults to a period of 9 and must be edited. Right-click the study, edit the indicator, change the period to **50**, and change the colour to **blue** (Interactive Brokers defaults it to purple).

The second is another **simple moving average**, edited to a period of **150** and coloured **green**.

The third is an **exponential moving average**, edited to a period of **20** and coloured **red**.

The fourth is another **exponential moving average**, edited to a period of **40** and coloured **blue**. Adam notes with mild exasperation that the platform kept reverting this one to purple and he had to edit it repeatedly to get blue.

Finally, **lock the layout** so the arrangement persists.

| Study | Type | Period | Colour | Trend role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Simple MA | 50 | Blue | Medium-term fast |
| 2 | Simple MA | 150 | Green | Medium-term slow |
| 3 | Exponential MA | 20 | Red | Short-term fast |
| 4 | Exponential MA | 40 | Blue | Short-term slow |

The result is a two-panel workspace: the scanner on the left, the chart on the right. Clicking a stock in the scanner displays its trend on the chart, and the trader can zoom in and out to assess the wave structure. Adam demonstrates by clicking Amazon, which he describes as being on a very nice uptrend, and reminds the reader of the entry timing: you want to enter when it retraces to the moving average.

#### Order Entry on Interactive Brokers

The order mechanics in Interactive Brokers differ from thinkorswim in ways that matter, and Adam walks through them on the live TAL trade.

The sequence is: in the option chain, select the underlying — TAL — then select the expiration, in this case **16 October**. Open the **Strategy Builder**. Select the short strike, in this case **60**, and click **Sell**. Select the long strike, **55**, and click **Buy**.

Two warnings follow, and both are emphatic.

The first concerns the **default price**. When the spread is built, Interactive Brokers populates a default credit — in this case **30 cents**. Adam's assessment is blunt: never trust that, always ask for more. He calls the default price stingy and notes that he finds thinkorswim gives better prices, so he uses the thinkorswim mid-price as a reference for what to ask for on Interactive Brokers. In this case he bargained the price up to **45 cents**.

The second, and more serious, concerns the **sign of the price**. On Interactive Brokers a negative price denotes a credit. Adam warns that sometimes the platform defaults the order to a **debit**, and states that he has made that mistake before. The rule is absolute: when placing these bull put spreads, **always ensure the price is entered as a credit, and it must be a negative number.** A positive price on a spread the trader intends to sell means paying to enter a position that should be paying them.

Once the price is set, click **Submit**. The margin used is displayed on the order screen for the ratio check.

The fill process mirrors thinkorswim. Adam submits at 45 cents and waits. When it does not fill immediately he offers 44 cents — again ensuring the minus sign is retained — and updates the order. It fills at **44 cents**. His summary of what happened on the full position is that he got filled on **20 contracts at 45 cents** and **two contracts at 44 cents**, on the way to his 23-contract target. He also placed the same trade on his thinkorswim account, where it filled at 45 cents.

The ratio check on the TAL trade: maximum profit of **$45** per contract against a maximum loss and buying power of **$455**. Adam calls this close enough to ten times to be acceptable — it is 10.1 to 1 — while stating that anything more than that he would not take. The return arithmetic is $45 on $450 of buying power, a **10 percent return in 46 days**.

His guidance on how far to negotiate is the same constraint expressed differently: if you do not get filled you can bargain a bit, putting 44 or 43, but do not go too low, because if you go too low you do not get a good risk-to-return ratio. The target he restates is that for $1 of credit you want $10 of buying power.

#### Closing Positions on Interactive Brokers

The closing workflow on Interactive Brokers has one navigation detail worth recording. The portfolio view shows all positions mixed together, which becomes unmanageable when a trader holds spreads alongside other instruments. The fix is to use the portfolio **filter** control and change it from **All** to **Combos**, which isolates the option combinations — all the bull put spreads — into a clean list. Adam also increases the font size for legibility.

To close a position: highlight it, **right-click → Close**, which builds the closing order for the full contract quantity. The closing price is entered as a **negative** value, since closing a short spread is a debit.

The fill negotiation for closing runs in the opposite direction from opening — the trader must offer progressively *more* to get out. On the Okta position of 10 contracts, Adam first tries to close at **zero**, doubting it will fill. It does not. He offers **one cent**. It does not fill. He offers **two cents**. It does not fill. He offers **three cents**, and the order fills, first partially and then completely. His summary of the principle is that you have got to keep offering a higher price until it gets filled.

On the Teledoc position of 17 contracts he tries **two cents**, does not fill, moves to **three cents**, and gets a partial fill followed by completion.

These are trivially small debits against credits of $457 and roughly $900 respectively, which is exactly the point of the profit-taking rule: when only a couple of cents of extrinsic value remain, the remaining upside is not worth the overnight risk, and the closing cost is negligible.

---

### Part Six: The Consolidated End-to-End Process

Everything above can now be compressed into a single ordered procedure that runs from a blank screen to a filled order and onward to a closed position. This is the summary Adam gives, expanded with the detail established in the preceding sections.

#### Step One: Find a Stock Candidate
