Every day, when the market opens — and specifically not before it opens, because option-derived values are stale pre-market — run the saved scanner. Adam uses thinkorswim's Stock Hacker by preference, and the Interactive Brokers Mosaic Market Scanner where thinkorswim is unavailable.

The scan filters for an IV percentile (or, on Interactive Brokers, a 52-week IV rank) of **35 percent and above**, an average daily volume of at least **one million shares**, a share price of at least **$50**, and a market capitalisation of at least **$30 billion**, restricted to optionable stocks and excluding pink sheets and OTC listings.

Save the output as a dated watchlist and work through it name by name. For each candidate, examine the daily chart and confirm that the **20 EMA is above the 40 EMA**, that the **50 SMA is above the 150 SMA**, and — the part the scanner cannot do — that the **price has retraced to a strong level of support** after a wave down rather than sitting extended after a wave up. Prefer names that are bouncing off a moving average over names that have broken through one. Reject any biotech or pharmaceutical name on sight.

Then check the earnings calendar. If earnings are due before expiration, or within the 30 to 45 day window generally, skip the trade. The only permitted exception is a trade the trader intends to close before the announcement.

#### Step Two: Choose the Options

Open the option chain for the selected name. Before anything else, confirm the options are liquid — the fastest check is whether a **weekly option series** exists, and the confirming check is that the bid-ask spread is not wider than roughly **30 to 40 cents**.

Choose the expiration. The sweet spot is **20 to 30 days**, with a broader acceptable range of **30 to 45 days**; shorter is preferred because it recycles capital faster, but the chain sometimes forces a longer choice.

Choose the short put strike at a delta of approximately **10**, accepting anywhere in the **9 to 15** band and never exceeding 15. Confirm that the resulting strike sits roughly **15 percent below** the current market price, relaxing that guideline toward 10 percent only for demonstrably low-volatility large caps.

Choose the long put **one to two strikes below** the short put, same expiration.

Verify the IV reading independently of the scanner, on thinkorswim via **Trade → Option Statistics**, confirming the current IV percentile is 35 or above.

#### Step Three: Check the Ratio

Build the spread — on thinkorswim by right-clicking the short strike and selecting **Sell Vertical**; on Interactive Brokers via the **Strategy Builder**, clicking Sell on the short strike and Buy on the long strike.

Click **Confirm and Send** to display the maximum profit and maximum loss. Confirm that **the buying power (equal to the maximum loss) is not more than ten times the net credit received.**

If the ratio fails, test other strike combinations — different long strikes, different short strikes within the delta band — until one satisfies it. If none does, the trade does not exist and the candidate is discarded.

#### Step Four: Size the Position

Divide the account's fixed per-trade premium target by the credit per contract to obtain the contract count. Confirm that adding this position does not push **total open premium** above the monthly target, or **total buying power used** above the allocated capital, or the **number of open positions** above ten.

#### Step Five: Analyse Before Committing

Run the proposed position through the **analyse tab**. Establish where the short strike sits relative to the current price on the chart. Identify the price at which the position would lose three times the credit — the point of no return — at entry, at the midpoint of the trade, and near expiration, so the cut-loss schedule is understood before any capital is at risk. Optionally simulate a volatility increase of around 30 percent to see how much the schedule deteriorates under a volatility shock.

#### Step Six: Place the Order

Always use a **limit order**, placed at the **mark price** while the market is open, with the price **locked**. On Interactive Brokers, ensure the price is entered as a **negative** number to denote a credit, and do not accept the platform's default credit, which is systematically stingy — use the thinkorswim mid as a reference and ask for more.

If the order does not fill, lower the credit in one-cent increments, re-checking after each adjustment that the ten-to-one ratio still holds. If lowering the credit far enough to fill would break the ratio, cancel the trade.

#### Step Seven: Record It

Log the entry date, the underlying, the short put strike, the contract count, the expiry date, the premium collected, and the buying power used in the trade journal. Recompute the control totals: total open premium, maximum risk at three times, and total buying power used.

#### Step Eight: Monitor Daily

Every day, review every open position on both the profit and loss graph and the chart. On the graph, confirm the current price remains comfortably distant from the short strike and that the unrealised loss, if any, is inside three times the credit. On the chart, with the short strike drawn as a red horizontal line, confirm the distance and confirm the uptrend is intact. Grade each position as safe, watched, or actionable. Budget roughly an hour a day for a portfolio of this size.

Ignore paper losses observed while the market is closed; re-check them at the open.

#### Step Nine: Exit

Close the position when any of the following occurs.

The position has realised **90 percent or more** of its maximum profit, in which case close it and recycle the buying power into a new trade.

**Earnings** are scheduled before expiration, in which case close before the announcement regardless of profit or loss.

The loss has reached **three times the net credit**, in which case close — unless the loss is demonstrably driven by an increase in implied volatility while the stock remains in an uptrend, above support, and not falling, in which case the position may be held as an explicit judgement call.

The **trend has broken** — the 20 EMA has crossed below the 40 EMA, or a strong support level has broken with price falling fast — in which case close immediately, typically realising a loss of only one to two times the credit.

It is **expiration day**, in which case close before the 4pm Eastern close no matter how far out of the money the spread appears to be, paying whatever small debit is required.

Update the journal, mark the trade closed, and return to Step One.

---

### Closing Reflections on the Process

Three things about this framework deserve emphasis as the chapter closes, because they are easy to read past and hard to recover from if missed.

The first is that **the ten-to-one structure is a fiction the trader maintains only by acting**. Every number in the strategy — the 10 percent monthly return, the 30 percent doomsday drawdown, the claim that a 90 percent win rate produces a profitable expectancy — depends on the assumption that losses are realised at three times the credit rather than ten. Remove the discipline and the arithmetic inverts: a single unmanaged loss at ten times the credit erases ten winners, and the 85 percent realistic win rate is no longer sufficient to produce a positive expectancy. Adam says this repeatedly and in different words, and the repetition is not padding. It is the load-bearing wall.

The second is that **the entry criteria are a conjunction, not a menu**. A stock that passes the scan but has broken its 50-period moving average is a marginal candidate. A stock that passes every technical test but is a biotech is not a candidate at all. A spread that satisfies delta and distance but fails the ten-to-one ratio does not get taken at a worse price; it gets abandoned. The strategy's edge lives in the intersection of the criteria, and the discipline of the intersection is what produces a scan output of nine names rather than nine hundred.

The third is the psychological point embedded in the Spotify story, and it is the one that most separates traders who can run this process from traders who cannot. Adam closed a position for a $654 loss that, had he left it alone, would have delivered a $910 profit. The price missed his strike by cents and reversed. He states he has no regrets and explains why: he followed his rules, there was no way to know, and everything is clear only in hindsight. A trader who takes the opposite lesson from that episode — who concludes that cutting was a mistake because the outcome was favourable — will hesitate the next time the 20 EMA crosses the 40 and support breaks, and the next occurrence will be the one that does not reverse. The rule is judged by the distribution of outcomes it produces, not by the outcome of the instance in which it was applied.

That is the operational backbone. The strategy is the easy part.

---

# Part VIII — The Diagonal Spread & The Bull Bang Collar

## The Diagonal Spread and the Bull Bang Collar

### Part One: The Diagonal Spread

#### The problem the strategy exists to solve

Every strategy in this curriculum begins with a limitation of the strategy that preceded it, and the diagonal spread is no exception. In the basic course the student learned to sell covered calls: buy one hundred shares of a fundamentally good company, hold those shares for the long run because you genuinely believe the business will be worth more in five years than it is worth today, and then sell a call option against that stock position every month with roughly thirty days to expiration, collecting premium each cycle. The appeal of that strategy is not subtle. Even if the share price goes absolutely nowhere for a full year — sideways, flat, drifting in a range — the accumulated premium from twelve monthly call sales can produce a twenty to twenty-five percent return on the capital tied up in the shares. That is a return generated purely from the passage of time, from the decay of extrinsic value in options you have sold to somebody else, and it requires no directional heroism at all.

The challenge, as Adam puts it plainly, is that owning one hundred shares of stock is expensive. If you want to run covered calls on Apple and Apple trades at two hundred dollars, one hundred shares is twenty thousand dollars of capital committed to a single name. A trader with a small account looks at that number and concludes, correctly, that the covered call strategy is simply not available to him. The rule of the covered call is unforgiving in this respect: you cannot sell a call against fifty shares, or against sixty shares, or against ninety-nine shares. The option contract represents one hundred shares of deliverable stock, so you must own one hundred shares before you are permitted to write a single covered call. There is no partial version of the trade. For any of the Dow Jones index names that Adam prefers for this strategy, the practical minimum capital to begin a covered call programme is around ten thousand dollars, and for many of the large-capitalisation technology names it is very much more than that. Bang points out that a covered call on Microsoft or Facebook, at the prices prevailing when he recorded the lesson, would require roughly thirty-five thousand dollars to buy the underlying hundred shares before a single cent of premium could be collected.

There is a second, subtler problem that Bang emphasises even more strongly than the first, and it is the problem of diversification. Suppose you have a ten thousand dollar account and you want exposure to Alibaba at one hundred and sixty dollars a share. You cannot buy one hundred shares. You could buy sixty or seventy shares, spend most of your account doing it, and then you have a completely undiversified portfolio riding on a single Chinese technology stock. If that stock continues to decline — and Bang is candid that a stock you have judged cheap can always get cheaper, because "market can behave very differently" — you have no other positions to carry you. His own account, which he shows on screen during the lesson, illustrates the point: he had taken real damage on some Chinese positions and had underperformers elsewhere, yet the account overall was doing fine because other parts of the portfolio were outperforming and covering the losses. "You cannot be a hero every day," he says. A ten thousand dollar account needs to be divided into at least five or ten different positions, and if buying a single round lot consumes the whole account, that diversification is arithmetically impossible.

The diagonal spread is the answer to both problems simultaneously. Instead of buying one hundred shares of stock, you buy a single call option contract that is deep in the money, with a long time to expiration, and you use that option as a synthetic substitute for the shares. Against that long call you then sell short-dated out-of-the-money calls, month after month, exactly as you would if you owned the stock outright. The capital required collapses to a fraction of the share purchase, the maximum loss collapses with it, the return on investment expands because the denominator has shrunk, and — because you now need only fifteen percent of the capital per position — you can hold five or six positions where before you could hold one.

#### The lease-to-rent analogy

Both instructors reach for the same analogy, and it is worth stating carefully because it explains not just the mechanics but the economics of the trade.

In the covered call strategy, Adam says, you own an apartment and you rent it out by the day. You have paid the full purchase price, you hold the deed, and the rental income is pure yield on an asset you own outright. That is a fine business if you can afford the apartment.

In the diagonal spread, you do not own the apartment. You lease it — you take a long-term lease, paying the landlord for the right to occupy the property for a fixed period — and then you sub-let it on short-term contracts at a higher rate. Bang notes that this is a real business model in Vietnam, where people lease an apartment or a landed house for a year or two and then rent it out on a monthly, weekly or even daily basis, sometimes dividing the property into rooms and letting to several tenants at once. The economics of the business are simple: you are betting that the aggregate of the short-term rents will exceed the cost of the long-term lease. If it does, you have generated income on a property you never had to buy.

The mapping onto the option structure is exact. The long-term lease is the deep-in-the-money long-dated call: you pay a premium up front for the right to control one hundred shares for the next several months. The short-term sub-lets are the monthly out-of-the-money calls you sell: each one brings in a rent cheque. If the sum of the rent cheques exceeds the decay on the lease, you profit. This is why the strategy is sometimes called "lease to rent," and why it is also widely known by a blunter name — the poor man's covered call. Bang uses that name explicitly: "I mean, you don't have a lot of money, but you want to do covered call. That's what the name is all about."

Bang extends the analogy in a way that turns out to be the most important single idea in the lesson. If you lease a property and fail to find a tenant — because a pandemic has stopped all travel, say, and no one is booking your Airbnb — then every single day that the house sits empty costs you money. You are paying the lease, paying the utilities, and receiving nothing. That empty house is precisely what a naked long call looks like: an asset bleeding time value every day with no offsetting income. The entire purpose of the second leg is to find a tenant who pays your bills.

#### The construction, leg by leg

The diagonal spread is a two-legged position. What makes it a *diagonal* rather than a *vertical* or a *calendar* is that the two legs differ along both axes of the option chain at once.

A vertical spread uses two different strikes in the same expiration month. A calendar spread — sometimes called a horizontal spread — uses the same strike in two different expiration months. A diagonal spread uses a different strike *and* a different expiration on each leg, which is why it is drawn as a diagonal line across the grid of the option chain rather than a horizontal or vertical one. Each of those two differences is doing specific work.

The difference in *expiration* buys you the theta asymmetry. The long leg is placed far out in time, where time decay per day is slow; the short leg is placed close in time, where time decay per day is fast and accelerating. The net effect is that you lose a little each day on the leg you own and gain a lot each day on the leg you have sold. The difference in *strike* buys you the directional profile. The long leg is placed deep in the money so that its delta is high and it behaves like stock; the short leg is placed out of the money so that it starts with no intrinsic value at all and consists entirely of extrinsic value that can decay to zero in your favour.

| | Leg 1 — the long call | Leg 2 — the short call |
|---|---|---|
| Direction | Buy to open | Sell to open |
| Moneyness | Deep in the money | One to two strikes out of the money |
| Delta target | 80 delta or above (Adam); 70 to 80 delta (Bang) | Roughly 30 delta, or at a technical resistance level (Bang) |
| Expiration | 3 to 6 months (Adam's preference is about 6); 3 to 9 months (Bang) | 30 to 40 days (Adam); 2 to 4 weeks, or 30 to 45 days (Bang) |
| Function | Stock replacement — the "long lease" | Income generation — the "short-term tenant" |
| Composition of premium | Mostly intrinsic value, small extrinsic component | Entirely extrinsic value, zero intrinsic |
| Repeated? | No — held once, closed at 30 DTE | Yes — rolled roughly monthly, about five times over the life of the long call |

The long leg is bought deep in the money for a reason that has nothing to do with cheapness and everything to do with the composition of the premium. Bang works through this explicitly on Taiwan Semiconductor. With the stock at roughly one hundred and eight dollars, the at-the-money one-hundred-and-ten call for January 2022 was priced at six dollars and eighty cents, or six hundred and eighty dollars for the contract. That looks like a bargain — you control one hundred shares for six hundred and eighty dollars instead of ten thousand eight hundred. But every cent of that six hundred and eighty dollars is extrinsic value, and extrinsic value goes to zero at expiration with mathematical certainty. If the stock is still at one hundred and eight in January, the entire six hundred and eighty dollars is gone. "So I will lose 100% of $680," he says, and adds, "I'm not recommending it."

Move down to the ninety-five strike, where the delta reads 0.77, and the picture changes completely. That option costs fifteen dollars and eighty cents, or one thousand five hundred and eighty dollars for the contract — more than twice the at-the-money call in absolute dollars. But of that fifteen dollars and eighty cents, only two dollars and fifty-five cents is extrinsic value; the remaining thirteen dollars and change is intrinsic value, the real, hard difference between the ninety-five strike and the one-hundred-and-eight stock price. If the stock sits perfectly still until January, you get back thirteen dollars and you lose two dollars and fifty-five cents. Your maximum time-decay bleed on a leg costing fifteen hundred and eighty dollars is two hundred and fifty-five dollars, not the whole thing.

This is the definition of "deep in the money" that matters for the strategy. Bang notes that technically any call strike below the current market price is in the money, and the lower you go the deeper you are; what he means operationally by "deep" is the 70-to-80-delta region, and Adam pushes it slightly further to 80 delta and above. The reason for the high delta is stated as a mechanical fact about the option: delta is the sensitivity of the option price to the underlying. A 0.77 delta means that when the stock rises one dollar — from 108 to 109 — the option rises seventy-seven cents, from 15.80 to 16.57. A 0.90 delta means the option rises ninety cents on the same move. That is very nearly the behaviour of one hundred shares of stock, which is exactly what you want from a stock-replacement leg. Adam frames it the same way: "For every $1 increase in a stock price, it means that a call will increase by 80 cents for 80 delta. And for 90 delta, you increase by 90 cents, which is very similar to owning the shares in the first place."

There is a cost to this substitution, and Bang is careful not to hide it. If you buy the ninety-five call at fifteen dollars and eighty cents and eventually exercise it, your all-in cost per share is ninety-five plus fifteen eighty, or one hundred and ten dollars and eighty cents. The stock is available in the open market at one hundred and eight. You are paying roughly two dollars and eighty cents per share more than the market price, and that premium is the price of the option — the price of controlling the shares for five months while committing only fifteen percent of the capital. "It's not a bad deal at all," he concludes, because fifteen hundred and eighty dollars against ten thousand eight hundred is about fifteen percent of the capital for essentially the same exposure.

The short leg is the tenant. It is sold out of the money so that it has no intrinsic value whatsoever — its entire price is time value plus volatility premium, and both of those components are guaranteed to reach zero at expiration. Adam's rule is one strike out of the money, or at most two; Bang's rule is roughly 30 delta, or, better, wherever the chart tells him resistance lies. The expiration is short precisely because theta accelerates as expiration approaches, so the option you have sold decays faster, in dollars per day, than the option you own.

#### Why the theta arithmetic works

This is worth stating in its own right because it is the engine of the strategy, and Bang demonstrates it live on the platform in a way that makes the point unmistakable.

With only the long ninety-five call in place, the analysis tab reported a theta of negative one dollar and seventy-nine cents. Every single day that passes — weekday or weekend, because time decay does not observe market holidays — that position loses one dollar and seventy-nine cents. Over the life of the option that accumulates to the two hundred and fifty-five dollars of extrinsic value it started with. This is the empty house.

Then he adds the short leg: sell the September 17 one-hundred-and-fifteen call for eighty-two cents. The net debit of the position drops from fifteen dollars eighty to fourteen dollars ninety-eight, because the eighty-two cents collected is subtracted from the cost of the long call. And the theta flips sign. "Original one was negative 1.79. Now it's positive two." Every day the trade now brings in about two dollars purely from the passage of time, before any consideration of price movement at all.

That sign change is the whole strategy in one number. Bang returns to the analogy: "I don't have to worry about my house being left empty, because I have somebody using my house and paying the bills." The trade is now paid to wait.

The mechanism behind the flip is straightforward once the two decay rates are compared directly. Bang lays it out with the JPMorgan trade. The short 113 call, with forty-three days to run, carried two dollars and forty-three cents of extrinsic value, all of which would decay to zero by June 28 if the stock stayed put. The long 100 call, with one hundred and twenty-seven days to run, carried one dollar and seventy-five cents (he also quotes it as one dollar seventy-eight) of extrinsic value in total — and, crucially, it would not lose all of that in forty-three days. It would lose only a portion, perhaps a third, perhaps fifty-five cents, because it has four months of life remaining and decay is back-loaded. So over the same forty-three-day window the short leg surrenders two dollars forty-three and the long leg surrenders fifty-five cents. The difference is yours.

Bang then extends the arithmetic across two cycles. Sell the June call for 2.43, let it expire, sell a July call for another 2.40 or so, and you have collected roughly five dollars against a total extrinsic loss on the long leg of perhaps one dollar seventy-five. Net, you have banked around three dollars thirty of pure time premium. If the stock also rises — from 112 to 113, say — you pick up an additional dollar of intrinsic value in the long call as a bonus on top. That is the good case. The bad case is symmetric: if the stock falls, the long call loses intrinsic value while the short call, having had no intrinsic value to begin with, has nothing to give back to you. "So your risk is on the downside."

#### The payoff profile and why it is curved

When you pull up the analyse tab on a diagonal spread, the profit-and-loss picture looks, at first glance, exactly like a covered call. There is a rising left-hand section, a bend, and then a flat plateau to the right. Bang says it directly on the JPMorgan trade: "the P&L chart looks almost the same. You don't have the risk on the upside, you have the risk in the downside."

But there are two important departures from a genuine covered call, and both of them favour the diagonal.

The first is that the downside is truncated. In a real covered call, if the stock goes to zero you lose the entire value of the shares — eleven thousand dollars on a JPMorgan position, ten thousand eight hundred on a Taiwan Semiconductor position. In the diagonal, the most you can lose is the net debit you paid to open, because that is the entire capital committed and neither leg can produce a liability beyond it. On the JPMorgan trade the net debit was eleven dollars and twenty-one cents per share, or one thousand one hundred and twenty-one dollars, and Bang states the consequence flatly: "even when JPMorgan price drops to 80 or 70 or even 50 or even 0, I could not lose more than a thousand here." On the Taiwan Semiconductor trade the debit was fourteen dollars ninety-eight, or one thousand four hundred and ninety-eight dollars, against a ten-thousand-eight-hundred-dollar loss on the shares in the same catastrophe.

The second departure is that the P&L line is *curved* rather than composed of two straight segments, and this is a genuine structural feature rather than a graphical artefact. A covered call at expiration is piecewise linear: below the strike you own stock and gain dollar for dollar; above the strike you are capped and the line is horizontal. The diagonal is different because the two legs expire at different times. The blue line on the analysis chart represents the profit and loss *at the expiration of the shortest leg* — Bang is explicit about this: "when you do two legs, the P&L is only at the shortest leg expiration, which is September 17." At that moment the short call has expired and its value is a hard, known function of the stock price. But the long call has not expired. It still has months of life, and therefore it still carries extrinsic value, and that extrinsic value is itself a curved function of the stock price — largest when the stock is near the long strike, smaller as the option moves deeper in the money, smaller again as it moves out of the money. The long leg is also still exposed to implied volatility. So instead of a clean kink you get a smooth arc, and the position's value on any given day is a blend of the two legs' remaining optionality rather than a settled payoff.

This has a practical consequence that both instructors exploit. Because the long leg has not expired, the profit shown on the chart at the short leg's expiration is not the end of the story — it is a way-station. You close the short call, sell another, and the whole picture resets forward with the long leg still intact and now cheaper on a cost basis.

Adam adds a further consequence about the break-even. Because you have collected premium on the short leg, the break-even price of the combined position sits *below* the current stock price, which is not true of a naked long call. Bang measures it precisely on Taiwan Semiconductor: with the stock at roughly one hundred and eight and a bit, the break-even at the September 17 expiration is one hundred and seven dollars and eighty-four cents. "That means I can afford my share price to drop a little to still be profitable." The premium collected is a cushion. And each subsequent roll adds another cushion on top of the last, which is why Adam stresses that "as you keep selling calls and collecting one more premium, you have a higher break-even price" — or, equivalently, a lower one, in the sense that the stock must fall further before you lose. On a naked long ninety-five call with no short leg, Bang's chart showed a break-even of one hundred and ten dollars and eighty-one cents, roughly two dollars *above* the market. Adding the short leg moved the break-even nearly three dollars in the trader's favour.

#### Entry rules and numeric thresholds

Adam structures the entry as a screening problem followed by an execution problem, and both stages have hard numbers attached.

**The market regime.** The diagonal spread is a bullish structure and it should only be deployed when the broad market supports it. Adam's condition is that the S&P 500 itself must be on a clear uptrend — the 50-day moving average above the 150-day moving average, and/or the index trading above its 200-day moving average. "When the whole market is in a bear market, please do not use the diagonal spread, not a good time."

**The company.** The strategy must be applied only to fundamentally strong companies, preferably large-capitalisation names, and Adam states a strong preference for constituents of the Dow Jones index. He is emphatic on the exclusion: "This strategy should never be used for small companies or companies that are very volatile." The fundamental test is rising sales revenue and rising net income for the last five years, which he demonstrates by navigating to Morningstar, entering the ticker, opening the financials section and then the full financial data, selecting the annual income statement, and confirming that both the revenue line and the net income line have trended upward across the five-year window.

**Valuation.** The stock must not be overpriced, and the screen he uses is the PEG ratio — the price-to-earnings ratio divided by the projected earnings growth rate. The threshold is a PEG below 1.5. Above 1.5 the stock is becoming expensive and it becomes risky to buy either the stock or the call. He does not compute this by hand; he reads it directly off Finviz. On Apple he demonstrates the arithmetic anyway: a P/E of 16.82 divided by a growth rate of thirty percent gives 1.29, comfortably inside the threshold. On JPMorgan, Bang reads the PEG as 1.23, likewise passing.

**The trend, on two time frames.** The stock must show a clear uptrend on both the ten-year chart and the one-year chart. The definition of "clear uptrend" is mechanical: the 50-day simple moving average (plotted blue) above the 150-day simple moving average (plotted green), with both moving averages sloping upward, and/or price above the 200-day moving average (plotted red). Adam is careful about the qualifier. Looking at the Apple chart he notes that the 50 was above the 150 but the 150 was sloping downwards, and says that is "not as great" a signal — the slope condition matters as much as the crossover condition. On the price action itself he wants higher highs and higher lows.

**Timing within the trend.** Because prices in an uptrend move in waves rather than straight lines, the entry point matters. Adam is explicit that the worst time to buy the long call is when price is extended at the high of a swing: "These are bad times to buy the call." The best time is after a temporary retracement, when price has pulled back near the 50-day or the 150-day moving average and is turning back up. His reasoning is that when price gets too far above the 50-day it tends to revert toward it, so entering near the moving averages both improves the entry price and reduces the odds of an immediate adverse move.

**Implied volatility.** The best time to enter is when the IV percentile is below 40. The logic is that the diagonal spread is net long vega — you own more time value in the long leg than you have sold in the short leg — so you want to be buying volatility cheaply. Bang states the same rule and the same reason: "when you buy a diagonal, you basically long vega. You need to make sure the IV is low before you enter." On JPMorgan he read the IV percentile at nineteen percent and judged it a good entry. On Apple, Adam read it at forty-five percent, noted that this was above his threshold, and said explicitly that in reality he would give it a miss — proceeding only because he was demonstrating mechanics. This is a useful piece of discipline to note: the rule was stated, the reading violated it, and the violation was named rather than glossed over.

**Earnings timing.** Adam prefers to enter right after the company has announced earnings, which he identifies on the thinkorswim chart from the blue earnings icons along the bottom. Entering after the announcement removes the event risk from the position and typically catches implied volatility after its post-earnings collapse, which is consistent with the IV-percentile rule.

**The long leg.** Expiration three to six months out, with six months being Adam's usual preference, though he notes there is nothing wrong with going out a full year and that he simply rarely does. Strike chosen by delta: 80 delta or above. Bang widens the expiration window to three to nine months and the delta window to 70 to 80, and in practice on Taiwan Semiconductor picked 77 delta at one hundred and fifty days.

**The short leg.** Expiration 30 to 40 days (Adam) or two to four weeks, quoted elsewhere as 30 to 45 days (Bang). Strike one to two strikes out of the money (Adam), or roughly 30 delta, or placed at a chart resistance level (Bang).

**Position sizing.** Adam's sizing rule is stated in terms of the loss you actually intend to take rather than the theoretical maximum. Twenty percent of the maximum loss should be no more than one to three percent of your entire capital — your net liquidation value. The logic is that since you will cut the trade at a twenty percent loss rather than riding it to zero, the twenty percent figure is your realistic worst case, and that realistic worst case is what should be held to one to three percent of the account. "One bad trade will not damage your portfolio that much and you can make it back easily in the next few winning trades."

#### The Nike worked example

Adam's first full example is on Nike, chosen because it is a large-capitalisation Dow Jones component with consistently rising sales and net income, on a long-term uptrend and currently on a medium-term uptrend as well, with the 50-day moving average above the 150-day and both sloping upward. The current price is $85.70.

The date is May 2019. He selects the October 18, 2019 expiration for the long leg, which is one hundred and sixty-seven days away — "roughly six months." Scanning the delta column for a reading near 80, he lands on the 75 strike. The market price of that call is $12.95, which for one contract of one hundred shares is $1,295.

The comparison to the covered call is immediate. One hundred shares of Nike at $85.70 costs $8,570. The long call costs $1,295, which is about fifteen percent of the share purchase. That ratio — roughly one-sixth to one-seventh of the capital — recurs throughout every example in the lesson.

For the short leg he selects the June 7, 2019 expiration, thirty-four days out. The stock is at $85.70, so one strike out of the money is the 86 strike. He notes the visual convention on the thinkorswim chain: in-the-money calls are shaded yellow, out-of-the-money calls are white, so you simply take the first white strike after the last yellow one. The 86 call sells for $1.77.

The net debit is therefore $12.95 minus $1.77, or $11.18 per share, which is $1,118 for the position. That is the capital committed and, at the same time, the theoretical maximum loss.

| Nike diagonal spread — May 2019 | | |
|---|---|---|
| Stock price | $85.70 | |
| Long leg | Buy 1 Oct 18 2019 75 call | $12.95 debit, ~80 delta, 167 DTE |
| Short leg | Sell 1 Jun 7 2019 86 call | $1.77 credit, 34 DTE, one strike OTM |
| Net debit | $11.18 | $1,118 per contract |
| Cost of 100 shares instead | $8,570 | Diagonal is ~15% of this |
| Max profit on first short call | $144.85 | Read off the analysis chart |
| ROI on first cycle | 12.9% | $144.85 ÷ $1,118, in ~30 days |
| Projected ROI over five cycles | 64.7% | 12.9% × 5 |
| Maximum theoretical loss | $1,118 | If stock collapses below ~$65 |

The analysis tab shows the profit and loss chart with profit above the zero line, loss below, and stock price along the horizontal axis from eighty-five to one hundred dollars. The green line is the profit and loss at the expiration of the short call. Adam reads the maximum profit off that line as $144.85, and is careful to flag what this number does and does not represent: "This maximum profit you see is for the first call that you're selling." Recall that the plan is to sell roughly five calls over the life of the long leg.

The return arithmetic follows. $144.85 divided by the $1,118 net debit is 12.9 percent, earned in about thirty days. Multiply by five cycles and the projected total is 64.7 percent on the initial capital. Adam is honest about how this compares to the rest of the curriculum: "it's not an astronomical return. It's not like 100, 300% return that, like some of our other strategies. So this is a lower return strategy, relatively low return, but it's a lot easier to execute."

The maximum loss is the net debit of $1,118, realised if the share price collapses. Adam points at the chart and says that if Nike were to drop all the way down to around sixty-five dollars, the long call would be very far out of the money and the entire debit could be lost. He immediately places that in context: losing $1,118 is still better than what an owner of one hundred shares faces, since that person has $8,570 at risk. But he also states the compensating disadvantage with equal force, and it is the central risk of the strategy. The share owner has holding power. If the company is good, he can simply wait, and the price will eventually recover. The diagonal spread holder cannot wait. "Time is against you. We don't have the holding power. The moment, you know, six months is up, that's it. If the price goes down and doesn't recover by then, you can lose your entire capital."

He then closes the loop on risk management, and this is the sentence that governs everything that follows: "We would usually start to cut our losses the moment we lose about 20% of our capital."

#### The Apple worked example

The second example is on Apple, and it is instructive partly because Adam walks through the order-entry mechanics and partly because he adjusts his cycle-count arithmetic to fit an expiration that is not quite six months.

The screening runs as before: Apple is a Dow Jones constituent; Morningstar shows five years of rising revenue and rising net income; Finviz shows a PEG of 1.29 against a 1.5 threshold; the ten-year chart is a clear uptrend. The IV percentile reads forty-five percent, which fails the below-forty rule, and Adam says so before proceeding for demonstration purposes only.

He picks the October 18 expiration for the long leg, which is one hundred and sixty-one days out — "slightly less than six months." Scanning the delta column for 80, he selects the 165 strike, priced at $38.75. For the short leg he considers June 7 at twenty-eight days and June 14 at thirty-five days, judges either acceptable, and takes June 14. With Apple at $272 — the figure he speaks, though the strike he then selects implies a price nearer $200, and the discrepancy is never resolved on the recording — he chooses the 202.5 strike as the first one out of the money. Its delta reads 42 and it sells for $5.62.

The order-entry mechanic is worth recording precisely because it is the fastest way to build the position without legging into it. Rather than clicking each leg separately, Adam right-clicks on the bid of a strike, selects "Buy," and then chooses "Diagonal" from the resulting menu. The platform immediately populates both a buy leg and a sell leg, which he then edits to the strikes and expirations he wants: buy October 18, 165 strike; sell June 14, 202.5 strike. Bang uses a different but equally quick route on the same platform: click to buy the long strike, then hold the Control key on Windows and click to sell the short strike, at which point the platform itself labels the resulting order a diagonal spread.

The combined net debit displays as $33.13 per share, which is $3,313 for one contract. Adam pauses here to make a point about accessibility: if that number is too large for your account, choose a lower-priced underlying. "You could choose a lower price stock like Intel. Because Apple is quite an expensive stock. To begin with, it's a $200 stock." The strategy scales down with the share price of the underlying, which is precisely what makes it useful to small accounts.

On the analysis tab, hovering over the peak of the curve gives a maximum profit of $816 for the first short call — he corrects himself from an initial reading of $814 after unchecking an overlay. That is $816 on capital of $3,313, or 24.6 percent, in thirty-five days.

Then comes the cycle-count arithmetic, which is the piece most students get wrong. The long call has one hundred and sixty-one days, but you will close the entire trade when the long call reaches thirty days to expiration. So the usable window is one hundred and sixty-one minus thirty, which Adam rounds to one hundred and thirty days. Each short-call cycle is about thirty-five days. One hundred and thirty divided by thirty-five is 3.7. You cannot sell seven-tenths of a call, so the conservative assumption is three cycles, not four.

| Apple diagonal spread — May 2019 | |
|---|---|
| Long leg | Buy Oct 18 165 call, $38.75, ~80 delta, 161 DTE |
| Short leg | Sell Jun 14 202.5 call, $5.62, 42 delta, 35 DTE |
| Net debit | $33.13 per share = $3,313 per contract |
| Max profit, first cycle | $816 |
| ROI, first cycle | 24.6% in 35 days |
| Usable window for rolls | 161 − 30 = 130 days |
| Cycles available | 130 ÷ 35 = 3.7, taken conservatively as 3 |
| Projected total profit | $816 × 3 = $2,448 |
| Projected total ROI | 24.6% × 3 = 73.8% in under six months |

Three cycles at $816 gives $2,448 in total profit, or, expressed as a rate, 24.6 percent times three, which is 73.8 percent return on capital in less than six months. Adam's verdict: "it's actually not a bad trade, something that we could consider."

The remaining execution steps are procedural but he enumerates them. Choose the number of contracts with the sizing rule in mind. Check the total net premium debit. Click confirm and send, and send it as a *limit* order, never a market order. Read the order confirmation box, which restates the maximum loss and maximum profit, and double-check it before transmitting. Then go to the Monitor tab, under Activity and Positions, and check whether the order has been filled or is still working. "Leave it till it is filled and be patient. Do not chase the trade."

#### Exit rules

Adam separates the exit rules into three categories, and it is important to keep them separate because they answer different questions: what to do with the short leg, what to do with the whole position on schedule, and what to do with the whole position when the thesis breaks.

**Managing the short leg.** When the short call approaches expiration and is far out of the money, do nothing — let it expire worthless and keep the entire premium. When the short call approaches expiration and is at the money or in the money, you must act: buy it back to close, accepting a small loss on that leg if necessary, and simultaneously sell a new call, one strike out of the money, with another thirty to forty days to expiration, collecting fresh premium. Adam gives "like five days to expiration" as the point at which this decision becomes live. The alternative trigger is profit-based: close and re-sell once seventy percent or more of the premium has been realised, without waiting for expiration at all.

**Closing on schedule.** The entire trade — sell the long call, buy back the short call — is closed once the long call has less than thirty days to expiration. This is not optional and it is not a judgement call. The reason is that the long leg's own theta accelerates sharply inside thirty days, which destroys the asymmetry the strategy depends on. "If you are buying the call with six months to expiration, once five months has passed and there's 30 days to [expiration], close the whole trade and do the whole thing all over again."

**Closing on a trend break.** This is the loss-cutting rule and it is defined mechanically rather than discretionarily. The trade is premised on the stock going up or going sideways; what destroys it is a sustained downtrend, because then the long call loses intrinsic value faster than the short call premium can offset, and left alone to expiration you can lose the entire debit. The signals are:

The 50-day moving average crossing below the 150-day moving average, *with* both moving averages having begun to flatten or slope downward. Adam is precise that the crossover alone is not the signal — on an uptrend both averages slope up, so it is the change in slope combined with the crossover that constitutes a trend change.

Or, price closing below the 200-day moving average with the 200-day itself sloping down.

He points at a real example on the Apple chart: the two-month bear market of the previous year, where the 50 crossed below the 150 and price crossed below the 200. "This would be a time to actually cut your loss and to close your diagonal spread." The result is a losing trade, but a contained one: "you would usually lose about 20% of the maximum capital."

#### Setting the stop by dollars, not just by chart

Bang adds a piece of technique that operationalises Adam's twenty percent rule in a way that is worth studying, because it converts a percentage rule into a specific price level before the trade is even placed.

On the JPMorgan trade, the maximum loss is the net debit of roughly $1,100. Twenty to twenty-five percent of that is $250 to $300. So the question becomes: at what stock price does this position show a $250 to $300 loss? He answers it directly off the analysis chart by reading the *red* line — the profit and loss as of today, or as of a chosen near-term date such as two weeks forward — rather than the blue expiration line. Moving along the red line until the displayed P&L reaches roughly negative three hundred dollars, he finds the stock price: one hundred and five dollars.

That number is then carried back to the chart, and this is the elegant part. With JPMorgan trading at $112, the $105 level coincides with a cluster of three separate support structures: the 50-day moving average, which is sloping up; the 200-day moving average, which is flat; and the 150-day moving average. For the stock to reach his stop it would have to break through all three lines. "Which is very unlikely. You have a good chance that the stock price will not drop below that. That gives you some more assurance that you will not lose $1,100. You lose about $200 maximum because you have very strong support here."

And if it does break? Then the premise is dead. "The stock is no longer in uptrend. The setup is no longer valid. You have to close early, cut loss and lose $300. That's the intent and that is the risk management plan as well."

This is the whole discipline in miniature: define the dollar stop from the position size, translate it into a price, check that the price sits behind meaningful technical support, and pre-commit to acting if that support fails.

#### The JPMorgan live trade, entry

Bang's live trade is the most complete worked example in the series because it is followed forward in time through a real roll.

The screening runs first. On Morningstar, JPMorgan's annual statements show total net revenue rising, interest income sloping up, and net income growing nicely across the five-year window. Bang's summary: "fundamentally, JP Morgan is a very solid Dow Jones stock, arguably one of the biggest banks in the world, very solid management." On Finviz, the PEG ratio reads 1.23, under the 1.5 threshold.

The capital problem is stated: with the share price around $112, buying one hundred shares costs more than $11,000, "which could be a lot of capital for a small account."

The technicals are mixed but acceptable. The stock has recently jumped after a good earnings report and has bounced above the 200-day moving average. The 50-day is sloping up and has crossed above the 200-day, and the 200-day itself appears to be sloping up. But the 150-day is still below the 200-day, so Bang refuses to call it a textbook uptrend: "it's not like 100% clear that it is on the uptrend... But I would say it's a short-term uptrend already established." He then switches the chart to a ten-year daily view and finds an unambiguous long-term uptrend, higher highs and higher lows. "So there's not a thing to worry about the trend."

The IV percentile reads nineteen percent — comfortably below forty, and Bang notes the reason it matters is the long vega exposure.

Now the construction. He wants three to six months on the long leg. The chain does not offer anything at exactly one hundred and eighty days, so he takes the closest available series at one hundred and twenty-seven days, which is a little over four months. Scanning the delta column he finds a reading of 79 — "which is about 80" — at the 100 strike. The market price is $13.75, or $1,375 for the contract, against $11,000 for one hundred shares: "almost like about 11 or 12% of your capital."

For the short leg he considers thirty-six days and forty-three days, judges either acceptable, and states his strike preference: one strike out of the money. With the stock at $112, he argues that the 112 strike is effectively at the money, so the first genuinely out-of-the-money strike is 113. He builds the two legs with the Control-click method and the platform labels it a diagonal spread: buy the September 20, 2019 100-strike call; sell the June 28 113-strike call. The net debit is $11.20 — "which is $1,120, which is just one-tenth of the capital that you need when you buy 100 shares. That's the beauty of this strategy."

The analysis chart confirms the shape: no risk on the upside, risk on the downside, but with the downside truncated at the debit. Maximum profit occurs at the short strike of 113 and reads $226 on the blue number. Against capital of $1,117 that is twenty percent — "20% for 43 days. A little more than a month, you get 20% max return on investment."

He then considers the likely rather than the maximum outcome. Given that the stock has crossed above the 200-day and is bouncing off that level, the realistic scenario is a move up into the profit region, producing somewhere between $210 and $265 of profit — still roughly twenty percent on capital in about forty days.

He places the order at the mid price. The broker blocks buying power of "one one two something" — the exact figure is stated as $112.3 elsewhere in the recording, including commission. It fills. The Monitor tab confirms: JPMorgan, bought the 100, sold the 113, paid 11.211.

#### The JPMorgan live trade, five weeks later

Bang returns to the recording on June 21, thirty-six days after entry on May 16 (May 17 crossing midnight Singapore time). The short call now has one week to expiration.

The price action is the interesting part. On entry the stock was at $111.9. Now it is at $111.24 — he also quotes it as $111.18 at the moment he presses the roll button. Either way, the stock is *down* about sixty to sixty-five cents per share over the five weeks. A holder of one hundred shares would be showing a loss of sixty to seventy-two dollars.

The diagonal spread, by contrast, shows a P&L Open of positive fifty-four or fifty-five dollars. Bang decomposes it: the long leg is losing $145, and the short leg is making more than that loss, so the net is positive. The stock went down and the position made money. This is the cushion effect of the collected premium, working exactly as the break-even calculation predicted.

The value decomposition at the roll makes the mechanism explicit. The long 100 call, bought at $13.65 per share, has declined to $12.20 — a loss of $1.45. The short 113 call, sold at $2.44, has declined to $0.46 — a gain of $1.98. The spread as a whole has therefore *increased* in value from $11.21 to $11.74, a gain of $0.53 per share or $53 for the contract.

| JPMorgan diagonal — entry vs. roll | At entry (16 May) | At roll (21 Jun) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stock price | $111.90 | $111.18 | −$0.72 |
| Long Sep 20 100 call (127 DTE at entry) | $13.65 | $12.20 | −$1.45 |
| Short Jun 28 113 call (43 DTE at entry) | $2.44 | $0.46 | +$1.98 (to the seller) |
| Net spread value | $11.21 | $11.74 | +$0.53 |
| Position P&L | — | +$53 | 4.7% on ~$1,121 in 36 days |
| Stock-only P&L (100 shares) | — | −$72 | — |

Fifty-three dollars sounds small in absolute terms, and Bang says so, but he insists on measuring it against the capital actually deployed: $53 on roughly $1,121 is 4.7 percent in thirty-six days. Annualised at the same cadence — repeating every thirty-six days through the year — that is something on the order of forty-seven to forty-eight percent. And he draws the comparison that makes the case for the whole strategy: an owner of one hundred shares over the same thirty-six days would be down $72. The diagonal made $53. "Which is a swing of like $125, which is not bad at all."

#### The rolling schedule and how repeated rolls cut the cost basis

The roll is the operational heart of the strategy, and Bang's rule of thumb is specific. He sells the short call with five to six weeks — roughly one month to one and a half months — to expiration, and he rolls one week ahead of the expiration date. The trigger conditions on this occasion were all satisfied at once: it was exactly one week before expiration; the share price was almost exactly at the entry point, so no directional decision was being forced on him; and the short option had already given up most of its value. Sold at $2.44 and now at $0.46, roughly $2 of the $2.44 had been captured, which he calls "maybe 80% of the profit has been realized." His conclusion: "No point to wait for another week. And I just roll it so that I can have a fresh new set of premium."

Note that this eighty percent figure is consistent with Adam's stated seventy percent trigger — both instructors are pointing at the same idea, which is that the last slice of premium is not worth the remaining gamma risk and the opportunity cost of not having a fresh, fully-priced short call working for you.

The mechanic on thinkorswim is direct. Right-click on the leg you want to roll and select "create rolling order." The platform proposes buying back the expiring 113 call and selling the same strike in the next available series, which in this case was July 5. Bang rejects that suggestion because July 5 is only two weeks out, short of his five-to-six-week window, and manually changes the expiration to July 26. That roll collects an additional $1.19 per share, or $119 for the contract.

Before sending it he checks the effect on the position's shape. Without the roll, the chart is the familiar covered-call profile with no upside risk. With the roll, and looking forward to a date such as July 12, "the chart continued to look like a cover call. And I do not have the risk in the upside as well." The roll preserves the structure. He sends it; the fill shows the June 28 call closed for forty-seven cents and the new July 26 call sold, giving him a new diagonal spread with the original long leg and a fresh short leg.

Now the crucial piece of accounting, which is the answer to how a diagonal spread makes money over multiple cycles. The $119 collected on the roll is subtracted from the cost basis of the position. The trade was opened for a net debit of $1,121. After the roll it stands at $1,002. "So it brings down my cost by a hundred nineteen dollars." Bang then generalises: "If I keep doing this one, I keep rolling and reducing my cost further down, eventually my cost will go down, and if share price stays here or even increases, I can close my long option trade eventually at the higher price and pocket the profit."

This is the mechanism that makes the strategy work even in a flat market. Each roll is a permanent reduction in the amount of money you have at risk in the position. The long call's value may drift with the stock and with time, but the cost basis against which that value is measured ratchets downward with every premium collected. After five rolls the position may cost you very little, and at that point almost any surviving value in the long call is profit.

| Cost basis ratchet — JPMorgan | Amount | Running net debit |
|---|---|---|
| Long Sep 100 call purchased | −$1,365 | −$1,365 |
| Short Jun 28 113 call sold | +$244 | −$1,121 |
| Jun 28 call bought back to close | −$47 | −$1,168 |
| Short Jul 26 113 call sold | +$119 (net of buyback: quoted as $119 collected on the roll) | −$1,002 |

Bang also inspects the Greeks of the newly rolled position and reports what they tell him. Net theta is around $1.67 to $2, "meaning every single day passes, I collect about $2 regular income. Imagine if I do it for 10 contracts, every day I got $16 to $20." Delta is positive, so a rise in the share price adds money. Vega is slightly positive, so an increase in implied volatility adds money — and, he notes, the reverse is true as well.

#### Selecting the short strike from the chart

Bang's Taiwan Semiconductor demonstration adds a refinement to strike selection that Adam does not stress, and it is worth separating out because it changes the trade from a mechanical delta rule into a technical judgement.

The setup: TSM had run to $142 late in the prior year, peaked, retraced, and then traded sideways in a range for five or six months while the broader market continued higher. Bang offers the possible explanation that some investors mistakenly lump Taiwan Semiconductor in with Chinese companies and sold it alongside the China complex, while the company itself was "running flat out 24-7" without the capacity to serve demand. Fundamentally he regards it as the dominant chip manufacturer in the world and notes that its intrinsic value, from an earlier analysis, was something like $150 against a market price of $108.

The chart carried three moving averages — the 200-day in red, the 150-day simple moving average in green, and the 50-day in blue — plus two indicators Bang adds to Adam's standard set. The first is Bollinger Bands, which tell him whether price is stretched outside its normal trading range; a move well below the lower band suggests oversold conditions and a possible bounce. The second is the stochastic oscillator, which at the time read oversold and was reversing upward, indicating buyers stepping in to grab cheap shares.

He then draws the support line. At approximately $108 there is a level that was previously a swing high; price broke through that resistance, retraced back to it, and it held as support, bouncing twice. The third retracement to that level was in progress. He is careful about the state of confirmation: the candle was still red, so the reversal was not yet confirmed. "If it turns bullish pin bar, you see some bouncing, then it just gives me more confidence." His stated plan is to take a smaller position now and add on Monday if a bullish pin bar confirms — "when I'm not so sure, I enter first with a smaller position" — while still respecting his diversification limit.

Now the short strike. Rather than reaching for a delta, Bang reasons about where the stock will run into trouble. The 200-day moving average sits above price at about $115, and the 50-day and 150-day are also sloping down toward roughly that area. So $115 is the first meaningful resistance. His conclusion: "if I think the stock price won't go beyond 115, at least in the next month or so, even if it rebounds, but it will hit that ceiling and maybe it returns back... I will sell a call option at the strike price of 115."

He sells the September 17 115 call — less than a month out — for eighty-two cents.

This is a materially different way of choosing the strike than "one strike out of the money," and it is arguably better suited to a range-bound chart. If your technical read says the stock will bounce but stall at a specific level, selling the call at that level captures the maximum premium consistent with your directional view while making assignment unlikely. Bang's own summary of the principle: "The beauty of the option is if it starts to go up and you see the resistance, you can make money from the resistance also."

#### The Taiwan Semiconductor payoff arithmetic

The completed position: buy the January 21, 2022 95-strike call at $15.80 with one hundred and fifty days to expiration and 0.77 delta; sell the September 17 115-strike call at $0.82. Net debit $14.98 per share, or $1,498 for the contract. That is also the maximum loss, and the broker blocks exactly that amount of buying power.

The analysis chart, with the short leg's September 17 expiration as the reference date, shows several things at once.

If the stock simply stays where it is at roughly $108, the position makes $35. Compare this to the naked long call, which would have lost $255 in the same scenario. That difference — from a $255 loss to a $35 gain on an unchanged stock — is entirely the work of the second leg.

The break-even is $107.84, below the current market price, which means the stock can drift down slightly and the trade is still profitable.

There is no loss zone on the upside at all. The profit line rises to the short strike and then flattens. "No risk at all if the stock price goes up. It goes up and you'll be making money in this trade."

The risk zone is the downside, and it is capped at $1,498 in the total-collapse scenario, versus $10,800 for a shareholder.

If the stock reaches the $115 resistance where Bang has placed his short strike, the profit reads almost $600. Against capital of $1,498, call it $1,500, that is forty percent — and the short leg expires in under a month. "40% return on investment. Man, that is a good one. And it's not even a year. This is like less than a month."

The comparison to owning shares is the argument in a single pair of numbers. A shareholder who bought one hundred shares at $108 for $10,800 and saw the stock reach $115 would make $700. Seven hundred dollars on ten thousand eight hundred is 6.5 percent. Bang's verdict: "Is 6.5% good? Yeah, not bad, comparing to putting money in the bank. Yeah, I can take 6.5 anytime. But how is it compared versus using option to trade? I don't know about you, but I like 40%."

| Taiwan Semiconductor diagonal — August 2021 | |
|---|---|
| Stock price | ~$108 |
| Long leg | Buy Jan 21 2022 95 call, $15.80, 0.77 delta, 150 DTE |
| — intrinsic / extrinsic split | ~$13.25 intrinsic / $2.55 extrinsic |
| Short leg | Sell Sep 17 115 call, $0.82, at chart resistance |
| Net debit / max loss | $14.98 = $1,498 per contract |
| 100 shares would cost | $10,800 |
| Capital used vs. shares | ~15% (roughly one-sixth) |
| Theta, long call alone | −$1.79 per day |
| Theta, completed diagonal | +$2.00 per day |
| Break-even, long call alone | $110.81 (above market) |
| Break-even, completed diagonal | $107.84 (below market) |
| P&L if stock unchanged at Sep 17 | +$35 (vs. −$255 on the naked long call) |
| P&L if stock reaches $115 | ~$600 = 40% ROI in under a month |
| Same $115 move, owning 100 shares | $700 = 6.5% ROI |

He adds one more observation about theta that is easy to miss. On the completed spread, if the stock rises toward the short strike the theta improves further — "if it goes up here, it's $4 a day. If it doesn't go up, if it stays right here, still $2 a day." Extrinsic value is greatest at the money, so as the underlying approaches the short strike the option you have sold has more time value to surrender each day.

#### The full catalogue of risks

The instructors are unusually candid about what can go wrong, and the risks fall into distinct categories.

**Expiry risk, which is the fundamental risk.** This is the one Adam identifies as the essential trade-off against a covered call. A shareholder has unlimited holding power; if a good company's stock falls, he can wait years for it to recover. The diagonal spread holder has, at most, the life of the long call. "The moment, you know, six months is up, that's it. If the price goes down and doesn't recover by then, you can lose your entire capital." No amount of correctness about the business protects you if the recovery arrives after your option has expired.

**A collapse in the underlying.** If the stock falls far enough that the long call goes deep out of the money — on Nike, below roughly $65 — the entire net debit is lost. This is the theoretical maximum loss and it is realised only if you fail to apply the loss-cutting rules. Adam's position is that this should never actually happen: "we will never allow ourselves to lose the entire capital... We would usually start to cut our losses the moment we lose about 20% of our capital."

**Trend reversal.** Related but distinct: the stock need not collapse for the trade to fail. It merely needs to enter a sustained downtrend, in which the long call bleeds intrinsic value faster than the short call premiums can offset. The mechanical exit signals — 50-day crossing below the 150-day with both flattening or sloping down, or price closing below a downward-sloping 200-day — exist precisely to catch this before it becomes a collapse.

**A gap through the short strike.** The short call is the leg that caps your profit, and if the stock gaps sharply higher through the short strike you do not participate in the move above it. Bang addresses this head-on as the acknowledged disadvantage: "of course, it caps your upside. If you're holding shares and the share price goes to the moon, you get all the full benefit, unlimited profit there. But if you sell a call option above that level, then you cap your upside profit. But hey, again, I'm happy with 40% return on investment." There is a related mechanical concern, which is that a short call driven deep into the money near expiration is exposed to early assignment, and Adam's handling of it is the roll: when the short call is at the money or in the money near expiration, close it and re-sell rather than letting it sit. The economic consequence of a gap through the strike is that on the roll you will be buying back the short call at a loss, and while that loss is offset by the gain in the long call, your subsequent roll must be placed at a higher strike, which changes the premium you can collect.

**Assignment on the short leg.** Because the short call is out of the money at entry, this is not the base case, but it becomes live if the stock rallies through the strike. Note that in a diagonal spread you do not own the shares to deliver — you own a long call — so the resolution is different from a covered call. This is the practical reason the discipline of rolling rather than letting an in-the-money short call ride is enforced.

**Volatility risk.** The position is net long vega. Bang confirms this when he reads the Greeks off the rolled JPMorgan position: "Vega slightly positive means if the implied volatility increases, I will also earn extra money from here. And the reverse is true as well." A collapse in implied volatility after entry hurts the long leg more than it helps the short leg, which is exactly why the entry rule requires an IV percentile below forty. Entering at high IV means buying your long-dated vega expensive and risking a volatility crush.

**Wrong-company risk.** Both instructors circle back to this repeatedly. The strategy has no defence against a business that deteriorates. This is why the screening — five years of rising revenue and net income, PEG below 1.5, Dow Jones preference, explicit exclusion of small and highly volatile companies — comes before any consideration of the option chain.

**Concentration risk.** Bang's framing is that the strategy's capital efficiency is not merely a convenience but a risk control in its own right. Because a position consumes only fifteen percent of the capital that shares would, you can and should hold five or ten positions instead of one. "You cannot be a hero every day... You can have a conviction, but you can be wrong as well. So you cannot put all your money in one stock." He is candid that he has personally paid the price for overtrading and overconfidence in individual securities.

**Management burden.** The final disadvantage Bang names is time. Unlike buying and holding shares, the diagonal spread requires you to return to the position roughly monthly to roll the short leg. He judges the trade-off worth it — "I think 40% or 30% or 20% a month is worth the effort. Because it's not much effort anyway, when you do it for a long time... rolling the 115 call to another month, it's just a matter of a few minutes."

#### What the strategy is not

It is worth closing this half of the chapter with the warning Bang delivers with more force than anything else in the lesson, because it defines the strategy by contrast.

"We're not teaching a simple strategy that you just buy a call and then leave it there, right? Because buying a call, like 90% chance you'll be losing money. That's a losing strategy. We're not teaching that."

He is explicit about the audience he has in mind: newer traders who buy naked calls on AMC or GameStop hoping the stock will go up eight or ten times. Some of them do hit the jackpot and post their winnings publicly. "But I tell you that there are not many of them. Millions of others who lost money never post anything."

The diagonal spread is the disciplined version of the same bullish impulse. It uses a fraction of the capital that shares require, it caps the downside at a known dollar figure, it converts negative theta into positive theta so that the passage of time works for you rather than against you, it produces a break-even below the current market price rather than above it, and it can be rolled indefinitely to ratchet the cost basis downward. In exchange it caps the upside at the short strike and imposes a hard deadline via the long call's expiration. Adam's characterisation of the return profile is the fair summary: not spectacular, but reliable and easy to execute — "a lower return strategy, relatively low return, but it's a lot easier to execute."

---

### Part Two: The Bull Bang Collar

#### What problem this strategy solves

The Bull Bang Collar is Bang's own construction, and it is best understood as the same idea as the diagonal spread applied to a different base position. In the diagonal spread the base position was a deep-in-the-money long call, and the problem was that this long call bled theta every day it waited for the stock to move; the solution was to sell a short-dated out-of-the-money call against it, converting the position from negative theta to positive theta. In the Bull Bang Collar the base position is a Bull Bang — a three-legged bullish structure — and the problem is exactly the same. A Bull Bang is a negative-theta trade. If the stock goes up, the trade wins handsomely and quickly. If the stock goes sideways, or takes a long time to make its move, the trade bleeds. The Bull Bang Collar bolts a fourth leg onto the structure, a short out-of-the-money call, and that fourth leg does the identical job: it flips the sign of theta so that the trader is paid to wait.

Bang opens by placing the strategy in its family: "It is a similar concept of holding shares and selling a covered call to collect additional income while we're waiting for the share price to go up. And this is just similar to that... Instead of holding shares, you're holding a Bull Bang trade or position, and now, while you're waiting for your share price to go up, you get additional income by selling a call option above your current Bull Bang strikes."

He also situates it within his own results. He describes the Bull Bang Collar as one of the strategies that brought in a lot of profit for him during the year in question, alongside Sniper X, the plain Bull Bang, the calendar spread and the diagonal spread, and notes that members of his Option Tactics Playbook community had seen him use it repeatedly and had asked for a dedicated video on it.

#### The base position: the Bull Bang

Before the collar can be added, the three-legged base must be understood. A Bull Bang consists of a long call, positioned at or just out of the money, financed by a bull put spread placed well below the current price.

The long call is the profit engine. Bang's rule for it, which he states explicitly in answer to a community question about strike selection, is that he buys the call at the money or slightly out of the money, with a delta of roughly 50, sometimes 45, sometimes 40, depending on how the price is moving. In practice on the platform he takes the first out-of-the-money strike. On Netflix with the stock at $491.36 he buys the 495 call. On Salesforce with the stock at $227 to $228 he buys the 230 call. On Alibaba at $265 to $267 he buys the 270 call, and when demonstrating the strike-selection logic on a hypothetical February position with Alibaba at a different level he picks 265 as the first out-of-the-money strike.

The short put is the financing leg. Its job is to bring in premium that pays for a substantial part of the long call, and its strike is chosen from the chart rather than from the option chain. Bang's primary rule is to place it at a support level: "I typically choose the strike at the support level." On Netflix he sells the 455 put, which sits at the 200-day moving average. On Salesforce he sells the 200 put, again at the 200-day moving average. On Alibaba he sells the 250 put at what he identifies as the last swing low. His fallback rule, for occasions when no clean support level presents itself, is a delta rule: "My favourite is to sell at about 30 delta put." On the platform he demonstrates this by holding Control and selling a put reading 30 or 33 delta, noting with satisfaction that on Alibaba the 30-delta strike happened to coincide with the 250 support level anyway.

The long put is the insurance leg, and it exists purely to define and cap the downside. It is bought below the short put, and Bang gives a specific and practically important spacing rule: five points below the short put, and at absolute maximum ten points. His reason is a capital reason rather than a risk reason: "I don't go more than 10 points because if you go too wide in terms of the strike difference, the buying power will be very significant." The width of the put spread *is* the margin requirement, so a wide spread ties up capital the strategy is trying to conserve. On Netflix he buys the 450 put against the 455 short put, a five-point spread. On Salesforce he buys the 195 against the 200 short put, again five points. On Alibaba he buys the 245 against the 250 short put, five points once more. In every live example the spacing is exactly five points.

The result is a position that profits strongly if the stock rises, has a defined and modest maximum loss if the stock collapses, and — crucially for what follows — decays every day that the stock does nothing.

Bang states the flaw of the plain Bull Bang without hedging: "The problem with Bull Bang is if the price does not go up or it takes a lot of time for it to go up. While I'm waiting, every day passes I will lose some money because time decay works against me. So Bull Bang trade is a negative theta trade. I don't want that to happen. I want to be in a situation that, hey, when I'm waiting for it to happen, for the share price to go up, I get paid to wait."

He quantifies it on Salesforce. Simulating the three-legged January Bull Bang alone, the analysis tab reports a theta of negative fifteen to sixteen dollars per day. "That's quite something. I mean, if you have to wait for a long time, it could eat into your premium quite a lot." On the Alibaba Bull Bang the figure is negative sixteen dollars per day. Over a forty-day hold that is six hundred dollars of decay working against a position whose whole maximum profit might be eight or nine hundred dollars.

#### The fourth leg: the collar

The Bull Bang Collar adds one leg. You sell a call, out of the money, at a strike *above* the long call strike of the Bull Bang, with a shorter expiration than the Bull Bang's.

| Bull Bang Collar — four legs | Action | Strike placement | Expiration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Leg 1 | Buy call | At the money or first strike OTM; delta ~40–50 | Bull Bang expiry (1–3 months) |
| Leg 2 | Sell put | At a chart support level, or ~30 delta | Bull Bang expiry (same as leg 1) |
| Leg 3 | Buy put | 5 points below leg 2; maximum 10 points | Bull Bang expiry (same as leg 1) |
| Leg 4 | Sell call | Above leg 1's strike, at a resistance level | Shorter — 1 to 2 weeks, rolled repeatedly |

Legs one, two and three share a single expiration and constitute the Bull Bang. Leg four is the collar, and it is the only leg that is rolled.

Bang is careful about the word "collar" because the structure differs from what most traders mean by it. A standard collar is built on top of a *stock* position: you own one hundred shares, you buy a protective put below and you sell a call above, and the sold call finances the bought put. The Bull Bang Collar keeps the economic shape — protection below, capped upside above — but replaces the stock with a long call and replaces the naked protective put with a put *spread*. The consequences of that substitution are significant. Capital required drops sharply because a long call costs a fraction of one hundred shares and a put spread has a defined width. The maximum loss becomes a small, known number instead of the full value of the shares. And the position acquires an expiration date, which the stock version does not have.
