The difference from the plain Bull Bang is simply the presence of leg four, and Bang enumerates exactly what it buys you: additional income while waiting, a lower net cost of entry, a break-even that moves down toward or below the entry price, a better risk-to-reward ratio for the same magnitude of move, and — the point he cares most about — theta that works in your favour instead of against you.

#### The cardinal rule on the short call strike

There is one rule in this strategy that Bang states more forcefully than any other, returns to repeatedly, and describes as dangerous to break.

**Never sell the collar call at a strike lower than the long call strike of the Bull Bang.**

He states it in the lesson: "Note number two, never sell call at a lower strike price than the long call strike. So in this particular case, I would never sell below the 495 call." And he gives the reason: "Because if I sell below that and the share price shoots up very sharply, I could lose the difference between the two call strikes as well. It's a very dangerous situation. I would never do it."

The mechanism is straightforward. If your long call is at 230 and you sell a call at 225, you have created an inverted call spread. Above 230 the two calls move together and your net delta from the pair is roughly zero, but between 225 and 230 the short call is gaining intrinsic value while the long call has none, so you lose the five-point difference. Bang demonstrates this on the analysis chart during the Salesforce trade: "in case you sell this one below your long call — so long call is 230 and if you sell 225 — you see you will be losing money if the share price goes up a lot. That's a trade-off. And I don't want that to happen because I'm bullish. I want to create enough room for the upside potential."

Selling *at* the long call strike is permitted. In the Salesforce management he rolls the collar down to 230, which is exactly his long call strike, and says so explicitly: "my long call is 230, so I can afford to roll it to 230, but not lower." He repeats the point earlier: "I can choose to roll to 230, which is equal to my long call. It's okay."

There is a corollary that governs what to do when the trade goes against you. If the stock has fallen far enough that selling at any strike above your long call brings in a trivial premium, you have run out of useful things to do: "In case you enter a Bull Bang and then the share price, instead of going up, it goes down, and then if you sell a too high call strike, you will not get a decent premium — then you need to sell at minimum at the long call strike. In case you sell at the long call strike and the premium is too little, it's not worth it, then in that case it's better to close the trade completely."

#### The trade-off in strike selection

Within the permitted range — anything at or above the long call strike — the choice of collar strike is a direct trade-off, and Bang states it as note number one of the entry rules: "when I sell a lower strike, I could collect more premium, but that would mean I will cap the upside potential more. So there's no free lunch here. I want to collect more premium, I sell a lower call strike, and I cap more upside. But if I want to unleash or increase the room for the upside potential, then I would sell a higher strike call."

His preferred method for resolving the trade-off is not a delta rule but a chart rule: sell the call just above the resistance level the stock is expected to encounter. "I would sell a call option which is, in other words, I create a collar at the strike price just above the resistance level." The reasoning connects the strategy to the market view. If the chart says the stock will rally into resistance and stall there, then a call sold at resistance is unlikely to be breached, and the premium collected is compensation for accepting a cap you did not expect to hit anyway. When no resistance is visible, the choice becomes discretionary: "if I don't see any resistance, I would have to make a decision whether I want to sell higher or I sell lower... If I see the price really bullish, then I would sell a higher strike price. Or I don't sell it at all — let the Bull Bang run. But if I am cautiously bullish, I know there's some upside but I'm not sure that it can break some level, then I would sell the call at that level."

His summary is that there is no mechanical formula: "there's no hard rule in choosing the strikes in the Bull Bang or Bull Bang Collar trade."

#### The outlook: cautiously bullish

The sentiment behind the trade is precise and Bang uses the same phrase throughout: cautiously bullish. Not bullish, and certainly not neutral.

"The reason for the trade is I'm bullish on the stock, but I'm cautiously bullish. Therefore, instead of just buying a Bull Bang to benefit from the stock price going up and get protected at the same time, now I'm selling a call option on top of that because I'm cautiously bullish. I'm waiting for the stock price to go up, and then I collect money while I'm waiting for it to happen. So in exchange for that, I'm willing to cap my upside potential."

The specific market conditions that produce cautious bullishness rather than outright bullishness recur across the live trades. The first is that the stock faces a visible resistance level that it may not clear in the near term. The second is that the stock has fallen sharply on news and shows early technical signs of a bounce that has not yet been confirmed — Bang repeatedly notes that he would prefer to see a bullish pin bar close before committing. The third is that the broad market itself looks stretched and due for a pullback, which he checks by looking at the S&P 500 and NASDAQ futures before the open.

On the day he entered Salesforce and Alibaba, all three conditions were present. S&P 500 futures were down fifteen points and NASDAQ futures down thirty. "So it could be a down day. So I'm just cautiously bullish right here because the market has been going up over the past few days and weeks and it could be due for a pullback. And therefore I'm just not going to go all in with Bull Bang, but go with a Bull Bang Collar where I will sell a call in the short term to wait for the price to rebound."

The final piece of the outlook is the underlying quality filter, which is the same as everywhere else in the curriculum: "especially I'd like to use this strategy on good fundamental stocks that are on the uptrend setup."

#### Entry rules and numeric thresholds

Gathering the rules scattered across the four videos gives the following.

**Sentiment.** Bullish, but cautiously so, on a fundamentally good stock in an uptrend. The specific trigger is that the stock faces a resistance level you are not confident it will clear in the short term.

**Long call.** Bought at the money or at the first strike out of the money. Delta target roughly 50, acceptable range 40 to 50.

**Short put.** Placed at a chart support level — a prior swing high that has turned support, a moving average, or a swing low. If no support level is identifiable, use roughly 30 delta.

**Long put.** Five points below the short put; ten points is the absolute maximum, because the strike width is the buying power requirement.

**Bull Bang expiration.** One to three months. In practice Bang works from roughly 38 days to roughly 73 days in the examples, and he explicitly compares a 38-day January expiration against a longer February expiration before choosing.

**Collar call strike.** Above the long call strike, never below, and equal to it is acceptable. Placed at the resistance level the stock is expected to meet.

**Collar call expiration.** One to two weeks. Bang states it as his preference: "For the short call that I'm selling, it's one to two weeks. So you can imagine that every one or two weeks I can roll my call option so that I can reduce the cost of my Bull Bang trade even further. By doing so, I always have the positive theta for my trade. Time is my friend." The collar expiry must be equal to or shorter than the Bull Bang expiry. In the live trades the collar was sold with 10 days, 11 days and 16 days to run.

**The theta test.** This is the entry rule that is unique to this strategy and it is worth stating as a rule in its own right, because Bang applies it as a live filter on the platform rather than as an abstraction: *the completed four-leg structure should have positive theta*. If it does not, the trade has failed its own purpose and the strikes or expirations must be adjusted until it does. He works through this iteratively on Salesforce, and the process is instructive enough to record in detail below.

**Position sizing and buying power.** The buying power blocked by the broker is the net debit paid plus the width of the put spread. Bang states the formula explicitly on Netflix: "the max loss again, that is a put strike difference plus the debit I'm paying, which is 455, the two strikes of the put options, plus 18.55. And that is also the buying power that the broker blocks me."

#### The Netflix example, constructed

The teaching example is Netflix, and Bang builds the case for it before touching the option chain.

The fundamental view is stated personally and briefly: "Netflix is a fast-growing stock. In fact, I'm one of the loyal customers. I'm using it almost every day... and I believe in the long term Netflix will dominate the whole movie streaming business."

The technical setup is the reason for the specific structure. The stock is at $491.36. For the past four or five months it has traded up and down within a range rather than trending. There is a strong support level at around $475 where price has bounced repeatedly. The 150-day moving average is sloping up and provides support at the current price. Below that, the 200-day moving average is also sloping up and provides a second support level. And overhead there is a previous swing high at $520, which is the resistance he expects the stock to encounter: "Looks like the immediate resistance would be around 520. 520 is a previous swing high, and if it breaks this one it can go higher. Now, I'm not sure it's going to break in the short term. Maybe it continues to go up, but that would take some time. In the meantime, I say if it hits 520, I would be happy with that profit already."

That single paragraph determines the whole structure. The long call goes just above the current price. The put spread goes down at the support cluster. The collar call goes at $520, the resistance.

| Netflix Bull Bang Collar — teaching example | | |
|---|---|---|
| Stock price | $491.36 | |
| Leg 1 | Buy Jan 15 2021 495 call | First strike OTM, 46 DTE |
| Leg 2 | Sell Jan 15 2021 455 put | At the 200-day moving average |
| Leg 3 | Buy Jan 15 2021 450 put | 5 points below leg 2, caps downside |
| Leg 4 | Sell Dec 11 2020 520 call | At resistance, 11 DTE |
| Net debit | $18.55 | $1,855 per contract |
| Put spread width | $5.00 | $500 |
| Buying power blocked | $2,355 plus commission | (also quoted as ~$2,356) |
| Break-even | ~$488 | ~$3 below current price |
| Maximum loss | $2,355 | Put width + debit |
| Maximum profit | Just under $2,000 | Achieved with stock at $520 at collar expiry |

The structure and its logic, in Bang's words: "on the downside I got protected, because I have the Bull Put with the protection there, and I place it at the very strong support level below the 475, at the 200 moving average, and they cap the max loss right below that... On the upside I give myself enough room for the price to go up from 495 to 520, that is 25 points. And the short option that I'm selling would be a short-dated option, 11 days, so that the time decay will be very fast so it works in my favour."

Note the twenty-five point runway. The long call is at 495 and the collar call is at 520, so the position participates fully in every dollar of the first twenty-five dollars of upside and stops participating thereafter. That runway is the quantity the strike-selection trade-off is really about: sell the collar lower and you shorten the runway but collect more rent; sell it higher and you lengthen the runway but collect less.

#### The payoff arithmetic

The shape of the Bull Bang Collar's profit and loss chart is distinctive and Bang describes it as a mountain. Reading it from left to right: on the far left, below the long put strike, the loss is flat at the maximum. Between the long put and short put strikes the loss line rises. Between the short put strike and the break-even the position is still losing but improving. Above the break-even the position profits, and the profit rises steeply through the long call strike up to the collar call strike, where it peaks — this is the tip of the mountain. Above the collar strike the line flattens, or, if the collar was sold at too low a strike, it declines.

The maximum profit is read by hovering the mouse over the tip of the mountain. On the Netflix teaching example that figure is stated as "about a thousand nine hundred dollars or so" and elsewhere as "about a thousand something, almost two thousand." It is achieved if the share price sits exactly at the collar strike of $520 when the collar expires.

The maximum loss follows a formula that Bang gives twice. It is the difference between the two put strikes, plus or minus the entry price — plus the debit if you paid one, minus the credit if you received one. "That would be similar to the case of the Bull Bang: the two strikes of the put spread, plus or minus the entry price that you collect or you pay at the entry. Sometimes you get the debit, sometimes you get the credit, and you just need to add or subtract that from the put strike difference." On Netflix: $500 of put spread width plus $1,855 of debit equals $2,355.

The break-even is the price at which the mountain crosses the zero line on the way up. On Netflix it is approximately $488, which is about three dollars below the entry price of $491.36. This is a meaningful feature: the position is profitable even if the stock drifts slightly lower, which is not true of a plain long call and is the direct result of the premium collected from the put spread and the collar call together.

There is an important qualification about the upside. Bang says of the Netflix structure that "essentially I have no risk on the upside because the 520 that I sell there is high enough. If I sell lower, my upside can have some risk. If the price goes up strongly, I could have some risk. But I sell high enough, it creates a big room for my upside profit." The phrase "no risk on the upside" means the profit line does not fall back below zero no matter how high the stock goes — it flattens rather than declining. Whether that is true depends on how far above the long call strike the collar was sold and how much premium was collected. He demonstrates the dependency on Salesforce, where a collar sold at 240 against a long call at 230 produced a visible dip on the far right of the chart: "at some point in time I would be losing money if the share price goes up a lot." His judgement there was that the dip lay so far out of reach in ten days that it did not matter.

#### Working the theta filter live: the Salesforce construction

The Salesforce trade is the most valuable passage in the entire lesson because Bang does not simply present a finished structure — he iterates toward one on screen, adjusting expirations and strikes until the position passes his theta test, and explains each adjustment as he makes it.

The setup first. Salesforce had released robust earnings but guided lower, and more importantly had announced the acquisition of Slack Technologies. Since that announcement the stock had dropped about twenty percent, down to a strong support level at about $218 which was a previous swing high now turned support, with the 150-day moving average sloping up and also providing support. Price had dipped below the lower Bollinger Band and was now reversing back inside it, and the stochastic oscillator was reversing out of oversold. "I like these kinds of setup. So many factors are indicating that a rebound is soon to happen."

With the stock at $227 and futures pointing to an open around $228, the intended structure was: buy the 230 call, sell the 200 put at the 200-day moving average, buy the 195 put for protection, and sell a call at $250, which he identified as the 50-day moving average and therefore a plausible resistance.

**Iteration one: the plain Bull Bang, January expiration.** He builds only the three legs, in the January 15 expiration at 38 days, and analyses it. Using the platform's price-slice feature he simulates ten days forward to December 18 and sets the slices at plus and minus fourteen dollars, which is the one-standard-deviation move the market was pricing for that period. A fourteen-dollar rally produces a $734 profit; a fourteen-dollar decline produces a $756 loss. "So it's almost one-to-one risk-reward ratio, which is not bad." Theta is negative fifteen to sixteen dollars per day.

**Iteration two: add the 250 collar, January expiration.** He holds Control and sells the December 18 250 call, ten days out, collecting about $1.30. The net debit becomes about nine dollars. Re-analysing, the same fourteen-dollar rally now produces $828 and the same fourteen-dollar decline produces a $625 loss. "So basically I improve the risk-reward ratio here. When I win, I win more; when I lose, I lose less, for the same magnitude of the movement." But the theta test fails: "even after I sell the call option, the 250 call, I still won't be able to convert my trade into a positive theta trade. If the price stays right here I would still be losing $15 or $16 per day." The diagnosis is explicit: "the reason for this one is because the premium I collect from the 250 call there is very little. Not enough. Only $1.30. And not enough to offset the decay of the Bull Bang that I am buying, because the Bull Bang that I chose here has relatively short DTE."

**Iteration three: lengthen the Bull Bang to February.** Reasoning that a longer-dated Bull Bang decays more slowly, he converts all three legs from January 15 to February 19. Theta improves — "now lower" — but is still not positive, "because the 250 strike price that I sell is having very little premium."

**Iteration four: lower the collar strike to 240.** With the long call at 230 he is free to sell anywhere at or above 230, so he tries 240. The chart's right-hand side now shows a discernible slope: "you see, the slope here is steeper. At some point in time I would be losing money if the share price goes up a lot, but very unlikely, right? Because the share price right now, in the next 10 days, it's unlikely it will go beyond 280 something. So I think 240 is still safe." He also names the trade-off directly: "If you change it to 250, you see the upside potential is bigger because there's no dip there. But if you choose the 240, there will be a dip or the upside will be capped more. But I would say the risk is low from the upside standpoint." Theta is now "almost positive already."

**Iteration five: lower the collar strike to 235.** "If I really want to completely turn this one to positive, probably I need to sell something like 235. Then it turns positive theta. The reason for it is, next 10 days, if I sell 235, I would collect almost four dollars. That's why the time decay from these four dollars in the next 10 days will overcome the time decay of my Bull Bang." He then checks the consequence for the profit zone: with the February Bull Bang and the 235 collar, the profit zone runs up to about $258. With the stock at $228 that is thirty points of runway in ten days. "I don't think it's going to cross that level, so I'm okay with selling 235."

**Iteration six: compare February against January on return on capital.** Having found a structure that works, he asks which expiration gives the better return. The February version has a maximum profit of $651 against a buying power block of $1,500, which is 43 percent. The January version costs less premium because it is shorter-dated, still collects the same $4 for the 235 collar, and produces a maximum profit of $595 to $600 against a buying power block of about $1,150 to $1,153, which is 52 percent. "So in this case I would have a better return on investment if I choose a shorter DTE, because I would pay less. And the theta is positive for me."

He selects the January version and summarises the method: "This is a thought process, right? I will simulate different scenarios — long DTE, short DTE, higher strike price, lower strike price. Look at the max profit, the capital, return on investment, and compare versus different trades."

| Salesforce — the iteration table | Bull Bang expiry | Collar strike | Theta | Max profit | Buying power | ROI |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bull Bang only | Jan 15 (38 DTE) | none | −$15 to −$16/day | — | — | — |
| + 250 collar | Jan 15 | 250 (Dec 18) | still −$15 to −$16/day | — | — | — |
| Lengthen | Feb 19 | 250 (Dec 18) | negative, improved | — | — | — |
| Lower collar | Feb 19 | 240 (Dec 18) | almost positive | — | — | — |
| Lower collar again | Feb 19 | 235 (Dec 18) | positive | $651 | $1,500 | ~43% |
| **Chosen** | **Jan 15** | **235 (Dec 18)** | **positive** | **~$595–600** | **~$1,150** | **~52%** |

The lesson embedded in that sequence is that the four variables — Bull Bang expiration, collar expiration, collar strike, and the resulting theta — are not independent. Lengthening the base reduces its decay but costs more capital and lowers the return on that capital. Lowering the collar strike collects more rent but shortens the runway. The trader's job is to find the combination where theta is positive, the runway is longer than the stock is likely to travel before the collar expires, and the return on the blocked buying power is attractive.

#### The Alibaba construction

The Alibaba entry, made the same morning, is a compressed version of the same process and adds one variable Bang had not adjusted on Salesforce: the collar's expiration.

The setup: Alibaba was bouncing after several volatile days driven by headlines about the US Congress voting on potentially delisting Chinese stocks. Bang's read was hedged — "it's not 100% being bullish, but at least it's not bearish, like HD or McDonald's right now" — but the trend structure was clean: the 50-day moving average above the 150-day above the 200-day, all three sloping up, with the 150-day providing support at the current price. His conclusion: "bullish setup long term, uptrend. Short term maybe sideways, but gets some support from 150 moving average right here... Alibaba is a very solid stock, very good fundamental stock, so I don't mind entering it right now."

The stock was at $267. He builds the Bull Bang in January: buy the 270 call as the first out-of-the-money strike, sell the 250 put at the last swing low, buy the 245 put five points lower.

Analysing the three legs alone with the same ten-day, fourteen-point standard-deviation slices: up fourteen gives $680, down fourteen gives a $770 loss — "almost one-to-one ratio, not too bad." Theta is negative sixteen.

For the collar he looks at the chart and identifies resistance at $280, which is a previous swing high, ten points above his long call strike. The December 18 280 call brings in about two dollars. The net debit for the four legs is $7.25. But the theta test fails again: "It's not entirely positive on theta yet."

He tries 275 instead, which brings in about three dollars — "theta is almost positive, right? Still negative. But if it goes up from here, it will be positive for me." He is not satisfied, and rather than lowering the strike further and sacrificing runway, he lengthens the collar instead: "I still want to create more room for capital appreciation, but I want to move this one to December 24, which is about 16 days from now. So then I have a positive theta trade in this case, because I collect more premium, longer time, and that more premium pays for the decay of the long Bull Bang that I have."

This is the alternative lever. Rather than selling a nearer strike, sell the same strike further out. You collect more premium for the additional time, which is what the theta arithmetic requires, and you keep the runway intact. The cost is that you cannot roll as frequently and you are committed to the cap for longer.

The final structure and its numbers: buy January 15 270 call, sell January 15 250 put, buy January 15 245 put, sell December 24 280 call. Simulated to expiration with fourteen-point slices, a rally gives $800-plus and a decline gives $500-plus — "so risk-reward ratio is like 1 to 1.5. If I win, I win one and a half; if I lose, I lose one. So it works in my favour." Theta is positive. Maximum profit is $845 to $850 against a buying power block of $1,129 to $1,130, which is 75 percent. "Very good return on investment. This one is very good, love it, because I like it."

He sizes it up on the strength of that: "let me increase the number of contracts to three contracts. So then my capital would be around $3,400 and I could — I mean, if it just goes up, I could get about a thousand plus profit already." In the event he entered two contracts on each of his two platforms.

| Alibaba Bull Bang Collar — 8 December 2020 | |
|---|---|
| Stock price | ~$265–267 |
| Leg 1 | Buy Jan 15 270 call |
| Leg 2 | Sell Jan 15 250 put (last swing low, ~30 delta) |
| Leg 3 | Buy Jan 15 245 put |
| Leg 4 | Sell Dec 24 280 call (previous swing high, 16 DTE) |
| Net debit as first built (280 collar, Dec 18) | $7.25 |
| Theta, Bull Bang alone | −$16/day |
| Theta, final structure | positive |
| ±$14 simulated move | +$800s / −$500s; ~1 : 1.5 |
| Max profit | $845–850 |
| Buying power | $1,129–1,130 |
| Max ROI | ~75% |
| Filled at | $6.30 to ~$6.40 per contract, two contracts per platform |

#### Order entry across three platforms

Bang deliberately demonstrates the same trade on three different brokers, because his community had asked how to place a four-legged order somewhere other than thinkorswim.

On **thinkorswim** the construction is by Control-click. Click to buy the long call, then hold Control and click each additional leg — sell put, buy put, sell call. The platform assembles the combined order and prices it as a net debit. This is the platform he uses for all analysis, and he says why: "I normally do all the analysis like this on thinkorswim because it has very good features. This is one of the best platforms for option trading."

On **Interactive Brokers** the route is through the Option Trader window. Type the symbol, choose Stock/SMART, load the option chain, select the expiration — he notes that the monthly January 15, 2021 expiration is the third Friday of the month and may need to be expanded from a collapsed list — and then use the Strategy Builder feature. Within Strategy Builder he adds each leg in turn. He notes one significant limitation of the account he was using: no live pricing. This forces a workaround he uses repeatedly, which is to price the trade on thinkorswim first and then key that price into Interactive Brokers manually.

On **tastyworks** the route is the Trade tab and then the Table view. Select the January 15 series, click to buy the 230 call, sell the 200 put, buy the 195 put, then open the December 18 series and sell the 235 call. The four legs assemble into a single order. His verdict: "tastyworks is getting more popular, and in fact it's a quite decent platform and I like it," and later, "if you cannot open the account with thinkorswim, tastyworks is very decent and their customer service is the best."

The pricing behaviour at the open is worth recording because it is realistic rather than idealised. Before the open, Salesforce showed a net debit of $6.52 on Interactive Brokers and $6.50 on tastyworks. The market opened with the stock up a dollar fifty, so the debit rose. Bang bid $6.80 on Interactive Brokers, was not filled, raised to $6.90, and was filled. On tastyworks he bid $6.80 against a market of $6.75, was not filled, raised five cents, and eventually filled at $6.85 against a market of $6.80. His comment: "I paid at fair market value; $6.80, $6.85 doesn't matter."

On Alibaba he was filled on one platform at $6.30 and left a working order at $6.50 on the other, which is where he draws a line: "I'm not going to chase too much. I just leave it there, $6.50. I draw the line in the sand right there. If it doesn't fill at this price, it's okay. I already got the one position and I have a few other bullish positions. I'm not so keen. If it doesn't, I give it a pass." He invokes Adam's phrase directly: "let the [trade] come to you and don't chase her, Adam always likes to say."

#### Exit rules

Bang lays out four distinct exits, each triggered by a different circumstance.

**Exit one: the stock rallies sharply and the short call goes into the money.** The trigger is not the moneyness itself but the delta. "My rule is when the short call option gets into the money and the delta of that call option exceeds 80, then it's time to roll."

The reasoning for the delta threshold is precise and worth understanding, because it is not the reasoning most traders assume. Bang goes out of his way to dismiss the assignment fear first: "I know many of you may be freaking out and say, hey, will I be exercised? I just want to clear this one out of your mind. Your short call gets into the money — it doesn't mean it will be automatically exercised. No, that's not the case, because even when it gets into the money, the extrinsic value in that call is still significant. Then the call option buyer won't exercise it. Because the moment he or she exercises, he or she will forfeit the extrinsic value and that will become your extra profit." He adds from experience: "It's very unlikely that your short option will be exercised the moment it gets into the money. It's going to happen — I've been trading options for many years and this is one of the very rare situations."

So the reason to roll at 80 delta is not assignment. It is participation: "When the short call delta exceeds 80, every dollar increase in the share price, you have to give $80 to the other guy. So therefore your incremental profit is very little. Sometimes it's not even worth it. So for you to take advantage of the share price continuing to go up, then it makes sense to roll the strike up so that you can create more room for capital appreciation."

The action is to roll up and out: "I would typically roll the call option that I sell there to a higher strike. And often I also roll it out in time to the following week at a higher strike price. Hopefully I pay a little debit, or maybe some debit, that's fine. But sometimes I could get a credit for the rolling as well. Depends on how deep the price has gone beyond the strike price. So it's not an issue. Just roll it up and out in time to create more potential for upside appreciation."

**Exit two: remove the collar entirely.** If the momentum is so strong that even a rolled collar would cap a move you expect to continue, close the short call outright. "You just close the short call option, take the loss from the call option. That's fine, because you make more money from the base Bull Bang trade. Just remove the collar, unleash the upside potential and let the Bull Bang trade run. That could be a very bullish trade." He attaches a strict condition and states his own base rate: "You do it only when you are 100% convinced that the share price will continue to go up. But normally I'm not that convinced. I just roll it up higher and out in time."

**Exit three: take profit when the move is exhausted.** "When I think the share price has run enough, it seems to be overstretched and it could be due for a pullback, then I would take the profit off the table. Just close the trade, close all legs at the same time, close the trade and take the profit."

**Exit four: cut the loss at fifty percent of maximum.** "I always have the pre-defined max loss for the trade. In this case $2,355, but normally I would mentally cut loss at 50% of the max loss. So in this case, if I lose like $1,200, I just close the trade. Because chances are, when I lose that kind of money, the bullish setup is no longer valid. It could be breaking to the downtrend already. So cut loss early, especially when the bullish setup is no longer valid, and avoid hitting the max loss."

#### The Netflix trades managed to their conclusion

Bang entered two Bull Bang Collars on Netflix using the structure from the lesson, and following both to their conclusion illustrates the roll mechanic and the profit-taking discipline better than any abstract rule.

**Trade one** was entered on November 30 during a live monthly coaching session with his students, at a net debit of $18.19 — slightly better than the $18.55 quoted in the prepared lesson, since prices had moved. The structure was exactly as taught: January 15, 2021 495 call, 455 put, 450 put, plus the December 11 520 call which had eleven days to run at entry.

By December 8, eight days later, Netflix had risen from $491 to about $515 — "almost 25 points." The position showed more than $1,000 of open profit against blocked capital of about $2,350, which is roughly forty percent in eight days.

Bang deliberates on screen about whether to hold or close. The case for holding is that the $520 collar is still above the market, so if price continues up toward $520 while time runs out, the current-day curve merges into the expiration curve and the position approaches its maximum of nearly $2,000. The case for closing is discipline: "in trading, sometimes you just need to be disciplined — not just discipline in cutting loss, but also discipline in taking profit. Because if you are too greedy and the market pulls back, your profit can disappear as well."

He closes it. His stated arithmetic: entered at about $18, closed at $28, realising roughly $1,000 of profit — "almost like 40% of profit already. I'm happy with that 40% over the past eight days." Later in the same session he refines the fill: he worked the closing order down from $28.70 to $28.60 to $28.40 as Netflix drifted lower during the day, and filled at $28.40.

The closing mechanic is itself a lesson, because thinkorswim does not offer a one-click close for a four-legged custom structure. "You cannot just right-click and close the trade, because the create-closing-order options here — none of those allows you to close the four-legs trade. But this is a strategy I created, so they don't have that built-in kind of selection for you to choose." He gives two workarounds. The first is to build the closing order leg by leg: go to the January 15 series, sell to close the long call, Control-click to buy to close the short put, Control-click to sell to close the long put, then Control-click into the December series to buy to close the short call. The second, which he prefers, is to go to Monitor, Account Statement, filter by symbol and by a lookback of ten days, find the original opening trade in the trade history, right-click it, and select "create opposite order," which assembles the entire closing order in one step. He notes he had two contracts and closed only one, leaving one open.

**Trade two** was entered on December 2, three days after the first, at exactly the same strikes and expirations. Because Netflix had already risen, the debit was higher: $22 instead of $18, "$4 higher because the price has gone up. It's okay."

This trade tells the more instructive story. On December 8 it was profitable but less so than trade one. Bang held it. Then Netflix retraced. By December 11, the expiration date of the 520 collar, the stock had fallen back to about $500 — essentially back to the entry level — and the profit had evaporated: "for making some good profit, now the profit disappeared because price has retraced almost to the same level where I entered the trade."

Rather than closing at a small gain or a small loss, he rolled the collar. The 520 call expiring December 11 was rolled to the 520 call expiring December 18 — same strike, one week out — collecting $3.50. This is the "paid to wait" mechanic in its purest form: the stock had done nothing, the position had gone nowhere, and the roll converted the passage of that week into $350 of cash.

The wait paid off. Over the following week Netflix rallied strongly, crossing $520 and reaching as high as $530 or more. On December 17, judging the move overstretched and due for a retracement, Bang closed the whole position for a credit of $32.

The accounting on trade two is worth setting out in full because it shows how the rolls enter the arithmetic.

| Netflix Bull Bang Collar, trade two | Amount |
|---|---|
| Opened 2 December at a debit of | $22.00 |
| Closed 17 December at a credit of | $32.00 |
| Profit on the four-leg structure | $10.00 = $1,000 |
| Plus: credit collected rolling the 520 collar from 11 Dec to 18 Dec | $3.50 = $350 |
| **Total profit** | **$13.50 = $1,350** |
| Buying power: debit $2,200 + put spread width $500 | $2,700 |
| **Return on capital** | **~50%** |
| Holding period | 2 December to 17 December — under three weeks |

Bang's summary of it: "So actually I generated a return of 50% in this trade, $1,350. And that's exactly what I informed my OTP community, because this is a trade that I entered for the OTP portfolio... in a matter of — so December 2nd to December 19 — less than three weeks, which is very good."

And the principle he draws from it, which is the strategy's central claim: "This is how I kept the trade, rolled it one more round. I'm waiting for the price to recover. While I'm waiting, I get paid at the same time. And when the price rebounded, I closed the trade for a good profit. That is the concept of being paid to wait. When the price is not in your favour, you just need to wait, as long as it takes, because the time is on my side. I don't have to worry about the time decay at all. So I'm fine to wait as long as it takes for the price to recover."

Note also that his decision on December 8 to close trade one and hold trade two turned out to be right in both directions — trade one banked forty percent before the retracement, trade two survived the retracement because the collar was rolled and then captured the subsequent rally for fifty percent. Neither outcome was foreseeable; both were the product of having a rule for each situation.

#### The Salesforce trade managed: break-even in a falling market

The Salesforce position demonstrates the strategy's defensive property, and it is arguably the single most persuasive piece of evidence in the four videos.

Entered December 8 with the stock at about $228. By December 18, the expiration of the 235 collar, Salesforce was at $225 to $226. The stock had fallen two dollars. In a plain Bull Bang, this is a losing outcome — the long call has lost value, time has passed, and nothing has come in to compensate. Bang states the expectation: "In a typical Bull Bang trade, you need the price to go up for the trade to be profitable. If the price just goes sideways or even drops, the trade will lose money."

The actual result on Interactive Brokers was an unrealised profit and loss of negative $15. Fifteen dollars. Bang decomposes it leg by leg: the long 230 call had lost $400; the put spread, netting the short 200 put against the long 195 put, had brought in about $20, essentially nothing; and the short 235 call had produced almost the entire $400 needed to offset the long call's loss.

"So that's the beauty of Bull Bang Collar. The share price doesn't go anywhere — in fact it drops — but the trade managed to be break-even because the profit that I generated from the short call pays for the long call and pays for the Bull Bang trade. This is the concept of being paid to wait. Again, I don't mind waiting longer as long as it's not crashing. Even if we go sideways or slightly drop, like in this case, I'm okay. The trade is still okay, not losing money at all."

The identical position on tastyworks showed the same result: put spread up about $20, long call down $430 to $440, short call up almost $400, net loss $30. He notes the consistency approvingly: "same trade, different platforms should have the same performance."

**The December 18 roll.** With the collar expiring that day and the short 235 call worth only three to five cents, Bang faced the strike-selection decision again. The chart showed Salesforce finding support at about $220 and beginning to bounce, with short-term resistance at about $230. The coming week was the Christmas week — only four trading days, with expiration on Thursday December 24 rather than Friday.

He laid out the trade-off explicitly before deciding: "If I roll to 230, which is the lowest right, I would get about $2 premium in four days, which is not bad. But I want to have more room for capital appreciation — then I need to roll it to a higher strike, which is about 235. Then I collect about $1 premium. So that is the consideration: rolling lower I get more premium but I cap more on the upside; rolling to a higher strike I have more room for capital appreciation but I collect less premium." And he set a conditional rule for the open: "If the price opens up very strongly today, I could just roll it higher to 235. If it's flat or slightly down, then I roll to 230 to collect a meaningful premium."

The market opened flat. He rolled to 230 — equal to his long call strike, which is permitted, and he says so: "my long call is 230, so I can afford to roll it to 230, but not lower." Given that only four trading days remained and he did not expect the stock to move more than four or five points in a narrow range, the shortened runway was an acceptable price for the larger premium.

The mechanic on tastyworks is a right-click on the leg and "quick roll." The platform proposed rolling to the same 235 strike, which would have collected 89 to 90 cents. Bang overrode it by clicking on the strike field and dragging it to 230. The resulting order bought to close the December 18 235 call at three to five cents and sold to open the December 24 230 call, for a net credit of about $192.

On Interactive Brokers the same roll had to be priced manually because of the absence of live data. He right-clicked the 235 leg, selected the December 24 230 call as the replacement, then switched to thinkorswim, built the identical roll there to read the price — $2.10 — switched back, entered $2.15 as his credit to bargain slightly, and was filled. His comment: "you always need to bargain."

**The December 24 roll.** With the stock at $229, up a dollar fifty on the day, and the 230 collar showing thirty-three to thirty-nine cents of remaining value that would decay to zero by the one o'clock Eastern close of the half-day Christmas Eve session, Bang chose to roll rather than squeeze the last cents: "if I wait a little longer I could get a little more value here, but it's too late, it's Christmas Eve anyway. So I will roll it."

He rolled the 230 call from December 24 to December 31, same strike — noting that January 1 is a holiday so the following week's expiration also falls on a Thursday. The credit was about $2.41 as first quoted, and the fill required working the price down: he tried $2.26, then $2.25, then $2.24, and was eventually filled around $2.22 to $2.24 as Salesforce drifted.

**The running profit and loss.** At the December 24 roll the Interactive Brokers screen showed the position at a $265 loss. Bang immediately corrects the reading: "it's not the real loss, because last time I have rolled it for one more round for about $380 profit from the short call." Adding the $387 realised on the previous roll to the $265 open loss leaves the position roughly $100 to the good.

"Now, we say $100 is not a big deal, but consider that the price has not gone anywhere. Since I entered, maybe it's slightly up, it's sideways basically. But I keep rolling like this. Eventually the short call will bring the profit to the trade."

He then states the position he is content to hold indefinitely: "next week about this time I will open up the account and roll it again, and if the price has not recovered and continues to go sideways like this, I have nothing to worry about, because the time is on my side. In this Bull Bang Collar trade, time works in my favour."

That sentence is the strategy in one line. A plain Bull Bang held through three weeks of a flat, slightly declining Salesforce would have lost real money to theta. The collared version, rolled twice, was marginally profitable.

#### The Alibaba trade managed: the loss

The Alibaba position is the counter-example, and Bang narrates it without softening.

On December 24 news broke that the Chinese government had launched an antitrust investigation into Alibaba and Ant Financial. The stock, which had been at $264 to $265 the previous week, plunged to about $224 — a drop of more than thirty points in a single session. At $224 the price was below both put strikes, meaning the position was at or approaching its maximum loss.

The position, two contracts, showed a loss of $1,900 against a maximum loss of about $2,300. Bang's assessment: "there's still about $400 left in the trade to save. If I want to close the trade today, right now, I can save the $400 so that my trade doesn't hit the max loss, because I still have time until the expiration, which is January 15. And that's what I'm going to do."

He explains why he does not wait for a recovery: "for the trade to turn around to break even or even profitable, it's very unlikely in the next two weeks or so. The price has to go beyond at least my short put here, and it's still a loss. If I want to really make a profit it has to recover somewhere to 260, which is very unlikely. I don't think it's going to happen in the next two weeks or so. I'm going to take the loss, swallow the bullet, and just move on."

He also acknowledges that his own rule was overrun by the gap: "normally in a Bull Bang trade or a Bull Bang Collar trade I would cut loss at about 50% of the max loss, which is $1,200. But in this case, because the price [dropped] so sharply, I could not cut at that level. And right now, if I cut the loss, I probably lose about 70, 75% of the max loss. It's still okay, it's still about 20, 25% or 30% value left, and I would like to do so. And it's better to just salvage whatever value is left rather than hoping the price will recover — and chances are it won't, and I lose another $400 from here."

This is an honest and important admission, and it identifies the strategy's principal risk directly. The fifty-percent-of-maximum-loss rule works when the stock declines through your levels in a continuous fashion, giving you an opportunity to act at the level you chose. It does not work when the stock gaps thirty points overnight on regulatory news, because there is no trading at the intervening prices. The rule protects against drift, not against gaps.

The closing mechanic on Interactive Brokers: highlight the four legs, right-click, and "close as a strategy," which fits all four into a panel and constructs the reverse of the entry — buy to close the short put, sell to close the long call, sell to close the long put, buy to close the short call. Because Alibaba had crashed, the closing order was a debit rather than a credit, which he checks explicitly: "when I enter it's a debit, now it's also a debit, because [the stock] has plunged, correct." The market price was $3.30; he bid lower to bargain and was filled at $3.24 to $3.25, realising the $1,900 loss against a maximum of $2,300.

**The good mistake.** The tastyworks copy of the same trade tells a small and instructive side story. On December 18, when he was rolling Salesforce, Bang had also rolled the Alibaba collar from the December 18 280 call down to a December 24 275 call — and then realised, on the Interactive Brokers copy, that he need not have done so, because that collar had a week left to run. "I make a mistake when I roll it in tastyworks. I should have not done it. Anyway, from 280 I rolled it down to $2.75. I got extra credit. That's okay. That's a mistake, but it could be a good mistake."

It was. The premature roll collected extra premium, and that premium became a downside buffer when the crash arrived. On December 24 the tastyworks position showed a larger raw loss of $2,200, but the roll had banked $387 — the 280 call had expired worthless and the 275 call sold in its place was profit — so the true loss was about $1,800, better than the $1,900 on the un-rolled Interactive Brokers copy. His comment: "you see, sometimes like this you make a mistake but it's a blessing in disguise."

The mechanism generalises even if the anecdote was luck: every roll executed while the trade is still healthy permanently reduces the cost basis, and a reduced cost basis is a smaller loss in a disaster.

**The closing discipline.** Bang ends the series on the loss rather than on the wins, and his framing is worth quoting because it is the emotional counterpart to the numeric rules: "in trading you cannot expect to win all the time. There will be losing trades, especially once in a while you have some bad news that hits your trade badly. In that case just stay disciplined, stay with your predefined risk management plan and stick with that, cut loss and move on — because the sooner you can get over the losing trade, the faster you can regain your energy and focus for new trades. There are so many good opportunities out there."

He also notes that the damage was widespread among his community and not specific to this structure: "I know a lot of folks in the community got hit also, either by Bull Put spread, Bump Extreme, or Bull Bang or Bull Bang Collar. Things like this happen."

#### Advantages

Gathering the benefits Bang enumerates.

The position has genuine upside profit potential, inherited from the Bull Bang. Unlike a pure income strategy, a Bull Bang Collar makes real money when the stock moves in the intended direction, and does so with leverage, because the long call gives high delta exposure for a small outlay.

The risk is defined and limited. The long put caps the downside at a known dollar figure computable before entry — the put spread width plus the net debit — and the broker blocks only that amount of buying power. Bang calls this out repeatedly as "very low capital or buying power because it's a risk-defined trade. The broker will not block the huge capital from you."

The short call generates additional income while you wait for the stock to move. This is the incremental benefit over the plain Bull Bang.

Time decay works in your favour rather than against you, which is the reformulation of the previous point and the one Bang treats as decisive. It is also the property that makes patience possible: the trader can wait for a technical thesis to play out over weeks without the position degrading in the meantime.

The risk-to-reward ratio improves for the same magnitude of move. On Salesforce, adding the collar to the Bull Bang changed a fourteen-point outcome from +$734 / −$756 to +$828 / −$625. "When I win, I win more; when I lose, I lose less, for the same magnitude of the movement."

Repeated rolls ratchet the cost basis down, exactly as in the diagonal spread. Every credit collected on a roll is a permanent reduction in what the position has at risk, which is why the Salesforce trade could be marginally profitable after three weeks of a stock that went nowhere, and why the prematurely-rolled Alibaba position lost less than its twin.

The returns on blocked capital are high. The realised Netflix trades produced approximately forty percent in eight days and fifty percent in under three weeks. The projected maximum returns at entry were 52 percent on Salesforce and 75 percent on Alibaba against their respective buying power requirements.

#### Risks and disadvantages

The upside is capped at the collar strike. This is the price of the income and Bang states it without qualification: "of course, when you sell a call option you cap the upside potential at the short call strike. There's no free lunch here. You get additional income; in exchange for it you have to cap the upside potential for the trade." The mitigation is strike selection — "if you really want to have a decent room for the upside potential, then sell a higher strike call; but if you want to go for a higher premium, then sell a lower strike" — and the exit rules, which allow you to roll the cap up and out or remove it entirely if the stock breaks out.

The inverted-spread risk if the rule on strike placement is violated. Selling the collar below the long call strike creates a structure that loses money on a strong rally, which is perverse in a bullish trade. "In any case, don't sell below the long call strike."

No dividends. This is the disadvantage relative to a genuine collar or a covered call built on stock. "In the case of the collar strategy or the covered call strategy where you own the shares, you would earn dividends if the company happens to pay a dividend during the time you're holding the shares. But when you hold an option position, you don't get the dividend."

Gap risk, which is the risk that actually materialised. The fifty-percent-of-maximum cut-loss rule assumes the ability to transact at the level where you decided to exit. A regulatory announcement, an earnings shock, or any overnight news that moves the stock thirty points removes that ability, and the loss taken is whatever the market offers on the reopening. On Alibaba the intended exit was $1,200 and the realised exit was $1,900, or roughly seventy to seventy-five percent of the maximum.

Assignment risk on the short call. Bang argues persuasively that this is rare, because a call buyer who exercises early forfeits the remaining extrinsic value, which becomes the seller's profit. But the risk is not zero — "it's going to happen; I've been trading options for many years and this is one of the very rare situations" — and it is one more reason the 80-delta roll rule exists.

The negative-theta failure mode. The strategy's headline claim is positive theta, but Bang's own iterations show that a carelessly constructed Bull Bang Collar does not achieve it. A collar sold too far out of the money, or too close to expiration, may bring in a dollar or two against a Bull Bang decaying at fifteen or sixteen dollars a day, in which case you have capped your upside and gained nothing. The theta reading on the analysis tab is the check, and it must be performed before entry.

Execution complexity. Four legs across two expirations is not a trivial order. Bang encountered a real consequence of this during the Salesforce roll on Interactive Brokers, when the newly rolled leg appeared to have gone to the wrong strike. After checking the order log he established that his execution had been correct and that the confusion arose from an unrelated bear call spread with ten contracts in the same expiration: one contract had netted off against his new short call and the remaining legs had been displayed separately. "So very messy... Sometimes you have multiple trades and it happens to be in the same expiration as well, and you execute the trade and it just cancels out." The lesson is that overlapping positions in the same underlying and expiration can be netted by the broker's position display in ways that make individual strategies hard to read.

Management burden. Like the diagonal spread, this strategy requires you to return to it every one or two weeks to roll the short leg. Bang treats this as a feature rather than a cost — each roll is another premium collected and another reduction in cost basis — but it is nonetheless work that a buy-and-hold position does not require.

#### The two strategies compared

It is worth closing by putting the two structures of this chapter side by side, because they are the same idea implemented on different bases and the differences are instructive.

| | Diagonal spread | Bull Bang Collar |
|---|---|---|
| Legs | 2 | 4 |
| Base position | Deep ITM long call (80+ delta), 3–6 months | Bull Bang: ATM/OTM long call (40–50 delta) + short put at support + long put 5 points lower, 1–3 months |
| Income leg | Short OTM call, 30–40 days, 1–2 strikes OTM or ~30 delta | Short OTM call, 1–2 weeks, at resistance and never below the long call strike |
| Substitutes for | 100 shares in a covered call | A stock collar |
| Capital vs. 100 shares | ~10–15% | Debit plus put spread width; typically $1,100–$2,700 in the examples |
| Downside protection | None beyond the capped debit | Explicit long put defining the floor |
| Base theta before the income leg | Negative | Negative |
| Theta after the income leg | Positive | Positive if correctly constructed — must be verified |
| Downside if wrong | Debit lost; long call bleeds intrinsic value with the stock | Capped at put spread width plus debit; loss accrues quickly once below the short put |
| Rolls | Roughly monthly, about five times over the long call's life | Every one to two weeks, indefinitely |
| Cut-loss rule | 20% of maximum loss (Adam); ~20–25%, translated to a price level behind support (Bang) | 50% of maximum loss |
| Roll trigger | 70% of premium realised (Adam) / ~80% (Bang), or in the money near expiration | Short call in the money with delta above 80 |
| Outlook | Bullish long-term, neutral to slightly bullish over the next 30 days | Cautiously bullish, facing a specific resistance level |

The common thread is unmistakable. In both cases the trader begins with a bullish position that costs money to hold, recognises that the cost is a daily theta bleed, and sells a short-dated out-of-the-money call to convert that bleed into income. In both cases the price of the conversion is a cap on the upside. In both cases the short leg is rolled repeatedly, and every roll permanently reduces the cost basis of the position. And in both cases the governing metaphor is the same: you have leased an asset, and your job is to keep a tenant in it.


---

# Part IX — The DS Hammer Strategy

## The DS Hammer Strategy

### Introduction: The Diagonal Spread, Version 2.0

The DS Hammer is the second-generation diagonal spread, and Adam Khoo introduces it as a strategy he had personally tested to his own satisfaction before teaching it. The abbreviation "DS" stands for Diagonal Spread; the DS Hammer is what he calls the "diagonal spread version 2.0," a structural refinement of the diagonal spread taught earlier in the course, which he retroactively renames "DS 1.0." The whole point of the refinement is capital. The DS Hammer, in his words, "will benefit from a moderately bullish price movement using a fraction of the capital." Everything else about the strategy — the direction it wants, the shape of its payoff, the way it is managed week after week — follows from that one design decision.

In its skeletal form the position is unremarkable and will look familiar to anyone who has traded a calendar or diagonal before. You buy a long-dated call and you sell a short-dated call at a higher strike. Two legs, two different expiries, two different strikes. What makes it the *Hammer* rather than the classical diagonal is where the long strike sits. In the DS 1.0 you buy a deep in-the-money call with a delta somewhere between 70 and 90, which functions as a stock substitute and costs a great deal of premium. In the DS Hammer you buy an at-the-money or near-at-the-money call with a delta between roughly 50 and 60. That single change cuts the entry debit roughly in half, and because the debit *is* the capital and *is* the maximum loss, halving the debit halves both.

#### Where the name comes from

The name is a physical analogy and Adam builds the whole conceptual frame around it. Imagine you are pulling a nail out of a plank of wood. You can do it with a pair of pliers — grip the nail head, and haul. It works, but it takes a lot of effort, and you fight the wood the entire way. That, he says, is the DS 1.0: you can still get the job done, "but you will use more effort, more capital."

Now imagine you use a claw hammer instead, and before you start pulling you slide a small block of wood under the hammer's head. The block raises the fulcrum, converts a short awkward lever into a long efficient one, and the nail comes out with far less force. The nail still comes out — same result — but the effort is dramatically reduced.

In the DS Hammer, **the at-the-money long call is the wood block**. "When you use a hammer to pull the nail, you put the wood block there, you use less effort. So the at-the-money call is like a good block that helps reduce the capital you use in the trade. And you get the same result with less capital, less effort." Throughout the module he refers to this leg as "the good block" or simply "the leverage." The hammer, then, is not a chart pattern and it is not a candlestick — a reader coming from technical analysis might reasonably expect the "hammer" to refer to the bullish reversal candle, and it does not. It refers to the mechanical advantage of a lever with a block under it.

This distinction matters practically as well as rhetorically, because it tells you what the strategy is optimizing for. It is not optimizing for maximum profit in dollars. It is optimizing for **return on capital employed**. The absolute profit of a DS Hammer is roughly comparable to the absolute profit of the corresponding DS 1.0 — you are still capturing the same directional move in the same underlying — but you are capturing it on half the money. The ratio therefore roughly doubles, and it is that doubling that lets Adam set a profit target range of **+50% to +150% return on investment** where the DS 1.0 target was a more modest +50%.

#### The strategy in one paragraph

The DS Hammer is a moderately bullish, two-legged, defined-risk options position. Leg one is a long call bought near the money, with a delta of roughly 50 to 60, expiring three to nine months out. Leg two is a short call sold at approximately the one-standard-deviation strike, with a delta of roughly 20 to 25, expiring in one to three weeks. The trade is entered for a net debit, and that debit is simultaneously the capital committed and the maximum possible loss. The short call is rolled repeatedly — every week, every two weeks, whatever the option cycle dictates — and each roll harvests additional credit that permanently reduces the net cost basis of the position. The trade is closed when the accumulated return on that original capital reaches somewhere between 50% and 150%, or cut when it reaches negative 50%.

---

### Part One: The Anatomy and the Rulebook

#### The two legs and the reasoning behind each

Every element of the construction earns its place, and it is worth being explicit about what each leg is actually doing before we get to the numbers.

**Leg one — buy a near-at-the-money call, three to nine months to expiry.** This is the engine of the trade. It is the leg that gives you directional exposure to the underlying and it is the leg you are hoping will appreciate. Adam is explicit that the reason for choosing the at-the-money strike rather than the deep in-the-money strike of DS 1.0 is not that he expects it to perform better — it is purely to reduce the cost of the trade. "As I said, the intent of buying near-at-the-money is to reduce the cost of the trade. And I call it the good block." The three-to-nine-month expiry is inherited unchanged from DS 1.0. It has to be long-dated for two reasons that reinforce each other. First, a long-dated option has a low theta per day relative to its premium, so the leg bleeds slowly rather than collapsing under time decay. Second, and more importantly, the long leg is the *inventory* against which you sell short calls, and you want that inventory to last many cycles. A six-month long call gives you something like twenty-four to twenty-six weekly rolls, or twelve to thirteen fortnightly rolls, and each of those rolls is a credit. If the long leg only had a month to run you would get one or two rolls and the whole compounding mechanism of the strategy would never engage.

**Leg two — sell an out-of-the-money call at approximately the one-standard-deviation strike, one to three weeks to expiry.** This is the income engine and the risk reducer. Selling it does three things at once. It reduces the net entry debit, and therefore reduces both the capital and the maximum loss. It flips the net theta of the position positive, so that the passage of time works for you rather than against you. And by being repeatedly rolled it generates a stream of credits that grind the cost basis of the position lower and lower over the life of the trade. Adam's ideal expiry for this leg is the shortest one that still pays a worthwhile premium: "In some [volatile] stocks, I could sell a weekly call. In some less volatile stocks, I have less premium. I could sell two or three weeks out." The strike is set at approximately one standard deviation above the current price, which in practice lands at a delta of roughly 20 to 25, and the strike is a tunable expression of your directional view — "if you are more bullish, you can sell a higher strike. If you're less bullish, you can sell a lower strike to collect more premium."

#### The complete entry checklist

Adam sets out five families of entry conditions. They are worth stating carefully because he returns to them, item by item, on every live trade in the module — before entering the Nvidia trade he literally says "so let's go point by point," and works down the list.

##### Rule 1 — Option liquidity, defined by three tests

Liquidity is the first filter and Adam treats it as non-negotiable, because a strategy that requires you to roll a short option perhaps a dozen times over its life will be destroyed by transaction friction if the market in that option is thin. He applies three specific tests.

The first and most important is that **the underlying must have weekly options**. This is a hard gate: "if the stock doesn't have weekly options, I would not touch it." The logic is structural rather than aesthetic — the entire management framework rests on rolling the short call at intervals of one, two or three weeks, and without weekly expiries you simply cannot construct that cadence. You would be forced into monthly rolls, which means fewer credits, worse strike granularity, and long periods where an in-the-money short call cannot be adjusted at a sensible price.

The second test is the **bid-ask spread**, which he wants tight enough that the round trip does not eat the premium. His rule of thumb is expressed two equivalent ways: "0.4 for the $100 stocks or 0.4% of the stock price." So on a $100 stock he wants the bid-ask on the option to be no more than about forty cents; on a $200 stock, no more than about eighty cents; and so on proportionally. Anything tighter than that threshold he treats as good liquidity. In practice the stocks he actually trades in this module are dramatically better than the threshold — on Nvidia, checking the 180 and 190 strikes, he observes that "bid and ask is like just 10 cents difference, which is very good," and on Alphabet the spread is "only five cents different."

The third test is **open interest**, where his floor is modest: "anything more than 100 on the open interest, that would be good." Again the live examples clear it by an order of magnitude — Nvidia open interest at the strikes he examines is "like 10,000."

| Liquidity test | Threshold | Nvidia (1 Aug 24) | Alphabet (1 Aug 24) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weekly options available | Mandatory — no weeklies, no trade | Yes | Yes |
| Bid-ask spread | ≤ 0.4% of stock price (≈$0.40 on a $100 stock) | ~$0.10 | ~$0.05 |
| Open interest | > 100 contracts | ~10,000 | "huge" |

##### Rule 2 — The technical setup must be neutral to bullish

The second condition is a chart condition, and Adam frames it in the negative first because the failure mode is so expensive. "I would not do it on the stock that is on the steady downtrend or secular downtrend. That would be a suicide trade." The DS Hammer has a long call as its core; a stock in a persistent, grinding decline will destroy that long call while simultaneously forcing you to roll the short call down and down for shrinking credits until you hit the stop loss. He names Lululemon and another persistently declining name as the kind of chart he refuses.

What he wants instead is any chart that has stopped going down. "Only do it when the stock has shown that it has stopped declining, stabilizing, bottomed already, and ideally recovering on the way up." Beyond that stabilized-and-recovering pattern he accepts two other setups explicitly: a **dip on an uptrend** — a retracement inside an established upward move, which is the setup he uses for both Nvidia and Alphabet on 1 August — and a **breakout pattern**. The unifying idea is that any bullish setup qualifies, and the neutral-but-no-longer-falling setup qualifies too, because the strategy makes money in a sideways tape.

##### Rule 3 — Expiry selection for each leg

The long call expires **three to nine months** out. The short call expires **one to three weeks** out, with the exact choice governed by premium: sell the weekly if the weekly pays, and stretch to two or three weeks if the stock is quieter and the weekly premium is thin.

There is a refinement Adam applies to the long leg that is not part of the formal rulebook but which he uses on every single live entry in this module, and which is worth elevating because of how consistently he does it: **he prefers to buy a long call that expires after the underlying's next earnings release**. On Nvidia, entering on 1 August, he reasons: "the earnings for Nvidia normally happens in the late February. So the last one, when they release in February, that is 21st of February. So if I buy the one that expired in March, that means I will buy the one that expired after the February earnings. I prefer to long an option that expire after earnings because that option normally will have better value because it expires after the earning." He applies the same reasoning to Alphabet ("this one I can go to February because Google normally release earning by end of January. So February is after the earnings, which is good"). The economic content of the preference is that an option spanning an earnings event carries the implied volatility of that event in its price, and an option holder benefits from that embedded event premium; the qualifier he attaches is that he will only reach for the later expiry "if the price is not so much more expensive compared to February or January."

##### Rule 4 — Strike selection for each leg

The long call is bought **near at the money**. In practice the available strike grid rarely offers an exact at-the-money strike, and Adam's habit when forced to choose is instructive. On Amazon at $182.50 he faces a choice between 180 and 185 and says plainly "either 180 or 185, it's fine," choosing 180. On Alphabet at $173, facing 170 or 175, he articulates the trade-off explicitly: "If I'm more bullish, I choose 170. If I'm less bullish or want to reduce the cost, I choose 175." The lower strike is more in the money, higher delta, more expensive, more directional; the higher strike is cheaper and less directional. In every live example in this module he ends up choosing the slightly-in-the-money strike and lands on a delta between 62 and 63.

The short call is sold **near the one-standard-deviation strike**, which corresponds to a delta of **20 to 25**. The mechanic he uses to find that strike is not delta-based, however — it is the platform's one-standard-deviation indicator, which for a chosen expiry reports the expected absolute move of the underlying between now and that expiry. He takes that number, adds it to the current stock price, and sells the nearest listed strike at or above the result. The delta of 20 to 25 is a consequence of that, not the input to it.

##### Rule 5 — The economics must clear two numeric screens

Two quantitative gates must be passed before the order goes out.

The first is that **maximum risk equals the entry debit**, which is a structural fact rather than a test, but Adam states it as a rule because it defines the capital: "Max risk for the trade is equal to the entry debit, and that is also the capital that I use in the trade."

The second is a genuine screen: **the trade must show a maximum return on investment of at least 25% at entry, before any rolling**. The calculation is done off the risk profile chart. You find the peak of the profit-and-loss curve at the short call's expiration date — the tipping point, which sits at the short strike — read the dollar value of the maximum profit at that point, and divide it by the net debit. "If it is more than 25% at the entry, that would be good enough. Most of my trades, I get more than 25%."

The third gate is graphical rather than numeric: **the payoff chart must show no risk on the upside**. Read the profit curve to the right of the short strike; it should decline as the underlying rises past the short strike, but it must not cross below zero. "If the stock price goes higher, the trade would still be profitable, though it would be less profit if the stock price goes much higher, but it won't dip into a below zero line." This condition is a check that the construction is correct — that the long call's intrinsic value grows fast enough to outrun the short call's losses at any price. In practice he sometimes describes it as "no risk on the upside, or very limited risk on the upside. The stock price needs to go up a lot for the trade to lose money," which acknowledges that on some strike combinations there is a theoretical far-upside loss zone that is simply unreachable in the timeframe.

#### The entry rules as a single table

| # | Rule | Specification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Option liquidity | Weekly options mandatory; bid-ask ≤ 0.4% of stock price; open interest > 100 |
| 2 | Technical setup | Neutral to bullish only — bottomed and recovering, dip on uptrend, or breakout. Never a steady or secular downtrend |
| 3a | Long leg expiry | 3 to 9 months; prefer an expiry that falls after the next earnings release if not materially more expensive |
| 3b | Short leg expiry | 1 to 3 weeks; choose the shortest tenor that still pays a worthwhile premium |
| 4a | Long leg strike | Near at the money; delta 50–60 (in practice he accepts 62–63 when the grid forces a slightly ITM strike) |
| 4b | Short leg strike | Current price plus the platform's one-standard-deviation move for that expiry; delta 20–25. Raise if more bullish, lower if less bullish |
| 5a | Max risk | Equals the net entry debit, which is also the capital committed |
| 5b | Return screen | Max profit at short-call expiry ÷ net debit ≥ 25%, before any rolling |
| 5c | Payoff shape | No risk on the upside — the curve must stay above zero at all prices above the short strike |

#### The illustrative Amazon construction

Adam builds a full example in the introductory lesson using Amazon trading at **$182.50**.

For leg one he goes to the option chain and selects the **January 2025** series, which shows **175 days to expiration** — "which is nearly six months, which is good, right, between three to nine months." The chain offers no strike at 182.50, so he must pick 180 or 185; he picks **180**, and pays the mark price of **$20.65**.

For leg two he selects the **16 August 2024** series, **21 days to expiration**, three weeks out and comfortably inside the one-to-three-week band. He then reads the platform's one-standard-deviation indicator for that expiry, which tells him "the market expects the stock price to move up or down by **$17.70**." Adding that to the spot price of $182.50 gives approximately $200, and $200 is a listed strike, so that is what he sells, collecting **$2.42**.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | DTE | Strike | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy call | 17 Jan 2025 | 175 | 180 | −$20.65 |
| 2 | Sell call | 16 Aug 2024 | 21 | 200 | +$2.42 |
| | **Net debit** | | | | **−$18.23** |

One contract therefore costs **$1,823**, "and that is my max loss, and that is the capital I use in the trade as well."

The risk profile of the constructed position shows a "very decent profit zone," a **probability of winning of 52.6%** before any rolling, and — critically — the current stock price sitting inside that profit zone with the break-even point "slightly below the current stock price, which gives me some margin for error." Hovering over the tipping point of the profit curve gives a maximum profit of **approximately $1,300**, and $1,300 divided by the $1,823 capital gives a **maximum return on investment of 71.3% before rolling** — comfortably clearing the 25% screen.

It is worth pausing on the probability figure, because 52.6% sounds unimpressive for a strategy Adam claims has a high win rate. His answer is that the entry probability is not the operative probability. "When you construct the trade at the entry, the trade would have more than 50% probability of winning, but if you keep rolling the short call, you will increase the probability of winning for the trade. And most of my trades would have 80% or more in terms of probability of winning." Every roll adds credit, every credit lowers the net cost basis, and every reduction in cost basis pushes the break-even point lower and widens the profit zone. The 52.6% is the starting value of a number designed to increase.

#### The payoff profile and its arithmetic

The shape of the DS Hammer's payoff at the short call's expiration is worth spelling out carefully, because the management rules only make sense against it.

**Maximum loss** is the net debit, realized if the underlying falls far enough that both calls expire worthless. In the Amazon illustration this is $1,823 per contract. It is a true floor — there is no scenario, however violent, in which you can lose more than you paid. This is one of the strategy's central selling points, and Adam contrasts it repeatedly with holding stock: "Trading stock, if it gaps down significantly, even with stop loss [you can lose more]. This one, you know exactly how much your max loss, and you cut loss at 50% of that."

**Maximum profit** occurs at the short strike on the short call's expiration date. At that price the short call expires exactly worthless while the long call has captured the entire move from the long strike up to the short strike, plus retains all its remaining extrinsic value. Adam does not compute this analytically; he reads it off the platform's profit curve by hovering at the peak. In the Amazon illustration it is approximately $1,300 against $1,823 of capital, for 71.3%.

**Break-even** at short-call expiry sits slightly below the entry stock price, which is the structural signature of a well-constructed DS Hammer.
