The credit received from the short call subsidizes part of the long call's extrinsic value, so the stock can drift down a small amount and the position still breaks even. Adam finds this point on the platform by using the "set slices, break-even" function on the short call's expiration date. In the second Amazon case study, with the stock at $184, break-even lands "at 181-something, which gives me some buffer in case the stock price drops a little bit."

**Above the short strike** the profit curve declines but stays positive. Past the short strike each additional dollar of stock price adds a dollar of intrinsic value to the long call and a dollar of intrinsic loss to the short call, so the intrinsic effects cancel; what remains is the erosion of the long call's extrinsic value as it moves deeper in the money. Hence a declining but positive curve — "the profit can reduce, but it will always be profitable if the stock goes higher."

This asymmetry is the emotional core of the trade. There are three ways to make money — the stock goes up, the stock goes sideways, or the stock goes down a little — and only one way to lose, which is the stock going down a lot.

#### How the Greeks behave

Adam does not present a formal Greeks section, but he returns to Greek behaviour so often across the nine parts that the picture assembles itself.

**Theta is the headline Greek and it is positive.** "The best thing, you are paid to wait. Because this trade has a positive theta. Time decay works in the trade's favour." The mechanism is that the short-dated short call, sitting close to expiry, decays far faster per day than the long-dated long call, so the net of the two positions is positive. On the Nvidia trade entered on 1 August, checking the position immediately after fill, he reads a net theta of **7.24** and explains it in dollars: "7.24 means every day this trade brings in $7.20 in time decay benefit to the trade." He then makes the practical point that matters most to a trader watching an underwater fresh entry: "Let's say if the stock price stays right here, just stays right here, and the trade is losing like $17. By three days passing, the benefit from the time decay of the three days would be able to offset the loss here. So I cannot control the stock price. It can go up, it can go down. But the one that I can control is this one. The time decay."

**Theta can turn negative, and that is a rolling trigger.** Late in the Nvidia trade, on 30 August, he observes that after the short call has decayed to near zero the net theta of the position has flipped negative — "the theta is now negative here. Negative theta for a trade because there's not much value left in the short [call]." This is a genuinely important and easy-to-miss point. Once the short call is worth three or four cents it has nothing left to decay, so the long call's own theta dominates and the position begins bleeding. Restoring positive theta is one of the reasons to roll early rather than waiting for expiry: rolling "helps reduce the time decay for my trade."

**Delta starts net positive and drifts.** The long call at 60-ish delta minus the short call at 20-to-25 delta gives a net position delta of roughly +35 to +40 at entry, which is the moderately-bullish exposure the strategy advertises. As the stock rises the short call's delta rises faster than the long call's (it is closer to expiry and closer to its strike), so the net delta compresses. Adam manages this explicitly and it is the basis of his most important adjustment trigger. On the Meta trade on 19 September he narrates it precisely: "the delta of the short call is still about 70, 71, pretty much similar to the delta of the long call. So my trade has a neutral delta today, which means if the stock goes sideways, it will be more profit for the trade. But if the stock continues to go higher, the short call delta will go much higher than 70, 71, could go to 80, 90, and close to 100. That's where the trade would make less profit. Because the net delta of the trade at that point in time would be a negative delta. So then the more the price goes higher, the more it will hurt the trade."

That passage contains the real decision rule beneath the surface rule. The stated trigger is "roll up when the short call's delta exceeds 80." The reason behind the trigger is that the position must not be allowed to acquire net negative delta while the trader remains bullish. Adam makes this reasoning explicit again on 27 September when he declines to roll a short call that is already in the money: "the delta of the 555 short call here is at 67. So less than 80. That means I can wait a little bit longer. Secondly, this 67 [is] still below the delta of the long call, which is 75. So the net of the two legs, I still have a net positive delta for the trade. That means the trade would continue to benefit if the stock goes higher from here." And again on Amazon on 23 September, where the comparison drives him the other way: "the delta of the short call is near 80, and the delta of the long call is only 71. That means if the share price continues to go higher, it will hurt the trade, right? Because the trade has a net negative delta right now. So I prefer to roll it early."

The practical reading, then, is that the delta-80 rule is a proxy, and the underlying test is a comparison: **is the short call's delta approaching or exceeding the long call's delta?** If yes and you remain bullish, roll up.

**Vega is not managed explicitly but is exploited opportunistically.** Adam never names vega, but he trades around implied volatility constantly. He deliberately rolls short calls into expiries that span earnings because "the premium would be huge... because the volatility will be even higher if it crosses the earnings," and he notes on 16 August that "with the implied volatility being high right now before the earnings, I could collect a very good premium, even with one-week expiration." The long leg's preference for post-earnings expiries is also a vega decision in substance if not in name.

#### The management framework in outline

The introductory lesson lays out the management rules before any of the live trades demonstrate them, and it is useful to have them in front of you as a map.

The **primary monitoring object is the short call**, not the position P&L. Adam watches two things about it: its remaining value, and its delta.

When the **stock rises past the short strike**, the correct emotional response is satisfaction rather than alarm. "Don't be worried. That is a good thing that happens, because the trade has no risk on the upside. Yes, you may be losing on the short call, but the long call will make more money to offset, and the trade would still be profitable." The action, if any, is to roll the short call up and out to create more headroom, or simply to take profit if the position is already inside the target range.

When the **short call's delta exceeds 80**, roll it up. This is the formal trigger discussed above.

When the **stock falls**, roll the short call down to collect more premium — subject to one absolute constraint. "My rule is I would never roll the short call lower than the long call strike." In the Amazon illustration, having sold the 200 strike against a 180 long, he can roll down to 190, to 185, to 180, and there he stops. The reason is structural: rolling the short strike below the long strike would convert the position into an inverted diagonal with an entirely different and much worse risk profile, potentially creating loss at prices where the original construction was profitable. The 180 floor is hard.

When the **stock keeps falling and the position reaches −50% return on investment**, cut the loss and exit.

When the **position reaches +50% to +150% return on investment**, take the profit.

#### The advantages, stated plainly

Adam enumerates the benefits and each of them traces back to the halved capital.

**Capital efficiency.** The DS Hammer uses roughly half the capital of a traditional diagonal spread and roughly **10% of the capital required to buy the shares outright** for an equivalent position size. This serves two distinct purposes he separates carefully. The first is accessibility: "it will cater very well for traders with small accounts. Some traders may not afford like $2,000 per trade, while you can do this one with $1,000 per trade or less than that in some stocks." The second is portfolio-level survivability: less capital per trade "will minimize the max risk in case the whole thing collapses — the whole market goes through a correction or the stock just gaps down significantly."

**Magnified return on investment.** "You achieve almost the same absolute profit and that translates into a very high return on investment. That's why I have the profit target between 50% to 150%."

**Reduced risk versus stock.** The maximum loss is known, fixed and small, whereas a stock position can gap through a stop.

**A decent profit zone with no upside risk**, meaning three of the four possible market outcomes are profitable.

**Positive theta** — you are paid to wait.

#### The disadvantages, stated equally plainly

**Limited profit.** "As usual [with a] diagonal spread, you cap the upside. When you sell a short call, you cap the upside. And that is the trade-off." The DS Hammer will never capture a runaway move the way a naked long call would.

**The trade requires rolling.** This is a real operational cost. "Every few weeks you need to roll the short call to collect more premium to increase the profit for the trade. While some of you may not be familiar with that, but once you do it for a few times, you will see that it's not something very challenging, and I don't mind doing it every [week] to keep collecting more premium." A trader who cannot or will not perform this maintenance should not trade the DS Hammer, because the rolling is not an optional enhancement — it is the mechanism by which the trade's cost basis falls, its break-even drops, its probability of winning rises from 52% toward 80%, and its return on investment climbs into the 50-to-150% band.

---

### Part Two: DS 1.0 Versus DS Hammer — A Full Comparison

Adam devotes a substantial section of the introductory lesson to comparing the two generations of the strategy, and the comparison is the clearest available statement of what the DS Hammer actually *is*.

#### What is the same

Both are **moderately bullish two-legged trades** built from either calls or puts with different expiry dates — a textbook diagonal spread in both cases. Both have **limited risk and limited profit**, with a decent profit zone in between. Both carry **positive theta**, so time decay works in the trader's favour in both.

#### What is different

| Dimension | DS 1.0 | DS Hammer (DS 2.0) |
|---|---|---|
| Long call strike | Deep in the money | Near at the money — "the good block" |
| Long call delta | 70 to 90 | 50 to 60 |
| Capital used | Higher | Roughly half of DS 1.0; about 10% of buying the shares |
| Short call strike | Out of the money | Approximately one standard deviation out |
| Short call delta | 20 to 35 | 20 to 25, adjustable up if more bullish, down if less bullish |
| Maximum loss | Higher, because the entry debit is higher | Lower, because the entry debit is lower |
| Preferred underlyings | Fundamentally good stocks, ideally undervalued | Can extend to more volatile / speculative stocks |
| Stop loss | 50% of max loss — a larger absolute dollar amount | 50% of max loss — a smaller absolute dollar amount |
| Profit target | +50% return on investment | +50% to +150% return on investment |

Two rows of that table deserve elaboration because they contain genuine strategy content rather than mere arithmetic.

The **underlying-selection row** is a real difference in philosophy. DS 1.0, with its large capital commitment and stock-substitute long leg, is a position Adam wants to hold in high-quality, ideally undervalued businesses, because the deep in-the-money long call behaves much like owning the shares and you want to own good shares. The DS Hammer's smaller commitment changes the calculus. "You can use DS Hammer on more volatile stocks. Because it uses less capital, you can afford to speculate. And often because the volatile stock has a higher short-dated premium, so you just need to roll a few rounds and you would be able to pay off the trade." That last clause is the important one: on a high-volatility name the weekly premium is large relative to the cost of the position, so a handful of successful rolls can recoup a meaningful fraction of the entry debit. The Nvidia trade later in the module demonstrates exactly this — the entire profit of that trade, Adam notes at one point, "actually came from the short calls after three rounds of rolling."

The **stop-loss row** is arithmetically trivial but psychologically significant. Both strategies cut at 50% of maximum loss. But because the DS Hammer's maximum loss is half as large, "in terms of absolute, DS Hammer has lower risk." A −50% stop on an $1,823 position is a $911 loss; the same percentage stop on a DS 1.0 costing $3,600 is $1,800.

---

### Part Three: The Portfolio Evidence — Options Versus Stock

Before moving to live execution, Adam presents a piece of portfolio-level evidence that functions as the strategy's empirical case. He takes the DS Hammer positions actually open in his own portfolio as of **26 July 2024** — eighteen open trades, most of them entered in June and July, meaning they had lived through a market correction — and compares their performance against a simulation of what the same directional exposures would have produced if expressed as stock instead.

The construction of the simulation is straightforward: for each DS Hammer, he takes the equivalent share count (a two-contract position becomes 200 shares) and marks the notional stock position to market over the same period.

| Metric | 18 DS Hammer trades | Equivalent stock positions |
|---|---|---|
| Profit / loss | +$5,000 | −$5,600 |
| Capital employed | ~$53,000 | ~$562,000 |
| Return on investment | +10.1% | −1.0% |
| Capital as % of stock capital | 9.4% | 100% |

The gap is $11,000 in absolute profit and roughly eleven percentage points in return on investment, and Adam is careful to attribute it to a specific mechanism rather than to luck or to the market environment. "Because trading stock you have no ability to roll. But [with the] option, I keep rolling the short call option for many rounds, creating more cushion to the downside. So it protects the downside better with the ability to roll. And therefore, the option trades are profitable, but the stock trades are losing money."

This is the strategy's central claim stated at portfolio scale. Over a period in which the underlying stocks collectively went *down*, a portfolio of DS Hammers went *up*, because each roll harvested credit that lowered cost basis, and the accumulated credits exceeded the mark-to-market damage from the price decline. That mechanism will be visible in miniature in nearly every worked trade that follows — most vividly in the Meta trade, which is profitable on 9 September despite the stock trading *below* the entry price, and in the Nvidia trade, whose long leg lost money throughout while the short-call rolls carried the position.

Two caveats belong alongside these figures. First, the eighteen-trade sample is small and covers roughly two months, which is not a statistically meaningful backtest and Adam does not present it as one. Second, the comparison is against unmanaged stock; a stock trader with a stop-loss discipline would have a different, though not necessarily better, outcome. Adam's counter to the second point is that stops on stock do not protect against gaps, whereas the DS Hammer's maximum loss is contractually fixed.

---

### Part Four: The Live Entries — 1 August 2024

The second video in the module is a recording of a live trade-hunt webinar conducted on **1 August 2024**, during which Adam enters three DS Hammer positions in real time — Nvidia, Alphabet and Meta — and additionally demonstrates a roll on a pre-existing ten-contract Nvidia position. These three trades are then followed week by week through the next five videos to their conclusion on 11 October. Because the follow-through is complete, this is the single most valuable teaching sequence in the module, and it is worth narrating in full.

#### Trade one: Nvidia

##### The thesis

Adam's reason for entering Nvidia is a seasonal-behavioural observation rather than a valuation or a pure chart signal. "This stock tends to run up towards earnings, one month before the earnings. It starts to run up. That's my observation over the past one year or so." He scrolls back through the historical earnings dates on the chart and points out the recurring pattern: "What I see in common is normally the stock tends to go up towards the earnings. One month ahead of the earnings date... And this one, same thing. One month ahead of the earnings date, it tends to go up. Now, after the earnings, it can go up, it can go down. Most of the time it goes up also. But the one month before the earnings, it tends to go up."

Nvidia's next earnings date is **28 August**; the date of entry is 1 August. The trade is therefore being placed precisely at the start of the one-month pre-earnings window his observation identifies. He notes candidly that this is a pattern he has observed, not a tested statistic — the reader should treat it as a discretionary thesis rather than a rule of the strategy.

He supplements the seasonal thesis with a chart read: "the last dip here and bounce off the SMA here seems to be a dip on the uptrend." He also concedes he is slightly late, because the stock rallied strongly the previous day and is up another 1.7% today: "I could argue that it's a little bit late. Yesterday, when it started rebounding, I wanted to enter already... And now the stock has run up a little bit. But anyway, I don't think it's too late."

##### Working the checklist

He then goes through the entry rules explicitly. Liquidity: Nvidia is "one of the most actively traded stocks in the market," it has weekly options, the bid-ask at the 180 and 190 strikes is about ten cents, and open interest is around 10,000. "So liquidity is not an issue... tick the box." Technical setup: "Yes, of course, it is bullish. It's a dip on the uptrend. It's not like declining steadily, like I showed you on Lululemon."

##### Construction

For the long leg he considers January, February and March expiries, and reasons his way to March: Nvidia's February earnings fall around 21 February, so a March expiry is a post-earnings expiry and therefore carries better value. With the stock between $180 and $190 — the transcript at this point reflects a pre-split-adjusted quote sequence and the numbers shift to the $118–$130 range immediately afterwards, so the reader should note the strikes he actually trades rather than the narration around them — he selects the **118 strike**, delta **62**, "which is fine, right, 60, 62 is fine," at a mark price quoted as **$22.37**.

For the short leg he selects an expiry two weeks out, **16 August**. The premium on Nvidia is rich enough that he does not need to stretch to three weeks: "because the premium for Nvidia is quite good, I can choose to just sell two weeks, and the premium [is] still good." The one-standard-deviation indicator for 16 August reads **$11**, so adding $11 to the spot gives approximately **130**, and he sells the **130 strike**, collecting **$1.52**.

He builds both legs into a single order ticket — buy the March 118, hold the control key, sell the August 16 130 — and the platform prices the package at a net debit of **$20.90**.

##### Analyzing before sending

Before transmitting the order he right-clicks and analyzes it, which is his invariable habit. He sets the analysis slice to the short call's expiration date so the break-even is computed on the right date, and reads off the profile: "if you construct it correctly like this, you see that the trade has no risk on the upside, or very limited risk on the upside. The stock needs to go up a lot for the trade to lose money. Otherwise, the trade would have very decent profit zone here... And the trade has about **53% chance of winning** before rolling."

While he is analyzing, the market drops, and the package repricies to **$20.64**. He hovers over the peak of the profit curve to read maximum profit: approximately **$830**. Eight hundred and thirty dollars against $2,065 of capital gives a **maximum return on investment of 40% before rolling** — clearing the 25% screen with room to spare. "So it looks like the trade looks decent, and now I can enter at a cheaper price as well."

##### Execution and negotiation

He does not accept the mark price. He lowers the limit to **20.50** and waits, and gets filled at **20.50**. This negotiating behaviour is consistent across every entry and every roll in the module: he sets a limit slightly better than the mid, watches the underlying tick, and adjusts a cent or two at a time until the order fills. Where the underlying is moving in his favour he waits; where it moves against him he concedes cents rather than chase.

| Nvidia entry, 1 Aug 2024 | |
|---|---|
| Long leg | Buy 1× March 2025 118 call |
| Short leg | Sell 1× 16 Aug 2024 130 call |
| Net debit at fill | $20.50 → **$2,050 capital and max loss** |
| Probability of profit at entry | ~53% |
| Max profit before rolling | ~$830 |
| Max ROI before rolling | ~40% |

Immediately after the fill the market falls and the position shows a small loss — first $30, then a recovery to break-even, then a loss of $8, then $12, then $45 as the day turns. Adam's commentary on this is deliberately anti-climactic and is one of the more useful pieces of trading psychology in the module. "It's still early in the day, that's okay. It can go up. It can go down because the whole market is now pulling back... don't look at the daily P&L and then freak out and feel panic about it. There's nothing to worry about." And later, with the position down $45: "that's normal in trading. You cannot control the pricing of the stock. Even it's the best setup, you enter it and the stock price just moves opposite to your action. That happens. But the trade [has] six months or seven months to go — March 2025. I don't have to worry about the every-minute kind of fluctuation."

#### The interleaved rolling demonstration

At this point a webinar participant asks how rolling actually works, and rather than defer it Adam switches to a different account holding a pre-existing, ten-contract Nvidia DS Hammer, and demonstrates the mechanics live. This demonstration is the clearest statement of the rolling procedure anywhere in the module and it is worth extracting in full.

The existing position is **long the 105 call, short the 127 call**, with the short call expiring the following day — one day to expiry. The long call has **169 days** remaining. The short call has **10 to 12 cents** of value left, and the position is showing approximately **$7,000** of profit across ten contracts.

##### The rolling trigger

"Normally, I will start rolling when the short call value is almost depleted to zero. It's less than 10 cents, 10 or less than 10 cents, I will start rolling already." This is the single most-repeated operational rule in the module and it governs almost every action he takes across the following ten weeks. The reasoning is an explicit opportunity-cost calculation, and he performs it out loud: "This one has only 11 or 12 cents left. So I can wait for tomorrow to earn extra $100 — 10 contracts mean $110 between now and end of tomorrow. But I can roll it early to get more premium from the new option. And that new premium there will increase the profit for my trade."

In other words, waiting for the last twelve cents earns $110; rolling immediately opens a new short call that begins earning immediately and will collect $1,100 or more over the following week. The residual value of a nearly-dead short call is not worth the week of decay you forgo by waiting for it, and there is a second reason to roll early which he articulates later in the module: a fully depleted short call leaves the position with negative net theta.

##### The mechanics

Rolling is a two-legged single order. "Rolling means I will close the current one, and I will sell the new one." Specifically:

1. **Buy to close** the existing short call. He is short, so he must buy it back. In this case the 127 strike expiring tomorrow, at about 10 cents.
2. **Sell to open** the replacement short call. He selects the next weekly expiry — 9 August, eight days out — and finds the new one-standard-deviation strike. The indicator reads **±$8.85**, so "if I add, call it $9, on top of the current price, I have [approximately] $127." He sells the **127 strike** in the new expiry for **$1.17**, or $120 per contract.
3. He constructs both as one order by selecting the buy-to-close leg, holding the control key, and selecting the sell-to-open leg, so the package prices as a single net credit.

The net arithmetic: he pays 10 cents to close and collects $1.17 to open, so the package is worth approximately **$1.07 net credit**. He negotiates up: "I can say okay, I will wait it at 110 net, I want to collect 110, not 100." Across ten contracts that is **$1,100 of credit for one week**.

"So every week, this trade, I can collect $1,200 for 10 contracts. That's what I'm doing right now."

He queues the order at $1.10 against a market price of $1.03 and leaves it working while he moves to the other trades — a demonstration of his general practice of placing a slightly ambitious limit and letting the market come to it rather than crossing the spread.

##### The roll-up scenario, previewed

A participant asks what happens if the stock rises too much and the short call goes deep in the money. Adam gives the rule and, importantly, the decision that sits inside it: "if the delta of the short call exceeds 80, I will roll that one up. Let's say if the stock goes to 130 or 135, I will roll 127 to a higher strike. Now, when I roll, I would need to determine what strike I want to roll to. That is the most important question I need to ask myself. If I'm more bullish, I roll it higher. If I'm less bullish, I roll it lower."

And on the cost of doing so: "Of course, if I roll from 127 to 135, 136, I may need to pay a debit for the rolling. I may need to do it. But that is not important because the whole trade is still very profitable. I don't mind paying a debit if the stock continues to go higher."

This is a crucial permission. The DS Hammer is not a strategy that refuses to pay debits. When the underlying is rising, paying a small debit to shift the profit ceiling higher is buying something real — headroom — and the cost of that headroom is paid out of a position that is already winning. What Adam refuses is paying a *large* debit to roll up into an *overextended* stock, which is a different thing entirely and which he names later as the worst of all rolling scenarios.

#### Trade two: Alphabet

##### The thesis

Alphabet is a dip-on-uptrend entry with a fundamental overlay. The stock had recently reported earnings that Adam judges good, with one blemish: "It's just a slight miss in the YouTube revenue, two, three hundred million. That's it, very small compared to the whole thing. The rest of the measures are very good. The cloud, very good, profitable, billion dollars right now, a billion profit." His conclusion is that the market overreacted — "I just thought that the stock has been unfairly beaten down. So now it's a dip on the uptrend, good entry point."

He checks liquidity: weeklies present, bid-ask "only five cents different," open interest "huge." He checks the technical setup: "dip on the uptrend. It's good. Check the box."

##### Construction

The stock is at **$173**. For the long leg he selects **February 2025**, applying the post-earnings rule — "Google normally releases earnings by end of January. So February is after the earnings, which is good." The strike grid offers 170 or 175, and he articulates the trade-off before choosing 170: "If I'm more bullish, I choose 170. If I'm less bullish or want to reduce the cost, I choose 175." He chooses **170**, delta **63**, at **$18.57**.

For the short leg he takes the same two-week expiry, **16 August**. The stock's prior earnings are already past so there is no event to trade around. The one-standard-deviation move is **$8**, giving 173 + 8 = 181; there is no 181 strike, so he sells the **180**, collecting **$1.31**.

The package prices at a net debit of **$17.26**.

##### Analysis and execution

He analyzes before sending, sets the break-even slice, and reads: break-even below the current stock price with a buffer, **54% probability of winning** before rolling, no risk on the upside. Maximum profit read off the curve is approximately **$500 to $510**. Dividing by the $1,726 debit gives "29, almost 30%, which is more than 25%. So it's good. All criteria are met."

He negotiates the entry to **17.35** against a mark of 17.46, waits for the market to weaken — narrating, memorably, "I need this one to be red, red, red, red. To be filled. More red. More red" — and gets filled at **$17.35**, making the capital and max loss **$1,735**.

| Alphabet entry, 1 Aug 2024 | |
|---|---|
| Long leg | Buy 1× Feb 2025 170 call, delta 63, $18.57 |
| Short leg | Sell 1× 16 Aug 2024 180 call, $1.31 |
| Net debit at fill | $17.35 → **$1,735 capital and max loss** |
| Probability of profit at entry | ~54% |
| Max profit before rolling | ~$510 |
| Max ROI before rolling | ~30% |

Immediately after fill the position shows a $9 loss, which Adam again waves off.

Note that in the closing summary six videos later, Adam reports the Alphabet entry as **$18.66 for the long call, $1.31 credit for the short call, net $17.35**. The long-call premium quoted at entry ($18.57) and in the summary ($18.66) differ slightly; the net debit of $17.35 is consistent across both accounts and is the figure that governs all subsequent arithmetic.

#### Trade three: Meta

##### The thesis

Meta is a different kind of entry: it is a post-earnings momentum entry, taken the day after the report. Meta reported the previous evening and the stock is up **8%** on the day. Adam's general practice is to wait after earnings — "normally, I would wait for a few days for the thing to settle, especially if the stock plunges after the earnings" — but he distinguishes the direction of the reaction: "In this case, it is positively reacted, so actually I don't mind entering it here because if the stock reacts positively, the momentum tends to carry on in the next few days."

He considers Amazon as an alternative, which is reporting earnings that same day, and notes that trading through an earnings event does not concern him. But he prefers Meta on conviction and enters Meta instead.

##### The capital warning

Meta at $510 is an expensive stock and the DS Hammer on it costs roughly $6,000 per contract. Adam interrupts the construction to issue an unusually direct risk warning, and repeats it twice: "because the stock price is higher than normal stocks, so the risk per trade is higher. Now, if you're not comfortable with this high-priced stock, just skip it. Go with a smaller one. Like Amazon, [which is] less than half of this price." And again after pricing it: "Again, if you're not comfortable with high capital stock like this, just skip it completely. It's your own money at the end of the day. You need to be comfortable with that. Otherwise, just choose a smaller-priced stock. I like [Meta], so I don't mind doing this."

This is the position-sizing rule of the strategy stated in plain language. The DS Hammer's maximum loss is small relative to stock, but it is not small in absolute terms on a $500 underlying, and the capital-efficiency argument does not exempt a trader from sizing to their own account.

##### Construction

The stock is at **$510**. Long leg: **February 2025**, strike **510** — an exact at-the-money strike for once — at approximately **$64.55** per the later summary. Short leg: two weeks out to **16 August**. The one-standard-deviation move is **$30**, giving 510 + 30 = **540**, and he sells the **540 strike** for approximately **$4.95**, described in the moment as "almost $5."

The package prices at approximately **$5,900**, and after negotiation he fills at **$59.60**, making the capital and max loss **$5,960**.

##### Analysis

The profile shows **53% probability of winning**, "almost no risk on the upside," and a break-even "a few points below the current stock price." Maximum profit read off the curve is **$2,000**. Two thousand against $5,988 of capital gives **33% maximum return on investment before rolling** — again clearing the 25% screen.

He negotiates from 59.6, watches the mark move to 60.25 against him as Meta's momentum strengthens, and eventually gets filled.

| Meta entry, 1 Aug 2024 | |
|---|---|
| Long leg | Buy 1× Feb 2025 510 call, ~$64.55 |
| Short leg | Sell 1× 16 Aug 2024 540 call, ~$4.95 |
| Net debit at fill | $59.60 → **$5,960 capital and max loss** |
| Probability of profit at entry | ~53–54% |
| Max profit before rolling | ~$2,000 |
| Max ROI before rolling | ~33% |

##### The stop loss made concrete

With the Meta position on the screen, Adam does something he does not do for the other two: he locates the stop loss geographically on the profit chart. "Now, this trade has about $6,000 max loss. So the moment the stock dropped to somewhere here, **450**, where it hits $3,000 loss, which is half of my max loss, I will cut loss."

He then attaches the discipline speech that goes with it, which applies to both directions: "in trading, you cannot be 100% winning. There will be times when the whole thing goes against you. And you need to be disciplined in cutting losses. You also need to be disciplined in taking profits if it gets to good profits. Don't be too greedy."

#### The four scenarios, enumerated

With all three positions open, Adam pauses to enumerate every scenario that can occur between now and the short calls' expiry on 16 August, and the response to each. This is the complete adjustment decision tree of the strategy and it deserves to be set out formally.

**Scenario one — the stock rises but stays below the short strike.** This is the best case. The short call decays toward zero while the long call appreciates. "Guess what? The 540 short call there will be depleting its value to near zero. Then when it goes below 10 cents, I will roll that 540 to another week, another two weeks to collect more premium." The theoretical optimum is that the stock finishes exactly at the short strike on expiry day, which is where maximum profit lives — "the best would be it moves to 540 and expires on that day. That's where you get the max profit. But most of the time, you won't be able to get the max profit."

**Scenario two — the stock rises past the short strike.** Second-best. "Don't worry. The short call may be losing money, but the trade would still be profitable. It's still very profitable here." The monitoring object is the short call's delta. "If the delta of the short call goes beyond 80, you roll it up and out further in time to create more headroom for the upside."

He then demonstrates a roll-up hypothetically on the fresh Meta position. The short 540 currently has a delta of **24** — "nothing to worry about." He walks through what would happen as the stock rises: "the 24 will become 30, become 45, become 50, become 60, become 80, the higher the stock price becomes." And then the action: "if this short call delta exceeds 80, I will buy to close this one, and I go to, let's say, two weeks from now, and I sell a higher strike. I would sell like 560 at the lower delta."

The pricing target for a roll-up is stated precisely, and it is one of the most useful numbers in the module: **exchange the old short call for a new one of equal or greater value.** "Let's say I do it right now. I buy to close this one. I pay $4.70 to close. And I go to 560 and I sell 560 expiring in a month and I collect also $4.70. So that means I exchange this one for this one, same value. But the new one has a higher strike price. That means my trade will have more headroom for the upside. That's the way I roll it. Roll it up and roll it out. Ideally, I exchange the old one for the new one with the same value, or the new one would have more value [and] I would exchange the option for a credit. That one [is] even better."

The mechanism being exploited here is that moving *out* in time adds extrinsic value while moving *up* in strike removes it, so by choosing the right combination of new strike and new expiry you can usually raise the ceiling for approximately zero net cost. Time is the currency you spend to buy headroom.

**Scenario three — the stock goes nowhere.** "It's okay. The trade would still make some money. There's still money here, a few hundred dollars." This is the positive-theta case, and it is why the strategy tolerates a "neutral to bullish" technical setup rather than requiring a bullish one.

**Scenario four — the stock falls.** The losing case. "I can roll the 540 down to 530 or down to 520, or at minimum I roll it down to 510. I will not roll it below the 510 because the 510 is the long call strike. My rule is never roll the short call below the long [call strike]."

He is explicit that rolling down has diminishing returns and about what happens as it exhausts itself. "If I keep rolling at 510 and the stock keeps going down and I cannot roll it further, that means I collect less and less and less premium every time I roll, which is fine. By rolling like that, you buy time for the stock to recover. So if the stock recovers, eventually, you make all the money back. Now, in case the stock never recovers — at some point in time, it keeps going down and you hit the stop loss. And I exit the trade at the stop loss."

That is the honest account of the strategy's failure mode. Rolling down buys time; it does not manufacture a recovery. If the stock does not come back, the position dies at −50%.

| Scenario | What happens | Action |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Stock rises, stays below short strike | Short call decays to near zero; long call appreciates. Best case | When short call value < ~$0.10, roll out to a new expiry at a new one-SD strike, collecting credit |
| 2. Stock rises past short strike | Short call loses, long call gains more; net position still profitable | Monitor short-call delta. If it exceeds 80 (or exceeds the long call's delta), roll up and out for even value or a credit |
| 3. Stock goes sideways | Positive theta accrues; modest profit | Roll on schedule when short call depletes |
| 4. Stock falls | Position loses; break-even is above spot | Roll the short call down for more premium — but **never below the long call strike**. Continue until recovery or until −50% ROI, then cut |

#### The exit rules restated

He closes the webinar by restating the three operating rules that govern everything after entry:

"Roll the short call upon expiry or when the delta exceeds 80. Take profit between 50% to 150% return on investment. Cut loss when it hits 50% of the max loss."

---

### Part Five: First Rolls — 16 August 2024

Two weeks after entry, all three short calls expire on the same day. In the interim the market has been extremely hostile. Adam catalogues what happened: "there were some massive sell-offs in the market because of the yen carry trade, because of Warren Buffett selling [the] Apple stake, because of Middle East political tensions. And for Nvidia, particularly, there was news that the latest chip that the company will launch would be delayed — the Blackwell." A macro shock and a company-specific shock arriving together in the first two weeks of a trade is close to a worst case, and the sequence is therefore an unusually good test of the framework.

#### Nvidia: from −40% to +20%

Nvidia fell from approximately $120 at entry to **$95** at the trough. Adam quantifies the drawdown against the stop loss with precision, and this is the single most important risk-management moment in the module: "At that point in time, the trade was losing money, but the loss was not at the stop loss. I think it's about **40%, negative 40% return on investment**. So it's not at 50 yet. So I held onto the trade and continued to wait."

A 40% adverse excursion against a 50% stop is uncomfortably close, and it is worth being clear about what the rule demanded: the rule demanded that he hold. Had the stock fallen another few dollars he would have cut and the subsequent recovery would have been irrelevant. This is not a story about the wisdom of holding losers; it is a story about following a pre-committed threshold in both directions.

The stock recovered to **$124** by 16 August, slightly above the entry price. The short 130 call is therefore going to expire worthless, with **three cents** of value left. The position has swung from a 40% loss to a profit of **approximately $520, or +20% return on investment**. That is not in the profit target range — "it's still not at my profit range, which is plus 50% to plus 150% return on investment. So I would continue to hold on to the trade, keep rolling the short call and collecting more premium and wait for the stock to go even higher."

##### The roll decision

He is still bullish, for the reason he entered: "as I mentioned at the trade setup, Nvidia stock tends to rally ahead of the earnings. Now, the rally has started, but the earnings will be coming in the next two weeks. So then I would expect the rally to continue to go a little bit further."

He chooses a **one-week** roll rather than two, for an explicit volatility reason: "with the implied volatility being high right now before the earnings, I could collect a very good premium, even with one-week expiration." Elevated pre-earnings implied volatility means a one-week option is paying like a two-week option, so he takes the shorter tenor and keeps optionality.

The new expiry is 23 August, seven days out. The one-standard-deviation indicator reads **$7.80**, call it $8. Adding $8 to $124 gives **$132**, and the 132 strike pays about **$1.10**. He sanity-checks the yield: "one week, $1.10 is almost 0.8%. So not bad. So if you keep collecting 0.8% a week, that would be like 3-plus percent per month."

He also looks one cycle ahead and previews the earnings premium: "the next one I expect to collect even more because the next one will be crossing the earnings. So the one that expires next week on August 23rd, that one is still before earnings. But the one after that would be huge. The one that expires on 30th of August, the premium would be huge." He checks: the 132 strike expiring 30 August, which spans the 28 August earnings, is quoted at **"$4 plus"** — roughly four times the pre-earnings weekly. "Huge, because the volatility will be even higher if it crosses the earnings."

Execution: buy to close the 130 at two cents, sell to open the 23 August 132. He queues at $1.07, reduces to $1.05, then to $1.00, and finally fills at **$0.98** as the market sells off during the negotiation. Note the direction of the concession — a falling market lowers the value of the call he is selling, so the achievable credit shrinks while he waits, and he takes what he can get rather than hold out for a price the market has moved away from.

#### Alphabet: rolling down while losing

Alphabet is the problem child. Entered at $174, the stock has fallen about $10 to the $164 area, and it has fallen for a specific reason: "Google received an unfavorable ruling from the DOJ, from the US government, and the government could potentially break up the company, and that has put the stock price under pressure."

The position is losing **approximately $500, or −29% return on investment**. Against a −50% stop, that is a live but not yet triggered loss. "So it's still not at the stop loss, which is negative 50. So I will roll this one also, buying time for the stock to recover... I believe Google is fundamentally good stock and it will recover. So I just need to buy more time."

##### The roll

The 180 short call has no value and expires today. He rolls **out two weeks** rather than one — the opposite tenor choice from Nvidia, and for the opposite reason: Nvidia had an earnings event coming that made the near expiry rich, Alphabet has nothing, so he stretches for premium. "For Nvidia, I roll it to next week because the week after that will be earnings. For Google, I just rolled it out straight to two weeks from now to collect a little bit more premium."

The one-standard-deviation move for the 30 August expiry is approximately **$7**. Adding $7 to the stock price of approximately $165 gives **$172.50**, which is a listed strike. He sells it for about **$0.77**.

He then performs the mandatory check, and states it aloud, which is exactly the discipline the rule requires: "And by the way, the new one I'm selling, 172.5, is still above the long call, which is 170, which is good." The floor held with $2.50 to spare. Had the stock fallen a further few dollars, the one-standard-deviation calculation would have pointed at a strike below 170 and he would have been forced to sell 170 itself — collecting less premium — rather than follow the indicator down.

He fills at **$0.78 net credit**, buying back at one cent and selling the new call at 79 cents.

#### Meta: rolling up into all-time highs

Meta is the star. Entered around $510–520, it "has recovered very strongly, and even went above the entry point. Today, it's already at $529." Adam notes that Meta too had a drawdown — "at the trough, the loss was at about, I think it's about 25, 30%, still not at my stop loss. So I held onto it" — and it has since turned profitable, showing **$1,300-plus profit, +22% return on investment**. Still short of the 50% target.

The 540 short call has **14 cents** left and expires today. He rolls out one week, to 23 August.

The strike selection here introduces a technique that becomes increasingly important through the module: **combining the one-standard-deviation calculation with a chart-based resistance level**. The one-standard-deviation move for the coming week is **$18**, and $528 + $18 = **$546**. He then checks that against the chart: "Remember, 546 will be a new all-time high because the last swing high, that is 542. So it's a right strike price. I mean, the stock could break through it, but I think that would be a little bit of resistance in the next one week or so."

There is no 546 strike, so he sells the **545**, collecting **$2.71** — "so for one week, I got $271. And I still have plenty of headroom for the upside. And there will be resistance up there also."

He negotiates from $2.60, reduces a cent, and fills at **$2.54**.

The logic being applied is that the ideal short strike satisfies two independent conditions at once: it is roughly one standard deviation away, meaning the option-implied probability of it being breached is low; and it sits at or above a technical level where price has previously stalled, meaning the chart-implied probability of it being breached is also low. When the two agree, the strike is chosen with more confidence than either method alone would justify. He repeats this pattern on Nvidia on 12 September and on Amazon on 25 October.

#### The 16 August rolls in summary

| Trade | Old short call | New short call | Net credit | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nvidia | 130, 16 Aug (2¢) | 132, 23 Aug | +$0.98 | 1-week tenor to exploit high pre-earnings IV; roll **up** on recovery |
| Alphabet | 180, 16 Aug (1¢) | 172.50, 30 Aug | +$0.78 | 2-week tenor for premium; roll **down** on decline, checked against 170 long strike floor |
| Meta | 540, 16 Aug (13¢) | 545, 23 Aug | +$2.54 | 1-week tenor; roll **up** to a strike at a new all-time high, doubling as resistance |

---

### Part Six: The Home Stretch — Nvidia and Meta to Close (27 September – 11 October 2024)

Between the 16 August rolls and the next update Adam actually gives us, six weeks pass in the transcript record, and by the time the recording resumes on **Friday 27 September** the Nvidia and Meta positions have each been rolled several more times without a dedicated video — the roll history for that stretch survives only in the closing recap Adam narrates on 11 October, and it is folded into the summary table below rather than reconstructed scene by scene. Google, meanwhile, does not reappear in the surviving footage at all between 16 August and its exit; its ending is likewise known only from that same closing recap. What the 27 September and 11 October recordings *do* show directly is the last live decision points on Nvidia and Meta, and they are worth walking through in the same detail as everything before them, because they are the moments where the delta-comparison rule and the profit-target discipline are applied under real, camera-visible pressure.

#### 27 September: Nvidia rolls again, Meta is left alone on purpose

Adam opens by noting the date explicitly — "two weeks after I wrote the short call of Nvidia" — and reports that the stock has drifted from about $119 on 12 September to $122 on 27 September, a gain of roughly $3, with some chop in between ("it went down, it went up, it is retracing again"). The trade's profit has grown from roughly $500 to roughly $600 on that move. In return-on-investment terms the position sits at **33%**, still short of the 50%-to-150% target band.

The short call — struck at 131, the strike he had rolled to on 12 September — is expiring that same day with its value depleted, so there is, in his words, "no point to wait longer." He closes it and rolls out two weeks to **11 October**, and rather than moving the strike he keeps it at the **same 131 level**, reasoning that the one-standard-deviation indicator for the new expiry reads plus-or-minus **$9**, which added to the roughly $122 stock price lands almost exactly back on 131. The roll collects a net credit of **$1.25**, or $125 for one contract, negotiated down from an opening ask of $1.25 to a fill after the market moved a little — the transcript shows him queuing at 1.25 and getting filled there after a small back-and-forth. This is the fifth rolling round of the Nvidia trade counting from entry, and it brings the running cost of the position down to **$1,995** — just under the original $2,050 capital, meaning the accumulated credits from five rolls had by this point repaid almost the entire initial entry debit even before the position's own directional gains are counted.

The Meta position, by contrast, gets no action at all on this date, and Adam is explicit that this is a decision rather than an oversight. The short call he had rolled up to earlier — the 555 strike — is now in the money, with the stock having pushed above it, yet he declines to roll. His stated reasoning runs through the delta-comparison test in full: "the delta of the 555 short call here is at 67. So less than 80. That means I can wait a little bit longer. Secondly, this 67 still below the delta of the long call, which is 75. So the net of the two legs, I still have a net positive delta for the trade. That means the trade would continue to benefit if the stock goes higher from here." He adds that an in-the-money short call sold above the current retracement level would actually give some downside protection if Meta pulls back toward 555, which he calls "the best scenario" for the position's remaining two weeks. As of that day the Meta trade, net of $136 already realized in losses from earlier rolling rounds, is showing a profit of **$2,388**, a return on investment of **40%** — again inside striking distance of, but not yet inside, the profit-target range. The short call on that position still has two weeks left to run, so there is, as he puts it, "no action that I need to take today on this trade."

#### 11 October: closing both trades on the same day, for two different but related reasons

Two weeks later, on **Friday 11 October**, both surviving positions are closed in the same recording, and Adam's stated logic for closing each one is worth separating out because it illustrates a genuine judgment call rather than a mechanical rule.

**Nvidia** has continued to run. The stock, which sat at roughly $124–125 at the last roll, is now trading at about **$135**, a ten-point move in two weeks, and the 131-strike short call is deep in the money. A pure application of the roll-up rule would say: the delta has certainly cleared 80, so roll up and out to create more headroom. Adam instead declines to roll, and gives two reasons. First, a chart reason: the stock is "approaching the all-time high, which is 140.76," and the stochastic indicator he prefers is reading "highly overbought," so he expects "a pullback before it breaks out to a new all-time high." Rolling up under those conditions would mean paying a debit to buy headroom just before the stock retraces — which he names directly as "the worst scenario" among all the rolling situations the strategy can produce: "roll the short call up, paying a big debit, and see the stock right plunging." Second, and independently sufficient on its own, the trade has already reached the profit-target range: it is showing a return on investment of **61%**, comfortably inside the 50%-to-150% band. His conclusion is to bank the win rather than pay to extend it into a stretched chart: "why not just take the profit and run? And then if there's a pullback, I can consider re-entering the trade."

He closes the position by buying back the near-worthless 131 short call and selling the March 2025 118 long call in a single two-legged order, negotiating the exit price up from a first attempt at $25.45 down to a fill at **$25.42**. The trade's final realized profit comes to **$1,247** (he separately reads it as "$1,248" a few lines earlier in the recording, and the two figures are close enough to be the same number stated twice with a small rounding slip), which against the original $2,050 of capital is a return on investment of **60.8%**.

**Meta** is closed for a related but distinct reason. The stock has continued rallying since the 555 roll — up from roughly $570 at the time of that roll to nearly **$587** on 11 October, almost twenty points higher — and the 555 short call is now deep in the money. Adam again declines to roll it up, citing the same worry about paying a large debit into an overextended stock. But unlike Nvidia, the Meta trade has not quite reached the 50% floor of the profit-target range: it is showing **44%** return on investment. He treats that as close enough to count: "though the profit has not been at 50% yet, but 44 is good enough... call it a good trade." He closes both legs together — buying back the 555 short call and selling the February 2025 510 long call — starting his ask around $73.9 (against a mid near $73.8) and working it down through $73.52 to a final fill of **$73.72**, netting a total realized profit of **$2,602** on the $5,960 of original capital, a return on investment of **43.7%**.

#### The Nvidia trade, entry to close, in full

Adam narrates the complete roll history of the Nvidia position immediately after closing it, and the sequence — five rolls between entry and exit — is the clearest single illustration in the whole module of how repeated small credits compound into a materially lower cost basis over the life of a trade.

| Date | Action | Detail | Credit / debit | Running trade cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Aug 2024 | Entry | Buy 118 call (Mar 2025) $21.86; sell 130 call (16 Aug) $1.36 | Net debit $20.50 | $2,050 (capital / max loss) |
| 16 Aug 2024 | Roll 1 | Short call 130 → 132 (higher strike, more headroom) | +$0.98 ($98) | $1,952 |
| 23 Aug 2024 | Roll 2 | Short call 132 → 146, expiry crosses the 28 Aug earnings | +$2.58 ($258) | $1,694 |
| 30 Aug 2024 | Roll 3 | Short call 146 → 130 (rolled down after a price drop) | +$1.22 ($122) | $1,572 |
| 12 Sept 2024 | Roll 4 | Short call 130 → 131 | +$1.52 ($152) | $1,420 |
| 27 Sept 2024 | Roll 5 | Short call 131 → 131, same strike, two weeks out | +$1.25 ($125) | $1,295 |
| 11 Oct 2024 | Close | Buy back short call; sell long call for $25.42 | Exit credit $2,542 | — |

Note that the table's running-cost column shows $1,295 after the fifth roll where the video's own recap states $1,995 — the recording itself gives the figure as "$1,995" when narrating that step and the arithmetic of summing the five credits against the $2,050 entry debit (2,050 − 98 − 258 − 122 − 152 − 125 = 1,295) does not match that stated number; both figures are reproduced here as spoken, without resolving the discrepancy, since the source is inconsistent at that point. Whichever running-cost figure is correct, the closing arithmetic Adam gives is unambiguous: an exit credit of $2,542 against the trade's cost produces a final profit of **$1,247**, a return on investment of **60.8%**, realized over what he calculates as **71 days** from entry to close.

#### The Meta trade, entry to close, in full

The Meta position went through six rolling rounds — one more than Nvidia — reflecting the more volatile, harder-charging path the stock took over the same period, including one roll-down when the price pulled back mid-sequence.

| Date | Action | Detail | Credit / debit | Running trade cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Aug 2024 | Entry | Buy 510 call (Feb 2025) $64.55; sell 540 call (16 Aug) $4.95 | Net debit $59.60 | $5,960 (capital / max loss) |
| 15 Aug 2024 | Roll 1 | Short call 540 → 545 (higher, more headroom) | +$2.54 ($254) | $5,706 |
| ~22 Aug 2024 | Roll 2 | Short call 545 → 550 | +$2.65 ($265) | $5,441 |
| ~29 Aug 2024 | Roll 3 | Short call 550 → 540 (rolled down after a price drop) | +$3.05 ($305) | $5,136 |
| 12 Sept 2024 | Roll 4 | Short call 540 → 545 (higher again) | +$3.55 ($355) | $4,781 |
| 19 Sept 2024 | Roll 5 | Short call 545 → 555 (higher again, more headroom) | +$0.31 ($31) | $4,755 (per the video's own arithmetic; the actual subtraction of $31 from $4,781 gives $4,750, a $5 discrepancy left as stated) |
| 11 Oct 2024 | Close | Buy back short call; sell long call for $73.52 | Exit credit $7,352 | — |

Against that running cost the exit produces a final profit of **$2,602**, a return on investment of **43.7%**, over the same **71 days**.

#### Google's ending, as recapped

The Google (Alphabet) position, whose entry and first roll were covered above in Part Five, does not get its own dedicated monitoring video in the surviving material between the 16 August roll and its eventual exit — the only account of what happened to it comes from the closing recap Adam gives at the end of the 11 October video. According to that recap, the position was rolled down a second time on **30 August**, from the **172.50** strike it held after the first roll down to **170**, exactly at the long call's own strike — the hard floor the rule never permits crossing — for a credit of **51 cents** ($51), which brought the running trade cost down to **$1,606**. The stock continued to decline, and on **9 September**, thirty-two days after entry, it hit the stop-loss threshold. Adam exited by collecting **$5.54** ($554) against the $1,606 cost, for a loss on the trade of **$1,052** (he also gives the closing table figure as a loss of "$152,000," which is plainly a transcription artifact for $1,052 and is treated here as such). Divided by the original $1,735 capital, that loss works out, by his own explicit division, to **negative 60.6%** return on investment — though the summary table he reads a few lines later states the figure as **negative 69.6%**. Both numbers are given in the source; they are not reconciled here, and the reader should treat the loss as being in that vicinity — a loss modestly larger than the strategy's own 50% stop threshold, consistent with the fact that a short call sitting at the exact floor strike cannot be rolled down any further to cushion a continuing decline, so the position rides the last leg of the fall essentially unhedged on the short side.

#### The three-trade portfolio, as Adam totals it

With all three of the 1 August entries now closed, Adam totals the results in a single table.

| Trade | Final P&L | Return on investment |
|---|---|---|
| Nvidia | +$1,247 | +60.8% |
| Meta | +$2,602 | +43.7% |
| Google (Alphabet) | −$1,052 (stated once as −$152 in the summary, treated as a transcription artifact) | −60.6% (also stated once as −69.6%) |
| **Total** | **+$2,797** | **stated as +28.7%** |

The stated combined return of "positive 28.7%" does not correspond to any of the ordinary ways of aggregating the three individual returns — it is neither the simple sum of the three percentages (which would be roughly 44 or 34, depending on which Google figure is used) nor an obviously capital-weighted blend of them under the capital figures given elsewhere in the module. It is reproduced here exactly as narrated, without an attempt to reconstruct the arithmetic behind it, since the source gives no further detail on how it was computed. What is unambiguous is the dollar total: three trades entered together on the same day, carried through a macro-driven correction, a company-specific earnings surprise, and — in Google's case — an adverse regulatory headline, netted a combined profit of $2,797. Adam's closing comment on the set is the same one he returns to throughout the module: "there's no like invincible kind of strategy here. There will be losing trades, there will be winning trades all the time. As long as you continue to trade this one over the long run and it generates a good return for you, that is good enough."

### Part Seven: The Amazon Trade — A Complete Cycle (30 July – 8 November 2024)

Running in parallel with the Nvidia/Alphabet/Meta cohort, and narrated as a separate real-time teaching example rather than as part of the 1 August webinar, is a fourth DS Hammer position on Amazon. It is the single most fully documented trade in the entire module — nine roll-or-hold decisions recorded across ten separate updates, from construction on 30 July 2024 through to a final close on 8 November 2024 — and because every decision point survives on tape, it is worth treating as the definitive worked example of the strategy's management framework operating over its full, intended lifespan.

#### Entry: 30 July 2024

Amazon is trading at **$184** on the morning of the entry, half an hour after the market opens on a day Adam describes as "kind of flat." He goes to the option chain and selects the **January 2025** series, which shows **171 days to expiration** — about six months, comfortably inside the three-to-nine-month window for the long leg. There is no listed strike at exactly 184, so he faces the familiar choice between 180 and 185 and picks **180**, slightly in the money, with a delta of **63**.

For the short leg he selects **16 August 2024**, seventeen days out — a touch under three weeks, at the outer edge of the one-to-three-week band. The one-standard-deviation indicator for that expiry reads **plus or minus $16.80**; adding roughly $16 to the $184 stock price lands on **200**, which is a listed strike, and he sells it, collecting a mark price of **$2.56**.

The package as first priced would cost **$18.77** to enter — he pays $21.32 to buy the long call and collects $2.56 for the short call. Before sending the order he analyzes the risk profile on the platform, moving the "set slices" break-even date to the short call's expiration. The break-even sits at approximately **$181**, "slightly below the current stock price," which he reads as a favorable buffer. The probability of winning at entry is almost **55%**, and the maximum profit read off the peak of the curve is approximately **$1,240**, which against the entry cost gives a maximum return on investment before any rolling of about **66%** — comfortably clearing the 25% screen. He also locates the stop loss on the chart in dollar and share-price terms at the same time: "stop loss will be half of this price, which is about... $990... when the supply drops to about $160."

He negotiates the fill as the stock ticks higher during the process, raising his limit from the initial $18.77 in small increments to keep pace with the market, and the position is ultimately filled with a final recorded cost that the closing recap states plainly: the long call cost **$21.48**, the short call collected **$2.62**, for a net entry debit of **$18.86**, or **$1,886** of capital — the number that governs every percentage calculation for the rest of the trade's life. (The live recording's spoken numbers during negotiation — "18.77," then a garbled "$186.86" — are consistent with this $1,886 figure once read as dollars-per-contract rather than as a raw price.)

| Amazon entry, 30 Jul 2024 | |
|---|---|
| Long leg | Buy 1× Jan 2025 180 call, delta 63, $21.48 |
| Short leg | Sell 1× 16 Aug 2024 200 call, $2.62 |
| Net debit at fill | $18.86 → **$1,886 capital and max loss** |
| Probability of profit at entry | ~55% |
| Break-even at short expiry | ~$181 |
| Max profit before rolling | ~$1,240 |
| Max ROI before rolling | ~66% |
| Stop-loss level (chart) | Stock near $160, loss near $990 |

#### 16 August 2024: the first roll, down, into a losing position

By the time the short call expires, Amazon has fallen hard — Adam attributes the decline specifically to an earnings report that "missed the expectations," which sent the stock lower before it partially recovered — and on 16 August the stock sits at about **$177–178**, down six to seven points from entry. The trade is showing a loss of **$400 to $412**, a return on investment of roughly **negative 21%**. He notes that a week or ten days earlier, at the trough of the move, the loss had been close to negative 45%, "close to the stop loss" but not through it, which is why the position was held rather than cut.

The 200-strike short call has expired worthless with nothing left to harvest, so he rolls. He selects a two-week expiry and, being still bullish that the earnings miss was overdone, rolls to the new one-standard-deviation strike, which the indicator puts at about **$8 above the current price** — $177 plus $8 gives roughly **$185**, which is where he sells, collecting **$1.34** (stated in the live recording as "1.30-something" and confirmed in the closing recap as $1.34, or $134 for one contract). He explicitly reasons through the yield before accepting the trade: "if I could get anything between 1.5 to 2% yield from the premium a month, that could be good enough... $1.30 for two weeks... times two [for a month]... $2.60 divided by the current stock price, 177, that is 1.5%. That's good enough."

#### 30–31 August 2024: rolling down again as the decline continues

A week or so later — recorded on Saturday 31 August because, Adam explains, he had not recorded the prior day — the 185-strike short call has expired worthless, and the stock, having been roughly flat and then rebounding strongly the day before, is back near where it had been a week earlier. He had already rolled the prior evening, selling a new short call at **182.50**, the one-standard-deviation strike at the moment of that roll, for a credit later confirmed at **89 cents** ($89). The trade's overall loss has not meaningfully improved on net — it is "still losing about $400" — because the newly sold 182.50 call is itself underwater following the subsequent bounce, offsetting the benefit of the roll. Across the two rolling rounds completed so far, he notes having realized **$395** of credit from the two closed short calls, even as the position as a whole remains in a loss. He reiterates the stop-loss discipline: the position is not close to the negative-50% threshold, and if the stock continues to recover, he expects the loss to turn around.

#### 12 September 2024: rolling up as the recovery takes hold

By 12 September the stock has recovered to about **$185**, pushing the 182.50 short call into the money one day before its expiry. Its delta has not yet crossed 80, but Adam elects to roll a day early rather than wait, on the now-familiar reasoning that being bullish argues for acting before the trigger rather than at it. The loss on the position has already shrunk from over $400 to under $200 — he reads it as **$196** at this point — evidence that the accumulated rolling credits are starting to outpace the drag from the in-the-money short call.

He rolls out two weeks to **27 September**, and this time explicitly targets a strike that lets him avoid paying a debit: buying back the 182.50 call costs about $2.80, so he looks for a new strike paying roughly the same amount, and finds it at **187.50**, priced around $2.90. The roll nets a small credit of **20 cents** ($20 — narrated in the moment as "16" cents before settling on this figure in the closing recap). He confirms the strike sits at a level he expects to act as resistance, citing the stochastic indicator reading into overbought territory, and reasons the stock "could go a little bit higher... but it will not go a lot more from here" — a forecast that, as the next update shows, does not hold for very long.

#### 23 September 2024: rolling up again, paying a small debit for headroom

Eleven days later the stock has continued climbing past his expectation, trading near **$192**, roughly $7 above the level at the last roll, and the 187.50 short call — now four days from its own expiry — is deep enough in the money that its delta is "approaching 80." Crucially, Adam compares that delta directly against the long call's own delta, which by this point has fallen to **71**: "if the share price continues to go higher, it will hurt the trade, right? Because the trade has a net negative delta right now." This is the same comparison test articulated on the Amazon illustration and the Meta hold decision earlier in the module, applied here in the direction that argues *for* action rather than against it.

He rolls out three weeks, to **18 October**, choosing a target strike, **192.50**, specifically to minimize the debit paid — "I don't want to pay a lot when I roll it up, especially now the stock price is a little bit overextended" — and after negotiating from an opening bid of 25 cents up through 32 and 35 cents as the stock moved against him mid-negotiation, fills at a net debit of **35 cents** ($35). This is the only true debit roll recorded on the Amazon trade — every other roll in its history is a net credit — and it lands exactly on the principle stated earlier in the module: rolling up costs money when the underlying is already running, and the cost is worth paying because it buys headroom on a position that is winning. By this point the trade, which had been solidly underwater for weeks, is "almost turned around" and nearly at break-even.

#### 18 October 2024: rolling at the same strike as the stock consolidates

By 18 October the stock has pulled back roughly $2.50 from the level at the last roll, so the 192.50 short call — now expiring that day — finishes essentially at the money with only a few cents of value left. Rather than adjusting the strike, Adam rolls to the **same 192.50 level**, one week out, reasoning through the same trade-off he names on every roll where the chart looks stretched: rolling to a slightly lower or equal strike than the pure one-standard-deviation calculation would suggest ("$195 or so") sacrifices a little theoretical headroom in exchange for a better premium and, in his words, better downside protection. He collects **$1.33** ($133) for the roll. The trade's profitability, despite the stock having drifted down over the three weeks since the last action, has nonetheless turned from its earlier loss into a genuine profit: **8%** return on investment.

#### 25 October 2024: rolling up into a resistance level ahead of earnings

One week later the stock is essentially flat, still near **$189**, and Adam notes explicitly that a flat stock is good for this trade — theta continues to work regardless. The 192.50 short call, again down to a few cents of remaining value, is rolled with an eye toward Amazon's upcoming earnings release on **31 October**, meaning the new expiry will span the event and should carry richer premium as a result. He selects the following week, **1 November**, and again layers a chart consideration on top of the one-standard-deviation math: the indicator suggests **$13** above the current price, pointing to roughly **202.50**, and he notes independently that the prior swing high sits at **201**, so his chosen strike sits just above that level — "the stock right will need to break out to a new all-time high to hit my short call strike, which is a very good strike price to sell because I sell at the resistance level." He fills the roll at a net credit of **$1.75** ($175, after negotiating down a cent or two from an opening $1.76). The trade's profit at this point stands at roughly **$240 to $245**, a return on investment of about **13%**.

#### 1 November 2024: rolling again after a blowout earnings reaction

Amazon's earnings, released after hours the prior evening, beat on both revenue and profit and came with a raised forecast; the stock gaps up about six percent, or roughly twelve dollars, and is trading near **$199** the next morning — about ten points above where it had been rolled the previous week. Adam observes with some satisfaction that the 202.50 strike he had chosen specifically because it sat just above the prior swing high has done exactly the job he intended: the stock rallies hard but "could not break above that swing high" before the short call's expiry, so the position captures essentially the entire earnings pop without the short call being forced deep in the money. He rolls the now-worthless 202.50 call out one more week, to a new one-standard-deviation strike roughly **$7 to $8** above the current price — he computes it as **$205** — and, because he intends to keep riding the rally rather than lock in the current profit, sets his sights on the higher end of the target range: "I will aim to get a higher end of my profit target range, which is maybe 100% return on investment or even higher." The trade at this point is already showing close to **$1,000** of profit, technically inside the 50%-to-150% band, but he elects to hold rather than close, judging the earnings momentum strong enough to justify staying in. The roll to 205 fills at a net credit that the live recording gives as **$1.29** (queued at $1.26, adjusted to $1.23, then filled at $1.29 as the market dipped), though the closing recap a week later states the credit for this specific roll as **$1.20** ($120) — the two figures are close but not identical, and both are given here as stated in their respective recordings.

#### 8 November 2024: closing at the high end of the range

By Thursday 8 November — one day ahead of the 205 short call's own Friday expiry — the stock has broken out further still, past the prior resistance and into new all-time-high territory, trading around **$211**, comfortably above the 205 short strike. The trade is now showing more than **$1,500** of profit, a return on investment of **80%**, solidly inside the target range and closer to its upper half than its lower one. Facing the same choice he had faced with Nvidia and Meta three and a half weeks earlier — roll up for a debit into a stock that looks overextended, or bank the gain — Adam chooses to close: "I really don't want to roll the 205 up paying a big debit when the stock price is overextended. I would rather take the profit here because the profit is good."

He closes both legs in one order — buying back the 205 short call and selling the January 2025 180 long call, which by this point has 71 days left to run — negotiating the exit from an opening ask of $27.80 down through the mark near $27.75 to a final fill of **$27.75**. The closing recap he gives immediately afterward puts the final numbers precisely: the short call was bought back for **$6.03**, the long call sold for **$33.78**, netting the stated $27.75, and against the running trade cost after all the rolling credits, the trade produced a final profit of **$1,523** in the live recording and **$1,525** in the closing summary a few minutes later — again two very close but not identical figures, both reproduced as given. Divided by the original $1,886 of capital, the return on investment comes to **80.9%**, achieved over what Adam calculates as **100 days** from entry to close.

Of the four trades documented in this module, the Amazon position is the one that most completely demonstrates the strategy's central thesis in a single continuous arc: it opens roughly a third underwater within three weeks of entry, is nursed through two consecutive down-rolls without ever approaching the stop-loss threshold, turns the corner as the underlying recovers, absorbs a debit roll to keep pace with a genuine rally, benefits from a strike chosen jointly by statistical and chart logic that happens to cap the stock exactly at its own resistance level through one full cycle, rides a blowout earnings reaction almost entirely uncapped because the short strike had been placed above the point the stock could not immediately clear, and finally exits near the top of the intended profit range having taken seven separate rolling actions across fourteen weeks. Every one of the management rules stated in Part One is visible doing real work somewhere in that sequence.
