### Part Eight: The Consolidated Rulebook

Having now watched the framework operate across four complete trade lifecycles — one cut at a loss, three closed at a profit — it is possible to restate the DS Hammer's rules as a single operating manual, incorporating not only the formal entry checklist from Part One but the refinements that only became visible once real trades were followed week by week.

**Construction.** Buy one call three to nine months from expiry, at or near the money, with a delta of roughly 50 to 60 (in practice, whenever the strike grid forces a choice, Adam consistently takes the slightly in-the-money strike over the slightly out-of-the-money one, landing on deltas in the 62-to-63 range across every live entry in this module). Prefer, where the cost difference is not too large, a long-dated expiry that falls after the underlying's next earnings release, since an option spanning an earnings event carries the elevated implied volatility of that event in its price. Sell one call one to three weeks from expiry, at approximately the platform's one-standard-deviation strike for that expiry, which corresponds to a delta of roughly 20 to 25; raise the strike for a more bullish view, lower it to collect more premium if less bullish. Enter for a net debit; that debit is simultaneously the capital committed and the maximum possible loss.

**Entry screens.** Confirm weekly options exist on the underlying — without them, do not trade it. Confirm the bid-ask spread on the strikes in question is no wider than about 0.4% of the stock price. Confirm open interest exceeds roughly 100 contracts. Confirm the chart is neutral to bullish — bottomed and stabilizing, a dip on an established uptrend, or a breakout — and never a steady or secular downtrend. Confirm, from the risk-profile tool, that the maximum return on investment before any rolling is at least 25%, and that the payoff curve shows no risk on the upside past the short strike.

**The roll trigger, restated precisely.** Roll the short call once its remaining value has depleted to below roughly ten cents — waiting for the literal final cents of a dying option to decay is not worth forgoing a full week of a freshly sold option's decay, and letting a short call fully expire worthless anyway leaves the position with negative net theta in the interim, since a depleted short leg can no longer offset the long leg's own time decay.

**The roll-up trigger.** Roll the short call up and out once its delta approaches or exceeds 80 — or, more precisely and more usefully, once its delta approaches or exceeds the long call's own delta, at which point the net position delta turns negative and further stock appreciation begins to work against rather than for the trade. When rolling up into a stock that is still trending in an orderly way, paying a modest debit for the extra headroom is acceptable, because that debit is being paid out of a position that is already winning. When the stock looks overextended — chart-wise, an approach to an all-time high; indicator-wise, an overbought stochastic reading — avoid rolling up for any meaningful debit, since the combination of paying up and then watching the stock pull back is, in Adam's own words, the single worst outcome the management process can produce. In that situation the better action is often simply to close the trade if it is already inside the profit-target range, rather than pay to extend it.

**The roll-down floor.** When the stock falls, roll the short call down to collect additional premium and buy time for a recovery — but never below the strike of the long call. That floor is structural, not a matter of preference: a short strike below the long strike inverts the position's risk profile. If the stock keeps falling once the short call has already been rolled down to the floor strike, further rolls collect progressively smaller credits, and eventually the position is running with no further room to hedge the short side at all.

**Strike selection as a joint test.** Where possible, choose the new short strike so that the platform's one-standard-deviation calculation and an independent chart level — most often the most recent swing high — point to approximately the same price. A strike that is statistically unlikely to be reached *and* sits at a level where the chart has previously shown resistance is a stronger placement than either signal alone, and the Amazon trade's 25 October and 1 November rolls, both explicitly placed just above the prevailing swing high, are the clearest demonstrations of the technique paying off.

**Earnings and volatility.** Where an earnings release falls within reach of the short call's next natural roll date, prefer to roll into an expiry that spans the event rather than one that falls just before it — implied volatility, and therefore premium, rises as an event approaches, and a roll that crosses the event captures materially more credit than one that does not. This same logic underlies the preference for a long-dated call that expires after the next earnings release rather than before it.

**Tenor choice for the short leg.** Default to the shortest expiry that still pays a worthwhile premium — often weekly on a liquid, volatile name. Stretch to two or three weeks on a quieter stock where the weekly premium is thin. When implied volatility is elevated ahead of a known event, a short tenor can pay as richly as a longer one normally would, which is itself a reason to prefer the shorter expiry in that specific window and preserve flexibility for the following cycle.

**Exit rules.** Take profit when the position's return on investment, measured against the *original* entry capital net of all subsequent rolling debits and credits, reaches somewhere in the 50%-to-150% range — with the specific point chosen inside that range often depending on whether the underlying's momentum still looks intact (favoring the top of the range) or the chart looks stretched (favoring an earlier exit even a little below 50%, as with the Meta close at 44%). Cut the loss once the position's return on investment reaches negative 50%, regardless of conviction about an eventual recovery — the Google trade is the module's own demonstration of why this threshold exists and of what happens when a short-side floor is reached before the stock stops falling.

---

### Part Nine: Closing Synthesis

Four trades, entered across a two-month window in the back half of 2024, close out this module of the course, and it is worth standing back from the individual arithmetic to say plainly what the sequence, taken as a whole, actually demonstrates.

Three of the four trades made money — Nvidia at 60.8%, Meta at 43.7%, Amazon at 80.9% — and one lost money, Google, at a return on investment the source states inconsistently as either negative 60.6% or negative 69.6%, but in either case a loss modestly beyond the strategy's own 50% stop threshold, a consequence of the short call having already been rolled all the way down to its structural floor at the long call's strike before the stock's decline continued. None of the four outcomes was known in advance, and Adam does not pretend otherwise; his own framing of the three-trade Nvidia/Meta/Google cohort — "there's no like invincible kind of strategy here" — applies with equal force to Amazon's eventual success. What distinguishes the four trades is not that three "worked" and one "failed" in some sense that could have been predicted at entry, since all four passed the same entry screens, cleared the same 25%-return threshold, and showed the same absence-of-upside-risk on their payoff charts at the moment of construction. What distinguishes them is what happened after entry, and specifically how the management framework was or was not able to absorb the divergence between what the chart implied at entry and what the stock actually did over the following weeks.

Google is the instructive failure precisely because the framework worked as designed and the trade still lost money. The rule that forbids rolling the short call below the long call's strike is not a suggestion that can be waived when a name looks fundamentally sound; Adam's own conviction that "Google is fundamentally good stock and it will recover" turned out to be wrong within the trade's own time horizon, and once the short call had been rolled down to 170 — the floor — there was no further mechanism available to cushion the continuing decline. The stop-loss threshold existed for exactly this situation, and it did its job: the loss was large, but it was bounded, and it was bounded at a level the trader had chosen in advance rather than one the market chose for him. Contrast this with what an unmanaged, unhedged long stock or long call position would have suffered over the same decline, with no credits accruing and no floor beneath the loss until the position was closed outright.

Amazon is the instructive success for a related but opposite reason: it is not a story of a trade that simply went up and stayed up. It fell roughly six to seven percent in the first two and a half weeks after entry, on a disappointing earnings report, and sat at a loss approaching negative 45% — five points from the stop — before recovering. Nothing in the framework told Adam in advance that the stock would turn; the two down-rolls that carried the position through that stretch were bets that time, not conviction about a specific catalyst, would eventually work in the trade's favor, exactly as the "sideways or slightly down" scenario in the entry framework anticipates. What separates Amazon's outcome from Google's is not superior foresight at entry — both trades were built the same way, against the same rules, with similar probabilities of winning at construction — but simply that one underlying recovered before its trade hit the floor and the other did not. The strategy did not predict which would happen; it was constructed, in both cases, to survive being wrong for a while, and to profit modestly from being wrong for a while and then right, or to lose in a bounded and pre-chosen way from being wrong and staying wrong.

The Nvidia and Meta trades sit between these two poles and show the third recurring pattern in the module: winners that are cut short of their theoretical ceiling not because the rules demanded it, but because the trader judged the marginal reward for staying in — squeezing a position already at 44% or 61% up toward 100% or 150% — no longer worth the marginal risk of paying a debit to roll up into a stock that looked, by both chart structure and momentum indicator, overextended. This is a discretionary overlay on top of the mechanical rules, and Adam treats it as such rather than dressing it up as another fixed threshold: the 50%-to-150% profit range is a band, not a single number, precisely because the decision of where inside that band to exit depends on a read of the underlying's condition at the moment, not on a formula.

Running beneath all four trades, and stated or demonstrated dozens of times across the nine parts of this module, is the single mechanical fact that makes the whole approach work: every roll of the short call, whether up, down, or sideways in strike, is structured to produce a credit far more often than a debit, and each credit permanently lowers the capital at risk in the position without requiring the underlying to have moved at all. Across the four trades combined, dozens of individual rolls were executed, the overwhelming majority of them for credits ranging from a few cents to a few dollars per contract, and it is the patient accumulation of those credits — not any single directional call — that Adam repeatedly identifies as the mechanism separating a portfolio of DS Hammers from the equivalent stock position over the same stretch of calendar time, exactly as the eighteen-trade portfolio comparison in Part Three had already shown in aggregate before any of these four individual trades were even entered. The strategy's name comes from a lever and a block of wood; its results, across four fully documented lifecycles, come from a much less picturesque mechanism — a short option sold and resold, week after week, patiently, at a strike chosen by a formula and checked against a chart, never below a floor, rarely for a debit, until either the target is reached or the stop is hit.

# Part X — The C2D Strategy (Calendar to Diagonal)

## The C2D Strategy: Calendar to Diagonal

### What C2D Stands For

C2D is not an acronym for a Greek, an indicator, or a proprietary formula. It is a description of a sequence. The "C" is the **calendar spread** — the trade you put on first. The "D" is the **diagonal spread** — the trade the calendar becomes once the market gives you the signal to upgrade it. The "2" is the ordinary English word "to." C2D therefore means, quite literally, *calendar-to-diagonal*: you enter as a calendar, and when the underlying is ready to run, you convert that same position into a diagonal so it can run with it.

Adam introduces the strategy as a combination of two structures he first shared publicly at the Black Market 2025 event, and he is careful to frame it as a two-step process rather than as a single static position. Step one is to enter the trade as a C trade — a calendar spread. Step two is to upgrade the C trade into a D trade — a diagonal spread — the moment the market has stabilised and looks ready to rebound or has already started to rally. That is the whole architecture in two sentences, and everything else in this chapter is detail hung on that frame.

The reason the strategy exists at all is a specific market problem. Imagine the market is volatile, pulling back, and you genuinely do not know whether it has bottomed or whether it is about to resume its climb into a year-end Christmas rally. That is not an unusual condition; it is the normal condition for most of the time most traders are looking at charts. The honest answer to "where does this go next?" is "I don't know." A directional trade in that environment is a coin flip with a decay tax attached. What C2D does is refuse to make you guess. You enter with a calendar spread, which pays you while you wait, protects you if you are early, and caps your loss at a number you know before you click. Then, once the chart resolves the uncertainty for you, you convert the position into something that participates in the upside you were waiting for.

Adam summarises the appeal of the entry structure with two claims. First, you collect rent while you wait for the market to stabilise and go up. Second, if you are wrong and the market continues down, your downside risk is protected and limited. He contrasts this explicitly with buying stock: "It's not like you buy a big chunk of Nvidia now and then suddenly it goes down 10 points next week." With a calendar spread you know exactly what your maximum risk is at the moment of entry, and you cannot lose more than that number. Those two properties — being paid to wait, and having a hard-capped loss — are what make it rational to take a position at all when you cannot see the next move.

The strategy is therefore designed, in his own words, for a **choppy market with bullish recovery prospects**. Not for a runaway bull market, where a simple long call or a straight diagonal would be superior from the start. Not for a collapsing bear market, where nothing bullish belongs on the book. For the messy middle, where a stock has fallen or stalled, is grinding around a level, and where you believe the eventual resolution is upward but cannot date it.

### The Two Legs, and Why Each One Exists

A calendar spread has two legs. Adam's mnemonic is deliberately childish and therefore memorable: like a human being, it needs two legs; you cannot do it with one. The point of the joke is that each leg on its own is a bad trade, and that the virtue of the structure comes entirely from the combination. He spends a substantial portion of the first lesson establishing exactly why each leg alone is bad, because unless you understand that, you will not understand what the pairing is fixing.

#### Leg One: the Long-Dated Call — the "Lease"

Leg one is to **buy a long-dated call option**. Long-dated, in his loose but usable definition, means anywhere from roughly three to nine months out, or beyond. Short-dated means a few weeks — one, two, three, or four weeks. He is explicit that these are his own working terms rather than formal industry definitions, and that they are loosely bounded on purpose.

The reason the long leg must be long-dated is the shape of the time-decay curve. Options lose value over time, but not linearly. At the beginning of an option's life the decay is slow; as expiration approaches, the decay accelerates, and most of the money is lost in the final few weeks or even the final few days. If you draw the value of an option against time, you get a curve that is nearly flat at the left and falls off a cliff at the right. Buying long-dated therefore parks you on the flat part of that curve, where the daily bleed is small and manageable.

He demonstrates this live on the platform rather than asserting it. Taking Amazon with the stock at roughly $220 and buying the February 220 call with about 90 days to expiration for a mark price of $18.18 per share — $1,818 for one contract — the platform's theta reads approximately **$10 per day**. A crude arithmetic estimate would be $1,818 divided by 90 days, or about $20 per day. The reason the actual figure is only half that is precisely the non-linearity: at 90 days out you are on the shallow part of the curve. He then simulates the calendar forward on the analysis tab, and the audience watches theta climb as the date advances, eventually exceeding **$20 per day** as the option nears expiration. He steps the simulation back to the actual date, 23 November, and theta returns to roughly $10. The lesson is delivered by demonstration: the closer to expiration, the faster the decay.

The economic metaphor that runs through the entire strategy is introduced here. Buying the long-dated call is **leasing** an asset. Many people want to invest in property for rental income — they buy a property, rent it out for a two or three percent annual yield, and hope the property appreciates. But buying property is enormously capital-intensive; in Singapore that is easily a few million dollars. The equivalent in the stock market is buying 100 shares and selling covered calls against them. That works, but 100 shares of Meta costs roughly $60,000 and you need a full 100 shares before you can sell even one covered call. Adam's point is that this capital intensity puts the covered-call income strategy out of reach for most retail accounts.

The long-dated call replaces the shares. Instead of buying the property, you **lease** it — you take a one-year lease from the landlord and then sublet it on short terms, Airbnb-style, to collect rent. You do not need millions of dollars to control the asset; you need only the lease payment. Applied to options: you do not need $22,000 to control 100 shares of Amazon; you need the $1,818 premium for the long call. The capital requirement collapses and the return on invested capital rises correspondingly. "You lease to rent. You don't buy to rent."

Before moving on, Adam takes the time to teach the call option itself for anyone new. A call gives you the right to buy 100 shares at the strike price by the expiry date. If Amazon trades at $220 and you want 100 shares but do not have the $22,000 — perhaps you are waiting on a year-end bonus two or three months away — the risk is that by the time the cash arrives the stock has run and the $220 entry is gone. Buying the February 220 call locks in the right to buy at $220 for the next 90 days regardless of how high the stock goes, and it costs $18.18 per share, or $1,818 for the contract. He likens it to putting down a deposit to reserve a property: the deposit locks in the agreed price no matter how much the property appreciates afterwards.

The pros and cons of that single long call are then laid out plainly. On the upside, the potential is effectively unlimited — if good news takes Amazon from $220 to $300, you profit enormously on a $1,818 outlay rather than a $22,000 one. On the downside, your maximum loss is the premium paid and nothing more; even if Amazon went to zero you would lose $1,818, whereas 100 shares bought at $220 and falling to $120 would cost you $10,000. That capped loss is genuinely valuable.

But the disadvantage is decisive. Time decay works against you every single day. If the stock simply does not move for 90 days, the entire $1,818 — which is all time value, all "hope value" — is lost. At roughly $20 per day on average, weekday or weekend, holiday or not, you wake up every morning slightly poorer. Early on it might be only $10 a day; in the final weeks it accelerates to $30, $40, $50, even $60 a day. The consequence is that the stock must move up fast enough not merely to be right, but to outrun the decay.

His analogy for this is swimming against the current. If you stop swimming, the river carries you backwards. You can overcome it by swimming very hard, but it is exhausting and the destination is far. He labels this condition **low probability of winning**, and he does not soften it: "buying a single call option is a losing game." He adds the personal confession that gives the claim weight — in twenty years of trading options, the first seven were spent doing exactly this kind of thing, and he lost money most of the time. Many retail traders keep doing it because they do not fully understand how the decay works and remain hopeful that tomorrow's move will overcome it.

So leg one alone is a losing game. It is only worth doing because of what leg two does to it.

#### Leg Two: the Short-Dated Call — the "Rent"

Leg two is to **sell a call option at the same strike price with a much shorter expiry**. Continuing the Amazon example, with the long February 220 call already bought, he looks at the 5 December expiry — thirteen days out, roughly two weeks — at the same 220 strike. The premium there is $6.45 per share, or $645 for one contract. Same stock, same strike, shorter expiry, smaller premium. He walks through the option chain on the platform so that students can see where the numbers come from rather than taking them on trust: you open the trade tab, type in Amazon, pull up the option chain, and read the mark price at each expiry and strike.

This is the **rent** side of the metaphor. Having leased the property long-term, you now rent it out short-term. And when you are a landlord collecting rent, you want time to pass quickly, because faster time means the current tenancy completes and you can sign the next one. Time is on your side. The same is true for an option seller: as the seller of that 220 call, decay works in your favour.

Considered alone, selling that call makes money in three of four scenarios. If the stock falls, you keep the $645. If it goes sideways, you keep the $645. If it rises slightly, you still keep most or all of it. Only if it rises a lot — beyond the $6.45 of premium collected — do you begin to lose, and beyond that point your risk is unlimited.

Adam is blunt about this: selling a naked call is not merely risky but "suicidal." He argues it is more dangerous than selling a naked put without cash securing it, because a put's downside is bounded by the stock going to zero while a call's upside is not bounded at all. His analogy: you do not own a property, but you promise to sell one to somebody, and then the property price goes through the roof. You are now obliged to deliver something you must buy at any price the market demands.

So leg two alone is a dangerous game, with capped profit of $645 and uncapped risk.

The conclusion is the thesis of the whole lesson: do not do one, do not do two, do both simultaneously. Doing both at the same time is exactly what a calendar spread is, and the combination cures the specific defect in each leg.

### The C Trade Assembled

Putting the two Amazon legs together gives the canonical calendar spread:

| Leg | Action | Underlying | Strike | Expiry | DTE | Premium per share | Cash flow (1 contract) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (lease) | Buy to open | AMZN call | 220 | 20 Feb 2026 | ~90 | $18.18 | −$1,818 |
| 2 (rent) | Sell to open | AMZN call | 220 | 5 Dec | 13 | $6.45 | +$645 |
| **Net** | **Debit** | | | | | **$11.73** | **−$1,173** |

The net debit of $11.73 per share, or $1,173 per contract, is simultaneously three things: the capital required, the maximum possible loss, and the net entry price. Adam repeats this identity because it is the anchor for every risk calculation that follows. You cannot lose more than $1,173 on this position — not if Amazon gaps down, not if it goes to zero, not under any circumstance.

Notice what the $645 of collected premium has already done before a single day has passed. It has cut the capital from $1,818 to $1,173, a reduction of roughly one third, achieved instantaneously at entry with no waiting. And because capital equals maximum risk in this structure, it has cut the maximum risk by the same third. That is the first benefit, and it is banked at the moment of execution.

The second benefit is the transformation of theta from enemy to ally. Adam demonstrates this on the platform in three steps, and the demonstration is worth reproducing carefully because it is the single most important mechanical insight in the strategy.

| Position analysed | Platform theta (per day) | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Long Feb 220 call alone | −$10 | You pay the landlord $10 a day |
| Short 5 Dec 220 call alone | +$23 | The tenant pays you $23 a day |
| Both legs together (the C trade) | **+$13** | Net rent collected: $13 a day |

He puts it in the language of the metaphor: "I pay the landlord ten and I collect twenty-three from the guy who rents my home. So net, I still have a net profit of thirteen dollars a day." And he adds the important caveat that the $23 figure will itself accelerate as the short call approaches its own expiry, which is exactly what you want, because the tenant's contribution grows while the landlord's charge stays comparatively flat.

The swimming analogy inverts. You are no longer swimming against the current; you are swimming with it. Even if you stop swimming — even if the stock does nothing at all — the current carries you towards your destination. And because of that, the probability of winning is materially higher than it was for the naked long call.

The third benefit follows from the second leg's presence: the unlimited upside risk of the naked short call is eliminated. Because you own a long call at the same strike, however far the stock runs, your obligation on the short call is covered by your right on the long call. Maximum risk on either side is the $1,173 you paid, full stop.

#### The costs of the structure

Nothing is free. The calendar spread has two clear disadvantages, and Adam names both.

The first is that **profit is capped**. Unlike the naked long call, which has unlimited upside, the calendar's profit tops out. The peak of the payoff diagram is a point, not a ramp.

The second is that the calendar spread has **two loss zones**. The payoff diagram is a triangle: one profit zone in the middle, flanked by a loss zone on the left and a loss zone on the right. If the stock falls a lot, the trade loses. If the stock rises a lot, the trade also loses. This second property — losing when you are right about direction — is counterintuitive and is precisely the problem that step two of C2D exists to solve.

The third practical cost, which he raises when listing disadvantages, is management effort. A calendar spread is not a set-and-forget position. Every time the short call approaches expiry you must roll it, which is the direct analogue of having to find a new tenant every few weeks. "It kind of, you need to put some effort to make money. You need to actively look for tenants to rent on your house."

### Which Charts Qualify: the Setup

Before any of the mechanics matter, the trade has to be placed on the right chart. Adam names three acceptable setups for a C trade:

The first is a **stock dipping on an uptrend**. The trend is clearly, visibly up, but the stock is currently retracing within it. This is his stated favourite.

The second is a **stock consolidating near support**. From the chart you can see the stock has bottomed and is now stabilising or basing, and it looks ready to rally.

The third, described more loosely, is any setup that reads as **neutral to mildly bullish**.

He then tests these criteria against four real charts, polling the audience each time. The exercise is worth recording in full because it demonstrates how much judgement sits behind the apparently simple rules.

#### Amazon — yes

The Amazon daily chart shows all the moving averages — the 200, the 150, the 50 — sloping up together, which establishes that the long-term, mid-term and short-term trends all point higher. The price structure shows higher highs and higher lows. Against that clean uptrend, the stock is currently retracing and testing the 50-day moving average, which has served as support before: it bounced off that level on the most recent test and had dipped below it and recovered many months earlier.

So the stock is dipping on a solid uptrend *and* it is near support — two of the three qualifying conditions at once. Long-term the chart is bullish; short-term, because the retracement is still under way, it reads as somewhat neutral. Roughly 99% of the audience voted yes, and Adam agreed. His reasoning for tolerating the unfinished retracement is instructive: the retracement may well continue a little further before the stock turns, but that is acceptable because the calendar spread has decent downside protection. Even if he is early and the stock keeps falling, the trade retains margin for error.

#### Salesforce (CRM) — yes, with more debate

Salesforce peaked at $369 over the preceding year and had fallen substantially, trading at $227. It appeared to be testing the $230 level, which, zoomed out over several years, had repeatedly acted as support — the stock had fallen to it and bounced off it again and again, and was now testing it once more.

This is the second qualifying setup: consolidating or bottoming near support. Trend-wise both long-term and short-term read as neutral, because the stock has been at that level for a long time. The vote split roughly 80/20 in favour, and Adam sided with the majority while acknowledging the controversy. His argument is a piece of technical reasoning worth stating explicitly: the longer a stock holds above a support level, the more powerful the eventual rebound tends to be. The stock had been accumulating at that level for a long time, and every dip below $230 was being bought.

He is candid about the residual risk. If the stock totally collapses, he loses money. But the maximum loss is limited and known in advance, and the structure's downside margin for error makes the setup acceptable.

#### Adobe — no

Adobe had been in a steady multi-year decline, printing lower highs and lower lows, with every moving average sloping down. It had just broken below the $332 support level and looked set to continue lower. Short-term, also bearish.

The audience was unanimously negative and Adam concurred without qualification. His phrasing — "this chart looks horrible" — is not analysis so much as verdict. He does add an important discipline point: fundamentally the stock might be undervalued, but that is a separate conversation. We are talking about trading here, and from the technical standpoint it is not a good setup for a calendar spread.

#### Eli Lilly — no

Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind the GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, had recently moved up sharply in a parabolic manner, and the stochastic — the momentum indicator Adam prefers — showed the stock extremely overbought. In his experience a stock in that state is due for a pullback soon.

The majority said no and he agreed emphatically: do not chase it, do not FOMO. The reasoning is specific to the structure rather than generic risk aversion. A sharp pullback from here would hurt the C trade. The calendar has some margin for error on the downside, but only a limited magnitude of it. If the stock drops a lot, the C trade is hurt too.

The four cases together define the boundary. The calendar spread wants a stock that is quiet, based, or gently retracing inside an uptrend. It does not want a stock in free-fall, and it does not want a stock stretched to a parabolic extreme with a violent mean reversion pending.

### The Entry Checklist

Beyond the chart, Adam gives a checklist of construction and quality rules. These are the numeric thresholds that determine whether a candidate trade is actually worth entering.

**Liquidity.** The underlying should have high liquidity, meaning that when you want to buy there is a willing seller and when you want to sell there is a willing buyer. The practical test he gives is simple: check that the stock has **weekly options**. If weeklies exist, the name is widely traded and the bid-ask spreads will be tight enough to get in and out. Amazon obviously passes.

**Long leg construction.** Buy a call **near or at the money**, expiring in **three to six months**, or up to nine months if you prefer more runway. With Amazon at $220.69 at the previous Friday's close, the 220 strike is at the money.

**Short leg construction.** Sell a call at the **same strike**, expiring in **two to four weeks**. The short expiry is chosen to sit in the fast part of the decay curve so that the rent arrives quickly.

**Capital and risk.** The net debit of the two legs is simultaneously the capital, the maximum risk, and the entry price. There is only one number to remember.

**Maximum return on investment test.** Hover the cursor over the apex of the payoff triangle on the platform's analysis tab. That value is the maximum profit at the short call's expiration. Divide it by the net debit. **The result should be at least 25%.** More is better. For the Amazon example, the apex reads approximately $420 against a $1,173 capital base:

$$\text{Max ROI} = \frac{420}{1173} = 35.8\%$$

That comfortably clears the 25% threshold, so the trade qualifies. Adam is careful to note that this 25% figure is measured **before rolling**. Because the C trade will typically be rolled through many rounds, each collecting fresh premium, the realised return often ends up far above the static maximum — which is how some of his trades return more than 100%.

**Probability of profit.** Ideally the probability of finishing inside the profit triangle should be around 50% or higher.

That checklist, stated as a compact table:

| Criterion | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Liquidity | Weekly options available; tight bid-ask |
| Technical setup | Dip on uptrend, consolidation near support, or neutral-to-bullish |
| Long leg | Near/at the money, 3–6 months (up to 9) |
| Short leg | Same strike, 2–4 weeks |
| Capital / max risk | Net debit of the two legs |
| Max ROI (pre-roll) | ≥ 25% |
| Probability of profit | ≈ 50% or better |

### Reading the Payoff Diagram

The risk profile of the calendar spread on the platform is the triangle already described: a profit zone in the middle bounded by breakevens on each side, with the zero line separating profit above from loss below.

For the Amazon trade, with the stock at $220 and the short call expiring in two weeks, the **lower breakeven sits at $211.70**. That means the stock can fall roughly $9 from entry and the trade would still be profitable at the short call's expiration. This is the concrete content of the phrase "margin for error on the downside." You are not merely protected in the sense of having a capped loss; you have a band of adverse movement in which you still make money. Only if the stock falls a great deal do you enter the left-hand loss zone, and even then the maximum loss is $1,173.

Adam contrasts this with equity trading, where a stop loss is only as good as the next opening print: "You trade stock, you buy it, you put a stop loss. But what if the stock gaps down much below your stop loss? You will be filled." The option position has no such gap risk on the downside, because the loss is bounded by construction rather than by an order type.

### Managing the C Trade: Three Scenarios

Once the C trade is live, everything that happens next falls into one of three cases, and each has a defined response.

**Scenario one: the stock stays flat.** Keep rolling the short call to a new two-, three- or four-week expiry to collect more premium. When the current short call expires in two weeks, you roll to another two weeks. This is finding a new Airbnb tenant when the last one moves out. Because the rent collected exceeds the lease cost, repetition compounds into profit.

**Scenario two: the stock starts to rally.** The moment you see the consolidation end, or the stock has clearly bottomed and is ready to rally, upgrade the C trade to a D trade. This is step two, covered in detail below. Once upgraded, the upside loss zone is eliminated and the position has room to profit as the stock climbs. After the upgrade and a subsequent rally, take profit between **50% and 150% return on investment**, with most exits falling in the **50% to 100%** band.

**Scenario three: the stock collapses.** Cut the loss at **50% of maximum loss**. With maximum loss at $1,173, that means exiting at roughly a $600 loss. The virtue of this rule is that you know the maximum in advance and choose not to let the trade run to it. Adam adds an encouraging structural note: if you have been in the trade for some time and have rolled the short call several rounds, the accumulated premium has both increased profit and lowered net risk, which makes the stop loss progressively harder to reach.

Summarised:

| Scenario | Trigger | Action | Target |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flat | Stock hovering near strike | Roll short call out 2–4 weeks, same strike | Collect repeated premium |
| Rally | Consolidation ends / stock turns up | Upgrade C → D (roll short call up and out) | Exit 50–150% ROI, usually 50–100% |
| Collapse | Loss reaches half of max loss | Cut the trade | −50% of max loss (≈$600 on $1,173) |

### The Full Benefit Case for the C Trade

Adam consolidates the advantages into a list that is worth walking through in prose because each item has a number attached.

The first is **capital optimisation**. Buying 100 shares of Amazon requires $22,000. One Amazon calendar spread requires $1,173. Dividing gives roughly **5% of the capital** for a position that participates meaningfully in the same underlying. He draws the direct practical consequence: traders with small accounts can now participate. You no longer need a six-figure account. A $5,000 account can hold several of these trades at once.

The second follows arithmetically from the first: because the capital base is small, any profit translates into an outsized **return on investment**. His typical C trade take-profit band is 50% to 100% ROI, and he frames this as the mechanism by which wealth is actually built.

The third is **risk reduction on two axes simultaneously**. The premium collected on the short call cuts the maximum loss from $1,818 to $1,173, and the presence of the long call eliminates the unlimited upside exposure that a naked short call would carry. Both improvements come from the same single action of adding leg two.

The fourth is that the trade retains a **decent profit zone with a decent probability of winning**, and that it can be upgraded to a diagonal to ride an uptrend.

The fifth, and the one he emphasises most, is that **time is now your friend — you are paid to wait**. The net positive theta means that doing nothing is profitable. This inverts the entire emotional experience of holding a long option position.

The sixth is that the structure can be used on **speculative stocks**. Adam does not mind putting calendars on speculative names, because those names typically carry very rich short-dated premium, which means the rent you collect each cycle is large.

Against those, the disadvantages are the three already named: capped profit, two loss zones, and the ongoing management burden of rolling.

### Worked Example One: Humana — Being Wrong and Winning Anyway

The Humana trade is presented specifically to demonstrate that the C trade can be wrong on direction and still profitable, which is the claim most students find hardest to believe.

The setup was a stock in a steady decline that appeared to have found a strong support level — structurally similar to the Salesforce chart discussed earlier. When the stock retraced back towards that support, Adam entered. The trade was taken in his IBKR account in what he identifies as his OTP portfolio.

| Element | Detail |
|---|---|
| Entry date | Late April |
| Stock price at entry | ~$260 |
| Long leg | Buy 260 call, November expiry, $34.00/share |
| Short leg | Sell 260 call, 6 May expiry (~2 weeks), $13.16/share |
| Contracts | 2 |
| Net entry price | $21.10/share |
| Capital / max loss | $4,220 |

The long call cost roughly $3,400 per contract, so $6,800 for two; the short calls brought in roughly $1,300 each, or $2,600 collected. The net debit of $21.10 per share across two contracts is the $4,220 figure that anchors the whole trade.

The thesis at entry was that Humana had bottomed, was consolidating and bouncing around, and could be due for a rebound. Within a few days of entry the stock gapped down significantly. Adam does not soften this: "I was wrong, completely wrong."

On 16 May, the short call's expiry, he had to roll. The mechanics are instructive. He had originally collected $13.16 for the short call; he bought it back for **12 cents**. In other words, because the stock had fallen so far, the call he sold expired almost worthless and he retained essentially the entire premium. He then sold a new short call — but because the stock had dropped so much, the new call at the same strike brought in only **$1.78**.

The metaphor absorbs this cleanly. The rental market crashed along with the property market; he could no longer find a good tenant at the old rate and had to cut the rent to fill the unit. But he kept it rented, "even for a smaller rent, just enough to buy me time for the better market."

He rolled six times in total. Crucially, he rolled to the **same strike price** every round — he never upgraded to a diagonal — because upgrading requires rolling to a higher strike, and with the stock stuck at a low level he could not raise the rent. The position stayed a pure calendar for its entire life.

He exited below his entry price, when the stock had recovered only a little. On the spread itself he lost: he paid $21.10 to enter and collected $19.00 to exit. But once all six rounds of rent were counted, the trade produced **$1,700 of profit, a 40.3% return on investment**, despite him being entirely wrong on direction.

That result is the strongest single argument for the strategy. The stock fell after entry, never recovered to the entry price, and the trade still returned over 40%. Adam is honest that this is not an ideal trade — the ideal version has the stock cooperate — but he calls the outcome "the power of the C trade" precisely because it makes money in the case where a stock position would have lost.

### Step Two: Upgrading the C Trade to a D Trade

The C trade's weakness is the loss zone on the right. If the stock rallies and you do nothing, the position moves into that zone and you end up losing money on a move you correctly anticipated. This is, as Adam puts it, "a very sad thing." You do not want to miss the opportunity when the stock recovers.

The upgrade is therefore mandatory, not optional, when the stock starts to move. **The way you upgrade is to roll the short call to a higher strike price and a further expiry date.**

Mechanically, rolling means two simultaneous actions. You **buy to close** the existing short call — you originally sold to open it, so you close it by buying it back — and at the same time you **sell to open** a new short call at a higher strike with more days to expiration. The long call is untouched. The lease with the landlord remains exactly as it was; only the tenancy changes.

The metaphor here is the most precise one in the whole course. You have leased the house and rented it to a tenant. Now you want the property back so you can re-let it at a higher rate. So you negotiate: "Hey tenant, is there a way I can compensate you for the rent, but I really need to get my house back?" You pay the tenant something to move out early, and then you re-let to a new tenant at a much higher rental — creating extra headroom on the upside.

The resulting structure is a **diagonal spread**, which also has two legs. Leg one is the original long call, unchanged — the same contract with the landlord. Leg two is the new short call at a higher strike and later expiry. The difference between a calendar and a diagonal is exactly one thing: in a calendar the two strikes are equal, in a diagonal they differ.

#### The timing and cost of the upgrade

Normally you do not upgrade immediately after entry. The stock usually needs time to stabilise before it rallies, and there is a real financial advantage to waiting: by the time the stock starts to move, the original short call has already decayed some value, so buying it back is cheaper. You can upgrade at a lower cost, and sometimes even for a credit.

But Adam works through the worst case explicitly, to show that even the unfavourable version is acceptable. Suppose you have just entered the Amazon C trade — long Feb 220, short 5 Dec 220 collected at $6.45 — and Amazon immediately moves up sharply. Can you upgrade at once? Yes.

| Action | Strike | Cash flow per share |
|---|---|---|
| Buy to close short call | 220 | −$6.45 |
| Sell to open new short call | 230 | (less, being further OTM) |
| **Net roll cost** | | **−$2.95 debit** |

Because 230 is further out of the money than 220, it collects less premium, so the roll costs a net debit of $2.95 per share, or $295 per contract. The trade's total cost rises from $1,173 to $1,468.

That cost purchases something measurable. The payoff diagram changes shape: the upside loss zone is eliminated, or at worst reduced to a small residual zone far above the current price. The maximum profit rises from approximately **$420 to $650**. The profit zone widens. And the maximum return on investment rises from 35.8% to **44%**:

$$\frac{650}{1468} = 44.3\%$$

So even in the worst case — upgrading immediately, paying full freight — the trade is improved on every dimension that matters: the upside risk is removed, the maximum profit is higher, the profit zone is wider, and the return on capital is better. That is the entire justification for step two.

Adam adds the important note that when time has passed before you upgrade, the roll may cost far less, and sometimes you collect money for upgrading. Rolling **for a credit** — getting paid to improve your position — is the ideal case, and later in the live trades we will see it happen repeatedly.

The C-to-D comparison, side by side:

| | C trade (calendar) | D trade (diagonal) |
|---|---|---|
| Long leg | Feb 220 call | Feb 220 call (unchanged) |
| Short leg | 5 Dec 220 call | Later-expiry 230 call |
| Strikes | Same | Different (short higher) |
| Capital | $1,173 | $1,468 |
| Max profit | ~$420 | ~$650 |
| Max ROI | 35.8% | 44% |
| Upside loss zone | Present | Eliminated or minimal |
| Net delta | Typically negative once ITM | Positive |

That final row — net delta — is the concept that dominates the live trade management later in the module, and it deserves stating plainly here. When the short call is at or below the stock price, its delta grows and can exceed the long call's delta, making the position's net delta negative: further upside *hurts* you. Rolling the short call up restores a positive net delta so that further upside *helps* you. Every rolling decision in the live trades is ultimately a decision about the sign of net delta.

### Worked Example Two: Meta — Wrong Again, and Still Paid

If Humana proves that a calendar can survive being wrong on direction, the Meta trade proves something narrower and more useful: that the C-to-D upgrade can be executed at the very end of a losing sequence, on the single day the stock finally cooperates, and that this one act converts an accumulated grind into a respectable return.

Adam entered Meta on 29 September as a plain calendar spread. The long leg was a call expiring 19 December; the short leg was a call expiring 10 October. He paid a net debit which he quotes twice in slightly different forms — first as $36.95 and then as "the exact one is $36.69" — so the capital committed was somewhere in the region of $3,695 for a single contract, and the precise cent-level figure is not resolvable from the recording. What matters is the order of magnitude: roughly $3,700 of capital, which is also the maximum loss, against a stock trading at $750 a share. To hold 100 shares of Meta at that price would have required $75,000. The calendar controlled the same 100 shares of exposure for about five per cent of the money, which is the same capital ratio the Amazon illustration produced.

The thesis was the favourite setup. The Meta daily chart was in a clean uptrend, and every previous dip to the 50-day moving average had been bought. On 29 September the stock was dipping to that same moving average again, and Adam was betting on the same rebound that had occurred every prior time. He is careful, in the retelling, to point out that the chart made this look like an easy call, and that the chart was wrong.

The stock did not rebound. By 10 October, the day the first short call expired and had to be rolled, Meta had fallen from $750 to around $720 — a thirty-point decline in eleven days. Here the mechanics that Humana demonstrated repeated themselves. The first short call had been sold for roughly $13.00 per share, or $1,300 for the contract; with the stock thirty points below the strike it expired worthless or near enough, and the entire premium was retained. But the replacement tenant was much poorer. The new short call sold on the roll brought in only $345 for the contract, barely a quarter of what the first one had paid.

The consequential number is what the trade's profit and loss read at that moment. Despite a thirty-point adverse move in the underlying, the position was down **five dollars**. The rent collected from the first tenant had almost exactly offset the decline in the value of the long call. That is the entire downside-protection claim of the structure expressed as a single arithmetic fact: a four per cent fall in a $750 stock, absorbed by a position that ended the period essentially flat.

The second roll went the same way. Meta continued lower, dropping below $700. The new short call collected only $260. The trade's cumulative loss widened — to $193. Adam pauses on the comparison deliberately, because it is the comparison that justifies the whole approach. From an entry at $750 the stock had now fallen roughly fifty points. A holder of 100 shares would have been down $5,000. The calendar spread was down $193. The transcript at this point contains a garbled figure for the maximum loss — it is rendered as "$3,06", presumably a mangling of the $3,695-ish capital quoted at entry — so the exact denominator he cites for that comparison cannot be recovered from the audio, but the ratio he is drawing is unambiguous: the realised loss was under two hundred dollars against a maximum possible loss of several thousand.

Then the stock turned. On the next rolling day Meta had recovered and the trade's profit and loss flipped to **positive $650**. The rent on that roll was much better too: over $600 collected for the new short call, because the stock had come back towards the strike and the option he was selling was once again close to the money. This is the mechanical asymmetry that makes the strategy work over multiple cycles. When the stock falls, the short call expires worthless and you keep everything, but the next rent is small. When the stock recovers, the rent gets rich again. Either way you collect something.

The last roll of the sequence was the upgrade. Up to this point Adam had been rolling at the same strike — the original 750 — which is to say the position had remained a pure calendar throughout the decline, exactly as Humana had. On the final roll he moved the short call **up from 750 to 795**, converting the calendar into a diagonal and creating forty-five points of upside headroom above the entry price. And he was paid to do it. In his words, he rolled it up to 795 "yet I am paid for that rolling" — a credit roll, the ideal case described in the theory section, achieved because time had already eroded the old short call while the recovering stock had restored premium in the further-out expiry.

After that upgrade the stock rallied to slightly above the entry price — he estimates $755 against an entry of $750 — and because the loss zone on the upside had been removed, the trade did not merely survive the rally but was maximised by it. The position's profit reached **$972**.

He closed there, and the reason matters for the exit rules. $972 on roughly $3,695 of capital is **26.3% return on investment**, which is below his stated 50% target. He was not at his profit objective. What made him close was that earnings were due immediately afterwards, and earnings are a binary event that can destroy an accumulated profit in a single overnight gap. He describes the decision as a judgement call — "somehow my hunch tells me that I should lock in the profit" — and notes in hindsight that the stock did lunge on the earnings release, so the timing was validated. The principle to extract is not "always close before earnings," because he explicitly holds a different trade through earnings later in the module for a specific structural reason. The principle is that a decent profit in hand, sitting in front of a binary event, is a legitimate reason to take an exit below target.

The Meta sequence, laid out as a ledger of what each roll did:

| Event | Stock | Short call action | Premium | Trade P&L at that moment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 29 Sep entry | $750 | Sell 750 call, 10 Oct expiry | +$1,300 | — (capital ≈ $3,695) |
| 10 Oct roll 1 | ~$720 | Buy back near zero; sell new | +$345 | −$5 |
| Roll 2 | <$700 | Sell new short call | +$260 | −$193 |
| Roll 3 | recovering | Sell new short call | +$600-plus | +$650 |
| Final roll — the upgrade | recovering | Roll **750 → 795**, further expiry | **credit** | — |
| Exit (pre-earnings) | ~$755 | Close both legs | — | **+$972 (26.3% ROI)** |

### Worked Example Three: GLD — Twelve Rolls and the C↔D Oscillation

The gold ETF trade is the longest-duration example in the module and it teaches something none of the others do: the C-to-D conversion is not a one-way door. You can go C to D, and then back to C, and then to D again, many times over, as the stock oscillates. The strategy's name describes the intended terminal state, not a promise that the journey there is monotonic.

The setup was again the favourite one. GLD was in a clear uptrend, but it had a resistance level at approximately $317 to $318 which it had tested and failed. Before Adam's entry it had approached that swing high, been unable to break above it, and pulled back. Because the pullback was occurring inside an uptrend, it read as a dip on an uptrend — the highest-quality C trade setup by his own ranking.

He entered at the end of May with a calendar at the 303 strike, which was around the market price at the time, using **two contracts**. The spoken cost figure is "$109 and two contracts. So I pay $2,100 basically," which is internally inconsistent — $2,100 across two contracts implies $10.50 per share, while "109" implies $10.90 and a $2,180 outlay. The capital is therefore approximately $2,100, and the precise per-share debit cannot be recovered from the recording.

What followed was months of nothing resolving. The ETF ground sideways, testing the resistance level repeatedly and pulling back each time. Adam narrates the position's profit and loss as it wandered, and the sequence is worth recording precisely because it is the emotional reality of running these trades and it is almost never shown honestly:

| Stage | Trade P&L |
|---|---|
| Shortly after entry | +$27 |
| Next check | near +$300 |
| After a pullback | +$68 |
| Deeper pullback | −$98 |
| Recovery | almost +$900 |
| Failed the resistance, sharp pullback | −$400 |
| Rolling day | +$316 |
| Next rolling day | +$285 |
| Next rolling day | +$246 |
| Rally begins | +$886 |
| Broke above resistance | +$1,011 |
| Final exit | **+$1,350** |

He rolled **twelve times** — he counts them off the screen — and along the way he upgraded to a diagonal on multiple occasions and then, when the price fell back, rolled the short call back **down** to convert the diagonal into a calendar again. "I keep switching my trade between C and D and C and D, C and D many times." This is the single most important practical lesson in the GLD case. The upgrade is not a graduation you achieve once; it is a steering input you apply whenever the balance of risk shifts, and it can be reversed when the stock fails to follow through. Rolling up when the stock rallies creates headroom; rolling back down when the stock falls restores rent, because a lower strike sits closer to the money and therefore collects more premium.

The terminal state was a diagonal with the short call at **318** — fifteen points above the original 303 — chosen deliberately because 318 was the resistance level itself. When GLD finally broke out to a new high above that resistance, the position had exactly the headroom it needed, and Adam exited for **$1,350**, which against roughly $2,100 of capital is a **63 to 64% return on investment**.

His post-mortem on the exit is unusually candid and is the best short statement of his exit philosophy in the entire module. Looking back at the chart after the fact, gold kept running, and had he continued holding and continued upgrading — "D, D, D plus" — the trade would have made considerably more. He does not treat this as an error. "I never complain when I make profit. Profit is profit, and profit is profit. 63, 64%. It's good enough. I don't look back in regrets, especially when I make profit." The rule that generated the exit was the rule that was supposed to generate it: take profit inside the 50-to-100% band. The rule did its job. Regret about foregone upside is not evidence that the rule is wrong, and a trader who lets that regret rewrite the rule will eventually hold a winner all the way back to a loss.

### The Live Trade Hunt: Three Entries on 26 November

Everything to this point has been either illustration or retrospective. The remainder of the module is a live sequence, recorded across roughly two months from 26 November 2025 to 22 January 2026, in which three trades are entered in front of the class and then managed to completion with every roll shown, every price negotiated on screen, and every profit-and-loss figure reconciled in a spreadsheet. This is the part of the module that actually teaches management, and it is worth reading as one continuous narrative rather than as three separate case studies, because the decisions in each trade are repeatedly made by comparison with the other two.

#### Trade one: Microsoft

Adam introduces Microsoft with an apology. The stock had already gone up on the day of the webinar, which makes the entry slightly late — "a little unfortunate because Microsoft has gone up today. A bit too late, but I think it's still okay to enter it right now." His confidence came from the structure of the pullback rather than from the day's move: Microsoft had retraced a long way and had held the 200-day moving average as support for the first time since the April selloff. It tested that level, held above it for three days, and rebounded on the day of the entry.

The decision he articulates at this point is the cleanest statement of the strategic fork in the entire course. If he were neutral, he would enter at the money as a calendar — buy a call and sell a call at the same strike. If he were **more bullish, he would go straight to the D trade** and skip the calendar stage entirely. The C trade is not mandatory; it is what you enter when you are not yet convinced. Because Microsoft had already run that day, he chose caution: enter as a calendar, and upgrade later if the bullishness is confirmed.

The construction followed the checklist exactly, with one refinement that had not appeared in the theory. He wanted the long call to expire **after** the earnings date, because an option that still has an earnings event ahead of it holds its value very well. Microsoft's earnings were due in January, so a February expiry cleared them; March would also have worked but cost roughly $400 more, and he chose February to keep the capital down.

| Leg | Action | Strike | Expiry | DTE | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long | Buy to open MSFT call | 485 | February 2026 | ~3 months | ~$27.00 |
| Short | Sell to open MSFT call | 485 | 4 December | 9 | $6.70 |
| **Net** | Debit | | | | quoted ~$20; **filled $20.62** |

The short leg was slightly under two weeks — nine days — rather than the canonical two to four, and Adam flags the compromise openly. Nine days decays very fast, which is good, but it also caps the maximum profit, which is why the trade only barely passes his quality test. The premium collected cut the cost of the long call from $27 to roughly $20: "more than one quarter — you cut almost like one third, actually."

On the analysis tab the payoff triangle gave a lower breakeven around **$475**, about ten dollars below the stock, and an upper breakeven at **$498**, about thirteen dollars above it. Adam frames this as the entry question in its most concrete form: if you believe Microsoft can move more than ten dollars down or thirteen dollars up in the next nine days, including the Thanksgiving holidays, then this is the wrong trade and you should construct something else. If you believe it will stay inside that band, this is the right trade.

The apex of the triangle read about **$510** of maximum profit. Against $2,060 of capital that is **just about 25%** — the threshold met but not exceeded. He accepts it explicitly on the grounds that the short leg is unusually short: with a Thanksgiving holiday and a half-day Friday inside those nine calendar days, the real trading-day count is closer to seven, and a 25% static return over seven trading days is a good rate even if the absolute number is unimpressive. Had he sold a full two-week call the maximum would have been comfortably above 25%.

He negotiated the fill rather than paying the mark, starting the order at $20.62 and getting filled there immediately. The trade went on the book at a capital and maximum-loss figure of **$2,062**, showing an immediate loss of two dollars — which he notes is entirely normal, because a spread will always show a small plus or minus straight after entry as the mid-prices settle. The number he directs attention to instead is theta: **+$22 per day**. "Weekday, weekend, doesn't matter. It brings me $22 a day. Tomorrow, day off, I also got $22. Friday, half day, I also get $22. Saturday I also get $22."

#### Trade two: ExxonMobil

The XOM chart is presented as almost a textbook illustration of the criteria. Over a full year the stock had gone sideways, and over three years it had done much the same, but inside that range it was printing higher highs and higher lows, with the 200-day, 150-day and 50-day moving averages all sloping up — "not like parabolically up, but steadily up, which is beautiful. Just good for this C trade." The recent behaviour was a repeating rhythm of rise, retrace, rise, retrace, and at the moment of entry the stock had retraced back to the lower boundary of the ascending channel.

Two additional pieces of evidence supported entry. The first was the position within the channel, which put the stock at the bottom of its own trend line with a plausible case that the day's action was the beginning of the next leg up. The second was the stochastic, which was near oversold. Adam walks back through the chart and identifies four previous instances where the stochastic reached that region and the stock bounced each time — "every time, right? Every time." He states the conclusion as an instruction rather than an observation: when you see that bounce, upgrade the trade immediately.

The construction differed from Microsoft in one respect. Because XOM's premiums are cheap in absolute terms, he could afford a longer-dated long leg without inflating the capital, so he bought March rather than February.

| Leg | Action | Strike | Expiry | DTE | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long | Buy to open XOM call | 115 | March | ~4 months | $5.70 |
| Short | Sell to open XOM call | 115 | 5 December | 9 | $1.60 |
| **Net** | Debit | | | | $4.17 theoretical; **filled $4.23** |

At $417 per contract this is the cheapest structure in the module, and Adam makes the point directly at the small-account trader: "those who have a small account, this one is good. You cannot lose more than $417." He then chose to trade **three contracts** rather than one, for a total capital and maximum loss of **$1,269**, on the grounds that a single contract would not be worth the management effort for him personally — while explicitly telling students that one contract is entirely sufficient if they are practising.

The three-contract payoff showed a profit zone from **$112 to $118** and a maximum profit of **$376**, which against $1,269 is **29%** — comfortably above the 25% floor. He negotiated a fill at $4.23 and the position showed a $1.50 profit and a theta of **+$18 per day** on entry.

#### Trade three: Accenture

Accenture had been consolidating for a long time around $243, and when Adam zoomed the chart out to a five-year view, that level revealed itself as a support that had held repeatedly across many years — dip, bounce, dip, bounce, hold above, hold above. It was the Salesforce pattern again: a long accumulation at a level that keeps getting bought.

The construction ran into a small practical obstacle worth recording because it will happen to every student eventually. The stock was at $248, so the at-the-money strike would have been 248 — but no 248 strike existed. The chain offered 245 and 250. Adam chose **245**, which is slightly in the money, noting that 248 would have been better if it were available. This is the correct default: when the exact at-the-money strike is not listed, take the nearest available strike and accept the small directional tilt it introduces.

| Leg | Action | Strike | Expiry | DTE | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long | Buy to open ACN call | 245 | February | ~3 months | ~$19.80 |
| Short | Sell to open ACN call | 245 | 5 December | 9 | ~$6.90–7.00 |
| **Net** | Debit | | | | quoted $12.90; **filled $13.30** |

The profit zone ran from **$236 to $255**. Adam assessed it as "not great, not huge," but acceptable given how long the stock had been contained inside a narrower range than that. His stated worry was asymmetric and is worth quoting because it inverts the intuition most students bring: "I'm not worried much on the downside, to be honest, because it has very strong support here. I'm worried that the stock could break out very fast, very soon. In that case, I need to be nimble to upgrade my trade immediately." The risk he was actually managing at entry was the upside risk — the risk of being right.

The maximum profit read **$433** against a quoted $1,295 of capital, or **33%**, which he liked. He then made and immediately corrected an error about the earnings date, initially saying earnings were far away and then locating them on **18 December**. The correction changed the management plan: the 5 December short call would not cross earnings, and neither would the first roll, but the roll after that would. He flagged it as a problem to be solved later rather than a reason not to enter — which is exactly what happened, and that earnings date turned out to be the source of the best roll in the entire module.

He negotiated from $12.90 up towards the mark price of $13.35 and was filled at **$13.30**, giving a capital and maximum loss of **$1,330**.

The three entries, side by side:

| | Microsoft | ExxonMobil | Accenture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entry date | 26 Nov 2025 | 26 Nov 2025 | 26 Nov 2025 |
| Stock at entry | ~$486 | ~$115.5 | ~$248 |
| Long leg | Feb 485 call, ~$27.00 | Mar 115 call, $5.70 | Feb 245 call, ~$19.80 |
| Short leg | 4 Dec 485 call, $6.70 | 5 Dec 115 call, $1.60 | 5 Dec 245 call, ~$6.95 |
| Contracts | 1 | 3 | 1 |
| Net debit filled | $20.62 | $4.23 | $13.30 |
| Capital = max loss | **$2,062** | **$1,269** | **$1,330** |
| Profit zone | $475 – $498 | $112 – $118 | $236 – $255 |
| Max profit / ROI | $510 / ~25% | $376 / 29% | $433 / 33% |
| Theta at entry | +$22/day | +$18/day | not stated on screen |

Total capital at risk across the three positions was **$4,661** — less than the cost of 100 shares of Microsoft alone, for exposure to three different underlyings in three different sectors.

### Two Days Later: the First Upgrades, 28 November

The market did to all three positions exactly what Adam had warned it might. Two trading days after entry, all three stocks had risen, and all three trades were therefore in the one state the C trade handles badly: profitable, but with the profit about to be strangled by the short call.

Microsoft had jumped almost six dollars, from around $486 to roughly $492. The trade was showing about **$85 to $100** of profit, and Adam narrates the problem precisely: "the higher the stock goes up, the less the profit will become, because it's going out of the profit zone of the trade." The profit zone was $474 to $498; entry had put the stock in the middle of it and two days had pushed it towards the upper edge. If the stock kept going, the position would first stop making money and then start losing it.

The remedy was the upgrade, and Adam's search for the right roll shows how the cost of an upgrade is actually assessed at the screen. He looked first at buying back the 485 call expiring the following Friday, which would cost almost $10, and selling the 490 call expiring the week after that, which would bring in almost $10. "So it's almost like an eco-swap" — an even swap. Five points of extra headroom purchased for a rounding error. He quoted the roll at a debit of **28 cents**, negotiated it down, and was filled at **25 cents**, meaning the entire upgrade cost **$25** on a $2,062 position.

He is careful to note the residual limitation, because it would be dishonest not to. The stock was already at $491 or $492, so a 490 short strike is still in the money and still caps the upside. "But at least it's not as much capping as $485." The upgrade did not eliminate the cap; it moved it, and moving it was worth twenty-five dollars.

Accenture had risen three dollars to $250, putting the 245 short call five points in the money. Here the roll was less generous. Buying back the 245 cost $7.70 and selling the 250 collected almost $7.00, for a quoted debit of about **90 cents** — and this is where Adam states one of the two numeric rules that govern every roll decision in the module: "To me, less than $1 is still fine." Under a dollar of debit for five points of headroom is acceptable. He also names the alternative he rejected: he could have rolled two weeks out instead of one, which would have crossed the earnings date and produced a big credit, but he wanted to preserve that fat earnings-crossing premium for a later roll rather than spend it now. That decision is the first appearance of an idea that recurs throughout — an earnings-crossing expiry is a resource, and you should spend it when you need it most.

The Accenture fill was ugly and instructive. He started at 85 cents, moved to 90, and the mark price kept climbing as the stock rose during the negotiation — to $1.05, then past a dollar. "The more it goes up, the more expensive my rolling will be, so I need to chase a little bit here." He was filled at **$1.10**. The lesson embedded in that sequence is that a roll is a live transaction whose price moves against you in exactly the circumstance that makes you want it, and that ACN's liquidity is materially worse than Microsoft's — a direct consequence of the liquidity criterion in the entry checklist.

ExxonMobil produced the best roll of the three. The stock was at $116, one point above the 115 strike. Adam checked 117 first, which would have cost about 55 cents for three contracts' worth of movement, then checked 116 and found it was "almost a free upgrade." He submitted the order at **zero debit** for three contracts and it filled. "I upgraded my trade up by $1 for zero debit. I did not pay anything extra. I exchanged the 115 expiring on December 5th for the 116 expiring a week after."

The three upgrades of 28 November:

| Trade | Old short call | New short call | Headroom gained | Roll cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | 485, exp. 5 Dec | 490, one week later | +5 points | **$25 debit** (1 contract) |
| ExxonMobil | 115, exp. 5 Dec | 116, one week later | +1 point | **zero** (3 contracts) |
| Accenture | 245, exp. 5 Dec | 250, one week later | +5 points | **$110 debit** (1 contract) |

"All three C trades have now become D trades," he says at the close of that session. "So then it will have much bigger upside headroom from now on."

### The Master Variable: Net Delta

The Saturday review recorded on 29 November is the theoretical heart of the entire live sequence, and it converts the rolling decision from a matter of feel into a matter of reading one number.

Adam opens by showing what the three positions looked like **before** the rolls, using the Excel tracker he distributes with the curriculum in both a thinkorswim and an Interactive Brokers version. All three trades were profitable on 26 November because the stocks were still inside their profit zones. But every one of them had a **negative net delta**:

| Trade (pre-roll, 26 Nov state) | Net delta | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | −13 | A $1 rise in MSFT costs the trade $13 |
| ExxonMobil | −21 | A $1 rise in XOM costs the trade $21 (3 contracts) |
| Accenture | negative (value on screen, not spoken) | A $1 rise in ACN costs the trade |

All three simultaneously had **positive theta**, so each day that passed still paid. That combination — positive theta, negative delta — is the signature state of a calendar spread whose short call has gone in the money, and it is precisely the state the upgrade exists to cure. Adam states the objection in one sentence: "I don't want the price increase to hurt my trade, especially if I'm bullish."

The mechanism by which net delta goes negative deserves stating plainly, because Adam explains it repeatedly and it is the single piece of Greek arithmetic a C2D trader must internalise. The position is long one call and short one call. Its net delta is the long call's delta minus the short call's delta. When the short strike sits above the stock, the short call's delta is below 0.50 and the long call's — being at or in the money and much longer dated — is higher, so the net is positive. But as the stock rises through the short strike, the short call's delta climbs past 0.50 and keeps climbing, while the long call's delta, already high, has much less room to grow. At some point the short delta exceeds the long delta and the net flips negative. From that moment the position is short the stock, and every further dollar of the rally you were waiting for takes money out of your account.

Rolling the short call up resets this. A higher strike is further out of the money, so its delta is lower, so the subtraction comes out positive again. That is the whole content of the upgrade expressed in Greeks, and it is why Adam checks the two deltas explicitly before committing to a roll — as he does later with Accenture, comparing a 72-delta short call against an 85-delta long call and concluding "so that means my new trade would have a positive net delta after I roll. So this is a decent rolling."

After the 28 November rolls, all three positions read positive delta and positive theta. "So total portfolio, if you call this one a portfolio, it has positive delta, it has positive theta." That pair of signs is the target state of a managed C2D book: paid to wait, and rewarded if the stock rises.

### The Inflated P&L Problem, and Why You Need a Tracker

Immediately after establishing net delta, Adam raises what is probably the most practically valuable warning in the module, because it concerns a systematic error that every broker platform makes and that will make an unmanaged trader believe he is richer than he is.

When you roll, you close a leg. The realised profit or loss on that closed leg is a real cash event. But the broker's position screen reports the profit and loss of the **currently open** legs only; once a leg is closed it drops out of the display, and its realised result vanishes from the number on screen. "The broker removes the P&L of the closed legs. And not just thinkorswim — all other brokers do the same."

The Microsoft roll makes the size of the distortion concrete. He had sold the original 485 call for **$6.93** and bought it back on the roll for **$9.74**. That is a realised loss of **$281** — real money paid to the first tenant to break the contract early. He then sold the new 490 call for **$9.49**, almost exactly funding the buyback. After the roll the platform displayed a profit of **$364**. The true profit, once the $281 realised loss is subtracted, was **$83**.

The same distortion applied to the other two. ExxonMobil showed **$167** on the platform against a true **$35** once its $132 realised roll loss was counted — collected $1.64, paid $2.08, across three contracts. Accenture showed **$199** against a true **$45** after its **$154** realised loss — collected $6.46, paid $8.00. Across the three positions, **$567** of realised rolling losses had been erased from the broker's view, converting a true portfolio profit of **$163** into an apparent one of $730.

| Trade | Platform-displayed P&L | Realised roll loss hidden | True P&L |
|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | $364 | $281 | **$83** |
| ExxonMobil | $167 | $132 | **$35** |
| Accenture | $199 | $154 | **$45** |
| **Total** | **$730** | **$567** | **$163** |

The correction extends to the payoff diagram as well, and Adam is emphatic about it.
