The risk-profile curve the platform draws after a roll is also computed only from the open legs, so the entire curve — the current profit-and-loss line, the at-expiration line, the breakevens, everything — sits too high by exactly the amount of the realised roll loss. His instruction is to mentally shift the whole curve down: "just bring it down by 281. Everything on the curve, just bring it down by 281, and essentially you have the right curve." Do the same to the expiration line. Only then are you looking at your actual breakevens.

This is why the Excel tracker exists and why he updates it on camera after every single roll for two months. The tracker records the original premium collected, the buyback price, and the resulting realised profit or loss on every closed leg, and carries that number forward. Without it, he says flatly, "it is very hard to track what is the real P&L of the trade" — you will look at the platform, see $364, feel pleased, and be wrong by three hundred dollars.

He also uses the Saturday session to state a rule that governs how a roll should be interpreted at the moment it happens, and which he repeats almost every time he rolls thereafter: **rolling itself does not change the profit or loss of the trade.** At the instant of the roll you have simply exchanged one option for another at fair value. The Microsoft trade was making about $83 before the roll and about $83 after it. What changes is not the P&L but the Greeks — the delta sign and the theta rate — and the future distribution of outcomes. His reasoning for why this must be true is a good sanity check: "if it changed the P&L after the trade, that means I don't need to do anything, I keep rolling to create more profit." A structure that manufactured profit through rolling would be a money machine, and there are none.

The corollary is the second tradeoff he names on that Saturday. Rolling further out in time buys a bigger credit and reduces the debit, but it slows the rent. Before the roll ExxonMobil's theta was **+$18 per day** with one week to expiry; afterwards it was **+$12 per day** with two weeks. "The new trade has two weeks to expiry for the short call, and the old one has only one — it expires faster, and therefore time decay is faster. Each day I collect a little less, but it's important to know that now the new trade has a positive delta." That is the exchange every up-and-out roll makes: you pay for directional headroom with theta.

He also notes a small honest embarrassment in the ExxonMobil roll, and it is worth preserving. Measured after the fact, the rolled position was making **$35** where the unrolled position would have been making **$54**. Rolling had cost him nineteen dollars of realised profit, because the stock dipped in the hours after he rolled. He does not hide it and he does not treat it as a mistake: "But it's okay. What is important now, the trade has a net positive delta." The roll is not judged by whether it improved the P&L in the next four hours. It is judged by whether it put the position on the right side of the next move.

### The Sweet Spot Doctrine, and the Discipline of Not Rolling

The 2 December session introduces the concept that governs every decision to hold. Adam calls the short call's strike the **sweet spot** of the trade, and the rule is that when the stock sits at or near that strike, you do nothing.

Microsoft had gone nowhere in the two intervening sessions — $492 on the Friday, $491.50 on the Tuesday. That is exactly what the position wanted. "As long as the price stays near the sweet spot of the trade, the longer it stays there, the more profit it will generate." The trade was making **$110** and about **5% return on investment**, up from $83 and 4% two days earlier, which is what a $20-a-day theta looks like when nothing happens. He states the projection explicitly: at roughly $20 per day with eleven days remaining, the short call would contribute something like another $200 if the stock simply stayed put.

Three separate reasons are given for holding rather than acting, and together they constitute the negative form of the rolling rule — the conditions under which you should keep your hands off the position. The trade still had positive delta, so a further rise would help rather than hurt. The theta was strong at $20 to $21 a day. And there were eleven days to expiration, so there was no deadline pressure. On the chart, Microsoft had rallied into a level that had been support and was now acting as resistance, and Adam's read was that it would take time to break through. "I don't know if it's going to break above the resistance level or not. So this is okay" — an explicit acknowledgement that the correct response to genuine uncertainty is to let theta work rather than to guess.

ExxonMobil got the same treatment for the same reasons: trading at $116, right at its new 116 strike, profit up from $35 to $54, positive delta intact, and **$453** of extrinsic value still sitting in the short call with ten days to run. If the stock stayed put, that $453 would decay to zero and become profit. No action.

Accenture, by contrast, had broken. News had emerged that the company was partnering with OpenAI to build AI capability for its business, and the stock had jumped two consecutive days to around $259 or $260, ten dollars above the 250 strike Adam had rolled to only two trading days earlier. The short call was now ten points in the money and the position's net delta had gone to **−8**: every dollar of further rise cost eight dollars. Adam spells out the compounding: "$1, it will hurt the trade by $8. If it goes up by $2, it will hurt the trade by $16. So every dollar, it will hurt the trade more and more."

But he does not roll on the Greek alone. He goes to the chart first, and this ordering is the procedure: the Greeks tell you the position has a problem, the chart tells you whether the problem is worth paying to fix. Accenture had bottomed at the $243 support, rallied, and was now pressing against resistance around $259 — exactly where it was trading. The stochastic was rising and near overbought, and his experience was that a stock in that state usually pushes a little higher before turning. He therefore judged a breakout more likely than a rejection, and only then decided to roll.

### The Earnings-Crossing Roll: Accenture, 2 December

The Accenture roll of 2 December is the best single demonstration in the module of how to obtain a large upgrade for nothing, and the technique generalises.

The position needed a big move: the short call was at 250 with the stock at $259, and Adam wanted to reach 260 — a **ten-point** upgrade, twice the size of anything he had attempted so far. Rolling ten points up would ordinarily cost real money, because the option you buy back is deep in the money and expensive while the one you sell is far away and cheap.

It cost nothing, and the reason is the date. The expiry he rolled into, **19 December**, sits immediately after Accenture's earnings on **18 December**. Options that contain an earnings event carry inflated implied volatility and therefore inflated premium, because the market is pricing in the possibility of a large gap. The 260 call expiring 19 December was at or slightly out of the money and yet was quoting around **$11.50** — enough to fund the entire buyback of the in-the-money 250 call.

Adam states the generalisation directly: "every time I roll it to a new expiry which crosses the earnings, I typically can get a good premium. So in this case, you see, I can roll it up a lot, but I pay a little bit, because the 260 that I'm rolling to will have a very good premium. So it's almost like a free upgrade. I upgrade my apartment to a penthouse for almost zero additional cash."

He quoted the roll at a **$35 debit**, then noticed the stock ticking down and re-quoted for a credit, then walked the price back down through ten cents to **zero** and was filled. He bought back the 250 expiring 12 December for **$11.55** and sold the 260 expiring 19 December for **$11.55** — an exact wash. The tracker recorded another realised roll loss (he had collected $6.90 for the 250 and paid $11.55 to close it), bringing Accenture's cumulative realised rolling losses to **$619**.

The position after the roll was in a state worth pausing on, because it looks worse than it is. It was still showing a small loss once the $619 of realised roll costs were counted. But it now had positive delta, strong positive theta, and — crucially — **$1,135** of extrinsic value sitting in a short call that was now out of the money with the stock at $259 and the strike at 260. "If the stock just stays here until the expiry date, this one will decay to zero, and that will turn around the trade and make the trade very profitable." A position showing a paper loss with eleven hundred dollars of decay ahead of it is not a losing position; it is a position that has not yet been paid.

### Reading the Delta Comparison: ExxonMobil and Accenture, 3 December

The following day produced three separate lessons in a single session, one per trade, and they are best read as a set because each illustrates a different branch of the decision tree.

**Microsoft demonstrated downside protection under a bad headline.** News broke that Microsoft had warned its AI sales would be slow, and the stock fell **eight dollars** to around $481. The trade remained profitable. Adam explains the mechanism: "because of the stock price drop today, the profit that I'm making from the short call is actually more than offset by the hurt that I'm seeing in the long call." The short call, being nine points out of the money now, was losing value fast, and that loss was Adam's gain. This is the same protection the Humana and Meta trades demonstrated retrospectively, observed live on a single-day eight-dollar drop. No action was taken: the position still had positive delta, decent theta, and **$400** of extrinsic value in the short call to be earned over nine days.

**ExxonMobil demonstrated the delta comparison and the roll-distance tradeoff.** The stock jumped two dollars to above $117, putting the 116 short call in the money. Adam reads the Greeks off the screen: "the delta of the short call is 64, which is more than the delta of the long call. As a result, the trade has a net negative delta." A one-dollar rise now cost **$15**.

He then priced three different rolls in front of the class, and the comparison is the clearest exposition of the tradeoff in the module:

| Candidate roll | Headroom | Cost | Theta consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 116 → 117, one week out (19 Dec) | +1 point | ~10c debit ($30 for 3 contracts) | faster decay, shorter wait |
| 116 → 118, one week out | +2 points | larger debit | — |
| 116 → 118, two weeks out | +2 points | ~$2.10 (cheaper per point) | slower decay, longer wait |

His reasoning for choosing the first is explicit and is the rule: "That 118 would be more bullish rolling, and the 117 is less bullish rolling. I prefer a faster theta benefit." He was moderately bullish, not strongly bullish, so he bought a modest amount of headroom and kept the fast rent. He started the order at a five-cent debit, was not filled, raised to ten cents, and was filled — **$30 total** for three contracts. Bought back the 116 at $2.47, sold the 117 at $2.37.

The general principle underneath is that the amount of headroom you buy should be proportional to the strength of your directional conviction, and that rolling further out in time is the lever you pull when you want more headroom without paying more cash — at the price of a slower theta.

**Accenture demonstrated that an in-the-money short call is not automatically a problem.** The stock had jumped another five dollars to $266, putting the newly-sold 260 call in the money with a delta of **61**. Under the naive rule — "short call in the money, must roll" — this would demand immediate action. Adam does not roll, and his explanation is the definitive statement of the actual rule: "in the money means more than 50 — now 61 — is still lower than the delta of the long call. So net, because of that, the trade still has a net positive delta. So I don't have to worry about the stock going higher."

**The trigger is not moneyness. The trigger is the sign of net delta.** A short call can be in the money and the position can still be positively exposed to the upside, provided the long call's delta is higher. That is normally the case when the long call is deep in the money and long dated, because such an option has a delta approaching 0.90 or higher, and the short call has to go very deep before it can beat that. He adds the forward-looking caveat that keeps this from being complacency: "if it goes up too much, too fast, then it will turn negative. Then that's one I have to consider. But right now, it still has a positive delta, and especially it has a positive theta, so I'm paid to wait." The position that had been losing money the previous day was now profitable, purely because the stock had continued in the direction he had rolled to accommodate, with **$900-plus** of extrinsic value still to be earned over sixteen days.

### Rolling at Zero: Microsoft, 12 December

The 12 December session opens with the market selling off hard, money rotating out of AI technology names into defensives, and Microsoft down to **$477** — sixteen points below the 490 short strike. That short call was expiring the same day with **zero** value left. The position was still profitable relative to entry, which Adam offers as further evidence for the downside-defence claim.

The roll here is not an upgrade. It is a pure rent collection, and it introduces the tool Adam uses when he has no directional view: the **one standard deviation** move. With the stock at $477 and a one-standard-deviation move of about $13, the strike one standard deviation above the market is $490 — the same strike he already held. So he rolled **490 to 490**, one week out, collecting **$174**.

His justification for choosing that strike is worth recording in full because it is the logic of selling premium in its purest form: "490 is about one standard deviation above the current stock price. That means the stock needs to go up to hit my short call strike, which is unlikely. But if it goes there, then the trade will still have a lot of headroom for upside. And it looks like I will collect this premium for free again, because there's a very good chance for the stock not to go beyond 490, and therefore I keep rolling it to buy more time for the stock to recover."

Three things are being purchased with that single roll. Time for the thesis to work. A premium that is likely to be kept in full. And a strike far enough away that if the stock does rally hard, the position profits rather than suffers. Rolling to a strike one standard deviation out of the money is the default action when you have no opinion, and it is the reason Adam keeps returning to that measure — it is the market's own estimate of how far the stock is likely to travel, and selling beyond it is selling something the market says probably will not happen.

The same session produced the module's clearest example of **deliberately not rolling in order to keep a negative delta**. ExxonMobil had risen to $118.80 and the 117 short call was in the money, flipping net delta negative. The naive response would be to roll up. Adam looked at the chart instead: XOM was testing a long-standing resistance around $120 which it had failed at repeatedly, and his read was that a pullback was more likely than a breakout. And a negative delta position **profits** when the stock falls.

"So that means I will not roll it now, because if the stock declines, it will benefit the trade because it has a negative delta. So I will wait. I wait for the pullback to happen before I roll." He also notes there was one full week left before expiry and **$200-plus** of extrinsic value still in the short call, so there was no deadline forcing his hand. He states the condition under which he would have acted: "unless I'm very bullish on the stock price going higher right now, which I'm not."

This is the point at which the strategy stops being mechanical. Negative net delta is not a defect to be corrected reflexively; it is a directional exposure. If you are bearish over the next week, negative delta is what you want. The rule is not "always restore positive delta" — it is "make the sign of your delta agree with your view of the chart."

### Holding Through Earnings: Accenture, 17 December

The 17 December decision is the most sophisticated in the module. Accenture was due to release earnings before the open the following morning, the short call was expiring in two days, and the position was carrying a deep in-the-money short call with the stock at approximately $276 against a 260 strike — **sixteen points** in the money.

Since the previous review the stock had gone up six points and the trade's profit had **not moved**: it was $280 before, and $280 now. That is what a capped position looks like. "The stock went up six points, but the trade did not generate more profit."

Adam lays out the state of the Greeks. Net delta was still slightly positive, so a further small rise would help. Theta was strongly positive, because **$361** of extrinsic value remained to be earned over two days — an unusually rich figure precisely because the earnings event was still ahead, stuffing the option with what he calls "hope value." That hope value would collapse the moment earnings were released.

The decision was whether to roll the short call up before the event or hold it deep in the money through it. To answer it, he simulated. The options chain's expected move was **plus or minus $19** — the market's own estimate of the post-earnings range. He shifted the analysis-tab price slider $19 up and $19 down and read the resulting profit and loss off the payoff curve:

| Post-earnings scenario | Stock | Outcome for the position |
|---|---|---|
| Up $19 | ~$295 | Still inside the profit zone; makes a little less, no significant risk |
| Unchanged | ~$276 | Best case for theta; profit improves as extrinsic decays |
| Down $19 | ~$257 | **Very profitable** — stock falls towards the strike with two days to expiry |
| Down $27 (to $250) | $250 | Still profitable at expiration |

The asymmetry is what makes the decision. Holding a short call sixteen points in the money is, in effect, holding a large cushion. If the stock crashes, the short call loses value dramatically and the position gains; the cushion absorbs the fall. If the stock gaps up, the profit is capped but the position does not lose meaningfully, because the upper breakeven is far away. "By maintaining the short call in the money right now, it can protect the downside risk quite significantly."

He then priced the alternative and rejected it on cost. Rolling the 260 up to 265, one week further out, would have cost about **$2.65** for five points of headroom. His rule fires: "this is something I don't think is ideal, because I would have to pay more than half of the incremental headroom for my cash. My preferred rolling option would be if I roll it up for $5, I pay like less than $1 — or even better if I can roll it for a credit."

That gives the second numeric rule of rolling, and together with the first it defines the whole cost discipline of the strategy:

| Roll cost relative to headroom gained | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Credit (paid to upgrade) | Ideal |
| Less than $1 per $5 of headroom (under one fifth) | Good — take it |
| About one third of the headroom gained | Acceptable |
| More than one half of the headroom gained | Reject — do not roll |

The chart supported the same conclusion. Accenture had failed twice at a resistance level around $281 and was hovering below it, so the probability of a further melt-up seemed lower than the probability of a pullback. Combining the cost rule, the payoff simulation, and the chart, Adam held the deep in-the-money short call into earnings deliberately, as a hedge.

He was right. Accenture beat on the quarter — actual earnings of **$3.94** against an expectation of **$3.73** — but guided future earnings per share below expectations, and the market punished it. The stock opened down as much as **$9** at $264, recovered somewhat with the broad market, and settled around $270, down roughly $4. The trade's profit rose by nearly **$200**, from $280 to close to $480. "As I said, I maintain the short call deep in the money with the intention to cushion the downside risk in case the stock drops after the earnings, and it is now doing it."

He then declined to roll again the same day, on the basis of a behavioural observation about post-guidance selloffs: "based on my experience, the stock guided lower — typically the market will punish the stock, and it will last for a few days. So I'm not in a hurry to roll the short call up right now if I'm convinced that the stock could fall further from here. I could be wrong, but that's my bias." He also checked and rejected the available rolls on cost: 260 to 265 one week out would cost almost **$3**, and even two weeks out would cost **$1.60**. At 35% return on investment against a 50% target, he held.

The same session had good news elsewhere. Microsoft had jumped almost **twelve dollars** to near $488, right at the sweet spot below the 490 strike, and the position had swung from a small loss to a nice profit with **$186** of extrinsic value still to earn in one day. ExxonMobil had retraced two dollars to $116.60, back towards its 117 sweet spot, with **$200** to earn across three contracts over two days. Adam's summary of the whole book at that moment is a good statement of what a well-managed C2D portfolio feels like: all three trades doing well, none at the profit target, all being held while time does the work.

### Triple Expiry Friday: 19 December

All three short calls expired on 19 December, so all three had to be rolled in a single session. The three rolls are worth reading together because each was decided by a different consideration and each produced a different economic result.

**Microsoft rolled up and out for a credit.** The stock was rising on the day, the 490 short call was out of the money with almost no value left, and the chart suggested the stock could push a little higher before meeting horizontal resistance. Adam priced two candidate strikes for the following week's 26 December expiry: 492.5 would bring in $1.60, and 495 would bring in a figure he does not state cleanly. He chose **495**, bought back the expiring 490 for **$0.05**, sold the 495 for **$1.04**, and after negotiating from 99 cents down was filled for a net **99-cent credit**. "I just upgraded my trade for credit — for additional cash."

**ExxonMobil rolled up two points for a credit.** Here the chart was doing the work. XOM was showing higher highs and higher lows, the recent dip read as a dip on an uptrend, and momentum suggested more upside. "So look at the chart here, I'm bullish that the stock will go higher. So then definitely I want to go with the higher strike to make sure I have enough headroom for that side." Being more bullish than he had been on 3 December, he bought more headroom: he rolled the 117 up to **119** for the 26 December expiry, buying back at **$0.27** and selling at **$0.33**, and after walking the credit down from eight cents to seven to six was filled at **six cents credit** across three contracts. "I roll my short call up two points for a credit. That is a very good roll."

**Accenture rolled up five points for a debit, chosen against the one-third rule.** The stock had rebounded after the earnings drop to around $275, putting the 260 short call deep in the money and turning net delta negative again. The expiring call had to be bought back at about **$15**. Adam considered rolling to 265 one week out and found it would cost **$2.70** for five points — "more than half of my spread, which is not ideal." He then extended the expiry to **9 January**, which brought the cost down to roughly **one third** of the five-point spread, and that cleared his threshold.

Before committing he ran the delta check explicitly: the 265 call expiring 9 January carried a delta of **72**, against the long call's delta of **85**. Seventy-two is less than eighty-five, so the roll would restore a positive net delta. "So this is a decent rolling, because after that I would have a positive delta here." He negotiated from a 35-cent improvement upward through $1.40 and was filled at **$1.51** — buying back the 260 for **$15.31** and selling the 265 for **$13.80**.

The three rolls of 19 December:

| Trade | Roll | New expiry | Cash | Delta before → after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft | 490 → 495 | 26 Dec | **+$0.99 credit** | positive → positive |
| ExxonMobil | 117 → 119 | 26 Dec | **+$0.06 credit** (×3) | negative → positive |
| Accenture | 260 → 265 | 9 Jan | **−$1.51 debit** | negative → positive |

Adam updates the tracker on camera after each one and repeats the invariant every time: the profit and loss does not change at the moment of rolling. Microsoft was at about $330 before and $2,030 after — the second figure is the tracker's cumulative column rather than the trade P&L, and he reads them quickly, but the point he makes each time is the same: "the trade is still making around the same amount of profit, but it now has a significant upside headroom and also a positive theta." He closes with the standing instruction: "any trade that hits my profit target of around 50% return on investment, I will look to close it. Right now, they are around halfway there."

### The First Exit: ExxonMobil Hits Target, 24 December

On Christmas Eve, with the market open for an hour and trading thin, Adam closed the ExxonMobil position, and the way he closed it is the module's model of exit discipline.

The stock had risen beyond $119, past the short strike he had rolled to five days earlier. The short call's delta had therefore climbed above the long call's and the position's net delta had gone negative — a further rise would now cost money. Under the ordinary rules that would be a signal to roll up again. Adam says plainly that he could roll it, and that he is not going to, because the position had reached his exit criterion: **55% return on investment, $702 in absolute terms**.

The reasoning is a discipline argument rather than a market argument, and it is delivered without hedging: "because it already hit my profit target, by discipline, I just close it. You never know. If you are so greedy, yeah, you could get a little bit more profit, but what if the stock price drops a lot? It could wipe quite a big chunk of the profit."

The chart supplied a second, independent reason. XOM was pressing against a resistance around $119.90 to $120 that it had failed to break several times. "So if it cannot break above this one, chances are it will pull back again. And that will wipe out quite a big chunk of the profit of the trade. So I don't want that to happen. I just want to take the profit and run."

Two independent signals — the profit target and the resistance level — both said the same thing, and he acted.

The execution is instructive on its own. The tracker told him the closing trade should bring in about **$662** of credit. He entered the order to buy back the 119 short calls and sell the 115 long calls simultaneously as a single spread, three contracts, and started the negotiation **above** the expected price, at $670, working down through $665 and $663. He was filled at **$663** — a dollar better than the tracker's estimate. The long calls sold at **$7.60** and the short calls were bought back at **$0.97**.

Final result on the ExxonMobil trade: **$708 profit, 55.8% return on investment**, in four weeks, on $1,269 of capital.

He then walks through the housekeeping, which matters more than it sounds. The closed trade is moved to the closed tab of the tracker, its Greeks deleted because they are no longer live, and the realised profit hard-coded so the formulas do not keep recalculating against stale prices. The open book was now two positions.

In the same session he reviewed Accenture and chose to hold it despite the short call being in the money at 265 with the stock at $271. His reasoning combines both directions of exposure into one sentence that is the best summary of why a mildly in-the-money short call is a comfortable place to sit: "I don't need to roll it because the trade still has a positive delta — if the stock goes higher it would still benefit the trade. But if it goes towards the short call strike, which is $5 or $6 below the current stock price, the trade would still be doing fine. So I want to maintain the trade as it is right now to provide some protection on the downside. And at the same time, if the stock continues to go up, it will generate more profit. In the meantime, I am paid to wait, because the trade has a positive theta." The position was at 39% return on investment, below target, and there was nothing to do.

### Rolling on a Negative Theta Signal: Microsoft, 31 December

The New Year's Eve session introduces the last of the rolling triggers, and it is the one most students would never think to look for.

Microsoft's 497.5 short call, expiring on the Friday, had only **six cents** left in it. That is not merely a small number; it changes the sign of the position's theta. A calendar or diagonal has positive theta because the short call decays faster than the long call. When the short call has almost nothing left to decay, the long call's decay dominates and the net theta **goes negative** — the position starts paying rent instead of collecting it.

Adam names this explicitly as the reason to act: "there's no point to wait, because now the trade has a negative theta, because there's not much value in the short call to earn. So I need to roll it to make the trade more like positive theta so that I will benefit from the time decay."

This is a distinct trigger from the delta trigger. Delta tells you to roll **up**. Negative theta tells you to roll **out**. A trader watching only the delta will sit on an expiring short call with no premium in it, bleeding the long call's decay for days, wondering why the position keeps losing money in a flat market.

The strike selection used the one-standard-deviation tool again. Microsoft had declined about three dollars since the last review and was pulling back from a strong resistance at $492.30. Adam considered rolling down to 495 to collect more premium — around $2.00 instead of $1.50 — but the one-standard-deviation move was over $12, which put the boundary near $497, so he rolled to the **same 497.5 strike** one week further out to preserve headroom in case of a rally. He bought back at **$0.05**, sold the new call at **$1.47**, quoted the net at $1.45 and was filled at **$1.42 credit**.

He is honest about the imperfection of the result. After the roll the theta was not strongly positive but roughly neutral: "now the trade is no longer negative. It's not positive, but at least it's no longer significantly negative. So it's good." And he names the fix he chose not to take: "if I roll it out for two weeks, I have more extrinsic value and the trade would have a positive theta as well. But this one is okay, zero theta. That means when I'm waiting for the stock price to go up, the time doesn't hurt my trade." A zero-theta position is not collecting rent, but it is not paying it either, and that is enough while you wait for a directional thesis to resolve.

### The 30-Day Rule Appears: 8 January

The 8 January session is where the endgame becomes visible, and it introduces the hard constraint that eventually terminates every C2D trade regardless of profit or loss.

Microsoft had dropped six dollars to $476.20, erasing the profit and returning the position to near breakeven. The short call had one day left and three dollars of value in it, so it had to be rolled. Adam rolled out **two weeks** to 23 January, using the one-standard-deviation calculation once more: with the stock at $476.20 and a one-standard-deviation move of about $17, the indicated strike was $493.60, and he rounded to **495**. He bought back the expiring 497.5 for **$0.20** and sold the 495 for a credit; the net roll filled at **$2.07**.

Then he states the rule that governs the end of the trade: "that's going to be maybe the last rolling, because after this rolling — the next one in two weeks' time — the long call will be falling below 30 days to expiry. So a bit short in DTE, and then that is typically when I would close the trade."

The reason is the same decay curve that dictated the choice of a long-dated long leg at entry, running in reverse. The long call was bought three months out precisely so that its theta would be small. As it approaches expiry it moves onto the steep part of the curve and its decay accelerates until it overwhelms whatever the short call can collect. At that point the structure stops working: the rent no longer covers the lease. "The long call now is approaching the 30 days, and that's why you see the decay in the long call accelerate. That's why I say after this rolling, I would likely close the trade."

He commits to it in advance and unconditionally: "no matter what, I would close the trade in a week's time, whatever it is."

The same day he rolled Accenture, which had risen about five dollars and was showing **41 to 42% return on investment** — close to target. The 265 short call was ten points in the money with negative extrinsic value, meaning it had gone to a slight discount to intrinsic and the position's theta had turned negative. Both triggers were firing at once. He rolled **265 to 267.5**, two weeks out to 23 January, buying back at **$12.15** and selling at **$11.50** for a **$1.00 debit** after negotiating up from 87 cents while the stock rose during the order.

The delta check was run again before committing: the new 267.5 call carried a delta of **84 to 85** against the long call's **95**, so the net would be positive. And he articulates the double benefit of the resulting position: "if it goes down, it's okay, because I have $8.50 from the current stock price down to my new short call at 267.5." Eight and a half points of downside cushion and positive upside delta at the same time — the ideal configuration of a diagonal.

His summary of the two-position book at that point is measured and worth preserving as an example of realistic expectation-setting: the portfolio theta was approximately breakeven, which he notes is not ideal but acceptable; both trades had good upside headroom; and his forecast was that Accenture would probably reach the 50% profit target before the 30-day deadline forced a close, while Microsoft was genuinely uncertain — "it could be just break even, losing a little, making a little."

### The Dividend Trap: Closing Accenture, 12 January

The Accenture exit on 12 January is caused by a risk that has not appeared anywhere else in the module and that every seller of in-the-money calls must understand: **early assignment around an ex-dividend date.**

The position was in excellent shape. Accenture was at $279, the trade was making **$644** — **48% return on investment**, within touching distance of the 50% target. The short call was at 267.5, deep in the money, with only **$0.64 per share** of extrinsic value left in it.

The platform flagged that the following day, 13 January, was the **ex-dividend date**, and that the company would pay a dividend of **$1.63** per share.

Adam explains the arithmetic from the counterparty's point of view, which is the only way to see the danger. The person who owns that call can exercise it today, convert it into 100 shares, and become a shareholder of record in time to receive the dividend. Exercising costs him the option's remaining extrinsic value — $0.64 per share, or $64 — because exercising an option always throws away its time value. In exchange he collects $1.63 per share, or $163. Since $163 exceeds $64, exercising is rational, and a rational counterparty will exercise. "So if I don't take any action right now, there's a good chance that this short call will be assigned at the end of today."

That gives the general rule, which is worth stating in its own right because it applies to every short call in every strategy: **when the extrinsic value remaining in an in-the-money short call is less than the upcoming dividend, expect to be assigned.** If assigned, Adam would be short 100 shares and would owe the dividend to the buyer, which he describes as "kind of a hassle process to clear it."

Two remedies existed. He could roll the short call to a strike or expiry where the extrinsic value exceeded $1.63, which would remove the incentive to exercise. Or he could close the trade.

He priced the roll — up to 270, a week further out — and rejected it on three grounds simultaneously. It would cost a debit. It would deliver "a very slow theta decay benefit, which I don't like." And the chart showed the stock overextended and failing at resistance, so the likely path was down. "I don't want to pay a debit to roll my short call up, and then see the stock price pull back. That is the worst-case scenario of rolling, which I don't like."

That phrase deserves isolating, because it names the single worst outcome the strategy can produce: **paying cash to buy upside headroom immediately before the stock falls.** You have spent money to remove a cushion you then needed. It is the mirror image of the 17 December decision, where he kept a deep in-the-money short call as a cushion precisely because he thought a fall was likely.

So he closed, and he lists the three benefits of closing in order: it eliminates the assignment risk entirely, it releases the capital for redeployment, and it locks in a good profit at a level essentially at target.

The execution again shows the negotiation. The tracker indicated a closing credit of about **$23.35**. He queued there, was not filled, reduced to the mark price of $23.30, was still not filled, and noted that the bid-ask was wide because Accenture's liquidity "is not so great" — the same weakness that had cost him on the 28 November roll. He walked down to $23.10, observing that even there the return would be **47%**, and was finally filled at **$23.00**: the long call sold at **$34.72**, the short call bought back at **$11.72**.

Final result on Accenture: **$609 profit, 45.8% return on investment**, in seven weeks, on $1,330 of capital. Slightly below the 50% target, closed for a specific structural reason rather than because the target had been hit.

### The Loser: Closing Microsoft, 22 January

The Microsoft trade is the one that lost money, and Adam gives it as much airtime as the winners, which is the right editorial choice.

By 22 January the stock was at approximately **$446 to $447**. It had fallen about thirty-two points since the 12 January review, and roughly thirty-nine to forty points since the 26 November entry at $485. What had happened was a failure of the thesis in the most complete way available: the stock had been trading in a range, Adam had been hoping for the rebound, and instead it broke the support and "has since declined almost every day."

The position was losing about **$1,000**, and the short call expiring the following day had almost nothing left in it.

Three separate conditions all pointed to the exit, and he names them in order.

The first is the **30-day rule**, which he had pre-committed to two weeks earlier. "The long call expiry date is approaching, so the DTE is now falling below 30. As you know, normally I need to close the trade when my long call DTE is approaching 30 days or below, because at that point in time the remaining extrinsic value in the long call will decay very fast, and it will accelerate. So I want to close it to avoid the negative theta which hurts the trade every day."

The second is the **stop loss**. "The return on investment is also approaching my stop loss anyway." The rule from the theory section was to cut at 50% of maximum loss; maximum loss was $2,062, so the stop sat around $1,031, and the position was at roughly $1,000.

The third is the **collapse of the thesis**. "At this point in time, I have no hope that the stock can recover in time and above the long call strike here so that I can roll." With the stock at $446 and the long call struck at 485, a recovery of nearly forty points inside a month would be required for the position to become workable again, and there was no reason to expect it.

Before executing, he makes the comparison that reframes the loss. A thirty-two-point decline since the last video, on 100 shares, would have cost **$3,200**. The option position, controlling the same 100 shares, lost about **$1,000** — "one third of the loss that you could have incurred had you held the stock instead. So that just gives you another perspective that, hey, trading options, you actually reduce the risk in case the price goes against the trade."

He closed by buying back the short call for **$0.01** and selling the long call for **$3.90**, for a net closing credit of **$3.89** after starting the order at $3.90 and shaving a cent.

Final result on Microsoft: a loss, initially recorded as **$998 and −48% return on investment**.

That figure was then corrected on camera, and the correction is itself a teaching moment about record-keeping. Reviewing the trade history in the platform, Adam discovered he had failed to update the tracker with the correct premium for the last short call sold on 8 January. He had left the previous round's figure of **$1.47** in the cell, when the premium actually collected on that roll was **$2.90**. Correcting the entry reduced the loss to **$936**, or **−45.4% return on investment**. A single un-updated cell had misstated the result of the trade by sixty-two dollars, and there is no way to catch that other than reconciling against the broker's trade history.

# Part XI — The Iron Condor

## The Iron Condor

### 1. Where the Iron Condor Comes From

Everything in this chapter is built out of material you already own. In the credit spread lessons you learned two separate trades that look, at first glance, like opposites. The first was the bull put spread, which you sell when you are moderately bullish — when you think the price is going to go sideways or go up. You sell a put at one strike, you buy a further out-of-the-money put below it for protection, and you collect a net credit. As long as the price does not drop far enough to fall below the strike price of the put you sold, you keep the whole credit. The second was the bear call spread, which you sell when you are moderately bearish — when you think the price is going to go sideways or go down, but not go up too much. You sell a call at one strike, you buy a further out-of-the-money call above it for protection, and again you collect a net credit. As long as the price does not rise beyond the strike of the call you sold, you keep the whole credit.

Read those two descriptions carefully and you will notice something. Both of them contain the word *sideways*. The bull put spread pays maximum profit if the price goes sideways or up. The bear call spread pays maximum profit if the price goes sideways or down. There is therefore a region of price behaviour — sideways — where *both* trades win at the same time. That observation is the whole idea of this chapter. The iron condor is what you get when you execute both credit spreads simultaneously on the same underlying, with the same expiration date, and let them collect premium together.

To be precise about the terminology: when you sell both spreads at the same time you have sold an iron condor. It is sometimes called a *short* iron condor to distinguish it from the long version, which is the mirror-image debit structure that nobody in this course trades. Throughout this chapter, when we say "iron condor" we mean the short iron condor — the version where you are the net seller of premium and you collect cash into your account on the day you open the position. Every credit strategy in this course shares that character: money arrives up front, and the job of the trade thereafter is to keep as much of it as possible.

The short iron condor is ideal when you are neutral on market direction, or neutral on the direction of a particular stock price. In other words, when you think the stock is going to keep going sideways but within a certain range. The range matters. The profit zone of a short iron condor can be quite wide — wider than the profit zone of most of the directional strategies in this course — and as long as the price stays inside that range you collect the maximum profit the position is capable of paying.

There are two reasons to love this structure, and they are worth stating clearly at the outset because they determine everything that follows.

The first reason is that you do not have to predict a direction. The iron condor is a non-directional strategy. You do not need the price to go up. You do not need the price to go down. Whether the price drifts up a little, drifts down a little, or does nothing at all, you are profitable. For a trader, the value of removing the directional guess from the equation is enormous. Most trading losses come from being wrong about direction, and the iron condor simply declines to make that bet.

The second reason is more subtle and more powerful, and it is a genuine structural edge rather than a preference. With a short iron condor you get double the premium for the same risk you took on either the bull put spread or the bear call spread individually. That claim needs to be justified arithmetically, and the next section does exactly that.

### 2. Why the Risk Does Not Double When the Premium Does

Recall the risk-to-reward profile of a single credit spread. When you sell a bull put spread with $5 between the strikes and collect roughly $1 of credit, the maximum risk — which is also the buying power the broker sets aside from your account — is roughly $4 per share, or $400 per contract. That is the width of the spread minus the credit received. In reality you will never lose that $4, because you cut loss a lot earlier: the rule taught in the credit spread lessons is that you exit the moment the price drops and hits the strike price of the put you sold, and in practice that produces a loss of about $1.50 rather than $4. So in a bull put spread you are effectively risking $1.50 to make $1.

The same arithmetic applies to the bear call spread. Every $1 of credit collected comes with a maximum theoretical risk of about $4 per share, the buying power used is again about $4, and again you cut loss the moment price hits the strike of the short call, so the realistic loss on a losing trade is about $1.50. Risk $1.50 to make $1.

Now put both on at once, and ask the critical question: does your risk double?

It does not. The risk stays the same. The reason is structural and it is the single most important idea in this chapter. Think about what has to happen for you to lose money. Once you have entered the trade, the price can either go up and hit your upper stop, or it can go down and hit your lower stop. It cannot do both. It is going to be one or the other. The stock cannot simultaneously break out above your short call and break down below your short put, because the moment it violates one boundary you close the entire position and go home. Therefore, when you enter both spreads, your risk is only one spread's worth of risk — but because you entered both spreads, you collect two spreads' worth of premium.

So you get double the premium and not double the risk. Instead of collecting $1 of credit you collect both sides, and the total credit is roughly $2. But the risk remains the same. In fact, when you look at the numbers, you find that for every $2 of credit you collect, your maximum risk is not four times the credit. Your maximum risk is at most about two times, which is $4 — because the maximum theoretical loss on the structure is the width of one spread ($5) minus the total credit received ($2), which is $3, and the buying power blocked is of that order. And in reality you will never lose that, because you cut loss the moment one of the boundaries is hit, and when that happens your estimated loss is usually about $1.

Read the last two sentences again, because they contain the whole reason experienced income traders reach for this structure. In a single credit spread you were risking about $1.50 to make $1. In the iron condor you are risking roughly $1 to make $2. The risk-to-reward profile is dramatically more favourable, and it is more favourable not because you took on more directional risk or more size, but purely because of the geometry of selling two spreads that cannot both lose.

The table below summarises the comparison for a $5-wide structure, using the round numbers from the lesson.

| Measure | Bull put spread alone | Bear call spread alone | Short iron condor (both) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Credit collected per share | ~$1.00 | ~$1.00 | ~$2.00 |
| Theoretical max loss / buying power | ~$4.00 | ~$4.00 | ~$3.00–$4.00 (one spread's width less total credit) |
| Max loss as multiple of credit | ~4× | ~4× | ~1.5–2× |
| Realistic loss when the stop is hit | ~$1.50 | ~$1.50 | ~$1.00 |
| Effective risk-to-reward | risk $1.50 to make $1 | risk $1.50 to make $1 | risk $1 to make $2 |

That final row is the thesis of the strategy. Everything else in this chapter — strike selection, delta bands, credit minimums, position sizing, exit rules — exists to make sure that the trade you actually put on genuinely has that profile and not some degraded version of it.

### 3. The Payoff Diagram: Building the Tent

The risk-to-reward chart of an iron condor is simply the risk-to-reward chart of the bull put spread superimposed on and combined with that of the bear call spread. It is worth building the picture in stages, because the shape explains the rules.

Start with the bull put spread. Imagine you enter with the stock somewhere in the middle of the chart. From that entry price, the price can go up and you make maximum profit; the price can stay exactly where it is and you make maximum profit; the price can even go down some distance and you still make maximum profit. You only lose money if the price drops too far below a particular point, and that point is the strike of your short put. Below that, the profit line slopes downward until it flattens out at the maximum loss, which is where your long put — the protective wing — takes over and caps the damage.

Now the bear call spread on its own. Again enter with price in the middle. The price can stay where it is, or it can go down, and either is fine — you make maximum profit. It can even go up a certain distance and you still make maximum profit. You only get into trouble if the price goes beyond the upper boundary, which is the strike of your short call. Above that the line slopes downward until the long call caps it.

Put both together and you get the iron condor. Now imagine you enter the trade with the stock price right in the centre. The price can go up, the price can go down, the price can stay sideways, and in every one of those cases you make the maximum profit — as long as it stays within the range. If the price goes up too much, beyond the upper break-even point, you lose money. If it goes down too much, beyond the lower break-even point, you lose money.

The result is a shape that is often called the profit tent, though "tent" undersells it — a tent implies a single peak, and the iron condor's profit region is a flat plateau, not a spike. The plateau runs from the short put strike to the short call strike, and everywhere on that plateau you earn exactly the same maximum profit, which is the total credit received. Outside the plateau, on each side, the payoff slopes down through a break-even point and then flattens at maximum loss once the long wing engages. In profile it looks like a table with two short legs on either side — a wide flat top with two ramps descending to two floors.

Four numbers describe this shape completely, and you should be able to compute all four before you ever click confirm on an order.

| Quantity | How it is computed |
|---|---|
| Maximum profit | Total net credit received × 100 × number of contracts |
| Maximum loss | (Width of one spread − total net credit) × 100 × contracts |
| Upper break-even | Short call strike + total net credit per share |
| Lower break-even | Short put strike − total net credit per share |

Notice which strikes do *not* appear in the break-even formulas. The long call and the long put — the wings — do not affect where you break even at all. They affect only the maximum loss, by capping it. This is worth internalising: the wings are insurance, and like all insurance they cost you premium and do nothing whatsoever until disaster strikes. Their entire job is to convert an undefined-risk position into a defined-risk one, so that a catastrophic gap cannot take more from you than a known, bounded number.

A live illustration of the structure will make it concrete. In the lesson, an iron condor was already open on TXN, alongside others on Adobe, ADP and Viva. The TXN position consisted of a bull put spread selling the 155 put and buying the 150 put beneath it, and a bear call spread selling the 170 call and buying the 175 call above it. That is the whole architecture: strikes at 150 / 155 / 170 / 175, with the two inner strikes short and the two outer strikes long, everything $5 apart on each side, and a 15-point gap in the middle where the price is currently sitting.

Displaying the legs one pair at a time on the analysis tab makes the construction transparent. With only the put legs checked, you see the bull put spread: current share price sitting comfortably above the structure, maximum profit if price rises, maximum profit if price stays flat, maximum profit even if price falls somewhat, and losses only below the 155 short put strike. Uncheck those and check only the call legs, and you see the bear call spread: maximum profit if price collapses, maximum profit if price stays flat, maximum profit if price rises somewhat, and trouble only beyond the 170 short call. Check all four boxes and the two diagrams fuse into the iron condor, with its flat plateau running from 155 to 170 and its two descending ramps outside.

### 4. The Four Legs, Formally

It helps to have the construction laid out as a table, because the iron condor is the first four-legged structure in this course and the leg bookkeeping is where beginners make errors.

| Leg | Action | Option type | Strike position | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy | Put | Furthest out-of-the-money, $5 below leg 2 | Downside wing — caps maximum loss on the put side |
| 2 | Sell | Put | Delta 23–28, below support | Primary income leg on the downside; defines the lower edge of the profit plateau |
| 3 | Sell | Call | Delta 23–28, above resistance | Primary income leg on the upside; defines the upper edge of the profit plateau |
| 4 | Buy | Call | Furthest out-of-the-money, $5 above leg 3 | Upside wing — caps maximum loss on the call side |

Reading the strikes from lowest to highest, the pattern is long-short-short-long: buy the low put, sell the higher put, sell the lower call, buy the higher call. Both short options are out of the money at entry, one below the current price and one above it. Both long options are further out of the money still. All four legs share the same expiration date. All four legs are traded in equal quantity.

The two shorts do the earning. The two longs do the protecting. The distance between a short and its wing — the width — is what determines both the maximum loss and the amount of buying power the broker sets aside.

### 5. When To Deploy: The Neutral Outlook and the Chart

You deploy an iron condor when you are neutral on the asset's direction. You do not know whether the price is going up, you do not know whether it is going down, and you think it is going to go roughly sideways within a certain range. That is the best time to use a short iron condor.

The important discipline here is that "neutral" is not the same as "no opinion." A trader with no opinion is guessing. A trader with a neutral opinion has looked at the chart and formed a positive view that price is contained. You want to see the containment on the chart before you put the trade on.

What that looks like in practice is a stock in a range, with visible structure on both edges. The example used in the lesson was Lowe's (LOW). The chart showed a stock in a slight uptrend — making higher lows — but making roughly the same highs each time, producing a wedge-like consolidation pattern. It waves up, comes down, goes up, comes down, and stays inside a band. There was a visible level of resistance at around $221 and a visible level of support at around $192, with the stock trading at about $203 in between. That is the picture you want: a resistance the stock has repeatedly failed to exceed, and a support it has repeatedly failed to break.

Why the visible support and resistance matter is straightforward once you connect them to the structure. When you construct an iron condor, you want to create the bear call spread *above* the resistance and the bull put spread *below* the support. If you do that, then price has to break structure — has to do something it has repeatedly failed to do — before your position is even threatened. The support and resistance are not magic, but they are places where buyers and sellers have previously shown up in size, and putting your short strikes on the far side of them gives you a buffer that is earned by the chart rather than imagined.

There is a second, softer confirmation available from the moving averages, and it is a useful sanity check because it is hard to argue with. When a stock is in a clear uptrend, the moving averages slope upwards and stack in order, with the 50-period above the 150 and the 150 above the 200. When a stock is in a clear downtrend, the moving averages slope downwards and stack in the reverse order, with the 200 above the 150 and the 150 above the 50. But when a stock is going sideways, the moving averages criss-cross each other. They tangle. They look, in the phrase used in the lesson, like wool or a string that has been knotted up. When you see the strings knotted, that tells you the stock is going sideways — and a sideways stock is what the iron condor is built for. The same observation was made again on Berkshire Hathaway in the case study: the 200, the 150 and the 50 moving averages were crossing each other back and forth, which is exactly the signature of a range.

So the chart test has two parts, and you want both: a range with identifiable support and resistance edges, and moving averages that are tangled rather than stacked and sloping.

### 6. Underlying Selection and Liquidity

You can trade an iron condor on any asset. It works on futures, on indices, on ETFs, on individual stocks. Different traders specialise differently, and the lesson is explicit that this is a matter of expertise rather than doctrine: Adam's expertise is in individual stocks, so he trades iron condors on stocks; Bang prefers oil futures and commodity futures, and does exactly the same trade there with the same logic.

For those trading stocks, the selection criteria are conservative and specific. You want fundamentally good businesses — good companies. Generally that means stocks within the S&P 500, large companies. You do not want to trade this on small companies or speculative companies. The reason is not snobbery; it is gap risk, which we return to below. Large, well-capitalised, widely-held companies gap less violently and less often than small speculative ones, and the entire iron condor thesis is a bet against violent movement.

ETFs are also perfectly tradeable, with one caveat: ETFs usually do not pay as much premium as individual stocks, because their implied volatility is lower. The diversification inside an ETF damps its volatility, and damped volatility means thinner option premium. So you can trade them, but you will more often find that the credit falls short of the minimums we are about to set.

Liquidity deserves its own paragraph because the iron condor is a four-legged trade. Every leg you add is another bid-ask spread you must cross, both on the way in and on the way out. A structure with four legs crosses eight spreads over its life. On an illiquid underlying with wide markets, those eight crossings can eat a meaningful fraction of the credit you were trying to collect. That is why the lesson insists on high liquidity, tight bid and ask, and — as a preference rather than an absolute rule — the presence of a weekly option series.

The weekly-series criterion is a proxy for liquidity and choice. Stocks with weekly option series generally have more liquidity, more strike prices available, and consequently better trades on offer. On the ThinkOrSwim platform you confirm this simply by opening the option series list and looking for entries labelled "weeklys." If you see them, the criterion is met. If you do not see them, the stock fails that particular preference. But it is a good-to-have, not a must — there are times when a stock with a good iron condor setup and good premium simply does not have a weekly series, and the trade can still be taken.

Berkshire Hathaway Class B, the subject of the extended case study later in this chapter, was chosen in part on exactly these grounds. It is a blue chip, extremely solid, and at the time of the trade the company was sitting on approximately $300 billion in cash. It is a company run conservatively for a very long time by a manager who habitually holds large cash balances, partly because the insurance operations require cash reserves as protection. The liquidity was good, the bid-ask was good, and weekly options existed. It is exactly the kind of underlying the strategy is designed for: large, stable, boring.

### 7. The Earnings Exclusion

The largest single threat to an iron condor on an individual stock is a gap. If the stock gaps up, it can open way above your short call strike and, occasionally, straight past your long call, delivering the maximum loss without ever giving you the chance to exit at your intended stop. If it gaps down, it can open far below your lower break-even in exactly the same way. That is the fundamental risk of trading this structure on individual stocks rather than on indices, and you cannot eliminate it completely.

But you can mitigate most of it, because most large gaps are not random. They cluster around scheduled events, and the dominant scheduled event for an individual stock is the earnings announcement. It is usually during earnings that a company gaps up a lot on good news or gaps down too much on bad news. Gaps can certainly occur outside earnings, but the concentration around earnings is overwhelming.

The rule that follows is simple and it is close to absolute in practice. Do not trade iron condors when the stock is going to announce earnings soon. Concretely: if earnings fall within your 30-to-45-day window, do not take the trade. If you do enter a position and earnings are approaching while the trade is still open, you close the trade before earnings are announced. Always. It is simply too risky to hold an iron condor through an earnings report.

There is one softening of the rule, stated honestly in the lesson. If the setup is very good, the trade may still be entered even though earnings are coming — but not too close. Earnings must be at least about 30 days away. And even then, the trade will be closed before the announcement rather than held through it.

This exclusion is what killed the Lowe's example. Everything else about Lowe's qualified. The chart was ranging between support at $192 and resistance at $221 with the stock at about $203. The moving averages were knotted. The IV percentile read 36, comfortably above the 30 threshold. Weekly options existed. But below the chart on the ThinkOrSwim platform sat a blue icon indicating an earnings announcement, and clicking it revealed earnings scheduled for the 23rd of May before the market opened. The recording date was the 15th of May. That is less than ten days away. In ten days you cannot extract much profit from an iron condor, because iron condors and credit spreads make their money slowly through theta decay — the longer you hold, the more you make. So the trade was not taken in reality. It was used as a teaching example only, and the lesson is explicit about that: it was the only stock available on the day that met the other criteria, and trades do not appear every day. Some days you see nothing. Some days you see several.

Berkshire Hathaway, by contrast, passed this test cleanly. The company had released earnings the week before the trade was placed, which meant there would be no more earnings for roughly the next 90 days — the entire life of a 41-day option and then some.

### 8. Implied Volatility Rank

The second environmental criterion is implied volatility. Ideally you want to trade stocks whose current IV percentile — also called IV rank — is 30 and above.

The reasoning is direct. When the IV percentile is 30 or higher, options are relatively expensive compared with where they have traded over the past year, which means premiums are higher, which means you get more premium for the same structure. Since you are a net seller of premium in every iron condor, selling when premium is rich is straightforwardly better than selling when premium is thin.

You should treat this as a strong preference rather than an inviolable law. Sometimes the IV percentile is below 30 and you still get good premiums; it happens. So this is not an absolute rule, but it is a good thing to have, and the credit test described in the next section is the real gate. If IV rank is low, you will usually discover that fact anyway, because the credit will fail to reach the minimum and you will discard the trade for that reason instead.

On ThinkOrSwim you find the number under Today's Options Statistics on the Trade tab. On Lowe's it read 36, which satisfies the criterion.

There is a related Vega point that belongs here, though its consequences show up during management rather than at entry. Because you are short net premium, you are short Vega: you want implied volatility to fall after you enter. If volatility drops after entry, the position gains value faster — on the analysis chart, dragging the volatility adjustment widget negative causes the purple current-P&L line to rise and you make money faster. Conversely, if you enter an iron condor and volatility rises instead of falling — the stock becomes more volatile — the purple line drops lower and you will see unrealised losses initially, until theta decay catches up and makes up for it. This is not a failure of the trade. It is the normal behaviour of a short-Vega position in a rising-volatility environment, and understanding it in advance is what stops traders panicking out of positions that are behaving exactly as designed.

### 9. Choosing the Expiration: The 30-to-45-Day Window

The sweet spot for days to expiration is 30 to 45 days.

That window is chosen as a compromise between two opposing forces. Longer-dated options carry more absolute premium, so a 90-day iron condor collects more credit than a 40-day one — but it collects it far more slowly, because theta decay is gentle far from expiration and accelerates as expiration approaches. Shorter-dated options decay fast, but they carry so little premium that you cannot reach the credit minimums without moving your short strikes uncomfortably close to the money, which destroys the very wide profit zone that makes the strategy attractive. Between 30 and 45 days you get enough absolute premium to satisfy the credit test while sitting in the part of the decay curve where time is starting to work meaningfully in your favour.

Within the window, the shorter expiration is preferred when it works. Given a choice between a 33-day and a 40-day expiry, the shorter one is preferable because it expires faster, meaning you reach maximum profit sooner; the faster it expires, the more money you make per unit of time. But the shorter expiry must still pay enough credit, and often it does not. That is exactly what happened on Lowe's. Selling the 190 put and buying the 185 put in the 16 June series — 33 days out — produced a net credit of only 88 cents, below the 90-cent floor. Entering the same two strikes manually rather than through the right-click vertical dialog produced 80 cents. Either way, 33 days did not pay enough. Moving out to the 23 June expiry — 40 days — the same 190/185 put spread produced 91 cents, which cleared the minimum. So the 40-day expiry was used, and the choice was made by the credit, not by preference.

Bang's practice on futures runs slightly longer. His preferred timeframe for trading iron condors is anywhere between 45 and 60 days, or one-and-a-half to two months. In the crude oil example he selected a 62-day expiration because a 45-day series was not available and 62 was close enough to 60. On the Berkshire trade, working within Adam's stock framework, he selected 41 days from a choice of 35 or 41, preferring the 41-day series specifically because it was a monthly option, and monthly options usually carry higher liquidity than weeklies.

That last point is a useful refinement of the weekly-series rule. You want the *stock* to have weekly options, because that indicates depth and choice across the chain. But when you actually pick your expiration, the monthly series is often the better instrument to trade, because open interest concentrates there and the markets are tightest.

### 10. Strike Selection: The Delta 23–28 Band

Once the expiration is chosen, the strikes are chosen by delta, and the same band applies to both short legs.

The short put is selected at a delta of 23 to 28. The short call is selected at a delta of 23 to 28. That is the sweet spot for both.

The logic behind the band is a direct trade-off, and it is worth articulating because it explains why the band has both a floor and a ceiling. The lower the delta you choose, the better in one respect — a lower delta means the strike sits further away from the current market price, further out of the money, and therefore less likely to be threatened. But if it is too far away, too far out of the money, you will not collect enough premium to make the trade worth doing. So there is an optimal region between those pressures. Well above 28 delta, the strike is too close to the market price and you may get hit too fast. Much below 23 delta, you do not get enough premium. Between 23 and 28 lies the balance.

There is a second, deeper reading of delta that makes the choice more intuitive. The delta of an out-of-the-money option is a rough approximation of the market's estimate of the probability that the option finishes in the money. A 25-delta short put therefore carries roughly a 25% chance of finishing in the money and roughly a 75% chance of expiring worthless. Doing that on both sides gives you a structure where, at entry, the market's own pricing implies a high probability that price finishes between your short strikes. That is the statistical foundation of the trade, and it is why the strategy can tolerate a moderate loss rate and still be profitable: you are structurally winning most of the time by design.

In practice you scan the delta column of the option chain and pick the strike whose delta lands inside the band, choosing the middle of the band where possible. On the Lowe's 23 June chain, the put side showed a strike at 25 delta, which is ideally central, so the 190 put was the short put. On the 16 June chain, the closest was 24 delta at the same 190 strike, with 31 too high and 18 too low. On the call side of the 23 June chain, the available delta inside the band was 23, at the 220 strike, so the 220 call was the short call.

On Berkshire Hathaway the chain did not offer a clean 25. The available choices bracketed it: 21 on one side and 27 on the other. Twenty-one would be too low, so 27 was selected, and that put the short put at the 465 strike. On the call side the same 27-delta reasoning selected the 495 strike as the short call. Both sit inside the 23-to-28 band, and the resulting structure had a 30-point-wide profit plateau running from 465 to 495 with the stock trading in between.

Bang's futures practice again differs, and the difference is instructive rather than contradictory. On crude oil futures he sells both short legs at 10 delta, not 25. With 10-delta shorts you have roughly a 90% probability on your side — meaning a high probability of winning — and the profit zone is correspondingly enormous. The cost is that a 10-delta option collects very little premium, which is precisely why the risk-to-reward on that trade looks so lopsided: in his crude oil example the maximum profit on five contracts was $850 against a maximum loss of $4,150. That is a fine trade if the 90% probability is real, and it is a completely different balance of probability against payoff from the 25-delta stock version. Neither is wrong. They are different points on the same trade-off curve, and you should understand which point you are choosing and why.

### 11. Wing Width and the Credit Test

Having chosen each short strike by delta, you place each wing a fixed distance beyond it. The default distance is $5.

For the put side: sell the short put at 23–28 delta, then buy the long put roughly $5 below it. For the call side: sell the short call at 23–28 delta, then buy the long call $5 above it. Most of the time — the lesson estimates 95% of the time — $5 is the width used.

The exception is high-priced stocks. On a stock trading at $500 or $1,000 or more, the option chain may not offer strikes at $5 intervals, and you are forced to a $10 minimum width. That is acceptable, but it changes the credit requirement, and the adjustment is mechanical: if the width doubles, the required credit doubles.

Here is the credit test in full, because it is the single most important numerical filter in the strategy.

For a $5-wide spread, you want a credit of at least 90 cents, and preferably $1.00 or more, **per spread**. If you get more than a dollar — $1.20, $1.30 — that is a great trade. But 90 cents is the floor. If you cannot get at least 90 cents, you throw the stock away and look for another one. It is a waste of your time.

Since the iron condor consists of two spreads, entering the whole structure as one order requires double the per-spread credit. For a $5-wide iron condor the minimum total credit is $1.80, and the preferred total credit is $2.00 or more. Above $2.00 is even better.

For a $10-wide structure everything doubles again. A $10-wide single spread requires at least $1.80 to ideally $2.00. A $10-wide iron condor therefore requires at least $3.60 to ideally $4.00 in total credit per contract.

| Width of each spread | Minimum credit per spread | Preferred credit per spread | Minimum total iron condor credit | Preferred total iron condor credit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $5 | $0.90 | $1.00 | $1.80 | $2.00 |
| $10 | $1.80 | $2.00 | $3.60 | $4.00 |

The reason this test exists is that it enforces the risk-to-reward ratio automatically. If you collect $2.00 on a $5-wide iron condor, the theoretical maximum loss is $3.00 and the ratio of max loss to max profit is 1.5. If you collect only $1.00 on the same structure, the maximum loss is $4.00 and the ratio is 4.0 — you would be back to the poor economics of a single credit spread while carrying a four-legged position. The credit minimum is therefore not an arbitrary preference; it is the mechanism by which the structural advantage described in Section 2 is actually delivered.

A worked example of the $10 case was given on Chipotle, a stock trading around $2,000 per share. Selecting a roughly 25-delta put at the 1940 strike and buying $10 below at 1930, then selecting a roughly 25-delta call at 2175 and buying $10 above at 2185, produced a total credit of exactly $4.00 — precisely the target for a $10-wide iron condor. That is what a correctly-scaled high-priced-stock iron condor looks like.

There is a second constraint that runs alongside the credit test and cross-checks it. For an iron condor, you want the maximum loss — which is also the buying power that will be used from the account — to be roughly 1.5 to 1.8 times the maximum profit, and not more than that. If the ratio exceeds 1.8, the credit is too thin relative to the width and the trade should be rejected. The two tests are two views of the same underlying quantity, and they should agree; if they disagree you have made an arithmetic error somewhere.

### 12. The Complete Worked Setup on Lowe's

It is worth walking the Lowe's example end to end, because it demonstrates every calculation in sequence even though the trade was ultimately rejected on the earnings rule.

**Underlying and chart.** Lowe's (LOW), an S&P 500 constituent, trading at about $203. Visible resistance around $221 and visible support around $192. Moving averages criss-crossing, indicating sideways action.

**Environmental filters.** IV percentile 36, above the 30 threshold. Weekly option series present. Earnings scheduled 23 May before the open, with the current date 15 May — a failure of the earnings rule, and the reason the trade was not taken for real.

**Expiration.** The 16 June series, 33 days out, was tested first and rejected because the put spread paid only 88 cents. The 23 June series, 40 days out, was used.

**Put side.** The 25-delta strike was the 190 put, so sell the 190 put and buy the 185 put $5 below. Net credit 91 cents — above the 90-cent floor, though below the $1.00 preference.

**Call side.** The 23-delta strike was the 220 call, so sell the 220 call and buy the 225 call $5 above. The market credit was 89 cents, marginally below the floor. Rather than discard a trade that close to acceptable, the correct action is to place a limit order at 90 cents. If the market fills you, you have your minimum; if it does not fill, you do not get the trade, which is the correct outcome. So the call side was priced at 90 cents.

**Total credit.** 91 cents plus 90 cents equals $1.81 per share, or $181 per contract, since one contract covers 100 shares.

**Maximum profit.** $181 per contract. This is confirmed on the analysis chart, where the green line — the profit and loss at expiration — plateaus at 181 across the whole region between the short strikes.

**Profit plateau.** From 190 to 220. If the price remains between 190 and 220 at expiration, you collect the full $181.

**Maximum loss.** $319 per contract, which is also the buying power used from the account. Check the arithmetic: the width of one spread is $5.00, the total credit is $1.81, and $5.00 − $1.81 = $3.19, which is $319 per contract.
