The figure read off the platform and the figure computed by hand agree exactly.

**Ratio test.** $319 divided by $181 is approximately 1.76. The requirement is that maximum loss should be between 1.5 and 1.8 times maximum profit, and 1.76 sits inside that band. Compare this with the individual credit spreads, where the maximum loss is four times the credit received, and the improvement is stark. This is the concrete demonstration that iron condors have a more favourable risk-reward profile — that they are, in that specific sense, safer.

**Break-evens.** The upper break-even is the short call strike plus the total premium received: 220 + 1.81 = 221.81, shown on the platform as about 221.8. The lower break-even is the short put strike minus the total premium received: 190 − 1.81 = 188.19, shown as about 188.18. (The transcript renders the credit as "1.18" at this point in the arithmetic, which is a transposition of 1.81; the resulting break-evens quoted, 221.8 and 188.18, are consistent with $1.81 and are the numbers used throughout.)

**Estimated loss at the stop.** The purple line on the analysis chart shows the current-date profit and loss. Hovering the cursor at the upper break-even of about 221.8 shows the purple line at $90.07. So if price rises to the upper break-even and you close the entire trade there and then, your estimated loss is about $90 per contract.

**Final risk-reward.** Risking about $90 to make $181. That is risking $1 to make $2. The rule is absolute: for an iron condor, always make sure you are risking a dollar to make $2 or more. If the ratio is worse than one-to-two, it is a bad trade and you do not take it.

**Chart overlay.** With the break-evens computed, they are drawn on the price chart in red — the point of no return on each side. The upper red line at 221.8 sits *above* the resistance at about $221. The lower red line at 188.18 sits *below* the support at about $192. So the profit zone fully contains the trading range, with margin on both sides. Price would have to break resistance *and* then travel further, or break support *and* then travel further, before the trade is in danger. Over the next 40 days, price can go up, go sideways, or go down, and as long as it does not touch 221.8 or 188.18, it is a profitable trade. Visually, that looks like a reasonable proposition, which is exactly what the chart test is meant to establish.

Everything about the trade qualifies except the earnings date, and the earnings date alone is sufficient to reject it.

### 13. A Note on the Short Put and Support

One refinement deserves emphasis because it is easy to miss inside the larger procedure. When examining the Lowe's put spread on its own, the lower break-even was computed at about 189 (the round number used in the walkthrough before the call side was added, since with only the put spread on the credit was 91 cents and 190 − 0.91 ≈ 189.09). The question then asked was whether 189 is far enough below the current price, and the answer came from the chart: yes, because there is a visible support level above it. If price falls, it ought to hit the support and bounce.

The principle generalises. Ideally you want the strike price of your short put to sit below a support level, so that it is protected by structure and will not get hit easily. Symmetrically, you want the strike of your short call to sit above a resistance level. The delta band tells you roughly where the strike should go; the chart tells you whether that particular strike is a good place for it. When the two agree — when the 25-delta strike happens to sit just beyond a structural level — you have a much better trade than when the delta band lands you in the middle of open air.

### 14. The Greeks: Theta as the Engine

The iron condor is a positive-theta position. Theta is the engine of the entire strategy, and if you understand nothing else about the Greeks, understand this.

The mechanism is visible directly on the analysis chart, where two lines are drawn. The green line is the profit and loss at expiration — the final payoff diagram, the tent with the flat plateau. The purple line is the profit and loss as of the current date, and it is a flattened, sagging version of the green line. At entry, the purple line sits well below the green line everywhere, because the options you sold still contain substantial time value that you have not yet earned.

Now advance the date on the simulator. Move from 15 May to 16 May, then further. As time passes, the purple line starts to move higher and higher and higher, until eventually it reaches the green line on expiration date. That is theta decay made visible. It is why, for an iron condor, the longer you hold it, the more money you make, until you make the maximum on expiration.

Three practical consequences follow, and each of them corrects a common beginner error.

The first consequence is that you should expect to be unprofitable at the very start. When you enter an iron condor, you may look at it a day later and say: the stock price is staying within the range, so why am I not making money? In fact you could be losing money initially, because the purple line at entry sits below zero across much of the range and can drop further before it starts to climb. You have to wait for the purple line to rise. You have to be patient and wait for the options to decay. Bang put the same point in different words on the Berkshire trade: it is a slow-burning kind of trade, you do not see profit overnight, the profit comes very slowly over time and especially slowly in the first few days, and as time passes and you get nearer to expiration the decay accelerates and you see more benefit. He also said, correctly, that this makes it a boring trade — and that in options trading, boring is good, because too exciting a trade is dangerous.

The second consequence is that your risk shrinks over time. Because the purple line rises toward the green line, the loss you would suffer by cutting at a break-even point gets smaller the longer you have been in the trade. At entry, hitting the upper break-even on Lowe's would cost about $90. Later in the trade, hitting the same price would cost less, because more time value has already been earned and banked into the position. Bang made this explicit on Berkshire: the longer he is in the trade and the price stays within the profit zone, the less risk he has, because if he has to close at one of the exit points he would close at almost break-even, or for a very tiny loss. The worst-case scenario is that the price starts moving sharply one way or the other in the first few minutes after entry, before any decay has accumulated. After a few days, and certainly after a few weeks, the trade is almost certainly making money even if he has to exit at a boundary.

The third consequence is that theta gives you a running daily number you can monitor. On the crude oil iron condor, five contracts produced a positive theta such that if the oil price stayed at the same level and everything else stayed the same, each day that passed would bring roughly $15. Later, holding two oil iron condors simultaneously, the combined theta was about $25 per day — and, as Bang pointed out, theta does not care whether it is a weekday or a weekend; every day that passes, it pays. When he checked the position after the first night and found it showing a small $50 loss, his verdict was that the P&L was not important and that a small loss or profit in the first few days is very normal; the key part is that theta is positive and working. That is the correct way to read an iron condor in its first week.

### 15. The Greeks: Vega, Delta and Gamma

**Vega.** The iron condor is short Vega, because you are net short options. If volatility drops after entry, the purple line rises and you make money faster — the analysis platform's volatility adjustment widget demonstrates this directly: set a negative volatility adjustment and the purple line lifts. If volatility rises instead — the stock gets more volatile — the purple line drops lower and you may see unrealised losses. Those losses are not a signal to panic; they are a temporary mark-to-market effect that theta decay will offset over time as the purple line eventually jumps up to the green line. But you must understand this in advance, because a volatility spike early in a trade can show a loss even while price sits perfectly in the centre of your profit zone.

This is also, incidentally, why the estimated loss at a break-even point is an estimate and not a guarantee. If the price really goes up to the break-even or drops down to it, you may not lose exactly the $90 the chart showed at entry. You may lose less, if enough time has passed; you may lose a bit more, if volatility has risen sharply. It is an estimate.

**Delta.** At entry, a well-constructed iron condor is close to delta-neutral, because the short put's positive delta and the short call's negative delta roughly cancel. That is the mathematical expression of being non-directional. As price moves toward one side, the position acquires a directional delta pointing against you — the tested short option's delta rises and the position starts behaving like a directional trade you did not want. This is precisely what delta-based monitoring detects, and it is the basis of Bang's adjustment trigger discussed below.

**Gamma.** Gamma is the rate of change of delta, and it is the risk that grows as expiration approaches. Near expiry, an option whose strike sits close to the current price develops enormous gamma: small price moves produce large delta swings and large P&L swings. This is why an iron condor that is comfortable at 40 days can become alarming at 3 days even with the price in the same place — the payoff line has hardened from the gentle purple curve into the sharp-cornered green tent, and price is now sitting on a knife-edge rather than a cushion. It is one of the strongest arguments for taking profit early rather than holding to the last day, and it underlies the profit-taking rules in the next section.

### 16. Position Sizing

Sizing comes before order entry, and it is treated with unusual seriousness in the lesson for a good reason: there is no 100% winning trade. Any trade you enter could be a losing trade. Over many trades you should have more winners than losers, and your winners should make more than your losers lose, so that net you make a profit. But on any individual trade you could lose. So as a trader, never think about how much you are going to make on a trade. Always think about how much you are going to lose, and whether the amount you lose is going to destroy your account.

The sizing method taught here is deliberately conservative and proceeds in four steps.

1. **Determine the estimated loss per contract if you cut at a break-even point.** Read it off the analysis chart by placing the cursor at the upper or lower break-even and reading the purple line. On the Lowe's trade this was about $91 per contract.
2. **Multiply that estimated loss by 1.5 to build in a buffer.** The estimate can be exceeded in reality, particularly if volatility rises. On Lowe's, $91 × 1.5 = about $136. So it is safe to assume that if you cut loss on this trade you will lose at most $136 per contract.
3. **Compute your risk budget as 2% of account size.** The general rule is that you never risk more than 2% of your account on any one trade. Your account size here means your net liquidation value (NLV).
4. **Divide the risk budget by the buffered per-contract loss, and round down.**

Two worked examples make it concrete. With a $10,000 account, 2% is $200. Dividing $200 by $136 gives 1.47, so you can trade exactly one contract — one contract risks $136, which is within the $200 budget, whereas two contracts would risk $272, which exceeds it. With a $100,000 account, 2% is $2,000. Dividing $2,000 by $136 gives about 14.7, which rounds down to 14 contracts.

| Account NLV | 2% risk budget | Buffered loss per contract | Contracts (rounded down) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $10,000 | $200 | $136 | 1 |
| $100,000 | $2,000 | $136 | 14 |

Note carefully what this method does *not* do. It does not size by maximum theoretical loss, and it does not size by buying power. It sizes by the loss you actually expect to take when you obey your own exit rule. That is only legitimate if you genuinely obey the exit rule. If you are the kind of trader who lets losers run past the stop, this sizing method will under-estimate your risk severely, and you should size by maximum loss instead. The 1.5× buffer is the concession to imperfection — it covers the case where slippage or a volatility spike makes the exit worse than the chart predicted — but it does not cover the case where you simply refuse to exit.

The seriousness of the exit rule is stated with some force in the lesson: never allow the trade to go too high or too low, let it expire, and hit the maximum loss. That is described as unforgivable, with the promise of a personal visit and a slap should it occur. The humour is doing real work — it is marking the difference between a strategy with a defined, survivable loss and a strategy where one bad trade removes several months of income.

### 17. Order Entry: Two Legs at a Time, or All Four at Once

There are two ways to get into an iron condor, and the choice between them is genuinely a matter of experience.

**Method one: enter the two spreads separately.** Place the bull put spread as one vertical order and the bear call spread as a second vertical order.

The advantage of doing it this way is flexibility on exit. If you entered separately, you can close one side and keep the other. Suppose the stock rallies and your bear call spread becomes a loser. You can close just the bear call spread for a loss and keep the bull put spread running to near expiration to collect its maximum profit. That is a genuine benefit, and it is why the experienced trader in the lesson enters his own positions this way.

The danger is execution risk. If you enter the bull put spread first and the stock price moves too much before you get the second order in, you may not get filled on the bear call spread at the price you want. You then end up holding one spread and not the other, or holding the second spread at a bad price, and the overall trade does not look the way you designed it.

**Method two: enter all four legs together as a single iron condor order.** This is the safe method and the one recommended for beginners. Because the whole structure trades as one instrument, you get all four legs or none of them, and you get them at a known net credit.

Mechanically on ThinkOrSwim, you right-click on one of the strikes — for instance the 190 put on the Lowe's example — and choose Sell, then Iron Condor. The platform immediately generates all four legs. You then edit the strikes to the ones you actually want: for the put side, sell 190 and buy 185; for the call side, sell 220 and buy 225. The platform will not know which strikes you intend, so you must set them yourself. It then displays the market price, which is the net credit for the whole structure — on the Lowe's example, $1.80.

For method one, the individual spreads are built either by right-clicking a strike and choosing Sell, Vertical — which automatically constructs the two-leg spread — or by clicking legs manually. The manual method requires you to remember one convention: when you are buying, you click on the ask; when you are selling, you click on the bid. So to sell the 190 put you click the bid at 190, which produces a quantity of minus one, and then you hold the Control key and click the ask at 185 to add the long leg. The Control key is what keeps the existing legs in the order rather than replacing them. Bang uses exactly this technique on both the crude oil and Berkshire examples: click the first leg, then hold Control for every subsequent leg, building all four in sequence.

**Negotiating the fill.** Whichever method you use, you must place a limit order. Click the lock icon on the price field so the broker will only fill at your limit price or better. Never send an iron condor as a market order.

The recommended technique is to start greedy and walk down. On the Lowe's example the market credit was $1.80, which is the bare minimum, so the sensible opening bid is $2.00 — always try at least $2.00 first. Send it in, go to the Monitor tab, and see whether it fills. If it does not, replace the order at $1.95 and wait. If that does not fill, try $1.90. Keep bargaining until you get filled, but never go below $1.80 for a $5-wide iron condor. It is exactly like haggling: you are selling something and you want as much for it as you can get, and each step down is a concession you make only when the market refuses your price.

The same fishing technique applies to individual spreads. On the Lowe's put spread, with 91 cents available, you might try 95 cents first and lower it to 93 or 92 if it does not fill within a few seconds. Sometimes you do get lucky and get filled at a higher credit, and there is no harm in asking. What there is harm in is going below the floor because you are impatient.

Bang demonstrated the same behaviour in reverse on the crude oil trade. He had 17 cents showing and locked it, then decided that if he really wanted the fill he would go down to 16 cents, which he expected to execute. He right-clicked, chose cancel-and-replace, reduced to 16, confirmed and sent — and it filled at 16. On Berkshire he started at $2.20 for the credit and reduced the price to get filled, noting that as long as it was more than $2.00 it was fine, and filling at $2.15. He remarked that he had perhaps reduced it too quickly, which is an honest observation: aggressive walking-down leaves money on the table, and patience is usually rewarded.

One pleasant detail worth noting from the Berkshire entry: after execution, the cash balance in the account rises immediately, because this is a trade where you collect cash up front rather than paying it. Two contracts at $2.15 brought in $430, and the account cash moved from about $2,000 to about $2,400 as a result.

### 18. The Entry Procedure, Step by Step

Bringing all of the above together, here is the complete entry sequence in order.

1. **Choose a stock or ETF to trade.** Ideally find one in a range within a visible support and resistance level. Prefer large S&P 500 companies with good fundamentals. Confirm the range with criss-crossing moving averages.
2. **Check the environmental filters.** IV percentile ideally 30 and above. No earnings results coming soon — and if earnings are coming, you must be able to get out of the trade before they hit. A weekly option series is preferred but not required.
3. **Choose the date to expiration.** The sweet spot is 30 to 45 days. Prefer the shorter expiry within the window if it pays enough credit; monthly series often offer better liquidity than weeklies.
4. **Build the bear call spread.** Go to the call option chain, sell the call at a delta of 23 to 28, and buy the call $5 above it. Confirm a credit of at least 90 cents, preferably $1.00 or more.
5. **Build the bull put spread.** Go to the put option chain, sell the put at a delta of 23 to 28, and buy the put $5 below it. Confirm a credit of at least 90 cents, preferably $1.00 or more.
6. **Analyse the combined structure.** Look at the iron condor risk-to-reward chart. Read off the upper and lower break-even prices, the maximum profit, and the estimated loss if you cut at either boundary.
7. **Apply the risk-reward test.** Confirm you are risking $1 to make $2 or more. If you cannot get at least $2 of reward per $1 of risk, it is not a good iron condor and you do not take it. Cross-check that maximum loss is between 1.5 and 1.8 times maximum profit.
8. **Overlay the break-evens on the price chart.** Draw both break-even levels in red as the points of no return, and satisfy yourself that price would have to break structure to reach either one.
9. **Size the position.** Take the estimated loss per contract at a break-even, multiply by 1.5, and divide 2% of your net liquidation value by that number. Round down.
10. **Enter the trade as one four-legged iron condor order** — the safest approach, particularly for beginners. Place a limit order with a minimum of $1.80 to $2.00 per contract for a $5-wide structure, or $3.60 to $4.00 for a $10-wide structure. Start higher than the minimum and walk down until filled.
11. **Confirm and send, then check the fill.** Go to the Monitor tab, then to Activity and Positions, and check the trade status to confirm the order filled. Once it is filled, you are done for the day.

### 19. What Real Positions Look Like

Four live iron condors were open in the account at the time of the lesson, and reviewing them is instructive because they show the range of outcomes the criteria actually produce in practice. All four were entered as separate spreads rather than as single four-legged orders, which is the experienced trader's method.

**Adobe.** Five contracts. The bull put spread was entered for $1.05 and the bear call spread for $0.90. Both are above the 90-cent minimum. Adding them gives $1.95 in total credit per contract for the entire iron condor. With the share price at $335 and having drifted down since entry, the maximum profit on the position was $975 for five contracts — which is $1.95 × 100 × 5, confirming the arithmetic. If price continued down and the lower boundary was hit, the estimated loss was about $249.56, call it $250. So the trade was risking $250 to make $975, a risk-to-reward ratio of about 1 to 3.9. On the upside the estimated loss at the upper boundary was about $349, giving $975 ÷ $349 ≈ risking $1 to make $2.7. Both ratios comfortably exceed the one-to-two minimum, and the downside ratio of nearly one-to-four is exceptional — which is precisely why the trade was taken.

**ADP.** Five contracts. Bull put spread entered for $1.01, bear call spread for $0.90, total credit $1.91 per contract. Maximum profit $955 for five contracts. At the time of review the position showed an unrealised profit of $317 on one component and an unrealised loss of $40 on another — a good reminder that unrealised P&L fluctuates during the trade and that as you near expiration it becomes more and more profitable, provided the stock stays in range. Price was sitting between the two break-evens. The estimated loss on a downside cut was described as pretty minimal, making this another small-risk, large-reward configuration.

**TXN.** Five contracts, with the 150/155/170/175 structure described earlier. The bull put spread was entered for $0.91 and the bear call spread for $1.38, giving a total credit of $2.29 per contract. That is well above the $2.00 preference and is described as the kind of good deal you get once in a while. Maximum profit for five contracts was $1,145 — again exactly $2.29 × 100 × 5.

**Viva.** The bear call spread was entered for $1.30 and the bull put spread for $0.90, giving $2.20 total credit for the entire iron condor. Another good deal. Five contracts, maximum profit about $1,100. Critically, Viva had earnings coming up on 31 May, so the position had to be closed before that date regardless of how it was performing. This is the earnings rule applied to an open trade rather than to a candidate.

Two general observations emerge from this set. First, a normal target is to collect roughly $1,000 of credit per iron condor position — which, at $2.00 or so of credit per contract, implies about five contracts as a typical size for that account. Second, the credit actually achieved varies considerably: $1.91, $1.95, $2.20, $2.29. The minimum of $1.80 is a floor that gets cleared, not a target that gets hit.

| Position | Put spread credit | Call spread credit | Total credit | Contracts | Max profit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adobe | $1.05 | $0.90 | $1.95 | 5 | $975 |
| ADP | $1.01 | $0.90 | $1.91 | 5 | $955 |
| TXN | $0.91 | $1.38 | $2.29 | 5 | $1,145 |
| Viva | $0.90 | $1.30 | $2.20 | 5 | ~$1,100 |

### 20. Trade Management: How Often To Look

Once the trade is on, how often should you look at it? At least once a day.

The practical routine described is shaped by trading US markets from Singapore, where the market opens around 9:30 p.m. local time and closes around 4 or 5 a.m. There is no need to be awake for the whole session, and no attempt is made to be. The routine is to look at the trade when the market opens, and to look at it again before going to sleep, checking whether the price is near the lower or upper points of no return. If it is near one of them, close for a loss. If it is still far away, leave it alone.

That is a deliberately low-maintenance regime, and it is appropriate to the structure. An iron condor with 40 days to run and short strikes at 25 delta is not a position that requires minute-by-minute attention. What it requires is that you notice, reliably, when price approaches a boundary — and once a day is enough for that on a large-cap stock in a range.

### 21. Taking Profit

You do not always hold an iron condor to expiration. In fact you usually should not.

**Adam's rule.** If 80% to 90% of the maximum profit has already been realised — meaning the purple line has risen almost to the green line — and there are still more than 10 days to go, close the trade, take the 80% to 90%, and open the next trade.

The reasoning is one of risk-adjusted return. The last 10% to 20% of an iron condor's profit is the slowest and most dangerous portion to collect. It requires you to sit through the final days when gamma is largest, when a single sharp move can convert a large winner into a loser, and when the remaining premium available is trivial. Closing early converts a probabilistic outcome into a realised one and frees the capital to be redeployed into a fresh position with a full 30-to-45-day decay runway ahead of it.

**Bang's rule.** Take profit at half or more than half of the maximum profit, achieved in less than half the time. The logic is a rate-of-return argument: if you can generate the majority of the profit in a fraction of the time, that is already a very good trade, and you can always recycle your capital into a new trade to boost return on investment. You do not have to wait another three or four weeks to collect the remaining quarter or third of the profit, and while you are waiting you are still carrying the risk that price moves sharply one way or the other.

The two rules are different points on the same trade-off and the lesson is explicit that this is a matter of personal preference. Adam prefers 80% to 90%, which normally means staying in the trade almost until expiry. Bang prefers half-the-profit-in-less-than-half-the-time, which means shorter holds and more turnover. Both are defensible. What matters is that you have a rule and that the rule is expressed as a percentage of maximum profit rather than as a dollar figure, so that it scales with position size and with the credit you happened to collect.

The crude oil trade illustrates the mechanics of an early close beautifully. Entered on 14 December 2018 for 16 cents per barrel on five contracts, the position was reviewed on 28 January 2019 with 17 days still to run. Oil had gone out to around $46 and come all the way back to about $52 — almost exactly where it started, which is the best possible scenario for an iron condor. The remaining premium to buy the position back was 1 cent, or $50 across five contracts. Against a maximum profit of $800, closing at that point realised $750. The reasoning given for closing rather than waiting is exactly the risk-adjusted argument: there is no point waiting another 17 days to squeeze out the last cent or two; better to close, move on, and release the capital for a new trade — because you never know, and in the next 17 days the market can move widely or sharply one way or the other and hurt the trade again. There is no point being greedy for the last one or two cents.

When the market would not fill at 1 cent, the price was raised to 2 cents, giving back $100 instead of $50 and realising $700 instead of $750. That is the correct instinct: the last $50 is not worth the risk of remaining in the position, and it certainly is not worth several more days of exposure. The order filled about ten minutes later at 2 cents.

It is also worth noting the patient version of the same decision. Before raising the price, the plan stated was to leave the order at 1 cent overnight and, if it did not fill, to come back tomorrow and do the same thing — because every day that passes the premium decays further and eventually goes to zero, so if you cannot close at 2 cents today, there is a better chance tomorrow, or even at 1 cent. Time is on your side when you are closing a short premium position, which is the mirror image of the fact that time is against you when you are opening one.

### 22. Cutting Loss

The exit rule on the loss side is stated with unusual bluntness, and it is the same rule from both instructors with a small difference of emphasis.

**The trigger.** The moment the price goes too high or too low and hits the upper or lower break-even point, close the entire trade and take the loss. Both spreads are closed, not just the tested one. The break-even is the point of no return.

**The expected loss.** The estimated loss at that point is roughly half of the credit received. For every dollar of credit collected, a losing trade loses about 50 cents. That is fine — as long as you do not risk too much of your capital, you will have losing trades, but over time your winning trades will more than make up for them, and that net profit is how you grow an account.

Bang's version on Berkshire adds a useful refinement. He noted that if you want to be safer you can close when the short strike is hit rather than waiting for the break-even, which on that trade meant closing at $495 rather than $497.15. The two are very close to each other, so for simplicity he was prepared to use the break-even. He also framed the loss size as a fraction of the credit: cut loss at one-third, or at most half, of the premium received. Most of the time he would cut at about one-third; occasionally, if volatility changes, he might have to cut at about half. With $2.12 to $2.15 of credit in hand, that meant cutting at about $100 in the worse case and about $75 in the normal case.

Those two framings — "roughly half the credit" and "one-third, at most half" — are consistent in practice, and both are estimates rather than guarantees, for the Vega reasons discussed earlier. What is not an estimate is the trigger. The break-even is hit, or the short strike is hit, and you are out.

The reason the rule is so rigid is that the maximum loss on an iron condor, while defined, is large relative to the credit. On the Lowe's structure, allowing the trade to expire at maximum loss would cost $319 per contract against a maximum profit of $181. Taking that loss once undoes nearly two full winning trades. Taking it because you did not want to admit a loser is the specific behaviour the strategy cannot survive.

### 23. Adjustment: Delta-Based Early Warning

The break-even stop is a hard exit. Before you reach it, there is an earlier warning system available, and Bang demonstrated it on the crude oil position.

The rule is to watch the short strikes. Whichever side price is moving toward, that is the short strike in danger, and you monitor its delta.

On the crude oil trade, entered with both short strikes at 10 delta, oil dropped from about $52 to about $46 over five or six days, putting the short put at 41.5 under pressure. Six days after entry, with 56 days remaining out of the original 62, the delta of the 41.5 short put had risen from 10 to 23. The stated rule was that when the short strike's delta exceeds 25, action is required. At 23, the position was still inside the adjustment rule, so no action was taken — but the instruction was to watch it closely, because if price continued to move, that 23 would become 25, then 26, then 27, and that is where action becomes necessary.

This is a genuinely useful management layer because delta is a forward-looking measure. Price can sit some distance from your short strike and still show a rising delta if volatility has expanded or if time has passed, and the delta captures both effects. Watching delta gives you notice before the price-based stop is triggered.

Note carefully that the 25-delta threshold on that trade is meaningful *because the position was opened at 10 delta*. A short strike that has gone from 10 delta to 25 delta has more than doubled its probability of finishing in the money — that is a substantial deterioration. For a stock iron condor opened at 25 delta, the same threshold would be meaningless, since the position starts there. The transferable principle is not the number 25; it is that you set a delta threshold materially above your entry delta and treat crossing it as a call to action.

What action? In the crude oil sequence, the trade never crossed the threshold — oil recovered all the way back to about $52 by 28 January and the trade went through no adjustment at all, which is exactly why it was so profitable. So the transcripts do not show an adjustment being executed on that position. The general adjustment menu is discussed in the next section.

### 24. Adjustment: Rolling, and Why It Is Usually Declined

There is a well-known family of adjustments for iron condors, and the lesson is candid about the fact that they exist, that experienced traders use them, and that they are nonetheless declined here in favour of simplicity.

The adjustments in question are as follows.

**Rolling the tested side out and away.** If the stock is rallying and about to hit your upper strike, you close the losing bear call spread and reopen another one at higher strike prices, using the credit from the new spread to offset the loss on the first. This is what is meant by rolling. The equivalent on the downside is closing the tested bull put spread and reopening it at lower strikes.

**Rolling out in time.** Instead of, or in addition to, moving the strikes, you close the position in the near expiration and reopen in a later one, buying more time for price to return to your range and collecting additional credit for the extra duration.

**Rolling the untested side in.** If price has moved up and your call side is threatened while your put side has become nearly worthless, you can close the put spread cheaply and re-sell it at higher strikes closer to the money, collecting fresh credit that widens your break-evens on the tested side. This is the classic "roll the untested side toward the money" adjustment.

**Closing one side only.** If you entered the two spreads separately, you can simply close the losing spread and hold the winning one to expiration. This is the flexibility advantage of separate entry described in Section 17: if the stock rises and the bear call spread becomes a loser, close the bear call spread for a loss and keep the bull put spread running to near expiration to collect its maximum profit.

Of these, only the last is actually practised in the lesson. The position on rolling is stated plainly: some people roll, but personally the preference is not to, because it keeps things simple. If it is a losing trade, get out, and go to the next trade.

The reasoning is worth taking seriously, because it is not laziness — it is a claim about how prices behave after a range breaks.

The argument runs as follows. Consider a stock consolidating around $50 between roughly $45 and $55, with an iron condor placed around that range. If the stock breaks out above the resistance, what tends to happen next? It tends to keep going higher. A stock in consolidation that breaks out of the consolidation tends to break out and keep running. So if you roll your call spread up, you can get hit again, and lose more, and roll again, and lose more. The very event that damaged your trade — a breakout — is evidence that the range assumption underlying the trade has been falsified, and rolling into a higher range is a bet that the assumption is true again, immediately after the market told you it was false.

This is exactly what happened on a Google iron condor. Google suddenly shot up, broke above resistance, and broke out of its consolidation. The moment it hit the upper break-even, the whole trade was closed for a loss and a new trade was sought elsewhere. The alternative — closing the upper spread and reopening one with higher strikes — was declined for precisely the reason above.

The preferred alternative is to redeploy the capital into a different stock that is still in a consolidation, where the range assumption is still intact and where you therefore have a better chance of making money playing the range, rather than re-entering a stock that has already broken out.

The analogy offered is memorable and it captures the reasoning better than any technical argument: it is like going on a date that did not turn out well. If the first date went badly, cut loss and date another person you could have chemistry with. Why would you want a second date with the same person?

The honest caveat is also given. You should only roll if you are very, very convinced that price is going to come back down — which you may believe, and you never know. It is a different style, not a forbidden one. But for spreads, rolling is a lot of work to keep track of, and the simpler discipline is to cut loss on the loser, re-enter a new trade, and take profits on the winners.

Here is the adjustment decision tree as actually practised.

| Situation | Action |
|---|---|
| Price comfortably inside the profit zone, purple line rising | Do nothing. Check once a day. |
| Short strike delta rising materially above entry delta (e.g. 10 → 25 on the oil trade) | No action yet at the threshold; watch closely, expect to act if it continues. |
| 80–90% of max profit realised with more than 10 days remaining (Adam) | Close the whole trade, take profit, redeploy. |
| More than half of max profit realised in less than half the time (Bang) | Close the whole trade, take profit, redeploy. |
| Earnings announcement approaching while position is open | Close the whole trade before the announcement, regardless of P&L. |
| A major scheduled macro event approaching (e.g. Fed decision) with most of the profit already banked | Close the whole trade and eliminate event risk. |
| Price touches a short strike | Optional safer exit: close the whole trade here. |
| Price touches a break-even point | Mandatory exit: close the entire trade for a loss (~⅓ to ½ of credit). |
| Tested side losing, position was entered as two separate spreads | Optionally close only the tested spread; hold the untested spread to near expiration for its full credit. |
| Range has broken out decisively | Do not roll into the breakout. Close, and find another consolidating stock. |

### 25. Assignment and Pin Risk

Two related hazards attach to the final days of any short-option structure, and the management rules above are designed largely to make them irrelevant.

**Assignment risk** arises because the short legs of an iron condor are American-style options on a stock, and can be exercised by their owner at any time before expiration. If the stock closes through your short call and the holder exercises, you are assigned short 100 shares per contract; if it closes through your short put and the holder exercises, you are assigned long 100 shares per contract. In either case you also hold the corresponding long wing, which means the total position remains defined-risk — you can exercise your long option to close out the stock position, or the broker will do so at expiration — but you will have a stock position in the account overnight, with the associated margin requirement, and the mechanics are considerably more disruptive than simply closing a spread.

**Pin risk** is the specific case where the stock finishes almost exactly at one of your short strikes on expiration day. You do not know whether the option will be exercised or not, and you therefore do not know whether you will be flat or holding stock on Monday morning. The uncertainty is genuinely unmanageable in the moment, which is why it is avoided rather than handled.

The management framework in this chapter avoids both hazards structurally rather than by any special assignment technique. The short strikes are placed at 23 to 28 delta, well out of the money, so that they should never be threatened at all in a normal outcome. If price does approach a short strike, the exit rule fires and the position is closed — either at the short strike (the safer version) or at the break-even. And the profit-taking rule closes winners with days or weeks left rather than carrying them into expiration week where gamma and pin risk both spike. In both the case studies in this chapter, the position was closed before expiration: the crude oil condor with 17 days to run, and the Berkshire condor with roughly one and a half days to run. Neither was held to settlement.

It is worth stating the general principle plainly: an iron condor that reaches expiration day with price near a short strike is a management failure, not a normal outcome. The rules exist to make sure you are never in that situation.

### 26. Failure Modes

It is worth cataloguing what actually goes wrong with this strategy, because each failure mode maps to a specific rule and understanding the mapping is what makes the rules stick.

**A strong trend through one wing.** This is the primary failure mode and it is the one that costs real money. The stock is in a range, you sell an iron condor around the range, and then the range breaks — decisively, with follow-through — and price runs through your short strike and toward your long wing. The Google trade described earlier is exactly this: a consolidation that broke out and kept running. There is no clever adjustment that reliably rescues this; the reason the range trade worked was that the range existed, and once it does not exist, the reason has gone. The defence is threefold: place the short strikes beyond structural support and resistance so that a break is required before you are threatened; exit at the break-even without hesitation; and do not roll into the breakout, because a broken consolidation tends to keep running.

**An earnings gap.** The stock gaps up or down on an earnings announcement, opens beyond your break-even or even beyond your wing, and you never get the chance to exit at your intended stop. You can take the maximum loss this way — rarely, but it happens. The defence is the earnings exclusion: do not open a position with earnings inside the expiration window, and close any open position before earnings are announced.

**An unscheduled gap.** Gaps can occur outside earnings too, and no rule eliminates them. The defences are partial but real: trade only large S&P 500 companies rather than small speculative ones, and keep position size within 2% of account value so that a maximum-loss event on one position is survivable rather than catastrophic. This is the residual risk of the strategy and it is why the wings are bought rather than the trade being run as a naked strangle.

**A volatility spike.** Implied volatility rises after entry, the purple line drops, and the position shows an unrealised loss even though price has not moved. Traders who do not understand Vega panic out of perfectly good positions at exactly the wrong moment. The defence is understanding: the loss is a mark-to-market effect, theta will offset it as time passes, and the position is only genuinely damaged if price actually approaches a boundary.

**Impatience in the first week.** The trade shows a small loss or no profit at all in the first few days and the trader concludes it is not working. Bang's oil position was down $50 after the first night; the Berkshire position showed only a small profit at first. Both were fine. The defence is knowing in advance that the purple line starts below the green line and rises slowly, and that the meaningful indicator in the first week is that theta is positive, not that P&L is positive.

**Accepting insufficient credit.** The trader finds a beautiful chart, computes the credit, gets 75 cents per spread instead of 90, and takes the trade anyway because the setup looks so good. This silently converts the risk-to-reward from one-to-two into something much worse and destroys the entire structural advantage of the strategy. The defence is the credit floor, applied without exception: below 90 cents per $5-wide spread, throw the trade away and look for another stock.

**Widening the strikes to chase premium.** A related error is moving the short strikes closer to the money — buying more premium with more delta — to reach the credit minimum on a stock that will not otherwise pay it. This narrows the profit plateau and raises the probability of being tested, and it is the wrong solution. The right solution is a different stock or a different expiration.

**Illiquidity.** Four legs in and four legs out on a wide-market underlying can consume a substantial fraction of the credit. The defence is the liquidity criterion: tight bid-ask, high volume, preferably weekly series available, and preferably the monthly expiration where open interest concentrates.

**Failing to exit.** The largest failure mode of all is simply not obeying the stop. The maximum loss on a $5-wide iron condor with $1.81 of credit is $319 per contract against a maximum profit of $181, so a single trade taken to maximum loss undoes nearly two winners. Worse, the position sizing method taught here is calibrated to the *expected* loss at the stop, not the maximum loss, which means that a trader who does not exit is carrying roughly 2.3 times the risk they believe they are carrying. The rule is stated in the strongest terms available: never let the trade go too high or too low, expire, and hit maximum loss. That is unforgivable.

### 27. Bang's Crude Oil Iron Condor, End to End

Before the Berkshire case study, it is worth walking the crude oil trade through in full, because it is a complete life-cycle example on a futures underlying and it demonstrates the strategy working exactly as designed on an entirely different asset class.

**Rationale and date.** The trade was entered on Friday 14 December 2018 — recorded just after midnight Singapore time, so Saturday locally but still Friday in the US. The underlying was crude oil futures, ticker /CL. The reason for the trade was that the week before, OPEC had decided to cut production, the oil price had stabilised as a result, and it had been trading sideways for several days. The expectation was that oil would continue to be range-bound for some time, which is the correct precondition for an iron condor.

**Expiration.** The preferred timeframe was 45 to 60 days. No 45-day series was available; the closest was 62 days, which was close enough to 60. That is the two-month expiration.

**Strike selection.** Both short legs were placed at 10 delta. On the put side, the 10-delta strike was 41.5, so the 41.5 put was sold. On the call side, the 10-delta strike was 62.5, so the 62.5 call was sold. Note that the platform may not show a delta column on the call side by default; if it is missing you go to the layout menu, choose Customize, scroll down, select Delta, and add the item.

**Wings.** Protection was placed $1.50 below on the put side, at the 40 strike, and $1.00 above on the call side, at the 63.5 strike. (The transcript is garbled around the put wing selection — it says "I typically choose $1.5. 41.5" and then names 40 as the strike bought — so the put wing is $1.50 wide at 41.5/40 while the call wing is $1.00 wide at 62.5/63.5. The narration later describes wanting "the same protection at the same $1 difference on the upper end," confirming the call side is $1 wide.)

**The four legs, in order of execution.** Sell one 41.5 put by clicking the bid; hold Control and buy one 40 put by clicking the ask; hold Control and sell one 62.5 call by clicking the bid; hold Control and buy one 63.5 call by clicking the ask. Four legs, one order.

**Credit and contract size.** One contract collected 16 cents per barrel, and one contract of oil is 1,000 barrels. At the moment of building the order the market showed 17 cents. Confirming a single contract showed a maximum profit of $117 and a maximum loss of $830, with the broker blocking only $710 because of the leverage granted on futures.

**Position size.** The account was significant enough to support more contracts, and five was selected. With five contracts the risk profile showed maximum loss of $4,150 and maximum profit of $850. That looks lopsided until you weigh it by probability: entering an iron condor with 10-delta shorts means roughly 90% probability on your side, so the chance of winning $850 is much higher than the chance of losing $4,150. That is the intent of the trade.

**Reading the profit zone.** On the analysis chart, the P&L curve initially does not display fully and must be zoomed by clicking the x-axis and dragging it inward several times. Then, from the right-hand menu, choosing Set Slices → Break Even → the expiration date displays the break-even points. They were 41.35 and 62.67. Between those two prices lies the profit zone; beyond them the trade loses money.

**Fill.** The order was initially locked at 17 cents. Because the market was drifting lower and the fill looked unlikely, and because the trade was wanted, the order was cancelled and replaced at 16 cents, which executed. Checking the Monitor tab confirmed one filled order, five contracts, four legs, filled at 16 credit.

**Immediately after entry.** P&L was zero, as expected on a fresh position. Theta was positive, which is the number that matters: if oil stayed at that level and everything else stayed the same, each passing day would bring about $15. The instruction given was not to worry about day-to-day P&L in the short term because it fluctuates, and to focus on theta being positive and working.

**Day one.** On Saturday 15 December, the S&P had dropped 50 points overnight — a significant move, with the market potentially heading into a correction. Oil had dropped $1.33 per barrel intraday but ended the day almost exactly where the trade was entered, which is good, because the entry itself had occurred around a $1.40–$1.50 decline. The position showed a small $50 loss. The verdict: not important, and very normal for the first few days of an iron condor. Theta was positive and working.

**Day six.** Checking in with the trade now at 56 days to expiration, down from 62. Oil had fallen from about $52 at entry to about $46 — a significant drop over five or six days. The position was down $600 cumulatively, with $250 of that coming on that day alone as oil dropped a further $1.50 to $1.60 per barrel. The management response was to watch the short strike in danger, which on a decline is the short put at 41.5. Its delta had risen from 10 at entry to 23. Since the rule is to take action when delta exceeds 25, 23 was still inside the adjustment rule and no action was required — but close monitoring was warranted, because continued movement would take it to 25, 26, 27, and then action would be needed.

**Day 45.** On 28 January 2019, about a month and a half after entry, oil was back at about $52 — essentially the price at which the trade was entered. That is the best scenario for an iron condor: after a violent excursion, price returned to where it started. The trade had gone through no adjustment at all, which is why it was so profitable. There were 17 days remaining.

**The close.** Buying the position back cost 1 cent, which across five contracts is $50 — a trivial amount of remaining time value. Against the $800 of premium collected, closing there would realise $750. The decision to close early rather than hold the last 17 days was made on risk-adjusted grounds. When the order at 1 cent did not fill, the price was raised to 2 cents, giving back $100 and realising $700. The order filled about ten minutes later. Note the platform colour convention observed here: selling shows in red or dark red, and buying to close shows in green.

**Full summary of the crude oil trade.**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Strategy | Short iron condor |
| Underlying | Crude oil futures (/CL) |
| Entry date | 14 December 2018 |
| Exit date | 28 January 2019 |
| Days in trade | 45 |
| Days to expiration at entry | 62 |
| Contracts | 5 |
| Short put / long put | 41.5 / 40 |
| Short call / long call | 62.5 / 63.5 |
| Short strike delta at entry | 10 on each side |
| Entry credit | $0.16 per barrel |
| Contract multiplier | 1,000 barrels |
| Total premium collected | 5 × 1,000 × $0.16 = $800 |
| Break-evens | 41.35 and 62.67 |
| Maximum profit | $850 (as shown on the platform for 5 contracts) |
| Maximum loss | $4,150 |
| Capital blocked | $3,600 |
| Exit price | $0.02 per barrel |
| Premium paid to close | $100 |
| Realised profit | $700 (before commissions) |
| Return on capital | $700 ÷ $3,600 = 19.4% |
| Annualised (19.4% × 365 ÷ 45) | ≈ 158% |

Two notes on that table. First, there is a small internal inconsistency in the transcript between the total premium collected computed as $800 (5 × 1,000 × $0.16) and the maximum profit shown on the platform as $850; the $800 figure is the one used in all the subsequent profit arithmetic, and $850 appears to be the platform's display at the 17-cent price the order was originally locked at. Second, the annualisation figure is stated in the transcript as "19.4 times 265 days divided by 45 days," which is plainly meant to be 365 days; 19.4 × 365 ÷ 45 = 157.4%, which rounds to the 158% quoted. The annualised figure assumes you repeat the trade back to back through the year and that every repetition makes the same profit, which is an illustrative assumption rather than a forecast.

The capital-blocked figure of $3,600 is also worth a comment, since the platform showed maximum loss as $4,150 for five contracts. The broker blocked less than the theoretical maximum because of the leverage granted on futures — the same phenomenon noted at entry, where one contract showed $830 maximum loss but only $710 blocked. The return-on-investment calculation correctly uses the capital actually tied up.

**What this trade teaches.** The oil trade is a near-perfect illustration of why the strategy works. Price left the profit zone's neighbourhood entirely — falling from $52 to $46 and putting the short put's delta up to 23 — and the position was down $600 at its worst. Had it been managed on a hair trigger it would have been closed for a loss. Instead the delta rule said 23 is not 25, the position was held, price returned to the entry level, and the trade finished with $700 of realised profit and a 19.4% return on capital in 45 days. The rules gave the trade room to be wrong temporarily without being wrong permanently. That is what a well-specified adjustment threshold buys you.

# Part XII — The Calendar Spread & Synthetic Long/Short Positions

## The Calendar Spread and Synthetic Long/Short Positions

### Part One — The Long Calendar Spread

#### The problem the calendar spread was invented to solve

Every strategy in this course exists because some earlier, simpler strategy left a problem unsolved, and the long calendar spread is no exception. To understand why it exists at all, it is worth walking through the chain of reasoning exactly as Bang lays it out at the opening of the lesson, because the structure of the trade only makes sense once you have felt the discomfort of the alternatives.

Begin with a market view. Suppose you look at a ten-year chart of SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, and you see what everybody sees: a long, persistent climb upward. Your conclusion is straightforward. Over the long run you believe the index, and therefore the ETF, will continue to rise. In the short run, however, you can also see that price is bumping into resistance, that it may go sideways for a while, that the market has already run a long way and could be sitting near the top of an exuberant move. You want exposure to the long-term uptrend, but you are not confident about the next few weeks, and you are acutely aware that a correction could arrive at any moment.

The obvious way to express that view is to buy the shares. But there is a capital problem. SPY is trading at $287 per share, so a round lot of 100 shares requires $28,700 of cash. For a small account, that is not merely inconvenient — it may be impossible. You simply cannot buy 100 shares if you do not have $28,700 sitting there, and if you did have it, committing all of it to a single ETF position is a concentration of capital that leaves nothing for anything else.

There is also a risk problem, and it is the more serious of the two. If the whole market collapses by 10 percent — a move of about $28 on a $287 ETF — a 100-share position loses $2,800. That is not a hypothetical figure invented to frighten you. In December 2018, the market fell roughly 20 percent into the year end. A 10 percent decline is therefore not unusual at all; it is a routine feature of equity markets that arrives every few years. So the shareholder has a downside of $2,800 on a 10 percent drop, on capital of $28,700, and no defined floor beneath that: if the market fell 20 percent the loss doubles, and if it fell 40 percent the loss doubles again.

So you reach for options, which is the correct instinct. If you are bullish on something, you can buy a call. And because your bullishness is a long-term view rather than a next-week view, you buy a long-dated call — something out at 270 days to expiration, roughly seven months, with a strike at the money, which at a spot price of $287 means the 287 strike. At that date and strike, the option costs about $13 per share, which for one contract of 100 shares is a cash outlay of $1,300.

Compare the two numbers side by side, because the comparison is the entire argument for using options in the first place. Owning the shares costs $28,700. Owning the seven-month call costs $1,300. The option gives you the same directional exposure for a small fraction of the capital, and that is the first benefit.

The second benefit is the loss profile. In the same 10 percent crash scenario, the shareholder loses $2,800. The call buyer cannot lose $2,800, because as an option buyer his maximum risk is the premium paid. He cannot lose more than $1,300 no matter what happens. The option position therefore has a hard floor beneath it that the stock position does not have.

And there is a third benefit that is easy to overlook and that Bang stresses because it matters enormously in practice. Even in the crash scenario, the long-dated option holder does not lose 100 percent of his maximum loss. He loses less, because he still has a great deal of time remaining in the contract. A seven-month option that goes 10 percent against you in the first month does not go to zero; it retains substantial extrinsic value, precisely because there are still six months in which the market could recover. That remaining time is not merely a consolation prize — it is a functional asset. It buys you time for the market to come back, which can reduce the loss or even turn the position profitable again. The phrase Bang uses is worth remembering: you won't lose more than what you pay, and even in the very worst case you lose only a portion of your max loss, as long as you have time on your side.

So far the option looks superior in every dimension. But there is a cost, and it is the cost that gives rise to the calendar spread. Over those 270 days, every single day that passes takes a piece of the $1,300 away. At first the decay is gradual and slow, but the longer you hold, the faster it accelerates towards expiration. To make money, you need the price to move enough to pay for that decay. If SPY does not move at all, or drifts sideways, the option buyer loses the entire $1,300 by expiration even though he was, in a sense, not wrong about anything — the market simply did not move.

This is the dilemma stated cleanly. There is no free lunch. Buy the shares and you have no time decay but you carry a large loss if the market crashes. Buy a long-dated option and you get downside protection but you pay for it with time value bleeding away every day. Either way, something is working against you.

The calendar spread is the resolution of that dilemma. If the problem with owning a long-dated option is that it decays, then the solution is to find somebody else to pay for the decay. And the way you find that somebody is by selling a short-dated option at the same strike.

#### The construction

In its most basic form, the long calendar spread is a very simple two-legged strategy: you buy a far-month option and you sell a near-month option, both at the same strike price. Same strike, different time frame. That is the whole thing.

The name varies. Most people call it a calendar spread, but it is also known as a time spread or a horizontal spread. The horizontal label is deliberately the opposite of the vertical spread you already know. A vertical spread uses the same expiration but different strikes; a calendar or horizontal spread uses the same strike but different expirations. That single sentence is the defining difference between the two families of spread, and everything that follows about the payoff shape flows from it.

Because the two legs share a strike, they cannot be netted against each other the way a vertical's legs can. In a vertical, the two strikes bracket a range and the payoff is a simple step between two levels. In a calendar, the two legs differ only in time, which means the whole position is a bet on the *relative* rate of time decay between the two expiries, and on where price sits relative to that shared strike when the near leg dies.

The mechanical rationale is this. Buying and holding a long-dated option decays its value day after day, so you need someone to pay for that decay. You therefore sell a shorter-term at-the-money call expiring in roughly 25 to 35 days. That short-dated option decays faster than the long-dated one — which is exactly what you want. The short-dated option is there to pay for the long-dated option. If the short leg's decay exceeds the long leg's decay, your net theta is positive, meaning every day that passes brings you money rather than taking it away. That is the beauty of using the long calendar spread: your net time impact goes from negative to zero or positive.

#### The SPY worked example, leg by leg

Bang builds the example on a live SPY option chain. The spot price is $287.70. The option statistics page shows an IV percentile of 25 percent, which is low, and low IV is precisely the condition under which this strategy should be entered — we will come back to why in the vega section.

He chooses the December 2019 expiration for the long leg, which is 217 days from the trade date. At the 287 strike, which is at the money, the mark price is $13.82 per share, so one contract costs $1,382.

For the short leg he stays at the same 287 strike but moves in to the June 21 expiration, which is 35 days out. The mark there is $5.52 per share, so selling one contract collects $552.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | DTE | Strike | Mark | Cash flow (1 contract) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long | Buy call | December 20, 2019 | 217 | 287 | $13.82 | −$1,382 |
| Short | Sell call | June 21 | 35 | 287 | $5.52 | +$552 |
| **Net** | | | | | **$8.30** | **−$830 debit** |

The net of what you pay and what you collect is a debit of $8.30 per share, or $830 for the one-contract spread. Set that beside the $1,382 you would have paid for the naked long call and the effect is immediate: the cost of owning the long-dated option has been cut by more than a third. And set it beside the $28,700 required to own 100 shares and the capital efficiency of the structure becomes almost absurd.

That $830 debit is also, and this is a definitional point rather than an estimate, the maximum possible loss on the trade. You paid a net debit; you cannot lose more than the net debit. What remains is the question of under what circumstances you would actually lose all of it, which we address below.

#### Why you sell at the money, and why the value must go to zero

Notice what kind of premium the short leg is. Because it is struck at the money, the entire $5.52 is extrinsic value. There is no intrinsic value in an at-the-money option at all. That matters, because extrinsic value is the part that decays to zero by expiration. If the share price does not go up, the whole $5.52 disappears, and it disappears into your pocket because you are the seller.

That is exactly what you are hoping for. You want the $5.52 to go to zero by June 21. As you approach that date, the option that was $5.52 will become something like $1.00, or less than $0.50, or $0.30. At that point you roll.

This also explains the strike-selection rule for the short leg, which Bang states as a rule rather than a preference: sell at the money or near the money, because the at-the-money strike has the highest extrinsic value. You want the short-dated option to give you the best possible premium, and since the premium you are harvesting is precisely the extrinsic component that decays to zero, the strike that maximizes extrinsic value is the strike that maximizes what you can harvest. Sell too far out of the money and you collect too little to finance the long leg; sell deep in the money and much of what you collect is intrinsic value that does not decay at all.

#### Rolling: the engine of the trade

Rolling is not an adjustment made under duress in this strategy. It is the ordinary operating cycle, the reason the position exists, and the source of nearly all of its return.

To roll means: close the short leg, keep the long leg. You bought the long-dated December option and you intend to keep it. What you are recycling is the near-dated short leg. So as the June 21 expiration approaches and the short call's price has collapsed toward $1.00 or $0.50 or $0.30, you buy it back. You sold at $5.52 and you buy back at, say, $0.50. You sold high and bought low, and the difference is realized profit. Then, with the cash in hand, you sell to open a new short call in the next cycle — perhaps rolling from June 21 out to July 19 — collecting another premium of a similar order, maybe another $5.52, maybe somewhat different depending on conditions.

Then you repeat. And repeat. The long leg has 217 days of life, and the short cycles are about 35 days each, so you can run the process roughly six times. If each round collects on the order of $5.50, six rounds is on the order of $33 to $35 of collected premium against the $13.82 you paid for the long leg. The combination of all the premium you collect from selling will be far more than the premium you paid for the long-dated option. That is the arithmetic that makes the strategy compelling: you are not hoping for a single large directional payoff, you are running a repeating harvest that pays for the asset you wanted to own anyway.

#### The payoff profile and why it peaks at the strike

Pull the position into the analysis tab of the platform and the payoff curve appears as the characteristic calendar tent: a hump centred on the shared strike, sloping away on both sides, crossing zero at two break-even points, and asymptoting toward the debit paid at the extremes.

The maximum profit is achieved when the short-dated option — the June 21 leg — expires exactly at the money, that is, with SPY at $287. The platform computes that maximum at approximately $500, achieved if SPY closes at $287 on June 21.

Why does the peak sit at the strike? Because at the strike, on the short leg's expiration day, two things happen simultaneously that are both maximally good for you. The short call you sold expires with zero value, so you keep every cent of the premium collected; and the long call you still hold retains the most extrinsic value it can have, because at-the-money options carry the greatest extrinsic value of any strike. Move away from the strike in either direction and you degrade both halves of that: the short leg gains intrinsic value against you if price rises through it, and the long leg loses extrinsic value as it moves away from the money in either direction.

The break-even points on this SPY structure sit at approximately 276 on the downside and 300 on the upside. Bang describes that as a very wide profit zone — roughly 25 points of range on a $287 underlying. As long as the price stays within that band, the position continues to make money.

Achieving the exact peak is, as he says, very difficult. You will normally end up somewhere on the flank of the tent rather than at its summit, and that is fine. The trade is designed to be profitable across a range, not at a point.

#### Theta: how time works in your favour

Inside the profit zone, the net theta of the two legs is positive. The short-dated at-the-money option decays faster than the long-dated at-the-money option, so the combined position gains value as each day passes. Bang describes the sensation vividly: every day you hear a *ching, ching* as money comes in.

But this is conditional, and the condition is exactly the profit zone. The moment price moves beyond the profit zone — higher than $300 or below $276 in the SPY example — theta turns negative, and negative theta hurts. That is not a subtlety; it is the single most important operating signal in the entire strategy, because it converts a vague notion of "the trade is going against me" into a precise, mechanical, observable trigger. When price exits the profit zone, the very force that was paying you begins charging you instead, and you must act.

The way you act is by moving the short leg. If price drops below $276, you close the short 287 call and sell a lower-strike call instead. That widens the profit zone on the downside, brings price back inside the tent, and restores positive theta. The mirror applies on the upside: roll the short call up and out to push the upper break-even beyond the current price.

That is the entire management framework in one sentence: watch the profit zone, and when price leaves it, roll the short leg toward price until price is inside the zone again.

#### Return on the first cycle, and what to expect over many cycles

The $500 maximum profit figure applies to the first round only — the round in which you sold the June 21 call. Against capital of $830 (the net debit), that is a return on investment of roughly 60 percent over 35 days, achieved if price sits at $287 at expiry.

If you can run the cycle five times, 60 percent times five is 300 percent, and Bang is careful here to warn against exactly the arithmetic he has just performed. Do not expect 300 percent. That figure requires the underlying to sit precisely at $287 at every single short-leg expiration, which is not going to happen. He would be happy with half of it, or even 20 to 25 percent of it — which would still be a lot. The purpose of showing the multiple is to demonstrate that the return engine compounds across cycles, not to set an expectation.

#### When do you actually lose the maximum?

This is where the calendar shows its most attractive property, and it is a property that is easy to miss if you only look at the expiration payoff diagram.

Suppose you enter today and you are immediately unlucky: the whole market collapses and SPY drops to $270. On the platform, the pink line represents the P&L as of the following Friday (the trade is entered on May 17; the simulated line is May 24). At $270 on that near date, the loss is approximately $200 — not $830. You do not lose the maximum, because you still have an enormous amount of time in the long option and that option therefore retains most of its extrinsic value.

The only scenarios that produce something close to the maximum loss are extreme. Price would have to drop all the way to about $220 — a decline of roughly 25 percent from $287 — or, within the next month, jump up by about $3.60 per the transcript's figure. Bang immediately dismisses both as unrealistic within a single month: the whole market is not going to drop 25 percent or rise 25 percent in four weeks. So the realistic bad outcome is not the max loss at all. Even when price exits the profit zone, you lose a portion — maybe 10 percent, maybe 15 percent of the maximum — which on this structure is less than $100. That is why he characterises it as a pretty safe trade: you will not lose the $830 even in a bad market.

#### Vega: the second engine, and the second risk

The calendar spread has a second source of profit beyond time decay, and it is the reason the entry rule about implied volatility exists.

Look at the vega on each leg. The long December 287 call has a vega of 87. The short June 287 call has a vega of 36. Net, the position is long approximately 51 vega. That means a 1 percent increase in implied volatility increases the value of the position by about $51.

The reason the long leg has more vega than the short leg is structural rather than incidental: vega rises with time to expiration. A 217-day option is far more sensitive to a change in implied volatility than a 35-day option at the same strike, because there is far more remaining time over which a higher volatility assumption can act. Buy the long-dated leg and sell the short-dated leg at the same strike, and you are necessarily net long vega. This is not a choice you make; it falls out of the construction.

Now consider the magnitude. If the VIX — or, more precisely, the implied volatility of the S&P 500 — rises by 10 points, the position gains an extra $510 from volatility alone, on top of whatever theta has produced. That is a very large number relative to an $830 debit.

But it works in reverse with equal force. Every 1 percent drop in implied volatility costs $51. This is the vega risk, and it is the reason the entry rule is what it is: you enter when IV is low. If you enter at a 25 percent IV percentile, the probability of IV falling further from there is lower than the probability of it rising, so the asymmetry of the vega exposure is in your favour. If you were to enter the same structure at a 90 percent IV percentile you would have precisely the same net long vega but with the odds inverted, and a volatility collapse in the back month would damage the long leg far more than it would help the short leg.

On the platform this can be seen directly. With the volatility simulation set to zero change, the profit zone runs between about 278 and 300, marked by two vertical posts. Increase implied volatility from the current level and both the blue expiration line and the pink current-date line lift: the profit zone widens and the maximum profit increases at the same time. Higher volatility does not merely make you more money at a given price — it makes a wider range of prices profitable.

#### The entry rules, stated as rules

Pulling the entry criteria together, the framework is as follows, and every number in it is a threshold Bang states explicitly.

The first rule concerns implied volatility. You enter when IV is low. The recommendation is an IV percentile below 40, and lower is better — if you can find something in the 10th or 15th percentile, that is best. In the SPY example he takes the trade at an IV percentile of 25 percent and explicitly calls it low and therefore good for this strategy. The rationale is the net long vega established above: entering at low IV means you enter with a volatility tailwind more likely than a headwind, and when IV rises you collect a bonus on top of the time decay.

The second rule concerns the long leg's tenor. The long-dated option must be long enough — at minimum three months, and ideally six or seven months. The reason is arithmetic rather than aesthetic: the tenor of the long leg determines how many rolling cycles you can run, and the return of the strategy is the sum of those cycles. Three months gives you perhaps two or three rolls; seven months gives you five or six. In the SPY case the 217-day long leg supports roughly six cycles.

The third rule concerns the short leg's tenor. The short-dated option should sit somewhere between 25 and 35 days to expiration — call it a month — which conveniently turns the position into a monthly exercise you perform on a routine schedule.

The fourth rule concerns strike placement, and it is the sweet spot of the trade. You buy and you sell at the money, or very near the money. The reason to sell at the money is that the at-the-money strike carries the highest extrinsic value, and extrinsic value is what decays to zero and therefore what you are harvesting. You want the short leg to give you the best possible premium so that you benefit the most from option value decay.

The fifth condition is about the underlying's behaviour rather than the option chain. The strategy works very well in a market that goes sideways in the short term. Over the long term the underlying can go up — indeed you want it to, since you hold a long call — but the short-term hope is a market that ranges, so that each short-dated option expires worthless and you can sell a new one for a new premium.

#### The exit and management rules

There are three distinct exit triggers, and they are triggered by three quite different circumstances.

The first is the profit-zone breach. When price goes beyond the profit zone in either direction — jumping a lot or dropping a lot — you must adjust. The adjustment is to roll the short-dated option to a lower or higher strike, pushing the profit zone wider so that price falls back inside it. If you do this in time, you can usually accomplish it at break-even or at a small loss. This is the beauty of the strategy: you do not lose a lot when price moves against you, and you have time to adjust.

The second is the profit-taking trigger, and here the threshold is explicit. If the market chops around and goes nowhere, chances are that after 15 or 20 days you have already captured more than half the available profit — perhaps 70 percent of the maximum profit is already realized. In that case, rather than waiting another 15 days for the remaining 30 percent, close the short-dated option and sell a new one with another 25 to 35 days on it. Bang's rule of thumb is exactly this: there is no point waiting another 15 days to collect the remaining 30 percent when you could reset the clock and start a fresh cycle at full premium. The reasoning is a return-per-unit-of-time argument rather than a return argument — the first half of an option's life yields decay more slowly than the last stretch, but the last sliver of value takes disproportionately long to squeeze out, so you recycle.

The third is the terminal exit, governed by the long leg's remaining life. When you have rolled several rounds and the long-dated option has itself burned down in time, you close the whole trade at the latest 30 days before its expiration.
