The reason is that below 30 days the long-dated option's own decay accelerates sharply, and you no longer want to be holding it. This 30-day floor is a hard rule and it recurs in the live trades: it is the reason Bang closes the Facebook position when he does, and it is the reason he declines one extra roll that would have pushed the long leg under the threshold.

#### Pros, cons and further considerations

Summarised as a profile, the calendar spread is a limited-profit, limited-risk trade. The risk is very well defined: in the SPY example it is $830, you know exactly what your maximum loss is, and that maximum applies only in a worst case that is itself unlikely. In the far more likely case you lose only a portion of it. The maximum profit is likewise defined: as long as price is inside the profit zone you make some profit, and the peak sits at the strike at the short leg's expiration. On top of that you get the implied volatility benefit — if IV shoots up you receive an extra bonus on top of the time decay.

Everything explained so far uses calls, but the structure works identically on the put side. There is no material difference between a call calendar and a put calendar. People tend to use calls when they are slightly bullish on the long term and puts when they are bearish on the long term, but mechanically the two are close to equivalent, and the choice is largely yours.

Finally, although the standard textbook calendar is a non-directional trade — sell at the money, buy at the money, hope price sits right there or fluctuates around it — that is only one version. In practice Bang uses several variants, and each of the live trades that follows demonstrates a different one.

The first variant is the calendar as a *directional* trade. Instead of placing both legs at the money, you place both legs at the same out-of-the-money strike — a strike you expect price to travel toward. The tent then sits over your price target rather than over spot, and you profit if price migrates into it. The Facebook trade is this variant.

The second variant is the calendar as an *earnings* structure. You buy a long-dated option expiring *after* the earnings release, and to reduce its time decay you sell a short-dated option expiring *before* the earnings release. Because the short leg dies before the event, you carry no gap risk on it — the option you sold expires worthless just before earnings, and the premium collected reduces the cost of the long option you keep. You can then either hold that cheapened long option through earnings as a speculation or sell it before the event. Bang calls this his favourite scenario. The Pfizer trade is this variant.

The third variant is the *double calendar*, which is used when you have no idea which way price will move. You construct the trade in both directions at once and the resulting profit zone is very wide, so you profit whether price moves one way, the other way, or not at all. The Boeing trade is this variant.

#### Calendar versus diagonal: a side-by-side comparison

By this point in the course you have already learned the diagonal spread, and the resemblance between the two is close enough that the comparison deserves to be made explicitly.

Start with what they share. Both strategies have two legs, and both legs are on the same side of the chain — either both calls or both puts. Both deal with different expiration dates for the short and long options. In terms of risk profile, both give you a limited-profit, limited-risk structure. In terms of time decay, both carry positive theta, because in both cases you sell a short-dated option to finance a long-dated one. And in terms of volatility, both are net long vega, because in both cases the long leg has a longer tenor and therefore a higher vega than the short leg. When IV rises you benefit in both; when IV collapses you are hurt in both — which is why in both cases the entry rule is to enter when IV percentile is low.

Now the differences, which are structural and consequential.

**Strike placement.** The long calendar spread requires you to buy the long-dated option and sell the short-dated option both at the money. The long diagonal spread has you buy *in the money* for the long-dated leg and sell *out of the money* for the short-dated leg. The reason for that in-the-money long leg on the diagonal is that the diagonal replicates a covered call: the deep in-the-money long call stands in for the stock. In the QQQ demonstration Bang expands the chain to find the 80-delta strike and buys the 160 call for the long leg, then sells the 177 call — at the money or first out of the money — for the short leg.

**Cost.** Because the calendar buys and sells both at the money, the two premiums largely offset and the net debit is small. The diagonal buys an in-the-money option, which is expensive, and sells an at-the-money or first-out-of-the-money option, which is cheaper, so the net debit is much larger. In the QQQ example the calendar costs $4.71 and the diagonal costs $16.89.

**Maximum loss.** Since the debit is the maximum loss in both structures, the calendar's maximum loss is $4.71 per share and the diagonal's is $16.89 per share — $1,689 per contract.

**Profit zone.** The calendar is cheaper but has a narrower profit zone. The diagonal is more expensive but has a much wider one. On the QQQ chain, the calendar's profit zone runs from about 171 to 183 — roughly 12 points. The diagonal's profit zone runs from about 173 upward with essentially no limit on the upside: if the underlying keeps rising you remain profitable, because the structure is a synthetic covered call and a covered call has no upside *risk*, only capped upside *profit*.

**Risk location.** The calendar has risk in both tails. Sharp moves in either direction cost you money. The diagonal's risk is concentrated on the downside; it has essentially no upside risk, and the maximum loss of $16.89 is realized only on a significant decline.

**When to use each.** If you are long-term bullish and short-term *neutral* — expecting a narrow range — the calendar is the right tool. If you are long-term bullish and short-term either neutral *or bullish*, the diagonal is appropriate, since its profit zone extends into the upside.

| | Long calendar spread | Long diagonal spread |
|---|---|---|
| Legs | 2, same side | 2, same side |
| Expirations | Different | Different |
| Long leg strike | At the money | In the money (≈80 delta) |
| Short leg strike | At the money (same as long) | At the money / first OTM |
| Cost (QQQ example) | $4.71 | $16.89 |
| Max loss | $4.71 | $16.89 |
| Profit zone (QQQ) | ~171 to ~183 | ~173 and above, unbounded up |
| Risk | Both tails | Downside only |
| Theta | Positive | Positive |
| Vega | Net long | Net long |
| Best used when | Long-term bullish, short-term neutral | Long-term bullish, short-term neutral to bullish |

In the QQQ demonstration the calendar is built by buying the September 20 expiration, 113 days out, at the 177 strike (at the money), then holding the control key and selling the June 21 expiration, 22 days out, at the same 177 strike. The diagonal keeps the same September 20 long expiration but moves the long strike down to the 160 call at 80 delta, and sells the same June 21 177 call. The strike of the short leg is identical in both; the only thing that changes is where the long leg sits — at the money for the calendar, in the money for the diagonal.

---

#### Live trade one: Facebook, the calendar used directionally

The Facebook trade is the longest single trade demonstrated in the program, running roughly six weeks from entry through three rolls to a final close, and it illustrates almost every management principle described above.

**The setup.** The date is January 30, 2019, just past midnight Singapore time, which in US trading terms is still January 29. Facebook is due to report earnings in two days. The one-year chart shows the stock having fallen from a high around 219 down to something like 120-something, and since then it appears to be recovering — a short-term counter-trend bullish setup. Bang's reading is that a great deal of bad news has already been priced into the stock. Earnings may well be bad again, but his judgment is that the price will react positively because the bad news is already in the price.

**Sizing the expected move.** Spot is $145. Looking at the roughly two-week options, the market is pricing a move of about plus or minus $12 over that window — so the implied range is $133 to $157. His bias is upward rather than downward, so he structures the trade around price rising toward $157 or $160. He picks $160 as the target because it coincides with the 200-day moving average, a strong resistance level that may be difficult to break.

**The construction.** This is a directional calendar. Rather than placing both legs at the money at $145, he places both legs at the $160 strike — 15 points above spot, well out of the money and therefore cheaper. The long leg goes out to April, 79 days from entry, and costs about $3.50 per share. Bang notes that even at that out-of-the-money strike the premium is expensive, because Facebook's implied volatility is elevated ahead of the earnings release. To finance part of that $3.50, he sells the same $160 strike at a much nearer expiration — 17 days to expiration, February 15 — collecting roughly $1.00 per share even though the strike is well out of the money.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | DTE at entry | Strike | Price | Cash flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Long | Buy call | April 18 | 79 | 160 | $3.48 | −$348 |
| Short | Sell call | February 15 | 17 | 160 | ~$1.00 | +$100 |
| **Net debit** | | | | | **$2.48** | **−$248** |

The platform reports the net cost at approximately $2.46 at the moment of construction, and the fill ultimately lands around $2.45–$2.48; the summary figure Bang uses for the trade accounting is $2.48 per share, or $248 for the one contract, which is also his capital in the trade and his maximum loss.

Note what this achieves. Standing alone, the April 160 call would have cost $3.50, and for it to make money Facebook would have to travel to $160 and then a further $3.50 above that to break even. Selling the February leg cuts the trade cost by almost a third, and correspondingly lowers the price at which the structure starts working.

**The payoff.** Right-clicking to analyze the trade produces the typical calendar tent. Maximum profit is achieved if price closes at the $160 strike on February 15, the short leg's expiration, and the platform puts that maximum at $610. Setting slices to break-even at the expiration date shows the profit zone bounded by two posts.

The downside test is instructive. If he is wrong on direction and Facebook falls to $125 rather than rising, the blue line shows a loss of $171 — not the $245 maximum. He loses only a portion of the maximum because he still owns a long-dated option with roughly two months of life remaining. This is the same principle demonstrated on SPY: exiting an option position early, whether at a profit or at a loss, preserves the extrinsic value that a hold-to-expiry would have destroyed.

He locks the price, sends the order, finds the market asking a little more than $2.45, raises to the market price, confirms and sends, and the order fills.

**Two weeks later: the first roll.** Bang returns on February 14, the day before the short leg expires. Facebook did in fact release earnings two days after entry, and the price shot up — the direction call was correct. Price is now $163.

Pulling up the risk profile and plotting break-evens gives a profit zone of roughly $147 to $176. At $163 the stock is comfortably inside it — not at the ideal $160, but close enough. The position is showing a profit of roughly $300-something on the one contract; the platform reports a net profit of $344, of which $202 has accrued since opening.

The long April leg still has 60 days to run, and Bang is still bullish, so he keeps it. Only the February 15 leg is rolled. The mechanics on Think or Swim are simple: right-click the leg you want to roll and choose "create rolling orders," and the platform proposes a roll.

The platform's default suggestion is to roll from tomorrow's expiration to the following week, February 22, which would collect an extra premium of almost $1.00. Bang prefers a two-week cycle rather than a weekly one, so he changes the target date to March 1, two weeks out. Because the further expiration carries more time value, the credit is larger — almost $2.00.

He also considers a second dimension of the roll. Rather than rolling out at the same 160 strike, he could roll out *and up* — to 162.5, for example. That collects less credit, but it changes the payoff profile materially. Analyzing the rolled-up structure shows that you pretty much eliminate the risk on the upside: if the stock keeps rising, you always make money. Yes, the further up it goes, the less profit you make, but the line stays above zero. The maximum profit area shifts up to around 164–165. Rolling *out only*, without going up, collects more credit — almost $2.00 — but the profit curve declines significantly if price rises quickly, approaching zero on a sharp rally, and the maximum profit area stays around 160–161. It also starts losing below about $140, versus about $145 for the roll-up-and-out version.

The decision rule he articulates is directional: if you are biased that price will continue to rise, roll up and out; if you think price will stay at this level or drift slightly down, roll out and not up. Since the stock has already shot up and then declined somewhat, and he has no strong view on the next leg, he assumes range-bound behaviour and rolls out only, keeping the 160 strike and collecting almost $2.00.

The order fills. In the position window the February 15 leg now shows zero quantity — completely closed — and a new March 1 short leg appears. The long April leg is unchanged. Because both legs still share the 160 strike, the position remains a calendar rather than becoming a diagonal.

**February 26: the profit-zone watch.** About ten days later Facebook rises on good news about the China–US trade deal. Bang checks whether action is needed. Simulating the exact position — long April 18 160 call, short March 1 160 call — and setting slices to break-even at the March 1 expiration gives a profit zone of $155 to $165.36. Price is at $165. That is very close to the upper boundary but not yet outside it, and the combined position still shows a slightly positive theta precisely because price has not yet left the zone.

He explains what the adjustment would look like if it were needed. He would buy to close the March 1 160 call, cancelling the short leg, and simultaneously sell to open a new call at a later expiration and a higher strike — out and up. That would cost a small net debit but would push the break-even point from $165 out to $169.5. Within the widened profit zone, theta returns to positive and the daily income resumes.

The governing logic is stated plainly: if price goes so far out of the profit zone, theta turns negative, and when theta is negative every day that passes costs you money. So you watch, and when price leaves the zone you roll the short call either up and out or down and out depending on which side was breached. On this day it has not yet breached, so he takes no action, but he flags it for monitoring.

**March 1: the second roll.** It is Friday March 1 (just past midnight into March 2 Singapore time, still Friday in US trading hours). Bang describes his standing Friday routine: check the portfolio for options expiring that day and decide which need to be rolled or closed to avoid assignment.

Luckily, since the scare a few days earlier, price has come back down into the profit zone and is trading at $162 on expiration day — close to the 160 strike and, as he says, perfect for this setup.

The long April leg now has 48 days to go. That is still above the 30-day floor, so one more roll is possible: he would close the trade completely when the long call falls below 30 days to expiration, and 48 days leaves room for one more two-week cycle. So he rolls once more.

Again he right-clicks the expiring leg and creates a rolling order. The platform proposes buying to close the 160 call expiring today and selling the 160 call expiring next Friday. He overrides the date to March 15, two weeks out, noting that March 15 is also a monthly expiration and therefore should have very good liquidity — a liquidity consideration that matters for multi-leg fills.

The roll collects a net credit of $2.13. Because both legs share the 160 strike and differ only in time, that $2.13 is simply the time value of the two weeks between today and March 15.

He then does the running cost arithmetic, which is the most instructive part of the trade. The original debit was about $2.48. The first roll on February 14 collected almost $2.00 in credit, so the real cost of the trade after that roll was about $0.50. Rolling now for another $2.00-plus means the trade is guaranteed profitable — the cost basis goes negative. As he puts it, the trade will be locked in for at least $1.50 of profit. And if in two weeks the short call again expires within the profit zone, the remaining long April leg will be completely free and will have generated profit on top.

The order is placed at $2.17 against a market of $2.17, fills, and the position now shows the original April 18 long leg alongside a new March 15 short leg.

Checking the new profit zone by setting slices to break-even at the new expiration gives $155 to $165. That is the band to monitor: inside it the trade makes money; outside it, on either side, he must roll the short call lower or higher to bring price back in.

**March 14: the close.** Two weeks later Bang takes action — but not because the short leg is expiring. Technically there are still two days to go. The trigger is the profit-zone breach: Facebook is trading at about $172-something, well above the $165 upper break-even. The trade has gone out of the profit zone.

The evidence is visible directly in the position's greeks: with price outside the zone, theta has turned negative. Negative theta means every day that passes hurts, which inverts the entire rationale for holding the position. Today alone the trade shows a small loss, even though the trade is still profitable overall since the last roll.

He considers the alternative — rolling the short call out another two weeks and up to a higher strike such as 170 or 175, which would convert the position into a diagonal spread since the strikes would no longer match. But he rejects it, and the reason is the 30-day rule. If he rolls one more term, by the time he closes the trade the long option would have only about 20 days of life remaining, and his rule is to close the long option before its DTE goes below 30. Rolling now would push him under that threshold.

There is also a discretionary element he is honest about. If he waited, price might drop back to $165 and into the profit zone, and he would make more money. But price has broken through a very strong resistance level and may be on its way up. He does not know which way it goes from here, and by discipline he takes action when price goes outside the profit zone and is hurting him.

The close is done by right-clicking the trade itself and choosing "create closing order." He collects $145 for the contract — a credit of $1.45 per share — locks the price and sends. The fill goes through, the filled-orders window shows both Facebook legs closed, and the position statement shows zero quantity.

**Full trade accounting.** Bang summarises the entire six-week campaign, and the table below reproduces his arithmetic exactly.

| Date | Event | Per share | Per contract | Running cost basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Jan 29 | Open: buy Apr 160 call | −$3.48 | −$348 | |
| Jan 29 | Open: sell Feb 15 160 call | +$1.00 | +$100 | |
| Jan 29 | **Net debit at entry** | **$2.48** | **$248** | $248 |
| Feb 14 | Roll #1 credit (to Mar 1) | +$1.90 | +$190 | $53 |
| Mar 1 | Roll #2 credit (to Mar 15) | +$2.15 | +$215 | −$162 |
| Mar 14 | Close remaining spread | +$1.45 | +$145 | |
| | **Total profit** | | **$307** | |

The interpretation of the negative cost basis is worth dwelling on. After the second roll the cost basis is −$162, which means the trade has already returned more than it consumed. As Bang puts it, he has a guaranteed profit and nothing left to lose: $162 is the minimum he will make no matter what happens next. The final close for $145 adds to that, giving a total profit of $307.

Over 44 days from opening to closing, against the original $248 of capital committed, $307 of profit is a return on investment of approximately 124 percent. Bang attributes the result to two things: he got the direction right, having structured the trade as a directional calendar rather than a neutral one, and price then moved into his profit zone and fluctuated there over many weeks, which is exactly the behaviour that lets a calendar harvest premium repeatedly.

---

#### Live trade two: Pfizer, the calendar as an earnings structure

The Pfizer trade demonstrates a completely different use of the same structure — not a directional bet held over weeks, but a short, surgical construction designed to acquire a post-earnings option almost for free.

**The context.** The date is April 24, 2019, an hour or so after the open. Pfizer, one of the 30 Dow components and a fundamentally strong blue-chip pharmaceutical, has run up over a two-year window but has recently pulled back on political grounds — campaign talk about lower healthcare costs has hit the whole healthcare sector. On the two-year chart the stock has dropped to what Bang identifies as a very strong support level around $39, off which it looks likely to bounce.

Pfizer reports earnings on April 30. Bang wants long exposure through the event but does not want to own stock into a binary event, because a bad reaction would cost a great deal. So the question becomes how to use options to play earnings given both the fundamental and technical setup. Because earnings are on April 30, the natural expiration to use is May 3.

**The naive approach and its cost.** The straightforward play is simply to buy a call expiring after earnings. Spot is $39.37, so you could buy the at-the-money 39.5 call for $0.67 per share — $67 per contract. Ten contracts would cost $670. If you are right, the upside is uncapped. If you are wrong — if the stock drops, goes sideways, or rises but not enough to cover the premium — you lose the $670 or so. That is still an expensive way to play earnings, and expensive relative to a binary event whose outcome you genuinely cannot forecast.

**The calendar solution.** So Bang reduces the cost by financing the long option with a short one. He buys the May 3 39.5 call, which the platform prices at about $0.71 per contract's worth per share, and then sells the 39.5 call expiring April 26 — just two days away — collecting about $0.28 per share.

Holding control and clicking to sell builds the spread in one order. The combined cost of the two options drops from about $0.70 to about $0.41 — almost half. What he is hoping for is straightforward: by Friday, two days away, the April 26 39.5 call expires worthless, leaving him owning the May 3 option, purchased at a heavily subsidised price, to play the earnings event.

He does this for 10 contracts.

**The two-day payoff.** Analyzing the risk profile shows the blue line as P&L at the April 26 expiration and the pink line as P&L as of today. If you enter now and price stays exactly here, you break even; move either way today and you lose a little. But as time progresses toward Friday, if price stays where it is, the maximum profit is realized — the platform shows a maximum of about $189 if price sits still and the sold option expires that Friday.

Setting slices to break-even at the expiration gives a profit zone from $39.07 to $39.94 — almost a full dollar of range between now and Friday. On a $39 stock that is more than 2 percent in either direction. Not enormous, but not trivially narrow either, and Bang is comfortable with it.

**The volatility angle.** The option's implied volatility is at the 46th percentile — middle of its 52-week range, an average level. But with earnings approaching, Bang argues 46 is actually low, and he expects IV to rise as April 30 nears. He simulates this: adding 5 points of implied volatility takes the maximum profit from about $185 to nearly $300, and widens the profit zone from the original band out to roughly $38.8 to $40.2. That is the net-long-vega property of the calendar working exactly as described in the theory section, and in an earnings context the direction of the volatility drift is unusually predictable, since IV almost always rises into a scheduled event.

He also runs the reverse case: if IV drops — which he doubts, given the approaching event — the profit zone narrows.

**The second, higher-strike calendar.** Bang then considers the risk that price rises above 39.5 by Friday, which would put the short leg in the money and raise assignment concerns. Rather than only managing that risk, he opens a second, parallel calendar at a higher strike: buy the May 3 40 call, sell the April 26 40 call, same-strike calendar, one strike higher.

The logic is that the higher strike raises the probability that the short leg expires worthless on Friday, and because the long leg is now further out of the money relative to spot, its premium is cheaper. He is explicit about the trade-off: because the long-dated strike is significantly above the current price, his chance of making money on the long leg is lower than on the 39.5 structure, but the cost is correspondingly lower. In this second trade he would likely end up owning the long-dated option effectively for free, since the short leg should expire worthless.

The 40-strike calendar costs $360 for the 10 contracts. It fills immediately. The 39.5-strike order is still pending; the market is raising the price and Bang has to raise his own bid to get filled, which he eventually does at a slightly worse price.

| Trade | Long leg | Short leg | Net debit/share | Contracts | Capital |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Calendar #1 | May 3 39.5 call | Apr 26 39.5 call | $0.42 | 10 | $420 |
| Calendar #2 | May 3 40 call | Apr 26 40 call | $0.36 | 10 | $360 |
| **Total** | | | | 20 | **$780** |

The $780 is his total capital and his total maximum possible loss; it is also the amount his buying power is reduced by.

**The risk framing.** Bang draws the comparison that justifies the whole structure. Twenty contracts represent 2,000 shares of exposure. If you owned 2,000 shares and earnings were bad and the stock fell $1 per share, you would lose $2,000. Here, if he is completely wrong, he loses $750-odd in total — $420 on one trade and $350-odd on the other. And if he is right, the upside is unlimited. He adds a further reassurance grounded in option mechanics: even if the stock drops before earnings, a call expiring *after* earnings will not go to zero. It cannot. It only goes to zero after earnings and as expiration approaches.

**Friday, April 26 — managing the short legs.** Bang checks back a few days later, on the expiration day of both short legs. Pfizer is at $39.89.

The 39.5 pair is now in the money on both legs, and the short call expires at the end of today, so he must decide between allowing assignment and closing. The P&L since open shows a loss on the short call and a larger gain on the long-dated call, netting a profit of roughly $25 on the spread. Since the trade is profitable and he does not want to deal with exercise and assignment — which also carries an assignment cost — he simply closes both legs. He right-clicks the two legs of the 39.5 spread, closes at $0.44 credit, and sends. It fills. He makes about $25 on that spread.

The 40-strike spread he leaves alone. With price at $39.9 and less than an hour to expiration, he judges it will close below $40. If it does, the 10 short 40 calls expire worthless, he does nothing, and he pays no closing cost and no commission. Both legs of that structure are currently profitable — he is up almost $200 on the pair.

**Saturday morning — the outcome.** Bang records from New York at 10 p.m. Friday New York time (Saturday morning Singapore time). Pfizer closed at $39.97 — just shy of the $40 mark, which is, as he says, perfect. The short 40 calls expired worthless. On Monday they will simply be removed from the portfolio, leaving him the 10 long May 3 40 calls. He pays no commission and no buy-back premium. When you sell an option and price closes just below the strike, the seller gets the best possible outcome.

The interim accounting is as follows. Trade one — the 39.5 calendar — cost $420 and was closed for $440, a profit of $20. Trade two — the 40 calendar — had its short leg expire worthless, and the $0.07 per share credit, $70 for the 10 contracts, becomes profit. Total realized profit at this point is $90.

What remains is 10 contracts of the May 3 40 call, expiring after earnings, carried at an original cost of $0.43 per share. But if you apply the $90 of realized profit against that cost, the effective net cost of those 10 contracts is $0.34 per share. Bang underlines how remarkable that is: for a $40 stock, holding an at-the-money call expiring after earnings for $0.34 per share is less than 1 percent of the share value. You can hardly find anywhere or any stock where you can buy an at-the-money post-earnings option for under 1 percent of the share price. That, precisely, is what the calendar structure bought him.

**Monday, April 29 — the roll to more time.** Bang records from New Jersey at about 11 a.m. New York time, two hours into the session, the day before earnings. He holds 10 contracts of the May 3 40 call. Price is slightly down at $39.86.

He lays out the decision honestly. If he holds through earnings and the price stays flat or drops, he loses 100 percent of the premium remaining — but no more than that. The position's net liquidation value is about $500 for the 10 contracts, so $500 is the maximum he can lose from here. But of that, only $430 represents loss since he opened, because he has already realized some profit; his net maximum loss on the overall campaign is around $40 while the mark-to-market exposure from today is $500.

For the position to break even from here, the stock has to reach about $40.50, and beyond that he profits.

He is clear-eyed about the nature of the event: earnings is a binary event. We really do not know whether it will be good or bad, and even if it is good, we do not know how much has already been priced in and what surprise factor remains. So instead of simply holding, he runs scenarios.

Consulting the option chain for May 3, the platform indicates an expected move of roughly $1.20 to $1.30 in either direction based on current implied volatility. From $39.8, that means the stock could jump to about $41 or fall to about $38.6.

Analyzing the current 10-contract position: by Friday, if price stays below $40, he loses everything on the position, which from today's mark is $430–$500. If price rises to $41, his profit would be about $572. His break-even is around $40.44–$40.45, meaning the stock must move 50 to 60 cents from here just to get to flat.

Then he asks the key question: what if instead of holding a four-day option, he converted into a longer-dated option? The benefits of more DTE, in his framing, are twofold. First, if you are wrong you do not lose 100 percent immediately — the option retains value until much closer to its own expiry. Second, if you are right, you can still make good money.

He simulates buying the same 40 strike at 53 days to expiration — the June 21 expiration — and analyzes it against the same scenarios.

| Scenario by Friday May 3 | Hold May 3 40 call | Switch to June 21 40 call |
|---|---|---|
| Price falls to $39 | Lose ~$430 (most of position) | Lose ~$300-plus only |
| Break-even price | ~$40.43–$40.45 | ~$39.90 |
| Price rises to $41 | Profit ~$572–$590 | Profit ~$609 |

The comparison is one-sided. If price rises to $41 the longer-dated option makes more money. If price falls to $39 the longer-dated option loses less money. And the break-even point drops from about $40.44 to about $39.90, which is essentially at spot. Better protection if wrong, higher profit potential if right, and a much lower break-even — all three move in his favour, so whether price drops, goes sideways or rises, owning the longer-dated option is superior.

The execution is a roll: in the position window he sells to close the existing May 3 leg by clicking the bid, then holds control and clicks the ask on the June 21 40 call to buy to open, for 10 contracts. It is a net debit. He notes that unlike the near-dated option, this $0.40-ish of premium will not go to zero by Friday even if he is wrong.

The order sits pending. The market will not fill at $0.40, so he raises to $0.41 and it fills. He is now holding 53-DTE options rather than 4-DTE options.

The running position is: 10 contracts of the June 21 40 call at a total cost of $0.84 per share — the original $0.43 plus the $0.41 rolling cost — plus $90 of realized profit already banked.

**Tuesday, April 30 — earnings, and the close.** Pfizer releases earnings and they are good. The stock pops about 3 percent, crossing to $40.8. The direction call was correct. On the chart, the $39 level held as a very strong support and the stock bounced off it.

Bang checks how the roll decision performed. The June 21 40 call he now holds is up $0.55 per share. He also checks the counterfactual: had he held the May 3 option, it too would have gained about $0.50 per share. So the roll was a wash on the day — indeed slightly better, at roughly $0.57 versus $0.50 — but the point is that the roll gave him better protection had he been wrong and a slightly better absolute gain given that he was right. He calls it a good decision.

Now the exit question. He could wait longer for further appreciation, but he does not know whether the stock will hold; people will take profit. His reasoning is characteristically unsentimental: it is good profit in a matter of a week, so why not hit and run, take the profit, and release the capital for a new trade. There are plenty of new trades.

He right-clicks the 10 contracts and creates a closing order. The market is around $1.38 and he can bargain between $1.38 and $1.41; he tries $1.40, waits, and eventually reduces to get an immediate fill. The trade closes at $1.38.

**Full trade accounting.**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Remaining position at close | 10 contracts June 21 40 call |
| Cost basis | $0.84/share = $840 |
| Closing price | $1.38/share = $1,380 |
| Profit on this leg | $540 |
| Return on investment | $540 ÷ $840 ≈ 64% |
| Holding period for this leg | ~2 days |
| Plus previously realized | $90 |

The 64 percent return is earned over what amounts to two days for the final leg, within a campaign of about a week in total, and the $90 from the earlier expiry sits on top of it.

Bang draws out the general lesson. This is another way to play earnings using a calendar spread: use the short-dated option to finance the long-dated option, and make sure the long-dated option is the one that expires *after* the earnings. Because the short leg dies before the event, you carry no event risk on it, and the premium it hands you cheapens the option you actually want to hold. And if you then want to reduce your risk further, you can roll that option out into a longer-dated one, which improves your position in all three of loss, break-even and gain.

---

#### Live trade three: Boeing, the double calendar

The Boeing trade demonstrates the third variant — the double calendar, sometimes loosely called a double diagonal — used when you genuinely have no directional view but expect movement, or at least want to be paid whether or not movement occurs.

**The situation.** The date is March 15, 2019. Boeing has fallen almost 100 points since the 737 MAX accident, from something like $440 down to about $368 today, trading around $367.

The uncertainty is real and Bang does not pretend otherwise. On one hand, bad news keeps arriving: all countries have grounded the aircraft, and nobody knows when it will fly again. There will be significant liabilities; some airlines are already filing lawsuits and some countries as well. It is unknown whether the bad news is fully priced in or whether more decline follows. Some commentators suggest investigations could extend beyond the 737 MAX to other aircraft types, which would change the fundamentals of the company entirely. On the other hand, given the magnitude of the fall already, one could argue a lot of bad news is factored in, short sellers may be satisfied with their profits and may take them at any time, and the stock could bounce.

Bang maps both cases onto technical levels. If price continues down from $367, the next stop is around $350 — but to get there it must cross a key support around $360, where the 150-day moving average sits; below that, $350 is where the stock fluctuated for almost a year and should offer support. If instead it bounces, he would expect it to run to about $390, which coincides with a key resistance and with the 50-day moving average.

His honest assessment is 50-50: either down to $350 or up to $390. So he wants a structure that profits if price falls, profits if price rises, and still profits if price sits still.

**The naive version: a long strangle.** The obvious expression of "it will move but I don't know which way" is to buy a put and buy a call. Applying his general rule about not buying too little time — because very short-dated options decay fastest — he chooses at least 30 days, and settles on a 34-day expiration, April 18. He buys one 350 put and one 390 call.

The resulting payoff is the familiar strangle: profitable above about $400-something and below about $335-something, with a losing valley in between. The problem is cost. The put and call together cost almost $15 per share, so one contract is about $1,500. And rightly so — when you buy both a call and a put, theta hits you from both sides. If price does not move enough, you lose.

**Financing both sides.** So he finances both long legs by selling short-dated options at the same two strikes. He sells the 350 put and the 390 call expiring March 22, seven days out. The result is four legs: long April 18 350 put, long April 18 390 call, short March 22 350 put, short March 22 390 call. Because each pair shares a strike and differs only in expiration, the structure is two calendars side by side — a double calendar.

That reduces the cost from roughly $14 to $15 down to about $11 — a cut of about one third.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | Strike | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy | April 18 | 350 | Put |
| 2 | Buy | April 18 | 390 | Call |
| 3 | Sell | March 22 | 350 | Put |
| 4 | Sell | March 22 | 390 | Call |

**The payoff.** The P&L chart at the March 22 expiration produces a shape Bang later describes as rabbit ears: two humps, one over each strike, with a shallow valley between them and drop-offs at the extremes.

Maximum profit occurs when price closes at $350 on Friday March 22 — that maximizes the put-side calendar — or at $390 on that date, which maximizes the call-side calendar. Hovering the mouse gives a maximum of somewhat over $500 for a single contract.

Setting slices to break-even at the March 22 expiration gives a profit zone from about $341 to about $400 or $401. That is an exceptionally wide band. Sitting right where price is now makes money; going a little lower makes more; going a little higher makes more. Only beyond $341 on the downside or $400–$401 on the upside does the position lose.

The maximum loss is the debit paid — about $1,000 for one contract. But as with the single calendar, that maximum is only realized on extreme moves. Even a drop to $300 would not produce the maximum loss; price would have to go below $300. On the upside, the maximum loss requires something like $440 to $450 — and $450 is the all-time high. Expecting the stock to travel from $367 to its all-time high within a week is unlikely, so Bang is confident that price will not move beyond the profit zone in the next week.

That confidence is why he sizes up: he takes three contracts. Everything triples — maximum profit becomes about $1,600 and maximum loss close to $3,000.

**Execution and pricing.** He got filled about an hour earlier at $9.30 per share. Entering now would cost $9.60, because time has passed and that passage of time has already brought him money — the position is up roughly $90 to $100 within an hour.

He then repeats the whole trade on Interactive Brokers to demonstrate the mechanics on a second platform. In IB you click Option Trader, type the security into the top-left box, choose the stock, and use the strategy builder to enter leg by leg for a multi-leg trade. He selects the April 18 expiration and clicks the ask on the 350 put and the ask on the 390 call to buy both. Then he goes to the March 22 expiration and does the opposite: sells the 350 put and sells the 390 call. Four legs, with the strikes matched on each side — hence a calendar.

The IB price to enter is about $9.87. Cross-checking Think or Swim shows the market has moved and something around $9.70 may be achievable, so he starts bargaining at $9.65, sets three contracts, and transmits. IB shows a maximum loss of $2,904. The order fills partially and then fully, in two batches — one contract and then two — with the four legs filled at various prices, for three contracts at $9.65 in total.

**The theta calculation.** Bang notes the position's net theta is about $120. Every single day, assuming price and volatility are unchanged, this trade brings in about $120. Of course nothing is truly unchanged, but that is the tailwind he is trading with, and it is why an hour after entry the position already shows a profit — by the time of this note, $1,106 in the platform's running figure.

**March 21 — the review and close.** Bang checks back six days after entry, on March 21 (just past midnight Singapore time into March 22).

Boeing entered around $368, bounced right after entry, then dropped back, and since then has moved in a very narrow range, currently around $373. The trade is making money, but not as much as hoped. Had price reached one of the two humps — near $350 or near $390 — the profit would have been much larger.

There is a second reason the profit is smaller than expected, and it is the vega risk in action. When he entered a week ago, implied volatility was around 34 to 35 percent absolute. It has now dropped to 31. Looking at the position's greeks, the four legs — two long-dated and two short-dated — produce a net vega of positive 195. Long vega means he benefits if IV rises and loses if it falls. IV fell three or four points, which explains why the profit has not been as good as expected.

So the scorecard is split: theta worked for him and brought in a good deal of money, but vega worked against him and reduced the profitability. This is the honest statement of the calendar's dual exposure — the same net long vega that produces windfall gains when volatility expands produces disappointment when it contracts, and you do not get to choose which.

The exit trigger, however, is not the vega disappointment. It is theta turning negative. The short legs' extrinsic value has been almost entirely squeezed out: the 390 call and the 350 put are marked around $0.06 and a few cents. Waiting one more day would capture the last few cents from those two legs, but it would cost him a day of time value on the two long-dated legs. Net, theta has flipped negative. He wants positive theta so the position pays him daily; when it flips, the reason for holding has evaporated, and he closes.

**The volatility counterfactual.** Before closing he quantifies the vega damage. Simulating implied volatility back up by three points — to where it was at entry — shows the maximum gain rising to about $1,600 to $1,800, and at the current price of $373 with unchanged IV he would have made something like $800 today instead of the roughly $220 to $230 he actually has. The IV drop cost him several hundred dollars of profit. His comment is pragmatic: there is no way to know in advance whether IV will rise or fall, so you assume it stays the same, but you *do* know at entry that theta works for you, because you can compute it — $120 per day in this case.

**The close.** He right-clicks the whole trade and sells the entire four-leg package, collecting about $10.07 per share at the market. A four-leg order takes some time to fill, and he has to reduce his credit slightly before it goes through. He then repeats the close on Interactive Brokers — clicking the summary line of the four-leg trade and closing it — checking that the IB price of $10.05 matches the Think or Swim price, transmitting at that level.

**Full trade accounting.**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry date | March 15 |
| Exit date | March 21 (6 days) |
| Contracts | 3 |
| Entry price | $9.30/share |
| Capital committed | $2,790 (transcript states $2,790 as "$2,0 90"; the figure used for the ROI is the entry debit) |
| Exit price | $10.05/share |
| Premium collected on close | $3,015 |
| Profit before commissions | ~$225 |
| Return on investment | ~8% |

Bang's own framing of the entry capital in the summary is the premium paid at $9.30 for three contracts, and the closing premium collected is $3,015; the profit before commissions and costs is approximately $225, which he converts to roughly 8 percent return on investment over six days. He puts that in perspective: money in the bank earns perhaps 2 to 3 percent in a year; 8 percent in a week is not a bad return at all — especially with a profit zone stretching from about $340 to $400, so wide that he did not have to worry about the stock moving out of it within a week.

His closing observation is the one that summarises the entire lesson on the double calendar: the trade could have done much better had implied volatility not dropped so much, and it could also have done better if price had actually moved to one of the humps. But the structure was built so that all three outcomes — up, down, or sideways — were profitable, and the profit arrived on schedule from theta. That is what a well-built calendar does: it converts an admission of ignorance about direction into a position that is paid for waiting.

---

### Part Two — Synthetic Long and Synthetic Short Positions

#### What a synthetic is, and why it exists

The second half of this chapter deals with a structure that has a different character from everything else in the course. The calendar spread, the vertical spreads, the credit spreads, the iron condors — all of these are *option* strategies in the sense that their payoff shapes could not be produced by any stock position. They have humps, plateaus, tents and wings. The synthetic is different. Its entire purpose is to produce a payoff shape that is *identical to a stock position*, and its entire justification is that it does so using a fraction of the capital.

The strategy is also known as the risk reversal. It allows you to take a long position on a stock, or a short position on a stock, using just a fraction of your capital. The construction is very simple. If you want to go long a stock — if you want to buy it — then instead of putting up cash to buy the shares, you buy an at-the-money call option and, at the same time, you sell an at-the-money put option. Both options share the same strike and the same expiration.

That is the whole definition. Buy the at-the-money call, sell the at-the-money put, same strike, same expiry. Two legs, and the resulting position behaves like 100 shares of stock.

The reason it behaves that way is put-call parity, and while Bang does not use the phrase, the logic he walks through is exactly parity's logic and is worth stating explicitly because it explains why the equivalence is not an approximation but an identity.

Consider what you own and what you owe at expiration, strike by strike. Above the strike, the call you bought is in the money and pays you one dollar for every dollar the stock is above the strike; the put you sold is worthless and costs you nothing. So above the strike your P&L rises one-for-one with the stock. Below the strike, the call you bought is worthless; the put you sold is in the money and costs you one dollar for every dollar the stock is below the strike. So below the strike your P&L falls one-for-one with the stock. Above and below, in both directions, your position changes dollar-for-dollar with the underlying — which is precisely what a 100-share long position does. The call gives you the upside; the short put forces you to absorb the downside; together, the two obligations reconstruct the share.

That is the identity. Long call plus short put at the same strike and expiry equals long stock, adjusted for the strike level and the net premium paid or received. Reverse both legs — long put plus short call — and you get short stock.

Bang expresses the delta consequence in the simplest possible way: when you are long the stock line, if the stock goes up by $1 you make $100; if it drops $1 you lose $100, because you own 100 shares. The same is true here. If it goes up, one to one. If it goes down, one to one. The synthetic has a delta of approximately 1.00 per contract from the moment it is put on, and it stays there, because the long call's positive delta and the short put's positive delta sum to one across the whole range.

#### The problem being solved: the Home Depot setup

The motivating example is Home Depot. Bang looks at two charts side by side. On the left is a ten-year chart, which is one way up — a very bullish, steady uptrend over the past decade — and beneath it a row of small icons marking the quarterly dividend, showing that this has been a very good dividend payer alongside fantastic price performance. On the right is a one-year chart showing the stock above its moving average lines. The company has just released earnings; the icon at the bottom marks yesterday's report, which was not bad. The price initially dropped and then bounced right back up, closing positive.

Price is $191.45, above the 200-day moving average, and above the 50-day. From a technical standpoint the stock has run up, retraced, and is now bouncing off the 200-day moving average, and Bang is convinced it will have a bullish run.

The natural expression is to buy shares and hold long term. The obstacle is capital. One hundred shares of Home Depot at $191.45 requires a cash outlay of more than $19,000. For a small account that is a great deal of money, and even for a larger account it ties up an uncomfortable share of the portfolio in a single name.

So consider the plain call. Buy a roughly two-month call — 59 days, expiring in July — and you pay $6.05 per share, or $605 for one contract. That is far less capital than $19,000. Before expiration you would not lose 100 percent of the $605 even if you are wrong; if the stock drops and breaks down you might lose $300 or $400 depending on how far it falls, with $605 as the hard ceiling on the loss.

But the plain call has the same defect it had in the calendar-spread discussion. Even if you are right about direction, if the stock does not move *enough*, you still lose. To break even, the stock has to move at least $6 upward, and every day that passes eats premium. So the plain call gives you low capital and defined risk but demands a large move. That is not the optimum way to trade.

#### The construction, leg by leg

The long synthetic resolves this by financing the call with a put.

Price is $191.45. Bang goes to the option chain, finds the July expiration at 59 days, and buys the 190 call — slightly in the money — at a mark price of $6.05 per share. He then sells the 190 put at the same expiration, collecting a mark of $5.17 per share.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | DTE | Strike | Mark | Cash flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy call | July | 59 | 190 | $6.05 | −$605 |
| 2 | Sell put | July | 59 | 190 | $5.17 | +$517 |
| **Net** | | | | | **$0.88** | **−$88 debit** |

The net is a debit of $0.88 per share — $88 for the contract — which is very close to zero. The reason it is a debit rather than a credit is that with spot at $191.45 the 190 call is slightly *in* the money and the 190 put is slightly *out* of the money, so the call is worth marginally more than the put. Had he chosen a strike above spot the relationship would invert and he would take in a credit.

Bang's framing of this near-zero cost is the essential point: the premium collected from selling the put is almost enough to pay entirely for the call. You have acquired 100 shares' worth of directional exposure without paying for it.

#### Capital efficiency and margin

Here is where the strategy earns its place. The broker does not block $19,145 of buying power for this position. Because the short put is the only leg carrying obligation, the margin requirement is computed on that leg, and the platform blocks $4,292. Bang states the general rule: the broker typically blocks 20 to 25 percent of the total share value. On a share value of just over $19,000, $4,292 is roughly 22 percent.

The consequence is a multiplier on return, and it is arithmetic rather than magic. You are using one fourth or one fifth of the capital that the share position would require, and the dollar profit on a given move is *identical* because the delta is identical. Same profit, lower capital, so the return on investment is four to five times higher. That is the entire economic argument.

Bang adds two situational reasons this matters especially. First, the strategy is particularly powerful for traders who do not have access to CFDs. Some platforms — Think or Swim among them — do not offer CFDs at all, and some jurisdictions do not permit them. Traders in those situations have no conventional route to leverage, and the synthetic gives them one-to-four or one-to-five leverage without needing any special instrument.

Second, and this is a real cost advantage rather than merely an access one, a CFD position accrues financing cost because you are borrowing money to hold it. The synthetic does not. As long as you hold the put and the call simultaneously, you pay no financing cost. That is why you can comfortably hold this structure at a long date to expiration; Bang's own preference is two to three months, but the absence of carry means longer tenors are entirely viable.

#### The risk profile

The payoff profile is exactly like stock performance. It is a straight line through the strike, rising one-for-one above it and falling one-for-one below it.

The break-even point is the strike price plus the debit paid: $190 plus $0.88 gives $190.88. Above that price the position profits; below it, it loses.

Maximum profit is unlimited. When you hold a stock the maximum profit is unlimited, and the same is true here — there is no cap on the upside.

Maximum loss is where the honest accounting has to happen, and Bang does not soften it. Similar to owning shares, the maximum loss is the full value of the position down to zero: the put strike, which is also effectively the break-even, times the share count. In this case the maximum loss is on the order of $19,000 — the same maximum loss you would face owning 100 shares outright.

This is the crucial asymmetry between the synthetic and every other option strategy in the course. The synthetic is not a defined-risk trade. Your capital *committed* is $4,292, but your capital *at risk* is roughly $19,000. Those numbers are not the same, and confusing them is the single most dangerous mistake available in this strategy. The margin block is not a maximum loss; it is merely a deposit. If Home Depot went to zero you would owe the full amount on the short put and the fact that the broker had only reserved $4,292 would not protect you at all.

Put another way: the synthetic gives you the capital efficiency of leverage while giving you exactly the risk of the unleveraged share position — measured in dollars. Measured against the capital you actually posted, it gives you four to five times the risk *and* four to five times the return. There is no free leverage; there is only leverage.

#### Entry rules

The entry rules follow directly from the fact that this is a stock position dressed in option clothing.

The first rule is that stock selection is identical to picking a stock for long-term holding. You have to do all the fundamental and technical analysis and feel comfortable with the name. Choose a stock you are very comfortable with, because when you buy a call and sell a put you are trading the bullish side with full one-to-one exposure. On the fundamental side, do all the steps of analysis. On the technical side, make sure there is a bullish setup — a breakout from consolidation, a dip on an uptrend, a reversal into a new uptrend, or a capitulation setup. Those are the standard bullish entries, and they apply here unchanged.

The second rule concerns time to expiration, and here the strategy is unusually permissive. You may choose any DTE, depending on your time frame. Bang typically chooses one to three months, most often two to three, but he explicitly says nine-month options are fine too, and LEAPS are acceptable. The reason there is no strict rule is the reason given above: with no net time decay and no financing cost, holding longer does not cost you anything.

The third rule concerns strike selection. Ideally you choose at the money or near at the money, and the reason given is a market-microstructure reason rather than a theoretical one: at-the-money strikes carry the highest liquidity, the bid-ask spread is narrow, and you can therefore trade more fluidly. On a two-legged position where you will have to unwind both legs at once, a narrow spread on each leg is worth a great deal.

The fourth consideration is implied volatility, and the answer here is unusual and important enough to deserve its own section.

#### Vega: why implied volatility does not matter

For essentially every other strategy in this course, the implied volatility entry condition is central. For the synthetic, it is close to irrelevant, and the reason is structural.

When you buy a call you are long vega. When you sell a put you are short vega. Both options are at the same strike and the same expiration, so their vegas are almost identical in magnitude. They therefore offset each other, and the net vega of the position is approximately zero. No matter whether IV is high or low, you can put this strategy on; it will not affect you.

Bang demonstrates this directly on the platform rather than asserting it. With the Home Depot position loaded — long the 190 call, short the 190 put — he opens the volatility simulation and increases implied volatility. The P&L chart does not change. Essentially no visible movement in the line at all, because the long vega is offset by the short vega. Implied volatility has a neutral impact on the profit or loss for the trade.

He repeats the demonstration on the split-strike Twitter structure described below, and gets the same result: changing volatility moves the chart not at all, for exactly the same reason.

This is a genuine advantage, and it is easy to underrate. It means you never have to wait for an IV percentile condition to be satisfied before expressing a directional view. It means an IV crush after earnings cannot damage you. It means you can enter into elevated volatility without paying a volatility premium. The synthetic is a pure directional instrument, stripped of the volatility exposure that contaminates most option positions.

#### Exit rules

The exit rules, like the entry rules, are stock rules rather than option rules. You exit exactly as you would exit a stock position: when the stock reaches your target price, exit; when it hits your stop loss, exit.

The mechanical requirement is that you must close *both* legs at the same time. You are holding a long call and a short put, so to unwind you sell the call to close and buy the put back to close, in a single reverse order at the same strike and expiration. This unwinds the whole position. Closing only one leg would leave you with either a naked short put or a bare long call — two completely different positions with completely different risk — so the two legs must be treated as one instrument on the way out just as they were on the way in.

#### Variant one: the short synthetic

Everything above has been on the bullish side, but the same structure builds a bearish position by reversing both legs. Instead of buying a call and selling a put, you buy a put and sell a call, at the same strike and expiration. The result is a synthetic short stock position.

Bang's example is Gilead. The chart shows a textbook downtrend: the moving average lines are sloping down, the 200-day is above the 150-day which is above the 50-day, and price is below all of them. Every time the stock hits a resistance level such as the 150-day moving average, it drops back down. Price is now $66.36 and appears to be hitting the wall again, suggesting another leg lower.

He constructs the short synthetic at the 65 strike, July 19 expiration: buy the 65 put, sell the 65 call. Because the put is out of the money and the call is in the money at a spot of $66.36, the call fetches more than the put costs, and the trade takes in a **net credit of $1.06** — the reverse of the Home Depot case, and for the mirror-image reason.

The risk profile is exactly that of a short share position. The break-even is $66.06. Maximum profit is achieved when the stock goes to zero: a decline of $66.06 per share, giving a maximum profit of $6,606 on one contract. Maximum loss is unlimited on the upside, exactly as with shorting shares — if you are wrong and the price jumps, you face a very heavy loss with no ceiling.

This is the point at which the risk discussion becomes most serious. On the long synthetic the maximum loss is large but bounded, because a stock can only fall to zero. On the short synthetic there is no bound at all. The short call leg is a naked short call, and a naked short call has theoretically unlimited liability. A takeover bid, a surprise approval, a short squeeze — any of these can move a stock 50 or 100 percent overnight, and the short synthetic absorbs the whole of it. This is why the position must be treated with exactly the same seriousness, sizing discipline and monitoring as an outright short sale of shares, and never as an option spread.

| | Long synthetic | Short synthetic |
|---|---|---|
| Leg 1 | Buy call | Buy put |
| Leg 2 | Sell put | Sell call |
| Strike/expiry | Same for both | Same for both |
| Equivalent to | Long 100 shares | Short 100 shares |
| Delta | ≈ +1.00 | ≈ −1.00 |
| Net cost (Bang's examples) | $0.88 debit (HD) | $1.06 credit (GILD) |
| Break-even | Strike + debit | Strike − credit |
| Max profit | Unlimited | Strike less credit × 100, at stock = 0 |
| Max loss | Full share value to zero | **Unlimited** |
| Net vega | ≈ 0 | ≈ 0 |
| Net theta | ≈ 0 | ≈ 0 |

#### Variant two: the split-strike synthetic

The second variant relaxes the requirement that both legs share a strike. You do not have to buy and sell at the same strike; you can split them. Buy the call at one strike and sell the put at another.

Doing so defines a range. Above the call strike is your profit zone; below the put strike is your loss zone; between the two strikes is a flat, roughly break-even region. In effect you are saying: when the stock breaks out above a certain level I want to profit from there, and at a certain lower level I don't mind owning the shares — because if the trade runs to expiration with price below the put strike, you will be assigned and will own the stock at that price.

On the bullish side, that means buying an out-of-the-money call and selling an out-of-the-money put simultaneously.

**The Twitter example.** Twitter is trading at $37.47. The one-year chart shows the stock having broken up after a good earnings report, hitting $40, and then retracing back to around $37.47, where it has been fluctuating in a narrow range for the past few weeks.

Bang's fundamental case is that Twitter is arguably the second-biggest social media platform after Facebook. In Asia it is not especially popular — mainly the Philippines and Indonesia — but in Europe and the US it is very popular, boosted by President Trump's constant tweeting, and he expects the coming election cycle to make it more popular still as people follow political candidates. Fundamentally the company has turned around and produced very good financials in the last quarter. He is bullish and wants to hold long term.

He splits the strikes: buy the 40 call and sell the 36 put. The logic behind each strike is explicit. He buys the 40 call because a break above $40 opens the upside — the next swing high resistance sits somewhere around $47 or $48, giving a lot of profit room between 40 and 48. He sells the 36 put because $36 is a support level, and if price falls below it and stays there to expiration, the worst case is that he is assigned and owns the stock at $36 — a discount to the current $37.47, and a price at which he is entirely happy to own it. Selling a put creates the obligation to own the shares at the strike, and here that obligation is a feature rather than a defect.

Because this is a long-term hold, he selects a 122-day expiration, out to September 2019.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | DTE | Strike | Mark | Cash flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy call | September 2019 | 122 | 40 | $2.85 | −$285 |
| 2 | Sell put | September 2019 | 122 | 36 | $2.89 | +$289 |
| **Net** | | | | | **$0.04** | **+$4 credit** |

The net is a four-cent credit. Not merely near zero cost — negative cost. The put premium more than pays for the call he wants to own for the long term.

The resulting profile is flat in the middle, rising above 40 and falling below 36. Maximum profit is unlimited once price breaks above $40. Maximum loss is the short put strike less the credit collected: $36 minus $0.04 equals $35.96, so $3,596 if the stock goes all the way to zero.

The buying power blocked is $887, which is roughly 23 to 24 percent of the share value. Instead of committing $3,700 to buy 100 shares, he commits less than $1,000 — about a quarter of the capital.

The split-strike variant is worth understanding as more than a technical curiosity, because it changes the character of the trade. The same-strike synthetic is a pure share substitute. The split-strike synthetic is something closer to a financed long-term accumulation plan: you get free upside optionality above one level, you accept share ownership below another, and you pay nothing — or are paid — for the privilege. It is, in effect, a cash-secured put and a long call funded by each other.

#### Comparing the bullish strategies: straight call, bull call spread, long synthetic

Because the synthetic is a third way to express a bullish view alongside two you already know, Bang lays them out in a comparison table and then demonstrates all three on SPY.

**The SPY demonstration.** SPY is at $279 and Bang believes the 200-day moving average is strong support from which the ETF will bounce. He chooses a 50-day expiration, about two months.

The straight call is simply buying the 279 call for $6.33.

The bull call spread refines the view. He is bullish, but he thinks price will face resistance at $287, where the 50-day moving average will act as a ceiling. So he buys the 279 call and sells the 287 call to collect $2-plus of premium, bringing the net cost to less than $4.

The long synthetic buys the 279 call for $6-plus and sells a put at around $278, producing essentially zero cost or a small credit — a negative cost for the trade. Analyzing it shows two legs, a small break-even zone, and a line that is essentially the share: unlimited risk and unlimited profit.

**Strategy.** The straight call is simply buying a call and paying a premium. The bull call spread buys a call and, to reduce the cost of owning it, sells a higher call to collect some premium, so the cost is the net of the two. The long synthetic buys a call and sells a put, so the put premium pays for the call, and the net cost is essentially zero or very low.

**Cost.** The straight call costs $6-plus, which is expensive. The bull call spread costs less than $4. The long synthetic costs essentially zero, sometimes a small debit, sometimes a credit.

**Time decay.** The straight call has the highest decay, because you paid the highest premium, so every day that passes costs you. The bull call spread pays a smaller net debit, so it still faces decay but more slowly, with a smaller net impact. The long synthetic has essentially no time decay at all, because the long option's decay and the short option's decay offset one another. That is the same offset logic that neutralised vega, applied to theta.

**Maximum loss.** On the straight call, the loss is capped at the premium paid — $633 in this case — and if you close before expiration you follow the pink line and lose less, because time value remains. On the bull call spread, the loss is capped at the net premium paid, $3.93 per share or $393, and again closing early usually means losing less than the maximum. On the long synthetic, the maximum loss is the highest of the three: it is like owning the shares, so if the stock goes to zero you lose all the way down, and the loss can be significant.

**Profit potential.** The straight call has unlimited profit, and exiting before expiration can capture extra value because time value remains inside the option. The bull call spread has profit capped at the short strike — in this example you cannot make more than $407 — and if you close before expiration you generally will not even have the full capped gain, because time remains in the trade. This is a real disadvantage Bang stresses: with a vertical you cannot collect the maximum profit even when price rises a great deal; you have to wait until expiration. The long synthetic again has unlimited profit, with no cap on the upside.

**Implied volatility.** The straight call is long vega, so if IV increases you make more money; simulating an IV increase lifts the pink line and raises the maximum profit. The bull call spread is long vega on one leg and short vega on the other, so the net is a small positive vega; simulating an IV change moves the pink line and shifts the break-even slightly, but not much, and you will not get a large benefit. The long synthetic is completely vega-neutral, so you get no benefit from IV at all — moving the simulation changes nothing.

**When to use each.** If you are very bullish and convinced the share price will rise enough to overcome time decay, the straight call is appropriate — but you have to be right, because if price drops you lose, if it goes sideways you lose, and even if it rises but not enough you lose. If you are bullish but not so convinced, and you believe there is a resistance level that will cap the move, the bull call spread suits: consciously or moderately bullish, with a lower cost if you are wrong. And if you are *super* bullish — Bang's phrase — the synthetic is the tool, because it is like owning the share: if it goes up you make a lot of money, and if you are wrong you lose a lot of money as well.

| | Straight call | Bull call spread | Long synthetic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Construction | Buy call | Buy call, sell higher call | Buy call, sell put |
| Cost (SPY example) | $6.33 | ~$3.93 | ≈ $0 or credit |
| Time decay | Highest | Slower, smaller net impact | None (offsets) |
| Max loss | Premium paid ($633) | Net debit ($393) | Full share value to zero |
| Max profit | Unlimited | Capped ($407) | Unlimited |
| Early exit | Extra time value retained | Cannot reach max gain early | Linear, no time distortion |
| Vega | Long | Slightly long | Neutral |
| Conviction required | Bullish, must be right | Moderately bullish, capped view | Super bullish |

#### Comparing the bearish strategies: straight put, bear put spread, short synthetic

The bearish comparison mirrors the bullish one exactly, and Bang demonstrates it on Goldman Sachs.

**The Goldman demonstration.** The chart looks very bearish: the moving average lines are sloping down and price is now below all three of them. The stock is trading at about $184 to $185 and Bang's premise is that it drops further.

The straight put is simply buying a put with about 49 days — almost a month and a half — at the money or slightly in the money. With price at $184.50 he buys the 185 put, which costs $775 for one contract. The chart shows the familiar shape: if price rises you lose the premium; if it falls, ideally toward zero, you make a great deal; and if it does not move anywhere, you lose the entire $775.

The bear put spread reduces that cost. He still buys the 185 put but also sells the 175 put, which cuts the cost roughly in half. The chart takes on the Z shape of a vertical debit spread: maximum loss $365 and maximum gain $365, a risk-reward ratio around one to two by his description of the structure, which he calls pretty good.

The short synthetic goes furthest. He buys the 185 put and sells the 185 call — at the money — to offset it entirely. The cost is almost zero, and in fact it comes out as a credit, meaning he collects money; the call premium is more than enough to pay for the put. Analyzing it produces a straight line, similar to selling short 100 shares: if the stock drops he makes a lot of money, and if it jumps from here he loses a lot, with no protection whatsoever on the upside.

**Cost.** The straight put pays the highest premium and therefore faces the highest decay as time passes. The bear put spread pays about half, so decay still hurts but more slowly. The short synthetic pays almost zero or a negative amount, so time decay does not affect it at all.

**Maximum loss.** With the straight put, the maximum loss is the premium paid — you cannot lose more than that. With the bear put spread, the maximum loss is the net debit of the two legs. With the short synthetic, it is similar to shorting shares: when the price drops you make a lot, but when the price rises you can lose a lot, so the risk is highest of the three if you are wrong on direction.

**Profit potential.** The straight put has the highest potential if you are right. The bear put spread caps profit at the lower strike you sold — buying 185 and selling 175 means profit stops accruing once price reaches 175, and below that you gain nothing further at expiration. The short synthetic has essentially unlimited profit down to a stock price of zero.

**Break-even, and why it is the decisive comparison.** Bang runs the break-evens on the platform, and this is where the case for the synthetic is at its sharpest.

| Bearish structure | Break-even | Move required from $185 |
|---|---|---|
| Straight 185 put | $177.24 | ~$8 down |
| Bear put spread 185/175 | ~$181.35 ($185 − $3.65) | ~$3.50–$4 down |
| Short synthetic at 185 | ≈ $185 (current price) | None |

The straight put requires the stock to fall almost $8 before you make a cent. The bear put spread, because its cost is lower, requires only about $3.50 to $4. The short synthetic, because its cost is essentially zero, breaks even right at the current price — the stock merely has to stay where it is or drift slightly down for you to make money.

This is the deepest advantage of the synthetic, and it generalises to the bullish side too. Cost is lowest, therefore break-even is best. Every dollar of premium you pay is a dollar the stock must move before you are even. Reduce the premium to zero and you remove that hurdle entirely — you have converted the trade from "I need a large move in my direction" into "I simply need to be right about direction."

**When to use each on the bearish side.** If you are bearish and want defined risk with a large potential payoff, buy the put and accept that price must drop meaningfully. If you are bearish but think there will be a bottom, sell at that bottom — the lower strike — to collect premium that reduces your cost while still earning a decent profit; that is the bear put spread. And if you are *super* bearish, trade the short synthetic, which is like shorting the share.

**Implied volatility.** The pattern is identical to the bullish side. The long put gives you the highest vega. The bear put spread has a long option giving long vega and a short option giving short vega, netting to slightly positive, so you retain some benefit if IV rises. The short synthetic is vega-neutral: IV up or down, it does not matter.

---

#### Live trade one: Home Depot, split-strike long synthetic

Bang now trades the Home Depot idea live, and immediately adapts the theoretical structure to the day's price action.

**The entry.** The date is May 22 in US trading hours (just past midnight of May 23 Singapore time). The stock has dropped about $2 to $3 versus the pre-market and now trades at $188.40.

He restates the fundamental case: Home Depot is the largest home-improvement retailer in the US, fundamentally very good, and paying a strong dividend. He pulls the ten-year daily chart to show the one-way-up trajectory and quarterly dividends, and notes the dividend yield is about 2.9 percent — almost 3 percent, which is good for a US company. On the one-year chart the stock has recently reversed into an uptrend and is bouncing off the 200-day moving average, with the 50-day sloping up. He treats the 200-day at this level as very strong support; the stock dropped after earnings and bounced right off it.

The problem is the same as before: 100 shares at these prices would cost about $18,800, a big part of his portfolio, and he does not want to tie that much capital into one stock.

The lesson structure was buy the 190 call and sell the 190 put. Because the stock has now dropped, that structure would actually come in at a credit today — better than the lesson's terms. But instead of taking the better price, Bang deliberately gives himself a buffer on the downside in case price falls further. He keeps the call at 190 but drops the put to 185. That way price must fall below $185 and stay there to expiration before he is assigned or loses money — the split-strike variant used as a risk cushion rather than as a yield enhancement.

He chooses 58 days to expiration, roughly two months.

| Leg | Action | DTE | Strike | Cash flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy call | 58 | 190 | debit |
| 2 | Sell put | 58 | 185 | credit |
| **Net at build** | | | | **−$0.15 debit** |
