Checking the P&L profile, the blue line is the payoff at expiration and the pink line is the payoff as of today; as time passes toward expiration the pink line converges onto the blue. The profit zone runs from 190 upward. Below 185 is the loss zone.

He tries to get filled cheaply. The debit shows around $0.08 to $0.10, and he sends at that level. The broker confirmation shows buying power blocked of close to $3,870 — roughly 20 to 22 percent of the share value. Instead of tying up $19,000 he commits less than $4,000, one fourth to one fifth of the capital, which magnifies the return by four or five times when the trade works.

The order sits pending; the market is not coming to him and the stock is now bouncing back upward. He raises his bid to $0.15, then decides that paying the market price is not a big deal — 15 or 30 cents is immaterial on a trade of this size — and pays up. **The fill comes at $0.30 debit.** The position shows two legs and a minor mark-to-market loss of about $5, which he correctly dismisses as unimportant.

**The exit plan, stated at entry.** Because this is effectively 100 shares, Bang defines the exit in share terms.

His profit target is around $208 to $210, roughly 20 points above entry. At 100 shares, 20 points is $2,000.

His stop is defined by both a technical level and a dollar risk. If the stock drops 10 points from $188 down to $178, he loses 10 points, which is $1,000 — perhaps 1 percent of his account — and that is where he cuts. He identifies the technical logic: he believes the current level is very strong support, but there is another swing low that could serve as a bottom around $181, and if price breaks below that and travels to $178, the bullish setup is no longer valid, the trend has reversed downward, and he must cut loss and move on.

He then makes an important process point about how to implement that stop. He does not set a stop loss in the platform. His reasoning, which he says he has explained several times, is that if you set a machine stop on an option, when it triggers it dumps your option at whatever the market price happens to be — and in options the bid-ask spread can be very wide, so a mechanical stop can fill you at a terrible price. He prefers to manage the trade manually, actively monitoring every single day and executing the stop himself when the level is reached.

He also frames the monitoring cadence realistically: in one day you will not see the stock move 10 points, but over a few weeks you can, and when it does you have to be nimble either to cut the loss or to take profit early.

**Two weeks later — the exit.** Bang checks back on June 6, a little more than two weeks after the May 22 entry.

Since entry, price has never dropped below the green line at $185, which is exactly where he sold the put — the buffer was never tested. The 200-day moving average held as support, with the 150-day available as a last line of defence beneath it. The stock bounced, and now trades around $197, up almost eight points since entry.

The question is what to do. His original target was around $207, a previous swing high that would have delivered roughly 20 points or $2,000. But on closer inspection he realises that price is now facing a nearer resistance at about $197, where the 50-day moving average is sloping up, and the stock has already hit that level twice before and dropped back down each time.

So he changes the plan and takes early profit. The logic he gives is a risk-management logic rather than a target logic: within two weeks he has made good money, and he wants to lock it in so that he cannot lose it. If price subsequently breaks above the resistance, he can jump right back in.

The position shows a profit of $800-plus since open: he paid $0.30 and it is now worth $8.33, so he is up about $803. To close, he highlights both legs, right-clicks and creates a closing order, which reverses both: sell the call he bought, buy back the put he sold. The credit shown is almost $8.30.

He bargains. He asks $8.30, hoping to make exactly $800 of profit, while the market hovers at $8.24. He waits, then lowers to $8.25, then to $8.24 at the market. Price is dipping, so he goes a little lower still, and **fills at $8.21**.

**Full trade accounting.**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry date | May 22, 2019 |
| Exit date | June 6, 2019 |
| Holding period | 15 days |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Entry debit | $0.30/share = $30 |
| Buying power blocked | ~$3,800 (≈22% of share value) |
| Exit credit | $8.21/share = $821 |
| Profit | $791 |
| Return on capital committed | >20% in 15 days |

The return calculation is the point of the whole exercise, and Bang states it explicitly: $791 divided by the buying power tied up in the trade gives more than 20 percent in 15 days. He used much lower capital than buying the shares would have required, so when the trade works the return on investment is significantly higher — magnified by four or five times.

Note that a shareholder who bought 100 shares at $188.40 and sold at roughly $196.61 would have made the same $791 in dollars. But he would have made it on $18,840 of capital, which is a return of about 4.2 percent, not 20 percent. Identical dollars, one fifth of the capital, roughly five times the return. That single comparison is the entire thesis of the synthetic strategy.

---

#### Live trade two: Facebook, split-strike long synthetic held to near expiry

The second live trade runs longer, endures an adverse move, and finishes with a specific management decision about assignment that the Home Depot trade never reached.

**The thesis.** Bang is trading his real money account. He wants a stock he can hold long term, and settles on Facebook. More than two billion people have Facebook accounts, making it by far the largest and still fastest-growing social media network in the world. The fundamentals are very strong: the company makes enormous amounts of money, carries very low debt, and grows fast. And the ecosystem argument is important to him — people who leave Facebook go to Instagram or WhatsApp Messenger, and both belong to the same company. He is very bullish long term and wants to own it in his portfolio.

Price is around $185. One hundred shares would cost almost $19,000, which would block a big chunk of his portfolio capital, and he does not want that. He could buy a call, but on Facebook a call is expensive. So the synthetic is the answer.

**The technical case and strike selection.** The stock has recently reversed into an uptrend, breaking through the 200-day moving average and now also trading above the 50-day. The last earnings release a few weeks earlier was very good; the stock jumped close to $200 and has since retraced to about $185.

He identifies strong support around $180, where the 50-day moving average is sloping up. That determines the put strike: when he sells a put he wants to sell somewhere at or below $180, because he does not want price dropping below the put's strike. On the call side, he judges that a break above $190 — and ideally above $200 — opens unlimited upside. That determines the call strike.

So he buys the 190 call and sells the 180 put. The break-even zone sits between $180 and $190; above $190 is the profit zone; below $180 is the loss zone.

**Execution.** For a synthetic he can choose any DTE, but his preference is two to three months, so he picks July 19 at 58 days.

He buys the 190 call at $5.55 — expensive, which is exactly why he needs to offset it. Then, holding the control key, he clicks the bid on the 180 put to sell it.

| Leg | Action | Expiry | DTE | Strike | Price | Cash flow |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy call | July 19 | 58 | 190 | $5.55 | −$555 |
| 2 | Sell put | July 19 | 58 | 180 | (not stated) | credit |
| **Net at build** | | | | | **$0.65** | **−$65 debit** |

Analyzing the trade confirms the geometry: break-even anywhere between $180 and $190.65, with a small loss of about $65 in the flat middle region that he treats as effectively break-even. Above $190.65 is profit; below $180 is loss.

He states the maxima plainly. Maximum profit is unlimited or infinite, because there is no cap on the upside. Maximum loss is about $18,000, because if the stock went to zero he would lose on 100 shares, exactly as an owner of 100 shares would — though he notes this is an unlikely scenario.

Then the capital arithmetic. With Facebook at $185.45, the share value of 100 shares is $18,545. The broker blocks $3,712 of buying power. Dividing $3,712 by $18,545 gives roughly 20 percent. He does not need to use $18,000; he uses about a fifth of it, so if he makes money the return on investment is magnified by five times.

The order sits pending, fluctuating between $0.65 and $0.75. He raises the debit slightly and **fills at $0.68**. The position shows two legs, currently at roughly break-even.

**The exit framework, again in share terms.** Because the position is similar to owning 100 shares, the exit criteria are share criteria. He names a profit target and then, more usefully, describes how to set the stop by portfolio risk rather than by chart level alone.

If his portfolio is $100,000 and he is willing to risk 1 percent, that is $1,000, which at 100 shares means a 10-point move: from $185 down to $175 is his cut point. If his risk tolerance is 2 percent — $2,000 per trade — then he can afford to let it fall to around $165 before cutting. The choice of stop is therefore a choice about position sizing and portfolio risk, and the synthetic's one-to-one delta makes the translation from dollars of risk to points of stock movement trivially direct.

**The adverse move.** After entry the stock went badly against him. It dropped and he lost money on the position. But because he had conviction in the stock and had deliberately chosen a roughly two-month expiration, he treated the dip as temporary and short term, expecting price to find support and rebound. He also notes the layered support beneath him: the 150-day moving average sloping up, and beneath that the 150-day and 200-day converging around $160-something.

This is where the tenor choice pays. A trader holding a one-week option through the same drawdown would have been destroyed by time decay before the recovery arrived. The synthetic has no net time decay at all, so the drawdown cost him nothing except unrealized loss — the position simply tracked the stock, exactly as shares would have done, and waited.

And the stock did rebound, strongly, off the support level. By the time he reviews the trade, price has fully recovered to his entry level and beyond, breaking above $190 and in fact above $200 — the previous swing high set on the strong earnings announcement.

**The July 12 review and the decision to close.** Bang is still very bullish. He argues that the $200 swing high, formerly resistance, now becomes support. The stock has been hit by bad news in recent days — regulators, and President Trump himself, saying they will not permit Facebook's proposed Libra digital currency to operate without very strict rules — and yet under all that bad news the stock has managed only a little dip. He reads that as the bad news being priced in, and believes price will continue higher, perhaps recovering to the $218 level it achieved before.

So the reason he closes is not a change of view. It is two operational reasons.

The first is a calendar problem. The trade has only seven days to expiration; today is Friday July 12 and expiry is July 19. He is going on a long vacation for the next two weeks. He will continue to monitor but does not want to become a heavy trader on vacation, and he cannot be certain he will have a good internet connection by next Friday. He prefers to close now rather than leave it and have to rush the close before expiry.

The second reason is an assignment problem, and it is the most instructive part of the trade. With price where it is, the 190 call will very likely expire *in the money*, which means he would be assigned and would end up owning 100 shares of Facebook. The 180 put will expire worthless, so that leg gives him no trouble. But 100 shares of Facebook would take up something like $20,000 in his portfolio — which is precisely the capital commitment the synthetic was constructed to avoid.

This deserves emphasis because it is the assignment consideration unique to the synthetic. The structure is designed to give you stock exposure *without* stock ownership. If you carry it into expiration in the money, that design collapses: the option converts into the very share position whose capital cost you were avoiding, and your buying power requirement jumps overnight from a fifth of the share value to the whole of it. A synthetic held to expiry is not a synthetic any more; it is stock. Therefore the position must be actively closed or rolled before expiration, and never allowed to drift into the expiration weekend on autopilot.

The mirror case is equally real. Had price fallen instead, the short put would have finished in the money and he would have been assigned the shares that way — obliged to buy 100 shares at the put strike. Either leg can deliver stock, depending on which direction the stock moved, and only one of them can be in the money at a time.

**The close.** He highlights the two legs — the 190 call and the 180 put — right-clicks and creates a closing order. The system builds the reverse: sell to close the 190 call, buy to close the 180 put, simultaneously. The credit shows $11-plus.

He bargains, raising his ask to $11.40 to get more money on the sale, and sends it. He waits, hoping the stock will rebound a little during the session to lift the fill. Being keen to close and get to bed before his trip, he reduces to $11.35 — and the trade closes. Checking the filled orders, the actual credit received was **$11.38**, better than the order he sent out. The position shows zero quantity on both legs.

**Full trade accounting.**

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Entry date | May 22, 2019 |
| Exit date | July 12, 2019 |
| Holding period | 51 days |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Entry debit | $0.68/share = $68 |
| Buying power blocked | $3,712 (≈20% of share value) |
| Theoretical max loss | ~$18,000 (stock to zero) |
| Exit credit | $11.38/share = $1,138 |
| Profit before commission | $1,070 |
| Return on capital committed | ~29% in under two months |

Bang is careful to distinguish two numbers that are easy to conflate, and it is worth repeating his own framing. The $68 he paid is *not* his maximum loss. The buying power blocked, $3,712, is not his maximum loss either. His maximum loss, in theory, is about $18,000 — realized only if Facebook went to zero, which is unlikely but is the honest theoretical number.

The profit of $1,070 against $3,712 of committed capital is almost 29 percent in less than two months. His summary of why: this is a strategy for a bullish position where you have strong conviction, and you use it because it blocks much less capital, so when you make money it magnifies the return on investment by four or five times. In this case he got the direction right, made money, used less capital, and therefore earned a very good return on investment.

---

#### Risks and assignment considerations, gathered

Because the synthetic looks so attractive on the return line, it is worth gathering every risk the lessons raise into one place, since they are scattered across three videos.

The first and largest risk is that this is not a defined-risk strategy. Every other structure in this course — verticals, condors, calendars — has a maximum loss equal to a debit paid or a spread width less a credit. The synthetic does not. Its maximum loss on the long side is the entire share value down to zero; on the short side it is unlimited. The margin the broker blocks is a fraction of that, and the gap between the margin and the true exposure is exactly the leverage you have taken on. If you size the position by the margin requirement rather than by the notional share value, you will be four to five times larger than you think you are.

The second risk is unlimited loss on the short synthetic specifically. The short call leg is naked. There is no upper bound on a stock price, and therefore none on the loss.

The third risk is assignment, in two directions. On a long synthetic, if price is above the call strike near expiry, exercise leaves you owning 100 shares and consuming the full share value in buying power — the outcome Bang closes the Facebook trade specifically to avoid. If price is below the put strike, the short put is assigned and you are obliged to buy 100 shares at the strike. The split-strike variant makes the second case a deliberate choice rather than an accident — in the Twitter structure Bang explicitly says the worst case is owning the stock at $36, a discount level he is happy with — but it is a choice you must have made consciously in advance.

The fourth consideration is that a synthetic must be exited as a unit. Both legs close together; closing one leaves a naked short option or an unfinanced long option, and either is a materially different trade from the one you designed.

The fifth is the execution risk that follows from the fourth, and it is why Bang refuses to use machine stop losses on this position. An automated stop dumps the option at whatever market price prevails, and option bid-ask spreads can be very wide. He monitors manually every single day and executes the stop himself.

The sixth is dividends and the missing income, which follows implicitly from the structure. The synthetic replicates the *price* exposure of the share, not the share itself. In the Home Depot case Bang specifically praises the roughly 2.9 percent dividend yield as part of the fundamental case for the stock, but a long synthetic holder receives no dividend, because he owns no shares. That is a real economic difference from ownership and one reason the option prices at the two legs are not perfectly symmetric.

And the seventh — which is really the absence of a risk rather than a risk — is volatility. Vega is neutral, theta is neutral, and neither an IV crush nor the passage of time will hurt you. Every other structure in the course requires an implied-volatility judgment at entry. This one does not.

#### When Bang would use a synthetic instead of the stock itself

Pulling the threads together, the decision rule that emerges from the three lessons is fairly precise.

You use a synthetic rather than shares when you have a strong, high-conviction directional view on a stock you would genuinely be willing to own — the Home Depot, Facebook and Twitter cases are all long-term holdings he wants in his portfolio — but where the capital required to buy the shares outright would tie up an unacceptable share of the account. You are not changing the trade; you are changing how much cash the trade consumes.

You use it when you want leverage and have no other route to it: no CFD access on your platform, no CFD permission in your jurisdiction, or an account too small for CFDs — and you want that leverage without paying a financing cost, which the synthetic uniquely provides.

You use it when the cost of the alternative option expressions is too high relative to the move you expect. The straight call requires an $8 move on Goldman or a $6 move on Home Depot before you break even; the synthetic breaks even essentially at spot. If you are confident in direction but not in magnitude, removing the premium hurdle is worth more than the defined risk you give up.

You use the split-strike variant when you want a cushion or an accumulation plan — buying the out-of-the-money call for the upside, selling the out-of-the-money put at a level where you would happily own the stock, and paying nothing or being paid for the combination.

And you do *not* use it when your conviction is only moderate. That is what the bull call spread is for. The synthetic is the super-bullish or super-bearish instrument in the toolkit, and Bang's own language reflects that: bullish for the straight call, moderately bullish for the spread, and for the synthetic, *oh man, this is like super bullish*. It is like owning a share — if it goes up you make a lot of money, and if you are wrong you lose a lot of money as well.

---

# Part XIII — The Bull Bang & The Earnings Probability Spread

## The Bull Bang and the Earnings Probability Spread

### Two Inventions, One Chapter

Most of the strategies taught in an options curriculum are inherited. The bull call spread, the iron condor, the calendar, the collar — these are structures with decades of literature behind them, catalogued in textbooks, argued over on message boards, priced into every broker's strategy builder as a named preset you can select from a dropdown. You learn them because the market has already agreed on what they are.

The two strategies in this chapter are different. Neither of them appears in the standard literature. Both were invented by Bang Van Ban, Adam Khoo's trading partner, out of dissatisfaction with what the standard structures could deliver. And in both cases the inventor tells the same story about discovering he had built something new: he traded it for months, found it worked, went looking for its name, and could not find one.

The first, which Bang originally called the **protective bullish synthetic** and which his students renamed the **Bull Bang**, solves a problem that every retail trader eventually runs into — how to get long exposure to an expensive stock without tying up the capital to buy it, without paying the financing cost of a CFD, without bleeding time decay from a long call, and without the naked-downside exposure that a synthetic long carries. It is a three-legged structure that replicates a hundred shares of stock, finances itself to nearly zero cost, and buys a disaster hedge on the downside, all in one order.

The second, which Bang calls the **earnings probability spread** — and which he sometimes calls the **Christmas tree spread**, because of the shape the strikes make on the option chain — solves a different problem entirely. Earnings announcements are the one scheduled event in a stock's life where a violent, discontinuous price move is not merely possible but likely. Every retail trader wants to bet on that move. Almost every retail method of doing so is bad: buying the stock exposes you to a gap through your stop; buying a call exposes you to an implied volatility that has already been bid to the sky and is guaranteed to collapse the morning after. The earnings probability spread is a six-option, three-strike structure that costs $14 to $200 per contract, that is *short* volatility so that the post-announcement IV crush works for you rather than against you, and that routinely produces risk-to-reward ratios of one-to-five, one-to-ten, and occasionally one-to-fourteen.

They are grouped in one chapter because they share a philosophy. Both are built on the observation that raw directional exposure is the most expensive way to express a directional view. Both dismantle that exposure into components, sell the components the market overpays for, buy back the ones that cap the disaster, and keep the residue. Both are cheap, both are defined-risk, and both are aggressive. Neither is a set-and-forget structure — each requires you to be at the screen at the right moment, and much of what follows is about exactly when that moment is.

---

## Part One: The Bull Bang

### The Problem the Bull Bang Was Built to Solve

Bang introduces the strategy by walking through, in order, every conventional way of getting long a stock, and showing what breaks in each one. This is worth following carefully, because the design of the Bull Bang is a direct response to each failure in turn. It is a strategy that can only be understood as a sequence of fixes.

The example he uses is Microsoft. On the day of the lesson the stock is trading at **$126.24 per share**, and Bang has just shown a ten-year chart. He likes the company: strong fundamentals, fast growth, generating a great deal of cash every year, paying a good dividend. This is a stock he wants long-term exposure to. The question is purely how to get it.

**Option one: buy a hundred shares.** The obvious answer, and the one most investors default to. The problem is arithmetic. A hundred shares of Microsoft at $126.24 costs **more than $12,000**. For most retail accounts that is a significant chunk of total capital committed to one name. Worse, the capital is not merely committed, it is exposed: if the market crashes, if the company reports a bad quarter and gaps down, if a recession arrives, if the trade war escalates, the position can lose thousands. And a stop loss does not save you from a gap. Bang is explicit about this: if the stock gaps below your stop, "my stop loss cannot help reduce my loss, because it gapped below the stop loss and I'm out at the lowest possible price." He points to the December correction as an example of a market-wide event that hurt a great many holders of good stocks. Buying a hundred shares, he concludes, "may not be the optimal way to hold the stock long term."

**Option two: use a CFD.** A contract for difference gives you the leverage without the capital outlay. Bang rejects it for three separate reasons. First, platform: he prefers to trade in thinkorswim rather than Interactive Brokers, and thinkorswim does not offer CFDs. Second, jurisdiction: students in the United States, and in several European countries, have no access to CFDs at all. Third, and most importantly, cost: "if you do it, you also need to pay a financing cost for it. So it's not a free lunch." A CFD is a leveraged loan wearing a derivative's clothing, and you pay for the loan every day you hold it.

**Option three: buy a call option.** Now we are in options territory, and the improvement is real. Bang prices it out: buying the **125-strike call** on Microsoft, slightly in the money, with roughly two months to expiration, costs about **$5.50 per share**, so **$550 per contract**. Against $12,000 for the shares, that is a dramatic reduction in capital. And the second benefit is structural — $550 is the absolute maximum you can lose. "Even in case of the large gap down, I cannot lose more than that." A long call is a defined-risk instrument by construction.

But the long call introduces a defect the stock did not have: **time decay**. To break even at expiration, the stock must rise by the full premium above the strike. With a 125 strike and $5.50 paid, Microsoft must be at **$130.50 or above by expiration** for the trade to make money. Every day that passes without a move erodes part of that $5.50. You are not merely betting on direction; you are betting on direction *and* speed. As Bang puts it: "for me to break even, the stock price has to go at least $5.50 above my strike price."

**Option four: the synthetic long.** This was covered in the previous lesson, and Bang assumes it — he suggests watching that lesson first if you have not. The synthetic long combines a long call with a short put to replicate a hundred shares. The put premium collected finances the call premium paid. Done at the same strike it is a pure synthetic; done at different strikes it is a **split-strike synthetic**.

The improvements are substantial. Premium cost collapses toward zero — "you could have a zero cost trade as well." Capital requirement is far lower than owning the shares: the broker blocks somewhere between **20% and 25% of the share value**. On this Microsoft example, selling the 125 put to finance the call results in buying power blocked of about **$2,000**, which Bang describes as roughly a fifth or a sixth of the share value. There is no CFD needed, so no jurisdictional problem and no financing cost. And because the trade is close to zero cost, "you have no time decay, essentially no time decay, because the put premium you collect will be enough to pay for the call premium you buy."

But one defect remains, and it is the big one. "You don't have the protection on the downside. It's similar to owning a hundred shares. You have unlimited potential profit, but you also could lose a lot in case the share price crashes." The short put is a naked short put. If Microsoft goes to zero you are obligated to buy a hundred shares at 125 and you lose $12,500. The synthetic long has fixed the capital problem and the theta problem but reproduced the stock's disaster risk exactly.

That is the gap the Bull Bang fills.

### The Structure: Three Legs, One Order

The Bull Bang adds one leg to the split-strike synthetic — a long put, further out of the money, same expiration — and that single addition changes the risk profile from unlimited-loss to defined-loss, halves the capital requirement again, and costs a few tens of dollars.

Bang states the construction in its most compact form at the top of the lesson: **"Leg number one, buy a call option. Leg number two, sell a put option. And leg number three, sell a further out of the money put option, which is lower. All options are at the same expiration."** The transcript's "sell" in leg three is an ASR error — every subsequent description, every worked trade, and the entire risk logic of the strategy make it unambiguous that leg three is a **purchase** of a lower-strike put. It is the reinsurance leg.

Here is the Microsoft trade laid out leg by leg with the numbers Bang shows on screen:

| Leg | Action | Contract | Strike | Premium per share | Cash flow | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy 1 call | July 19 expiry | 130 | $3.22 (mark) | −$322 | Bullish exposure; unlimited upside |
| 2 | Sell 1 put | July 19 expiry | 125 | $3.90 | +$390 | Finances leg 1; adds bullish delta |
| 3 | Buy 1 put | July 19 expiry | 115 | not stated | −$111 (implied) | Reinsurance; caps downside |
| | | | | **Net debit** | **−$43** | |

Microsoft is at $126.24. Expiration is 19 July, **55 days from the day of the lesson**. The net debit across all three legs is **43 cents per share, or $43 for one contract**. Bang does not read out the price of the 115 put on screen; the $111 figure above is the arithmetic residual implied by the $322 paid, $390 collected, and $43 net debit that he does state. Treat it as an inference, not a quoted price.

Now the reasoning for each leg, in Bang's own logic.

**Leg one, the long call, is the direction.** "Because I buy a call option, that means I am bullish. I'm bullish on the direction of the stock. That's why the name is such a bullish strategy." He buys the 130 call, which is above the current 126.24 — this is a deliberate choice, and it is what makes the structure a *split-strike* synthetic rather than a pure one. He is defining where his profit begins.

**Leg two, the short put, is the financing.** "I will sell a put option with the same date to expiration and I use the premium I collect there to finance the cost of the option I buy in the call side." He sells the 125 put and collects $3.90 — more than the $3.22 he paid for the call. On these two legs alone he takes in a net credit. "Buy a call, sell put — essentially I create a synthetic spread, and that's why the name is synthetic."

**Leg three, the long put, is the reinsurance.** This is the leg that names the strategy. "When I sell a put, I have no protection on the downside. If it drops to zero, I lose a lot of money. So I need to buy a reinsurance to protect just in that case." The analogy Bang uses is precise and worth keeping: selling the 125 put is selling an insurance policy on Microsoft's price. "I cannot just sit tight and collect and hopefully everything will go my way and I collect that premium. I have to protect myself as well. In this case, I buy a lower put as a reinsurance to protect me in case of a significant gap down in the stock." An insurer who writes policies and buys no reinsurance is solvent until the first catastrophe. The 115 put is Bang's reinsurance treaty.

And this is why the strategy carries the name **protective bullish synthetic**: "it's like you own a share, and now you buy a protective put. So now you don't have the share, but you use the synthetic spread to replicate the share, and you buy a protective put — hence the name is protective bullish synthetic." The Bull Bang is a synthetic covered position: synthetic stock plus a protective put, assembled from three options.

The name "Bull Bang" itself came later and from outside. Bang traded the structure across his portfolios for several months, found it consistent and powerful, went looking for what the industry called it, and found nothing: "I could not find one. There's no name for this strategy. In fact, I have read quite a few books on options and none of the books that I read have talked about this strategy." He named it protective bullish synthetic and taught it in his live course, and a student named Verma began calling it the Bull Bang strategy. He kept the name — simple, and, as he says, "in fact, it's very powerful like a bull."

### How the Bull Bang Relates to the Bull Bang Collar

Students arriving at this lesson have already been taught the Bull Bang Collar in an earlier module, and the relationship between the two structures is worth stating explicitly because the names invite confusion.

A collar, in its classic form, is a stock position plus a long protective put plus a short call — you own the shares, you buy downside insurance, and you sell an upside call to pay for the insurance. The cost of the protection is that you have capped your upside at the short call strike.

The Bull Bang is the collar's mirror image on the question of what gets capped. It replaces the *stock* with a synthetic (long call plus short put), keeps the *long protective put*, and — critically — **does not sell an upside call.** The upside is left completely open. "I have a huge profit zone. And there's just no limit to it. I have no cap on the upside. And this is similar to owning a hundred shares."

So the two structures divide the space cleanly. Both use a long put as the disaster hedge. The collar finances that put by selling away the upside; the Bull Bang finances it by selling a put *below* the position, converting the downside from unlimited to a defined ten-point band. The collar is what you use when you already hold shares and want protection at the cost of capped gains. The Bull Bang is what you use when you do not want to hold shares at all, want the leverage that comes from not holding them, and are unwilling to give up the upside.

The summary Bang gives at the end of the theory lesson makes the trade-off explicit: **"limited risk and at the same time unlimited profit potential. Normally you don't have this going together."**

### When to Use It: Outlook and Chart Setup

The Bull Bang is a bullish strategy, but Bang is careful to specify a particular *flavour* of bullish. It is not the structure for a screaming, high-conviction, everything-lines-up bull trade — for that you would want more delta and less insurance. It is the structure for what he calls **cautiously bullish**.

"I use this one when I'm bullish on the stock, especially I'm bullish but I'm not one hundred percent sure, because the market condition is so nervous." He is filming during a period of trade-war headlines. "So I'm bullish on the stock, but the stock may be affected by the bigger economic environment. So I'm cautiously bullish on the stock. But in the long run, I believe the stock will go up. So that's why I buy a protection just in case the market collapses."

That gives the first entry condition. **The stock must be fundamentally good.** Bang states this as a prerequisite in every worked example, and in the bottom-fishing examples it does most of the work: the whole thesis is that a good company has been mispriced by a non-fundamental force.

The second condition is technical, and he enumerates four acceptable setups:

1. **A breakout from consolidation** — the stock has been ranging and is breaking upward out of the range.
2. **A dip within an existing uptrend.** This is the Microsoft case: "in the case of Microsoft right here, it's just a dip on the uptrend."
3. **A reversal into a new uptrend**, or a capitulation setup where selling has exhausted itself.
4. **Bottom fishing** — which Bang treats as a distinct fourth case and which he uses "a lot."

The bottom-fishing case deserves its own treatment because it is where Bang says the strategy earns its keep, and because two of the three live trades in this module are bottom-fishing trades.

His screen example is **CVS**, one of the thirty Dow Jones Industrial Average components. The stock has been dropping heavily. The cause is political rather than commercial: US presidential candidates campaigning on cheaper healthcare and single-payer proposals, which has beaten down the entire healthcare sector, CVS included. Bang's read is that the damage is sentiment, not substance. "I know the stock fundamental is good. Technically it's not so good. But now, it looks like it finds some support. And I think this is like bottoming out." He notes a PE ratio of **7**, which he calls "extremely low for a Dow Jones stock."

The technical structure he is reading is a repeatedly tested horizontal support. "It has bottomed to the key support level here at **52** many times. One, two, three, four — maybe the fifth one is coming. And it could break through that level." That last clause is the honest part. He is not claiming the support will hold. He is claiming that he is willing to bet it holds *because he has cheap insurance if it does not*.

The hypothetical construction he sketches for CVS shows how the setup maps to strikes: "Maybe I long a call option at 55, 56 here. I sell 52, and I buy a 48 to protect." The long call is placed above the market where he expects the bounce to carry; the short put is placed **at the tested support level**, because that is the price at which he is genuinely willing to be assigned; and the long put is placed **below the support**, so that if the support fails, the failure is capped. The short put strike is not chosen from a delta table. It is chosen from the chart.

He states the underlying willingness plainly in a later trade: "I'm confident that the stock has found some temporary bottom. It's 160, it will bounce. If it goes there, then... I think the stock's fundamentally good, I could just own the stock also. I could get the stock assigned to me because I sell a put here — I have the obligation to take the shares if the stock drops below that 160 level." This is a crucial point about the psychology of the middle leg. You are short a put. You must be prepared to own the shares at that strike. If you are not, you have chosen the wrong strike.

### Entry Rules and Numeric Thresholds

Pulling the rules together from the theory lesson and the three live trades:

| Rule | Specification | Source of the number |
|---|---|---|
| Directional bias | Cautiously bullish; fundamentally sound underlying | Required for the short put — you may be assigned |
| Chart setup | Breakout from consolidation, dip in uptrend, reversal/capitulation, or bottom fishing at tested support | Four named setups |
| Days to expiration | **1 to 3 months acceptable; 2 to 3 months preferred** | "My preference of this strategy, normally two to three months" |
| Long call strike | Near the money, split slightly above spot; at or near the level where the expected move begins | Liquidity and profit-zone definition |
| Short put strike | Near the money below spot, or at the charted support level; **highest liquidity, tightest bid-ask** | "Normally I choose somewhere near the current price so that I have the highest liquidity, the bid and ask spread" |
| Long put strike | Far enough below to be cheap; near enough to give real protection — a judgement call | "If you buy too low, it may not give you sufficient protection. If you buy too high, then you pay a lot for that reinsurance. You have to be balanced" |
| Net premium | **Small debit; sometimes zero; occasionally a net credit** | "Sometimes you can get a zero cost as well. Sometimes you even get a credit" |
| Implied volatility | **Low IV preferred but not required** — the strategy is only slightly net long vega | See the vega discussion below |
| Capital blocked | Roughly **8–10% of share value**, versus 20–25% for the unprotected synthetic | Microsoft: $1,047 blocked against $12,000 of stock |

Two of those rows need expansion.

**On expiry selection**, Bang gives the reason in the Pfizer trade: "you need to give the trade enough time — two to three months — for it to play out, so that every day time goes, you don't lose a lot of money, because the theta will decay slower if you have a longer trade." A longer-dated option decays more slowly per day. Since the Bull Bang is a small net debit, theta is already close to irrelevant, but the longer expiry makes it more irrelevant still, and more importantly it gives the thesis room to be right on a delay.

**On the choice of the long put strike**, there is no formula. Bang explicitly frames it as a comfort-and-cost balance, and the three live trades show three different distances:

| Trade | Spot at entry | Short put | Long put | Width | Width as % of spot |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Microsoft (illustration) | 126.24 | 125 | 115 | 10 points | 7.9% |
| UNH (live) | ~227 | 210 | 200 | 10 points | 4.4% |
| Pfizer (live) | ~41.6 | 41 | 36 | 5 points | 12.0% |
| 3M (live) | 164–165 | 160 | 150 | 10 points | 6.1% |

The width of that put spread *is* the max loss, so choosing it is the same act as choosing your risk. Bang's Pfizer choice — a five-point wide spread on a $41 stock — is proportionally the widest of the four and reflects the fact that Pfizer's strikes are spaced widely relative to its price.

### The Payoff Profile: Full Arithmetic

The Bull Bang's P&L at expiration has three distinct regions, and Bang describes the shape in the transcript as looking "like a stairs." Working from left to right on the price axis:

**Region one — below the long put strike.** Both puts are in the money. The short put loses one point for every point the stock falls; the long put gains one point for every point it falls. They offset exactly. The loss is frozen at the strike width plus the debit paid. On the Microsoft example: the difference between the 125 put sold and the 115 put bought is **10 points, or $1,000 per contract**, plus the **$43** net debit. Bang rounds it in the transcript to "in total, my max loss is $1,000" and adds "that's my max loss, before commission — commission a few dollars on top." Strictly the figure is $1,043 plus commissions.

**Region two — between the short put strike and the long call strike.** This is the flat middle. All three options expire worthless: the 130 call is out of the money because the stock is below it, the 125 put is out of the money because the stock is above it, and the 115 put is far out of the money. You lose exactly the debit paid, $43. Bang calls this **the break-even zone**: "I would normally call the difference in the two strikes — the call that I buy and the put that I sell — I normally call that zone as a break-even zone. In this case it's not really break-even, it's $43 loss if the stock stays right there until expiration, which is about two months. That's small compared to the potential profit."

**Region three — above the long call strike.** The call goes into the money and the position gains dollar for dollar with the stock, exactly as a hundred shares would. There is no cap. The break-even is the call strike plus the net debit: **130 + 0.43 = $130.43**. Above $130.43 at expiration, the position is profitable, and it stays profitable without limit.

So, formally, for a Bull Bang with long call strike $K_c$, short put strike $K_{sp}$, long put strike $K_{lp}$, and net debit $D$ per share:

| Quantity | Formula | Microsoft example |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum loss | $(K_{sp} - K_{lp}) + D$, per share, ×100 | $(125 − 115) + 0.43 = $10.43 → **$1,043** |
| Loss in the flat zone | $D$ | $0.43 → **$43** |
| Upside break-even | $K_c + D$ | 130 + 0.43 = **$130.43** |
| Maximum profit | Unlimited | — |
| Downside "full loss" threshold | $K_{lp}$ | **115** |

The visual comparison Bang draws is that "the max loss area is very small as compared to the max profit, because the max loss is limited." On a chart with price on the horizontal axis, the losing region is a ten-point band; the winning region extends to the right edge of the page.

### The Pink Line: Why Early Exit Beats Expiration in Both Directions

The single most operationally important feature of the Bull Bang is something Bang returns to in every video: the difference between the **blue line** (P&L at expiration) and the **pink line** (P&L as of today, or any chosen date before expiration) in the thinkorswim analyze tab.

For most defined-risk spreads the pre-expiration line is *worse* than the expiration line on the profitable side, because you have not yet harvested full extrinsic value. The Bull Bang is the opposite, and the reason is that the position is **net long options** — long a call, long a put, short only one put. There is residual extrinsic value in the long call that you capture by closing rather than expiring.

**When you are right**, closing early pays more. "If you look at the chart, before the expiration, if you make money and you close the trade, you make more than if you keep it until the end of the expiration, because there's still some time value in the call option when you exit. That's why you can make more money."

**When you are wrong**, closing early loses less. "If you are wrong, the stock drops all the way down, and you cut loss early — look at the pink line. Your loss would be lower than your max loss. Even if it drops to 115 right here, chances are you don't lose $1,000."

This asymmetry — the pre-expiration curve sits above the expiration curve on *both* wings — is the reason the management framework for this strategy is built entirely around early exit. There is no scenario in which holding to expiration is the plan.

The 3M trade quantifies it precisely. Twenty days into a forty-five-day trade, with the stock at $174, Bang shows the analyze tab: **"if I exit today I will get at the pink level. The pink level is $537. If I keep the trade until the expiration, it will go down to $334."** Same position, same stock price, $203 difference — entirely time value in the long call that expiration would burn.

And symmetrically on the loss side, on the same screen: "in case I'm wrong, the stock price dropped — look at the pink line. I can exit early and I lose less than if I keep the trade until expiration. I could lose $1,000 if I keep until the expiration, but if I exit early, I could lose just half of them."

### Greek Behaviour Over the Trade's Life

**Delta.** The Bull Bang is constructed to have a delta profile close to long stock across the profit region. The long call contributes positive delta; the short put contributes positive delta; the long protective put contributes a small negative delta that only becomes material when the stock approaches it. Near the money, before the trade has moved, total delta is meaningfully positive but less than 100 — the split strikes mean neither the call nor the put is at the money. As the stock rallies through the call strike, the call's delta rises toward 1.00 and the short put's delta decays toward zero, so total position delta converges on roughly +100, i.e. a hundred shares. This is precisely what Bang means when he says a synthetic "will perform exactly like you long a stock."

**Theta.** Approximately neutral, by design. This is the central selling point against the naked long call. "Because you have almost zero cost trade, you have no time decay, essentially no time decay, because the put premium you collect will be enough to pay for the call premium you buy." In the three-legged version the long protective put adds a small amount of theta bleed back in, which is why the trade is a small debit rather than free, but the magnitude is trivial: $43 on Microsoft, $12 on Pfizer, $50 on 3M. Bang's closing summary is explicit: "you pay almost zero or a very small debit on a trade, so you don't have to worry much about your time decay. Unlike buying a call, which also gives you a limited risk and unlimited profit, the time decay is an issue — it's a big concern when you buy a call. In this particular strategy, it's not a big issue."

**Vega.** This is the subtlest of the three and Bang treats it carefully. Count the legs: "when you buy a call, you long the vega. When you buy the lowest put to protect, you also long the vega. So you long two vegas, and when you sell the put, the middle one, you short the vega. So net of the three, you still have a **positive vega, but it's not very significant**."

The consequence is a small, favourable tilt: rising implied volatility helps you slightly. "When IV increases, you get some extra benefit from vega as well."

Bang then does something valuable — he demonstrates it live rather than asserting it. He opens the Microsoft position in the analyze tab, advances the simulated date to the following week, and drags the implied volatility slider upward while narrating what moves. The result: **"Only the pink line is moving. And actually it's widening your profit zone. When IV increases, you get extra benefit — the profit zone is widening and also higher. But in this case, not a lot. You see, it's moving very slowly. And the blue line is unchanged."**

The explanation for the blue line's immobility is a clean piece of options first principles: **"at the expiration, all extrinsic value goes to zero, and the extrinsic value has two components inside — the time value and the volatility premium. So at the expiration date there will be no more volatility premium inside, there will be no more time value inside. That's why the blue line doesn't change when I change the volatility."** (The transcript renders "extrinsic" as "intrinsic" here; the argument only works with extrinsic, and the substance is unambiguous.) Volatility is a property of extrinsic value alone. At expiration extrinsic value is zero by definition, so the terminal payoff is volatility-independent. Every option position on earth has this property.

The practical conclusion Bang draws is permissive rather than restrictive: **"the IV has a little impact on the strategy. You don't have to worry — should I enter this one when IV is low or when IV is high? It doesn't matter much."**

That said, in the Pfizer live trade he does check it and does prefer low IV, on the grounds that the structure is fundamentally a net-buying strategy: "when you buy a call, you have to check first what the volatility is right now in terms of ranking or percent. So I go to Pfizer and I open up the *Today's Options Statistics*. IV percentile of **16%**. So it's low. It's the right time to buy. And when you use a protective bullish synthetic, it's also a net buying strategy. So it's low IV, so it's good." Reconciling the two statements: low IV is a mild positive and a good habit, but it is not a gating criterion the way it is in a genuine volatility strategy.

### Live Trade One: UNH — An Earnings Bet with the Bull Bang

The first live trade is instructive because it uses the Bull Bang for something the theory lesson does not emphasise: a short-dated event bet. It is also the trade that loses.

**The setup.** The date is 15 April in US trading time (Bang films after midnight Singapore time, so he refers to it as 16 April). UnitedHealth Group — one of the largest US health insurers and a blue chip — has fallen from **$246 to $223 over three days** and is bouncing today, currently at **$227**. The cause, again, is political: Bernie Sanders campaigning on cheap healthcare insurance, "and it hurt the stock very badly."

The thesis has two parts. Fundamentally the stock is intact: "a lot of people have done fundamental analysis, and they find the stock continues to be very solid, having very good fundamentals, and it should be a good candidate for a long-term holding." Technically there is a floor: looking at a two-year chart, "it has a very strong support level at around **210**." And there is a catalyst: UNH reports earnings tomorrow, 16 April.

Bang frames the two-sided possibility explicitly. "It can drop another 10, 15 points from here and could hit that bottom and bounce. But for the stock to drop to that level, the news has to be very bad tomorrow. Now if, however, the news is good, any positive news could pop the price right back up to a pre-crisis level. It could go back to 240, 250, or even higher. That is the zone that I'm playing right here."

And he states the alternative he is rejecting: "if I buy the stock right here, I risk myself a lot of capital, because buying a hundred shares would cost me **$22,000** right now, and if the stock continued to crash from here I could lose a few thousand dollars easily."

**The construction.**

| Leg | Action | Expiry | Strike | Premium | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Buy 1 call | 3 May | 240 | $2.39 | Expiry after earnings; strike at the pre-crisis level he expects a recovery to reach |
| 2 | Sell 1 put | 3 May | 210 | not stated | At the two-year support level; the price at which he'd accept assignment |
| 3 | Buy 1 put | 3 May | 200 | not stated | Below support; the disaster hedge |
| | | | | **Net debit $1.02** | **$102 for one contract** |

Two structural choices deserve comment.

First, **expiry selection is driven by the event**. "Because I'm bullish on the stock after the earnings, I will need to buy a call option expiring after the earnings. So earnings is tomorrow, April 16, and I choose May 3rd — just three weeks from now, just to be sure that we have enough time for the trade to play out." Three weeks is far shorter than the two-to-three-month preference from the theory lesson, and it is short deliberately: the trade is about a single event, not about a multi-month thesis, and Bang wants a few weeks of buffer rather than a few months of decay.

Second, **the strike placement is entirely chart-derived**. The 240 call is at the pre-crisis price. The 210 put is at the multi-year support. The 200 put is beneath it. Bang narrates the reasoning for the short put in a single sentence that captures the whole psychology of leg two: "I need to sell something like 210, because I believe 210 is a strong support level. When I sell a put option at 210 strike price, I'm obligated to take the shares if it drops below 210 and stays there until expiration date — which I believe wouldn't be the case, because it has a strong support level here."

And then the reason for leg three, in the same breath: "what if the earnings is so bad that it crashes down to below 210 or even below 200? What is my plan? So then I will need to buy a reinsurance to protect myself in the case of a disaster."

**The risk profile at entry.** Bang reads four numbers off the analyze tab, distinguishing carefully between the tomorrow-line and the expiration-line:

| Scenario | Stock price | P&L tomorrow (16 April) | P&L at expiration (3 May) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Crash to 200 | $200 (−27 from spot) | **−$650** | −$1,100 (max loss) |
| Flat, 210–240 | any | small loss | **−$102** (the debit) |
| Recovery to 240 | $240 (+14 from spot) | **+$660** | ≈ break-even to −$102 |
| Beyond 240 | >$240 | unlimited | unlimited |

The maximum loss figure of $1,100 is the 10-point put spread width ($1,000) plus the $102 debit, which Bang states as "my max loss is $1,100 when the stock price crashes below 200 and stays there until the expiration date, which is on May 3rd. My max profit is indefinite. It's unlimited because I don't cap my upside potential."

The tomorrow-line is where the management plan lives, and Bang articulates it before he needs it: **"tomorrow or the next few days I need to take action. If I'm wrong, I lose money, I don't want to lose the max — I lose half of them. If I'm right, I don't want to hold until expiration, I want to close it early so that I can earn profit more than the profit I would have at expiration."** Note the asymmetry in the table that justifies this: at 240 the trade makes **$660 tomorrow** but roughly **nothing at expiration**, because at expiration the 240 call is exactly at the money and worth zero intrinsic. If you are right on a three-week trade about a one-day event, waiting three weeks destroys the entire gain.

Bang also does the responsible thing with position sizing and disclosure: he sends the trade to his students as a note, and adds, "for those who want to follow me with real money, do your homework and play with the money you can afford to lose. For me, it's a bet. So I just see how it goes tomorrow."

**The outcome.** The next morning, 16 April, UNH reports **very good earnings**. Pre-market trading pushes the price close to **$240** — exactly Bang's profit target and the strike of his long call. And then the market opens and the stock immediately reverses, falling from 240 to **below 220**, approaching his short put strike.

The reason is that the political overhang did not care about the earnings. "It continued to be beaten down by the continued political campaigns going on. Bernie Sanders continues to talk about cheaper healthcare, and it's affecting across the board in the healthcare sector. So with that, I don't know when that campaign is going to stop. But what I know is the stock did not respond very well to the positive news from the earnings, **and my theory is not valid anymore.**"

This is the correct exit trigger, and it is a thesis-based one rather than a price-based one. The event happened; the event was good; the stock ignored it. Whatever edge the position was built on has been disproved. "So I would need to cut loss and move on from here, so that I can minimise my loss to a minimal level."

**Unwinding.** The mechanics matter because thinkorswim has no built-in preset for this structure. "To unwind the position, I need to do the reverse. I need to sell that call. I need to buy back the put at 210. And I need to sell the put protection at the lowest strike price." All three legs, one order, simultaneously.

| | Entry (15 April) | Exit (16 April) |
|---|---|---|
| Net premium per share | −$1.02 debit | +$0.30 credit |
| Per contract | −$102 | +$30 |
| Capital blocked | ~$1,000 | released |
| **Result** | | **−$72 before commissions** |

Bang quotes the closing credit as 24 cents while placing the order and 30 cents on the fill; the summary uses 30 cents and a **$72 loss**. His framing of that number is the point of the whole video: **"the stock dropped about $6.00. If I have bought a hundred shares, that would mean I have lost $600. Now I'm losing less than $100."**

One day in the trade. Thesis tested and rejected. Ninety-eight percent of the equivalent stock loss avoided. "So that is the beauty of using options to speculate or to bet on the stock moving one way or the other. And when you lose, you don't lose a lot, because you know exactly what's your max loss, what's your max gain."

### Live Trade Two: Pfizer — The Trade That Goes Nowhere

The second live trade is the most useful of the three, precisely because nothing happens. Every strategy course is full of winners and dramatic losers; the neutral outcome is where you learn what a structure costs you when you are simply wrong about timing.

**The setup.** Pfizer, a pharmaceutical company and a Dow component — "very blue chip." Bang shows a one-year chart: "in general, the stock is on the uptrend. All the moving averages are sloping up, with the exception of the 50 moving average which is sliding or sloping down, but the middle and long-term trend is still on the way up." The stock is at **$41**, above its 200-day moving average, and the 200-day has been repeatedly successful as support: "it has bounced off the 200 moving average a few times, and every time it just bounces back up. So I'm betting that it will bounce off the moving average one more time and then go up from here."

He checks implied volatility first — **IV percentile 16%**, low, which he considers a green light for a net-buying strategy.

He selects expiry: **64 days**, "more than two months, which is fine," consistent with the two-to-three-month preference.

**Building the trade on screen.** Bang constructs it incrementally, showing the risk profile at each stage, which makes this the clearest exposition of why the third leg exists.

*Stage one — the naked call.* "If I'm very bullish on the trade, I just buy at the money. So about 42, I can just go and buy the 42 call. And I pay $1.80." He immediately names the defect: "just buying a call would be expensive, because every day goes and if the stock price doesn't move up strongly enough, I would lose money."

*Stage two — add the short put, creating the synthetic.* "There's no better way than just selling a put option, to use the premium to pay for the premium you buy from the call. Because I'm paying like a dollar or so on the call side, I would look for another put which has a similar premium, which is the **41 put**, so that I can collect a similar amount to pay for my call option." He control-clicks the bid side of the 41 put to add the leg.

The result: **a net debit of one cent.** "So it's almost zero cost kind of trade. And that will perform exactly like you're long a stock, because now you buy a call which is bullish, and you sell a put which is also bullish. So you do both legs bullish. So it has to be super bullish for this trade. And that is equal to going long on the stock."

He then right-clicks to analyze the two-leg version and reads the numbers off the confirmation screen — and this is the moment the third leg justifies itself:

| Two-leg synthetic (42 call / 41 put) | |
|---|---|
| Max profit | Infinite |
| Max loss | **$4,100** (stock to zero, assigned 100 shares at 41) |
| Buying power blocked | **$878** |
| Net debit | $0.01 |

"Max loss will be $4,100, meaning if the stock price goes all the way to zero and I have to buy the stock at 41 and a hundred shares, that is $4,100. That's the worst case."

*Stage three — add the protective put.* "What if the stock drops, and drops a lot, in a disaster or catastrophic event? Then I will lose a lot on the downside. So to protect that scenario, I will go and search for an insurance, a cheap insurance, to buy some protection from the downside." He shops the put chain and takes the **36 put** — five strikes below his short put. "That will cap my loss, which is the difference between 41 and 36."

| Three-leg Bull Bang (42 call / 41 put / 36 put) | |
|---|---|
| Max profit | Unlimited |
| Max loss | **$514** ($5 spread × 100 + $14 debit) |
| Buying power blocked | **$517** |
| Net debit | $0.14 |

The comparison is the whole lesson in one table. Paying **13 additional cents** — $13 per contract — cuts the maximum loss from $4,100 to $514, an 87% reduction, and cuts blocked capital from $878 to $517, roughly in half. As Bang puts it: "I cut my max loss down significantly, from $4,000-plus to only $500. Now, the other benefit of this trade is because my trade is now capped on the downside risk, the broker will consider it as a lower-risk trade, and now they block less capital for me. So that is another beauty of the trade. When you buy a cheap insurance, it not only protects you from the downside, but it also reduces the capital that will be tied up in the trade. And then if you make money, that would translate into a much better return on investment for you."

**The chart logic for the strikes.** Bang goes back to the price chart to justify the placement, and it is the same three-part reasoning as CVS and UNH. The **41 put** is at a level "which seems to be a very strong support level over the past year or so — many times it dipped lower and it bounced back. So I sell it for that reason." The **36 put** is the cap "if I'm wrong, it crashes down." And the **42 call** is where he expects the bounce off the 200-day to carry: "I buy a call at 42, which is at the black arrow here, because I expect now it's bouncing off the 200 moving average and it goes up from there."

**Execution.** Bang watches the mark drift — "now I pay only $11 for the trade instead of 14, because the price is dropping." He sends at that level, does not fill, and then does something worth noting for anyone learning order mechanics: "I wait for a while and see if it fills. If not, then I change my debit to be a little bit higher to get it filled. Let's raise it a little bit." **Filled at 12 cents.** His justification for not haggling: "I only like two cents, or two dollars, for the trade."

**The pre-stated management plan.** Before walking away, Bang fixes his rules, and this is the clearest statement of the Bull Bang profit-and-loss framework in the module:

> "My max loss in this trade is $514. My bet is the stock price will go up from here, but if it breaks down and I lose money, my target is: if I lose **half of the $500 here, which is $250 or so**, then I close the trade, because my theory is wrong — the stock price breaks through the key support level. And also, I always target to lose a maximum of half of the money."

And on the upside: "let's say if the stock price goes all the way to something like 45, from currently below 42, I'm going to make $3 up and that would be $300. So that would be good, because I'm paying only $12 now. If I make like $200, that is super profitable... If I make more than $250 or ideally $300, that's a good trade for me and I may consider to take early profit."

So the framework is symmetric around half the max loss: **cut at −$250, consider taking profit at +$250 to +$300.** On a $12 debit, +$250 is a twentyfold return on premium paid; on $517 of blocked capital it is roughly 48%.

**The outcome: nothing.** Bang returns on **17 May**, the expiration date, 64 days after entry on 14 March.

"When I entered here — you see the black arrow — I entered around March 14, 15. The price was at about **41.6**. And right now, the price is also at **41.56**. So it's almost exactly where I entered about three months ago."

The path was not flat, though. "There was a time after I entered the stock was up and I made some money on the trade. But then after that it dropped all the way, because of the political reason. There's a political campaign going on in the US when people talk about healthcare for everyone, cheaper healthcare, single-payer kind of thing, and it hit the whole sector badly. So the stock has dropped after that, and since then it has recovered and gone back up to the same level as when I entered."

At $41.56, the stock sits precisely in the middle of the break-even zone between the 41 put and the 42 call. Every leg expires worthless:

| Leg | Strike | Status at $41.56 | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long call | 42 | Out of the money (price below strike) | Expires worthless |
| Short put | 41 | Out of the money (price above strike) | Expires worthless |
| Long put | 36 | Far out of the money | Expires worthless |

Bang's decision is to do nothing, and he explains why: "I don't need to do anything because I already hit the max loss, which is $12, and I don't want to close it to incur the commission and closing costs. I will not be exercised because all options will be expired." He checks the marks to confirm: "the market value of these three legs is down to almost zero for all legs."

| Pfizer trade summary | |
|---|---|
| Entry date | 14 March |
| Expiry date | 17 May |
| Days in trade | 64 |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Entry debit | $0.12/share = **$12** |
| Capital blocked | **$512** |
| Exit | Expired worthless, $0 collected |
| **Net loss** | **$12** |

His verdict is worth quoting in full because it is the honest accounting of what a neutral outcome costs: "So this trade, I do not make money as I expected, but I also do not lose money. So it's a neutral trade. We do another trade. It's just part of the long-term winning plan. Sometimes you get profit, sometimes you don't. That's fine too." And the counterfactual: "Much better than if I had held a thousand dollars in the hundred shares here for the last two months — I could not use that capital for any other trade. In this case, I only put a fraction of the money there and it goes nowhere. I lost $12."

That is the strategic argument for the Bull Bang stated in its purest form. Owning a hundred shares of Pfizer for 64 days would have tied up **$4,160** to earn a loss of four cents per share. The Bull Bang tied up **$512** to lose $12. When your thesis simply fails to materialise — which is the most common outcome in trading — the Bull Bang's cost of being wrong is trivially small, and your capital was available the whole time.

### Live Trade Three: 3M — Bottom Fishing, and a 52.8% Return in 20 Days

The third live trade is the winner, and it is the pure bottom-fishing application.

**The setup.** The date is 4 June in US trading time (5 June, past 1 a.m., in Singapore). The stock is **MMM, 3M** — a Dow component, a good dividend payer, "a very good company."

The damage is severe. "The stock has dropped quite a lot over the past two months or so, since it set the high at about almost **220**, down all the way to **160**, and now hovering at 164-165 — which is a **25% drop** from the high." (Bang says "25% drops from the high" in the transcript; 220 to 164 is a fall of about 25.5%, so the figure checks out.) The causes: "bad earnings and also a lot of headline issues on the China and US trade war." Today, the whole market is bouncing strongly after several bad days, "mostly the trade wars and a lot of tariffs things that Trump talks about — increasing tariffs for China, Mexico, India, and who else next. So today it seems to be like some institutionals just locked in their profit and the market rallied today."

Bang is unusually candid about the weakness of the technical case, and this candour is exactly what makes the Bull Bang appropriate here: **"there's no guarantee that 3M has hit the bottom. Technically there's no support here. So it can continue to go down, but I just use this strategy because I do have a protection on the downside in case I'm wrong."**

That sentence is the strategic thesis of the entire module. He is taking a trade he knows is unsupported by the chart, on a company he trusts, at a price he thinks is a gift, *because the structure makes being wrong survivable*. The description he gives of the method is memorable: "I also often use this one for bottom fishing, meaning buy good stock that has been beaten down to death, and now I just go collecting dead bodies."

**The construction.** Expiry chosen: **45 days**.

*Stage one — the naked call.* "Buying a call at the money here, I would pay about **$485**. So if the stock goes nowhere in the next 45 days, I lose $485, which may not be a good way to trade."

*Stage two — the synthetic.* He buys the call slightly above the market: "maybe I buy a little higher than the current market price — **$170**, I pay **$2.64**." And he sells the **160 put** to finance it, with the strike chosen entirely from the chart: "why am I selling 160? Because the last time when it dipped, it dipped to about $159 or 160. So I believe 160 could be the last swing low. It could be the support level right now. That's why I'm selling 160. I don't want the stock price to drop below that."

The premium relationship is favourable: "I sell 160 to collect premium, and that premium is more than enough to pay for the 170 call." Two legs, therefore, would be a net credit.

He shows the two-leg risk: "between the two strikes that I buy a call here and sell a put, I break even or make small money. Below that I would lose money — a lot. I could lose all the way when the stock price drops to zero. But I could make unlimited profit also if the stock price goes up."

*Stage three — the reinsurance.* He adds the **150 put**. "To protect the 160 put here, I buy a lower put to cap the downside."

| 3M Bull Bang | | |
|---|---|---|
| Leg 1 | Buy 1 × 170 call, 45 DTE | −$2.64 |
| Leg 2 | Sell 1 × 160 put, 45 DTE | credit, not stated |
| Leg 3 | Buy 1 × 150 put, 45 DTE | debit, not stated |
| **Net debit** | | **$0.50/share = $50** |
| Max loss | (160 − 150) × 100 + $50 | **$1,050** (Bang states $1,000-odd) |
| Capital blocked | | **$1,050** |
| Break-even (expiry) | 170 + 0.50 | **$170.50** |
| Max profit | | **Unlimited** |

Bang narrates the P&L shape: "between the two legs, 170 call and 160 put, I'm losing a little money, which is the cost of the reinsurance, basically 63 or $60 [the quoted mark at that moment]. If the stock goes nowhere in the next 45 days, I lose a little money. But if it recovers, I would make all the money on the upside. If I'm wrong, the stock continues to drop, then my max loss would be $1,050. And if I get out early — which is the pink line here — I could lose less. I could lose like $600, $700, depending on how deep the stock price could drop."

He then reads a symmetric ten-point scenario off the pink line, which is the cleanest single illustration of the strategy's risk-reward in the whole course:

| Move from $165 | Stock price | P&L on the pink line |
|---|---|---|
| **+10 points** | $175 | **+$648** |
| **−10 points** | $155 | **−$519** |

"So one to 1.2 kind of thing. That's my risk profile."

That ratio — roughly 1.25 units of gain per unit of loss for an equal-sized move in either direction — is the concrete meaning of the split-strike construction. The trade is not symmetric; it is tilted upward, and the tilt is paid for by the small dead zone between 160 and 170.

**Execution.** The mark is 50 to 52 cents. Bang bargains: "let's say I bargain to 50 and send it out." Filled almost immediately — "it should be filled anytime soon because now the market is active. Yeah, it's filled."

**The outcome: 20 days later.** Bang returns on **24 June**, exactly twenty days after opening, with 25 days still to run on the 45-day expiry.

3M has recovered from the entry price of **$164.12** to **$174.15** — up roughly ten points. "It seems to have found the bottom at about $159, and since then it's recovering."

Position status: "the stock price has recovered and gone above my $170 call that I bought there. So apparently my call option is in the money, and my put option is way, way out of the money, and it will likely be expired [worthless]."

Open profit: **$538**. "Remember when I entered I paid a little debit, which is $50; now it becomes $500-plus profit for me."

**The early-exit decision.** This is where the pink-line asymmetry converts from theory into money. Bang opens the analyze tab and reads both lines at the current price of ~$174:

| | Value if closed today (24 June) | Value if held to expiry (19 July) |
|---|---|---|
| P&L | **$537** | **$334** |

"From the chart, today the stock price is at 174, close to 174. If you look at the pink line, which is today, 24th of June — if I exit today, I could have more premium than if I keep the option until expiration. The blue line is P&L at expiration, which is a lower premium than I could have if I close it today. I will get at the pink level. The pink level is $537. If I keep the trade until expiration, it will go down to $334."

Holding for 25 more days, with the position *already right*, would cost **$203**. That is the entire argument for exiting a winning Bull Bang early, and the reason is simple: with the stock at 174 and the call struck at 170, the call has $4.00 of intrinsic value and roughly $1.30 of extrinsic. Expiration confiscates the extrinsic. Closing captures it.

And his framing of the general rule: "one of the benefits of this strategy is when you make profit, you exit early, you can get extra premium from the time value remaining in the call option. If I'm wrong, I lose money, I exit early, and I also lose less than the max loss as well."

**The honest arithmetic of the split strike.** Bang then addresses a question a sharp student would ask: the stock rose nine to ten points, so why is the profit only $530 rather than $900?

"Since I opened, the stock price has gone up almost like 9 to 10 points, maybe 9 points, but I'm only making $530. Why is that? Why am I not making $900? Because if I own a hundred shares, I could have made $900. **The reason is because I defined up front, for my trade, that my profit zone would be beyond $170, and my loss zone would be below $160. Between 160 and 170, I accept a break-even or a slight loss.** That's my game plan. I give myself some buffer. But if I had sold the put at 165 and bought a call at 165, I could have made $900-plus or even $1,000 today. But I gave myself some buffer, so **there's no free lunch here.**"

This is the trade-off at the heart of the split-strike synthetic, and it is worth restating in general terms. Widening the gap between the short put and the long call widens the dead zone, reduces the net debit (or creates a credit), moves the downside danger point lower, and gives up the first several points of any rally. Narrowing the gap to zero — a pure synthetic at a single strike — captures every point of the move but has no buffer at all and no cushion if the stock stalls. The Bull Bang trader chooses where on that spectrum to sit, and the choice is made *once, at entry*, by picking the two strikes.

He also decomposes the exit price to show where the value is: "in this case, 170 and above will be my profit zone. And now the stock price is 174. That means intrinsic value is $400. And now I can sell at $530. So I have $130-something extra when I close the trade today." Four hundred dollars intrinsic, roughly $130 extrinsic — the extrinsic being exactly what early exit harvests.

**Closing the position manually.** Bang emphasises that thinkorswim will not close this structure for you, because the platform has no preset for it: "in the normal trade, you could have one option here where you can choose to close the entire trade. But this three-leg strategy is different. This is my own way of trading, my own strategy. So the system doesn't know that there's such a strategy available. Maybe they know, but not popular enough. So they have not built in an automatic closing order. So I have to do it manually. I have to remember what is the trade that I entered, and I just need to do the reverse."

The mechanics, leg by leg, holding Control to build the multi-leg order:

| Position held | Colour in platform | Closing action |
|---|---|---|
| Long 170 call | green (long) | **Sell to close** |
| Short 160 put | red (short) | **Buy to close** |
| Long 150 put | green (long) | **Sell to close** |

"So here are the three legs. That is a reversal of the trade I'm holding."

**Working the order through a wide spread.** The initial ask on the combination is $6.10 credit. Bang notes the difficulty: "you can look at the bid and the ask spread here — it's quite wide, **25 cents**. So normally if you get the market price here, it's not easily get filled immediately.
