You have to wait for a while. If you are really keen, you may want to just reduce the credit — you may get it filled faster." He steps the price down: 6.10, no fill; down one increment, no fill; "so you look at the bid and ask, it's still like 20 cents. Probably you need to continue to go down to get it filled."

**Filled at $6.06 credit.** He notes the individual leg fill for the call: "the 170 call leg I sold at $6.37" — the other two legs netting against it to produce the $6.06 package.

**The full accounting.**

| 3M trade summary | |
|---|---|
| Entry date | 4 June 2019 (5 June Singapore) |
| Exit date | 24 June 2019 |
| Days in trade | **20** |
| Contracts | 1 |
| Stock at entry | **$164.12** |
| Stock at exit | **$174.15** |
| Stock move | **+$10.03 (+6.1%)** |
| Entry net debit | $0.50/share = **$50** |
| Capital blocked | **$1,050** |
| Exit net credit | $6.06/share = **$606** |
| **Net profit** | **$556 before commissions** |
| **Return on capital** | **52.8% in 20 days** |

Bang's own calculation: "$606 minus the $50 I paid at the beginning, so that's $556 before commission. If I calculate the return on investment, that translates into about **52.8% over 20 days**, which is very good return on investment."

He immediately adds the caveat that any honest teacher must: "if I continue to use this strategy for another 20 days, and if I could get the same return on investment, this could translate into a humongous return on investment. But again, **that assumes I'm right**. I'm just giving you an idea of what could be possible. But in this case, I picked the right stock at the right time using the right strategy."

### The Management Framework

Assembling the rules scattered across the four videos into a single operational framework:

**Profit-taking.** There is no fixed percentage-of-max-profit rule, because max profit is unlimited — the rule that governs credit spreads does not apply here. Instead, three triggers:

1. **A price target.** "When you hit the profit target — because there's no limit on the upside, if you have the target price in your mind, and when you see the stock price reaches that level, you may want just to exit it."
2. **A profit magnitude relative to premium and capital.** In the Pfizer trade the pre-stated target was **+$250 to +$300** against a $12 debit and $512 of blocked capital.
3. **The pink-line/blue-line gap.** When the position is deep enough in the money that the extrinsic value in the long call is material, closing captures it. The 3M trade closed with $130 of extrinsic on the table, harvested rather than surrendered.

The overriding instruction on all three is the same: **exit before expiration.** "If you exit early, you can get extra value, which is the time value remaining in the trade, and you can exit with extra profit as well."

**Loss-cutting.** Two triggers, and the first dominates:

1. **Thesis invalidation.** The UNH exit was not triggered by a price level. It was triggered by an event resolving against the thesis: earnings came in good, the stock ignored them, "my theory is not valid anymore." This is the highest-quality exit signal available and should be acted on immediately.
2. **A stop level, defined as a fraction of max loss.** Bang's stated default: **half the maximum loss**. "If I lose half of the $500 here, which is $250 or so, then I close the trade, because my theory is wrong." He generalises: "I always target to lose a maximum of half of the money." Alternatively a fixed dollar figure — "for example, I cannot lose more than $500 per trade."

The mechanism that makes a half-max-loss stop achievable is the pink line: because the pre-expiration curve is above the expiration curve on the downside as well, a stock sitting at your long put strike will not have produced max loss until expiration arrives. "Even if it drops to 115 right here, chances are you don't lose $1,000." You have time to get out for less.

**Closing mechanics.** Always close all three legs simultaneously in one combination order. "When you close a trade, remember you close all the legs together at the same time." Build the closing order manually — sell to close the long call, buy to close the short put, sell to close the long put — because the platform has no automatic close for the structure. Expect wide bid-ask spreads on a three-legged package and be prepared to work the price down in small increments to get filled.

**Doing nothing.** If all three legs are out of the money at expiration and worth approximately zero, the correct action is no action. Closing incurs commission on three legs to recover nothing. The Pfizer trade ended this way. This is only safe when all legs are genuinely out of the money — if any leg is in the money you must close, or face assignment.

### Every Risk in the Bull Bang

**Assignment risk on the short put.** This is the structural risk that never goes away. You have sold a put. If the stock trades below that strike, particularly near expiration or around an ex-dividend date, you can be assigned and required to buy a hundred shares at the strike. Bang's discipline for handling this is not a hedge — it is strike selection. He places the short put only at a level where he would genuinely accept ownership: "I think the stock's fundamentally good, I could just own the stock also. I could get the stock assigned to me because I sell a put here — I have the obligation to take the shares if the stock drops below that 160 level." If you would not want the shares at your short strike, you have chosen it wrongly.

**Gap risk beyond the long put.** The protective put caps the loss but does not eliminate it, and a gap can take you to the cap in a single session. The maximum loss — put spread width plus debit — is a real number that can be realised in one overnight move. On UNH that was $1,100 on a $102 debit; on 3M, $1,050 on a $50 debit. The insurance is real, but the deductible is roughly ten to twenty times the premium paid.

**The dead zone.** Between the short put strike and the long call strike, the trade cannot make money. If the stock spends the entire life of the position inside that band, you lose the debit and the opportunity — the Pfizer outcome exactly. This is the price of the split-strike buffer and it is paid in full whenever the stock goes nowhere.

**Under-participation in a rally.** As the 3M trade showed, a ten-point rally on a stock produced $530 of profit rather than the $900 a hundred shares would have made, because the first ten points fell inside the dead zone. The Bull Bang is a leveraged bet with a deductible on both sides.

**Wide bid-ask spreads on a three-legged package.** Six option legs on entry and exit (three each way) means six crossings of the spread. Bang encountered a 25-cent-wide market on the 3M close and had to work the order down through several price increments. In illiquid names this cost can eat a meaningful fraction of a small trade's profit. This is why he specifies choosing strikes "somewhere near the current price so that I have the highest liquidity, the bid and ask spread."

**Commission drag.** Three legs to open and three to close means six commissions per contract round trip. On a trade whose entry debit is $12, as in Pfizer, commissions can exceed the premium at risk. Bang's decision to let the Pfizer legs expire worthless rather than close them was driven purely by this: "I don't want to close it to incur the commission and closing costs."

**Timing risk on the exit.** Because the profitable exit depends on capturing extrinsic value before expiration, and because the loss-mitigating exit depends on acting before the expiration curve is reached, the strategy requires you to be present. The Bull Bang is not a position you set and forget.

**Thesis risk on bottom-fishing setups.** Bang's own warning on the 3M trade is the most important risk disclosure in the module: "there's no guarantee that 3M has hit the bottom. Technically there's no support here. So it can continue to go down." Bottom fishing is by definition trading against the prevailing trend. The reason it is defensible with this structure — and indefensible with a hundred shares — is that the structure caps the cost of being wrong at a known number.

**Non-fundamental price drivers.** Two of the three live trades were damaged by political news flow that fundamental analysis could not price. UNH and Pfizer were both hit by the same healthcare campaign rhetoric. Bang's conclusion after UNH is worth carrying forward: "I don't know when that campaign is going to stop." A thesis that says "the market is wrong about this good company" is only tradeable if the force making the market wrong has a foreseeable end.

### Summary of the Bull Bang

Bang closes the theory lesson with five points, and they serve as the compressed version of everything above:

| # | Benefit | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Limited risk with unlimited profit potential** | Long protective put caps the downside; no short call caps the upside. "Normally you don't have this going together." |
| 2 | **You define your own profit zone** | Splitting the call and put strikes lets you choose where profit begins and where loss begins. "At what price I will start making money. At what price I don't mind owning the share." |
| 3 | **Very low capital** | Less than 10% of share value blocked, versus 20–25% for the unprotected synthetic and 100% for the shares. Microsoft: $1,047 vs $12,000. |
| 4 | **Magnified return on investment** | Because the capital base is a tenth of the stock's, the same dollar profit is a ten-times-larger percentage return. 3M: $556 on $1,050 = 52.8% in 20 days. |
| 5 | **Almost no time decay** | Near-zero net debit means theta is close to neutral, unlike a long call where decay is "a big concern." |

And the sixth point, implicit in all the live trades: **early exit pays you twice** — more when you are right, less when you are wrong — because the pre-expiration P&L curve sits above the expiration curve on both wings.

# Part XIV — Psychology, Risk Management & Building the Business

## Psychology, Risk Management, and Building a Profitable Options Trading Business

### The Half of the Job That Nobody Teaches

By the time this lesson arrives in the course, the student has been handed an armoury. Bull put spreads, bear call spreads, iron condors, jade lizards, diagonals, calendars, the Crouching Bull, the DS Hammer, the C2D, the Bull Bang collar, synthetic longs and shorts, earnings probability spreads — each one dismantled into its entry criteria, its adjustment triggers, its exit rules, its behaviour under time decay and volatility shifts. It would be entirely natural for a student at this point to believe the work is done, that the remaining task is simply to execute what has been learned.

The instructor opens the psychology lesson by taking that belief apart. "Based on my 18 years of trading," he says, "strategy is just one part of a winning plan. In fact, it's not more than 50%." His split is explicit and it is even: fifty percent of the outcome comes from strategy — knowing which structure to deploy, where to place the strikes, when to enter and when to adjust — and the remaining fifty percent comes from psychology, which he immediately unpacks into two components. The first is risk management discipline, the mechanical business of sizing positions, defining losses in advance, and diversifying across strategies and underlyings. The second is emotional management, the far messier business of what happens inside the trader's head when the market moves against an open position and every instinct is screaming to hold on for one more day.

That second half, he argues, is what determines whether a trader survives long enough for the first half to matter. A strategy with a genuine statistical edge will still produce losing streaks, and a trader who abandons the strategy during those streaks never collects the edge. This is why the lesson is not an appendix to the course but a structural pillar of it. Everything taught in the preceding chapters is an engine; this chapter is the braking system, and an engine without brakes is not a vehicle, it is an accident waiting for a date.

Note in passing a small inconsistency in the source material worth flagging rather than smoothing over. In the psychology lesson the instructor refers to "my 18 years of trading" when describing his overall market experience, then a few minutes later says "several mistakes that I have made in my past 12 years of option trading," and in the business-building lesson he says "it takes me a very long time — in the 13 years right now." The figures are not contradictory if one reads the eighteen years as total market experience and the twelve or thirteen as options-specific experience, but the transcripts do not reconcile them explicitly and no attempt is made here to do so on his behalf.

### Everything Begins With the Risk Profile

The first concept in the lesson — the one everything else hangs from — is that no trade should ever be entered until its risk profile has been fully articulated. Not glanced at. Articulated, in numbers, in answer to a specific set of questions the instructor lists and then works through live on the platform.

He builds the example from the simplest possible starting point, deliberately, because the argument is about method rather than about strategy sophistication. Suppose you are looking at SPY. The market is up on the day. Technically, SPY is in an uptrend and has bounced off its 200-day moving average. The obvious, instinctive trade for a bullish trader is to buy a call. So you go out roughly two months — the platform shows seventy-two days to expiration — and you buy an at-the-money call. SPY is trading around 281 to 282, so you buy the 281 strike call.

Now, before the order goes anywhere, comes the interrogation.

**What is the profit-and-loss profile?** The platform draws it: the familiar hockey stick of a long call, losses capped and flat to the downside, gains rising without limit above the strike.

**What is the break-even point?** Set the slices on the analysis tab and read it off. The break-even is 289.07. SPY is at roughly 281 to 282 today. That is the first number that should give a buyer pause: the underlying must travel more than seven points, roughly two and a half percent, simply for the position to be worth what was paid for it.

**What is the maximum risk?** If the price falls and stays below the strike through expiration, the entire premium is lost. That premium is $807 for the single contract.

**What is the profit potential?** Unlimited to the upside, in the theoretical sense that a long call has no ceiling.

**What is the probability of winning?** Here the instructor makes his most important methodological point of the segment. The thinkorswim analysis chart displays a probability percentage attached to the region of the chart above the break-even line. For the price to finish profitable it must land to the right of that vertical line, and the platform reports the odds of that happening as **32% chance of winning and roughly 67% chance of losing money**. He then refines the loss side: the probability of losing the *maximum* — the case where SPY simply drops to 281 or below and stays there through expiration — is about **48% to 49%**. So the full distribution is roughly a third chance of profit, a half chance of total loss of premium, and the remainder somewhere in between.

Stop and consider what has just happened. A trader looked at a chart, saw an uptrend and a bounce off a major moving average, formed a confident bullish view, and reached for the most natural expression of that view — and the platform has just told him that the trade he was about to place wins less than one time in three. Nothing about the chart analysis was wrong. The directional read may well be correct. But buying an at-the-money call requires being right about three separate things simultaneously, and the instructor spells them out: "You have to have the direction right, you have to have the time right, and you have to have the price right" — meaning the underlying must not only move up, it must move up *enough*, and it must do so *before* the option expires. Three conditions in series, each with its own probability of failure, is how a confident directional view becomes a 32% proposition.

**What is the trade behaviour?** This is the last question and it is the subtlest. On the analysis chart there are two lines: a blue line showing the position's value at expiration, and a pink line showing its value today, at the current point in the time-decay curve. The blue line never changes; it is the terminal payoff. The pink line moves as the date moves. The practical consequence, which the instructor draws out explicitly, is that early exits do not land on the expiration payoff. If the trade goes your way and you close early, you capture extra value because there is still time premium left in the option — you make more than the expiration line suggests at that price. And if the trade goes against you and you close early, you do *not* lose the maximum, because there is still time value in the option working in your favour on the way out. You lose something in the middle, smaller than the max loss. This is the mathematical foundation of the entire cut-loss discipline that comes later in the lesson: getting out early is not merely emotionally easier, it is arithmetically cheaper, and the option's remaining time value is what makes it so.

### The Same View, Expressed as a Seller

Having established the method, the instructor uses it to compare two ways of holding the identical market opinion. Instead of buying the SPY call, he takes the same bullish thesis and expresses it as a cash-secured put.

Looking at the chart, he identifies strong support in the region of 274 to 275. His reasoning is stated plainly: "I believe it won't drop below 274." So he sells the 274 put at the same seventy-two days to expiration, removing the previous trade from the analysis so the two structures can be compared cleanly.

The risk profile that emerges is the mirror image of the long call in every dimension that matters.

**Maximum profit** is capped at the premium collected, which is $5.12 per share, or **$512** for the contract. If SPY rises — by a dollar or by fifty dollars — the outcome is the same $512. The seller has traded away the upside tail.

**Maximum loss** is, in his phrasing, indefinite. If the stock fell all the way to zero, the seller would lose the entire strike value on the way down: 274 times 100 shares, or **$27,400**. He is careful to characterise this correctly — "if it goes to zero, it won't happen, but mathematically, yes." The point is not that SPY will go to zero. The point is that a cash-secured put has a very large theoretical loss, and a trader who has not written that number down has not understood the position he is holding.

**Break-even** is the strike minus the premium: with the 274 put sold for $5.12, the break-even sits at approximately **268.7**. Read what that means against the thesis. The seller believed SPY would not fall below 274. He can be wrong about that — SPY can fall through 274 — and still make money, provided it does not fall below 268.7 by expiration.

**Probability of winning** is where the comparison becomes stark: the platform reports roughly **84% to 85%**. SPY is at 281. For the seller to lose money, it must fall well below 268.8. That is a very different proposition from needing a rally past 289.07.

**Contingency plan and capital requirement.** Because this is a cash-secured put, the seller must be prepared to be assigned 100 shares at $274. But the effective cash outlay is not $27,400, because the premium collected reduces the cost basis. The instructor computes it as roughly **$26,887 to $26,888** — the strike value less the $5.12 per share premium. That is the cash that must actually be sitting in the account, ready, before this trade is legitimate.

Set side by side, the two trades look like this:

| | Long 281 call, 72 DTE | Short 274 put, 72 DTE |
|---|---|---|
| Direction of view | Bullish | Bullish |
| Maximum profit | Unlimited | $512 (premium) |
| Maximum loss | $807 (premium paid) | $27,400 (theoretical, stock to zero) |
| Break-even | 289.07 | ~268.70 |
| Probability of profit | ~32% | ~84–85% |
| Probability of maximum loss | ~48–49% | Very small |
| Capital required | $807 | ~$26,887 cash secured |
| Wrong on direction, still profitable? | No | Yes, down to 268.70 |

Neither column is "better" in the abstract, and the instructor never claims otherwise. The buyer pays $807 for a lottery ticket with an enormous payoff and a two-in-three chance of expiring worthless. The seller ties up nearly twenty-seven thousand dollars to collect $512 with an eighty-four percent chance of success. What the comparison establishes is that these are radically different businesses, and that the trader must know which business he is in before the order is sent — not afterwards, when the position is already moving.

### Contingency Planning: Deciding in Advance What "Wrong" Looks Like

The most operationally useful passage in the first psychology lesson is the one where the instructor sits with the short 274 put and asks what he will actually do if the trade goes against him. He does not answer with a principle. He answers with numbers read off the pink line — the today-line — at specific prices.

Today is June 5th in the example. Suppose that one week from now SPY has fallen to 274, right at the short strike. What is the damage? He reads it: the position is down **$265**. Not the maximum loss, not anything close to it — a $265 unrealised loss on a position whose theoretical maximum loss is $27,400. That is what the time value remaining in the option buys the seller who exits early.

Suppose instead he decides to give the trade more room and sets his line at 270. If SPY reaches 270, the loss is close to **$500**. Still a small number relative to the structure's theoretical risk, and still a number he can absorb without damage.

So the menu of contingency plans, decided in advance, looks like this. Plan A: if SPY breaks 274 within the next week, cut the loss at roughly $265 and move on. Plan B: give the trade more room, accept a loss of roughly $500 at 270, and cut there. Plan C: accept assignment — take the 100 shares at an effective outlay of $268.87 per share — because the trader genuinely wants to own SPY at that price and has the $26,887 sitting ready. Plan D: never carry the naked risk in the first place, and instead buy a cheap far-out-of-the-money put alongside the short put as reinsurance, so that a full market meltdown cannot produce an unbounded loss.

All four are legitimate. What is not legitimate is having no plan, discovering SPY at 270 with a $500 unrealised loss, and only then beginning to think about what to do. "You need to have the plan," he says. "You need to have a contingency plan." The plan is the thing that turns a market move from an emotional event into an administrative one.

### The Pre-Trade Interrogation

The instructor then compresses everything above into a checklist he insists be run before any trade, in the form of questions with numerical answers.

The first is: **what is your worst-case loss?** The chart gives it. Read it and write it down.

The second follows immediately: **can you afford that loss?** And here the risk-per-trade rule appears. The question is whether the worst case sits "within your rule of one or two or five percent of your total capital." That is the entire numeric statement of risk per trade as it is given in this lesson — a band of **1%, 2%, or 5% of total capital** as the maximum acceptable worst-case loss on a single trade, with the trader choosing his own point on that band. If the answer is yes, the trade is permissible. If the answer is no, the trade must be restructured into a defined-risk form: "Don't sell like a cash-secured put, don't sell like a naked call. You just need to well-define in advance how much loss you can afford."

The third question is: **what is the reward for accepting the risk?** He frames the acceptable answers as ratios — "one to two, one to three" — and adds the special case of structures with limited loss and unlimited profit, such as the Bull Bang, where "you know how much your max loss is and you have unlimited potential profit. That could be a very good risk-reward ratio."

The fourth is: **where is the cut-loss point?** This is where the time-value insight from the trade-behaviour discussion pays off. "The beauty of options is when it goes down, but you still have time in your trade, you won't lose the max loss. You still have time value in the option, and then smaller than the max loss. But you need to define in advance what is the point where the market moves not in your favour and you move on and cut loss."

The fifth is the one that separates traders who last from traders who do not: **what if you are wrong?** His answer is bracingly humble for someone teaching a course: "No one can predict the market moves every single time. I can be right one time, but the next time I can be very wrong. I can be wrong many times in a row also. It's very hard. It's 50-50 chance, but it's hard to predict. Even if you get it right, you don't know how much it moves." Direction is roughly a coin flip; magnitude is a second, independent unknown; and the trader must build a plan that survives being wrong about both.

### Being Wrong and Still Getting Paid

There is a consolation embedded in this, and the instructor is careful to draw it out because it is the structural reason he prefers selling to buying. He returns to the short 274 put.

The thesis was that SPY would rise. Suppose it does: the seller collects the full premium, "500 plus dollars," and the trade closes at maximum profit. Now suppose the thesis is wrong and SPY falls. Does the seller lose? Not necessarily. As long as SPY does not fall below the break-even at roughly 268.7, the position remains profitable. Look at the line on the chart: the seller is wrong about direction, and still in the money.

"So that's the beauty of options," he says. "You can be wrong, but that doesn't mean that you will be losing money. You can be wrong and you still can make money, as long as it's not too far wrong."

This is the practical content of the phrase "play with the probability" that recurs throughout the lesson. The option seller is not being paid to forecast correctly. He is being paid to be approximately correct within a wide band, and to be compensated by theta for the time he spends waiting inside that band. It changes what a "wrong" trade means. For the call buyer, wrong means SPY failing to reach 289.07 in seventy-two days — an outcome that occurs about two-thirds of the time. For the put seller, wrong means SPY collapsing more than four and a half percent — an outcome that occurs about fifteen percent of the time.

### Take Care of the Risk and the Profit Takes Care of Itself

Before moving into the mistakes, the instructor delivers two framing statements he clearly regards as the heart of the lesson.

The first is about persistence. "Don't give up. I know there will be times you'll be very frustrated when we hit multiple losing trades in a row. I have gone through it many times, in fact. The key here is you need to be patient, you need to persevere to win in the long term." Note the framing: losing streaks are not evidence that the method is broken; they are a scheduled feature of any method with a win rate below one hundred percent, which is every method.

The second is the tagline he says he posts on the wall of every classroom he teaches in: **"Take care of your risk, and the profit will take care of you."** He explains the logic rather than leaving it as a slogan. "If you take care of your risk, the profit is just a result of it. You need to manage the risk and then the profit will come."

And then the analogy that best captures the entire selling business: "It's exactly like the insurance selling business. Insurance companies sell insurance to insurance buyers. What do they do? They just manage the risk. Because they know all the premium they collect will become their profit if they manage the risk properly. Just take out the risk, and then let the theta or the premium work in your favour."

An insurance company does not try to predict which houses will burn. It prices the premium, diversifies the book, buys reinsurance against catastrophic correlated events, and manages its exposure so that no single event can destroy it. Its profit is not a forecast; it is the residual left over after the risk has been properly managed. The option seller's business is identical in structure, and every rule that follows in this chapter is a version of one of those insurance-company practices: price the premium correctly (sell when IV is high), diversify the book (rule three), buy reinsurance (defined-risk structures), and never write so much exposure that a single correlated event can wipe out the firm (position sizing).

### Costly Mistake Number One: The Trade That Could Not Lose

The instructor structures the rest of the psychology material around his own failures, and he does not soften them. The first is the largest, and it is worth narrating in full because every element of it — the profitable pattern, the complacency that follows profit, the misunderstood instrument, the buffer that felt generous, the speed of the collapse — recurs in the trading lives of people who have never traded a volatility product in their lives.

"There was a time I did not understand what could go wrong with my trades," he says, "and I paid a hefty price for it."

The background requires understanding the instruments, and he takes the time to explain them properly. VIX is the volatility index, popularly called the fear index. Looking at a ten-year chart of VIX, the pattern is unmistakable: it spends most of its life subdued, hovering "between 10 to 16 or 17," and then once in a while it spikes violently — to 25, to 30, and in the extreme cases on his chart to around 50 or 53 — and after every spike it falls back down again within days or weeks. This behaviour has a name: mean reversion. VIX is, in his phrase, "a mean reversal asset."

But VIX itself cannot be owned. It is an index, exactly as SPX is an index. You cannot buy SPX; you can buy instruments derived from it. In the case of VIX, the primary derivative is the VIX future, ticker /VX — the slash prefix denoting a futures contract — which is constructed to replicate the index as closely as possible and which exhibits the same spike-and-revert behaviour.

Futures, however, carry expiration dates. A trader or investor who wants to hold a volatility position for an extended period must watch those expirations and keep rolling the contract forward, which is administratively tiresome and which many market participants would rather avoid. So exchange-traded products were created to solve that problem. VXX is an ETN — an exchange-traded *note*, as opposed to an ETF, an exchange-traded *fund* — designed to track the VIX future one-for-one. If the VIX future rises 1%, VXX rises 1%. If the future falls 1%, VXX falls 1%. UVXY is the leveraged version, tracking at twice the rate: the future up 1% means UVXY up 2%, the future down 1% means UVXY down 2%.

That two-times structure has a mathematical consequence that the instructor illustrates with the cleanest possible arithmetic. Start with $100. On day one you lose 10%, leaving $90. On day two you gain 10%, and 10% of $90 is $9, leaving $99. You have experienced a down-ten and an up-ten and you are down 1%. Repeat that pattern over a long series of days and the value decays relentlessly. This is the well-known drag on leveraged and volatility-linked products, and its effect on UVXY over ten years is spectacular. The chart he shows runs from a starting reference "like $6 million" down to $37 at the time of the lesson.

He is careful — and this is a good instinct in a teacher — to explain why the historical number is absurd rather than letting the student assume the product genuinely once traded at seven-figure prices. "The ETN did not start at 65 million. It started at like maybe 50. But because it kept decaying, every once in a while they just do the reverse split, meaning they combine the number of shares into one share. So 10 become one, 10 become one, 10 become one. So they have to restate the historical number to the new reference point. That's why they start with 50, but on the chart it becomes like 65 million at the beginning."

The visual consequence of that restatement matters for the lesson. On a ten-year chart, the last few years of UVXY look like a flat line pinned near zero. They are not flat. Zoom into 2016 and the product is falling substantially; zoom further and the individual spikes become visible. Move to 2017 and there are dramatic upward moves — one he points to runs from "like 12 or 13,000" on the restated scale up to "45,000," a move of roughly three times, occurring because the VIX future roughly doubled and the two-times product amplified it to three or four times. The chart's compression hid the violence. That, in itself, is a lesson about relying on long-horizon charts to assess short-horizon risk.

Now the trade. His reasoning was simple and, on its face, sound. "I look at the chart. I say, hey, there's only one way for UVXY to go, which is to go down." A product that structurally decays is a product whose call options should, over time, expire worthless. Selling naked calls on it should therefore be a reliable income machine — and the premiums were extraordinary.

He demonstrates the premium levels on the live chain at the price prevailing during the lesson, with UVXY at 37 and a thirty-day expiration:

| Strike | Distance above spot | Premium collected | Premium as % of share price |
|---|---|---|---|
| 37 (at the money) | 0% | ~$4.00 | more than 10% |
| 40 | ~10% above | ~$3.00+ | roughly 8–9% |
| 45 | ~20% above | ~$2.45 | — |
| ~45 (framed as a 30% buffer, roughly 10 points) | ~30% above | ~$1.70–$1.80 ($170–$180) | — |

Read the bottom row carefully, because it is the row that explains the disaster. Selling a call roughly thirty percent above the market — a buffer that in any normal equity would be enormous — still paid around $170 to $180 per contract on a thirty-day option. "I have 30% buffer. If the price goes up by 30%, I still am not losing money." The premium was rich precisely because the market was pricing the possibility of a violent upward move, and he was reading that richness as free money rather than as a warning. The two reasons he gives for concentrating there are worth quoting because they are exactly the two reasons that make such positions attractive to everyone who blows up in them: "One, I know the supply would go down in the long run. And number two, the premium is so good."

So he sold, heavily, mostly naked calls and some naked puts, across both VXX and UVXY. "I made a lot of money. I'm talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars." And with the profits came the complacency he names explicitly: "Because I made so quick and so much money on this, I became very complacent."

Then the market crashed and VIX surged. And here he makes the observation that anyone who has watched a volatility event will recognise: "VIX, they don't surge like just one day. They spike one day, and next day spike on top, and the next day they spike on top. They did it several days in a row."

The arithmetic of the destruction is straightforward once the mechanics are understood. The VIX future went from around $14 to around $30 — more than double — in a matter of days. UVXY, moving at twice the rate of the future, went up roughly four times over the same period. He had sold calls with a thirty percent buffer, and in some cases had felt fifty percent was generous. "Because now the price has shot up by three times, four times. And because I sold naked calls, I have no protection at all. And guess how much I lost? A lot. Because there's no protection. I did not buy insurance there. I just sold naked calls. And then, you know, 30% definitely not enough. Even 100% is not enough. It hit like 200, 300% — maybe that's enough."

The result, stated plainly: "Within a matter of a few days, I think within a week, all the profits that I made during the year were completely wiped out."

The anecdote he attaches to it is the human detail that makes the lesson stick. He was playing tennis. He checked the pre-market, saw VIX, and thought, "my God — then what could I do?" UVXY does not trade in those pre-market hours, so there was no action available to him. He continued his tennis game. When he finished, around half past ten, he checked the account. "All the profit is almost gone."

There are three distinct failures layered inside this single story, and it is worth separating them because they are independently avoidable.

The first is a failure of instrument understanding. He knew UVXY decayed. He did not adequately model what happened to it in the tail — that a doubling of the VIX future produced a quadrupling of UVXY, and that the very structure guaranteeing long-run decay also guaranteed short-run explosive upside. A product cannot decay towards zero over a decade *unless* it periodically explodes upward; the decay and the spike are two faces of the same construction.

The second is a failure of position structure. Naked short calls have unbounded loss. A vertical spread — buying a cheap far-out-of-the-money call against each short call — would have converted an unbounded catastrophe into a defined, survivable loss, at the cost of a portion of the premium. He did not buy the reinsurance. In his own words, applying his own insurance-company analogy against himself: "I did not have the proper risk management, which is a reinsurance."

The third is a failure of timing and adjustment. The position was not monitored in a way that permitted intervention, and by the time intervention was possible the move had already happened.

His summary of the lesson: "You need to understand the risk profile of any trade. And you need to make the adjustment on time. In this case, I did not understand what could go wrong with the trade. I did not have the proper risk management. So that's the learning. And it's a very costly mistake."

### Rule One: Be Disciplined

The rules of psychology and risk management now follow, numbered, and the first is the foundation for all the rest.

"Rule number one: be disciplined. There is simply no strategy that can guarantee a 100% winning rate. No strategy. There's no free lunch there. There are always pros and cons."

He immediately gives the mechanism behind the claim, which is more useful than the claim itself. Every option structure trades one desirable property for another. "If you want unlimited profit, buying a call, you will potentially lose your premium. If you want to have extra buffer, guess what, you have a smaller profit and you could still have some risk as well." There is no arrangement of strikes and expirations that produces high probability, high reward, and low risk simultaneously; the market prices these against one another, and every structure is a specific point on the same trade-off surface. The chapters on jade lizards, iron condors, diagonals and calendars are, from this vantage, a catalogue of different points on that surface rather than a ladder of increasingly good ideas.

The consequence is unavoidable: "No matter what strategy you use, and no matter how long you have been a master of a certain strategy — you thought you were invincible — guess what, there's no guarantee that you win 100% of the time. Therefore there will be losing trades, and sometimes many days in a row, many losing trades in a row. And that is part of the long-term winning plan."

That last phrase is the pivot of the whole psychology lesson. Losing trades are not the failure of the plan. They are a component of the plan. The plan is a distribution of outcomes, and the losing tail is a scheduled, budgeted, expected part of that distribution. A trader who has internalised this reacts to a loss by checking whether the loss was within the pre-defined size; a trader who has not reacts by questioning the method itself, usually at the worst possible moment.

From this follows the concrete instruction: "Well-define how much you can afford to lose. Once you have the contingency plan or you have the adjustment rule, you have the exit plan, you have all the criteria you set for yourself — please stick to it."

And then, with unusual candour, the acknowledgement that this is the hard part: "Now, I know it's easier said than done. But you will see yourself in a situation where you will keep asking yourself: what if I just hold on to it for a little while? What if I just wait for another day? What if I just wait to see how the market behaves before I make the adjustment?"

Those three questions are, in his experience, the exact linguistic form that indiscipline takes. They do not arrive announced as "I am about to break my rules." They arrive dressed as prudence, as patience, as sensible information-gathering. The instruction is blunt: "Don't let your emotion or ego or your hope make you hold on to a losing trade. That could potentially ruin your hard-earned money."

His formulation of the underlying principle deserves to be quoted exactly because it inverts the way most beginners think about trading: "Consistent profit does not come from being right all the time. You can be right, you can be wrong, you can be wrong, you can be wrong — as long as you are disciplined. If you lose, you lose a pre-defined, acceptable, affordable amount of money. You need to play with the probability and you need to play with the theta that works for you. You have to accept that there will be days where you lose money. And that's fine. That's part of the long-term winning plan."

### Rule Two: Adjust and Cut Loss on Time

The second rule addresses what happens after the discipline has been tested and the market has moved.

"You need to adjust your trade and you need to cut loss timely. No matter how much profit you have made, you will be wrong in any trade. Please stay with your rule. Don't screw up mentally and financially."

Then the single most dangerous behaviour a losing trader can exhibit, named directly: "The moment you lose, you could start making revenge trades. Revenge trade is like double down or double up — very emotional, very irrational trades, and that could be a perfect setup for a disaster. Don't do it. Be calm, be disciplined and stay with your game plan."

Revenge trading deserves dwelling on because it is the mechanism by which a manageable loss becomes an account-ending loss. The psychology is transparent: having lost money, the trader wants the money *back*, wants it back quickly, and wants it back from the same instrument that took it. The natural expression of that want is a larger position than the rules permit, in the same direction as the losing view, entered without the usual entry criteria being satisfied. Every risk control the trader has built is violated in a single order, and it is violated at the precise moment when his judgment is least reliable. The countermeasure is not willpower; it is a pre-committed rule that no new position may be opened on the same underlying, in the same direction, immediately after a loss on it, and that position size is set by the account rules rather than by how the last trade went.

The second half of rule two concerns the seduction of the imminent reversal. "Even if you know the market has gone up so much or dropped so much, there will be a bounce or there will be a reverse — please cut loss, please. Don't hope on it, because who knows how long the market can continue to move one way or the other. There's no woulda, shoulda, coulda. We just have to stick to the rule and move on. Cut loss, or just de-risk — remove the risk from your trade."

Note the two acceptable actions in that sentence. Cutting the loss is one. De-risking — restructuring the position so the remaining exposure is bounded, which is what all the adjustment techniques earlier in the course exist for — is the other. What is not on the menu is holding an unbounded losing position on the theory that it is "due" for a reversal.

### Protecting Capital: The Arithmetic of Drawdown

Rule two leads into the most quantitatively persuasive passage of the lesson, and one that every trader should be able to reproduce from memory.

"Rule number one: protect your capital. And what is rule number two? Well, very simple — remember rule number one. You need to protect your capital, because if you lose your capital, no matter how much return on investment you make, it won't translate into any profit at all. That is rule number one and number two and even number three."

Then the arithmetic, which he gives in three steps:

| Loss taken | Remaining capital (from a base of 100) | Gain required on the remaining capital to get back to 100 |
|---|---|---|
| 10% | 90 | **11%** |
| 25% | 75 | **33%** |
| 50% | 50 | **100%** |

The relationship is not linear and that is the entire point. A ten percent loss requires an eleven percent gain — barely more than the loss itself, and easily recovered inside a normal quarter. A twenty-five percent loss requires a thirty-three percent gain, which is a demanding year for most strategies. A fifty percent loss requires a doubling of what remains simply to return to the starting line, and a doubling is not something any honest trader can promise on demand.

His conclusion: "The more you let your loss snowball, the larger the profits you need to make to recover your capital. So cut loss early. The first loss is the best loss. The smaller one and the early loss is the best. Don't let the loss snowball and become a big drawdown in your account. It's very difficult to recover the capital if you lose a lot."

Combine this table with the earlier observation about the pink line — that an early exit from an option position does not incur the maximum loss because time value remains — and the case for cutting early becomes overwhelming from both directions at once. Early exits cost less in absolute terms because of the option's remaining extrinsic value, *and* the losses they avoid are exactly the ones that require disproportionate gains to recover. Waiting is expensive twice over.

### Costly Mistake Number Two: Knowing the Rule and Ignoring It

The second confession is, in one sense, worse than the first, because in the first he did not know what could go wrong, whereas in the second he knew exactly and did it anyway. "This is the mistake where, yes, I know the rule, but I did not adjust or did not cut loss on time."

The setting is late 2016 into early 2017, around the United States presidential election. Trump won. The market initially sold off sharply and then recovered with remarkable speed, after which it simply rallied, day after day.

His reaction was not an analytical one, and he identifies it as such: "I told myself, hey, how could Trump be a good thing for the world? That's my bias, that's my judgment. And I said, no way the market can continue to go up. It's a fake rally. That's what I said to myself. I told my friends as well: no way, the market just rallied because somebody was short covering, and then it has to die down. There's no way it will go up."

At that moment he was holding a large number of iron condors on SPX. The structure of an iron condor makes the exposure clear. Selling a bull put spread below the market and a bear call spread above it produces maximum profit when the underlying goes nowhere, and the maximum loss on either wing is substantially larger than the maximum gain on the whole position. As he puts it: "The best market condition for those trades is when the market goes sideways. If it goes one way or the other, I lose the max loss. And the max loss is much higher than the max gain in that particular trade. So I have a high probability of winning, but if the market moves so strongly one way or the other, I could lose a lot of money."

The market rallied and kept rallying. "I kept telling myself, no way. It already went up so much so fast. It has to drop. It has to correct." And the internal monologue produced exactly the sentence pattern he had warned about in rule one: "My emotion kicked in and urged me — hey, what if I just hold on to my trade for another day, maybe a few more days? There must be a correction. There must be a trend reversal. There's no way for it to continue to go up like this forever." His own verdict: "Guess what? I was completely wrong, and the market continued to go up no matter how much I wished it not."

Now comes the part of the story that is numerically precise, and it is the most instructive delta-management narrative in the entire course.

His rule was explicit. He entered the short strikes at a delta of 10. His adjustment trigger was a fifteen-point increase in that delta — "if it goes up by 15 points, that means at a delta of 25, I need to adjust."

| Short strike delta | Rule status | Action actually taken |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | Entry level | Position opened |
| 25 | **Adjustment trigger — the rule says act now** | Nothing |
| 35 | Well past the trigger | Nothing |
| 40 | Far past the trigger | Nothing |
| 50 | At the money; "that's when my emotion came in" | Nothing — "I kept telling myself it will go down" |
| 70 | Deep in the money | Nothing |
| 80 | Approaching maximum loss | Nothing |

"By the time it hit 80, I almost hit the max loss. So I let it go. So many trades at that point in time on iron condors, I just lost the max loss, which is significant."

Consider what the delta ladder represents. Delta on a short option approximates the probability of that option finishing in the money. At entry, delta 10 meant roughly a ninety percent chance of the strike expiring worthless. At delta 25 — the point at which his own rule demanded action — the odds had shifted to roughly three in four, still favourable but materially degraded, and the rule existed precisely to force action while the position could still be repaired cheaply by rolling, by closing the threatened wing, or by taking a small defined loss. At delta 50 the position was a coin flip. At delta 80 the market was telling him, with as much clarity as a market ever manages, that the outcome had been decided. Every rung of that ladder was a moment at which the loss could have been taken at a fraction of the maximum, and at every rung he substituted a forecast for a rule.

"I lost all the money that I made for several months, just during that period of time."

His stated lesson is a single word repeated three times, followed by a principle: "You need to be disciplined. Discipline, discipline, discipline. Discipline trumps conviction. Cut loss early, because that is cheaper. Even if you cut loss and the market reverses — move on. No woulda, shoulda, coulda, and no regrets. Just move on, as blindly as possible."

The phrase "discipline trumps conviction" is the compressed form of the whole lesson. Conviction is not worthless — it is what generates trade ideas in the first place — but when conviction and the adjustment rule disagree, the rule wins, every time, without debate. And the clause "even if you cut loss and the market reverses" is the hard part to swallow. A trader who cuts at delta 25 and then watches the market turn around will feel foolish and will be tempted to conclude that the rule cost him money. It did, on that one occasion. Across the distribution of occasions, it is the only reason he still has an account to trade.

### Rule Three: Position Sizing and Diversification

The third rule moves from the psychology of the individual trade to the architecture of the portfolio, and it carries the most important numeric threshold in the entire course.

"When you manage your risk, you need to have the right position sizing and diversification as well. You have one account. Don't max out your account capacity."

The threshold, given first in approximate form and later stated precisely in the business-building lesson: **leave roughly half of the account, or at minimum thirty percent of it, unused as margin buffer.** In his words here: "Often leave like half of the account, or 30%, for the margin to move, because when the market moves against you, the margin often goes up and you need this buffer to navigate through the tough time."

The reasoning behind this rule is one that trips up traders who have only ever thought about maximum loss. Margin requirement is not a fixed number set at trade entry. It is recalculated continuously by the broker, and it expands when the market moves against a position and when implied volatility rises. A trader who deploys ninety percent of his capital on the day he opens his positions has not merely left himself no room for new opportunities; he has left himself no room for his *existing* positions to require more collateral, which is exactly what they will do in the conditions where he most needs to remain in control. The buffer is not idle capital. It is the thing that prevents the broker from making his decisions for him.

The second half of rule three is diversification, and he specifies the dimensions along which it should occur: "Do have a diversified portfolio with several strategies, several securities, some long, some short, some directional, some non-directional, some commodity, some stocks, and ETFs, those kinds of things. Because that will help you have a more balanced portfolio and then you will minimise the chance of getting a big perfect storm in one day that could draw down your account significantly."

Read that list carefully, because it is a correlation rule stated in plain language rather than in statistics. Diversification across five *tickers* is worthless if all five positions are short puts on large-cap technology stocks, because on the day the market falls, all five lose together. Genuine diversification requires variation along multiple axes simultaneously: across underlyings, across asset classes (equities, ETFs, commodities, currencies), across directional stance (some bullish, some bearish, some neutral), and across strategy type (some directional, some non-directional). The phrase "perfect storm in one day" is the failure mode being guarded against — the day when every position in the book turns out to have been the same bet wearing different clothes.

#### Costly Mistake Number Three: Maxing Out the Account

The first of the two mistakes attached to rule three is about size.

"I over-traded many years ago. At times, I was so keen on certain trades, I was so overconfident that I could make money from those trades. So if you look at my portfolio statement at a point in time, I often maxed out my account capacity."

The consequence arrived in the form he had failed to anticipate — not a maximum loss on any single trade, but a margin call. "When the market moved against me, and it coupled with the implied volatility increasing, my account went into margin calls. The broker sent me some notification and reached out to me on the chat as well. They said I need to top up or they will force me to close some of the positions."

Note the compounding: the market moved against him *and* implied volatility rose. Those two things happen together, which is precisely the problem. A short-premium book takes a directional hit and a vega hit at the same moment, and the margin requirement expands on both counts, all while the account equity is falling. The buffer requirement exists because these three forces arrive as one event.

What follows is the operational nightmare that anyone who has been through it will recognise: "Normally when they close my positions, they're done at the market price. So I don't want that. I have to take action. So often I have to liquidate my positions at losses, because at the wrong time."

This is the essential point about forced liquidation, and it is why the buffer matters more than any other single number in the chapter. When a broker liquidates, it does so mechanically, at market, at whatever the bid-ask happens to be, in whatever order its risk engine prefers, at the single worst moment in the market's recent history. The trader loses not only money but agency — the ability to choose which positions to close, in what order, and at what price. And in the instructor's case, the anticipation of that outcome forced him to liquidate himself, on the same bad day, in order to avoid something worse.

His prescription is explicit: "Do not over-trade. Do not over-leverage. **Ideally just trade a maximum of 50% or 70% of your account capacity.** Leave the remainder for margin to increase, or sometimes just leave the cash there, because there will be some better opportunities that the market just offers you and you need to have enough margin to buy."

And then a sentence that reframes the buffer from defensive necessity to offensive asset: "The worst feeling that I have is, man, I maxed out my capacity, and now the market is offering me very good premium and I have no more capacity to trade. Don't do it. You have to leave some room in your account for a better opportunity."

That is a genuinely important reframing. A fully deployed account is not merely fragile; it is also blind. The best premium-selling opportunities appear exactly when volatility spikes — which is exactly when a maxed-out account is under margin pressure and cannot act. The trader with dry powder gets to be a buyer of opportunity in the moment when everyone else is a forced seller. This is, again, the insurance company analogy: the reserve capital is not dead weight, it is what allows the underwriter to write business at the best prices in the cycle.

#### Costly Mistake Number Four: All the Eggs in One Barrel

The second mistake attached to rule three is about concentration, and the story takes place in 2015 and 2016.

"I was trading a lot on oil futures, /CL. The strategies that I used were iron condors and strangles."

He pauses to define the strangle for students who have not met it, and the definition matters because it explains the risk: "Strangle basically, you sell a naked call and you sell a naked put out of the money without protection. So I don't have protections on both sides. I just sell naked call, naked put very far away from the current market price, have a high probability of winning. But if the price moves a lot, I can lose a lot of money."

Then the market. Over 2015 into 2016, oil fell from around the $60 level down to a bottom near $26 — a decline of well over half the price of the commodity. He places the low precisely in memory: "I think that was during the Chinese New Year 2016. I still remember that time."

The damage was not caused by any single bad trade. It was caused by the shape of the book. "My account was so concentrated on these two strategies and on oil, and when the market moved against me, it was a perfect storm that happened to me, and I suffered significant losses during that time."

Look at what "concentrated" meant here. Two strategies — iron condors and strangles — both of which are short-premium, both of which are non-directional, both of which lose when the underlying makes a large move in either direction, both of which are short volatility. And one underlying. When oil began its sustained collapse, every position in the account was the same position. The iron condors and the strangles did not diversify each other; they were correlated by construction. The high probability of winning on each individual trade was irrelevant, because the trades were not independent draws — they were one draw, repeated.

His lesson: "Please diversify your portfolio with several strategies and securities to avoid big drawdown days like the one I experienced."

### Rule Four: Be Patient

The fourth rule is about entry timing, and it rests on the volatility principle established throughout the course.

"Be patient. Wait for the right time to buy or sell options. When I say the right time, you have to stick to the rule: **buy when IV is low and sell when IV is high.** So you look at the IV percentile. If it's high, then it could be the right time to sell. If it's low, it could be the right time to buy."

Then the instruction that is hardest for an eager new trader to follow, and which he states as a positive action rather than an absence: **"Do nothing. It's still better than you do something that is not right."**

The cost of ignoring this is specific and it is a volatility cost rather than a directional one: "If I sell an option when IV is so low, and when IV spikes, I could lose a lot of money just from the vega, from the IV alone."

That is a point worth restating for emphasis. A short-premium trader who sells into low implied volatility is not merely collecting an inadequate premium; he is establishing a position with negative vega at the point in the volatility cycle where vega can only hurt him. The underlying can go absolutely nowhere — the directional thesis can be perfectly correct — and the position can still be deeply underwater purely because implied volatility rose from a low base. Selling premium is a business in which the entry price is the product, and low IV means the product is being sold below cost.

### Rule Five: Avoid Trading Through Key Events

The fifth rule identifies the specific occasions on which the probabilities the platform displays cease to be reliable.

"Avoid trading through key events. Those are the events that can move the price a lot."

His examples are drawn from the instruments he trades. "For example, if you trade oil, keep an eye on the OPEC meetings. Often they meet like twice a year — one in May or June, one in November or December. Those are the times when they could make some key decisions on oil production and it could be a big moving event for oil price." Beyond commodities: "Watch also for elections or referendums, the big ones that could also be movers or shakers in terms of affecting the market, or currencies, or commodities — especially when you sell options."

And then a sentence that belongs on the wall next to the risk tagline, because it addresses the real reason traders hold through events: **"The intent here is to make money, not to get excitement. We are in the business to make money, not in the entertainment business."**

This deserves unpacking, because the temptation to trade through an event is not usually framed by the trader as thrill-seeking. It is framed as opportunity — the premium is elevated before an event, sometimes dramatically, and the seller reasons that the elevated premium is compensation worth taking. Sometimes it is. But the elevated premium exists because the distribution of outcomes has genuinely widened, and the platform's probability numbers, which are derived from the current implied volatility surface, do not capture the binary, gap-risk character of an event outcome. The trader who sells into an event is not being paid extra for the same risk; he is being paid extra for a different and much fatter-tailed risk, and he must decide consciously whether he wants that business.

#### The Brexit Day: A Loss That Was Not Real

The instructor gives two event stories, and the first is unusual in that he did not lose money on it — which is exactly why it is instructive.

"On the Brexit day, I still remember, I think June 23, 2016, when the initial results from the Brexit referendum started to come out and people were so nervous. Oh my God, now the UK is going to separate from the European community. So a lot of uncertainty, a lot of headlines running around, and then people are so worried about the negative impact of the event."

He was at home, watching the market closely. What he observed was not a directional move but a structural one: "Certainly the uncertainty created a big liquidity collapse. Meaning, I look at the bid and the ask of any stocks or any securities, futures, gold, commodity, indexes, all the futures — certainly I see the bid and the ask widened significantly."

His explanation of *why* the spreads widened is the clearest short account of a liquidity event one could ask for: "Because the buyers don't want to pay a high price, because they don't know what's going to happen, and the sellers don't want to sell low, because they don't know what's going on, and therefore most of them just withdrew the orders from the system. And the ones that kept the order inside the system often put very weird prices."

The consequence for his account was immediate and alarming: "I look at my account and suddenly I see big losses." But the losses were an artefact, not a fact. "It's just because of the midpoints of the bid and the ask also being distorted, or completely whacked — no longer reflecting the true value of the assets anymore."

This is a genuinely important practical lesson for anyone trading multi-leg option positions. A position's marked value is calculated from the midpoint of the bid-ask spread on each leg. When liquidity evaporates and spreads blow out, the midpoint stops being an estimate of fair value and becomes an artefact of whichever stray orders happen to remain in the book. A four-legged iron condor has four such midpoints, each capable of being distorted, and the errors compound. The account statement can show a catastrophic loss on positions whose actual economics are unchanged.

His response was the correct one, and it required exactly the emotional control the lesson has been teaching: "Upon analysing it, I realised that, oh, this is a temporary loss only, because it's just driven by a lack of liquidity. So I just waited for the market to calm down and liquidity came back and then everything became settled. I still managed to make some adjustments after that. I did not lose money, so that's a good thing."

Consider the counterfactual. A trader who had panicked at the displayed loss and closed positions during the liquidity collapse would have transacted *against* those distorted prices — crossing enormous spreads, in size, in a market with no depth — and would have converted a phantom loss into a very real one. The discipline that saved him was the discipline to distinguish between a marked loss and an economic loss, and to know which market conditions produce the former without the latter.

#### The OPEC Meeting: A Loss That Was Entirely Real

The second event story ends differently. "The other event that happened at this time hurt my account significantly."

The setting is the end of 2016 — "November, December time" — and he prefaces it with a wry aside about that year: "again, that year was bad for me." OPEC met in Vienna. Before the meeting, Saudi Arabia had reached an agreement with Russia to cut oil production, and the oil price had already risen on that news. Then, at the meeting itself, "for the first time ever, all the OPEC members agreed to cut volume. And that caused about a 20% surge in oil price in a matter of a few days."

His reasoning for holding through the event was based on a track record, and the reasoning was not stupid: "I did not anticipate these guys' move, because OPEC has met many times. And they keep talking and no action at all. There has never been any follow-up or a system that can track the production from each of the OPEC members. So as a result, all OPEC members keep producing more than the quota."

That is a genuine, evidence-based prior. OPEC had a long history of announcing cuts that never materialised because there was no enforcement mechanism. What changed was precisely the thing his prior did not cover: "But this time, first time ever, they came out with the mechanism on how to track, and they also agreed on the production cut. All the oil traders got caught by surprise and the oil price spiked by 20%."

And here is the subtle and important part of the story, the part that distinguishes a directional loss from a volatility loss. His book was non-directional and short volatility, and he was holding through the event specifically to harvest the post-event volatility crush: "I did a lot of non-directional trades and I was so confident to keep the trades through the event, because I was hoping that after the event nothing is going to happen and the volatility will collapse and then I will benefit from my trade. Unfortunately, yes, volatility collapsed, but the price movement had significantly moved against me, so that hurt me a lot. It was a very bad month for me during that time."

Read that carefully. He was right about the volatility. Implied volatility did collapse after the meeting, exactly as he expected. And it did not save him, because the twenty percent price move blew through the strikes of his non-directional positions, and the gamma loss overwhelmed the vega gain. This is the specific trap of holding short-premium positions through binary events: the IV crush is real and is the reason people do it, but the IV crush is a small, bounded gain, while the price gap it accompanies is an unbounded loss. The trade is a bad one not because the volatility thesis is wrong but because the volatility thesis is the smaller of the two forces at work.

His generalisation extends the rule from commodities to equities: "So when you trade equities, for example, there will be certain strategies to trade earnings — for the rest of the strategies, it is advisable not to trade through the earnings event." That is a precise and correctly hedged statement. The course does contain a dedicated earnings strategy — the Earnings Probability Spread — which is *designed* around the event and prices the binary risk deliberately. Every other strategy in the course is not, and should be flat or reduced across the announcement.

### Rule Six: Trade the Math

The sixth rule is the shortest and the most mechanical, and it is the direct antidote to the SPX iron condor disaster.

"Please trade the math. Don't trade with your emotion or your rationale. Trade the market as robotic as possible. Only trade with what is in front of you, not what you or even anybody else think the market will do. Just look at the parameters, the numbers, the math. Delta hits a certain point — adjust. Or if the price drops, I hit the max loss threshold — move. Don't wait. Please take action as robotic as possible."

The word "rationale" in that opening sentence is doing important work and is easy to skim past. He is not only warning against emotion — against fear and greed and hope. He is warning against *reasoning*: against the narrative the trader constructs to explain why the delta at 40 does not really mean what the rule says it means. "How could Trump be good for the world?" was not an emotion. It was a rationale. It was an argument, with premises and a conclusion, and it was wrong, and it cost him several months of profits. The rule is that at the moment of decision, the delta reading outranks the argument.

And then the deliberately paradoxical instruction that closes the rule: **"Don't listen to other people, including yourself. Stick with the rule that you have before you enter the trade."**

"Including yourself" is the entire psychology curriculum in two words. The self that formulated the rule — calm, unpositioned, thinking about the distribution of outcomes — is a better analyst than the self that must apply the rule while holding a losing position. The rule is a message from the competent self to the compromised one, and the compromised self does not get a vote on whether to open it.

### Rule Seven: Assume the Worst Case

The seventh and final rule is a single line, and it is the natural conclusion of everything before it: "If you must speculate, please assume the worst case. Never assume the best case. **Plan for the worst and hope for the best.** That's what I do."

Notice the conditional at the front — "if you must speculate." Speculation is not forbidden. Later, in the portfolio-construction lesson, he will deliberately include a low-probability speculative position on CVS with a thirty-seven percent chance of profit, sized so that being wrong costs $876 against a $10,000 account. Speculation is permitted; unbounded, unplanned, best-case-assuming speculation is not. The difference between the two is whether the worst case was computed before the order was sent.

### The Watch-Out That Is Not Psychology: Commissions and Fees

The instructor closes the psychology lesson with something he explicitly flags as belonging to a different category: "This has nothing to do with psychology or risk management, but it's an equally important watch-out I need to share with you. Commissions and fees matter."

The scale of the problem grows with activity, which is precisely the trap for a trader who has just been told to trade small and trade often: "If you trade a lot like I do, especially multiple accounts, multiple trades per account, commissions and fees will add up a lot. It could be a significant cost and it can reduce your return on investment substantially if you don't watch it. You need to track them very closely, and call your broker or chat with them to clarify when you see something weird."

#### The Hidden Fee Story

His own experience: "One of my accounts got charged hefty fees. I got to know about it only at the end of the year, and we're talking about thousands of dollars of fees. And that one hit me a lot."

The cause was specific to the instrument class and the broker. "I traded a lot of commodity futures like oil or natural gas and stuff like that. On Interactive Brokers, they do charge some — what they call it — exposure fee, if you trade a big position on those commodities. And sometimes they charge you something they call overnight exposure, something like that. And it adds up a lot. So you need to watch that. I did not know it."

His comparison of the two brokers on this dimension is direct: "Now, thinkorswim, they are much cleaner on the fees they charge. There's no hidden charge. But Interactive Brokers, you need to watch. They do have some hidden fees there."

The failure here is not a trading failure at all — it is a bookkeeping failure, and it went undetected for a full year. That is what makes it worth including in a chapter about running trading as a business. A business that does not reconcile its costs monthly does not know its own margin.

#### The Commission Rule of Thumb

The actionable rule that follows is a clean, checkable threshold, and it is one of the most useful single numbers in the course for a small account.

"Avoid trading securities with low prices or low premiums. If you trade options on a penny stock, like $4, $5 stocks, the premium you get maybe a few cents, or ten cents, or twenty cents — it may not be worth the commission you pay. Don't trade those. **My rule of thumb is, in any trade, if the commission is more than 5% or 6% of your total max gain, don't trade it.**"

He notes that students routinely bring him trades that fail this test badly: "Some of you show me trades where the total commission could be 12, 15 or 20% of your max gain. What's the point? Keep the commissions a low percentage of your max gain."

This threshold quietly disqualifies whole categories of trade for a small account, and it does so for sound reasons. A four-legged iron condor on a cheap underlying, collecting fifteen dollars of premium against fourteen dollars of commission, is not a trade; it is a donation to the broker with a lottery ticket attached. The rule forces the trader upward in premium size, which in turn forces him toward liquid, appropriately priced underlyings — which is where he should be trading anyway. Applied to the portfolio he builds in the next lesson, the rule is comfortably satisfied: the oil iron condor collects $150 of maximum profit against about $14 of commission, which is roughly nine to ten percent — above his stated threshold, and worth noting honestly, though he does not flag it himself in the lesson.

Finally, on negotiating: "In my case, I also negotiate my own commission with TOS. Of course, as a new trader you may not be able to negotiate with them, but I've been trading with them for so many years, and with high volume, I have been able to negotiate with them for a much better commission." In the business-building lesson he quantifies this: he has renegotiated successfully **four times**, and the broker told him he has a very low rate compared with other traders in Singapore — in fact, lower than what he gets from Interactive Brokers. The last time he called, they could not go lower. He mentions that a bonus lesson covers the negotiation technique itself.

---

# Part XV — Choosing the Right Strategy, Assignment & Rolling

## Choosing the Right Strategy, Options Assignment, and Rolling Options

### Part One — When To Use Each Strategy: The Capstone Decision Framework

#### The problem this lesson exists to solve

By the time a student reaches this point in the course, the raw inventory of strategies has grown to roughly fifteen distinct constructions, and Adam opens the summary lesson by naming the emotional consequence of that inventory rather than the intellectual one. "By now you should have learned quite a lot of strategies on options trading," he says, "and some of you may be very overwhelmed or even like confused, or not know exactly when to use what strategies. So the intent of this lesson is just to sum it all up for you." That framing matters, because it tells you what kind of lesson this is. It is not a lesson that adds anything new. Every strategy discussed here has already been built leg by leg, priced, analysed and traded live in an earlier module. What this lesson adds is *selection* — the discipline of standing in front of a chart with a full toolbox and knowing, without deliberating for an hour, which single tool belongs in your hand.

The failure mode he is defending against is a real one and worth naming precisely. A trader who knows fifteen strategies but has no selection framework does not behave like a trader who knows fifteen strategies. He behaves like a trader who knows one — the last one he learned, or the one that worked most recently, or the one whose profit-and-loss diagram he finds most emotionally pleasant — and he applies it to every market condition he meets. That is worse than knowing three strategies well, because it produces confident misapplication. The iron condor trader who puts on an iron condor in front of an earnings release, the bull call spread buyer who buys premium when implied volatility is already at the ninetieth percentile, the covered call writer who sells calls into a collapsing stock — each of these traders knows the mechanics of his strategy perfectly. What he lacks is the two-question filter that would have told him this was the wrong week for it.

So Adam begins by taking inventory.
