From the basic course: buying a call outright; buying a put outright; buying a put to protect stock you already own against a crash; selling a cash-secured put to generate income or to acquire a good stock at a discount; and the two vertical debit spreads — buying a call and selling a further call against it to reduce the cost of the long option, and its mirror image on the downside, buying a put and selling a lower put to cut the cost of the long put. From the advanced course: the bear call spread; the bull put spread; the iron condor, which he describes as "completely non-directional"; the earnings probability spread for playing earnings releases; the diagonal spread, which he characterises as "similar to selling covered call but at a much less capital"; the calendar spread, which can be constructed to play one direction, no direction, or, remarkably, both directions at once; the synthetic spread, used "to replicate our owning shares or shorting shares"; and finally the protective bullet synthetic spread, which he calls the boom-bang strategy, used "to construct a bullish trade with a limited risk and very low cost at the same time."

That is the toolbox. Fifteen constructions, each with its own capital requirement, its own margin treatment, its own risk profile, its own ideal volatility environment. The rest of the lesson is about reducing that complexity to a decision you can make in thirty seconds.

#### The two questions that come before everything else

"Before we get to know when to use what," Adam says, "you need to ask yourself two key questions." Everything in the framework hangs off these two questions, and it is worth understanding why exactly two, and why these two.

**The first question is directional: are you bullish, bearish, or completely neutral on the stock price?** This defines whether you are taking a bullish trade, a bearish trade, or a neutral trade. Adam is explicit that there are three market directions here and that you must define your view for yourself before anything else happens. This is not a formality. A great many losing options trades are losing not because the strategy was badly constructed but because the trader never actually formed a directional view, put on a structure whose profit zone lay somewhere he had no opinion about, and then discovered his opinion only when the position started losing money. Forming the view first, explicitly, in words, is what allows the structure to be chosen to fit the view rather than the view to be retrofitted to the structure.

**The second question is about implied volatility: is IV high or low?** Adam gives a specific numerical threshold, and it is one of the few hard numbers in the entire framework. "The general rule of thumb is if it's more than 50 percent or 40 percent and above, it considers as high. Below 40, it's low." He is referring to the implied volatility percentile — the reading that tells you where current implied volatility sits relative to its own history for that underlying, not the absolute IV number itself. A stock with a 25 percent absolute implied volatility can be at a very high IV percentile if its own normal range is 15 to 20 percent; a stock with 60 percent absolute IV can be at a low percentile if it habitually trades at 80. The percentile is the meaningful reading because options are priced relative to their own history, and the question you are asking is whether today's premium is expensive or cheap by that stock's own standards.

And then the rule that follows from the reading, stated as simply as it can be stated: **"When IV is high, it's better to sell. And when IV is low, it's better to buy because you pay lower price."** That is the entire volatility half of the framework in one sentence. High implied volatility means option premium is rich, which means you want to be the party collecting premium — the seller. Low implied volatility means option premium is cheap, which means if you need to own an option you are buying it at a favourable price, and the strategies that require you to be net long premium become viable.

Adam is careful about what this framework does and does not promise. "If you know the direction of the trade and also the implied volatility situation, you can use the proper strategies to make money for you. And that's just increase the probability of you winning the trade." The claim is probabilistic, not deterministic. Correct strategy selection does not make a trade a winner. It removes the self-inflicted handicap of trading a structure that was fighting the volatility environment or pointing in a direction you did not actually believe in. That handicap, removed, shows up as a higher win rate over many trades — nothing more, and nothing less.

#### The four-quadrant map

Having established the two questions, Adam builds the visual device that organises the entire lesson: a four-quadrant chart. The horizontal axis runs from bearish on the left, through neutral in the middle, to bullish on the right. The vertical axis separates low IV at the bottom from high IV at the top. Every one of the fifteen strategies gets plotted somewhere on this grid.

The elegance of the device is that the two questions map onto the two axes, so answering the questions is literally the same act as locating yourself on the chart. Answer "mildly bullish" and "IV is low" and you have narrowed fifteen strategies down to the two or three that live in that region. What remains is a choice among close cousins, and that final choice is made on capital, margin, and how confident you are — not on direction or volatility, because those have already been spent.

What follows in the lesson is a walk through every strategy in turn, and for each one Adam does the same thing: he builds it live on the platform, pulls up the profit-and-loss analysis, reads the breakeven point off the chart, identifies the maximum profit and maximum loss, and from the shape of that curve *derives* where the strategy belongs on the grid. He never asserts a placement. He demonstrates it. That method is worth imitating, because it means that if you ever meet a strategy this course did not cover, you already know how to place it: build it, look at the profit curve, and ask where on the price axis the curve is above zero.

Nearly all of the demonstration uses SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, trading at approximately $283 per share on the day of recording, which is 6 June. The chart context matters for the trades he constructs: SPY has recently bounced off its 150-day moving average, which Adam describes as serving as "a very strong support level" — it had bounced there before and has now bounced a second time, and appears to be resuming its uptrend. Above the current price sits the 50-day moving average, which "could serve as a short-term resistance level." So the technical picture is a stock recovering off strong support with a plausible ceiling just overhead. That single setup is versatile enough to justify a bullish trade, a bearish trade, or a neutral trade depending on which feature of it you emphasise, which is exactly why he uses it for all the demonstrations.

#### The basic strategies, placed one at a time

##### Long call

The simplest possible bullish position, and the one Adam builds first. The entry rule for a straight long call is stated up front and is worth memorising: **choose two months or above days to expiration.** Before entering, he checks implied volatility: 26 percent, "which is low. It's a good time to buy here." That check is not decoration. Buying a naked long call is the purest possible expression of being long premium, so it is the strategy most punished by high implied volatility and most helped by low. Twenty-six percent passes the filter, so the trade is viable.

He selects the 71-days-to-expiration series and buys the 283 strike, at the money — noting that you can also choose slightly in the money — paying $7.40 per share, or $740 for the contract. He then pulls up the profit-and-loss analysis, isolating only the trade under study so no other position pollutes the chart.

What the chart shows is instructive. The zero line is breakeven; above it is profit, below it is loss. The blue line is the profit and loss at expiration; the pink line is the profit and loss as of the end of today, and can be dragged to any intermediate date. He drags it to 13 June, one week forward, to show how the curve migrates toward the expiration line as time passes.

The critical reading is the breakeven. With SPY at 283 and $7.40 of premium paid, the breakeven sits at "290-something" — the strike plus the premium. And the consequence, which Adam states bluntly, is this: "If the price stays right there until the expiration, you lose money. You lose some like 667." The stock can be exactly where you bought it, your directional view can be neither right nor wrong, and you have still lost $667 of your $740. That is the defining characteristic of the long call. It does not reward you for being right about direction. It rewards you only for being right about direction *by more than the premium you paid, within the time you allowed.*

"So apparently, you need a very strong price increase to make money. That means you are bullish on the stock." There is no limit on the upside — "you just make all the money when the SPY goes up" — but the position dies of time decay if the move does not come. It is therefore not a neutral trade and not a mildly bullish trade. **It is a strongly bullish trade, used when IV is low.**

##### Long put

The exact mirror image, built the same way. He buys the 283 at-the-money put and pulls the profit curve, which "looks the reverse of the long call, meaning if the price goes up, you lose money; if it goes down, you can make money." The breakeven is 275: the stock must fall from 283 all the way to 275 before the position turns profitable, and from there down to zero is all profit. If the stock does not move enough, you lose money; if it rises, you lose the maximum.

"So apparently there's a very [bearish trade] — it cannot be a neutral, it cannot be a bullish, it is a very [bearish]." **Strongly bearish, low IV.** The same logic that placed the long call places the long put: you are net long premium, you need a large directional move to overcome the premium paid, and you want to pay as little as possible for it, which means you want low implied volatility.

##### Covered call

Here the placement gets more interesting, because the covered call is the first strategy whose profit zone is genuinely wide.

The construction: buy 100 shares and simultaneously sell a call against them. If you already own the stock, you only need to sell the call — but Adam adds an important operational detail that traders new to this get wrong. The sale "has to be in the same platform so the system knows you are selling a call option against the stock that you're owning." If the broker cannot see the shares, it sees a naked short call, and it will margin you as though you had unlimited risk.

For the tenor, he goes shorter than he would for a long option: 34 days, expiring 10 July. And for the strike, the rule is the first out-of-the-money call — in this option series, the 285. He executes both legs as a single order by right-clicking and choosing the covered-stock order type, producing a two-leg ticket: leg one buys 100 shares of SPY, leg two sells one 285 call at 34 days. The net debit — the capital required to own the position — is **$28,000**. That number is the whole reason the diagonal spread exists, and it will return later.

The profit curve: breakeven at 280. So the stock can drop $3 from 283 and you still break even. If it stays exactly where it is, you make $500. If it rises through the strike, you hit maximum profit of $484.

Read the shape of that. "So apparently it's a bullish trade because I want the stock price to go up, or even neutral because if I stay right here, I can make the same profit. Or even if it goes slightly lower, about $3, I would still be profitable." The covered call makes money if the stock rises, if the stock does nothing, and if the stock falls modestly. It only loses if the stock falls meaningfully. So it sits **in the bullish quadrant but reaching left toward neutral and even slightly bearish** — a strategy for a mildly bullish view rather than a strongly bullish one, since the short call caps the upside at $484 no matter how far the stock runs.

And the volatility preference is stated explicitly: "Ideally if you can sell covered call when IV is high, it's better." Adam is using SPY at 26 percent IV for illustration only; in live trading, the covered call belongs in the **high-IV** half of the grid, because the entire economics of the trade come from the premium you collect on the short call, and that premium is larger when implied volatility is elevated.

##### Protective put

"The protective put is simple. You own the share and you want to protect the share from losing money if the stock price drops a lot." You are buying insurance. The motivation is worry about downside, so the option purchase itself is a bearish expression — you are buying a put because you fear a decline — even though the overall position, shares plus put, remains long the stock. Adam places it accordingly: the option leg is the bearish expression, purchased for protection rather than for profit.

##### Cash-secured put

The cash-secured put is where the framework starts to show its subtlety, because this is a strategy whose directional label depends entirely on what you intend to do if you are wrong.

The mechanics: you sell a put and hold enough cash to take delivery of the shares if the stock falls to the strike. Adam builds it on SPY at the same 34-day expiration. His reasoning is explicitly technical: "Now if the price is already at 282, I say, next time when it hits again to 275 here, it will bounce again." So he sells the 275 put — a strike he chose because the chart says it is support, not because it produced a particular delta or premium. And then the crucial sentence about intent: "It hits that level, I believe it will bounce, but it doesn't. Guess what? I'm willing to own SPY at 275 level, which is about $7 cheaper than, or $8 cheaper than the current price."

The profit curve: maximum profit of about **$331** if the stock stays at or above the 275 strike through expiration, and a breakeven at **272** — "which is more than $10 from here." Below 272 the position starts losing.

Now the placement argument, and it is a genuinely careful one. "So probably it's a bullish because I make all the money on the upside. Or slightly bearish, that's fine. It cannot be [strongly] bearish. [If] it's too much bearish, then I could potentially lose money if I'm not ready to take the share. But if my thesis is I'm willing to take the share, then it's fine." The summary line is one of the best in the lesson: **"So in this case, basically you are bullish, but in case you are wrong, you would still make money as long as you are not too wrong."**

That phrase — *you still make money as long as you are not too wrong* — is the defining property of every premium-selling strategy in the course, and it is why premium selling has a higher win rate than premium buying. The long call requires you to be right. The cash-secured put requires only that you not be badly wrong. Those are very different bars.

Placement: **bullish, extending into neutral and slightly bearish. High IV preferred**, because you are selling premium and want it to be rich.

##### Bull call spread

The bull call spread is the long call with the cost problem solved, and the placement follows directly from that.

Adam builds it on the same SPY setup. He buys the 283 at-the-money call, then looks at the chart for the resistance level: "I look at the short-term resistant level. I say, maybe we would have some resistance at 287." So he sells the 287 call. The economics of that single decision are dramatic: "So instead of paying $5 plus, now I'm paying only $2, which is less than half of my cost."

The profit curve: breakeven at 285 — the long strike plus the $2 net debit. "If the price goes up just $2, which is a net debit I pay here, then I break even. Beyond that, I will make money. If it goes all the way beyond the 287, I will make the max profit, which is $200, almost $200 there. And then if it drops, guess what, I lose the maximum $200." A one-to-one risk-reward: risk $200 to make $200.

He then demonstrates the width tradeoff by widening the short strike from 287 to 290. "Then you pay a little higher but you could have a better return if it's right. You make 374 if you are wrong, you lose 320 something. Slightly better return on investment for you." Widening the spread increases both the debit and the maximum profit, and in this case improves the ratio modestly — $374 of potential profit against $320-something of risk rather than $200 against $200. The tradeoff for that better ratio is that the stock must travel further to reach maximum profit, and more capital is at risk in the meantime.

The placement logic is about *confidence*, not just direction: "In this case you are bullish, but you're cautiously bullish. You're not 100% sure, you're not like totally convinced about the bullish side, so you can use the spread to reduce the cost in case you're wrong." **The bull call spread is the mildly-to-moderately bullish trade for low IV** — low IV because it is a net debit position, and you are still net long premium even after the short call offsets part of the cost.

##### Bear put spread

The exact mirror. He buys the at-the-money 283 put and sells the 275 put, choosing 275 for the same reason he sold it in the cash-secured put example — the chart says there is support there, so the stock is unlikely to blow through it. The cost saving is again dramatic: "If you buy a straight put, you pay $6. But now you sell a 275, you collect $3.33 to reduce your cost. So you cut your cost by more than half, instead of $6 [you pay] $2.69."

The profit curve is the reverse of the bull call spread: breakeven at **280**, meaning the stock must fall about $3 for the position to break even; maximum profit of **$50** below the short strike; maximum loss of "$270 something." Adam reads the ratio as "one to $1.5" — you are risking more than you stand to gain, which is characteristic of a debit spread whose short strike is close to the money.

"So definitely, if I do this, I want the stock price to drop. So it's a [bearish] trade." **Moderately bearish, low IV.**

That completes the basic strategies. The pattern that emerges from the six is clean: the two naked long options sit at the extreme ends of the direction axis in the low-IV half, because they need big moves and cheap premium. The two vertical debit spreads sit inboard of them — same direction, less extreme, still low-IV because still net debit. The two premium-selling strategies, the covered call and the cash-secured put, sit near the middle-to-bullish region and belong in the high-IV half.

#### The advanced strategies, placed one at a time

##### Bear call spread

"The name already suggests this is a bearish trade," Adam says, and then proceeds to demonstrate that the name is only half the story.

The construction, again driven by the chart: SPY at 283, and "from the chart you say it won't be able to break above 287 because it will face a strong resistance here." So he sells the 287 call. And then the protective leg: "I buy to protect myself at 295 because this is an all-time high. So I don't believe it will break through it." The reasoning for the long strike is as technical as the reasoning for the short strike — he is buying protection at a level the chart says the market is unlikely to reach.

He is explicit about why the long leg is not optional: "Because I will face unlimited risk on that upside, I need to buy a reinsurance to cap the risk." That word — reinsurance — recurs throughout the lesson for the protective long leg of every credit spread, and it is a useful mental model. You are the insurer, collecting a premium from the option buyer. The long leg is the reinsurance you buy to cap your own liability.

The profit curve: maximum profit of **$243**, earned if the stock stays where it is or falls. There is buffer above: "Even if I'm wrong, the SPY goes up instead of going down, I have some buffer here. If it goes to 287, I can stay there, I will still make the max profit." Breakeven at approximately **289**. Maximum loss of **$557** if SPY breaks to a new all-time high — a scenario Adam explicitly does not expect.

Then the number that reframes the whole trade: **62 percent probability of profit**, with 37 or 38 percent chance of losing money. That reading, available directly on the platform, is what turns the abstract shape of the curve into a decision.

And the placement: "So definitely if I do bear call spread, I'm bearish on the direction of the shares. Or at least I'm neutral. Because if neutral, I'm still making profit. Or slightly bullish, I'm still making money. As long as the price is not too strongly bullish, then I'm okay." **Bearish, extending into neutral and even slightly bullish. High IV**, because it is a credit spread and you want the premium you collect to be rich.

Note the asymmetry against the bear put spread. Both are bearish. But the bear put spread requires the stock to *fall* to make money, while the bear call spread makes maximum profit if the stock merely fails to rise. That is the fundamental difference between a debit spread and a credit spread in the same direction, and it is the reason the choice between them is a choice about how confident you are in the move actually happening rather than a choice about direction.

##### Bull put spread

The mirror image, and Adam constructs it with the same chart-driven logic. "You believe the price will continue to go up and then you just sell some option below here because you believe it won't break below that. It has very strong support level at 275. So you may want to just sell 275."

And then the reason for the long leg, stated with unusual clarity: "But again, if you just sell 275, you are naked, unless you want to buy the share at 275. If you don't, then guess what, you need to buy a reinsurance. So you would sell 275, but you need to buy some reinsurance at maybe 265 right here, just in case it drops on the way." This is the cleanest statement in the course of the relationship between the cash-secured put and the bull put spread: **they are the same directional bet, and the difference is whether you are willing to own the shares.** If you are, sell the naked put and hold the cash. If you are not, buy the lower put and turn it into a defined-risk spread.

Net credit: **$1.80 per share, or $180** for the position. The profit curve: maximum profit of $180 if the stock stays at 283 or rises; breakeven at **273**; and if the stock falls below 265, maximum loss of **$820**.

Adam then says something that many traders find counterintuitive and that deserves careful attention: "In this case, you see that the risk reward ratio is not in your favor because you have very good probability of winning the trade." He is pointing at the trade-off that governs all credit spreads. You are risking $820 to make $180 — a terrible ratio on its face. But the probability of profit is **70 percent**, with 30 percent chance of losing money. And then he does something more precise: he drags the probability line down to the 265 long strike and reads off that there is only a **16 percent** chance of losing the maximum, with **83 percent** chance of making money or losing less than the maximum.

That is the correct way to evaluate a credit spread, and it is worth stating plainly because so many traders get it wrong. The maximum loss is not the expected loss. The 30 percent of outcomes in which the trade loses money are not all outcomes in which it loses $820 — the great majority of them are outcomes in which the stock finishes between 273 and 265 and the loss is partial. Only 16 percent of outcomes produce the full $820. Judging a credit spread by its raw risk-reward ratio, without weighting by probability, will cause you to reject trades with positive expected value.

Placement: **bullish, extending into neutral and slightly bearish. High IV.** "You want the share price to go up, neutral or at minimum slightly down only. It cannot be too much down."

##### Iron condor

For the iron condor, Adam deliberately switches underlyings, and the switch is itself a teaching point. "Normally I don't do it with SPY. Let's say I do it with something else. Euro, for example, Euro slash 6E." He goes to the euro futures contract.

The chart context: "Euro right now, what is the trend? It's been up and down, like a wave, trending down. Recently it's recovered, but now it's dipping again. Now, you really don't know what is the next direction for the Euro. A lot of things could happen. You just need to play with your probability with the Iron Condor trade."

That is the iron condor thesis in one sentence: you do not know the direction, you are not pretending to know the direction, and you are constructing a position that profits from the absence of a large move rather than from the presence of a correct one.

The construction rules he states are specific. **Two months to expiration**, and **a delta of 10 on both short strikes.** He goes to the put side, finds the strike nearest 10 delta — settling for 11 delta since exactly 10 is not available — and sells the 1.10 put. He then buys the 1.09 put to protect the downside. On the call side he finds the 10-delta strike at 1.175 and sells it, then buys the 1.185 call to protect the upside, noting that he buys "the same distance, which is two strikes here" — the two wings are kept symmetric.

The result is four legs: short 1.10 put, long 1.09 put, short 1.175 call, long 1.185 call. Net credit collected: **0.0013**. One euro futures contract represents **125,000 euros**.

The profit curve is the classic condor tent. "There's two vertical lines there; within that will be profit zone because it's above zero line." Maximum profit is **$162.50**. The upper breakeven is at **1.1763** and the lower at approximately **1.097**, and outside those the position starts losing. Maximum loss if completely wrong: **$1,000**.

And the probability: **82 percent chance of winning**, with less than 10 percent of outcomes on each tail.

Then the management rule, which is arguably the most important sentence in the iron condor section: **"In this kind of trade, you never let the trade run through the adjustment point. I would never let the trade to hit the max loss. I need to adjust when the price moves sharply one way or the other."** The $1,000 maximum loss is a theoretical number describing what happens if you fall asleep. It is not the loss you should ever actually take. The iron condor is a managed position, and the 82 percent win rate assumes management.

Placement: **neutral, high IV.** "You don't want to take any direction. You want the stock price to be range bound and move up and down in a certain range so that you can pocket this profit. So definitely, this is the neutral trade."

##### Earnings probability spread

This is the strategy Adam reserves for earnings season, and its placement is unusual because it is directional in a way the others are not — you choose the direction at construction time, and the same architecture serves either.

The bullish construction is a one-by-three-by-two on the call side: "If I think the stock will jump up after the earnings, buy a call, sell three [calls], buy two calls up there." The bearish construction mirrors it on the put side: "If I think the stock price will drop after the earning, I will buy a put, I sell three puts and I buy another two puts lower."

"So it's kind of one by three by two kind of trade depending on what direction I choose. Sometimes I can structure it as a neutral trade as well, but it's very rare."

Placement: **either bullish or bearish depending on construction, used specifically around earnings events.** Because it is net short options in the middle of the structure, it is a strategy that benefits from the elevated implied volatility that precedes earnings and from the volatility crush that follows the announcement.

##### Diagonal spread

The diagonal spread is presented explicitly as the solution to a capital problem, and that framing is the key to its placement.

"Diagonal spread is the spread that you want to use instead of the covered call, because covered call you want to buy a hundred shares, sometimes it costs you a lot of money, and you want to use diagonal spread to reduce the cost."

The construction on SPY: instead of buying 100 shares for $28,000, you buy a deep-in-the-money call, far out in time, to serve as a stock substitute. He goes to the December expiration and buys the **256 strike**, choosing it by delta: "typically, you can go like 80-delta. So let's increase it to 80-delta here. You buy 256." Two properties of that choice matter. It is deep in the money, so it moves nearly one-for-one with the stock. And it is far out in time, "so that your option won't decay a lot" — the long leg is bought where theta is slowest.

Against that synthetic stock position, he sells the short call exactly as in a covered call: 34 days out, first out of the money, control-clicked to add it as a second leg.

"You look at the chart of the trade, it looks similar to a covered call. You pretty much don't have the risk on the upside; you have the risk on the downside because you don't have the protection there." Breakeven: the stock drops $3, from 283 to **280**.

Then the management cycle, which is where the strategy earns its keep: "After the short option expires, you can roll it to another term, which is in another month or 35 days. And then keep doing it." And the analogy: **"It's like a lease-to-rent kind of strategy. You lease a house and you do Airbnb to collect a daily or monthly rent to pay for the long-term lease."** The long deep-in-the-money call is the lease; the rolling short calls are the Airbnb income.

The second advantage is about catastrophic risk, and it is significant: "Even in the case of catastrophic event, you won't lose a lot. Because the max loss that you have is this money. It cannot be $2,000. That's it. You cannot lose more than that. Just one tenth of what the max loss can be if you own 100 shares." Owning 100 shares of a $283 stock exposes you to $28,000 of theoretical loss. The diagonal exposes you to roughly a tenth of that. Same income mechanics, a tenth of the tail risk.

Placement: **"If you do the diagonal spread, you are bullish or slightly bullish, or neutral it's fine too. But it cannot be bearish, because if it's too bearish then you would lose money as well. Slightly bearish, it's fine."** So: **bullish through neutral, tolerating slightly bearish.**

##### Calendar spread

The calendar is presented, like the diagonal, as a cost-reduction device — but for a different purpose.

"You want to own a long-term option. Maybe you do September, you buy a call at the money because you believe the share price will go up from here. But then it costs you quite a lot of money — still not as much as buying the shares, but still like $900 plus. So calendar spread is a strategy you can use to cut cost, reduce your cost of owning this option. So use the shorter-term option to finance part of the cost."

The construction: long the September at-the-money call, short the 36-day at-the-money call at the same 283 strike. The effect on cost: "So then you cut down your cost by half, from $9 plus now down to $4.40 something."

The profit curve is the calendar's characteristic tent: "You have a profit zone which is between the two vertical lines. There is a triangle." The width of that tent: "If the stock price drops like $6 from here or up by $6 from here, then it could go out of the profit zone." So roughly $283 plus or minus $6 — a profit zone of about $12 in width on a $283 stock, which is why calendars require monitoring.

Placement: **"That is kind of neutral trade. It's a neutral trade for calendar spread."** Adam also notes the flexibility: "This is a good way for you to trade in range, or bullish long-term short-term bearish, or neutral kind of trade."

##### Synthetic spread

The synthetic spread replicates a stock position without the capital outlay, and its placement is simply wherever the stock position would be.

"Synthetic spread is a strategy again you use it to replicate owning shares or shorting shares. So in this case, DTE is not so important. Just choose the DTE you want. You think the stock price will go up in three months, then choose the three months. But if you think it will go down in the next two months, choose two months."

He builds the bullish version at 71 days: buy the at-the-money call, sell the at-the-money put, same strike. The profit curve is a straight diagonal line: "It goes straight, as if you own 100 shares. So stock goes up by $1, you make $100. If it goes down $1, you lose $100. So one-to-one kind of thing."

The capital advantage is the point: "The broker will not block you a hefty amount of money. Normally, if you buy the shares, you need $28,000. This one maybe you need like $5,000." He then checks the actual figure on the platform and reports approximately **$6,000** — roughly a fifth of the capital for identical directional exposure.

He then introduces the split-strike variation, which converts the synthetic from a pure stock proxy into a defined-outlook structure: "You can also split the strike. If you don't want to buy and sell at the same strike, you can choose like buy 285 call and sell 281, for example. Now you have some credit there. So in this case, you split the strike, and then you define the profit zone for yourself. Beyond that certain level you make money; below certain level you're willing to own the share."

Placement: **bullish or bearish depending on which way you build it** — "it could be bullish synthetic spread or it could be bearish synthetic spread."

##### The boom-bang (protective bullet synthetic spread)

Adam's own favourite, and the most structurally interesting position in the course. "It's a very powerful strategy that I use a lot. This strategy is three legs. It allows me to construct a bullish trade with a low cost and limited risk. I have some protection on the downside and I have unlimited upside potential."

The construction on SPY, at a longer 106 days to expiration. The thesis first: "I believe the SPY will now break out above this level and it will go on the way up and maybe making a new high." So he buys the **290 call**, paying **$5**. To finance that, he sells a put well below the market — the **275 put**. But selling a naked put creates unlimited downside risk, so he buys a lower put as reinsurance: "I still have some credit. I will use this credit to buy some reinsurance somewhere at support at maybe 260."

Three legs, then: long 290 call, short 275 put, long 260 put. And the shape that results: **"The chart will look like a stair. In the middle could be a small loss or sometimes profit — I call it a break-even zone. Above that I will make unlimited profit. But if I'm wrong and the stock drops, I lose money; but because I buy a reinsurance, I cap my max loss. I cannot lose more than this level."**

That is a genuinely remarkable payoff diagram: unlimited upside, a flat near-zero-cost region across the middle, and a capped loss on the downside. It is what you would design if you could design anything.

Placement: **"It's a bullish trade, but a cautiously bullish trade."** Adam notes that when the structure prices out at zero cost or a credit, "it could be a neutral trade also," but he is clear about intent: "The intent of the trade is to bet on the upside of the stock. So it's a bullish trade. So that's definitely a bullish trade."

#### The master strategy-selection matrix

Everything above collapses into a single table. The following matrix maps market outlook against volatility regime and names the strategy Adam selects in each cell, together with the reason the placement holds and the capital consideration that often makes the final choice between neighbours.

| Outlook | Low IV (buy premium) | High IV (sell premium) | Why the placement holds | Capital / margin note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Strongly bullish** | Long call (2+ months DTE, ATM or slightly ITM) | — | Unlimited upside, but breakeven sits above the strike by the full premium; the stock must move hard and soon or the position dies of theta | Cheapest entry of any bullish trade ($740 in the SPY example) but the highest probability of total loss |
| **Strongly bullish, capital-constrained** | Synthetic spread (long ATM call + short ATM put); boom-bang (long OTM call + short put + long lower put) | Boom-bang when the short put is rich enough to fund the call outright | Synthetic replicates 100 shares one-for-one; boom-bang adds a capped downside and a flat breakeven zone | Synthetic ≈ $6,000 vs $28,000 for 100 SPY shares; boom-bang can be built at zero cost or a credit |
| **Moderately / cautiously bullish** | Bull call spread (long ATM call, short call at chart resistance) | Bull put spread (short put at chart support, long lower put as reinsurance) | Debit spread needs the move to happen; credit spread needs only that the move down does *not* happen | Bull call spread risk = net debit ($200 on the 283/287); bull put spread risk = width minus credit ($820 on the 275/265) |
| **Mildly bullish / income** | — | Covered call (own 100 shares, sell first OTM call, ~34 DTE); cash-secured put (short put at chart support, cash held) | Both profit if the stock rises, stalls, or falls modestly — "you are bullish, but in case you are wrong you would still make money as long as you are not too wrong" | Covered call = full share cost ($28,000); cash-secured put = strike × 100 held in cash |
| **Mildly bullish, capital-efficient income** | — | Diagonal spread (long ~80-delta LEAP-style call far out in time, short first OTM call ~34 DTE, rolled monthly) | Same income mechanics as the covered call with roughly one-tenth the catastrophic exposure — "lease-to-rent" | Around one-tenth the capital of the covered call; max loss capped at the long call's cost |
| **Neutral** | Calendar spread (long far-dated ATM option, short near-dated same strike) | Iron condor (short 10-delta put + long lower put + short 10-delta call + long higher call, ~2 months DTE) | Calendar profits from the near option decaying faster than the far one; condor profits from the underlying staying inside both short strikes | Condor blocks little capital on futures, which is why Adam prefers futures for it; four legs means four commissions |
| **Mildly bearish** | — | Bear call spread (short call at chart resistance, long higher call as reinsurance) | Makes maximum profit if the stock falls, stalls, or rises only modestly — 62 percent probability of profit in the SPY example | Risk = width minus credit ($557 on the 287/295) |
| **Moderately bearish** | Bear put spread (long ATM put, short put at chart support) | — | Needs an actual decline to profit; breakeven $3 below spot in the SPY example | Risk = net debit (~$270), reward $50 — a ratio of roughly 1 to 1.5 |
| **Strongly bearish** | Long put (2+ months DTE, ATM) | — | Mirror of the long call: needs a large, fast decline to overcome premium paid | Cheapest bearish entry, highest probability of expiring worthless |
| **Protecting an existing long** | Protective put (own shares, buy put) | — | Insurance against a crash; the put leg is a bearish expression bought for defence | Cost of the put is a drag on the stock position, so buy it when IV is low |
| **Around earnings** | — | Earnings probability spread (1×3×2 on the call side if bullish, 1×3×2 on the put side if bearish) | Direction chosen at construction; benefits from elevated pre-earnings IV and post-announcement crush | Ratio structure means the middle short legs dominate margin |

Two structural observations follow from reading down the columns.

First, **the low-IV column is almost entirely populated by net-debit strategies and the high-IV column almost entirely by net-credit strategies.** That is not a coincidence; it is the volatility rule expressed as a table. When premium is cheap you can afford to own it, so debit spreads and long options become viable. When premium is rich you want to be collecting it, so credit spreads and short-premium income strategies dominate. If you ever find yourself putting on a debit spread when IV percentile reads 70, or a credit spread when it reads 20, the table is telling you that you are fighting the environment.

Second, **the middle of the direction axis is the most crowded region of the grid, and it is crowded almost exclusively with high-IV strategies.** The covered call, the cash-secured put, the diagonal, the bull put spread, the bear call spread and the iron condor all live in or near the neutral zone. That is where the income strategies are, and it reflects a deeper truth about options: the highest-probability trades are the ones that do not require you to be right about direction, only that you not be badly wrong. The extremes of the direction axis — the naked long call and long put — are the lowest-probability trades in the entire toolbox, which is exactly why they are the cheapest.

#### Capital and margin as the deciding factor

Direction and volatility narrow the field. Capital usually makes the final choice, and Adam returns to capital repeatedly with specific numbers.

The reference point is 100 shares of SPY at $283: **$28,000**. Every capital-efficiency argument in the course is measured against that number.

The **synthetic spread** delivers identical one-for-one directional exposure for approximately **$6,000** — a little over a fifth of the capital. The tradeoff is that you have taken on the obligation of the short put, so a large decline hurts you exactly as owning the shares would.

The **diagonal spread** delivers covered-call income mechanics for roughly a tenth of the capital, and simultaneously caps the catastrophic loss at the cost of the long call rather than the full share value. Adam's phrasing on this deserves repeating: "just one tenth of what the max loss can be if you own 100 shares."

The **iron condor on futures** is the extreme case of the same argument. "The reason why I'd like to trade iron condors on these securities [is] because futures allow leverage. So it blocks me very little capital. And then when I make money, that translates into a very good return on investment." The condor's absolute dollar profit is modest — $162.50 in the euro example — but the return on capital deployed is what makes it worth doing.

And the **credit spreads** are themselves a capital argument relative to their naked equivalents. The bull put spread exists because the naked put requires you to hold the full strike value in cash; buying the lower put converts an obligation of $27,500 into a defined risk of $820.

The general principle running through all of this: **the same directional view can almost always be expressed at several different capital levels, and the right expression is the cheapest one that still gives you the risk profile you can live with.** A trader with $30,000 in an account who buys 100 shares of SPY has spent the entire account on one position. The same trader who buys a diagonal has spent roughly $3,000 and has $27,000 left to diversify across other trades — which, as we will see in the assignment module, is precisely the reasoning Adam applies when he converts 1,000 Biogen shares into ten LEAP calls.

#### Where he says explicitly not to use a strategy

Scattered through the lesson are the prohibitions, and they are as valuable as the placements.

**Never sell a naked call.** The prohibition is unambiguous: "If you are short a naked call, meaning you don't have shares and you don't have a long call, but you just sell a single call — well, you know the consequence of it. If the share price goes up, you could potentially have unlimited risk because it's not fully hedged." And on the discovery of an assignment on such a position: "The moment you see the assignment, you need to use the cash to immediately buy the short share to clear it up, to eliminate the unlimited risk potential there." Adam attributes the rule jointly: "if you do this — and Adam and me told you never do it."

**Never sell a put without the cash to take the shares.** "If you sell a put option without having enough cash on standby to buy the shares, what happens if the short put is assigned? Well, you will be taking on long shares. But because you don't have enough cash to take it, your cash will go down and will be a negative cash for your account. So in that case, you may be going into a margin call, and the broker may force sell the position at the price that's very unfavourable to you." The cash-secured put is cash-secured for a reason; the word is doing work.

**Do not use the iron condor on individual stocks with event risk.** This is one of the most specific pieces of advice in the lesson and explains his security selection: "Those are the securities that have no problem that individual stocks normally have. For example, quarterly earnings or M&A announcements or some management activities — like someone like Elon sending a Twitter and then it can turn the stock price upside down. Or even paying dividends. So futures, indexes — you don't pay dividend and they don't have those kinds of events. So when you do a non-directional trade like an iron condor, you don't want the stock price to gap up or down significantly."

**Do not use the diagonal spread, covered call, or cash-secured put into an earnings release.** The same logic applied to the income strategies: "Watch out for those stocks that you're trading. Avoid earnings or key events, because that's where you could potentially face a significant gap up or gap down. [If] you trade like diagonal spread or like covered call or sell a cash-secured put, you don't want the stock price to gap down or gap up a lot."

**Do not let an iron condor run to maximum loss.** "In this kind of trade, you never let the trade run through the adjustment point. I would never let the trade hit the max loss." The condor's stated maximum loss is a description of negligence, not a plan.

**Do not use the diagonal if your view is meaningfully bearish.** "It cannot be bearish, because if it's too bearish then you would lose money as well."

#### The commission caveat on multi-leg structures

One practical warning applies specifically to the iron condor and, by extension, to every four-legged structure. "The watch-out for you when you do the condor trade is it's a four-leg strategy, therefore you have to pay four times the commission. And futures also have a higher [commission]; index has the same commission as [stock] so it's good, but futures you need to pay higher. And forex — if you enter, and then sometimes you need to adjust, and then if you want to close to take profit early, you also need to pay another set of commissions for the four legs. So quite commission-intensive."

The arithmetic is worth doing explicitly. A four-leg position costs four commissions to open. If it needs one adjustment during its life — which, given the rule that you never let a condor run to maximum loss, is a realistic assumption — that is more commissions. And closing early to take profit costs four more. Against a maximum profit of $162.50 in the euro example, commission drag is not a rounding error. Adam's verdict is that it remains worthwhile — "but again, considering the good premium you can get, it's still worth it" — but the calculation has to be done, not assumed.

The calendar spread carries a different maintenance cost, not commissions but attention: "The watch-out is only that the profit zone is not wide enough, so it requires some high maintenance, meaning you need to watch and monitor the trade every single day."

#### Adam's own preferred strategies

The lesson closes with something more useful than a general framework: the specific short list of what he actually trades, and why.

**First, the iron condor** — but almost exclusively on futures and indexes. He names them: oil futures, euro futures, gold futures, natural gas futures, and on the index side SPX, NDX and Russell. Three reasons. Futures leverage means very little capital is blocked, which turns a modest absolute profit into a good return on investment. Futures and indexes have none of the single-stock event risk — no quarterly earnings, no M&A announcements, no chief executive moving the stock with a tweet, no dividends. And the condor's long wings cap the risk on both sides. The offsetting cost is the four-leg commission load.

**Second, a cluster of related income strategies**: the covered call, the diagonal spread, the cash-secured put, and the bull put spread. He groups them deliberately, and the grouping reveals the logic. The covered call is stock plus a short call. The diagonal is the same trade with a long call substituting for the stock, "which gives me a better use of capital because I do not need to buy 100 shares." The cash-secured put is selling a put below the market "ready to take the share at the discount; if not, then I can get the premium as my income." And the bull put spread is "same like cash-secured [put], but I buy a lower put to protect in case." Four strategies, one underlying idea: sell premium at levels where you would be content with the outcome either way.

**Third, the calendar spread**, valued for its versatility. "There are so many ways for you to trade it — directional or non-directional, or completely neutral, or in the case like Boeing in that video I play both directions at the same time. So I bet on both directions. You can use it to play earnings as well. It gives you a very good risk-reward ratio, or return on investment, with a very low cost, low risk type of trade."

**Fourth, the synthetic spread**, used when he wants to be long or short a single name — "normally I use it on the bullish side, so instead of buying 100 shares, I just use synthetic."

**Fifth, the boom-bang**, his own construction, deployed in two specific scenarios that are worth separating because they are genuinely different trades wearing the same structure. The first is as an entry vehicle for his value-momentum investing methodology: "in case I spot [a stock] that has very good fundamentals and also has a good technical setup — it's on the uptrend — and I enter, instead of entering with a stock, I enter using this three-leg strategy." The second is bottom-fishing: "sometimes I just go out there and go bottom fishing. A lot of good stocks for some reasons — for example, healthcare stocks these days beaten down a lot by political reasons — and I say the fundamentals, those are good stocks, but they just happen to be in a bad sector and affected by other reasons than economic reasons. Then I say, okay, good stock, just got beaten down and looks like it's found some bottom already. Now it could be bouncing anytime soon. So I just go and bottom fish, use the boom-bang strategy to catch hopefully the bottom." And the reason the structure suits bottom-fishing specifically: "in case I'm wrong and the stock price continues to crash — guess what, I have the protection on the downside. So I cannot lose more than the well-defined risk that I have in the trade."

That last point is the whole argument for the boom-bang as a bottom-fishing tool. Bottom-fishing is a strategy with a poor hit rate by construction — you are buying things that are falling, and some of them keep falling. A structure with unlimited upside and a hard floor on the downside is precisely the instrument you want when your hit rate is low but your winners are large.

**Sixth, the earnings probability spread**, used "a lot also to play earnings, either on the bullish side or on the bearish side of the stock price movement."

Six strategies out of fifteen. That is the real lesson buried in the closing section: a professional who has taught fifteen strategies actively trades six of them, and the six he trades are the ones that suit his capital, his time zone, his temperament and his tolerance for monitoring. The master matrix tells you which strategy *fits a market condition*. Your own short list — which will be shorter than fifteen — tells you which of those you should actually be trading. Building that short list is the work that follows this lesson.

---

### Part Two — Options Assignment

#### Why this module exists

Adam opens the assignment module by identifying it as the single most anxiety-producing topic in the entire curriculum. "This is one of the most common questions or concerns that people have, and many of you have asked questions in different chat groups. Some of you even send me private messages or even call me because their options were exercised or assigned." The framing question he poses is deliberately provocative: "Option assignment — should you be worried or should you be happy?"

The answer, developed over four videos, is that in the overwhelming majority of cases you should be neither worried nor happy but simply methodical, and that in a meaningful minority of cases you should be actively pleased. But getting to that answer requires dismantling a misconception so widespread that it has embedded itself in the language traders use. People say "assignment risk." Adam's position is that the phrase is wrong, and he replaces it: **"I don't call it assignment risk. I just call it assignment probability or possibility. That's it. It's not a risk."**

Understanding why requires starting with the mechanics.

#### Exercise versus assignment: the two sides of one transaction

The first distinction is between two words that describe the same event from opposite sides of the trade.

**Exercising is a concept that belongs to the option buyer.** "When you buy a call option or you buy a put option and you want to convert your option into shares, you just exercise it. So the option buyer converts the option into stock — that is called exercising."

The mechanics of each are simple and follow directly from what the option contract entitles you to. If you own one call option and you exercise it, you now own 100 shares, because exercising a call means buying the shares at the strike price. Your share position goes up; your cash goes down. If you own one put option and you exercise it, you sell 100 shares at the put strike price. Your share position goes down; your cash goes up, "because you sell your shares, you collect cash."

**Assignment is the same event described from the option seller's side.** "Assignment is used from the option seller standpoint, the opposite side of the option buyer. So if you are short an option, either a call or a put, and your counterparty — which is the other side — exercises his or her option, you will be assigned stock, either long shares or short shares. It depends on call or put option."

The four possible outcomes, laid out explicitly:

If you are **short a call** and get assigned, you receive **negative 100 shares** — you are now short the stock, because your obligation was to deliver shares you did not have. Your share position goes down, but you are paid for those shares at the strike price, so your cash goes up.

If you are **short a put** and get assigned — the cash-secured put case, for instance — you receive **positive 100 shares**. You bought the stock at the strike, so your cash goes down by the strike price times 100.

The causal ordering between the two concepts is the point that resolves most of the confusion. **"The first one, which is exercising, has to happen first for the second one, which is the assignment, to happen later. If the number one does not happen, I guarantee you the second one won't happen. If the buyer of the option does not exercise, then you as a counterparty won't be assigned. It has to be triggered from the buyer standpoint."**

From that ordering follows the asymmetry of control, which Adam states as a formal rule: **"The option buyers, either the call buyers or the put buyers, are the only ones that control whether an option can be exercised or not. On the other hand, the option sellers have the obligation if assigned, and therefore have no control over when the option will be assigned."**

This asymmetry is the source of most of the anxiety, and it deserves to be sat with rather than skipped past. When you sell an option you sell away your own optionality. You have accepted a premium in exchange for a promise that someone else decides when to call in. Every rule in this module about probability, extrinsic value, dividends and expiration timing is an attempt to *forecast* someone else's decision, because you cannot *make* that decision. You can only make it economically unattractive for them.

#### Why assignment is not a risk

Now the central claim, and the reasoning behind it.

"Many of you perceive assignment as a risk. So is it true? Is an assignment a risk or not? Probably not. In most cases, it's not. Your position changes from being short a call option to being short shares. Or being short a put option, now being long shares. That's it. Different types of assets. **The assignment itself doesn't change the value of your account at the point of the assignment.**"

That final sentence is the whole argument and it is worth unpacking, because it is easy to nod at and hard to internalise when you are staring at a negative 100-share line in your account.

Consider the covered call. You own 100 shares of a stock and you have sold a call at some strike above where you bought them. The call goes deep in the money and is assigned. At the moment of assignment, you no longer own 100 shares — they have been sold at the strike price — and your cash has increased by the strike price times 100. Your account is worth what it was worth a second before. Nothing has been lost or gained by the act of assignment itself; you have exchanged one asset (shares) for another (cash) at a price you agreed to when you sold the call. Adam makes the point directly: "It's not a risk, and if you want to buy back 100 shares, use that money that you got paid there, buy 100 shares. No problem at all."

Or consider the picture he draws of the two counterparties: "The call buyer and the call seller transact in the assignment process. The call buyer says, 'I'm exercising my call option, give me the stock.' The call seller says, 'No problem, at the strike price, here's your shares.' So they change hands between cash and shares. That's it. It's not a risk. It's just different forms of assets."

There is one further structural reason assignment is not a risk when the assigned option is part of a spread. **"If the assigned option is part of a risk-defined spread — and we've learned spreads by now, a spread is an option trade that has at least two legs, three or four legs — so if it's a risk-defined spread, meaning you're long an option and short the other one, and the short option is assigned, then the long option will serve as a hedge against the risk."** The consequence for margin follows: "Therefore, if the short option is assigned but you're still holding on to the long option, the risk is still defined. So there's no unlimited risk. And therefore the broker will not block additional margin or buying power from you. They should not, because the trade is fully hedged."

That is a practically important statement. If you get assigned on the short leg of a properly constructed spread and your broker *does* block additional buying power, something is wrong — either with your understanding of the position or with the broker's handling of it — and it is worth a phone call rather than a panic.

#### The three reasons people panic anyway

If assignment is economically neutral, why do traders react to it as though the house is on fire? Adam identifies three specific triggers, and they are worth naming because recognising your own reaction as one of the three is most of the cure.

**First, the sight of a large short share position.** "For example, they sell a call on Microsoft, and now it gets assigned. Suddenly, they see they are short 100 shares of Microsoft, and they look at the negative hundred shares. They just freak out." The number is negative and large and unfamiliar, and the emotional response arrives before the arithmetic does.

**Second, the sight of a collapsed or negative cash balance.** "They are assigned positive shares, but their cash goes down significantly or even negative. And when they saw the cash being significantly negative, they just blow their mind." If you are assigned 100 shares of a $280 stock, $28,000 leaves your cash line. If the account did not have $28,000 in cash — because the position was a spread and the risk was defined by the long put, not by cash on hand — the cash line goes negative. That is alarming to look at and, in a properly hedged spread, entirely benign.

**Third, and most honestly, not knowing what to do.** "I don't know how to deal with this, how to handle the situation, and they just freak out." This is the one the module is really designed to fix, and the reason so much of it is spent on step-by-step platform mechanics.

#### Assignment scenarios on the short call side

Adam walks through three distinct situations, and the correct response differs in each.

**Scenario one: the covered call.** You own 100 shares, you have sold a call above the market, the stock has shot up, the call has gone deep in the money and been assigned. "Your 100 shares will be called away, because you basically have the obligation to serve the demand of the option buyer — because you are the seller here. So the buyer of the call option exercises and you get assigned; your shares will be sold at the strike price. And you will be paid for it, so therefore your cash will go up. So not a problem."

The action required: none, unless you want the shares back. "If you want to buy back 100 shares, use that money that you got paid, buy 100 shares. No problem at all."

**Scenario two: the short call is a leg of a spread.** Adam enumerates the strategies where a long call and a short call coexist, and the list is long: "You're talking boom-bang collar, you're talking about calendar spread, diagonal spread, iron condor, ESS [earnings sniper spread], or earning probability spread EPS."

What happens: "You will be assigned negative shares. But you don't have to worry because it's a spread, it has been fully hedged. You will be assigned negative shares, but your cash will go up accordingly. And for the remaining legs — the long call leg or even three other legs — [they] will remain unchanged."

The action required: "If you want, you just use the cash that you got paid and buy [back the] short shares to clear them, and then sell a new call to reinstate the trade."

**Scenario three: the naked short call.** The one you should never be in. "If you happen to be short a naked call and get assigned — guess what, you will be short shares. And that will be unlimited risk potential for you. And of course, you'll be paid for it. So the moment you see the assignment, you need to use the cash to immediately buy the short shares to clear it up, to eliminate the unlimited risk potential there."

The distinction between scenarios two and three is the entire argument for defined-risk trading. In scenario two, being assigned short 100 shares is an inconvenience you clean up at leisure, because the long call caps your loss if the stock keeps running. In scenario three, being assigned short 100 shares is an open-ended liability that must be closed immediately, because nothing caps it.

#### Assignment scenarios on the short put side

The same three-way division applies.

**Scenario one: the cash-secured put.** "If that is a cash-secured put, that means you already have cash on standby to buy the shares. So when that short put is assigned, you will be buying 100 shares, and you will use your standby cash over there to pay for it. So not a problem — again, different types of assets, from cash now to shares."

**Scenario two: the short put is a leg of a spread.** The list of strategies containing a short-put/long-put pair is again long: "We're talking bull put spread, bull put spread extreme, bear put spread, the calendar spread using put options, diagonal spread using put options, boom-bang has two put [legs] there, a boom-bang collar also has two puts there, iron condor, earning sniper spread which has two put legs there, and also earning probability spread using put options."

What happens: "You just get assigned positive shares. But your cash will go down and could potentially go negative as well, because you don't have enough cash to absorb the shares. But it's not a problem. It's not a risk, because you have the long put to hedge the downside for you. So the remaining legs will stay unchanged."

This is the scenario that triggers panic trigger number two — negative cash — and it is precisely the scenario in which negative cash is harmless. The long put is the hedge. The cash line looks bad and the risk is defined.

**Scenario three: the uncovered short put.** "If you sell a put option without having enough cash on standby to buy the shares, what happens if the short put is assigned? Well, you will be taking on long shares. But because you don't have enough cash to take it, your cash will go down and will be a negative cash for your account. So in that case, you may be going into a margin call, and the broker may force sell the position at the price that's very unfavourable to you."

The phrase "force sell at a price that's very unfavourable to you" is the operative danger. A margin liquidation is not executed at a price you choose or a time you choose. It is executed when the broker's risk system says so, which is frequently the worst possible moment.

#### Why early assignment is rare: the three-part argument

Having established what happens when assignment occurs, Adam turns to how often it actually occurs before expiration. The answer: **"Before expiration, options are very rarely assigned. Very rare. Because in most cases, there's just no benefit for the option buyer to exercise the option early."**

Three reasons, and understanding all three is what lets you assess your own positions rather than worry about them generically.

**Reason one: exercising forfeits all remaining extrinsic value.** "If he exercises his option before the expiration date, he or she will have to forfeit all remaining extrinsic value in the option. You remember that before expiration, the option value has two types of premium inside: the intrinsic value, which is the difference between share price and the strike price, and the second element, the extrinsic premium, which is time value and volatility premium. Now, the moment the option buyer exercises the option, he or she will need to forfeit the extrinsic value."

And then the sentence that converts this from a fact into a reason to be pleased: **"And you, as the counterparty of that transaction — you are the seller — you will be happy, because you now can earn that extrinsic value before the expiration, meaning you don't have to wait until the expiration."**

This is the mechanism behind Adam's claim that assignment can be a gift. The extrinsic value the buyer throws away by exercising early does not evaporate; it accrues to you. You collected premium for time and volatility that you no longer have to wait out. His summary elsewhere is blunt: "his loss becomes my gain."

**Reason two: exercising a call requires a large cash outlay for no additional exposure.** "By exercising, let's say a call option, the option buyer will have to fork out a bunch of cash to buy 100 shares. And that would be very unfavourable because he could have just used a fraction of that money to own a call option instead. So there's no reason why you'd want to pay more cash for the same exposure or access."

**Reason three: a deep-in-the-money call is already a stock substitute, and a better one.** "If the option buyer happens to buy the call option and the price goes up, he's very happy because he's making a lot of money, and he says, 'Now I can exercise my option to buy the share at a cheaper price,' because now the strike price is deep in the money. Yeah, he can do it. He can just exercise the deep-in-the-money call and hold 100 shares instead of holding a deep-in-the-money call. But remember, the deep-in-the-money call has a very high delta — almost 100 delta, 80, 90 delta, or 100 delta. Meaning if the share price continues to go up, the option value will go in the same tandem. One-to-one kind of thing. So owning a deep-in-the-money call option is as good as owning 100 shares, but using a fraction of the capital."

And there is a further advantage to holding the call rather than converting to stock, which is the downside protection embedded in the option: "That owning the money call also helps you prevent the downside risk in case the whole market collapses. Then you cannot lose more than the call option value, compared to losing a lot of money if you hold shares."

The practical instruction to option buyers that follows: "That's why, when you own a deep-in-the-money call option before expiration, if you want to continue to stay in the position, don't exercise. Just hold on to the in-the-money call."

Notice that this is advice to the *buyer* that happens to protect the *seller*. The rational buyer does not exercise early, which is why the rational seller rarely gets assigned early. The whole edifice of early-assignment probability rests on the assumption that your counterparty is behaving rationally — which is usually true, and occasionally is not, which is why the probability is low rather than zero.

#### Automatic exercise at expiration and the do-not-exercise request

The rule at expiration is mechanical and unforgiving. **"If the option expires in the money by at least one cent or more, then it will be automatically exercised by the system."**

Adam demonstrates with a live position. He is short one contract of a Pfizer 40-strike call expiring the following day, 16 July. The stock is at **$39.95**, so the call is out of the money by five cents. "If tomorrow the price closes at 40 and 0.01, then this option will be expired in the money by one cent. So if the price goes anywhere 40.01 or above, this option will be expired in the money and then it will be automatically exercised — and because I'm short a call option, I will be assigned negative 100 shares."

The instruction for option buyers facing the same knife-edge: "What if you are long a call option and you are not so sure if that call option will be in the money or out of the money by the time of the expiration? You'd better just close it, because if it's in the money by one cent or more then it will be automatically exercised by the platform, unless you choose not to."

That last clause opens the topic of the **do-not-exercise request**, and the mechanics differ meaningfully by broker.

On **thinkorswim**, there is no self-service control. "You need to send in what they call it, DNE — do not exercise — request. You need to send in a DNE request as soon as possible, ideally before the expiration." Adam relates a personal failure here: "I had one time when I argued with them that, hey, I told you I do not want to exercise, but you did not follow my request. He told me that it already missed the cutoff." His estimate of the required lead time: "for thinkorswim, I think you need to send them at least half an hour or one hour before the expiration time, which is 4 p.m." The method: "just go to the chat, to the support, and then create the chat and then tell them, hey, I'm having this position that could potentially be expired in the money, I don't want to exercise."

On **Interactive Brokers**, the process is systematic and self-service. "They have a tool for you to do it more systematically. You don't have to tell anybody. You will do it by yourself." He demonstrates with a BlackBerry 20 August 10-strike call, one contract, with the stock at **10.66**. The mechanic: right-click the option position, choose "option," and you get both an **exercise** button and a **lapse** button. "If I press this exercise button, my one call option here, one contract, will be converted into positive 100 shares. But I don't want to do it now. When it comes near to the expiration time, if you don't want to exercise it, you just go here, right-click, go to the option exercise and choose the lapse, meaning you don't want to exercise." Critically, the control is time-gated: "You cannot do it right now because it's not near the expiration time. But when it comes very near to expiration time, you will be able to tell the system whether you want to let it lapse or you want to exercise."

On **tastyworks**, there is no lapse button. "You cannot use the lapse button, but you need to either call them on the trade desk — they have a phone number there — or you need to email their trade desk before the expiration time, telling them that, hey, I don't want to exercise this option even if it expires in the money. You need to tell them in advance."

The general instruction: "That depends on what broker you're talking about, and if you have other brokers you need to check out the mechanism applicable for that broker as well."

#### Dividends and the ex-dividend date

The single most common early-assignment scenario in equity options is the one that occurs around a dividend, and this section is where the module becomes genuinely quantitative.

The setup: "Company pays dividends once in a while — once every quarter or once every six months. And if you happen to own options or [be] short options near to the ex-dividend date, your brokers often send an alert to you. They send a notification telling you that, hey, you're owning this option or you're shorting this option that will be paying dividend tomorrow, and your risk will be high or low."

Adam then gives a three-part decision procedure. It is one of the few genuinely enumerated procedures in the course, and it should be run in order.

1. **If you are short a put, stop worrying — there is nothing to assess.** "If you are short a put option, you don't have to worry about it. Because your counterparty is a put buyer. And there's no incentive for the put buyer to exercise the put option before the dividend date. Because if he does it, actually he will be short shares and he would owe the dividend to you. So it won't happen." The logic is exact: exercising a put makes the buyer short the stock, and a short stock position across an ex-dividend date owes the dividend. The dividend is an argument *against* early put exercise, not for it. Adam's summary: "So anything to do with the put option — [ignore it]. Number one."

2. **If you are short an out-of-the-money call, stop worrying.** "It doesn't make sense for the call buyer to exercise an OTM call option. If he does that, what it means is he agrees to buy the shares at the strike price which is above the market price. Why would he want to do it? He could just use the money to buy at the market price. Why does he want to buy at the higher price above the market price? It doesn't make any sense. So you are the counterparty; you don't have to worry about OTM call options, because OTM call options are very highly unlikely to be assigned."

3. **If you are short an in-the-money call, do the comparison.** "You have to consider this case carefully. You have to look at the extrinsic value of the short call there. If the remaining extrinsic value of the short call is greater than the dividend that the company is going to pay, then there's very little chance that the option could be assigned to you." The reasoning: "Because your counterparty, the call option buyer — if he exercises the option, he will need to forfeit all the extrinsic value, and that doesn't make sense, because that means he forfeits more value than the value of the dividend itself. He would not do it."

So the whole dividend question reduces to a single comparison performed on a single leg: **remaining extrinsic value in the short in-the-money call versus the dividend per share.** Extrinsic value larger, and the buyer loses money by exercising, so he will not. Dividend larger, and exercising becomes profitable for him, so he might.

#### The MasterCard worked example

Adam demonstrates the comparison on a live position, and the numbers are worth following closely because they show how large the margin of safety usually is.

The position is an iron condor on MasterCard (MA), consisting of a bear call spread and a bull put spread. On the call side he is short the **375 call** and long the **380 call** to cap the upside. On the put side he is short the **365 put** and long the **360 put** to cap the downside. Four legs.

The date is **7 July**, and MasterCard goes ex-dividend the following day, **8 July 2021**. Clicking the dollar-sign marker on the chart reveals the dividend: **$0.44 per share.**

Step one of the assessment is the dividend, now known: 44 cents.

Step two is the extrinsic value in the short in-the-money call. And here Adam applies the filter from the procedure above: "We don't care about the put side. As we say, forget about the put side. Now, if you have the call that is OTM, don't care about it. Also, what you need to pay attention to is the short call that would be potentially in the money."

The stock is at **$376**, so the 375 short call is in the money by $1. The extrinsic value column on thinkorswim shows the extrinsic value of that short call as **almost $6 per share**.

The comparison: $6.00 of extrinsic value against $0.44 of dividend. It is not close. "So obviously, the call option buyer — my counterparty, the one who bought this one from me — will not exercise his or her option, because if he does it, what happens? He will need to forfeit this money, almost $6 per share. Gone. In his account, he immediately sees a loss of $6 per share by exercising his call option."

And then the reframing that captures the entire attitude of the module: **"And his loss will become my gain. So I would be more than happy if he does it. I tell you he doesn't. But if he does, for some stupid reason, I would be very happy. It's like a mini jackpot for me."**

The conclusion is properly hedged rather than absolute: "So in short, is there a possibility that this 375 call be assigned today before the dividend date? Yes, anything can happen. Now, how probable is that? Very unlikely. In fact, if it happens to me, I would be happy to receive that extrinsic value ahead of time. So in that case, my trade will be very profitable."

#### Reading extrinsic value when your platform does not show it

Not every platform has an extrinsic-value column. Adam gives two methods for deriving it, and the second is genuinely elegant.
