**Method one is direct subtraction.** With the 375 call trading at $7 and the stock at $376, the intrinsic value is $376 minus $375 = $1, so the extrinsic value is $7 minus $1 = $6. "So a rough number, that's one [way]."

**Method two uses put-call parity.** "The other way of doing it is you look at this 375 strike price here — instead of looking on the call side, now you look on the put side. You see the value of the put option at that strike price is **$6.30**."

The reason this works is that an out-of-the-money option is *entirely* extrinsic value — it has no intrinsic value by definition. The put at the same strike is out of the money when the call is in the money, so its whole price is time and volatility premium, and by parity that is very nearly the same extrinsic value embedded in the call.

But there is an adjustment, and Adam explains why: "By now, the option pricing, both on the put side and on the call side, has factored in the dividend that will be paid out tomorrow. So what does it mean? It means that tomorrow, when the market opens, the price of MasterCard will be adjusted down by $0.44. For that reason, the put option has priced in the impact and the call option as well. So you need to subtract the 44 cents from this put pricing."

Doing that: $6.30 minus $0.44 = **$5.86**. Against the extrinsic-value column reading of "almost $6" — Adam settles on **$5.95** as the column value — the estimate is very close. "You see it's very close. $5.95. So close."

The rule stated compactly: **"Just look at the opposite side, at the put, same strike price, get the value of the premium, minus the dividend that will be paid out, and then you will have the extrinsic value [of the call]."**

#### When the extrinsic value is smaller than the dividend

Part 2 of the module opens by completing the other half of the comparison. "If the extrinsic value of the short call option is smaller than the dividend that the company is going to pay, the likelihood of being assigned is higher."

The response is a choice of two actions: **"In that case, you may want to consider rolling up the call strike to a higher strike, or simply just close the position — just avoid the possibility there."**

Rolling up works because it restores extrinsic value. A short call deep in the money has almost no time premium; a short call closer to or above the money has considerably more. Moving the strike up moves you back to a position where the buyer would lose more by exercising than he would gain in dividend, which restores the disincentive that protects you. This is the same logic that drives the delta-based rolling rule in the rolling module, and the two rules reinforce each other.

And if you do get assigned short shares across an ex-dividend date, the consequence is again not what it appears: "If in case you are assigned short shares before the ex-dividend date, you will owe the dividend to the shareholder, the one that is long shares. But in that case, it's not a risk either. Yes, your cash will be reduced because of the dividend you need to pay, but the short shares that you owe — the price will be adjusted down accordingly. **So it's a left pocket to right pocket. It's not a risk.**"

The reasoning is exact. On the ex-dividend date the stock price drops by approximately the dividend amount. If you are short the stock, that price drop is a gain on your short position, exactly offsetting the dividend you owe. Cash out, position value up, net zero.

#### Clearing an assigned position: platform mechanics

The third panic trigger — not knowing what to do — is addressed with step-by-step walkthroughs on three platforms. The opening instruction sets the tone: **"First of all, please don't freak out. When you see the assigned shares in your account, just relax."**

The situation being cleared: you were short a call as part of a spread, the short call was assigned, and you now hold negative 100 shares plus a remaining long call. Adam is careful to restate why this is safe before showing how to fix it: "I do have the long call to hedge my position. So it's not a risk. It's a defined risk. So if the shares go up, the short call here will lose money, but my long call will make money. So it's not a risk."

**On thinkorswim**, there are three routes.

The first and preferred route is to close both legs as a single order. "Just highlight the two legs — hold the control key and highlight two legs, right-click on it, and create closing order. And you see the system tells you that you will execute it in one order called buy-covered-stock. So you buy 100 shares and then you sell your long call option." The resulting ticket has two legs: buy 100 shares to clear the short stock, and sell the long call. Adam negotiates the price: with the market showing **$9.20**, he enters **$9.00**, paying $900. "So after you buy back, your cash will go down, but your position will be cleared."

The second route reaches the same order from the other direction. "Go to the trade tab, go to the position where your remaining long call is — this one, August 20th — and you want to sell this one and you buy 100 shares. So right-click on this leg and buy-covered-stock."

The third route is leg by leg, and Adam permits it while explaining why he does not prefer it. "Some of you ask me, can I just buy the share to clear it up first, and then I would decide what to do with the long [call] later on? Yes, you can do it. Just right-click, close, buy 100 shares at the market price. And then separately you can sell the call option." His reasoning against: **"I prefer to do it together because then I will get the best optimal pricing for both sides. Because if you buy the share, you have to pay at the ask price. And if you sell, you have to sell at the bid price. So that's not the optimal pricing for you."** Executing as a combination lets you work a single net price rather than crossing two separate spreads.

**On tastyworks**, the mechanics differ in one detail worth knowing. The position is BlackBerry: negative 100 shares and one long call. First, a display gotcha: "Sometimes you don't see the shares. Just make sure you click both stocks and options, because if you only click option, you don't see shares." Then the selection method: "You don't have the control key in tastyworks — just click and click, and right-click on it and close position." The system builds the same buy-100-shares-plus-sell-call order for a net debit. Adam negotiates: market is around **$8.97**, he enters **$8.90**, and shows how to modify: "If you are keen to get rid of this one quick, then just right-click, replace the order and change it to whatever market price, 8.97, and send it out."

**On Interactive Brokers**, again two routes. The quick one: "Just click on here, hold the control key, click the other leg, highlight two legs, right-click and close, and yes, 100% close as a strategy." But Adam finds the resulting display hard to read — "it's more difficult to read from this kind of format" — and prefers the Option Trader with its strategy builder. There, he goes to the expiration holding the long call, clicks to sell that contract, then adds the stock leg to buy 100 shares of BlackBerry, producing a two-leg order: sell one contract at the 10 strike expiring 20 August, and buy 100 shares to clear the short position. He negotiates toward the same **8.97** and transmits.

The closing summary across all three: **"Again, don't freak out when you see your option being assigned. It's just very simple. Just close the assigned shares and possibly the remaining options together, and then clear it up. That's it."**

#### Common mistake one: exercising your long leg

The first major mistake is exercising the remaining long option to offset the assigned shares, and Adam quantifies exactly what it costs.

The scenario: "When you trade an option spread — like a calendar spread or diagonal spread, or a plain vertical spread — and the short call leg is assigned, people tend to be rushing or panicking to exercise the remaining leg, which is the long leg." The panicked reasoning is understandable: "Oh my God, I'm assigned 100 shares here. So what I would do is I will go and exercise my remaining call option, right-click on the option and choose exercise. And then after that, he will be assigned 100 positive shares that offset the negative 100 shares."

It works. It is also expensive. "You can do it, but that will be wasting a lot of money. I mean, you lose some valuable money, and I would not do it."

The specific number in the demonstration: "If I exercise the long call, I will be losing this value, **96 cents, or 96 dollars for one contract**. That's a lot of money. This is extrinsic value remaining, because there's still like more than a month to expiration. So I forfeit that extrinsic value. And that could potentially be big money if you're talking big share price or higher number of contracts. Don't do it."

The correct action is to sell the long call in the market rather than exercise it, and Adam shows the arithmetic side by side. The stock is at **$10.66** and the long call strike is **10**. "If you exercise, what it means is you buy the share at $10 and the market price right now is 10.66, so the difference between your buying price and the market price is only **66 cents**. So you get the value of 66 cents. Whereas if you sell the option in the market, you get this money, **$1.25, $1.26**. Much better value."

$1.26 versus $0.66. Exercising throws away 60 cents per share, $60 per contract, because exercise captures intrinsic value only while selling captures intrinsic plus extrinsic. The rule: **"Don't exercise the long call when the short call is assigned, because you will forfeit the extrinsic value of your long call option. The best way is just to sell your long option to the market at the market value of the option, which means you can collect both intrinsic value and extrinsic value out of the option. And then after that, you can just buy to clear the assigned shares or sell to clear the assigned shares."**

#### The one exception: negative extrinsic value and wide spreads

There is exactly one circumstance in which exercising the long option is correct, and Adam demonstrates it on a real option chain.

"One rare case where you could or should exercise your long call: that is when your long call has negative extrinsic value, or no more extrinsic value, and the liquidity is very low, creating a big spread between bid and ask price. And if you sell your option, you have to sell at a lower price. In that case, you'd better exercise your option."

The example is Illumina, "a high price stock," trading at **$460.92**, with the option series expiring the following day — one day to expiration, 16 July. The strike under examination is **430**.

"If you happen to own a 430 call option, this option now is deep in the money, and the extrinsic value is actually negative." The bid-ask spread is wide because liquidity is poor: "Bid and ask prices are very far away from each other. So if you want to get rid of this one — I want to sell — you have to sell at a lower price, **28.2**."

Now the arithmetic that makes the decision: "The intrinsic value of this option is the difference between this and this. So if you do the math, **460.92 minus the strike price 430** — the intrinsic value in the option itself is **30.92**. So you want to sell at minimum at 30.92, if not more. So if you sell at a lower price at 28.2, of course you will lose some value there."

Selling into the bid captures $28.20. Exercising captures the full $30.92 of intrinsic value. The difference is **$2.72 per share, $272 per contract**, and it exists purely because the market is not offering a fair price. "In this case, it doesn't make sense to sell the option at the market price because there's no taker — because the bid and ask [are] so wide, because the liquidity is low. So in that case, you would exercise the option. It makes more sense to just exercise the option, converting the option into the shares and then sell the shares at the market price, and then you can get out at the better value."

The general principle: **exercise only when the market is offering you less than intrinsic value.** As long as the market will pay you intrinsic plus some extrinsic, selling wins. When illiquidity means the market will pay you less than intrinsic, exercise wins.

#### Common mistake two: letting a vertical spread expire when one leg is near the money

The second mistake is subtler and more dangerous, because the reasoning behind it is superficially sound.

The setup: "When you trade a vertical spread — vertical spread has two legs, and both legs have the same DTE, the same expiration — and one of the two legs is near at the money, you either forget to close the trade just before expiration, or you bet that both legs will be expired in the money or out of the money."

The tempting logic: "If both legs are to expire out of the money, then both legs will expire worthless, and you let it become worthless. Or if both legs are to expire in the money, then what happens is you will be assigned both long shares and short shares together, and the long shares and the short shares will offset each other. So in either case, you would be okay, because you will end up with zero shares. Because of that logic, you say, let's not close the trade to save the closing cost and commission."

The flaw appears when one leg is sitting right at the money. "That is a mistake that people may have, especially when one of the legs is too near at the money and it could be in the money any moment or out of the money the other moment. If you happen to have that situation, and a certain sharp price move just before the expiration — just a few seconds before expiration — and supposedly out-of-the-money option becomes now in the money: in that case one of your legs will be expired in the money and the other leg [out], and therefore you could be assigned shares, long shares or short shares depending on what side of the trade you are."

The consequences split by broker policy. "If you don't have enough money or funds, you will be subject to a margin call, and some brokers do not have the margin call policy — they just force sell your position just before the expiration in case you don't have enough margin to take the shares. But some brokers allow you to take the assigned shares. But then that would mean that now the profit or loss of the trade will be at the mercy of the stock price move. On Monday, when the price opens up and you are short, you are screwed. But Monday, if the price opens down and you are short a share, then you make more money. So it depends."

That phrase — *at the mercy of the stock price move* — is the real cost. You have converted a defined-risk position with a known maximum loss into an undefined overnight directional bet, and you did it to save a commission.

Adam demonstrates on his own Pfizer bear call spread: short the 40 call, long the 40.5 call, with the stock near 40. "Both legs are out of the money. I could make a mistake by saying, hey, both legs are now out of the money, the price should not move much tomorrow, and I just go for a vacation, forget about the position completely. And tomorrow, what happens if just before the expiration the price goes to 40.01? Then this leg will be expired in the money and this one will be out of the money, so then I will be assigned 100 shares. So on Monday when I open this account, I will see negative 100 shares."

And the scaling argument that makes this more than academic: **"Pfizer is a small price stock, so it's okay for me to absorb it. But if it happens to be like Amazon, for example — then we're talking about $300,000 cash requirement to buy 100 shares."** A one-cent move on a knife-edge strike in a $3,000 stock creates a $300,000 obligation over a weekend.

The verdict: "It's better just to close it before the expiration, both legs. Sometimes you can save cost, but it may not [be] worth it."

#### Index options, cash settlement, and AM expiration

A whole category of the assignment problem disappears when the underlying is an index rather than a stock, and a different problem appears in its place.

"First of all, you cannot own the index, but you can trade options on the index. The common indexes like SPX (S&P 500), NDX (Nasdaq), Russell, VIX — those are the indexes that are very common and people trade options on."

The consequence: **"If your options on those indexes expire in the money, there will be no share assignment, because it's not shares — you cannot own the index itself. So what happens is there will be a cash settlement. The difference between the index at the close and the strike price would be the cash that would be settled. So upon settlement, the cash will be either added or deducted from your account, and the amount is the difference between the strike price and the settlement price."**

But indexes carry a complication that stocks do not: two different expiration conventions living side by side in the same option chain.

"The normal option typically expires on Friday at 4 p.m. Eastern Time. So for those indexes like SPX, NDX and Russell, they do have weekly options that expire on Friday afternoon at 4 p.m. as well. However, for those indexes, they have different types of options, and they call it the AM expiration options — the option that expires in the morning on Friday."

Pulling up the SPX chain shows both: "They have options that expire on weeklies, like every Monday, Wednesday or Friday. And they have AM, the option that expires in the morning of the third Friday of the month." He points at the specific series: 16 July, the third Friday of July; the August third Friday; September 17, the third Friday of September.

The settlement mechanism for the AM series is unlike anything in equity options. **"For SPX AM expiration options, they use what they call SET, or set price, to settle the difference between SET price and the strike price."** What SET is: "To make it simple, it's very close to the opening price of SPX at the opening on the third Friday of the month. So tomorrow, July 16, is the third Friday, and at the opening of tomorrow's session, the opening price of SPX is used to settle the difference between strike price and market price."

But it is not literally the opening print, and the distinction matters: "The SET is not exactly the first tick of the SPX. It's a combination of multiple trades, weighted average for a period of time during the opening. And then they would publish that SET price about **30 to 60 minutes after the market has opened**."

How to look it up: "Just go to the website and type SET. You see S&P 500 index open settlement value. There's a chart. Every day you see a dot. That dot is the opening price of SPX during that day. And they will use that to settle the difference into your account or deduct from your account."

The equivalent settlement tickers for the other indexes: **NDX settles on XQO. Russell settles on RLS. VIX settles on VRO.**

And VIX is different in timing as well as ticker: "VIX is a little bit different. AM settlement is not on Friday morning, but it's on Wednesday morning. So VIX is a completely different animal. The timing is on Wednesday, not Friday."

The trap that catches traders repeatedly is the gap between last trading time and settlement time. **"For the options that expire in the morning on Friday — which is SPX, NDX and Russell — the settlement price is the opening price on Friday, but the last trading time for these AM expiration options is actually on the previous Thursday. So Friday is a settlement day in the morning, but the last trading time is 4 p.m. Eastern time of the prior Thursday, the day before."** And: "If there's a holiday, then everything is shifted one day earlier."

Similarly for VIX: "The settlement price is on Wednesday morning opening price, but the last trading time would be Tuesday, 4 p.m. Eastern time."

Adam has clearly watched students discover this the hard way: "Sometimes you forget and you say, oh, how can I — I cannot close my position, because it's already stopped trading."

The consolidated reference he presents covers: VIX, expiring Wednesday with last trading Tuesday, settled on the Wednesday morning opening price; SPX monthly, expiring the third Friday of every month, settled on the SET AM price, last trading day the previous Thursday; SPX weeklies, which expire Friday, Wednesday and Monday afternoons and whose last trading time is 4 p.m. Eastern on those same days; and NDX, following the same monthly-AM and weekly-PM structure with XQO as the settlement value.

#### The advantages and disadvantages of cash settlement

Cash settlement is a genuine convenience for some structures and a genuine hazard for others, and the dividing line is whether all legs share an expiration.

**The advantage: same-expiration structures can simply be allowed to expire.** "If all legs of an option spread expire at the same time, meaning the same DTE, then you can let the option expire and settle in cash. If it's in the money, it's settled for the difference between market price and the strike price. And that would be very useful when you trade strategies that have the same DTE for all legs — for example, you trade the vertical spread, credit or debit, which has two legs and both legs have the same DTE, so you can just let it expire."

He demonstrates with a live butterfly on SPX put options, all three legs expiring **19 July**, four days out, on a Monday. "I have a butterfly spread on the put side. I'm betting that SPX will drop in the next few days because it looks overstretched right now. So I have a butterfly spread where I buy this put and I sell this put two times, and then I buy [a lower put] to protect the downside risk of this leg. So three legs in the same trade, and these three legs will expire on the same day, at the same time. So if this one expires in the money, the settlement will be done. If it's completely out of the money for all three legs, then all legs will expire worthless."

Note the contrast with the equity case. This is exactly the structure Adam warned against leaving open in stock options, because a knife-edge close there produces unwanted share assignment. In cash-settled index options, the same negligence is harmless, because there are no shares to be assigned — only a cash difference computed from a single settlement price.

**The disadvantage: mixed-expiration structures must be closed.** "If the trade has two legs and the two legs have different expiration times — you can see this very commonly in the calendar spread, diagonal spread, where the long leg and the short leg have different expiration dates — if you trade that on the index option like SPX and NDX, you must close the trade before expiration in order to avoid a potential cash settlement risk."

#### The Snipex disaster scenario

The specific danger case gets its own extended treatment, and the arithmetic is alarming.

The setup: a Snipex or Snipex 4B trade in which "you sell AM and you buy PM" — the short leg is an AM-settled series and the long leg is a PM-settled series. "You forget to close it before the last trading time, which is the prior Thursday. And certainly on Friday you remember it, but you cannot act on the AM series anymore because it has stopped trading already, and it will be going through the settlement process."

Then the mechanical trap that prevents you from fixing it: "In the morning you cannot close this one; it's already stopped trading. You can [try to] close it, but the broker won't allow you to close it. Remember, you sell short this one and you buy this one. If you sell your long option here, the broker or the system or the platform indicates or implies that you will be left with a short option — which is this one. **They do not detect that that option has been going through the settlement process. The system still has that short option in your position. And therefore they don't allow you to close this long leg, because this short leg will become naked, and that will block a huge capital or buying power for you.**"

So you are frozen. The short leg cannot be traded because it has stopped trading; the long leg cannot be sold because the broker's risk system believes doing so would leave you naked short. You must sit through Friday with a position that has already been half-settled.

Now the exposure: "What happens between the opening and the closing on Friday? SPX drops. Because you shorted the AM, you will be settled based on the higher price [the morning SET], and then at the end of the day when the long call expires, you'll be settled at the lower price for your long option. So if SPX drops — 10 points drop between AM and PM time, times 100 — that is a $1,000."

The scaling: **"So SPX drops by $10 within Friday from opening to closing, one contract will be losing $1,000. And that's just one contract. Normally I trade Snipex, I trade multiple contracts and I trade multiple strikes as well. So imagine it could be like $20,000 if SPX drops like 10 points. And that is very normal for SPX to drop 10 points a day. It could drop 100 points a day, and it could blow up your account."**

The rule that follows is stated as an absolute, with an unusual escape clause: "When you trade Snipex 4B, the first rule is don't forget to close it. **If you have the habit of forgetting the trade, please don't trade Snipex or Snipex [4B]. Just ignore it, don't trade that.**"

That is worth pausing on as a piece of trading philosophy. Adam is not saying to try harder to remember. He is saying that if your temperament reliably produces a particular failure, the correct response is to stop trading the structure that punishes that failure. Strategy selection includes selecting against your own known weaknesses.

The one mitigation if it happens: "If you forget to close Snipex or Snipex 4B trades before the expiration and you let it expire in the money, on Friday, if you just recognise that you did that, then during the market you can contact your brokers and ask them to close the position for you, to mitigate the risk of SPX dropping during that day."

#### Assignment before and after expiration

Two summary statements close out the general treatment.

**Before expiration:** "If you are short a call or a put option and that call or put option gets assigned before expiration, should you be worried? The answer is no. In most cases, no, you don't have to worry. As I said, it is just different forms of asset holding — from options to shares, or options to short shares. That's it. There's no difference at the point of assignment. At the point of assignment, the value of your account should not change. In fact, you should be happy, because if the option buyer exercises his option before expiration, he would have to forfeit the extrinsic value ahead of time. And his loss becomes your gain."

**After expiration:** "That's very simple. It happens during the weekend, because the expiration normally is on Friday, and during Saturday and Sunday it will go through the assignment process. Just relax. You cannot do anything anyway, because this weekend, the market is closed, the platform is closed, and your broker closes their office. So you cannot contact them anyway. And don't be panicked or nervous about it. And some of you, I know, first-time experience it — you send me a private message, you call me on the phone. I understand it. But again, it's just the process. Relax the weekend. Enjoy your weekend. And on Monday, if you see the shares, just buy or sell to clear it up."

#### The assignment process behind the scenes: the OCC lottery

Who gets assigned, and why you cannot predict it.

**"The process of assigning a certain share to a specific seller of the option is performed based on a random automated lottery basis."** The consequence: "So if you get assigned, you won't know where you got those shares from — Mr. A or Lady B. You don't know who."

Adam illustrates with five buyers and five sellers. "Let's say four of the five option buyers decide to exercise options. The first question: who will get what? And the second question would be: who will be the lucky seller who won't be assigned?" With four exercises and five short positions, exactly one seller escapes, and which one is decided by draw. "The system just does a random lucky draw. And it could come out something like: hey, option buyer two, you'll be [getting] shares from option seller one... And option buyer number four says, I don't want to exercise. And the system also just generates the random outcome and says, hey, seller number two, you are [the] lucky guy, you won't get assignment at all, because one guy in the buyers decides not to exercise his option."

The institutional chain is then traced end to end using his own BlackBerry long call as the example. "If I just pretend [to] exercise — just right-click and choose exercise. Once I press the button, exercise, basically I will tell my broker, which is thinkorswim in this case, that I'm going to exercise my option, so give me my shares, give me 100 shares. In that case, I am the option buyer. I tell my broker, and thinkorswim has to fulfil my request, give me 100 shares, and then thinkorswim will tell **OCC — the Options Clearing Corporation** — telling them that, hey, Mr. Bang has decided to exercise his option, I have given him 100 shares, everything is valid, now you need to go and find me 100 shares."

"And OCC will do a random lottery selection and say: okay, Interactive Brokers, you will be selling 100 shares to Broker A, which is thinkorswim. So Interactive Brokers will be selected in that case. And within Broker B — with Interactive Brokers — they would need to do a random system to say who's the seller of the option [that] will get assigned."

And the final layer of variation, which is broker-specific: **"Depends on the broker. Some brokers use like a first-in-first-out kind of mechanism. Some brokers use a random lottery mechanism as well."**

The practical takeaway is that assignment is a two-stage random process — OCC randomly selects a clearing member, and the clearing member allocates internally by its own rule — and no amount of skill at your end influences either stage. What you *can* influence is whether exercise is economically attractive to the buyer in the first place, which returns you to the extrinsic-value comparison.

#### The five tricky situations: can you be assigned when...?

Part 3 of the module poses five specific questions about when assignment is possible, and the answers are counterintuitive enough to be worth memorising.

**One: outside trading hours, on an unexpired option.** "If the market is closed, meaning now we are outside the trading hours, but the option that you are short has not expired — still a week, two weeks, a month to go. Can that option be exercised or not? **The answer is yes.** Because you are the option seller. You have no control over when that option will be exercised. If [the buyer] likes to exercise for some reason, then you just need to receive the shares or short shares for the assignment."

**Two: while the stock is halted for trading.** "When a stock is halted for trading for some reason — maybe waiting for news of M&A, or there's some SEC investigation, or some pending announcement from FDA on drug development. The stock could be put on hold for trading for a period of time, sometimes just a few hours, sometimes a few days, sometimes even longer. So during that period of time, you are short an option. Can you be assigned or not? **The answer is yes, you could be assigned as well.** Again, the option buyer could decide to exercise and you just need to be ready to receive your shares or short shares." With a broker-dependent qualification: "Depends on brokers. Some brokers don't allow it, but some brokers allow that situation. So just check with your broker."

**Three: while the option is out of the money and unexpired.** "You are short an option and that option is OTM, [and] you feel very confident that, hey, no one will exercise. It doesn't make sense for the option buyer to exercise an OTM option. That is true — but if for some stupid reason the person decides to exercise it, even if it has not expired yet and it's still OTM, **you could still be assigned.** So that is what I'm saying earlier, that you have no control over [it]."

**Four: after the option has expired out of the money at 4 p.m. on expiration day.** "You thought that, hey, the ringing bell already done, 4 p.m., market closed, expiration already happened, and your short option has expired worthless or OTM. But the question is, can it still be exercised and assigned to you? **The answer is yes. Yes, yes — very tricky.**" This is the 90-minute window, and it gets its own full treatment below.

**Five: during regular trading hours.** Here Adam is unusually candid about uncertainty. "This is a very tricky one. I have checked around, I checked on the internet, and I don't see the answer for it. I know some of our community members have talked with the brokers, like thinkorswim, and they say that no, if you are the short seller of the short call or short put, during [trading] hours you won't get assigned. So the answer from the broker was you won't be assigned during the trading hours. **But I am not so sure that is the right answer or not, because I used to be on the other side. I'm the option buyer. And during the trading hours, I did exercise my call option for some liquidity issue. And the option did go through. So I imagine that if I could exercise my long option during the trading hours, technically somebody has to receive it during the trading hours.**" His verdict: "Final verdict on this? I don't know, but I think it could be assigned to you during the trading hours."

That is a model of intellectual honesty in a teaching context — the observed evidence from his own experience as a buyer contradicts the broker's official answer, and rather than pick one, he reports both and labels the conclusion uncertain.

#### The 90-minute window after expiration

Question four deserves expansion because it is the mechanism behind the module's most dramatic case study.

The avoidance rule first: "How could you avoid that scenario? Well, very simple. **Just close your short positions before the expiration time. Just make sure you close it. Even it has one cent or two cents, just close it. It's not worth the risk or the nuances that could happen.**" With one exception: "In case there's a lack of liquidity, and to buy back to close it you have to pay a significant debit, then in that case you just leave it there. But again, remember that there's a risk there. The risk could be very low, but it could happen."

Now the mechanism. Three facts combine to create the window.

First: "The option trading stops at 4 p.m. Eastern time on expiration day. That's clear. Everyone knows it. Except for the AM expiration options, which we talked about earlier."

Second: **"However, after the market closed at 4 p.m. on Friday, the underlying stock's trading continues, even after that, until I think 8 p.m. on that day."** So the option has stopped trading but the stock has not.

Third: **"The option can still be exercised up to 5:30 p.m. on that day. So still 90 minutes' extension for the option buyer to decide whether he or she wants to exercise or not."**

The consequence: "Because the after-hours stock trading is still there, what could happen is the stock price could shoot up or drop sharply after the market closes. So what is out of the money at 4 p.m. could well be in the money by 5 p.m. And vice versa."

Adam adds the broker caveat: "Some brokers may have different cut-off times. They have their own regulations and you need to check with your brokers. They normally want you to tell them earlier than 4 p.m."

Now the asymmetry that makes this dangerous rather than merely interesting. Consider a credit spread — a bear call spread or bull put spread — that appeared to expire worthless at 4 p.m. "Let's say you sell a bull put spread. And at 4 p.m. on Friday, you thought that your spread has expired worthless. Both legs are out of the money. And after the market closed, within like half an hour, certainly there's bad news, and the stock price plunges, and it hits your short put strike. So the short put strike is supposedly out of the money, but now suddenly becomes in the money. The problem is because the market has closed, your counterparty who bought that put option from you can decide to exercise his put option within 90 minutes."

And here is the asymmetry: **"And the broker won't let you know in time. He exercised it, but then they go through the process I mentioned to you — OCC, and then they choose different brokers, and they happen to choose you to be the assignee. Then in that case, they will tell you. Problem is they would tell you way later than 5:30 p.m. By the time you got to know it, it's too late for you to take action."**

The specific loss this creates: "On Monday you would certainly see that, hey, how can I get assigned shares? And then on Monday the stock plunges, your shares will be hurt. **Because if you knew that your counterparty, the put buyer, had exercised his option, you could have done the same thing for your long put option within 90 minutes. But you did not know. You only got notified way later than that.**"

That is the core injustice of the window. The 90 minutes are available to both parties in principle. In practice the buyer knows immediately what he has decided, while the seller learns of the assignment only after the window has closed. So the buyer can act on the exercise decision and the seller cannot mirror it. The hedge that would have neutralised the assignment — exercising your own long leg — is unavailable precisely because you do not yet know you need it.

#### The Pfizer and GE weekend demonstration

Adam does not merely describe the 90-minute problem; he deliberately runs two live positions into expiration to show what actually happens.

It is Saturday, 17 July, Singapore time. Two positions from the previous day's expiration are still displaying on the platform with a DTE of negative one.

**Position one: a Pfizer bear call spread.** Short one contract of the 40 call, long one contract of the 40.5 call. The stock closed Friday at **$40.35**. So the short 40 call expired in the money by 35 cents and the long 40.5 call expired worthless.

His base-case expectation: "I have to assume that during the weekend or on Monday, this negative one contract of the call option here will be assigned to me [as] negative 100 shares. I should receive negative 100 shares on Monday. And this one, because it expired worthless, it will be zero for me."

But the 90-minute window makes even that uncertain: "What could happen is this price can drop a lot after hours. Let's say it dropped to 39 right after the market closed within one hour, for some bad news. And therefore, the call buyer could decide not to exercise his option. So instead of receiving negative 100 shares on Monday, now I won't receive it, because my counterparty decides not to exercise. So it really depends on the other side. But I don't get to know until later, maybe on Sunday or on Monday, whether I will be assigned or not."

**Position two: a GE bear put spread.** Short one contract of the 13 put, long one contract of the 13.5 put. "I bought a bear put spread, betting that GE share price will drop. And it did. Therefore, both legs are now in the money. So I let it expire in the money, both legs, because I assume that the settlement will offset each other."

His base-case expectation: "On Monday I would see that my short option here will be assigned. Because I'm short the put option, I will be assigned positive 100 shares. But because my long put option has also expired in the money, so I will be assigned negative 100 shares. So these two will cancel out each other."

And the residual risk he explicitly identifies: "What I cannot control is whether this short put will be assigned or not. Because again, the put buyer could decide not to exercise. And in that case, I would be assigned only the negative shares here, and I would not have the offsetting positive shares on Monday."

He generalises this into the debit-spread version of the trap: "If you have a vertical debit spread — bull call spread or bear put spread — you buy a lower call and sell a higher call, and the spread expires in the money, both legs expire in the money. You thought that both sides would expire in the money and therefore you say, hey, during the weekend there will be assignment, the long shares will be offset by the short shares, and they'd be cancelled out, by Monday I should see zero. **But what happens is your counterparty, the one who bought the call from you, may decide not to exercise his call option. And therefore, on Monday, when you open up your account, you see you have a long share but not the offsetting short shares.**"

The general instruction: "So it depends. Within 90 minutes, it's a very tricky situation. So the best thing is, if you're really not sure, just close the spread, whether it's in the money or out of the money, before expiration time. Unless the bid and ask is so wide that you have to pay a lot for closing it — then it's okay, but keep in mind there's always risk over there."

**The resolution.** Adam returns the following Tuesday, 28 July 2020, to report what happened.

On Pfizer: "During the weekend I was assigned 100 shares of Pfizer at the short call strike price, which is 40." Then the market moved: "Now the market price has increased. So the last check I have here, the price has gone up to **41.46**. And I'm short 100 shares. That means I'm losing money here. So that is a consequence of letting the option expire in the money and getting assigned and the market moving against me. It could move the other way around as well. So in this case, I was unlucky to get the market price moving against me."

The account statement shows the mechanics precisely: "I sold 100 shares of Pfizer upon option assignment. And my cash was up by **$4,000**, because I sold 100 shares at $40 per share. So that is $4,000. So I received $4,000 in exchange for being short 100 shares."

On GE, both legs settled as hoped: "The assignment has happened also, and it offset each other. There are two parts. I sold 100 shares of GE upon exercise, because that is the long put that expired in the money. So I sold 100 shares and I got cash of **1,350**, because the [long] put strike was at 13.5. At the same time, my short put also expired in the money. And because I was short the put and the put was in the money, I had been assigned positive 100 shares. So I bought 100 shares of GE here upon option assignment. And the strike price of that short put was 13. So I paid **$1,300** to buy 100 shares of GE. So net, I received $1,350 and I paid out $1,300. So **$15 is my gain** from the spread. And the shares just offset each other. So I don't see any shares in my position statement, because the negative shares offset the positive shares."

That $15 is worth noting: it is $0.50 per share of spread width times 100 shares, less nothing, and it arrived exactly as designed. The GE trade is the case where letting a debit spread expire in the money worked perfectly. The Pfizer trade is the case where it did not.

Cleaning up Pfizer took one order: "Right now I'm short 100 shares. What I'm going to do is just right-click on it and create closing order. So buy 100 shares back to clear the position. There's a very tiny spread between bid and ask — I don't care, one cent. I just confirm and send. So now I already bought back 100 shares to clear my position. Now it's zero. Zero quantity. That's how you clear up the assigned position. Just simple, just buy to clear or sell to clear the assigned position."

#### Rolling the short call before assignment: the 80-delta rule

Part 3 also introduces a preventive rule that belongs equally to the assignment module and the rolling module, and it is worth stating here because its primary justification is assignment avoidance.

The rule: **"If my short call option's delta exceeds 80, I usually just roll it up and out in time to just create more room for capital appreciation on the upside."**

Because "delta" appears in two places on the platform with two different meanings, Adam disambiguates carefully. The delta he means is the per-share delta in the option chain — the column showing values like 0.85 for a 130-strike call on Apple. The delta shown in the *position* statement is something else: "This is an absolute delta value, which is basically the other delta, the column that I showed you earlier, times 100 and times the number of contracts."

He works an example on Abbott (ABT) to make the relationship concrete. He holds a cash-secured put, **three contracts**, at the **110 strike**. The position statement shows a delta of **52**. Where does 52 come from? "You go to the series where I have the short option, the put option — I sold three contracts — and the delta column is showing negative 17, or 0.17, times 300." The arithmetic: 0.17 × 300 = **51**. "So you have 51. 51 is a negative delta, and I'm short, so it becomes positive. Negative times negative becomes positive. So it's simple as that." The position statement's 52 is the option-chain delta scaled by 100 and by contract count.

Having established which delta he means, the reasoning for the 80 threshold: "If the short call is part of the spread I'm trading, and the price goes up strongly, the short call option could become deep in the money and the delta exceeds 80, 90, 95. So what it means is every single dollar increase in the underlying share price, you will be losing 0.8, 0.9, 0.95 from the short call option. So you will be losing almost one to one. Yes, of course your long call option would also gain, but the net of the two [is] minimum. **So you won't get the benefit of the price going up anymore.**"

That is the primary reason: a 95-delta short call against a 90-delta long call gives you a net position delta near zero, and you have stopped participating in the move you correctly predicted. "That's why I need to roll the short contract to a higher strike, meaning lower delta. [Then] I have the net positive delta of the two legs. So when the price continues to go up, I get benefit from the price moving."

And the secondary reason, which is the assignment connection: **"Besides, since the deep-in-the-money call has very little extrinsic value left, it could incentivise the option buyer, your counterparty, to exercise his or her option. So when you roll it up, the extrinsic value becomes more, [so] your counterparty has less incentive to exercise. That also reduces the possibility of being assigned."**

The two reasons are the same phenomenon viewed from two angles. Delta rises as extrinsic value falls; both are consequences of the option going deep in the money. Rolling up simultaneously restores your directional participation and restores the buyer's disincentive to exercise.

Adam then adds the three conditions he actually checks before rolling, which prevent the rule from being applied mechanically:

1. **Delta.** "The short call delta exceeds 80 — then that's one condition."
2. **Extrinsic value.** "I look at the extrinsic value remaining in that call option. If it's still significant, I would keep it. But if it's almost depleted — like there's only a few cents left, or ten cents left — [it's] not worth waiting for a few more days to get the last few cents. So it could be advisable to just roll it up, refresh the extrinsic value. You will get more extrinsic value to earn rather than just sitting there and earning almost zero."
3. **Whether the stock is overstretched.** "I would roll only when the stock price is not overstretched yet. Because if it's overstretched and I roll it up, and then it's due for a retracement, it pulls back — I may have to pay a debit to roll it up now, [and then] I get hurt for the price dropping and it will hit my long call."

The third condition is the subtle one. Rolling up when the stock is extended converts a comfortable position into an exposed one at exactly the wrong moment: you pay a debit to move the short strike higher, and then the stock retraces, so you have spent money to remove protection you were about to need.

Adam also gives a rough threshold for when early assignment genuinely becomes likely, and it is the tightest number in the module: **"Normally you see early assignment happen when the extrinsic value [is] reduced to less than 10 cents — a few cents — then there's a chance that somebody will exercise. That is the only scenario when I see the assignment is likely. Other than that, I don't have to worry."**

Ten cents. That is the operational trigger. Above it, early assignment is a theoretical possibility you monitor. At or below it, it is a live probability you act on.

#### The Biogen case study: a $45,000 loss turned into a $72,000 profit

The fourth video of the module is given over entirely to a single trade, and it functions as both a warning about the 90-minute window and a demonstration of repair technique. Adam introduces it as "one of the accidents that I experienced last year when I got assigned with a big position and experienced a hefty loss, [and] how I turned it around and made it a huge win."

**The entry.** On **28 October 2020**, Biogen (BIIB) is trading at approximately **$250**. The company is developing an Alzheimer's therapy — Adam refers to it repeatedly as an asthma drug in the transcript, but the subsequent discussion of the FDA advisory panel and the June 2021 approval decision makes clear it is the Alzheimer's programme — and option premium is elevated as a result. "The premium of the stock was very good, so I was entering a trade when the stock was trading at about 250."

The trade is a bear call spread: **short the 275 call, long the 280 call**, a $5-wide spread. The credit collected is **$1.37 per share**, and the size is **10 contracts**, for **$1,370** total credit. Expiration is **6 November** — Adam entered on a Wednesday for the following Friday, "so less than 10 days."

His confidence in the trade, and the reasoning behind it: "You can imagine that I was very confident, because between 250 and 275 there's quite a significant price buffer. So I'm very confident that I have a high probability of winning for this trade, especially [as] the expiration of the spread that I entered is just about 10 days to go. **Within 10 days, the price has to jump 25 points for me to lose money. So pretty safe, I would say.**"

The maximum loss is computed explicitly: "It's a $5 spread, and I collected $1.37. That means the max loss is 5 minus 1.37, times $1,000, which is 10 contracts. So the max loss of the trade is **$3,630**."

**The move.** "On November 4th, which is one week after my entry — from Wednesday to Wednesday — what happened was Biogen price spiked to 355." Walking the chart: "After I entered here, the next day it's still around there, the following day still around there. Next Monday it went up, but not significantly. The following Tuesday it dropped back down, so it's good — the trade was making good money. And then suddenly on Wednesday you see the price shoot through the roof. It actually went on the way to close to 360."

The 25-point buffer he had judged safe was exceeded by more than four times, in six days. "It shot through the two strike prices of my spread. So you can imagine that I sold 275, I bought 280, now the price shot through it. That means this trade was to lose almost the max loss already."

At this point the situation is unpleasant but entirely normal. A defined-risk spread has gone against him and will lose approximately $3,630. That is the number he signed up for.

**The halt.** "The following day, which is on Thursday, just one day before expiration, the stock trading was halted, waiting for the news from the advisory panel on the company's drugs. So it's halted, waiting for the news. And this news was big — it's supposed to be like a mover and shaker for the company. And it's just halted. **This is the first time I experienced the halt just before expiration date. I really did not know what would happen to my trade.**"

"So on November 6th, which is on Friday, on expiration day, the trading remained halted for the entire day. So I was very confused. Because I don't know what would happen to my trade, because both legs were in the money. So I assumed that because both legs were in the money, they both would have been assigned and offset each other. And the trade would have hit the max loss. That's my assumption."

That assumption is exactly the debit-spread logic from Part 3 applied to a credit spread, and it is exactly the assumption that the 90-minute window can break.

**The news.** "On Saturday, which is in Singapore time, Saturday morning, I woke up early. In New York time, it's still on Friday late afternoon. So I woke up about 60 minutes after the market had closed on the 6th of November. So imagine that it's like 5 p.m. New York time." He is, without planning to be, awake inside the 90-minute window.

"Certainly I saw the news and the stock price — the Biogen price from 360 plunged on the way down to **240** after hours on Friday."

The advisory panel had rejected the drug. And the implication for the trade was immediately unclear: "This is a very tricky situation, because if it plunged to 240, that means the option could have expired out of the money instead of in the money. Because my spread is 275 and 280. But I don't know how it would be traded in this case. **Is the 350, the price before halted, used as a reference, or the 240, the price after the market close?** I don't know which one would be used. I was very confused."

He tries to contact the broker and gets nothing: "I went to the platform. I chatted with TOS on the chat, but as you know, I got no reply from them. In normal times, during trading time, [you] send them a message, you have to wait for a few hours if you're lucky. And then they answer you and they disappear. Now it's during the weekend, on Friday late afternoon, everyone rushes for barbecue and beer and hangs out with friends and family. It's very understandable that no one replied."

**The discovery.** "I assumed that my 280 call, which is the long call, would have been exercised. And the 275 would also be exercised, because both would be in the money. And the assigned shares would cancel each other out. That was my assumption."

"During that weekend, I was checking out the platform, seeing the cash movement and the assignment to see how it goes, and I was [only] seeing that I was assigned a thousand shares. So that thousand shares is like my long call, 280. I was assigned 1,000 shares. So then in that case, the price that they used would be the price before halted, which is 350-something. That makes sense. But then that would mean that I should also have been assigned negative 1,000 shares because the short 275 call would have also been exercised. **But in this case, the negative 1,000 shares was nowhere to be found.**"

The cash statement tells the story: "I bought a thousand shares — which is an assignment, a thousand shares, because my 280 call is in the money, so I was assigned a thousand shares. That makes sense. And my cash was down by **$280,000** because of the thousand shares that I bought. But I saw nothing on the short side. I would have seen negative thousand shares and also corresponding **$275,000** cash up to offset, but I did not see it. **So my cash used to be $260,000. Now it went all the way down to a negative $19,000.** That makes me nervous."

**The confirmation.** "On the following day, which is on Monday, TOS office opened again. I chatted with them on the TOS platform, and they told me that the 275 short call was not exercised and I was not assigned a 1,000 shares."

So the position is: long 1,000 shares of Biogen at a cost basis of $280, with no offsetting short, in a stock that has just been rejected by an FDA advisory panel. "Now I'm holding my back, which is a thousand shares, and the share price — you see it plunged on the way to 240. And I don't have anything to offset it. So basically what it means is now I just hold my 1,000 shares, and the share price was trading at **235** on that Monday when it opened. And because I bought at 280, obviously **I was losing $45,000** just for this stupid assignment. This is one of the biggest losses I have experienced in one trade."

Two things are worth marking here. First, the loss is more than twelve times the $3,630 maximum loss of the spread as designed. The 90-minute window converted a defined-risk position into an undefined one after the fact. Second, the cause was not a mistake in construction or in management — the spread was correct, the strikes were reasonable, the position size was reasonable. The cause was that his counterparty was awake and he was not.

**Why the counterparty did not exercise.** Adam returns to this at the very end of the video, and the explanation is the cleanest possible illustration of the 90-minute asymmetry. "Apparently, the one who bought the 275 call from me was very nimble. Probably he was in [the New York] time zone. And he watched the news very closely. **So the moment after the news came out, right after the Friday close, he immediately told his broker not to exercise his option, because he already saw the price plunge all the way down to 240.** The 275 — if he let it expire in the money and held a thousand shares, he would have lost a lot of money. So he was very nimble. He told the broker not to exercise it. That's why he got out of that situation."

Note what the buyer did. He held a 275 call that was in the money by 75 points as of the halt price and out of the money by 35 points as of the after-hours price. Exercising would have handed him 1,000 shares at $275 in a stock trading at $240. He filed a do-not-exercise and walked away from a call that was nominally deep in the money — the exact scenario the DNE mechanism exists for.

Meanwhile, "For my case, during that time, I was sleeping. What could I do?" And the reflection: "So that's another disadvantage of trading in a different time zone. You cannot monitor the situation on time. But hey, we just have to deal with what we have."

**The repair.** This is the part of the case study that earns its four-video treatment, and the framing Adam puts on it first is deliberate: "There are different possible reactions I can do. Number one, I can blame the broker — and you know you never win. What could you do? You beat them, you go to the other broker. Fine, they don't care. They just get a new customer. They're not going to compensate you for that. They say it's not their fault. They say I should have told them well before the market closed. **But hey, that's a catch-22. How would I have known the stock price would plunge so that I told them not to exercise?** It's not going to happen. So [I'm] not going to blame the broker here. I could blame my wife, I could blame anyone else but me, or I could blame myself. Again, it doesn't solve the issue. The loss is the loss. So then the other reaction I could have is just focus my energy on: hey, how could I turn this around? How could I repair the trade? How could I make it a win for me? That's what I did."

The repair rests on a specific market observation. "One thing about Biogen stock is it has a very good premium, and there's a reason for it. The reason why the stock plunged from 350 down to 235 was because the advisory panel came out with a very negative conclusion to advise FDA that this drug is not qualified and they should not approve the Alzheimer therapy drug that this company is developing. And that's why the stock plunged. **But that is just the advisory opinion. The final decision by FDA was not to be made until mid-June 2021.** So six or seven months after that, there will be another round of final decision from FDA. And during that period of time, option premium stayed elevated. Very good premium."

That is the crux. A binary catalyst had been deferred, not resolved. The uncertainty that had crushed the stock kept implied volatility high for seven months, which meant that a holder of 1,000 shares could sell calls against them at unusually rich prices, month after month.

"Because of that unique situation, when I was holding a thousand shares, I just took advantage of it. I kept selling call options to collect premium — and premium is good — to reduce my cost of holding my shares. My cost basis is 280. I kept collecting more premium to reduce it."

The sequence of covered calls, as he narrates it:

**Round one, 10 November.** "I sold 10 contracts, a very short expiration, which is like November 13, just a few days after this. I collect **$3**, and the strike price **240**, just above the stock price."

**Round two.** "When it expired, I rolled the 240 to [260] to create more room for the stock price to appreciate further. For that rolling, I collected **$1.20**, and the expiration is about a month. So I rolled it out to a month, up 20 points, collecting some credit, creating more room for the stock price to recover."

**The capital restructuring.** After two rounds, a different problem became pressing. "I found out that holding 1,000 shares of Biogen cost me a lot of capital — **$280,000** capital. I don't have enough capital to do other trades. And from a diversification standpoint, I also need to reduce the capital on this trade so that I can diversify my trades as well."

The solution is the stock-replacement logic from the strategy-selection lesson, applied to a position he did not choose to be in. "So what happened was I decided to sell my 1,000 shares, and in exchange for it, I bought 10 contracts of deep-in-the-money [calls]. The stock was now **250** after it recovered a little bit. So deep in the money, **delta is between 70 to 80, and expiring in two years' time**. So actually I bought LEAPS options expiring in two years, deep in the money, and that serves as stock replacement. So I don't need to hold the stock anymore. Now I just hold the LEAPS option. And against that LEAPS option, I can sell covered calls — almost like covered call, but this is a diagonal spread."

The capital released: "Because of that, when I sold a thousand shares and I bought the 10 contracts here, I collected a credit of **166 times 1,000**. So I released **$166,000** capital. The trade used to block me $280,000 capital. Now it blocks me [$114,000]. So now I have cash to do other trades as well."

This is precisely the diagonal-spread argument from Part One, deployed as damage control. The position's directional exposure is essentially unchanged — a 70-to-80-delta LEAP behaves like the stock — but the capital requirement falls by about 60 percent and the catastrophic downside becomes capped at the LEAP's cost rather than the full share value.

**The continuing roll sequence.** "After I converted the shares into the deep-in-the-money call, I started to sell calls again."

- "After the **260** expired in December, I rolled it out to [the next month]."
- "When it expired again in January, I rolled it out to February. And I rolled it even further to **290**. From 260 I rolled it up to 290, and I collected a little credit. It's a good thing. I created more room for the trade to appreciate, still collecting some premium. **Just roll it up and out for a credit. That's a good thing.**"
- "In February, after the option expired, I rolled it again from 290, also to the same 290. The stock price was about flattish during that time. So I just rolled to the same strike price out another month, collected another **$6.30**."
- "In March, I rolled it to April. It [was] split into several fills here. But this time I rolled it *down*, because the stock price dropped, and I collected **$6.76**."
- "In April, I rolled it to May, from 280 I rolled it to [2]85, collected another **$9**."
- "By late May, I rolled it one more round to June 4, same strike price, collecting **$6**, just one week."

That last one is worth dwelling on. Six dollars of premium for one week of duration on a stock in the $300 range is an extraordinary rate, and the reason is entirely event-driven: "Why is it [that in] one week I can get $6? Because remember, it's close to the date when FDA was supposed to make a decision on whether or not they approved the drug. June 4 — it's just a few days before that decision. So I rolled it to June 4 and collected very good premium here."

The pattern in the rolls is worth extracting because it prefigures the entire rolling module: **when the stock rose, he rolled the short call up and out; when the stock fell, he rolled it down and out; when the stock was flat, he rolled out at the same strike.** In every case he collected a credit. The direction of the strike adjustment tracked the stock; the collection of premium was constant.

**The exit.** "Finally, on June 4th, just before the decision was released — the decision was on June 7 — I closed the entire trade. **I don't want to take the chance of whether it's approval or disapproval again, because that's just a binary event. I could lose a lot of money holding deep-in-the-money call options here.** So I decided to close the whole thing. I closed the June 4th [short call], and I closed the January [20]23, which is the two-year LEAP option. And I collected on average about **$100**."

**The result.** "So if you add up all this credit — 100 here, 5, 6 here, 9 here, 10 here, et cetera — it turned around the trade completely. It's more than 280. 280 is my cost. So you add up all of this, it's much more than that. Remember, I also released 166. If you add up all of this, it's well beyond 280. And that's why I turned the trade around. And that became my biggest win or [most] profitable trade in this year. **This trade alone brought me almost $72,000 year-to-date.** So it contributed a big chunk of my year-to-date profit."

"So from a $45,000 loss, I turned it around and made it $72,000 profit. **It's more than $100,000 swing for one trade.**"

**The postscript.** The stock's behaviour after his exit is instructive about the decision to close: "We know now, in hindsight, we saw the price shoot through like 400 plus after the FDA approved the drug. But this is very volatile. It went all the way there, stayed there at a high level, and it started to drift lower. It started to drift lower, lower, lower. Now it's trading around 330."

He closed before a binary event that went in the direction that would have profited him enormously, and he is untroubled by that. The reason is that the decision was correct at the time it was made regardless of outcome: he was holding ten deep-in-the-money LEAP calls into a coin-flip FDA verdict, and the downside of the wrong verdict was severe. "It's a lottery, it's a binary event." His closing observation on the underlying: "You need to have a very strong heart to stay on the trade of these kinds of stocks."

**The lesson he draws.** "See, accidents can happen to anyone, even to [an] experienced trader like me. There are still things that I don't know in the market. Assignment — this particular case is one of them. **The important thing is, after the accident, what could we do to turn it around? So that's [a] more important thing than trying to avoid the accident, because no one can avoid 100% of accidents. It will happen one way or the other.**"

And the closing statement of method: "In this case, I choose not to complain. I just keep my head down and I keep selling options to collect premiums to reduce my costs, and eventually the stock recovers and I make it all the way back. And it's a big turnaround. **The repair is not the same for all situations. But again, if you keep the attitude of 'how could I turn it around,' I think everything is possible.**"

That qualification — *the repair is not the same for all situations* — matters, and it should be held onto. The Biogen repair worked because of a specific and unusual combination of conditions: a deferred binary catalyst kept implied volatility elevated for seven months, the underlying was a fundamentally sound large-cap pharmaceutical rather than a speculative name, and the position was long stock rather than short stock, so selling calls against it was structurally available. Change any of those and the repair fails. A short-stock assignment in a stock that keeps rising cannot be repaired by selling calls. A long-stock assignment in a name with no premium cannot be repaired by selling calls either, because there is nothing to collect. What generalises from the case study is not the technique but the sequence: stop the bleeding, restructure to release capital, and then look for the specific feature of the situation that can be monetised repeatedly over time.
